l-skinwalker.why: NIDS ran the field investigation at the ranch under Bigelow
l-skinwalker.note: NIDS investigators including retired Army Col. John B. Alexander examined close to 100 incidents while conceding they could not obtain publishable evidence.

l-skinwalker.label: Colm A. Kelleher
l-skinwalker.why: led both the NIDS and BAASS science teams on the ranch
l-skinwalker.note: Sixteen years of continuous field presence across a private and then a federally funded program.

l-skinwalker.label: James T. Lacatski
l-skinwalker.why: Lacatski's visit is the documented link from the ranch to DIA
l-skinwalker.note: Lacatski contacted Bigelow after reading 'Hunt for the Skinwalker', visited the ranch and reported an experience there; Bigelow relayed this to Sen. Harry Reid.

l-skinwalker.label: Travis S. Taylor
l-skinwalker.why: Led instrumented field investigation at Skinwalker Ranch while serving as UAPTF chief scientist
l-skinwalker.note: The same person applied near-identical sensing methodology inside the classified task force and on a television production at the property NIDS and BAASS had studied, with no public account of any relationship between the two efforts.

defense-appropriations-aawsap.label: Defense Intelligence Agency
defense-appropriations-aawsap.note: The appropriation named DIA as the recipient agency to assess long-term and over-the-horizon foreign advanced aerospace threats.

defense-appropriations-aawsap.label: Harry M. Reid
defense-appropriations-aawsap.note: AARO's official history states the FY2008 and FY2010 Defense Appropriations Acts appropriated $22 million to DIA 'at the direction of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV)'.

defense-appropriations-aawsap.label: Daniel K. Inouye
defense-appropriations-aawsap.why: Appropriations chairman who provided the vehicle
defense-appropriations-aawsap.note: Inouye's control of the Senate Appropriations process allowed the $22M to be routed through the classified annex without floor debate on the allocation.

defense-appropriations-aawsap.label: Theodore F. Stevens
defense-appropriations-aawsap.why: provided bipartisan cover for the earmark
defense-appropriations-aawsap.note: Stevens, the senior Republican appropriator and former committee chairman, is consistently named with Reid and Inouye as one of the three senators behind the appropriation.

defense-appropriations-aawsap.label: DIA Letter to the Senate Armed Services Committee Listing AATIP Products
defense-appropriations-aawsap.note: That DIA had to introduce the program to SASC by letter in 2018 establishes the committee had no visibility during its life — the direct consequence of funding it through the classified appropriation.

kona-blue.label: 10 U.S.C. 119 — Special Access Programs: Congressional Oversight
kona-blue.why: A program can be designed and formally requested without ever crossing the congressional reporting threshold
kona-blue.note: AARO: 'KONA BLUE was not reported to Congress at that time because it was never established as a SAP and, therefore, did not meet the threshold for congressional reporting.' The government states the gap in its own defence.

kona-blue.label: United States Department of Homeland Security
kona-blue.why: DHS Deputy Secretary disapproved and terminated KONA BLUE approximately six months later
kona-blue.note: The AARO/DHS paper states the Deputy Secretary disapproved and terminated the PSAP roughly six months after it was established, and that KONA BLUE was 'never approved or formally established'. Neither official is named in the released text.

kona-blue.label: Harry M. Reid
kona-blue.why: Reid and Lieberman asked that the DHS prospective SAP be established with promised funding
kona-blue.note: AARO states 'Senators Lieberman and Reid asked that the PSAP be established with the promise of additional funding' - the same senator who created the DIA appropriation now seeking a DHS compartment.

kona-blue.label: Robert T. Bigelow
kona-blue.why: Bigelow's organisation was the anticipated contract performer for the proposed program
kona-blue.note: AARO notes the material 'was only assumed to exist by KONA BLUE advocates and its anticipated contract performers,' and that the proposed lines of effort mirrored the private sector organisation's AAWSAP work.

kona-blue.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
kona-blue.why: Volume I surfaced Kona Blue and framed it as the origin of crash-retrieval belief
kona-blue.note: AARO disclosed the DHS prospective SAP and used it to argue that witnesses mistook a rejected proposal for an operating programme.

kona-blue.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
kona-blue.why: Report offers KONA BLUE as the explanation for the reverse-engineering allegations
kona-blue.note: AARO identifies KONA BLUE as a prospective SAP proposed to DHS, never approved, whose advocates only assumed material existed. The proposal's own premise - consolidating alleged concealed holdings under DHS for proper oversight - presupposes the thing AARO says does not exist.

kona-blue.label: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)
kona-blue.why: successor attempt to house recovery and exploitation work
kona-blue.note: AARO describes KONA BLUE as a proposed UAP recovery and reverse-engineering SAP at DHS, rejected by DHS leadership; the same personnel and subject matter as AAWSAP.

kona-blue.label: Bigelow Aerospace
kona-blue.why: KONA BLUE was proposed by AAWSAP's contractor team after DIA cancelled the program
kona-blue.note: AARO records that when DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP its supporters proposed a new version to DHS under a special access program, with lines of effort closely mirroring those the private sector organisation had conducted.

kona-blue.label: United States Department of Homeland Security
kona-blue.why: DHS prospective special access program, terminated 10 February 2012
kona-blue.note: DHS Acting Deputy Secretary Kristie Canegallo transmitted the declassified Kona Blue records to the Deputy Secretary of Defense on 5 February 2024.

kona-blue.label: DHS Science and Technology Directorate
kona-blue.why: DHS Under Secretary for S&T established KONA BLUE as a Prospective SAP in 2011
kona-blue.note: 'In 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology (S&T) established KONA BLUE as a PSAP' - the government's own words in the joint AARO/DHS paper.

kona-blue.label: Lockheed Martin Corporation
kona-blue.why: The proposal's premise was that existing holdings would be moved into a structure Congress could see
kona-blue.note: AARO records the proponents' belief that creating the program under DHS 'would allow all of the technology and knowledge of these alleged programs to be moved under the KONA BLUE program' where it could be properly monitored by oversight committees.

kona-blue.label: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)
kona-blue.why: KONA BLUE was proposed as the successor to the cancelled DIA effort
kona-blue.note: AARO records that when DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP in 2012, 'its supporters proposed to DHS that they create and fund a new version' to restart UAP investigations and 'reverse-engineer any recovered off-world spacecraft'.

kona-blue.label: Lockheed Martin Advanced Development Programs (Skunk Works)
kona-blue.why: Alleges Lockheed-held material was to be transferred
kona-blue.note: The Kona Blue allegation concerns a proposed change of custodial agency for physical material held on the Lockheed side - a bureaucratic transaction that would leave programme proposals and declination correspondence.

kona-blue.label: Central Intelligence Agency
kona-blue.why: CIA alleged to have terminated the programme
kona-blue.note: Gerb's account has the CIA shutting Kona Blue down. Recorded here as an alleged act of the concealment apparatus rather than as an adjudicated fact.

kona-blue.label: Reality Check with Ross Coulthart (NewsNation)
kona-blue.why: Episode centred on the alleged Lockheed-to-DHS transfer
kona-blue.note: Gerb described Kona Blue to Coulthart as a DHS-brokered program in which Lockheed Martin material was reportedly diverted before the CIA shut it down.

kona-blue.label: Reid Letter to DEPSECDEF Requesting Restricted SAP Status
kona-blue.why: second attempt at the protection Reid was refused
kona-blue.note: Reid asked DoD for a restricted SAP over engineering of advanced technologies in 2009 and was refused; two years later the same circle proposed a recovery-and-exploitation SAP at DHS instead.

flir1-video.label: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
flir1-video.why: Primary sensor artefact of the 2004 encounter, released by DoD in 2020
flir1-video.note: The video leaked in 2007, was published by the New York Times on 16 December 2017, and was formally released by DoD on 27 April 2020 with the objects 'characterized as unidentified'.

flir1-video.label: New York Times, 'Glowing Auras and Black Money: The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program'
flir1-video.why: Published by the New York Times, reopening the subject
flir1-video.note: The DoD's own 2020 release statement acknowledges the videos circulated publicly after unauthorized disclosures in 2007 and 2017.

flir1-video.label: Chad Underwood
flir1-video.why: Underwood produced the FLIR1 tape on a follow-on sortie
flir1-video.note: Consistently reported since 2019 and never disputed by the Navy or Fravor, but not anchored to a primary record in this pass.

flir1-video.label: Chad Underwood
flir1-video.why: Credited with capturing the ATFLIR footage on 14 Nov 2004
flir1-video.note: Consistently reported since 2019 and never disputed by the Navy or by Fravor, but not anchored to a primary record in this pass.

gimbal-video.label: USS Theodore Roosevelt Encounters (2014-2015)
gimbal-video.why: January 2015 ATFLIR artefact from the same operating environment
gimbal-video.note: DoD released GIMBAL on 27 April 2020 as authentic and unidentified; AARO's published case slides contain no GIMBAL assessment.

gofast-video.label: USS Theodore Roosevelt Encounters (2014-2015)
gofast-video.why: January 2015 ATFLIR artefact from the same operating environment
gofast-video.note: GO FAST is the video Gallaudet says was attached to the recalled Fleet Forces Command safety message, and the one AARO later reanalysed on parallax grounds.

gofast-video.label: Jon T. Kosloski
gofast-video.why: AARO parallax reanalysis: no anomalous speed or flight characteristics
gofast-video.note: AARO's SASC case slides place the object at roughly 13,000 feet at about 45 mph with 60-knot winds. The analysis addresses apparent speed; it does not address the recall of the fleet safety message built on the same footage.

gofast-video.label: ODNI Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (25 June 2021)
gofast-video.why: 18 of 144 incidents showed unusual movement patterns; sensors not designed to identify UAP
gofast-video.note: 'In 18 incidents, described in 21 reports, observers reported unusual UAP movement patterns or flight characteristics,' and military sensors 'are not generally suited for identifying UAP.'

gofast-video.label: Fleet Forces Command 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' Email (Jan 2015, recalled)
gofast-video.why: The recalled fleet safety message carried the GO FAST video
gofast-video.note: Gallaudet's written testimony states the January 2015 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' email attached the GO FAST video and cited 'multiple near-midair collisions.'

aaro-fy2025-report.label: Americans for Safe Aerospace
aaro-fy2025-report.why: 'AARO did not receive reports indicating flight safety concerns during this reporting period'
aaro-fy2025-report.note: The same report records two cases of electronic or avionic interference attributed to UAP in proximity to an operational aircraft. The no-safety-concerns finding is a statement about AARO's intake, not about the sky.

aaro-fy2025-report.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
aaro-fy2025-report.why: 'No evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials'
aaro-fy2025-report.note: A categorical negative issued by the office whose access to waived and unacknowledged programs has never been established. Recorded as a denial artefact with its author and date.

aaro-fy2025-report.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
aaro-fy2025-report.why: 1,870 total cases; 319 new; 9 meriting further analysis
aaro-fy2025-report.note: The report also notes cases near sensitive installations with 'performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art' while adding 'No technical data accompanied these reports.'

aaro-fy2025-report.label: Jon T. Kosloski
aaro-fy2025-report.why: Signed out under his directorship, nine months late
aaro-fy2025-report.note: The FY2025 report covering June 2024-May 2025 was not released until 20 July 2026, roughly three months before the FY2026 report was due.

norad-northcom.label: February 2023 Alaska, Yukon and Lake Huron Shootdowns
norad-northcom.why: NORAD-controlled fighters destroyed three unidentified objects in four days
norad-northcom.note: Two F-16CMs of the Minnesota Air National Guard's 148th Fighter Wing destroyed the Lake Huron object with an AIM-9X at roughly 20,000 feet on 12 February 2023.

norad-northcom.label: Gregory M. Guillot
norad-northcom.why: Commander, NORAD and USNORTHCOM from February 2024
norad-northcom.note: Guillot's public statements on Langley and on the 2026 incursions are the command's authoritative position.

norad-northcom.label: Langley AFB Drone Incursions (December 2023)
norad-northcom.note: Guillot testified the Langley incidents dominated his assessment on taking command in February 2024 and were 'the centerpiece' of his review.

norad-northcom.label: FY2026 NDAA UAP provisions
norad-northcom.note: AARO must brief Congress on the number, location and nature of UAP intercepts by NORAD and US Northern Command since 2004 and the data collected during them.

pursue-releases.label: The Sol Foundation
pursue-releases.why: Sol issued press statements on each major PURSUE release
pursue-releases.note: Sol published statements dated 9 May, 22 May and 10 July 2026 responding to the PURSUE releases, positioning itself as the interpretive authority on the released record.

pursue-releases.label: February 2023 Alaska, Yukon and Lake Huron Shootdowns
pursue-releases.why: Lake Huron engagement video withheld until the May 2026 PURSUE release
pursue-releases.note: Infrared footage of the 12 February 2023 shootdown was released on 22 May 2026 via PURSUE, with the entry noting an unusual lack of substantiated chain of custody.

pursue-releases.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
pursue-releases.why: Release programme runs parallel to, not in place of, AARO reporting
pursue-releases.note: The Department of War states it 'will continue to conduct separate reporting on resolved UAP cases, as mandated by statute' - meaning the historical-records release and the contemporary programme reporting line remain separate. This structure allows maximal apparent transparency about the past while the present reporting is unchanged.

pursue-releases.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
pursue-releases.why: AARO identifies and stages the material released under PURSUE
pursue-releases.note: The Department of War's PURSUE site publishes on a rolling basis - releases 01 through 05 between 8 May and 7 August 2026 - with AARO identifying material and ODNI coordinating across agencies.

pursue-releases.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
pursue-releases.why: Run by the Department of War with ODNI support
pursue-releases.note: Created by presidential directive of 19 February 2026; five releases published between 8 May and 7 August 2026.

pursue-releases.label: Pete Hegseth
pursue-releases.why: Releasing authority; signed transparency statement on the portal
pursue-releases.note: Hegseth is the addressee of the presidential direction and the signatory of the statement published on the PURSUE portal.

pursue-releases.label: war.gov/UFO release portal
pursue-releases.why: Published through the Secretary's web estate, not AARO's
pursue-releases.note: All five tranches are posted at war.gov/UFO as paired document and video bundles, with video served from a CloudFront distribution; AARO links out to it rather than hosting it.

pursue-releases.label: Enigma Labs
pursue-releases.why: Enigma cross-referencing PURSUE files against its civilian sighting database
pursue-releases.note: After the first PURSUE tranche (roughly 160 files) posted to war.gov/ufo on 8 May 2026, Enigma Labs consultant Alejandro Rojas said the team was adding PURSUE elements to Enigma's maps and app so official cases could be cross-referenced 'against our database of over 200,000 public sightings.' He also criticised the drop for lacking coordinates, sensor parameters and altitude data.

pursue-releases.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
pursue-releases.why: Framed as enforcement of the records identified for public release under the 2026 disclosure push
pursue-releases.note: Burlison ties the demand to records 'Congress has directed to be identified, preserved, reviewed, and transferred for public release', naming NARA and Record Group 615.

pursue-releases.label: PURSUE Release 01
pursue-releases.why: First tranche, 8 May 2026
pursue-releases.note: 160 files - 117 PDFs, 29 sensor videos, 14 photographs - spanning 1944 to 2026, at least 100 carrying redactions.

pursue-releases.label: PURSUE Release 02
pursue-releases.why: Second tranche, 22 May 2026
pursue-releases.note: 64 files including 51 sensor videos in a DOW-UAP-PR050 to PR099 series; the 5.6GB video bundle is the largest of the five.

pursue-releases.label: PURSUE Release 03
pursue-releases.why: Third tranche, 12 June 2026
pursue-releases.note: 72 files with the FBI the largest contributor at 29 files, including a less-redacted CIA Robertson Panel record.

pursue-releases.label: PURSUE Release 04
pursue-releases.why: Fourth tranche, 10 July 2026
pursue-releases.note: 227MB of documents and 1.4GB of video spanning the 1940s to 2026, published without any stated file count.

pursue-releases.label: PURSUE Release 05
pursue-releases.why: Fifth tranche, 7 August 2026
pursue-releases.note: 41 files - 16 videos, 22 documents, 3 images - spanning 1953 to 2026 per the portal, with content reaching back to a 1950 case.

pursue-releases.label: Presidential direction to identify and release UAP files (19-20 February 2026)
pursue-releases.why: The directive is the stated basis of the release programme
pursue-releases.note: The war.gov/UFO portal attributes PURSUE to the President's direction to the Secretary of War, and AARO's own homepage links to it under the PURSUE name.

pursue-releases.label: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14
pursue-releases.why: Republished by the Department of War as CIA-UAP-015 in PURSUE Release 03
pursue-releases.note: The same 1955 Battelle report has now been published by the government three times across seventy years without the underlying case data ever being independently reanalysed.

pursue-releases.label: Navy Range Fouler Reports (72 reports, 2004-2021)
pursue-releases.why: Two decades of aviator records released only under external pressure
pursue-releases.note: The 2023 range fouler release came via FOIA; the 2026 PURSUE releases came via presidential directive. Neither came from the reporting system that was supposed to surface them.

pursue-releases.label: UAP Science Advisory Council
pursue-releases.why: Council established following the PURSUE releases
pursue-releases.note: Loeb's Medium account references a government disclosure release date of 12 June 2026 immediately before describing his tasking; the council's formation follows the release programme rather than preceding it.

pursue-releases.label: Christopher K. Mellon
pursue-releases.why: 'Data alone is not disclosure'
pursue-releases.note: Mellon's verdict on the first PURSUE drop of 8 May 2026 became the caucus's framing.

pursue-releases.label: NASA UAP Independent Study Team
pursue-releases.why: Metadata stripping defeats the study team's core recommendation
pursue-releases.note: NASA's panel identified missing sensor metadata as the principal obstacle to analysis; the 2026 releases removed exactly that metadata before publication.

pursue-releases.label: Timothy Gallaudet
pursue-releases.why: Said the absence of metadata made it impossible to conclude any object was truly anomalous
pursue-releases.note: A 2024 House witness assessing the 2026 executive release.

pursue-releases.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
pursue-releases.why: Release volume without release quality
pursue-releases.note: The Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies found Release #1 stripped 'critical metadata, such as time, date, location, range, altitude, speed,' recycled roughly 70 percent of the FBI files from the existing FOIA Vault, contained no material from DOE, DIA, NRO, NSA or CIA, and left a 1974-2015 gap.

pursue-releases.label: Tulsi Gabbard
pursue-releases.why: ODNI coordinating authority for the release programme
pursue-releases.note: Gabbard described the first release as an ongoing joint effort between intelligence and defence agencies; ODNI-numbered documents appear inside the war.gov series.

pursue-releases.label: Alejandro Rojas
pursue-releases.why: Catalogued the missing fields in the case summaries
pursue-releases.note: Rojas identified absent coordinates, sensor parameters and altitude data as the specific omissions that block independent kinematic analysis.

pursue-releases.label: Christopher K. Mellon
pursue-releases.why: 'Data alone is not disclosure' - the framing the House adopted
pursue-releases.note: Mellon conceded the scale of the retained holdings is itself a revelation while rejecting the sufficiency of context-free files.

pursue-releases.label: Ryan Graves
pursue-releases.why: Set the four-element test: provenance, sensor context, metadata, chain of custody
pursue-releases.note: Graves specified what a useful release contains; the Department's stated refusal to comment on or assess any file means PURSUE meets none of the four.

pursue-releases.label: Timothy Gallaudet
pursue-releases.why: Identified the missing metadata as the disqualifying defect
pursue-releases.note: Gallaudet welcomed the first open admission that UAP files had been shielded and said the absence of metadata made it impossible to conclude any object was truly anomalous.

pursue-releases.label: 'UAP Gerb' (Sam)
pursue-releases.why: Gerb analysed the PURSUE releases as they were published
pursue-releases.note: Gerb ran a livestream on 'UFO File Drop 1' on 12 May 2026 and discussed the release programme in his 2 March 2026 livestream on Trump's announcement, making him one of the first analysts working the released record.

pursue-releases.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act (Burlison amendment to the FY2027 NDAA)
pursue-releases.why: Statutory backstop for an executive release programme
pursue-releases.note: The amendment is framed as reinforcing PURSUE by creating statutory disclosure procedures rather than relying solely on executive-branch policy.

pursue-releases.label: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
pursue-releases.why: Executive-controlled release running in parallel to, and in tension with, the committee's compelled-production track
pursue-releases.note: The House caucus response has been to keep issuing letters on the premise that a curated release cannot substitute for compelled production.

pursue-releases.label: Presidential directive waiving UAP-related nondisclosure agreements
pursue-releases.why: PURSUE named as an authorized receiving channel for waived-NDA disclosures
pursue-releases.note: Senior officials described former officials meeting with cleared AARO or PURSUE task force officials who may waive applicable NDAs during authorized discussions, with information then routed through existing declassification procedures.

pursue-releases.label: AARO Historical Record Report, Volume II (unpublished)
pursue-releases.why: Raw files clear in weeks; the narrative volume has not cleared in two years
pursue-releases.note: The contrast maps where the sensitivity sits: imagery can be published on a cabinet order, analytic conclusions about the department's own history cannot.

pursue-releases.label: AARO Declassification Information Paper (September 2025)
pursue-releases.why: Process described as immovable was moved by cabinet direction in weeks
pursue-releases.note: The September 2025 paper's 'deliberate and time-intensive' declassification account is contradicted by five tranches and over a hundred sensor videos cleared between May and August 2026.

pursue-releases.label: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
pursue-releases.why: The statutory report never mentions the department's own release programme
pursue-releases.note: Publishing a statutory UAP report three tranches into the largest official UAP release in US history without acknowledging it places the office outside the authorship of the disclosure.

pursue-releases.label: National Archives UAP Records Collection (Record Group 615)
pursue-releases.why: Two parallel release architectures, only one statutory
pursue-releases.note: PURSUE publishes at will through the Secretary's website with no FOIA case numbers or exemption citations, while the statutory NARA collection publishes no compliance accounting - neither channel can be audited.

pursue-releases.label: AARO Official UAP Imagery releases (PR series)
pursue-releases.why: AARO's channel stops; the Secretary's channel starts
pursue-releases.note: AARO's last imagery release is 6 January 2026; the Department's first tranche is 8 May 2026 with 29 videos, and AARO published nothing further.

pursue-releases.label: House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets hearing, 9 September 2025 - 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'
pursue-releases.why: Hearing, then letter, then release - the causal spine of 2026
pursue-releases.note: The sequence runs from sworn testimony that video was being withheld, through a subcommittee chair's letter to the Secretary, to a release channel that bypassed the office entirely.

pursue-releases.label: ODNI Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (25 June 2021)
pursue-releases.why: The data-scarcity claim survives the release only because the parameters were stripped
pursue-releases.note: PURSUE falsified the claim that the imagery does not exist while preserving the claim that the data are insufficient, by publishing video without coordinates, sensor parameters or altitude.

dow-uap-file-release-2026.label: Kirsten E. Gillibrand
dow-uap-file-release-2026.why: Author of the statute publicly states the obligation is unmet
dow-uap-file-release-2026.note: Gillibrand: 'I will continue to fight to ensure the administration finally meets its legal obligation to the American people.'

dow-uap-file-release-2026.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (NARA Record Group 615)
dow-uap-file-release-2026.why: Agency compliance ran nineteen months past the statutory deadline
dow-uap-file-release-2026.note: The Sec. 1842(c)(1) agency review deadline fell on 17 October 2024; NARA's transfer guidance is dated April 2025 and the author of the statute described the May 2026 release as the administration only beginning to meet its legal obligation.

adam-research-project.label: EarthTech International / Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin
adam-research-project.note: Puthoff's Austin laboratory is where the specimens were characterised. No results have been published.

adam-research-project.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
adam-research-project.why: ADAM: acquisition and analysis of claimed exotic material
adam-research-project.note: Announced July 2019 as the Acquisition & Data Analysis of Materials project; SEC filings record the $35,000 purchase of the bismuth/magnesium-zinc and aluminium items.

adam-research-project.label: Materials and custody analysis
adam-research-project.why: Custody chain: anonymous source to Art Bell, to Linda Moulton Howe, to Carnegie DTM (1996), to Puthoff, to TTSA (2019), to the US Army
adam-research-project.note: Howe says the samples were tested by Carnegie Science's Department of Terrestrial Magnetism in 1996 and by Puthoff on several later occasions before TTSA bought them for $35,000 in 2019.

adam-research-project.label: Harold E. Puthoff
adam-research-project.why: Samples routed to laboratories founded by Puthoff
adam-research-project.note: TTSA partnered with Puthoff-founded laboratories to study the ADAM materials; Puthoff had already tested the same Howe samples privately, reporting in a 2012 letter that no anomalous outcome had been obtained.

adam-research-project.label: To The Stars Academy - US Army CCDC Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (17 October 2019)
adam-research-project.why: ADAM materials became the subject of a five-year Army CRADA
adam-research-project.note: On 17 October 2019 TTSA entered a CRADA with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering inertial mass reduction, metamaterials, quantum physics and beamed energy propulsion, with at least $750,000 in Army support and no public funding to the company.

adam-research-project.label: Steve Justice
adam-research-project.why: Justice, ex-Lockheed Skunk Works Advanced Systems director, fronted the acquisition
adam-research-project.note: Justice said the structure and composition 'are not from any known existing military or commercial application' and conceded the materials came from sources 'with varying levels of chain-of-custody documentation'.

adam-research-project.label: Steve Justice
adam-research-project.why: Public technical voice: material 'not from any known existing military or commercial application'
adam-research-project.note: A former Skunk Works program director staking his name on the claim is what gave ADAM standing with an Army laboratory.

adam-research-project.label: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy
adam-research-project.why: ADAM is the predicate for the Army agreement
adam-research-project.note: The CRADA lists mechanical/structural metamaterials and electromagnetic metamaterial waveguides — the exact subject matter ADAM claimed to hold.

ttsa-army-crada.label: AARO / ORNL Synopsis: Analysis of a Metallic Specimen
ttsa-army-crada.why: The privately held specimen passed from the company through the Army to AARO and then to ORNL
ttsa-army-crada.note: AARO confirms the organisation 'negotiated an agreement in 2019 with the U.S. Army to analyze the samples' and that AARO subsequently acquired the sample with stakeholder permission. This is the only fully documented custody chain in the entire domain.

ttsa-army-crada.label: Luis D. Elizondo
ttsa-army-crada.why: Named as TTSA's principal investigator on the Army agreement
ttsa-army-crada.note: Two years after resigning from OUSD(I), Elizondo is the named private-sector counterpart to an Army laboratory on an exotic-materials instrument.

ttsa-army-crada.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
ttsa-army-crada.why: TTSA executed a federal exploitation agreement over material it claimed was of unknown origin
ttsa-army-crada.note: CRADA 19-15 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation' with the US Army CCDC Ground Vehicle Systems Center was filed as Exhibit 6.28 to TTSA's Form 1-A, naming Army principal investigators and TACOM intellectual property counsel.

ttsa-army-crada.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
ttsa-army-crada.why: Executed CRADA with the U.S. Army, 10 October 2019, term to 30 September 2023
ttsa-army-crada.note: A real federal instrument, not a press release: signed by the GVSC Director and TTSA's Chief Content Officer, with TTSA's participation valued at an estimated $1 million in in-kind contributions.

ttsa-army-crada.label: U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command, Ground Vehicle Systems Center
ttsa-army-crada.why: Army counterparty; Detroit Arsenal ground vehicle laboratory
ttsa-army-crada.note: GVSC released the agreement text within a day of the announcement and withheld all associated correspondence four months later.

ttsa-army-crada.label: Federal Contracting Mechanics
ttsa-army-crada.why: a non-FAR instrument binding the Army to a private claimant of recovered material
ttsa-army-crada.note: Signed 10 October 2019 by the Director of the Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and announced 17 October 2019. A Cooperative Research and Development Agreement sits outside ordinary procurement, involves no exchange of appropriated funds to the partner, and protects the private party's proprietary data - which is exactly the class of vehicle this domain is about. The executed document is not public; sourcing is the partner's own contemporaneous FAQ.

ttsa-army-crada.label: Jeffery Langhout
ttsa-army-crada.why: Signed for the United States Army, 10 October 2019
ttsa-army-crada.note: The federal signature block is what makes the agreement citable as a government act.

ttsa-army-crada.label: Dr. Joseph Cannon
ttsa-army-crada.note: Named in the agreement alongside Bean Soave and quoted in the announcement calling TTSA 'an exciting, non-traditional source for novel materials'.

ttsa-army-crada.label: Kari DeLonge
ttsa-army-crada.why: Signed for To The Stars Academy, 10 October 2019
ttsa-army-crada.note: The corporate signatory on a materials-science agreement with an Army laboratory was TTSA's Chief Content Officer — the entertainment company was the legal spine.

ttsa-army-crada.label: Detroit Arsenal, Warren, Michigan
ttsa-army-crada.why: The CRADA was executed at Detroit Arsenal
ttsa-army-crada.note: GVSC Director Jeffery Langhout signed the agreement on 10 October 2019; the Army released the text on 18 October 2019.

ttsa-army-crada.label: ADAM Research Project (Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials)
ttsa-army-crada.why: ADAM is the predicate for the Army agreement
ttsa-army-crada.note: The CRADA lists mechanical/structural metamaterials and electromagnetic metamaterial waveguides — the exact subject matter ADAM claimed to hold.

garry-reid-memo-2017.label: Luis D. Elizondo
garry-reid-memo-2017.why: 'Aggrandized his role'; 'no job responsibilities related to the AATIP'
garry-reid-memo-2017.note: The first written denial of Elizondo's program role, produced inside OUSD(I) within a week of the NYT story and routed to the Secretary of Defense. Every later public denial restates it.

garry-reid-memo-2017.label: Garry P. Reid
garry-reid-memo-2017.note: Reid wrote the memorandum for record and the memorandum for the Secretary asserting Elizondo 'aggrandized his role'.

garry-reid-memo-2017.label: Air Force Office of Special Investigations
garry-reid-memo-2017.why: Records an AFOSI inquiry into possible mishandling of classified material
garry-reid-memo-2017.note: AFOSI examined the video handling and concluded the material was unclassified, closing the matter. Elizondo later alleged the inquiry was orchestrated against him.

foia-18-f-0324.label: John Greenewald Jr.
foia-18-f-0324.note: Four years and eight months to release eight pages describing an employee's resignation, during which the Department repeatedly characterised that employee in public.

foia-21-f-0938.label: Susan Gough
foia-21-f-0938.why: FOIA release of the Elizondo-Gough correspondence
foia-21-f-0938.note: The Department's own reading room hosts the most detailed public rebuttal of the Department's position on Elizondo.

navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.label: DD Form 1910 for GoFast, Gimbal and FLIR video files
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.why: Cleared the GoFast, Gimbal and FLIR files for internal distribution only
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.note: The form's stated purpose expressly excludes publication: research and analysis only, for a UAS threat database. This is the narrow basis on which the Navy later said no unrestricted release was ever authorised.

navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.label: DoD Statement on the Release of Historical Navy Videos, 27 April 2020
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.why: DoD authorises release, 27 April 2020; phenomena 'remain characterized as unidentified'
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.note: The Department also characterised the 2007 and 2017 public appearances as 'unauthorized releases' — a formal acknowledgement that material left the building improperly.

navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.label: Joseph Gradisher
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.why: Navy designates the objects as unidentified aerial phenomena, 10 Sep 2019
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.note: The single most consequential official concession of the period, made by a named service spokesman.

navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.label: Christopher K. Mellon
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.why: Received the three files in the Pentagon parking lot and passed them to the NYT
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.note: Mellon's own on-record account in The Phenomenon: 'I received the videos, the now famous videos in the Pentagon parking lot from a Defense Department official.' The handing official has never been identified.

navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.why: Hosted and distributed the three videos from 2017-2018
navy-flir-gimbal-gofast-videos.note: TTSA published the footage on its own platform, framing it as officially cleared — a framing the Navy contested in September 2019.

dod-video-release-2020.label: FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast Navy gun-camera videos
dod-video-release-2020.why: DoD authorises release, 27 April 2020; phenomena 'remain characterized as unidentified'
dod-video-release-2020.note: The Department also characterised the 2007 and 2017 public appearances as 'unauthorized releases' — a formal acknowledgement that material left the building improperly.

dopsr.label: DD Form 1910 for GoFast, Gimbal and FLIR video files
dopsr.why: Prepublication review chain for the video files
dopsr.note: The Navy later said DOPSR held no record of a request for unrestricted release of the videos in 2017 — consistent with the form's 'not for publication' framing.

dopsr.label: Grusch DOPSR Prepublication Clearance (FOIA 23-F-0946)
dopsr.why: Cleared Grusch's statements for open publication, 4 and 6 April 2023
dopsr.note: DoD's own prepublication review office read the specific words and released them. FOIA case 23-F-0946 documents the submissions of 7 March and 5 April 2023 and the approvals of 4 and 6 April 2023, along with internal reviewer correspondence.

dopsr.label: Imminent: Inside the Pentagon's Hunt for UFOs
dopsr.why: Manuscript reviewed and cleared by the Department's prepublication office
dopsr.note: A DOPSR clearance is not an endorsement of accuracy, but it is an affirmative Departmental determination that the assertions are not classified.

l-pentagon.label: Luis D. Elizondo
l-pentagon.note: The New York Times placed AATIP on the Pentagon's fifth floor; the Pentagon parking lot is where Mellon says he received the video files.

battelle.label: AARO / ORNL Synopsis: Analysis of a Metallic Specimen
battelle.why: Oak Ridge, operated by UT-Battelle, analysed the alleged 1947 crash specimen for AARO
battelle.note: AARO contracted ORNL in 2022; the laboratory assessed the specimen terrestrial in origin and incapable of functioning as a terahertz waveguide. Battelle thus appears at both ends of the file, in 1951 and in 2024.

battelle.label: Project BEAR (Battelle contract to Project GRUDGE)
battelle.why: Battelle's authorship of Special Report No. 14 was deliberately concealed behind an ATIC cover
battelle.note: AARO states that Battelle 'released a report under the cover of ATIC to maintain its anonymity.' The first public analytical product of the government's UFO investigation was ghost-written by a private contractor at the contractor's request.

battelle.label: Columbus, Ohio
battelle.note: Battelle Memorial Institute is headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, roughly sixty-five miles from Wright-Patterson Air Force Base at Dayton, which is the geographic fact underlying its Air Force analytical work in the 1940s and 1950s.

battelle.label: Mark Todd Peters
battelle.why: Came to MITRE directly from Battelle's executive suite
battelle.note: Peters was executive vice president for laboratory management and operations at Battelle Memorial Institute and previously president of Battelle Energy Alliance LLC and director of Idaho National Laboratory.

battelle.label: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (UT-Battelle, LLC)
battelle.why: Battelle co-operates ORNL through UT-Battelle, LLC
battelle.note: Contract DEAC0500OR22725, recorded at approximately $42.3 billion, running 1999-2030.

battelle.label: Project BEAR (Battelle contract to Project GRUDGE)
battelle.why: Battelle held the Project BEAR contract supplying the science behind Project GRUDGE and BLUE BOOK
battelle.note: AARO's own history records the contract, the questionnaire and punch-card work, and the resulting Special Report No. 14.

battelle.label: Project Stork (Project White Stork)
battelle.why: Battelle held the Air Force contract designated Project Stork
battelle.note: Under Stork, Battelle performed the statistical analysis of Project Blue Book's case files that became Special Report No. 14.

battelle.label: Roswell Incident
battelle.why: Alleged analysis of Roswell 'memory metal' via Wright-Patterson contracts
battelle.note: The allegation rests on the coincidence of timing between the 1947 recovery, the 1948-49 Battelle NiTi work, and the absence of the reports from both archives. No document connects the two directly.

battelle.label: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14
battelle.why: Battelle performed the statistical analysis under contract
battelle.note: Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus is the contractor identified throughout the literature; the report's own front matter does not name a contractor, which is why this is graded tier 2.

battelle.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
battelle.note: The research lineage from which nitinol shape-memory alloy emerged; researchers including Anthony Bragalia allege the corresponding reports are missing from both Air Force and Battelle archives.

battelle.label: UAP Gerb - Battelle Memorial Institute investigation
battelle.why: Alleges Battelle studied Roswell-derived shape-memory alloy
battelle.note: Gerb argues, following Jacques Vallee's paper trail, that Battelle studied a shape-memory metallic alloy recovered at Roswell now referred to as nitinol, while also building the USAF's machine index of UFO reports and helping quell public interest.

battelle.label: Howard C. Cross
battelle.why: Battelle's Air Force liaison for Blue Book-related work
battelle.note: Cross was the named point of contact between Battelle's Stork analysts and Wright-Patterson.

battelle.label: The MITRE Corporation
battelle.why: Executive pipeline from the 1950s UFO analysis contractor to the 2020s FFRDC under inquiry
battelle.note: Battelle ran Project Stork and produced Blue Book Special Report No. 14; seventy years later it supplied MITRE's chief executive. The connection is documented; the significance is inference.

blue-book-special-report-14.label: Air Technical Intelligence Center
blue-book-special-report-14.note: Issued 5 May 1955 under Project 10073, Study No. 102-EL-55/2-79 — the largest statistical study of UFO reports the US government ever produced.

blue-book-special-report-14.label: Project Blue Book
blue-book-special-report-14.why: 19.7 per cent of analysed objects were unknowns, rising with report quality
blue-book-special-report-14.note: 434 of 2,199 objects were classified Unknown, and the better the report quality the higher the unknown rate — the inverse of what misidentification predicts.

blue-book-special-report-14.label: Project Stork (Project White Stork)
blue-book-special-report-14.why: Stork produced Special Report No. 14, 5 May 1955
blue-book-special-report-14.note: Project No. 10073; roughly 3,200 cases analysed; the proportion of unknowns rose with the quality of the sighting.

blue-book-special-report-14.label: PURSUE - Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters
blue-book-special-report-14.why: Republished by the Department of War as CIA-UAP-015 in PURSUE Release 03
blue-book-special-report-14.note: The same 1955 Battelle report has now been published by the government three times across seventy years without the underlying case data ever being independently reanalysed.

blue-book-special-report-14.label: Battelle Memorial Institute
blue-book-special-report-14.why: Battelle performed the statistical analysis under contract
blue-book-special-report-14.note: Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus is the contractor identified throughout the literature; the report's own front matter does not name a contractor, which is why this is graded tier 2.

blue-book-special-report-14.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)
blue-book-special-report-14.why: Both official studies buried an unexplained residue under dismissive conclusions
blue-book-special-report-14.note: SR14 left 19.7 per cent unknown with quality correlating positively with unexplainedness; the Colorado project left roughly a third of its cases unexplained. Both summaries declared the subject unrewarding.

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: Sean M. Kirkpatrick
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: AARO's founding director left government for the laboratory that analysed AARO's specimen
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: Kirkpatrick departed AARO on 1 December 2023 and became Chief Technology Officer for Defense and Intelligence Programs at ORNL, a UT-Battelle laboratory that had supported AARO during his tenure.

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: AARO contracted ORNL in 2022 to test the magnesium alloy specimen
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: AARO's own words: 'In 2022, The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) contracted with Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) to conduct materials testing on a magnesium (Mg) alloy specimen.'

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: ORNL Synopsis: Analysis of a Metallic Specimen
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: Produced 'ORNL Synopsis: Analysis of a Metallic Specimen', April 2024
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: Released publicly July 2024; concluded the material is a terrestrial magnesium alloy, while stating that neither AARO nor ORNL could verify the specimen's historical origin.

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: Battelle Memorial Institute
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: Battelle co-operates ORNL through UT-Battelle, LLC
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: Contract DEAC0500OR22725, recorded at approximately $42.3 billion, running 1999-2030.

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: Sean M. Kirkpatrick
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: chief technology officer for defense and intelligence programs
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: The first AARO director joined Oak Ridge National Laboratory in December 2023 - the laboratory that performed both of AARO's published specimen analyses.

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: United States Department of Energy
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: DOE laboratory performed AARO's metallic specimen analysis
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: AARO's published materials analysis synopsis was produced with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, a DOE laboratory - meaning DOE analytical capability was the government's chosen instrument for testing alleged recovered material.

oak-ridge-national-laboratory.label: Sean M. Kirkpatrick
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.why: post-government employment at the DOE lab that supported AARO and later held the UAP material sample
oak-ridge-national-laboratory.note: Kirkpatrick became CTO for Defense and Intelligence Programs at ORNL, operated by UT-Battelle, immediately after leaving AARO. The post-employment question under 18 U.S.C. 207 has been raised publicly and never adjudicated.

ornl-metallic-specimen-report.label: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (UT-Battelle, LLC)
ornl-metallic-specimen-report.why: Produced 'ORNL Synopsis: Analysis of a Metallic Specimen', April 2024
ornl-metallic-specimen-report.note: Released publicly July 2024; concluded the material is a terrestrial magnesium alloy, while stating that neither AARO nor ORNL could verify the specimen's historical origin.

ornl-metallic-specimen-report.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
ornl-metallic-specimen-report.why: The government's only published materials analysis, produced by a Battelle-operated laboratory
ornl-metallic-specimen-report.note: Recorded as a denial artifact as well as a technical result: the chain of custody to any 1947 event was never established and the comparison baseline of failed magnesium alloys is admittedly incomplete.

green-fireballs-conference-1949.label: Los Alamos National Laboratory
green-fireballs-conference-1949.why: Held at Los Alamos; LANL's National Security Research Center holds the minutes
green-fireballs-conference-1949.note: LANL confirms the 16 February 1949 conference and its custody of the minutes in its own published account.

green-fireballs-conference-1949.label: United States Department of Energy
green-fireballs-conference-1949.why: AEC laboratories convened the February 1949 green fireball conference
green-fireballs-conference-1949.note: The green fireball events centred on the Los Alamos and Sandia complexes and produced a conference and the subsequent Project TWINKLE instrumented observation effort. Attested by the FBI and Air Force file material released through the 2026 PURSUE tranches.

green-fireballs-conference-1949.label: Los Alamos, New Mexico
green-fireballs-conference-1949.why: The green fireballs conference was convened at Los Alamos
green-fireballs-conference-1949.note: Edward Teller and Lincoln LaPaz were among the attendees; the laboratory's own account records that the phenomenon was ultimately dismissed as a national security threat.

green-fireballs-conference-1949.label: Edward Teller
green-fireballs-conference-1949.note: Attendance confirmed by LANL alongside Norris Bradbury and Frederick Reines, with FBI, AEC and military representatives present.

green-fireballs-conference-1949.label: Lincoln LaPaz
green-fireballs-conference-1949.why: Brought in by Kirtland intelligence officers; his assessment drove the conference
green-fireballs-conference-1949.note: LaPaz concluded the fireballs did not behave like meteors despite superficially resembling them.

grusch-icig-complaint.label: Irvin Charles McCullough III
grusch-icig-complaint.why: Filed the complaint as counsel; former ICIG filing with the ICIG
grusch-icig-complaint.note: The first Inspector General of the Intelligence Community drafted and filed the urgent-concern complaint with the office he previously ran. This is the strongest structural credential in the file.

grusch-icig-complaint.label: Inspector General of the Intelligence Community
grusch-icig-complaint.why: Determined the complaint credible and urgent, July 2022
grusch-icig-complaint.note: The statutory urgent-concern finding by the IC's own watchdog, which obliges transmission to the congressional intelligence committees. It is the highest-grade institutional validation in the disclosure record and has never been withdrawn.

grusch-icig-complaint.label: House Oversight hearing, 26 July 2023 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'
grusch-icig-complaint.why: Fourteen months from urgent-concern determination to public testimony
grusch-icig-complaint.note: The ICIG found the complaint credible and urgent in July 2022; Grusch testified publicly in July 2023 only after leaving government and clearing his statements through DOPSR. The intervening year is the period the reprisal complaint covers.

grusch-icig-complaint.label: David Charles Grusch
grusch-icig-complaint.why: Complainant of record, PPD-19 urgent concern, 25 May 2022
grusch-icig-complaint.note: Grusch testified he 'became a whistleblower through a PPD-19 urgent concern filing in May 2022 with the intelligence community inspector general.' The Debrief dates the filing 25 May 2022 and identifies counsel.

grusch-icig-complaint.label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
grusch-icig-complaint.why: An urgent concern complaint enters a system whose SAP layer is itself compartmented
grusch-icig-complaint.note: The ICIG PPD-19 route reaches the intelligence committees, but access to waived DoD programs is restricted by DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f to chairs, ranking members and staff directors.

grusch-dopsr-clearance.label: Defense Office of Prepublication and Security Review
grusch-dopsr-clearance.why: Cleared Grusch's statements for open publication, 4 and 6 April 2023
grusch-dopsr-clearance.note: DoD's own prepublication review office read the specific words and released them. FOIA case 23-F-0946 documents the submissions of 7 March and 5 April 2023 and the approvals of 4 and 6 April 2023, along with internal reviewer correspondence.

grusch-dopsr-clearance.label: The Debrief: Intelligence Officials Say U.S. Has Retrieved Craft of Non-Human Origin
grusch-dopsr-clearance.why: Clearance preceded publication by two months
grusch-dopsr-clearance.note: DOPSR approvals of 4 and 6 April 2023 preceded the 5 June 2023 Debrief publication. Kean and Blumenthal confirmed the clearance before publishing, which is why the Pentagon's response contested substantiation rather than authorization.

aaro-grusch-interview-memo.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
aaro-grusch-interview-memo.why: AARO's own record of nine interview attempts, June 2023 - January 2024
aaro-grusch-interview-memo.note: Released under DoD FOIA case 24-F-0266. It documents both the refusals AARO cites and the fact that AARO worked through intermediaries and Senate staff for five months before making direct contact.

aaro-grusch-interview-memo.label: David W. Abba
aaro-grusch-interview-memo.why: SAPCO director's March 2023 memorandum cited as AARO's access authority
aaro-grusch-interview-memo.note: Maj. Gen. David W. Abba, Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office, signed the memorandum AARO invoked in its invitations. SAPCO is the one office that could resolve the read-on denial and has never publicly addressed it.

icig.label: Grusch PPD-19 Urgent Concern Complaint to the ICIG
icig.why: Determined the complaint credible and urgent, July 2022
icig.note: The statutory urgent-concern finding by the IC's own watchdog, which obliges transmission to the congressional intelligence committees. It is the highest-grade institutional validation in the disclosure record and has never been withdrawn.

icig.label: Thomas A. Monheim
icig.why: Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, 2021-present
icig.note: Monheim held the office when the credible-and-urgent determination was made and when his office briefed House Oversight members in closed session on 13 January 2024.

icig.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
icig.why: Irreconcilable executive-branch findings on the same allegations
icig.note: The ICIG found the complaint credible and urgent in July 2022; AARO found no verifiable information from June 2023 and no firsthand knowledge in March 2024. Both are executive-branch determinations on the same body of allegations, and neither has been formally reconciled on the public record. Reasoning: no document exists in which either office addresses the other's finding.

atic.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
atic.why: ATIC and its successors were and are headquartered at Wright-Patterson
atic.note: The Air Technical Intelligence Center, formed in 1951 from Air Materiel Command's T-2 intelligence organisation at Wright Field, became the Foreign Technology Division in 1961 and NASIC in 1993, which remains at the base. Attested by USAF unit histories.

atic.label: Air Force Regulation 200-2
atic.why: ATIC was the terminal analytical authority under the regulation
atic.note: The regulation routes reports from base level through Air Defense Command and the 4602d Air Intelligence Service Squadron to ATIC at Wright-Patterson for final analysis.

atic.label: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14
atic.note: Issued 5 May 1955 under Project 10073, Study No. 102-EL-55/2-79 — the largest statistical study of UFO reports the US government ever produced.

atic.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
atic.why: ATIC and every legacy UFO project were located at Wright-Patterson
atic.note: SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book were all headquartered at Wright-Patterson AFB, the site of the Air Force's foreign materiel exploitation organisation and its successors.

atic.label: Project SIGN
atic.why: SIGN hosted by AMC intelligence at Wright Field, ATIC's predecessor
atic.note: The first official UFO project was placed inside the foreign materiel exploitation organisation rather than a research or air defence body — the structural fact underlying this entire domain.

atic.label: Howard M. McCoy
atic.why: McCoy ran AMC/T-2 intelligence, the exploitation node
atic.note: As Chief of Intelligence at Air Materiel Command, McCoy headed the organisation that received and exploited recovered foreign materiel and that hosted Project SIGN. Any 1947 recovery would have been processed here.

project-blue-book.label: NARA Record Group 615 — UAP Records Collection
project-blue-book.why: NARA holds the Blue Book series and is digitising legacy UFO records
project-blue-book.note: Approximately 42 cubic feet of Blue Book material on 94 rolls of microfilm (T-1206) sits alongside the new RG 615 accessions; NARA states no Blue Book document discusses Roswell.

project-blue-book.label: United States Air Force
project-blue-book.why: BLUE BOOK records transferred to the National Archives as 94 rolls of microfilm
project-blue-book.note: The records were permanently transferred to NARA and are held as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, T-1206.

project-blue-book.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)
project-blue-book.why: The Condon report was the stated basis for terminating Blue Book
project-blue-book.note: The Air Force terminated Project Blue Book on 17 December 1969 in response to the Condon findings, having received the report in November 1968.

project-blue-book.label: A Die-hard Issue: CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-1990
project-blue-book.why: CIA states the Air Force made misleading and deceptive public statements
project-blue-book.note: Haines writes that reconnaissance-programme secrecy 'led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public' — an agency of the US government confirming official deception on this subject.

project-blue-book.label: Minot AFB B-52 incident, 24 October 1968
project-blue-book.why: Blue Book declined to field-investigate an instrumented nuclear-site case
project-blue-book.note: The RADCAT directory records that Project Blue Book personnel did not send field investigators and the incident was written off despite interest from SAC generals including 15th Air Force's Maj. Gen. Nichols.

project-blue-book.label: Columbus, Ohio
project-blue-book.why: Project Stork / Blue Book Special Report No. 14 produced here
project-blue-book.note: In 1952 Project Blue Book contracted the Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus, Ohio to carry out the statistical study of 1947-1952 sighting reports that became Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, dated 5 May 1955; the Battelle group was associated with Project Stork.

project-blue-book.label: Air Force Regulation 200-2
project-blue-book.why: AFR 200-2 governed what Blue Book could say publicly
project-blue-book.note: For unexplainable objects, 'only the fact that ATIC will analyze the data is worthy of release'. Every Air Force public statement that unknowns were unimportant was made under a regulation forbidding discussion of them.

project-blue-book.label: 'CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90' (Gerald K. Haines, Studies in Intelligence, 1997)
project-blue-book.why: Blue Book investigators knowingly issued false explanations for U-2 sightings
project-blue-book.note: CIA records that Blue Book investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights attributed sightings to ice crystals and temperature inversions and 'were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public.'

project-blue-book.label: Edward J. Ruppelt
project-blue-book.why: Ruppelt was Blue Book's first director
project-blue-book.note: Ruppelt directed the project from March 1952 to August 1953, covering the Washington flap and the Robertson Panel, and later published the only insider account of the period.

project-blue-book.label: J. Allen Hynek
project-blue-book.why: Hynek was scientific consultant across SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book
project-blue-book.note: Twenty-one continuous years as the Air Force's own astronomer on the problem — longer than any other participant in the legacy system.

project-blue-book.label: JANAP 146 (CIRVIS/MERINT reporting)
project-blue-book.why: JANAP created a parallel reporting channel outside Blue Book
project-blue-book.note: JANAP 146(C) made UFO sightings a mandatory CIRVIS report under espionage-statute penalties while Blue Book handled the public-facing residue. Bolender confirmed the split in 1969.

project-blue-book.label: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14
project-blue-book.why: 19.7 per cent of analysed objects were unknowns, rising with report quality
project-blue-book.note: 434 of 2,199 objects were classified Unknown, and the better the report quality the higher the unknown rate — the inverse of what misidentification predicts.

project-blue-book.label: James E. McDonald
project-blue-book.why: McDonald reviewed Blue Book files and told Congress it was not an investigation
project-blue-book.note: Testifying on 29 July 1968 he told the House Science and Astronautics Committee that 'credible observers are observing relatively incredible objects' and that the subject deserved science rather than ridicule.

project-blue-book.label: Bolender Memorandum
project-blue-book.why: Memo recommended termination; Blue Book closed two months later
project-blue-book.note: Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans Jr. announced the termination on 17 December 1969, citing the Condon Report.

project-blue-book.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)
project-blue-book.why: The Condon Report was the stated basis for terminating Blue Book
project-blue-book.note: The Air Force cited the Colorado study, a National Academy of Sciences review and prior experience in ending the program on 17 December 1969.

project-blue-book.label: UAP Gerb - Battelle Memorial Institute investigation
project-blue-book.why: Battelle's Project Stork produced Special Report No. 14
project-blue-book.note: Project Stork was Battelle's contract supporting the Air Force UFO effort; it produced the statistical study issued as Special Report No. 14, a document available in the CIA reading room.

project-blue-book.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
project-blue-book.why: Blue Book was hosted at Wright-Patterson from 1952 to 1969
project-blue-book.note: Project Blue Book, like SIGN and GRUDGE before it, was hosted at this base under ATIC. Of 12,618 sightings studied, 701 remained unexplained at closure. Attested by USAF fact sheets.

project-blue-book.label: Project GRUDGE
project-blue-book.why: GRUDGE renamed Blue Book under Ruppelt in March 1952
project-blue-book.note: Ruppelt was placed in charge of the reconstituted GRUDGE in late 1951 and the project was renamed Project Blue Book in March 1952.

project-blue-book.label: Project Stork (Project White Stork)
project-blue-book.why: Stork was Blue Book's contracted analytical arm
project-blue-book.note: The Air Force's public UFO project outsourced its own analytical methodology to a private nonprofit, whose records were never federal records.

project-blue-book.label: United States Air Force
project-blue-book.why: Air Force ran the public UFO investigation 1952-1969
project-blue-book.note: 12,618 sightings were reported to BLUE BOOK, of which 701 remain 'Unidentified'. The Secretary of the Air Force announced termination on 17 December 1969.

project-blue-book.label: COMETA - Comité d'Études Approfondies
project-blue-book.why: adopts Hynek's Blue Book-era classification
project-blue-book.note: COMETA chapter 7.2 states that the strangest category D cases 'are generally labeled CE3s (close encounters of the third kind) according to the classification proposed by Professor A. Hynek, an astronomer and consultant to the USAF, within the context of the Blue Book Project'. Chapter 9 of the report separately surveys the organisation of research abroad.

project-blue-book.label: 1975 SAC Nuclear-Base Overflights (Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot)
project-blue-book.why: Occurred six years after the Air Force closed Blue Book on a no-threat finding
project-blue-book.note: The USAF fact sheet states Blue Book was terminated on 17 December 1969 on the conclusion that no UFO had ever indicated a threat to national security. The 1975 records document unidentified objects over nuclear weapons installations.

project-blue-book.label: 1952 Washington DC Sightings
project-blue-book.why: The flap occurred during Ruppelt's tenure and drove the record volume
project-blue-book.note: Blue Book case documentation for the 19 July 1952 Washington radar events survives; 1952 produced the largest single-year report volume of the program's history.

project-blue-book.label: Kenneth Arnold
project-blue-book.why: Arnold's case entered the official file series from the outset
project-blue-book.note: Army Air Forces intelligence investigated the sighting and the case documentation survives in the Blue Book record series now held at the National Archives.

project-blue-book.label: JANAP 146 (CIRVIS/MERINT reporting)
project-blue-book.why: The public statistics are the residue of a filter, not the corpus
project-blue-book.note: If national-security reports went up the JANAP channel as Bolender states, then the 12,618 sightings and 701 unknowns describe only what the filtered public program retained.

project-blue-book.label: Project MOON DUST
project-blue-book.why: MOON DUST was the retrieval function alongside Blue Book's public sighting file
project-blue-book.note: Blue Book was the acknowledged investigative programme; MOON DUST was a separate, quieter recovery and exploitation tasking that was never advertised to the public that Blue Book served.

condon-committee.label: Low Memorandum ("the trick would be...")
condon-committee.why: The memo states the intent to present differently to public and scientists
condon-committee.note: 'The trick would be, I think, to describe the project so that, to the public, it would appear a totally objective study but, to the scientific community, would present the image of a group of nonbelievers.'

condon-committee.label: Project Blue Book
condon-committee.why: The Condon report was the stated basis for terminating Blue Book
condon-committee.note: The Air Force terminated Project Blue Book on 17 December 1969 in response to the Condon findings, having received the report in November 1968.

condon-committee.label: United States Air Force
condon-committee.why: Air Force funded the University of Colorado study used to close BLUE BOOK
condon-committee.note: The termination decision rested on 'Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects' and a National Academy of Sciences review of it.

condon-committee.label: Edward U. Condon
condon-committee.why: Condon directed the study and wrote its conclusions personally
condon-committee.note: Condon authored the summary, conclusions and recommendations placed at the front of the report — the only section most readers and reporters ever saw.

condon-committee.label: Boulder, Colorado
condon-committee.why: The Condon Committee was hosted by the University of Colorado at Boulder
condon-committee.note: The Air Force contract was announced in October 1966 at $313,000, eventually exceeding $500,000, with Condon as director and Robert Low as coordinator.

condon-committee.label: Estimate of the Situation (1948)
condon-committee.why: The Condon Report is the primary documentary record of the Estimate's destruction
condon-committee.note: Section V Chapter 2 records the estimate's preparation, Vandenberg's rejection and the destruction of copies — the Air Force paying to put its own suppression on the record.

condon-committee.label: House Armed Services Committee UFO Hearing
condon-committee.why: Congressional pressure produced a contracted study, not oversight
condon-committee.note: Six months after the hearing the Air Force let contract 44620-67-C-0035 to the University of Colorado — pressure in, study out, closure following.

condon-committee.label: Project Blue Book
condon-committee.why: The Condon Report was the stated basis for terminating Blue Book
condon-committee.note: The Air Force cited the Colorado study, a National Academy of Sciences review and prior experience in ending the program on 17 December 1969.

condon-committee.label: Coronel de Aviación Sergio Bravo Flores
condon-committee.why: forwarded Chilean reports to the University of Colorado study
condon-committee.note: SEFAA records that part of the dozen reports gathered were sent to the University of Colorado, where the commission later known as the Condon Committee was working.

condon-committee.label: George Kocher
condon-committee.why: RAND was documenting the case for instrumented study as Condon was closing it down
condon-committee.note: DRU-1571 is dated November 1968; the Condon report recommending termination of Blue Book followed in January 1969.

condon-committee.label: James E. McDonald
condon-committee.why: McDonald attacked the Condon Report and was professionally destroyed
condon-committee.note: He publicly criticised the report on release, was ridiculed over his UFO work during 1971 congressional SST hearings on an unrelated technical subject, and died by suicide in June 1971.

condon-committee.label: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14
condon-committee.why: Both official studies buried an unexplained residue under dismissive conclusions
condon-committee.note: SR14 left 19.7 per cent unknown with quality correlating positively with unexplainedness; the Colorado project left roughly a third of its cases unexplained. Both summaries declared the subject unrewarding.

project-mogul.label: Roswell Incident
project-mogul.why: Mogul is the Air Force's 1994 identification of the debris
project-mogul.note: The 1994 USAF report attributed the debris to Project Mogul Flight No. 4, launched 4 June 1947 from Alamogordo, and acknowledged that the weather balloon account had been a cover story.

project-mogul.label: The Roswell Reports (USAF, 1994-1997)
project-mogul.why: MOGUL is the load-bearing element of the official explanation
project-mogul.note: The Air Force concluded the most likely source of the recovered wreckage was a Project MOGUL balloon train, replacing the weather balloon account it had maintained since 1947.

project-mogul.label: Nathan F. Twining
project-mogul.why: The AMC commander's 1947 assessment predates and undercuts the MOGUL account
project-mogul.note: Twining wrote in September 1947 that the phenomenon was real while noting the lack of recovered exhibits; the Air Force's 1994 position requires that his own command's exploitation centre never connected the wave to a programme it was cleared for.

project-mogul.label: GAO/NSIAD-95-187 — Results of a Search for Records Concerning the 1947 Crash Near Roswell
project-mogul.why: The MOGUL attribution cannot be tested against destroyed records
project-mogul.note: GAO reported the base's message traffic for the relevant years was destroyed without disposition authority, so the Air Force's reconstruction rests on inference rather than on the contemporaneous record.

bolender-memo.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
bolender-memo.why: The Bolender memo closed the base's public reporting channel while conceding another existed
bolender-memo.note: Brig. Gen. Carroll Bolender's 1969 memorandum recommended Blue Book's termination and stated that reports which could affect national security were never part of the Blue Book system - a statement about this base's own reporting architecture.

bolender-memo.label: Carroll H. Bolender
bolender-memo.note: Brig. Gen. Bolender, USAF Deputy Director of Development, signed the 20 October 1969 memorandum recommending Blue Book's closure and explaining why closure cost the Air Force nothing operationally.

bolender-memo.label: Project Blue Book
bolender-memo.why: Memo recommended termination; Blue Book closed two months later
bolender-memo.note: Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans Jr. announced the termination on 17 December 1969, citing the Condon Report.

bolender-memo.label: JANAP 146 (CIRVIS/MERINT reporting)
bolender-memo.why: Bolender names JANAP 146 as the channel Blue Book was not
bolender-memo.note: The memorandum states national-security UFO reports are made under JANAP 146 or AFM 55-11 and are not part of the Blue Book system — an official concession that the public program was never the collection channel.

bolender-memo.label: NARA Record Group 615 — UAP Records Collection
bolender-memo.why: No records series has ever been identified for the JANAP channel
bolender-memo.note: Blue Book's files went to NARA; whatever accumulated on the JANAP 146 side has never been named as a series, accessioned, or searched under any disclosure statute including the FY2024 NDAA.

afosi-kirtland-file.label: Air Force Office of Special Investigations
afosi-kirtland-file.why: AFOSI is the originating agency of the released Kirtland UFO file
afosi-kirtland-file.note: The file covering the Manzano Weapons Storage Area intrusions was released under FOIA and is archived in full by NICAP.

afosi-kirtland-file.label: Kirtland Air Force Base and Albuquerque, New Mexico
afosi-kirtland-file.why: The AFOSI Kirtland file is the documentary residue of the Bennewitz operation
afosi-kirtland-file.note: The AFOSI documents concerning the 1980 Kirtland incidents are the only contemporaneous official records of the observations that triggered the campaign against Bennewitz.

afosi-kirtland-file.label: Kirtland Air Force Base and Albuquerque, New Mexico
afosi-kirtland-file.why: AFOSI District 17 file generated at Kirtland AFB
afosi-kirtland-file.note: The 10 November 1980 record concerns observations by Kirtland security police over Coyote Canyon and the Manzano storage area.

afosi-kirtland-file.label: Paul Frederick Bennewitz
afosi-kirtland-file.why: Bennewitz's reporting generated the AFOSI Kirtland file
afosi-kirtland-file.note: The 10 November 1980 AFOSI record documents Kirtland security police observations of unexplained objects over Coyote Canyon and notes Bennewitz's photography and reporting.

afosi-kirtland-file.label: Richard C. Doty
afosi-kirtland-file.why: Doty was the AFOSI special agent associated with the Kirtland UFO file
afosi-kirtland-file.note: Doty served in AFOSI at Kirtland from 1979 and is the agent identified with the Kirtland UFO documents and with the subsequent contact with Bennewitz and Howe.

wilson-davis-memo.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
wilson-davis-memo.why: AARO's 2024 review does not mention the Wilson-Davis notes or Admiral Wilson
wilson-davis-memo.note: The most specific custody allegation in the modern record, whose author and subject are both alive and identifiable, is absent from the government's historical review.

wilson-davis-memo.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
wilson-davis-memo.why: AARO's report independently catalogues the same structural allegation the memo describes
wilson-davis-memo.note: AARO records a senior military officer describing a craft floating in a building with roughly 150 people working on it, in a program kept 'outside of government so the technology could remain proprietary' - the memo's central claim, restated in a DoD publication.

wilson-davis-memo.label: Eric W. Davis
wilson-davis-memo.why: Author of record of the notes of the alleged 16 October 2002 Wilson meeting
wilson-davis-memo.note: Notes attributed to Davis describing a meeting with former DIA director Vice Adm. Thomas R. Wilson surfaced in 2019 among the estate papers of Edgar Mitchell. Provenance is a private estate, not a government release; Davis has not publicly repudiated authorship.

wilson-davis-memo.label: Christopher C. 'Kit' Green
wilson-davis-memo.why: The memo pages entered public circulation from Green's document holdings
wilson-davis-memo.note: Green has acknowledged that documents left his possession without vouching for their contents; the provenance chain between 2002 and 2019 has never been established.

wilson-davis-memo.label: Thomas R. Wilson
wilson-davis-memo.why: Wilson denies the meeting and the substance attributed to him
wilson-davis-memo.note: Wilson's denial is recorded as a primary artefact. It is irreconcilable with Davis's confirmation of authorship, and no agency has attempted to resolve it.

wilson-davis-memo.label: Jesse Michels
wilson-davis-memo.why: Dedicated chapter on the Wilson-Davis memo with Davis present
wilson-davis-memo.note: Chapter at 37:56 of the 8 March 2026 episode, with the memo's named author-participant in the room - the closest to a primary-source interrogation of that document yet conducted in public.

wilson-davis-memo.label: Eric W. Davis
wilson-davis-memo.why: author of the notes at the centre of the custody claim
wilson-davis-memo.note: The memo records Vice Adm. Thomas Wilson being refused access to a program holding a recovered craft on the ground that it sat with a private aerospace contractor and he had no need to know. Davis has never authenticated it; Wilson has denied the meeting.

wilson-davis-memo.label: EG&G (Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier)
wilson-davis-memo.why: The meeting is reported to have taken place at an EG&G facility in Las Vegas
wilson-davis-memo.note: EG&G held the Groom Lake support and personnel-transport contracts; the reported venue matters because it places the conversation inside the contractor perimeter it describes.

wilson-davis-memo.label: David Charles Grusch
wilson-davis-memo.why: The 2002 notes and the 2023 sworn testimony describe the same access-denial mechanism
wilson-davis-memo.note: Both describe an appropriately cleared official being refused a read-on by programme security officers and contractor gatekeepers on need-to-know grounds. Twenty-one years apart, two officials describe the same wall.

thunder-scientific.label: Paul Frederick Bennewitz
thunder-scientific.why: Bennewitz founded and ran Thunder Scientific, a USAF instrumentation vendor
