dodig.note: The report is the OIG's own audit of Army General Fund compilation adjustments for FY2015. Attested by the report.

dow-financial-mgmt-hearing-2026.label: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
dow-financial-mgmt-hearing-2026.note: The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform held the DoW financial management hearing at which Deputy IG Mansfield testified. Attested by the OIG's publication of his statement.

dow-financial-mgmt-hearing-2026.label: Brett A. Mansfield
dow-financial-mgmt-hearing-2026.note: Mansfield was the Office of Inspector General witness at 'DoW Financial Management: Examining Progress and New Audit Approaches'. Attested by the OIG's publication of his statement.

ev-chile-navy-flir-2014.label: CEFAA / SEFAA - Chilean anomalous aerial phenomena office, Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
ev-chile-navy-flir-2014.why: analysed the Navy FLIR case for two years then released it
ev-chile-navy-flir-2014.note: The Chilean office published the raw sensor product without an explanation, three years before the US DoD authorised release of the Navy videos.

l-colorado-springs.label: Immaculate Constellation disclosure, October-November 2024
l-colorado-springs.why: The only provenance story ever attached to the report points at Schriever
l-colorado-springs.note: A self-identified whistleblower said in 2025 he located the material in a folder labelled '2018 Schriever Wargame'; Jason Colavito assessed the claimant had mistaken wargame documents for UFO revelations. Schriever Space Force Base is at Colorado Springs.

l-cambridge.label: The Galileo Project
l-cambridge.why: The Galileo Project is based at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics
l-cambridge.note: Avi Loeb founded the project in 2021 to build independent multi-modal observatories, addressing the structural problem that every high-quality UAP dataset is held by agencies that will not release it.

nimitz-2004.label: FLIR1 (Nimitz ATFLIR video, 14 Nov 2004)
nimitz-2004.why: Primary sensor artefact of the 2004 encounter, released by DoD in 2020
nimitz-2004.note: The video leaked in 2007, was published by the New York Times on 16 December 2017, and was formally released by DoD on 27 April 2020 with the objects 'characterized as unidentified'.

nimitz-2004.label: Raytheon (RTX Corporation)
nimitz-2004.why: Raytheon-built ATFLIR pod produced the FLIR1 record
nimitz-2004.note: The AN/ASQ-228 Advanced Targeting Forward-Looking Infrared (ATFLIR) pod is developed and manufactured by Raytheon. The FLIR1 'Tic Tac' video, the primary sensor artefact of the 2004 Nimitz encounter and later released by DoD, was recorded on an ATFLIR pod operated by a VFA-41 weapons systems officer. This is the only UAP-specific Raytheon link found: the company's role is as the builder of the sensor of record, not as a programme participant.

nimitz-2004.label: USS Princeton (CG-59)
nimitz-2004.why: Generated the primary sensor record of the encounter; no such data has ever been released
nimitz-2004.note: Fravor testified Princeton tracked the objects on Aegis for two weeks. No Princeton radar or CEC data for 14 Nov 2004 has appeared in any release, and the range fouler report says reporting 'terminated at 3rd Fleet.'

nimitz-2004.label: Southern California Operating Areas (W-291 and Baja approaches)
nimitz-2004.why: The encounters occurred in the Southern California operating areas
nimitz-2004.note: The Nimitz Carrier Strike Group was working up in the W-291 warning area and Baja approaches when Princeton began holding the tracks.

nimitz-2004.label: ODNI Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (25 June 2021)
nimitz-2004.why: Assessment window opens with the Nimitz encounter
nimitz-2004.note: The assessment's date range begins November 2004 - the month of the Nimitz intercept - and it resolved only one of 144 reports with high confidence.

nimitz-2004.label: United States Navy
nimitz-2004.why: Nimitz encounter was a Navy carrier strike group event; Navy released the FLIR video
nimitz-2004.note: The November 2004 encounters involved aircrew and sensors of the USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group. DoD authorized release of the unclassified Navy video 'taken in November 2004' through the Naval Air Systems Command FOIA reading room on 27 April 2020, stating the aerial phenomena in the videos 'remain characterized as unidentified.' The DoD statement itself dates the video but does not name the strike group.

nimitz-2004.label: USS Princeton (CG-59)
nimitz-2004.why: Princeton's SPY-1B held the tracks and vectored the intercept
nimitz-2004.note: Princeton had been observing the objects on Aegis for approximately two weeks, descending from above 80,000 ft to 20,000 ft, before vectoring the VFA-41 section.

nimitz-2004.label: Strike Fighter Squadron 41 (VFA-41 Black Aces)
nimitz-2004.why: Squadron that flew the intercept and produced the FLIR1 footage
nimitz-2004.note: VFA-41 put two sections into the event: the Fravor/Dietrich visual intercept and a follow-on aircraft whose ATFLIR produced FLIR1.

nimitz-2004.label: Navy Range Fouler Reports (72 reports, 2004-2021)
nimitz-2004.why: The 2004 incident is formally documented in the Navy's own range fouler reporting
nimitz-2004.note: The January 2023 FOIA release proves the encounter was reported inside the Navy through intelligence personnel and then died at Third Fleet with no dissemination process.

nimitz-2004.label: New York Times, 'Glowing Auras and Black Money: The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program'
nimitz-2004.why: The Nimitz footage was the visual centrepiece of the 2017 disclosure
nimitz-2004.note: The New York Times published the November 2004 footage alongside the AATIP revelation, converting a shelved incident into a national accountability story.

nimitz-2004.label: Knuth, Powell & Reali (2019), Entropy 21(10):939
nimitz-2004.why: Nimitz encounter analysed quantitatively in a peer-reviewed physics journal
nimitz-2004.note: A companion paper in the MaxEnt 2019 proceedings treated the Nimitz case specifically; this is the point at which the 2004 encounter entered the physics literature rather than the news cycle.

nimitz-2004.label: July 2019 Drone Swarms, USS Kidd / USS Russell and CSG ships off California
nimitz-2004.why: Same operating areas, fifteen years apart, same failure to attribute
nimitz-2004.note: Both events occurred in the instrumented Southern California naval training space, both were documented in Navy records, and neither produced an attribution.

nimitz-2004.label: FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 - secs. 1671-1673, NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefings and UAP classification-guide accounting
nimitz-2004.why: Congress set 1 January 2004 as the retroactive intercept floor
nimitz-2004.note: The first briefing under Sec. 1671 must cover intercepts 'during the period beginning on January 1, 2004' — the year of the Nimitz encounters.

nimitz-2004.label: Alex Dietrich
nimitz-2004.why: Flew wing on the 14 Nov 2004 intercept; observed the object for about five minutes
nimitz-2004.note: Dietrich and her WSO observed the object from roughly 8,000 feet above for about five minutes. She is named in the Navy range fouler report released 12 January 2023.

nimitz-2004.label: David Fravor
nimitz-2004.why: Intercepted the object as CO of VFA-41 on 14 Nov 2004
nimitz-2004.note: Fravor's sworn written statement to House Oversight places him as commanding officer of VFA-41 flying the intercept; the Navy's own range fouler report names him as aircrew.

nimitz-2004.label: House Oversight hearing, 26 July 2023 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'
nimitz-2004.why: Fravor testified to the 2004 encounter under oath in 2023
nimitz-2004.note: Fravor's written statement placed on the record that the incident was never investigated, no crew were questioned and no tapes were taken.

nimitz-2004.label: USS Jackson (LCS-6) Encounter, 15 February 2023
nimitz-2004.why: Same warning-area complex, same object morphology, nineteen years later
nimitz-2004.note: A transmedium tic-tac-shaped object in W-291 in February 2023 repeats the November 2004 description in the same Southern California naval training space, with no published government assessment of either sensor record.

nimitz-2004.label: USS Ronald Reagan Encounter and Logbook Tampering (2003-2004)
nimitz-2004.why: Same year, opposite ocean, same record-destruction behaviour
nimitz-2004.note: Reagan watchstanders describe deck log pages being torn out on a senior officer's order; Princeton crew describe recording media removed. Deck logs are federal records.

nimitz-2004.label: Kevin Day
nimitz-2004.why: Ran the Princeton air picture and vectored the intercept
nimitz-2004.note: As Senior Chief Operations Specialist Day was the air warfare coordinator holding the tracks. Fravor's sworn statement corroborates the substance of the radar picture Day describes.

nimitz-2004.label: Gary Voorhis
nimitz-2004.why: Voorhis describes removal or wiping of Princeton recording media
nimitz-2004.note: Voorhis, a CEC/Aegis technician, has said in public interviews since 2018 that he was directed to hand over or wipe recording media and that unrecognised personnel were aboard collecting. Reasoning: no primary record naming those personnel has been located.

nimitz-2004.label: Jason Turner
nimitz-2004.why: Turner independently corroborates the confiscation window
nimitz-2004.note: Turner is one of several Princeton crewmen in different divisions describing the same 48-hour window in the same terms. The convergence is evidentiary weight short of proof; no document confirms it.

d-coverup.label: Records & Archives
d-coverup.note: GAO found Roswell AAF outgoing messages for 1946-1949 destroyed with no disposition authority and no destruction certificate - concealment executed through the records system.

d-coverup.label: Aerospace Engineering & Advanced Projects
d-coverup.why: Black aircraft generated real cover stories
d-coverup.note: CIA's own historian states that U-2 and OXCART flights accounted for over half of late-1950s and 1960s reports and that false explanations were issued to protect them.

d-coverup.label: Official Denial
d-coverup.why: Denial is the public face of concealment
d-coverup.note: CIA's own historian records that false explanations were issued knowingly to protect classified overflights; the denial is the output of the concealment activity.

d-coverup.label: Intelligence Community
d-coverup.why: CIA convened the panel that recommended debunking
d-coverup.note: The Robertson Panel was convened by CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence, placing the recommendation inside the intelligence community rather than the Air Force.

d-coverup.label: Psychological Operations & Perception Management
d-coverup.why: Debunking recommended as a security measure
d-coverup.note: The Robertson Panel's January 1953 recommendation for a mass-media debunking programme is the documented point where concealment becomes an influence operation.

d-denial.label: The Cover-Up
d-denial.why: Denial is the public face of concealment
d-denial.note: CIA's own historian records that false explanations were issued knowingly to protect classified overflights; the denial is the output of the concealment activity.

d-denial.label: Roswell
d-denial.why: Four official explanations for one event
d-denial.note: Weather balloon in 1947, Project MOGUL in the mid-1990s, crash test dummies in 1997 - the sequence of explanations is itself the evidentiary object.

d-secrecy.label: Executive Policy & Directives
d-secrecy.note: DoDD 5205.07 is the directive-layer implementation of authority that derives from executive order rather than statute.

d-secrecy.label: Special Access Programs
d-secrecy.why: Statutory basis for the access tier
d-secrecy.note: 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDD 5205.07 are the legal and policy instruments that create the special access programme category; the SAP domain is the applied form of the secrecy-law domain.

d-secrecy-architecture.label: Congressional Oversight
d-secrecy-architecture.note: 10 U.S.C. 119's waiver provision reduces notification to eight members without staff, which is the specific point at which the secrecy architecture and congressional oversight collide.

d-secrecy-architecture.label: Special Access Programs
d-secrecy-architecture.note: The acknowledged/unacknowledged/waived tier structure defined in DoDD 5205.07 is the concrete mechanism by which the compartmentation architecture is built.

d-sap.label: Secrecy Law & Classification
d-sap.why: Statutory basis for the access tier
d-sap.note: 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDD 5205.07 are the legal and policy instruments that create the special access programme category; the SAP domain is the applied form of the secrecy-law domain.

d-sap.label: Secrecy Architecture
d-sap.note: The acknowledged/unacknowledged/waived tier structure defined in DoDD 5205.07 is the concrete mechanism by which the compartmentation architecture is built.

d-sap.label: Congressional Oversight
d-sap.why: Waived notification limits reporting to eight members
d-sap.note: The waiver authority in 10 U.S.C. 119(e) is the statutory provision congressional witnesses cite when describing why members cannot confirm a programme's existence.

d-sap.label: Program Structure & Management
d-sap.note: The November 2009 OUSD(I) memorandum reviewing a special access programme request for AATIP is the documented moment where a FOIA-visible programme was considered for conversion.

d-counterintel.label: Psychological Operations & Perception Management
d-counterintel.note: AFOSI is chartered for both counterintelligence and criminal investigation, and is the organisation named in the Bennewitz deception; the two domains share personnel.

d-counterintel.label: Witness Chain
d-counterintel.note: Administrative revocation of access is effectively unreviewable and can end a career without any finding; this is the inferred mechanism suppressing first-hand testimony.

d-oversight.label: Washington, D.C.
d-oversight.note: The July 2023 and September 2025 House Oversight UAP hearings, and the NARA records collection created by P.L. 118-31, are all seated in the District of Columbia.

d-oversight.label: Secrecy Architecture
d-oversight.note: 10 U.S.C. 119's waiver provision reduces notification to eight members without staff, which is the specific point at which the secrecy architecture and congressional oversight collide.

d-oversight.label: Disclosure Movement
d-oversight.note: Every enacted transparency provision came through committee process; the disclosure movement's instruments are procedural because the substantive question cannot be reached.

d-oversight.label: Records & Archives
d-oversight.why: Records law as the oversight instrument that worked
d-oversight.note: Subtitle C of P.L. 118-31 is the only binding UAP transparency outcome Congress has produced, and it operates through records custody rather than through programme access.

d-oversight.label: Special Access Programs
d-oversight.why: Waived notification limits reporting to eight members

d-oversight.note: The 26 July 2023 and 9 September 2025 House Oversight hearings converted witness accounts into sworn congressional record.

d-legal.note: DODIG-2023-109 exists because personnel used the Inspector General channel; the legal domain determines which disclosures are protected and which are prosecutable.

d-legal.label: Litigation
d-legal.why: Courtroom outcomes set the witness's risk calculus
d-legal.note: The dismissal in Cash v. United States and the withholding sustained in CAUS v. NSA together define the practical ceiling on judicial remedies in this field.

d-policy.label: Secrecy Law & Classification
d-policy.note: DoDD 5205.07 is the directive-layer implementation of authority that derives from executive order rather than statute.

d-disclosure.label: International & Allied Programs
d-disclosure.note: GEIPAN's published classification scheme and open case archive establish that an acknowledged state programme is possible, shifting the burden onto the concealment argument.

d-disclosure.label: Congressional Oversight
d-disclosure.note: Every enacted transparency provision came through committee process; the disclosure movement's instruments are procedural because the substantive question cannot be reached.

d-legacy.why: Retrieval is the programme's input stage
d-legacy.note: Grusch's sworn July 2023 account describes retrieval feeding a multi-decade exploitation effort; AARO's Volume I rejects the claim. Both are on the record.

d-legacy.label: Reverse Engineering
d-legacy.note: The legacy claim and the reverse-engineering claim are the same claim stated at different stages; AARO addresses and rejects both in Volume I.

d-recovery.label: Roswell
d-recovery.why: The founding case of the retrieval strand
d-recovery.note: Roswell is the origin of the crash-retrieval literature and the case against which every later retrieval claim is measured.

d-recovery.label: Chain of custody
d-recovery.note: The custody chain begins at the recovery site; every documented handoff is a scoring opportunity on the C axis.

d-recovery.label: Legacy Program
d-recovery.why: Retrieval is the programme's input stage
d-recovery.note: Grusch's sworn July 2023 account describes retrieval feeding a multi-decade exploitation effort; AARO's Volume I rejects the claim. Both are on the record.

d-reverse-engineering.label: Materials and custody analysis
d-reverse-engineering.note: Materials characterisation is the first step of any exploitation workflow and the only step whose outputs have been released - so far all conventional.

d-reverse-engineering.label: Legacy Program
d-reverse-engineering.note: The legacy claim and the reverse-engineering claim are the same claim stated at different stages; AARO addresses and rejects both in Volume I.

d-chem.label: Materials and custody analysis
d-chem.note: The Nolan-Vallee methodology paper specifies isotope ratio measurement as the discriminating test; the chemistry domain is where that test is run.

d-history.label: Records & Archives
d-history.why: The corpus is what survives the records fight
d-history.note: Almost every primary document in this field arrived through FOIA or archival release; historiography here is downstream of records law.

d-research.label: Astronomy & Astrophysics
d-research.note: The Galileo Project instrumentation papers and the VASCO archival work are the two productive observational programmes outside government.

d-bio.label: Medical & Injury Effects
d-bio.why: Biologics claim and documented injury record
d-bio.note: The bio claim has no released material; the medical domain has DIRD 26 and the Cash-Landrum clinical record, which is the auditable end of the same question.

d-bio.label: Biosensors and BioMEMS: A Survey of the Present Field
d-bio.why: subject domain: implantable biosensors and neuro-interface
d-bio.note: The contents cover brain-implanted BioMEMS micromachine neuroelectrodes, implantable sensors, microelectrode array fabrication, brain-machine interfaces, polymer BioMEMS electrodes, retinal devices and microscale therapeutic neurostimulation. This is the human-effects and human-interface leg of the AAWSAP survey, alongside Kit Green's field-effects paper and Richard Genik's three neuro deliverables.

d-bio.label: Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft
d-bio.why: subject domain: cognitive load limits on multi-vehicle control
d-bio.note: The commissioned question is how many unmanned vehicles a single human operator can control simultaneously - the human-factors constraint that would bound any swarming or multi-object control architecture. It forms a set with Genik's other two deliverables on limb-free control of external devices and on organic-molecule automation.

d-nuclear.label: Nuclear Weapons Complex Nexus
d-nuclear.why: Phenomenon and the security regime around it
d-nuclear.note: The sites where the correlation is strongest are governed by the Restricted Data regime rather than by DoD classification, which routes any resulting analysis outside the SAP framework.

d-witness.label: Legal Doctrine & Liability
d-witness.why: NDAs and IG channels bound what a witness may say
d-witness.note: DODIG-2023-109 exists because personnel used the Inspector General channel; the legal domain determines which disclosures are protected and which are prosecutable.

d-witness.label: Congressional Oversight

d-witness.note: The 26 July 2023 and 9 September 2025 House Oversight hearings converted witness accounts into sworn congressional record.

d-witness.label: Counterintelligence
d-witness.note: Administrative revocation of access is effectively unreviewable and can end a career without any finding; this is the inferred mechanism suppressing first-hand testimony.

d-aviators.label: San Diego, California
d-aviators.why: Homeport of the Nimitz strike group
d-aviators.note: The 2004 encounters occurred in the Southern California Operating Area worked by San Diego-based fleet units.

d-aviators.label: Propulsion & Field Physics
d-aviators.why: Reported kinematics set the physics requirement
d-aviators.note: Aviator accounts with sensor corroboration generate the acceleration and power figures that any propulsion hypothesis must satisfy.

d-aviators.label: Signals & Sensor Intelligence
d-aviators.why: Sensor corroboration is what makes the accounts arguable
d-aviators.note: Radar tracks and targeting-pod video convert a pilot's account into a multi-sensor event; DoD authenticated the imagery in April 2020 while declining to explain it.

d-ic.label: Intelligence Tradecraft & Analysis
d-ic.note: The federated IC structure determines which element collects and analyses, and the seams between elements are where an activity can be nobody's to report.

d-ic.label: The Cover-Up
d-ic.why: CIA convened the panel that recommended debunking
d-ic.note: The Robertson Panel was convened by CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence, placing the recommendation inside the intelligence community rather than the Air Force.

d-intel.label: Intelligence Community
d-intel.note: The federated IC structure determines which element collects and analyses, and the seams between elements are where an activity can be nobody's to report.

d-intel.label: Nuclear Weapons Complex Nexus
d-intel.why: Indications analysis on the atomic complex
d-intel.note: Hancock, Porritt and Grosvenor applied formal intelligence indications methodology to UAP reporting against the US atomic warfare complex.

d-funding.label: DIA Contract HHM402-08-C-0072 (AAWSAP / BAASS)
d-funding.why: the one instrument on the board where the appropriation-to-contract path is fully documented
d-funding.note: The AAWSAP prime contract, awarded 22 September 2008 to BAASS off solicitation HHM402-08-R-0211 through the DIA Virginia Contracting Activity, and released through DIA FOIA together with modification P00001. It is the concrete artefact that turns 'money moved through a classified channel' into a document with a number on it, which is what this domain exists to collect.

d-funding.label: Federal Contracting Mechanics
d-funding.note: The contract vehicle is the visible end of the money; the appropriation and transfer authorities are the invisible end.

d-funding.label: Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024 (Div. G of PL 118-31) - secs. 7341, 7343
d-funding.why: sec. 7343 conditions intelligence funding for UAP special- or restricted-access activity on prior disclosure to the committees
d-funding.note: Division G of P.L. 118-31 contains Sec. 7343, 'Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' The Joint Explanatory Statement records that it imposes a funding limitation for perceived insufficient transparency and a limitation on independent research and development indirect expenses, to be read consistently with DoDI 3204.01. This is a funding-channel provision, distinct from this act's membership of the enacted-statute domain.

d-funding.label: Military Intelligence Program (MIP)
d-funding.why: the second named channel, under SECDEF and USD(I&S) rather than the DNI
d-funding.note: The Military Intelligence Program is the defence-side counterpart to the NIP, managed by the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. DoD has disclosed a MIP appropriated topline annually since 2010 and request figures since 2012; the DoD Financial Management Regulation Vol. 2B Ch. 16 governs how intelligence programmes are budgeted and displayed. Topline-only disclosure is the same structural property as the NIP.

d-funding.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
d-funding.why: one of the two named channels through which US intelligence money is appropriated
d-funding.note: The National Intelligence Program is the DNI-controlled channel. Since FY2007, sec. 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act (P.L. 110-53) has required disclosure of the aggregate appropriated amount, and ODNI publishes request and appropriated toplines annually. Aggregate-only disclosure is precisely what makes it a channel this board can name but not itemise.

d-funding.label: FY2024 NDAA, Public Law 118-31 - Div. A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C (secs. 1841-1843), UAP Records Collection; Div. G (IAA FY2024) secs. 7341, 7343
d-funding.why: carries the first enacted funding limitation aimed at unreported UAP activity
d-funding.note: Beyond the Subtitle C records collection, P.L. 118-31 carries funding-side provisions that bar the obligation of funds for UAP activity protected under special or restricted access that has not been disclosed to the congressional committees, and bar charging UAP-related independent research and development as an allowable indirect contract expense. Congress legislating on the funding channel is the strongest available evidence that the channel is real.

d-funding.label: IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102 — contractor turn-in of 'non-earth origin or exotic' UAP material
d-funding.why: the Senate committee text that would have closed the channel at the contractor end
d-funding.note: As reported by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, the IAA FY2024 UAP provision would have required any person currently or formerly under federal contract holding UAP material or information derived from the Government to notify the AARO Director within 60 days and to make it available within 180 days, alongside the funding and IR&D limitations. Tier 2 rather than Tier 1 because the enacted counterpart differed substantially from the Senate-approved text, and because the section number carried on this node does not match the reported bill (see unresolved).

l-ft-meade.label: Signals & Sensor Intelligence
l-ft-meade.why: NSA holdings and the FOIA wall
l-ft-meade.note: The records at issue in CAUS v. NSA are held at Fort Meade, and AARO's current director came from the NSA research organisation based there.

l-langley-afb.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
l-langley-afb.note: The response to the Langley incursions ran through NORAD and USNORTHCOM; NORAD commander Gen. Gregory Guillot addressed the incursions in testimony to the Senate Armed Services Committee on 14 March 2024 and again publicly in October 2024.

l-langley-afb.label: Langley AFB Drone Incursions (December 2023)
l-langley-afb.note: Joint Base Langley-Eustis first observed unidentified uncrewed aerial systems over the installation on the evening of 6 December 2023, with multiple further incursions through the month. The episode is the location's whole reason for being on this board.

l-michigan-state.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
l-michigan-state.why: site of the DoD unsupported-adjustment study
l-michigan-state.note: Economist Mark Skidmore conducted the aggregation of unsupported journal voucher adjustments in DoD and HUD financial statements for 1998-2015 at Michigan State University. The aggregate figure is an accounting-adjustment total, not spending, and the distinction is why this is tier 2 rather than tier 1.

l-san-diego.label: Military Aviators & Operators
l-san-diego.why: Homeport of the Nimitz strike group
l-san-diego.note: The 2004 encounters occurred in the Southern California Operating Area worked by San Diego-based fleet units.

uapda-2023.label: FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 - secs. 1671-1673, NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefings and UAP classification-guide accounting
uapda-2023.why: Third consecutive Act enacted without the Senate's own passed text
uapda-2023.note: P.L. 119-60 contains no instance of 'eminent domain', 'non-human', 'legacy program' or 'reverse engineer'.

uapda-2023.label: Senate Armed Services Committee
uapda-2023.why: Never reported the Act; it existed only as a floor amendment
uapda-2023.note: No standalone UAP disclosure bill exists in the Senate in the 118th or 119th Congress, and no committee has ever marked the text up.

uapda-2023.label: Legislative Process (proposed and pending)
uapda-2023.why: passed one chamber, stripped in conference - the domain's instructive defeat
uapda-2023.note: The only text ever passed by a chamber of Congress legislating on the assumption that recovered non-human technology exists and is held in part by private entities. It rode to the Senate floor as an amendment, cleared the Senate as a division of S. 2226, and did not survive conference into P.L. 118-31 in that form. The mechanism of the defeat is the lesson, which is why it belongs to process rather than to statute.

uapda-2023.label: Eric Burlison
uapda-2023.why: Burlison could not get the UAP Disclosure Act onto the House NDAA in 2024 or 2025
uapda-2023.note: 'It was stripped out by the House last year, and I cannot get it onto the bill leaving the House this year.'

uapda-2023.label: Lockheed Martin Corporation
uapda-2023.why: The Senate voted to seize privately held recovered technology by eminent domain
uapda-2023.note: The Senate passed Division I of the NDAA on 27 July 2023 including Sec. 9010, and defined 'legacy program' to include 'commercial industry... and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin.' No named company is in the text; the provision only has meaning if some entity holds something.

uapda-2023.label: FY2023 NDAA Sec. 1673 (P.L. 117-263; 50 U.S.C. 3373b)
uapda-2023.why: Statutory NDA-voiding precedent behind the Act's whistleblower posture
uapda-2023.note: Sec. 1673(b)(1)(A) had already established that an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement'; the UAPDA extends that logic to records and material.

uapda-2023.label: FY2024 NDAA, Public Law 118-31 - Div. A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C (secs. 1841-1843), UAP Records Collection; Div. G (IAA FY2024) secs. 7341, 7343
uapda-2023.why: reduced to secs. 1841-1843 in conference
uapda-2023.note: Public Law 118-31 contains no eminent domain clause, no Review Board and no contractor inspection authority. Congress asserted jurisdiction over the paper and left the objects where they are.

uapda-2023.label: P.L. 118-31 Subtitle C — Secs. 1841-1843 (what survived)
uapda-2023.why: Fifteen sections reduced to three in conference
uapda-2023.note: Secs. 9001-9015 as passed by the Senate became Secs. 1841-1843 as enacted; the Review Board, Board personnel, record review, eminent domain, court-sealed materials and the $20,000,000 authorization have no enacted counterpart.

uapda-2023.label: New Paradigm Institute
uapda-2023.why: Running the campaign for Senate passage of the UAPDA
uapda-2023.note: NPI's front page as of August 2026 reads 'The House Acted. Now Tell the Senate to Pass the UAPDA', indicating House passage of a version and Senate inaction.

uapda-2023.label: S. 2226 (118th Congress) - Senate FY2024 NDAA vehicle for the UAP Disclosure Act
uapda-2023.why: incorporated as Division G, secs. 9001-9015
uapda-2023.note: S. 2226 as engrossed in the Senate contains Division G in full.

uapda-2023.label: S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 (Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act amendment)
uapda-2023.why: The amendment became Division G of the engrossed bill
uapda-2023.note: The text filed as S.Amdt. 797 travelled into S. 2226 as Division G, Secs. 9001-9015, which the Senate passed on 27 July 2023.

uapda-2023.label: Charles E. Schumer
uapda-2023.why: sponsor of S.Amdt. 797
uapda-2023.note: congress.gov lists Sen. Schumer as sponsor of S.Amdt.797, submitted 07/13/2023; the Congressional Record entry names him as the submitting senator.

uapda-2023.label: Kirsten E. Gillibrand
uapda-2023.why: cosponsor
uapda-2023.note: Named in the Congressional Record entry for SA 797.

uapda-2023.label: Marco Rubio
uapda-2023.why: cosponsor
uapda-2023.note: Named in the Congressional Record entry for SA 797.

uapda-2023.label: Martin T. Heinrich
uapda-2023.why: cosponsor
uapda-2023.note: Named in the Congressional Record entry for SA 797.

uapda-2023.label: Mike Rounds
uapda-2023.why: lead cosponsor
uapda-2023.note: First-listed cosponsor in the Congressional Record entry for SA 797.

uapda-2023.label: Todd Young
uapda-2023.why: cosponsor
uapda-2023.note: Named in the Congressional Record entry for SA 797.

uapda-2023.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board
uapda-2023.why: Secs. 9007-9009 create the Board as an independent agency
uapda-2023.note: The Act's enforcement rests entirely on the Review Board: it orders disclosure absent clear and convincing evidence and examines recovered material under Sec. 9010(b).

uapda-2023.label: Section 9010(a) — Exercise of Eminent Domain
uapda-2023.why: section of
uapda-2023.note: Section 9010(a) of Division G is the eminent domain command; it is the only provision in the Act that reaches physical material rather than records.

uapda-2023.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2024 (S.Amdt. 2610 to S. 4638)
uapda-2023.why: Verbatim refiling of the 2023 text
uapda-2023.note: The 2024 amendment reproduces the findings, definitions, Review Board, Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan and eminent domain command without softening.

uapda-2023.label: Mike D. Rogers
uapda-2023.why: Named as co-leading the effort to eliminate or alter the Act
uapda-2023.note: Rogers chaired House Armed Services through the conference and is named alongside Turner in contemporaneous reporting; no direct quotation ties him to a specific section.

uapda-2023.label: Mitch McConnell
uapda-2023.why: Named as supporting the effort against the Act
uapda-2023.note: McConnell is named with Speaker Johnson as backing the Turner and Rogers effort, while three Senate Republicans were cosponsors of the same text.

uapda-2023.label: The Hill
uapda-2023.why: Reported the fight over the UAP amendment in the FY2024 defence bill
uapda-2023.note: The Hill covered House members demanding transparency from leadership over whether the UAP Disclosure Act amendment would be retained in the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act. The article page could not be retrieved directly (the site blocked automated fetch), so this edge rests on the indexed headline and URL rather than a verified full text; date left null for that reason.

uapda-2023.label: Burlison UAP Records Disclosure Amendment, FY2027 NDAA
uapda-2023.why: Revives the review board and eminent-domain-era disclosure architecture stripped in 2023
uapda-2023.note: The FY2027 amendment restores the Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority and a statutory transfer timeline to NARA.

uapda-2023.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
uapda-2023.why: The 'outside of government so the technology could remain proprietary' formulation is what the eminent domain provision was written to defeat
uapda-2023.note: Section 9010 asserts federal eminent domain over recovered technologies 'controlled by private persons or entities.' Reasoning: the legislative remedy matches the mechanism AARO records interviewees describing; no drafting record ties the two documents.

uapda-2023.label: David Charles Grusch
uapda-2023.why: The Act's definitions are drafted around his allegations
uapda-2023.note: Grusch's allegations were published 5 June 2023; S.Amdt. 797 was filed 38 days later containing bespoke definitions of 'legacy program' and 'controlling authority' reaching private and academic holders.

s2226-118.label: S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 (Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act amendment)
s2226-118.note: congress.gov: 'Amends Bill: S.2226 - National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024'.

s2226-118.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
s2226-118.note: S. 2226 as engrossed in the Senate contains Division G in full.

samdt-797.label: Charles E. Schumer
samdt-797.note: Congress.gov lists Schumer as the sole sponsor of S.Amdt. 797, submitted 13 July 2023, with the text printed at 169 Cong. Rec. S2953.

samdt-797.label: Legislative Process (proposed and pending)
samdt-797.why: the filing instrument - where the process starts and where its text is fixed
samdt-797.note: Submitted 13 July 2023 by Senator Schumer for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, ordered to lie on the table, text printed in the Congressional Record at pages S2953-S2959. The amendment, not the bill, is the object that carries the disclosure text, which is the process fact this domain exists to record.

samdt-797.label: Kirsten E. Gillibrand
samdt-797.note: Gillibrand cosponsored Schumer's amendment while her own Sec. 1683 architecture was the statutory baseline it cross-referenced.

samdt-797.label: Marco Rubio
samdt-797.why: Original cosponsor while serving as SSCI Vice Chairman
samdt-797.note: Rubio cosponsored the eminent domain text while holding one of the eight most senior intelligence-access positions in Congress.

samdt-797.label: Martin T. Heinrich
samdt-797.note: Heinrich cosponsored while sitting on SSCI and representing the state containing Kirtland, Sandia, Los Alamos and Roswell.

samdt-797.label: Mike Rounds
samdt-797.note: Rounds is listed as an original cosponsor with sponsorship date 13 July 2023.

samdt-797.label: S. 2226 (118th Congress) - Senate FY2024 NDAA vehicle for the UAP Disclosure Act
samdt-797.note: congress.gov: 'Amends Bill: S.2226 - National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024'.

samdt-797.label: Todd Young
samdt-797.note: Young's signature gave the amendment a three-to-three partisan balance that let it travel in the bipartisan package.

samdt-797.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
samdt-797.why: The amendment became Division G of the engrossed bill
samdt-797.note: The text filed as S.Amdt. 797 travelled into S. 2226 as Division G, Secs. 9001-9015, which the Senate passed on 27 July 2023.

ndaa-fy2022.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
ndaa-fy2022.why: statutory basis for standing up AARO
ndaa-fy2022.note: The Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum of 15 July 2022 approved amendments to the AOIMSG direction 'to meet the DoD requirements in section 1683 of the NDAA for FY 2022,' establishing the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office to carry out the duties assigned to AOIMSG.

ndaa-fy2022.label: FY2022 NDAA Sec. 1683 (P.L. 117-81; 50 U.S.C. 3373)
ndaa-fy2022.why: Sec. 1683 is the UAP-office provision of P.L. 117-81
ndaa-fy2022.note: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (Public Law 117-81, 27 December 2021) is titled 'Establishment of office, organizational structure, and authorities to address unidentified aerial phenomena.'

ndaa-fy2022.label: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
ndaa-fy2022.why: office required to be established in coordination with the DNI
ndaa-fy2022.note: The FY2022 NDAA 'was enacted with a provision that requires the Secretary of Defense to establish an office, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence (DNI)'; the Deputy Secretary acted 'following coordination with the DNI' and copied the DNI on the AARO establishment memo.

ndaa-fy2022.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (UAPTF)
ndaa-fy2022.note: 'Consistent with section 1683 of the NDAA for FY 2022, I also direct the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (UAPTF) no later than the date the AARO is established, and to support the orderly transition of the UAPTF, including the transfer of any data, analysis, or other relevant material, to the AARO.'

iaa-2022.label: FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 - secs. 1671-1673, NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefings and UAP classification-guide accounting
iaa-2022.note: PL 119-60 sec. 1672(a): 'Section 413 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (division X of Public Law 117-103; 50 U.S.C. 3373a) is repealed.'

ndaa-fy2023.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
ndaa-fy2023.why: codified AARO in statute with a public reporting mandate
ndaa-fy2023.note: The James M. Inhofe NDAA for FY2023, signed 23 December 2022, gave AARO statutory authority and the annual reporting requirement now at 50 U.S.C. 3373(k).

ndaa-fy2023.label: FY2022 NDAA Sec. 1683 (P.L. 117-81; 50 U.S.C. 3373)
ndaa-fy2023.note: IAA FY2023 sec. 6802(a) rewrites sec. 1683 in full.

ndaa-fy2023.label: David Charles Grusch
ndaa-fy2023.why: Helped draft the UAP whistleblower protection language
ndaa-fy2023.note: The Debrief reports Grusch helped draft the UAP language in the FY2023 NDAA, signed December 2022, which permits authorized UAP disclosures without retaliation regardless of prior nondisclosure agreements - written by the person who would then need it.

ndaa-fy2024.label: Section 9010(a) — Exercise of Eminent Domain
ndaa-fy2024.why: No enacted statute contains the eminent domain language
ndaa-fy2024.note: P.L. 118-31, P.L. 118-159 and P.L. 119-60 contain zero instances of 'eminent domain' in any UAP provision.

ndaa-fy2024.label: P.L. 118-31 Sec. 1687 — limitation on funds for unreported programs
ndaa-fy2024.why: Sec. 1687 is the enacted funding bar on undisclosed UAP SAPs
ndaa-fy2024.note: The only enacted provision that conditions money on disclosure of special access UAP activity, including the independent research and development indirect-cost bar.

ndaa-fy2024.label: Funding Channels
ndaa-fy2024.why: carries the first enacted funding limitation aimed at unreported UAP activity
ndaa-fy2024.note: Beyond the Subtitle C records collection, P.L. 118-31 carries funding-side provisions that bar the obligation of funds for UAP activity protected under special or restricted access that has not been disclosed to the congressional committees, and bar charging UAP-related independent research and development as an allowable indirect contract expense. Congress legislating on the funding channel is the strongest available evidence that the channel is real.

ndaa-fy2024.label: Enacted Statute
ndaa-fy2024.why: P.L. 118-31 Subtitle C, secs. 1841-1843 - the UAP Records Collection as enacted
ndaa-fy2024.note: What survived conference from the Senate-passed disclosure title was a records collection at NARA, a duty to transmit and a postponement regime, without the Review Board or the eminent domain provision. NARA's published guidance to federal agencies implementing the collection is the observable proof that this part is law and operating.

ndaa-fy2024.label: Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024 (Div. G of PL 118-31) - secs. 7341, 7343
ndaa-fy2024.why: enacted as Division G of the FY2024 NDAA
ndaa-fy2024.note: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence publishes the enacted text as 'Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Division G of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024' (P.L. 118-31, 22 December 2023).

ndaa-fy2024.label: John F. Reed
ndaa-fy2024.why: Sponsor of S. 2226 and Senate conference principal
ndaa-fy2024.note: Reed introduced the vehicle on 11 July 2023 and signed the conference product that removed his own chamber's passed division.

ndaa-fy2024.label: Leidos Holdings, Inc.
ndaa-fy2024.why: The records collection reaches government-funded contractor-held records
ndaa-fy2024.note: Sec. 1841 defines the collection as record copies of all 'Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records' relating to UAP, technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence - a formulation that reaches services primes holding classified records under contract. No accounting of contractor holdings has been made.

ndaa-fy2024.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (Record Group 615)
ndaa-fy2024.why: Collection created by sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA
ndaa-fy2024.note: The surviving remnant of the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act. The 24 April 2025 release drew records from ODNI, OSD, the FAA and the NRC, with rolling additions - the statutory machinery any executive declassification directive must eventually run through.

ndaa-fy2024.label: National Archives UAP Records Collection (Record Group 615)
ndaa-fy2024.note: Sections 1841-1843 of P.L. 118-31 mandate the UAP Records Collection; NARA created RG 615 and issued transfer guidance to agencies.

ndaa-fy2024.label: FY2022 NDAA Sec. 1683 (P.L. 117-81; 50 U.S.C. 3373)
ndaa-fy2024.why: Sec. 1841 defines UAP by cross-reference to 50 U.S.C. 3373
ndaa-fy2024.note: The enacted collection statute borrows its definition from Gillibrand's section, but miscites it as 'section 1673(n)(8) of the NDAA for Fiscal Year 2022 (Public Law 117-81)' — conflating two different Acts.

ndaa-fy2024.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
ndaa-fy2024.note: Public Law 118-31 contains no eminent domain clause, no Review Board and no contractor inspection authority. Congress asserted jurisdiction over the paper and left the objects where they are.

ndaa-fy2024.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act (Burlison amendment to the FY2027 NDAA)
ndaa-fy2024.why: Restores the enforcement architecture stripped from the FY2024 sections
ndaa-fy2024.note: Sections 1841-1843 created a records collection without a review board, subpoena power or contractor reach; the 2026 amendment reintroduces all three.

ndaa-fy2025.label: Enacted Statute
ndaa-fy2025.why: P.L. 118-159 Div. G, secs. 6801-6802 - GAO review of AARO and the sunset of the audit cadence
ndaa-fy2025.note: Approved 23 December 2024. Sec. 6801 directs a GAO review of AARO's implementation of 50 U.S.C. 3373; sec. 6802 sunsets the GAO audit requirements attached to the Historical Record Report. Wiring it here fixes a degree-1 orphan and records the first enacted step in winding oversight machinery back down rather than up.

ndaa-fy2025.label: Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 (Div. F of PL 117-263) - secs. 6802-6803
ndaa-fy2025.why: sunsets the sec. 6803 GAO audit cadence
ndaa-fy2025.note: PL 118-159 sec. 6802 amends IAA FY2023 sec. 6803.

ndaa-fy2026.label: Senate Armed Services Committee
ndaa-fy2026.why: Disposed of with seventeen amendments and no open process
ndaa-fy2026.note: The only Senate floor amendment proposed to S. 1071 was SA 3961 by Senator Thune 'to improve the bill'; there was no amendment process in which the UAPDA could have been offered.

ndaa-fy2026.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
ndaa-fy2026.why: Third consecutive Act enacted without the Senate's own passed text
ndaa-fy2026.note: P.L. 119-60 contains no instance of 'eminent domain', 'non-human', 'legacy program' or 'reverse engineer'.

ndaa-fy2026.label: P.L. 118-31 Sec. 1687 — limitation on funds for unreported programs
ndaa-fy2026.why: Not renewed; the funding bar has lapsed since FY2024
ndaa-fy2026.note: Sec. 1687 restricts only funds authorised by the FY2024 Act; neither P.L. 118-159 nor P.L. 119-60 contains the phrase 'special access or restricted access'.

ndaa-fy2026.label: Roger F. Wicker
ndaa-fy2026.why: Chaired SASC for the FY2026 authorization
ndaa-fy2026.note: P.L. 119-60 originated as S. 1071 and was enacted 18 December 2025 with a three-section housekeeping subtitle and no disclosure regime.

ndaa-fy2026.label: Enacted Statute
ndaa-fy2026.why: P.L. 119-60, Title XVI Subtitle E - the enacted corpus reduced to housekeeping
ndaa-fy2026.note: Approved 18 December 2025, with three UAP sections requiring that AARO briefings cover NORAD and NORTHCOM intercepts and accounting for UAP classification guides. Recording it in the enacted domain alongside the 2021-2023 provisions is what lets a reader see the trajectory of what Congress has actually been willing to enact.

ndaa-fy2026.label: Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2022, Sec. 413 (Div. X of PL 117-103; 50 U.S.C. 3373a)
ndaa-fy2026.note: PL 119-60 sec. 1672(a): 'Section 413 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (division X of Public Law 117-103; 50 U.S.C. 3373a) is repealed.'

ndaa-fy2026.label: FY2022 NDAA Sec. 1683 (P.L. 117-81; 50 U.S.C. 3373)
ndaa-fy2026.why: FY2026 amends Sec. 1683(l) to add intercept briefings
ndaa-fy2026.note: Sec. 1671 of P.L. 119-60 adds a new paragraph (5) requiring NORAD and NORTHCOM intercept detail in AARO briefings, reaching back to 1 January 2004.

ndaa-fy2026.label: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
ndaa-fy2026.why: Congress set 1 January 2004 as the retroactive intercept floor
ndaa-fy2026.note: The first briefing under Sec. 1671 must cover intercepts 'during the period beginning on January 1, 2004' — the year of the Nimitz encounters.

ndaa-fy2026.label: Kirsten E. Gillibrand
ndaa-fy2026.why: Claims only the briefing-requirement update as her FY2026 UAP win
ndaa-fy2026.note: Gillibrand's FY2026 announcement lists 'language to update congressional briefing requirements for UAP', matching Sec. 1671 rather than any disclosure mandate.

iaa-2023.label: Enacted Statute
iaa-2023.why: Division F of P.L. 117-263 - the intelligence-side half of the same enactment
iaa-2023.note: Sec. 6802 rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373 to create AARO and inserted the 'unidentified anomalous phenomena' and 'transmedium' definitions; sec. 6803 attached a Comptroller General audit and briefing requirement to the Historical Record Report. Wiring it here fixes a degree-1 orphan and records that the statutory definitions the whole board uses were enacted in an intelligence authorization, not a defence one.

iaa-2023.label: FY2025 NDAA, Public Law 118-159 - Div. G (IAA FY2025) secs. 6801-6802, GAO review of AARO
iaa-2023.why: sunsets the sec. 6803 GAO audit cadence
iaa-2023.note: PL 118-159 sec. 6802 amends IAA FY2023 sec. 6803.

iaa-2024.label: Funding Channels
iaa-2024.why: sec. 7343 conditions intelligence funding for UAP special- or restricted-access activity on prior disclosure to the committees
iaa-2024.note: Division G of P.L. 118-31 contains Sec. 7343, 'Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' The Joint Explanatory Statement records that it imposes a funding limitation for perceived insufficient transparency and a limitation on independent research and development indirect expenses, to be read consistently with DoDI 3204.01. This is a funding-channel provision, distinct from this act's membership of the enacted-statute domain.

iaa-2024.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
iaa-2024.why: AARO reporting change and UAP funding limitation
iaa-2024.note: Division G contains Sec. 7341, 'Modification of reporting requirement for All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office,' and Sec. 7343, 'Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena' - the provision barring funds for UAP activity not disclosed to the AARO Director and congressional leadership.

iaa-2024.label: Enacted Statute
iaa-2024.why: Division G of P.L. 118-31 - enacted intelligence-side UAP provisions
iaa-2024.note: Division G carries Sec. 7341, modifying the AARO reporting requirement, and Sec. 7343, the funding limitation. The section list published by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence confirms both as part of the enacted division. Its separate membership of the funding domain rests on 7343's substance, not on its status as law.

iaa-2024.label: FY2024 NDAA, Public Law 118-31 - Div. A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C (secs. 1841-1843), UAP Records Collection; Div. G (IAA FY2024) secs. 7341, 7343
iaa-2024.why: enacted as Division G of the FY2024 NDAA
iaa-2024.note: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence publishes the enacted text as 'Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Division G of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024' (P.L. 118-31, 22 December 2023).

iaa-2024.label: IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102 — contractor turn-in of 'non-earth origin or exotic' UAP material
iaa-2024.why: section node of this act (section number needs verification)
iaa-2024.note: The board's section node is filed under this act. Caution: the contractor turn-in language (persons holding UAP material or 'non-earth origin or exotic' material to notify AARO and make it available within 180 days) is Sec. 1104 of S.2103 as reported by SSCI on 22 June 2023; the enacted Division G UAP sections are numbered 7341 and 7343. The '1102' designation in the node id is not confirmed against either text.

hearing-2023-07-26.label: Susan Gough
hearing-2023-07-26.why: Post-hearing statement rebutting the harm claims

hearing-2023-07-26.label: David Fravor
hearing-2023-07-26.why: Testified as former commanding officer, VFA-41

hearing-2025-09-09.label: Joe Spielberger

hearing-2025-09-09.label: Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets

hearing-2025-09-09.label: Project On Government Oversight
hearing-2025-09-09.why: POGO counsel testified at the UAP transparency hearing
hearing-2025-09-09.note: Joe Spielberger, senior policy counsel at the Project On Government Oversight, was a witness at the 9 September 2025 hearing 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection.' His written testimony argued that national security whistleblowers -- the category David Grusch and the military witnesses fall into -- lack an independent enforcement mechanism and are uniquely exposed to clearance-based retaliation.

hearing-2025-09-09.label: Anna Paulina Luna
hearing-2025-09-09.why: Chaired the Task Force hearing that seated operator witnesses
hearing-2025-09-09.note: The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets built the hearing around serving and former operators rather than programme officials.

hearing-2025-09-09.why: Held the UAP transparency and whistleblower protection hearing
hearing-2025-09-09.note: The hearing where the Crane reprisal letter entered the record and where Knapp and Mace put ongoing retaliation against Grusch into the official transcript.

hearing-2025-09-09.label: Alexandro Wiggins

hearing-2025-09-09.why: First active-duty Navy senior enlisted UAP witness before Congress
