missing-scientists-probe-2026.label: James Comer Jr.
missing-scientists-probe-2026.note: Comer and Burlison opened the investigation on 21 April 2026.

missing-scientists-probe-2026.label: William Neil McCasland
missing-scientists-probe-2026.why: His February 2026 disappearance is the trigger for the probe
missing-scientists-probe-2026.note: One of eleven people in nuclear or rocket technology who have died or vanished since 2022, per the committee.

uap-disclosure-forum-2026.label: Eric Burlison
uap-disclosure-forum-2026.why: Announced the Lincoln Laboratory production at the forum
uap-disclosure-forum-2026.note: Jordan Flowers credited Burlison with shaking the artifact loose: 'He's stopped asking politely.'

capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.label: Anna Paulina Luna
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.why: Asked the White House to grant immunity to whistleblowers who disclose locations of craft and technology
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.note: The immunity ask is the caucus's response to the failure of the whistleblower bills to move.

capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.label: Eric Burlison
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.why: Called on the President to waive all NDAs for UAP whistleblowers; described a dead drop to his office
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.note: 'For decades, the American people have been treated like children.'

capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.label: Timothy Floyd Burchett
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.why: Said an Area 51 tour would yield a T-shirt because the government would move everything else
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.note: A restatement of his 2023 line to Grusch about moving vans.

capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.label: David Charles Grusch
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.why: Returned to Capitol Hill and said political appointees have not complied with the disclosure law
capitol-disclosure-event-2026-06-09.note: His first Capitol appearance with lawmakers since the 2023 testimony.

l-eglin.label: Anna Paulina Luna
l-eglin.why: Accompanied Gaetz to Eglin; described 'the infamous Eglin Air Force Base incident' in 2025
l-eglin.note: Luna's 2025 opening statement attributes the lead to multiple active-duty Air Force pilot whistleblowers alleging an Air Force cover-up at Eglin.

l-eglin.label: House Oversight hearing, 26 July 2023 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'
l-eglin.why: The Eglin radar sequence and imagery were requested from the dais, 'subpoenaed if necessary'
l-eglin.note: No production of the Eglin material to the committee has been recorded as of August 2026.

l-eglin.label: Matthew Louis Gaetz II
l-eglin.why: Received a protected disclosure from Eglin and went to the base with Burchett and Luna
l-eglin.note: Initially refused images, radar and full crew access; obtained a photograph and one crew member after a discussion 'about how authorities flow in the United States of America.'

l-eglin.label: Timothy Floyd Burchett
l-eglin.why: Accompanied Gaetz to Eglin on the protected disclosure
l-eglin.note: Named by Gaetz on the record and again by Luna in 2025.

uap-records-review-board.label: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
uap-records-review-board.why: The Board was designed to bypass the intelligence committees
uap-records-review-board.note: Sec. 9007(b)(3)(A) routes nominations through congressional leadership, DoD, the National Academy of Sciences, nonprofit UAP research bodies and the American Historical Association — never through HPSCI or SSCI.

uap-records-review-board.label: P.L. 118-31 Subtitle C — Secs. 1841-1843 (what survived)
uap-records-review-board.why: Postponement authority returned to the original classifier
uap-records-review-board.note: Sec. 1843(a) vests the clear-and-convincing determination in 'the original classification authority' — the very offices the Review Board was created to review.

uap-records-review-board.label: Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan
uap-records-review-board.why: The Board must produce the Plan under Sec. 9009(c)(3)
uap-records-review-board.note: The Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan exists only as a Review Board product; removing the Board removed the Plan.

uap-records-review-board.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
uap-records-review-board.why: Secs. 9007-9009 create the Board as an independent agency
uap-records-review-board.note: The Act's enforcement rests entirely on the Review Board: it orders disclosure absent clear and convincing evidence and examines recovered material under Sec. 9010(b).

uap-records-review-board.label: Michael R. Turner
uap-records-review-board.why: Named as demanding removal of the Board's subpoena power
uap-records-review-board.note: The Board survives in no form in enacted law; Sheehan attributes the demand to Turner, and the conference produced no document naming who struck what.

controlled-disclosure-campaign-plan.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
controlled-disclosure-campaign-plan.why: AARO was to inherit the Plan's declassification logic
controlled-disclosure-campaign-plan.note: Sec. 9009(b)(6) required the Board to brief AARO on the Plan before terminating, and Sec. 9013(b)(2) required AARO to carry its requirements into standing guidance.

controlled-disclosure-campaign-plan.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board
controlled-disclosure-campaign-plan.why: The Board must produce the Plan under Sec. 9009(c)(3)
controlled-disclosure-campaign-plan.note: The Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan exists only as a Review Board product; removing the Board removed the Plan.

uap-records-collection-rg615.label: National Archives and Records Administration
uap-records-collection-rg615.why: NARA is custodian without power to compel transmission
uap-records-collection-rg615.note: The Archivist must preserve, index and publish, but Secs. 1842 and 1843 put identification, transmission and postponement in the hands of the agencies and their original classification authorities.

uap-records-collection-rg615.label: P.L. 118-31 Subtitle C — Secs. 1841-1843 (what survived)
uap-records-collection-rg615.why: Secs. 1841-1843 created RG 615 at the National Archives
uap-records-collection-rg615.note: The collection is the only concrete institution produced by the entire UAPDA fight.

uap-records-collection-rg615.label: Department of War release of UAP files
uap-records-collection-rg615.why: Agency compliance ran nineteen months past the statutory deadline
uap-records-collection-rg615.note: The Sec. 1842(c)(1) agency review deadline fell on 17 October 2024; NARA's transfer guidance is dated April 2025 and the author of the statute described the May 2026 release as the administration only beginning to meet its legal obligation.

uapda-2024-samdt-2610.label: IAA FY2025 Title LXVIII — Secs. 6801-6802 (P.L. 118-159)
uapda-2024-samdt-2610.why: Never called up; FY2025 enacted with no disclosure regime
uapda-2024-samdt-2610.note: The amendment was 'ordered to lie on the table' and received no vote; P.L. 118-159's only UAP content is a GAO review and a sunset on audit briefings.

uapda-2024-samdt-2610.label: Mike Rounds
uapda-2024-samdt-2610.note: S.Amdt. 2610 was submitted 11 July 2024 by 'Mr. ROUNDS (for himself and Mr. Schumer)' with the full text and the eminent domain clause intact.

uapda-2024-samdt-2610.label: Marco Rubio
uapda-2024-samdt-2610.why: Absent from the 2024 refiling; left the Senate January 2025
uapda-2024-samdt-2610.note: The 2024 amendment carries only Rounds and Schumer; Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich are not on it, and Rubio left the Senate the following January.

uapda-2024-samdt-2610.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
uapda-2024-samdt-2610.note: The 2024 amendment reproduces the findings, definitions, Review Board, Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan and eminent domain command without softening.

ndaa-fy2027-s4784.label: Roger F. Wicker
ndaa-fy2027-s4784.why: Reported an FY2027 NDAA containing no UAP provisions
ndaa-fy2027-s4784.note: S. 4784 as reported returns zero occurrences of 'unidentified', 'UAP' or a citation to 50 U.S.C. 3373.

ndaa-fy2027-s4784.label: 2026 Disclosure Symposium
ndaa-fy2027-s4784.why: Target vehicle contains no UAP provisions to amend
ndaa-fy2027-s4784.note: Rounds's stated plan is to attach the Act to the FY2027 NDAA; the reported bill has no UAP subtitle and his own markup announcement lists no UAP win.

ndaa-fy2027-s4784.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act - Burlison amendment to the FY2027 NDAA
ndaa-fy2027-s4784.why: House-adopted amendment against a Senate base text with no UAP provisions
ndaa-fy2027-s4784.note: The House framework must survive conference against a Senate reported bill (S. 4784, S. Rept. 119-127) containing zero UAP provisions - the second consecutive cycle in which the subject is absent from the Senate base text. The 2023 precedent is that the eminent-domain and review-board provisions were stripped in conference.

disclosure-symposium-2026.label: FY2027 NDAA as reported (S. 4784, S. Rept. 119-127)
disclosure-symposium-2026.why: Target vehicle contains no UAP provisions to amend
disclosure-symposium-2026.note: Rounds's stated plan is to attach the Act to the FY2027 NDAA; the reported bill has no UAP subtitle and his own markup announcement lists no UAP win.

disclosure-symposium-2026.label: Mike Rounds
disclosure-symposium-2026.why: Announces a fourth filing at an outside conference
disclosure-symposium-2026.note: Nine days after SASC reported a bill with no UAP content, Rounds announced the next UAPDA attempt at the 2026 Disclosure Symposium rather than in committee.

senate-armed-services.label: FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 - secs. 1671-1673, NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefings and UAP classification-guide accounting
senate-armed-services.why: Disposed of with seventeen amendments and no open process
senate-armed-services.note: The only Senate floor amendment proposed to S. 1071 was SA 3961 by Senator Thune 'to improve the bill'; there was no amendment process in which the UAPDA could have been offered.

senate-armed-services.label: Legislative Process (proposed and pending)
senate-armed-services.why: owns the only vehicle the disclosure text has ever ridden, and has never reported it
senate-armed-services.note: Every version of the Act - 2023, 2024 and the announced later attempts - has reached the floor as an amendment to a SASC bill rather than as a committee product, which means no committee report, no markup record and no members professionally invested in defending it in conference. A committee's non-action is a process fact and belongs in this domain.

senate-armed-services.label: John F. Reed
senate-armed-services.note: Reed chaired SASC through the only cycle in which a UAP disclosure regime reached an engrossed Senate bill.

senate-armed-services.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
senate-armed-services.why: Never reported the Act; it existed only as a floor amendment
senate-armed-services.note: No standalone UAP disclosure bill exists in the Senate in the 118th or 119th Congress, and no committee has ever marked the text up.

senate-armed-services.label: United States Senate
senate-armed-services.why: Committee of jurisdiction for DoD special access program reporting
senate-armed-services.note: SASC is one of the four defense committees to which 10 U.S.C. 119 reporting runs, and one of the two whose chairman and ranking member receive waived-SAP notification.

senate-armed-services.label: Waived SAP Notification Group
senate-armed-services.why: one of the six defense committees named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1)
senate-armed-services.note: Contributes two of the twelve seats: the chairman and the ranking minority member. Ordinary committee membership confers no entitlement.

senate-armed-services.label: Congressional oversight of special access programs
senate-armed-services.note: Same statutory provision; four committees, eight members.

senate-armed-services.label: Harry M. Reid
senate-armed-services.why: Set the leadership-discretion precedent the domain still runs on
senate-armed-services.note: The legacy effort was funded by leadership discretion outside the ordinary committee record, and every attempt to reach it since has likewise been a leadership floor amendment rather than a committee product.

senate-intelligence.label: IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102 — contractor turn-in of 'non-earth origin or exotic' UAP material
senate-intelligence.why: SSCI produced the contractor turn-in language
senate-intelligence.note: Sec. 1102 rode in the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024, Division M of the engrossed Senate bill.

senate-intelligence.label: Marco Rubio
senate-intelligence.note: Rubio's Gang of Eight access is what makes his cosponsorship of the eminent domain text evidentially significant.

senate-intelligence.label: Mark R. Warner
senate-intelligence.note: Warner chaired SSCI when it produced the contractor turn-in and the Historical Record Report requirement.

senate-intelligence.label: United States Senate
senate-intelligence.why: Committee of jurisdiction for intelligence community programs
senate-intelligence.note: SSCI's report language accompanying the FY2021 Intelligence Authorization Act produced the June 2021 ODNI Preliminary Assessment.

house-intelligence.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board
house-intelligence.why: The Board was designed to bypass the intelligence committees
house-intelligence.note: Sec. 9007(b)(3)(A) routes nominations through congressional leadership, DoD, the National Academy of Sciences, nonprofit UAP research bodies and the American Historical Association — never through HPSCI or SSCI.

house-intelligence.label: Michael R. Turner
house-intelligence.note: Turner chaired HPSCI from January 2023 to January 2025, spanning the conference in which the disclosure division was reduced.

house-intelligence.label: United States House of Representatives
house-intelligence.why: Committee of jurisdiction for IC controlled access programs
house-intelligence.note: Programs carried in the IC SAP control enterprise are reported, if at all, to the intelligence committees rather than to the defense committees.

house-armed-services.label: Mike D. Rogers
house-armed-services.note: Rogers has chaired House Armed Services since January 2023 and was a conference principal on the NDAA.

house-armed-services.label: P.L. 118-31 Sec. 1687 — limitation on funds for unreported programs
house-armed-services.why: Retained remedy routes back to the committees
house-armed-services.note: Sec. 1687 does not open anything to the public; it compels description to the defence and intelligence committees and congressional leadership.

house-armed-services.label: United States House of Representatives
house-armed-services.why: One half of the read-in gate described by Chairwoman Luna
house-armed-services.note: HASC leadership approval is required, together with HAC-D leadership, for a non-committee member to view specific program material.

house-armed-services.label: Congressional oversight of special access programs
house-armed-services.note: Under 10 U.S.C. 119(e) the chairman and ranking minority member of each defense committee receive the waived program information and the waiver justification.

national-archives.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (NARA Record Group 615)
national-archives.why: NARA is custodian without power to compel transmission
national-archives.note: The Archivist must preserve, index and publish, but Secs. 1842 and 1843 put identification, transmission and postponement in the hands of the agencies and their original classification authorities.

ttsa.label: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy
ttsa.why: TTSA executed a federal exploitation agreement over material it claimed was of unknown origin
ttsa.note: CRADA 19-15 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation' with the US Army CCDC Ground Vehicle Systems Center was filed as Exhibit 6.28 to TTSA's Form 1-A, naming Army principal investigators and TACOM intellectual property counsel.

ttsa.label: AARO / ORNL Synopsis: Analysis of a Metallic Specimen
ttsa.why: ORNL assessed the privately held 'crash' specimen as terrestrial
ttsa.note: The finding does not resolve the custody question it arose from: AARO notes the specimen's 'undocumented chain of custody and conflicting personal accounts' leave its historical origin unclear.

ttsa.label: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy
ttsa.why: Executed CRADA with the U.S. Army, 10 October 2019, term to 30 September 2023
ttsa.note: A real federal instrument, not a press release: signed by the GVSC Director and TTSA's Chief Content Officer, with TTSA's participation valued at an estimated $1 million in in-kind contributions.

ttsa.label: Christopher K. Mellon
ttsa.why: National Security Affairs Advisor / advisory board (2017-2020)
ttsa.note: A former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and SSCI minority staff director lending his name to the vehicle.

ttsa.label: Harold E. Puthoff
ttsa.why: Co-founder, VP Science and Technology, director
ttsa.note: Puthoff co-founded TTSA with Tom DeLonge and Jim Semivan in 2017; the company's materials work was routed to laboratories he founded.

ttsa.label: James 'Jim' Semivan
ttsa.note: A retired CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer accepting a named directorship in an SEC-registered UFO company is a deliberate reputational commitment.

ttsa.label: Kari DeLonge
ttsa.why: Chief Content Officer; highest cash-compensated officer FY2017
ttsa.note: $100,000 cash and options on 5 million shares at $0.003 valued at about $18.96m — the entertainment side held the equity.

ttsa.label: Encinitas, California
ttsa.why: Corporate base and Entertainment Division retail location

ttsa.label: Luis D. Elizondo
ttsa.why: Director of Global Security & Special Programs / Government Programs (2017-2020)
ttsa.note: The move placed the former AATIP director inside the private company then acquiring claimed exotic material and negotiating a federal research agreement over it.

ttsa.label: Steve Justice
ttsa.note: 31 years at Lockheed's Skunk Works, latterly Program Director for Advanced Systems, per the company's own filing.

ttsa.label: Thomas Matthew DeLonge
ttsa.why: Co-founder, President, interim CEO and controlling shareholder
ttsa.note: TTSA was a Regulation A public reporting issuer, which is why its holdings and agreements had to be filed with the SEC rather than remaining private.

ttsa.label: The Intercept
ttsa.why: Scrutiny of To The Stars Academy's media apparatus and financing
ttsa.note: The Intercept documented TTSA's SEC filing identifying it as a 'Motion Picture & Video Tape Production' concern, the undisclosed employment relationship between TTSA staff and the History Channel series 'Unidentified,' and reporter George Knapp's purchase of 400 shares of TTSA stock, which Knapp confirmed to The Intercept.

ttsa.label: ADAM Research Project (Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials)
ttsa.why: ADAM: acquisition and analysis of claimed exotic material
ttsa.note: Announced July 2019 as the Acquisition & Data Analysis of Materials project; SEC filings record the $35,000 purchase of the bismuth/magnesium-zinc and aluminium items.

ttsa.label: To The Stars Academy public launch, 11 October 2017
ttsa.why: Public launch and Regulation A+ offering, 11 October 2017
ttsa.note: Seven days after Elizondo's resignation took effect and nine weeks before the NYT story.

ttsa.label: FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast Navy gun-camera videos
ttsa.why: Hosted and distributed the three videos from 2017-2018
ttsa.note: TTSA published the footage on its own platform, framing it as officially cleared — a framing the Navy contested in September 2019.

ttsa.label: 'Unidentified: Inside America's UFO Investigation' (History Channel)
ttsa.why: TTSA production, executive produced by Tom DeLonge, History Channel 2019-2020
ttsa.note: The Entertainment Division supplying distribution for the Aerospace and Science claims.

ttsa.label: General Atomics
ttsa.why: Securities disclosure is why the TTSA arrangement is visible and a privately held prime's would not be
ttsa.note: TTSA's Reg A reporting obligations forced the CRADA into the public record. A privately held prime such as General Atomics has no equivalent obligation, which is the structural reason the documented case is a small company rather than a large one.

ttsa.label: Christopher C. 'Kit' Green
ttsa.why: Green served as an adviser to TTSA during the period of the material acquisition
ttsa.note: Green's association with the company is publicly acknowledged; the board has located no filing specifying his role or duties, and records the connection as an inference from public association rather than a documented officership.

ccdc-gvsc.label: Dr. Joseph Cannon
ccdc-gvsc.why: 21 Feb 2020: Army withholds 29 emails / 100 pages of Cannon's TTSA correspondence in full
ccdc-gvsc.note: CCDC FOIA Officer Joy L. Linton invoked exemptions (b)(4) and (b)(5) over an unclassified novel-materials collaboration the Army publicly described as origin-immaterial.

ccdc-gvsc.label: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy
ccdc-gvsc.why: Army counterparty; Detroit Arsenal ground vehicle laboratory
ccdc-gvsc.note: GVSC released the agreement text within a day of the announcement and withheld all associated correspondence four months later.

elizondo-resignation-letter-1.label: Luis D. Elizondo
elizondo-resignation-letter-1.note: Establishes his exact title and departure date in his own words on Departmental paper.

elizondo-resignation-letter-1.label: John Garrity
elizondo-resignation-letter-1.why: Submitted to his supervising official, hand-delivered
elizondo-resignation-letter-1.note: Elizondo's attorney Todd McMurtry confirmed the letter was hand-delivered rather than routed through standard channels; The Black Vault identifies the recipient as John Garrity.

elizondo-resignation-letter-1.label: To The Stars Academy public launch, 11 October 2017
elizondo-resignation-letter-1.why: Seven days from resignation effective date to corporate launch
elizondo-resignation-letter-1.note: The interval is short enough that the corporate vehicle must have been assembled before the departure. This is inference from dates, not from any document stating intent.

elizondo-resignation-letter-2.label: Luis D. Elizondo
elizondo-resignation-letter-2.why: Author, 4 October 2017; hand-delivered to the Secretary's office
elizondo-resignation-letter-2.note: The protest letter naming Departmental opposition to further UAP research as his reason for leaving.

elizondo-resignation-letter-2.label: James N. Mattis
elizondo-resignation-letter-2.why: Memorandum saluted 'Mr. Secretary'; NYT reported it as addressed to Mattis
elizondo-resignation-letter-2.note: The letter asks the Secretary to 'ask the hard questions'. Garry Reid's memo later questioned its 'uncertain provenance' — while the letter itself sits in the Department's own FOIA release.

dd-form-1910-2017.label: Luis D. Elizondo
dd-form-1910-2017.why: Submitted the clearance request for the three video files, 9 Aug 2017
dd-form-1910-2017.note: The form bears his name and OUSD(I) title. It is the documentary link between him and the AATIP-associated imagery, and it was approved 24 August 2017.

dd-form-1910-2017.label: FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast Navy gun-camera videos
dd-form-1910-2017.why: Cleared the GoFast, Gimbal and FLIR files for internal distribution only
dd-form-1910-2017.note: The form's stated purpose expressly excludes publication: research and analysis only, for a UAS threat database. This is the narrow basis on which the Navy later said no unrestricted release was ever authorised.

dd-form-1910-2017.label: Joseph Gradisher
dd-form-1910-2017.why: 'Neither the cognizant Navy offices nor DOPSR have record' of a 2017 unrestricted-release request
dd-form-1910-2017.note: A denial that is narrowly correct: the DD-1910 sought internal distribution and expressly said 'not for publication'. It rebuts TTSA's framing without rebutting the form's existence.

dd-form-1910-2017.label: Defense Office of Prepublication and Security Review
dd-form-1910-2017.why: Prepublication review chain for the video files
dd-form-1910-2017.note: The Navy later said DOPSR held no record of a request for unrestricted release of the videos in 2017 — consistent with the form's 'not for publication' framing.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Harry M. Reid
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Identified Reid as the senator who initiated and funded AATIP
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Reid told the Times 'I'm not embarrassed or ashamed or sorry I got this thing going' and called the appropriation 'black money'.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP / AAITP)
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Broke the program's existence, funding and Reid origin
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Cooper, Blumenthal and Kean disclosed the programme, the appropriation arranged by Sen. Harry Reid at Robert Bigelow's urging, and Elizondo's resignation.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)
nyt-2017-12-16.why: the program the New York Times revealed
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The 16 December 2017 story named the program, the $22M, Reid and Bigelow, and forced DIA to write the Senate Armed Services Committee three weeks later.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Independent media as the disclosure substrate
nyt-2017-12-16.why: the baseline against which the substrate shift is measured
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The 16 December 2017 story is the last time a US paper of record originated a legacy-programme disclosure. Every subsequent major disclosure - Grusch in 2023, Immaculate Constellation in 2024, the structural reconstruction in 2026 - went somewhere else first. This node is what makes the domain's central claim measurable rather than rhetorical.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: FLIR1 (Nimitz ATFLIR video, 14 Nov 2004)
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Published by the New York Times, reopening the subject
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The DoD's own 2020 release statement acknowledges the videos circulated publicly after unauthorized disclosures in 2007 and 2017.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Leslie Kean
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Co-byline with Helene Cooper and Ralph Blumenthal
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Kean and Blumenthal had cultivated the sources; Cooper supplied the Pentagon beat. The trio's byline is what moved the story from fringe to record.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Luis D. Elizondo
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Named him as the official who ran AATIP
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The article identified him, quoted his resignation letter and reported his move to TTSA — the act that made him the Department's problem.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
nyt-2017-12-16.why: The Nimitz footage was the visual centrepiece of the 2017 disclosure
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The New York Times published the November 2004 footage alongside the AATIP revelation, converting a shelved incident into a national accountability story.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Ralph Blumenthal
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Blumenthal shares the byline that broke AATIP and published two of the three videos.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Luis D. Elizondo
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Elizondo's resignation and the videos anchored the story
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Pentagon spokeswoman Dana White confirmed to Politico that Elizondo had directed AATIP.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Christopher K. Mellon
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Supplied the videos published with the story
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Mellon says he provided the files to the Times; the Times separately stated the Department of Defense was its on-the-record source for them.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: David Charles Grusch
nyt-2017-12-16.why: The New York Times did not publish the 2023 Grusch story
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The same two authors who wrote the paper's 2017 AATIP revelation took the 2023 crash-retrieval story elsewhere. Recorded as a denial-type edge because the decision not to publish is itself an act by an institution, and one that shaped what the public record looks like.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: Immaculate Constellation disclosure, October-November 2024
nyt-2017-12-16.why: The alleged programme is said to have been created in response to this story
nyt-2017-12-16.note: Shellenberger's whistleblower alleges DoD created Immaculate Constellation in 2017 after the New York Times published on AATIP. The claim is attributed, not documented.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: New York City
nyt-2017-12-16.why: The decisive act of the modern disclosure era was a New York editorial decision
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The story added institutional standing rather than new physical evidence; every subsequent official step follows it in sequence. Reasoning: chronological review of post-2017 official actions.

nyt-2017-12-16.label: The Debrief
nyt-2017-12-16.why: Successor venue to the 2017 New York Times story
nyt-2017-12-16.note: The 2017 NYT article and the 2023 Debrief article share two of three authors and a continuous line of argument; the change of venue between them is a data point about institutional appetite, not about the reporting.

ttsa-launch-2017.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
ttsa-launch-2017.why: Public launch and Regulation A+ offering, 11 October 2017
ttsa-launch-2017.note: Seven days after Elizondo's resignation took effect and nine weeks before the NYT story.

ttsa-launch-2017.label: Elizondo Resignation Letter #1, 3 October 2017
ttsa-launch-2017.why: Seven days from resignation effective date to corporate launch
ttsa-launch-2017.note: The interval is short enough that the corporate vehicle must have been assembled before the departure. This is inference from dates, not from any document stating intent.

unidentified-history-series.label: Christopher Sherwood
unidentified-history-series.why: The series premiere prompted the 1 June 2019 Pentagon denial
unidentified-history-series.note: The Intercept tested the Department's position because the series presented Elizondo as having led AATIP for eight years. Media pressure produced the operative denial.

unidentified-history-series.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
unidentified-history-series.why: TTSA production, executive produced by Tom DeLonge, History Channel 2019-2020
unidentified-history-series.note: The Entertainment Division supplying distribution for the Aerospace and Science claims.

elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.label: Garry P. Reid
elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.why: Named respondent; Reid removed from post by April 2022
elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.note: Separate DoD IG investigations substantiated ethics and information-handling findings against Reid. Defense officials told The Debrief he 'played a central role in obfuscating information' about UAP.

elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.label: Neill Tipton
elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.note: Tipton originated the 'no assigned responsibilities' formulation in May 2019.

elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.label: Susan Gough
elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.note: The Department's UAP spokesperson named in a whistleblower-reprisal complaint by the subject of her statements.

elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.label: Luis D. Elizondo
elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.why: Filed May 2021 naming Reid, Gough and Tipton
elizondo-dodig-complaint-2021.note: Alleged 'malicious activities, coordinated disinformation, professional misconduct, whistleblower reprisal and explicit threats'. No public adjudication has been released.

imminent-book.label: Defense Office of Prepublication and Security Review
imminent-book.why: Manuscript reviewed and cleared by the Department's prepublication office
imminent-book.note: A DOPSR clearance is not an endorsement of accuracy, but it is an affirmative Departmental determination that the assertions are not classified.

imminent-book.label: Luis D. Elizondo
imminent-book.why: Author; DOPSR review took approximately one year
imminent-book.note: 'What is in the book is what I was told I am allowed to talk about' — sworn testimony, 13 November 2024.

reckoning-book.label: Luis D. Elizondo
reckoning-book.note: HarperCollins promises 'previously undisclosed evidence'. Whether it went through DOPSR, and what was struck, is not yet public.

the-black-vault.label: Operação Prato (Operation Saucer)
the-black-vault.why: The American reporter's Prato dossier sits in Greenewald's archive
the-black-vault.note: A file titled 'Operação Prato', written by the US journalist Bob Pratt, is served publicly in the MUFON/Pratt document set at documents.theblackvault.com. It opens: 'Operação Prato, a Brazilian Air Force investigation of a prolonged UFO flap in 1977-78'. It names Captain Uyrangê Hollanda and his six sergeants, names Brigadier Protázio Lopes de Oliveira as the Belém base commander who shut the operation down after four months, and describes the interviews of hundreds of witnesses in Colares and about thirty other villages. This is the concrete answer to whether Prato material reached US hands: it did, through a working reporter, and it is now in the same FOIA archive that carries the Elizondo and Grusch-era US paper.

the-black-vault.label: John Greenewald Jr.
the-black-vault.why: Founder and operator of the archive that produced the primary record
the-black-vault.note: Nearly every document in this domain arrived through his requests.

the-black-vault.label: Los Angeles and Burbank, California
the-black-vault.why: The Black Vault runs the private FOIA archive from Los Angeles
the-black-vault.note: John Greenewald Jr.'s requests produced the GVSC/TTSA correspondence denial and much of the released AARO record.

the-black-vault.label: Capitão Uyrangê Bolívar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima
the-black-vault.why: Hollanda's account to an American reporter is preserved in the Pratt file
the-black-vault.note: Basterfield records that Pratt 'visited Colares for the first time in February 1979, then twice after that. He interviewed Captain Uyrange Hollanda, who had led the official investigation in the Colares region. Pratt was later able to secure brief summaries of 281 incidents in Colares and surrounding areas, plus maps, and twenty photographs.' Hollanda told him his team 'took about three hundred photos and we photographed eight different types of UFOs.' Tier 2: the interview and the 281 summaries are reported by a named researcher quoting Pratt's 1996 book, and the Pratt file at The Black Vault is the surviving public artefact of that chain.

l-encinitas.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
l-encinitas.why: Corporate base and Entertainment Division retail location

d-ffrdc.label: The Aerospace Corporation
d-ffrdc.why: Operates the only FFRDC dedicated exclusively to the space enterprise
d-ffrdc.note: Founded 1960 at Air Force insistence after the Ramo-Wooldridge conflict-of-interest problem; FY2024 funding approximately $1,309.8 million.

d-ffrdc.label: FAR 35.017 - Federally Funded Research and Development Centers
d-ffrdc.why: FAR 35.017 is the regulation that creates the seam
d-ffrdc.note: The subpart grants FFRDCs access to government and supplier data beyond a normal contractual relationship while requiring disclosure only to the sponsoring agency.

d-ffrdc.label: Institute for Defense Analyses
d-ffrdc.why: Operates the only FFRDC sponsored by the National Security Agency
d-ffrdc.note: IDA's Center for Communications and Computing is sponsored by NSA/CSS - the least publicly visible FFRDC in the country and the hardest for a committee to reach.

d-ffrdc.label: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
d-ffrdc.why: A UARC, not an FFRDC - the unexamined branch of the same mechanism
d-ffrdc.note: University Affiliated Research Centers carry FFRDC-like access without the FAR 35.017 sponsoring-agreement regime or NSF master-list registration; no congressional UAP letter has gone to one.

d-ffrdc.label: The MITRE Corporation
d-ffrdc.why: MITRE is the largest single operator of the FFRDC form
d-ffrdc.note: MITRE operates six of the 41 FFRDCs recorded by NSF, spanning defence/intelligence, aviation, tax, health, homeland security and cybersecurity sponsors - the widest sponsor spread of any operator.

d-ffrdc.label: RAND Corporation
d-ffrdc.why: RAND invented the institutional form the whole domain rests on
d-ffrdc.note: Incorporated 1948 out of Project RAND inside Douglas Aircraft; now operates four FFRDCs for the Air Force, Army, OSD and DHS.

d-ffrdc.label: Burlison UAP Records Disclosure Amendment, FY2027 NDAA
d-ffrdc.why: Would extend statutory disclosure to contractors holding covered records
d-ffrdc.note: The only proposed mechanism that would convert FFRDC holdings into records reachable by an independent review board with subpoena power, without sponsoring-agency consent.

d-ffrdc.label: Federal Contracting Mechanics
d-ffrdc.why: the FFRDC seam is a species of contracting mechanics, not a separate subject
d-ffrdc.note: FAR 35.017 is a procurement regulation. The records status, disclosure direction and sole-source features that make the FFRDC form load-bearing on this board are all properties of the contracting instrument, which is why the seam domain should hang off contracting mechanics rather than float beside it.

d-ffrdc.label: 'The MITRE Corporation - UFO Reverse Engineering, USO Tracking, & Legacy Programs'
d-ffrdc.why: Argues FFRDCs are the 'missing link' that lets programmes be vested outside government
d-ffrdc.note: The structural argument is independently supported by FAR 35.017's dual-access provision, whatever the status of the specific allegations.

far-35-017.label: The FFRDC Seam
far-35-017.why: FAR 35.017 is the regulation that creates the seam
far-35-017.note: The subpart grants FFRDCs access to government and supplier data beyond a normal contractual relationship while requiring disclosure only to the sponsoring agency.

far-35-017.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
far-35-017.why: The letter's legal theory rests on the FFRDC access provisions
far-35-017.note: Burlison argues FFRDCs 'often receive special access to government facilities, data, sponsor requirements, and sensitive technical information that ordinary private contractors may not receive' and therefore cannot be private vaults for federal records.

mitre-corporation.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE routes the answer back through its sponsoring agencies
mitre-corporation.note: A MITRE spokesperson said that if any relevant material is found, 'we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work' - restating the FAR structure under which disclosure runs to the sponsor, not to Congress.

mitre-corporation.label: Bedford, Massachusetts
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE founding site and original headquarters
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE was founded at Bedford, Massachusetts in 1958 as a spin-off from MIT Lincoln Laboratory, adjacent to Hanscom Air Force Base, and Bedford remains one of its two headquarters.

mitre-corporation.label: McLean, Virginia
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE McLean headquarters campus
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE holds dual headquarters in Bedford, Massachusetts and McLean, Virginia; the McLean office was established in 1963 and is where the defence and intelligence FFRDC customer relationships sit.

mitre-corporation.label: Federal Contracting Mechanics
mitre-corporation.why: the largest operator of the one acquisition form built to be non-competitive by design
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE operates multiple FFRDCs. FAR 35.017 permits an agency to meet special long-term research needs through a sponsoring agreement with a single operator outside full and open competition, and obliges the FFRDC to disclose its activities to its sponsor and to no one else. That is a contracting mechanism, and MITRE is its largest single instance.

mitre-corporation.label: The FFRDC Seam
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE is the largest single operator of the FFRDC form
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE operates six of the 41 FFRDCs recorded by NSF, spanning defence/intelligence, aviation, tax, health, homeland security and cybersecurity sponsors - the widest sponsor spread of any operator.

mitre-corporation.label: Donald M. Kerr
mitre-corporation.why: Chairman of MITRE's Board of Trustees from November 2018
mitre-corporation.note: Former director of Los Alamos National Laboratory, former director of the National Reconnaissance Office, former PDDNI - elected chairman at the same meeting that made Mike Rogers vice chairman.

mitre-corporation.label: The FFRDC / UARC / GOCO mechanism
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE is the exemplar instance of the mechanism
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE operates six FFRDCs and describes itself as providing long-term strategic partnership and stability to government sponsors - the documented properties on which the concealment thesis rests.

mitre-corporation.label: JASON
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE has administered JASON since 2002
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE provides management and logistics for the government's most sensitive standing scientific advisory panel; the contract was saved by an NNSA sole-source award in April 2019 after DoD declined renewal.

mitre-corporation.label: Jason Providakes
mitre-corporation.why: President and CEO through the entire modern disclosure sequence, 2017-2024
mitre-corporation.note: His tenure spans the December 2017 AATIP revelation, the UAP Task Force, the 2021 ODNI assessment, AARO's creation, and the Grusch testimony - the period Burlison's request covers.

mitre-corporation.label: Mark Todd Peters
mitre-corporation.why: President and CEO from 3 September 2024
mitre-corporation.note: Announced 27 June 2024 as MITRE's 10th president and CEO; the executive to whom Burlison's May 2026 request was ultimately addressed.

mitre-corporation.label: MIT Lincoln Laboratory
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE was spun out of Lincoln Laboratory Division 6 in 1958
mitre-corporation.note: 485 Lincoln Laboratory employees moved to the new corporation on incorporation, 21 July 1958, to continue SAGE systems engineering under Air Force sponsorship.

mitre-corporation.label: Center for Advanced Aviation System Development (CAASD)
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE operates CAASD for the FAA
mitre-corporation.note: CAASD gives MITRE the engineering authority over the civil air surveillance picture, under contracts DTFAWA10C00080 and 693KA822C00001.

mitre-corporation.label: Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute (HSSEDI)
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE operates HSSEDI for DHS Science and Technology
mitre-corporation.note: Created 5 March 2009; the DHS engineering franchise sits with the same operator now under congressional UAP records demand.

mitre-corporation.label: National Security Engineering Center (NSEC)
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE operates NSEC for the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
mitre-corporation.note: NSEC is MITRE's only DoD/IC-sponsored FFRDC, funded at roughly $1.43 billion in FY2024 and executed through Army task orders under IDIQ W56KGU18D0004.

mitre-corporation.label: Northrop Grumman Corporation
mitre-corporation.why: Named among the primes whose MITRE-related work Congress demanded an accounting of
mitre-corporation.note: Burlison's production requests cover MITRE work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC and Leidos.

mitre-corporation.label: Robert R. Everett
mitre-corporation.why: First technical director; carried SAGE engineering authority across from MIT
mitre-corporation.note: Everett joined MITRE at incorporation as first technical director and later became its president.

mitre-corporation.label: Samantha F. Ravich
mitre-corporation.why: Elected to MITRE's Board of Trustees, 19 May 2026
mitre-corporation.note: Elected three days before the Burlison production request was sent; former vice chair of the President's Intelligence Advisory Board.

mitre-corporation.label: Susan M. Gordon
mitre-corporation.why: Vice chair of MITRE's Board of Trustees from 31 October 2023
mitre-corporation.note: Former Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, elected vice chair three months after the July 2023 House Oversight UAP hearing.

mitre-corporation.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
mitre-corporation.why: Demands production of all MITRE UAP and reverse-engineering records back to 1930
mitre-corporation.note: More than 40 production requests with a 5/10/14/30/45-day compliance schedule; MITRE confirmed it was reviewing its archives.

mitre-corporation.label: UAP Gerb - The MITRE Corporation investigation
mitre-corporation.why: Alleged 2011 restriction on historical briefings about program incumbents
mitre-corporation.note: A policy act alleged to prevent even cleared personnel from being briefed on the programme's own history - concealment directed inward at the programme's own workforce rather than outward at the public.

mitre-corporation.label: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
mitre-corporation.why: Conditions any production on coordination with the sponsoring federal agencies
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets' - a compliance posture with an executive-branch veto inside it.

mitre-corporation.label: UAP Gerb - The MITRE Corporation investigation
mitre-corporation.why: Names MITRE as the central FFRDC node of the legacy portfolio
mitre-corporation.note: The investigation alleges MITRE's founding in 1958 carried a hidden second impetus beyond SAGE systems engineering: constructing a trusted long-term partner answerable only to its DoD customer to spearhead reverse engineering of recovered craft.

mitre-corporation.label: Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE is named among the FFRDC and contractor ecosystem supporting NAVAIR programs at Pax River
mitre-corporation.note: The FFRDC form grants privileged long-term access to classified holdings while barring manufacturing and competition; no allegation of custody attaches to MITRE.

mitre-corporation.label: 'The Pentagon's UFO Program Is Real [Here's How It Works!]'
mitre-corporation.why: Dedicated chapter 'The Role of MITRE' at 51:28
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE is given a named chapter inside the structural episode, seven months before Gerb published his full MITRE investigation - establishing that MITRE was already central to the model in January 2026.

mitre-corporation.label: RAND Corporation
mitre-corporation.why: MITRE was created on the RAND model as the Air Force's systems engineering counterpart
mitre-corporation.note: RAND, incorporated 1948 out of Project RAND, established the permanent contractor-operated analytical partner form; the Air Force replicated it for systems engineering in 1958.

mitre-corporation.label: Burlison production demand to MITRE (22 May 2026)
mitre-corporation.why: addressed to
mitre-corporation.note: MITRE confirmed it was reviewing its archives and said it would 'coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.'

mitre-corporation.label: 'The MITRE Corporation - UFO Reverse Engineering, USO Tracking, & Legacy Programs'
mitre-corporation.why: Alleges MITRE has held a Navy legacy reverse-engineering role since 1958
mitre-corporation.note: Allegations include exploitation of non-human technologies from late-1940s recoveries and all-source processing of data on a very large Atlantic USO; no primary document has been produced.

mitre-corporation.label: Battelle Memorial Institute
mitre-corporation.why: Executive pipeline from the 1950s UFO analysis contractor to the 2020s FFRDC under inquiry
mitre-corporation.note: Battelle ran Project Stork and produced Blue Book Special Report No. 14; seventy years later it supplied MITRE's chief executive. The connection is documented; the significance is inference.

mitre-corporation.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act - Burlison amendment to the FY2027 NDAA
mitre-corporation.why: would reach contractor holdings
mitre-corporation.note: The amendment extends disclosure requirements to covered government contractors - the only instrument that would reach the holdings Burlison sought from MITRE by letter in May 2026.

mitre-nsec.label: Dana (Keoki) Jackson
mitre-nsec.why: Runs MITRE National Security, the organisation containing NSEC
mitre-nsec.note: Any MITRE holdings on Special and Controlled Access Programs, materials analysis or classification guides would sit inside his organisation.

mitre-nsec.label: The MITRE Corporation
mitre-nsec.why: MITRE operates NSEC for the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
mitre-nsec.note: NSEC is MITRE's only DoD/IC-sponsored FFRDC, funded at roughly $1.43 billion in FY2024 and executed through Army task orders under IDIQ W56KGU18D0004.

mitre-caasd.label: The MITRE Corporation
mitre-caasd.why: MITRE operates CAASD for the FAA
mitre-caasd.note: CAASD gives MITRE the engineering authority over the civil air surveillance picture, under contracts DTFAWA10C00080 and 693KA822C00001.

mitre-caasd.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
mitre-caasd.why: FAA surveillance data - engineered by a MITRE FFRDC - is a named AARO data source
mitre-caasd.note: AARO draws on FAA radar and reporting; the systems engineering authority over that data belongs to MITRE's CAASD. No claim of filtering is made; the dependency is the point.

mitre-hssedi.label: The MITRE Corporation
mitre-hssedi.why: MITRE operates HSSEDI for DHS Science and Technology
mitre-hssedi.note: Created 5 March 2009; the DHS engineering franchise sits with the same operator now under congressional UAP records demand.

jason-advisory-group.label: High-Frequency Gravitational Wave Communications
jason-advisory-group.why: JASON found the underlying physics wrong two years before DIA published the DIRD
jason-advisory-group.note: In 2008 JASON reviewed separate HFGW work Baker had done for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and rejected it at the root: 'The proposed applications of the science of HFGW are fundamentally wrong,' and 'No foreign threat in HFGW is credible.' DIA published Baker's HFGW paper as an official Defense Intelligence Reference Document on 6 April 2010 regardless. This is the sharpest available evidence of AAWSAP's quality-control failure: the programme placed on a JWICS-hosted DIA reference series a topic the government's own senior scientific review body had already assessed as wrong and whose threat premise it had declared not credible. It is also the only case in the 38 where an external government review directly contradicts a published deliverable.

jason-advisory-group.label: United States Department of Energy
jason-advisory-group.why: NNSA rescued and now sponsors JASON after DoD declined renewal
jason-advisory-group.note: On 25-26 April 2019 NNSA issued a notice of intent to award a short-term sole source contract to MITRE for JASON management and logistics support, two weeks after OUSD(R&E) confirmed it was ending the contract.

jason-advisory-group.label: The MITRE Corporation
jason-advisory-group.note: MITRE provides management and logistics for the government's most sensitive standing scientific advisory panel; the contract was saved by an NNSA sole-source award in April 2019 after DoD declined renewal.

jason-advisory-group.label: Institute for Defense Analyses
jason-advisory-group.note: JASON has never been housed inside the government: IDA, then SRI International, then MITRE. Continuity of the panel has always depended on an FFRDC operator's contract.

af-atic-film-0352.label: Edward J. Ruppelt
af-atic-film-0352.why: Ruppelt is the briefer on the recording
af-atic-film-0352.note: The Blue Book director briefing military officials and scientists in March 1952, four months before the Washington, DC radar intrusions.

af-atic-film-0352.label: MIT Lincoln Laboratory
af-atic-film-0352.why: Holds the March 1952 Ruppelt 'flying saucer talk' recording
af-atic-film-0352.note: By 25 June 2026 Burlison announced the laboratory had agreed to disclose it - the first FFRDC-held UAP record obtained by Congress by naming the file.

af-atic-film-0352.label: Project Beacon Hill
af-atic-film-0352.why: The briefing was given into the 1952 Beacon Hill reconnaissance study circle
af-atic-film-0352.note: Burlison's press release names both items together; the inference is that Blue Book briefed the group designing US strategic aerial reconnaissance. No minutes produced.

beacon-hill-study.label: MIT Lincoln Laboratory
beacon-hill-study.why: Beacon Hill was convened in the MIT/Lincoln Laboratory complex for the Air Force
beacon-hill-study.note: The study shaped US overhead reconnaissance and its records sit in institutional rather than federal custody.

beacon-hill-study.label: AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52 ('flying saucer talk')
beacon-hill-study.why: The briefing was given into the 1952 Beacon Hill reconnaissance study circle
beacon-hill-study.note: Burlison's press release names both items together; the inference is that Blue Book briefed the group designing US strategic aerial reconnaissance. No minutes produced.

project-stork.label: Battelle Memorial Institute
project-stork.why: Battelle held the Air Force contract designated Project Stork
project-stork.note: Under Stork, Battelle performed the statistical analysis of Project Blue Book's case files that became Special Report No. 14.

project-stork.label: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14
project-stork.why: Stork produced Special Report No. 14, 5 May 1955
project-stork.note: Project No. 10073; roughly 3,200 cases analysed; the proportion of unknowns rose with the quality of the sighting.

project-stork.label: Project Blue Book
project-stork.why: Stork was Blue Book's contracted analytical arm
project-stork.note: The Air Force's public UFO project outsourced its own analytical methodology to a private nonprofit, whose records were never federal records.

pentacle-memorandum.label: Howard C. Cross
pentacle-memorandum.note: Two pages, reference G-1579-4, SECRET, unsigned, to Miles E. Goll at Wright-Patterson AFB.

pentacle-memorandum.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
pentacle-memorandum.why: Addressed to Miles E. Goll at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
pentacle-memorandum.note: No signed original has ever been produced by the Air Force or by Battelle.

pentacle-memorandum.label: Robertson Panel
pentacle-memorandum.why: Written five days before the panel met; per Vallee the panel was never briefed on its proposals
pentacle-memorandum.note: Vallee's conclusion is that a separate group had already decided what the panel could and could not discuss - contractor-side predetermination of an official scientific review.

pentacle-memorandum.label: Jacques F. Vallee
pentacle-memorandum.why: Discovered the memorandum in 1967 among Hynek's papers and named its author 'Pentacle'
pentacle-memorandum.note: Journal entry 18 June 1967; published in Forbidden Science (1992). H. C. Cross was later identified as the author.

aerospace-corporation.label: The FFRDC Seam
aerospace-corporation.why: Operates the only FFRDC dedicated exclusively to the space enterprise
aerospace-corporation.note: Founded 1960 at Air Force insistence after the Ramo-Wooldridge conflict-of-interest problem; FY2024 funding approximately $1,309.8 million.

aerospace-corporation.label: Eric W. Davis
aerospace-corporation.why: Employed by the FFRDC operator at the time of the 2019-2020 briefings
aerospace-corporation.note: The New York Times identified Davis as working for Aerospace Corp. when reporting his classified briefings on retrievals. The corporation has never publicly addressed whether it had any institutional role.

aerospace-corporation.label: UAP Gerb - Northrop Grumman & TRW investigation (Vol.2)
aerospace-corporation.why: Traces Stephanie O'Sullivan from TRW to ODNI to the Aerospace board
aerospace-corporation.note: O'Sullivan is a former TRW engineer, former Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence and a current Aerospace Corporation board member - a single career spanning prime contractor, IC leadership and FFRDC governance.

aerospace-corporation.label: Eric Burlison
aerospace-corporation.why: Named as a target of his records investigation
aerospace-corporation.note: Aerospace holds the technical judgement on national security space sensing; no letter to Aerospace has been made public as of 12 August 2026.

aerospace-corporation.label: UAP Gerb - The MITRE Corporation investigation
aerospace-corporation.why: Groups Aerospace Corporation with MITRE as the FFRDC layer
aerospace-corporation.note: Gerb's FFRDC thesis treats MITRE and the Aerospace Corporation as parallel instances of the same mechanism; the Aerospace link is reinforced by Stephanie O'Sullivan's board membership there after ODNI. The specific allegation against Aerospace is inference from the model rather than a separately documented claim.

rand-corporation.label: Santa Monica, California
rand-corporation.note: RAND was formed on 14 May 1948 and is headquartered at 1776 Main Street, Santa Monica, California, where it operates three of its four FFRDCs. This is where the contractor-operated analytical institution was invented.

rand-corporation.label: The FFRDC Seam
rand-corporation.why: RAND invented the institutional form the whole domain rests on
rand-corporation.note: Incorporated 1948 out of Project RAND inside Douglas Aircraft; now operates four FFRDCs for the Air Force, Army, OSD and DHS.

rand-corporation.label: George Kocher
rand-corporation.why: Published Kocher's 'UFOs: What To Do?' as DRU-1571, November 1968
rand-corporation.note: Issued two months before the Condon Committee report told the public the subject was closed; RAND has never withdrawn it.

rand-corporation.label: UAP Gerb - The MITRE Corporation investigation
rand-corporation.why: MITRE founded as the Air Force's successor to RAND
rand-corporation.note: The investigation restates the documented history that MITRE was established in 1958 as the Air Force's spiritual successor to RAND, tasked with systems engineering for SAGE.

rand-corporation.label: Jason Matheny
rand-corporation.why: President and CEO, arriving from IARPA and the White House OSTP
rand-corporation.note: Another instance of the pattern: the person setting a nominally independent FFRDC operator's research agenda previously ran the Intelligence Community's research arm.

rand-corporation.label: Samantha F. Ravich
rand-corporation.why: Doctorate from the RAND Graduate School
rand-corporation.note: Another instance of FFRDC-operator interlock: a MITRE trustee credentialed by RAND and serving on Idaho National Laboratory's national security advisory committee.

rand-corporation.label: The MITRE Corporation
rand-corporation.why: MITRE was created on the RAND model as the Air Force's systems engineering counterpart
rand-corporation.note: RAND, incorporated 1948 out of Project RAND, established the permanent contractor-operated analytical partner form; the Air Force replicated it for systems engineering in 1958.

rand-corporation.label: Eric Burlison
rand-corporation.why: Named as a target of his records investigation
rand-corporation.note: Burlison: 'my investigation is following the trail into RAND, MITRE, Aerospace Corp, MIT Lincoln Labs, and the Northrop Grummans of the world.' No letter to RAND has been made public.

ida.label: Charles A. Richard
ida.why: President of IDA after commanding US Strategic Command
ida.note: His STRATCOM tenure, 2019-2022, coincides exactly with the UAP Task Force period and the establishment of AARO.

ida.label: The FFRDC Seam
ida.why: Operates the only FFRDC sponsored by the National Security Agency
ida.note: IDA's Center for Communications and Computing is sponsored by NSA/CSS - the least publicly visible FFRDC in the country and the hardest for a committee to reach.

ida.label: JASON
ida.note: JASON has never been housed inside the government: IDA, then SRI International, then MITRE. Continuity of the panel has always depended on an FFRDC operator's contract.

kirtland-manzano-1980.label: Richard C. Doty
kirtland-manzano-1980.why: Filed the AFOSI complaint form documenting the incident
kirtland-manzano-1980.note: Complaint form dated 9 September 1980, District File No. 8017D93-0/29, 'alleged sighting of unidentified aerial lights in restricted test range'.

kirtland-manzano-1980.label: Kirtland Air Force Base and Albuquerque, New Mexico
kirtland-manzano-1980.why: Occurred at the Manzano Weapons Storage Area and Coyote Canyon
kirtland-manzano-1980.note: Manzano is a nuclear weapons storage area on the Kirtland footprint shared with Sandia National Laboratories.

kirtland-manzano-1980.label: Air Force Office of Special Investigations
kirtland-manzano-1980.why: AFOSI investigated the 1980 intrusions at the nuclear weapons storage area
kirtland-manzano-1980.note: The intrusions occurred at the Manzano Weapons Storage Area adjacent to Sandia National Laboratories; AFOSI ran the investigation and simultaneously ran the Bennewitz operation.

kirtland-manzano-1980.label: Sandia National Laboratories
kirtland-manzano-1980.why: A Sandia security guard is a named reporting party in the AFOSI file
kirtland-manzano-1980.note: A Sandia guard reported a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure at approximately 00:20 on 9 August 1980, with radio malfunction.

lanl.label: Los Alamos Green Fireballs Conference
lanl.why: Held at Los Alamos; LANL's National Security Research Center holds the minutes
lanl.note: LANL confirms the 16 February 1949 conference and its custody of the minutes in its own published account.

lanl.label: United States Department of Energy
lanl.why: DOE/NNSA management and operating contract; Los Alamos
lanl.note: Los Alamos is an NNSA laboratory operated under contract; its National Security Research Center holds and processes FOIA on the laboratory's classified historical record, including 1949 green fireball material.

lanl.label: Donald M. Kerr
lanl.why: Directed Los Alamos before the NRO and ODNI
lanl.note: The same individual later chaired MITRE's board - a single career spanning the contractor-operated weapons laboratory, national overhead reconnaissance, and the FFRDC now under records demand.

lanl.label: Jeremy Kenyon Lockyer Corbell
lanl.why: 'Sleeping Dog' document trove said to originate with a deceased LANL cybersecurity chief
lanl.note: Corbell states the materials came from the son of the laboratory's late former cybersecurity chief and include material on a claimed 1991 meeting at Los Alamos; the laboratory has not authenticated them.

llnl.label: United States Department of Energy
llnl.why: DOE weapons laboratory operating under Atomic Energy Act classification authority
llnl.note: Restricted Data classification is statutory rather than executive-order-derived, and is therefore untouched by presidential declassification directives of the kind driving the 2026 PURSUE releases.

llnl.label: United States Department of Energy
llnl.why: DOE/NNSA management and operating contract; Lawrence Livermore
llnl.note: Livermore is an NNSA weapons laboratory operating under DOE classification authority rather than DoD SAP authority.

llnl.label: Edward Teller
llnl.why: Co-founder and director of the Livermore laboratory
llnl.note: The scientist present at the first US conference on anomalous objects over nuclear sites went on to found the second weapons design laboratory.

jhuapl.label: The FFRDC Seam
jhuapl.why: A UARC, not an FFRDC - the unexamined branch of the same mechanism
jhuapl.note: University Affiliated Research Centers carry FFRDC-like access without the FAR 35.017 sponsoring-agreement regime or NSF master-list registration; no congressional UAP letter has gone to one.

uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.label: 'UAP Gerb' (Sam)
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.why: Author and publisher of the 7 August 2026 MITRE investigation
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.note: Published with a researcher using the handle 'Kerberos'; explicitly framed as aid to Burlison's inquiry.

uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.why: Published as declared support for the congressional inquiry opened 11 weeks earlier
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.note: Burlison's letter is dated 22 May 2026; the investigation was published 7 August 2026 and states it seeks to directly aid that inquiry.

uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.label: The MITRE Corporation
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.why: Alleges MITRE has held a Navy legacy reverse-engineering role since 1958
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.note: Allegations include exploitation of non-human technologies from late-1940s recoveries and all-source processing of data on a very large Atlantic USO; no primary document has been produced.

uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.label: The FFRDC Seam
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.why: Argues FFRDCs are the 'missing link' that lets programmes be vested outside government
uap-gerb-mitre-investigation.note: The structural argument is independently supported by FAR 35.017's dual-access provision, whatever the status of the specific allegations.

ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.label: The FFRDC Seam
ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.why: Would extend statutory disclosure to contractors holding covered records
ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.note: The only proposed mechanism that would convert FFRDC holdings into records reachable by an independent review board with subpoena power, without sponsoring-agency consent.

ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.label: Eric Burlison
ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.why: Author of the House-adopted UAP records disclosure amendment
ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.note: Revised text designated Version 2 on 15 July 2026 and adopted as part of the FY2027 NDAA later that month.

ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.why: Revives the review board and eminent-domain-era disclosure architecture stripped in 2023
ndaa-fy2027-uap-amendment.note: The FY2027 amendment restores the Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority and a statutory transfer timeline to NARA.

l-mclean.label: Central Intelligence Agency
l-mclean.why: CIA headquarters at Langley, within McLean
l-mclean.note: The CIA's George Bush Center for Intelligence stands in the Langley neighbourhood of McLean, Fairfax County, Virginia. Note this is a different Langley from Langley Air Force Base, which is at Hampton, Virginia.

l-mclean.label: The MITRE Corporation
l-mclean.note: MITRE holds dual headquarters in Bedford, Massachusetts and McLean, Virginia; the McLean office was established in 1963 and is where the defence and intelligence FFRDC customer relationships sit.

l-mclean.label: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
l-mclean.note: The Director of National Intelligence has been headquartered at the Liberty Crossing complex in McLean, Virginia since 2008, alongside the National Counterterrorism Center.

l-bedford-ma.label: The MITRE Corporation
l-bedford-ma.why: MITRE founding site and original headquarters
l-bedford-ma.note: MITRE was founded at Bedford, Massachusetts in 1958 as a spin-off from MIT Lincoln Laboratory, adjacent to Hanscom Air Force Base, and Bedford remains one of its two headquarters.

l-columbus-oh.label: Battelle Memorial Institute
l-columbus-oh.note: Battelle Memorial Institute is headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, roughly sixty-five miles from Wright-Patterson Air Force Base at Dayton, which is the geographic fact underlying its Air Force analytical work in the 1940s and 1950s.

l-columbus-oh.label: Project Blue Book
l-columbus-oh.why: Project Stork / Blue Book Special Report No. 14 produced here
l-columbus-oh.note: In 1952 Project Blue Book contracted the Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus, Ohio to carry out the statistical study of 1947-1952 sighting reports that became Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, dated 5 May 1955; the Battelle group was associated with Project Stork.

l-santa-monica.label: RAND Corporation
l-santa-monica.note: RAND was formed on 14 May 1948 and is headquartered at 1776 Main Street, Santa Monica, California, where it operates three of its four FFRDCs. This is where the contractor-operated analytical institution was invented.

l-los-alamos.label: White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico
l-los-alamos.why: Los Alamos and White Sands bracket the 1948-1951 green fireball reporting corridor
l-los-alamos.note: The 16 February 1949 conference at Los Alamos and the Project Twinkle instrumented observation effort in southern New Mexico both arose from reporting across this corridor.

l-los-alamos.label: Los Alamos Green Fireballs Conference
l-los-alamos.why: The green fireballs conference was convened at Los Alamos
l-los-alamos.note: Edward Teller and Lincoln LaPaz were among the attendees; the laboratory's own account records that the phenomenon was ultimately dismissed as a national security threat.

debrief-2023-06-05.label: Leslie Kean
debrief-2023-06-05.why: Co-author; vetted Grusch through Nell and the NASIC officer
debrief-2023-06-05.note: Kean built the story on named and verified corroborators rather than on Grusch alone, interviewing Karl Nell to establish standing and securing the pseudonymous NASIC officer on the record.

debrief-2023-06-05.label: Ralph Blumenthal
debrief-2023-06-05.note: Blumenthal, with Kean, had co-authored the December 2017 New York Times AATIP story; the same byline pair carried the Grusch story after national outlets declined it.

debrief-2023-06-05.label: Grusch DOPSR Prepublication Clearance (FOIA 23-F-0946)
debrief-2023-06-05.why: Clearance preceded publication by two months
debrief-2023-06-05.note: DOPSR approvals of 4 and 6 April 2023 preceded the 5 June 2023 Debrief publication. Kean and Blumenthal confirmed the clearance before publishing, which is why the Pentagon's response contested substantiation rather than authorization.

debrief-2023-06-05.label: House Oversight hearing, 26 July 2023 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'
debrief-2023-06-05.why: Publication to sworn testimony in fifty-one days
debrief-2023-06-05.note: The Debrief published 5 June 2023; the House Oversight subcommittee took sworn testimony 26 July 2023. The speed is itself a data point about congressional appetite in that window.

kirkpatrick-sciam-oped.label: Sean M. Kirkpatrick
kirkpatrick-sciam-oped.why: Bylined attribution of the allegations to circular reporting and unsupported belief
kirkpatrick-sciam-oped.note: Published 19 January 2024 under Kirkpatrick's own name, seven weeks before AARO's Historical Record Report advanced the same circular-reporting frame. The outgoing director pre-litigated his agency's conclusions in the press.

kirkpatrick-sciam-oped.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
kirkpatrick-sciam-oped.why: Op-ed advanced the report's analytic frame seven weeks early
kirkpatrick-sciam-oped.note: Kirkpatrick's 19 January 2024 circular-reporting framing appears as the analytic spine of the 8 March 2024 report - the departing director publishing the conclusion before the agency published the study.

grusch-v-chapman.label: David Charles Grusch
grusch-v-chapman.why: Plaintiff; suit dismissed with prejudice 6 August 2025
grusch-v-chapman.note: Filed 15 July 2024 in Loudoun County Circuit Court against Sheriff Mike Chapman and a Sheriff's Office employee. Dismissed with prejudice on 6 August 2025 on the reasoning that Virginia's mental health confidentiality statute reaches court files rather than police records. The outcome establishes that no legal shield protected the whistleblower's most sensitive records.

grusch-v-chapman.label: Ken Klippenstein
grusch-v-chapman.why: FOIA request that produced the records at issue in the suit
grusch-v-chapman.note: Klippenstein obtained Grusch's 2014 and 2018 Loudoun County emergency-custody police records under Virginia FOIA and published them in The Intercept on 9 August 2023; Grusch's civil action was against the Sheriff who released them, not the reporter.

crane-dod-reprisal-letter.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
crane-dod-reprisal-letter.why: No reply on the record as of 9 September 2025
crane-dod-reprisal-letter.note: A sitting member formally notified the Department that a whistleblower lost his clearance, promotion and medical retirement for a protected disclosure. Crane stated he was still waiting for a reply; Chairwoman Luna committed to follow up. Non-response is itself an artifact.

crane-dod-reprisal-letter.label: Elijah Crane
crane-dod-reprisal-letter.why: Author; wrote DoD 24 July 2025 on Grusch's reprisal
crane-dod-reprisal-letter.note: Crane enumerated three specific adverse actions - clearance removal, denial of promotion, loss of medical retirement - and entered the letter into the hearing record on 9 September 2025 reporting no reply.

crane-dod-reprisal-letter.label: David Charles Grusch
crane-dod-reprisal-letter.note: The only document in the public record that itemizes the adverse actions against Grusch. Each of the three actions generates its own internal DoD paper trail that has never been produced.

task-force-declassification.label: David Charles Grusch
task-force-declassification.why: Serves the Task Force via the Burlison advisory role
task-force-declassification.note: Burlison's announcement states Grusch's role includes serving on the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, the body that held the September 2025 UAP hearing and hosted the June 2026 press conference.

task-force-declassification.label: Anna Paulina Luna
task-force-declassification.note: Luna chairs the standing Oversight task force that converted the ad hoc 2023-2024 UAP hearings into a permanent investigative vehicle.

task-force-declassification.label: House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets hearing, 9 September 2025 - 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'
task-force-declassification.why: Held the UAP transparency and whistleblower protection hearing
task-force-declassification.note: The hearing where the Crane reprisal letter entered the record and where Knapp and Mace put ongoing retaliation against Grusch into the official transcript.

task-force-declassification.label: Capitol UAP Disclosure Press Conference
task-force-declassification.note: The Task Force staged the event on the Capitol steps with Luna, Burchett, Burlison and Moskowitz to pressure the White House to convert the February 2026 declassification announcement into actual releases.

press-conf-2026-06-09.label: House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets

uap-nda-waiver-directive-2026.why: Offers his office as a disclosure channel with counsel and congressional presence
uap-nda-waiver-directive-2026.note: Burlison - whose Special Advisor is Grusch - recommends that anyone using the NDA waiver request congressional presence alongside legal counsel. That recommendation is a direct read-through of what happened to the last person who used executive channels alone.
