nasa.label: NASA UAP Independent Study Team
nasa.why: NASA chartered and published the Independent Study Team report
nasa.note: The 16-member panel reported on 14 September 2023 with findings on data curation, satellite assets and the classification obstacle.

nasa.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
nasa.why: Civil-agency complement to the DoD-led resolution office
nasa.note: The Independent Study Team positioned NASA's expertise as supporting AARO within a 'whole-of-government framework', while acknowledging that much of the relevant military and intelligence data is classified.

nasa.label: Blue Marble Space Institute of Science
nasa.why: BMSIS research investigator seated on NASA's UAP independent study team
nasa.note: NASA's announced 16-member independent study team on UAP included Anamaria Berea, described by NASA as 'a research investigator with Blue Marble Space Institute of Science in Seattle.' That team produced the September 2023 public report and the recommendation that NASA build a UAP data pipeline.

nasa.label: David N. Spergel
nasa.why: Chaired the NASA UAP Independent Study Team
nasa.note: Spergel of the Simons Foundation chaired the 16-member panel.

nasa.label: Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada
nasa.why: NASA's UAP study cited as precedent and named as a proposed partner
nasa.note: The Sky Canada report cites NASA's September 2023 UAP Independent Study Report in its bibliography and lists NASA among the international entities the recommended Canadian lead organization should partner with to share data and methodologies.

nasa.label: PURSUE Release 01
nasa.why: Released Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 mission records
nasa.note: Apollo mission records including cockpit transcript describing 'very bright particles or fragments' appear in the first tranche.

nasa.label: PURSUE Release 03
nasa.note: Gemini crew debriefings and 1962 Cronkite-Cooper interview audio were published in the third tranche.

nasa.label: United States Department of Energy
nasa.why: Both hold analytical capability that could resolve material claims and neither has been tasked publicly
nasa.note: NASA's report identifies the classification of military and intelligence data as the binding constraint; DOE laboratories hold the analytical instruments actually used by AARO. Reasoning: the capability exists and the tasking does not.

usaf.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (Record Group 615)
usaf.why: Project BLUE BOOK records are held at the National Archives
usaf.note: 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, T-1206, permanently transferred to NARA - the Air Force is the one agency whose UFO records were fully accessioned, and they stop in 1969.

usaf.label: Project Blue Book
usaf.why: BLUE BOOK records transferred to the National Archives as 94 rolls of microfilm
usaf.note: The records were permanently transferred to NARA and are held as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, T-1206.

usaf.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)
usaf.why: Air Force funded the University of Colorado study used to close BLUE BOOK
usaf.note: The termination decision rested on 'Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects' and a National Academy of Sciences review of it.

usaf.label: Air Force Office of Special Investigations
usaf.why: Air Force felony investigative and counterintelligence field agency
usaf.note: AFOSI is the Air Force's independent investigative agency with units 'located at most Air Force bases worldwide', covering espionage, terrorism and counterintelligence.

usaf.label: Project Blue Book
usaf.why: Air Force ran the public UFO investigation 1952-1969
usaf.note: 12,618 sightings were reported to BLUE BOOK, of which 701 remain 'Unidentified'. The Secretary of the Air Force announced termination on 17 December 1969.

usaf.label: Air Force Research Laboratory
usaf.why: Single Air Force science and technology laboratory, Wright-Patterson AFB
usaf.note: AFRL consolidated the Wright, Phillips, Rome and Armstrong laboratories and AFOSR at Wright-Patterson - the installation named in every retrieval account since 1947.

cia.label: 'CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90' (Gerald K. Haines, Studies in Intelligence, 1997)
cia.why: CIA's own published history concedes the Air Force made deceptive public statements
cia.note: 'This led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily sensitive national security project.'

cia.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (Record Group 615)
cia.why: Produced no records for the first statutory UAP transfer
cia.note: NARA's 24 April 2025 release named only ODNI, OSD, the FAA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. CIA, which holds documented UAP equity, transferred nothing.

cia.label: Robertson Panel
cia.why: CIA convened and sponsored the panel, and concealed that sponsorship
cia.note: The panel was convened by the Office of Scientific Intelligence. The CIA's own history states that any mention of Agency sponsorship of the panel was forbidden.

cia.label: McLean, Virginia
cia.why: CIA headquarters at Langley, within McLean
cia.note: The CIA's George Bush Center for Intelligence stands in the Langley neighbourhood of McLean, Fairfax County, Virginia. Note this is a different Langley from Langley Air Force Base, which is at Hampton, Virginia.

cia.label: Howard P. Robertson
cia.why: Chaired the CIA-convened panel of January 1953
cia.note: Robertson chaired the panel at CIA's request; the report is the founding document of American UFO information management.

cia.label: Hoyt S. Vandenberg
cia.why: Vandenberg was DCI before becoming Air Force Chief of Staff
cia.note: He directed Central Intelligence in 1946-1947 and then held the top Air Force post from 1948, arriving at the destruction decision already fluent in compartmentation.

cia.label: William B. Adkins
cia.why: CIA officer detailed to NRO advanced systems
cia.note: Per his NRO bio: 'From 1997 to 2000, Mr. Adkins worked for the Central Intelligence Agency and was assigned to the NRO in the Advanced Systems and Technology Directorate, where he managed several technology development projects.'

cia.label: Robertson Panel
cia.why: CIA convened and staffed the January 1953 scientific advisory panel
cia.note: Convened by the Office of Scientific Intelligence under H. P. Robertson; the panel recommended debunking and the monitoring of civilian UFO groups.

cia.label: A Die-hard Issue: CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-1990
cia.why: CIA published its own institutional history of its UFO role in 1997
cia.note: Gerald K. Haines, the Agency's historian, published an eighteen-page account in Studies in Intelligence acknowledging the OSI effort, the Robertson Panel and the later U-2/OXCART attribution.

cia.label: KONA BLUE
cia.why: CIA alleged to have terminated the programme
cia.note: Gerb's account has the CIA shutting Kona Blue down. Recorded here as an alleged act of the concealment apparatus rather than as an adjudicated fact.

cia.label: Lockheed Martin Corporation
cia.why: CIA is alleged to have blocked the divestment of material from the contractor to BAASS
cia.note: Rep. Burlison read Christopher Sharp's reporting of a CIA block into the 13 November 2024 hearing and Elizondo replied 'What I can say is that it was blocked.' AARO separately records an interviewee claim that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.'

cia.label: H. Marshall Chadwell
cia.why: Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence who drove the CIA's 1952-53 UFO effort
cia.note: Chadwell's OSI memoranda are the internal record of CIA's decision to treat the subject as a security and public-opinion problem.

cia.label: Christopher C. 'Kit' Green
cia.why: Life Sciences Division, Office of Scientific Intelligence
cia.note: Green was the agency analyst to whom biological anomalies were routed, including oversight of the SRI remote-viewing work, before writing the AAWSAP injury study two decades later.

cia.label: 'The Pentagon's UFO Program Is Real [Here's How It Works!]'
cia.why: Dedicated chapter 'The Office of Global Access' at 43:04
cia.note: The Office of Global Access, an element associated with CIA's Directorate of Science and Technology, is given a named chapter; Gerb separately links CIA OGA to NRO, MITRE and the Executive branch in his NRO investigation.

cia.label: Comer-Luna letters to Rubio, Hegseth and Ratcliffe on UAP records, February 2025
cia.note: Ratcliffe had said as DNI that UAP exhibit technologies the United States does not have.

cia.label: Science Applications International Corporation
cia.why: SAIC held the government's remote viewing research line after it left SRI
cia.note: A documented instance of a deniable government research program in an anomalous subject moving wholesale into corporate custody, terminated after an external assessment.

cia.label: ODNI Memorandum ES 2026-00818 - Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver
cia.why: directed to release; absent from the statutory archive
cia.note: The Director of the Central Intelligence Agency is an addressee of the ODNI NDA-waiver memorandum and the CIA has no series in Record Group 615, whose transfer deadline passed on 30 September 2025.

cia.label: CSETI / The Disclosure Project
cia.why: Claimed 1993 UFO briefing of sitting CIA Director Woolsey (disputed)
cia.note: CSETI founder Steven Greer says he briefed sitting CIA Director R. James Woolsey on UFOs on 13 December 1993 at a dinner in Arlington arranged by John Petersen, and quotes a Petersen memo referring to sabotage of 'Project Starlight', the CSETI disclosure effort. Woolsey and the other attendees disputed this characterisation in a signed 16 September 1999 letter, saying it was a dinner party and that Greer's published account was distorted. Both accounts are on the record; the relationship is contested.

us-senate.label: Senate Armed Services Committee
us-senate.why: Committee of jurisdiction for DoD special access program reporting
us-senate.note: SASC is one of the four defense committees to which 10 U.S.C. 119 reporting runs, and one of the two whose chairman and ranking member receive waived-SAP notification.

us-senate.label: Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
us-senate.why: Committee of jurisdiction for intelligence community programs
us-senate.note: SSCI's report language accompanying the FY2021 Intelligence Authorization Act produced the June 2021 ODNI Preliminary Assessment.

us-senate.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (Record Group 615)
us-senate.why: Created by sections 1841-1843 of Public Law 118-31
us-senate.note: The collection is the surviving remnant of the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act after the review board and eminent domain provisions were removed in conference.

us-house.label: SAF/AAZ — Air Force Declassification & Special Programs
us-house.why: Air Force SAP directive bars congressional briefings without SAPCO approval
us-house.note: Air Force Policy Directive 16-7, 'Special Access Programs,' 29 December 2010, states: 'It is strictly forbidden for any employee of the Air Force or any appropriately accessed organization or company to brief or provide SAP material to any Congressional Member or staff without DoD SAPCO approval. Additionally, the Director, SAF/AAZ will be kept informed of any interaction with Congress.' This is the documented mechanism behind the recurring complaint that SAP-compartmented material cannot reach non-HASC/HAC-D members.

us-house.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
us-house.why: Committee finding of non-cooperation by DoD and the IC
us-house.note: Chairwoman Luna: 'A major barrier to this Committee's inquiry into UAPs has been the lack of cooperation and transparency from the Department of Defense and the intelligence community.'

us-house.label: Legislative Process (proposed and pending)
us-house.why: the chamber where the text was stripped in 2023 and where a successor passed in 2026
us-house.note: The House is where UAP oversight became public through the July 2023 Oversight hearing, where House leadership's role in the conference removal of the disclosure title became a contested question, and where the Burlison amendment was adopted on 22 July 2026. Both the defeat and the advance ran through the same chamber.

us-house.label: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
us-house.why: Single point of congressional liaison for every DoD special access program
us-house.note: DoDD 5205.07 requires personnel to notify the Director, DoD SAPCO and OA SAPCO directors when briefing Congress or congressional staff with SAP material, and bars contractors from providing such material without specific approval. The office being overseen is notified before the overseer is briefed.

us-house.label: House Armed Services Committee
us-house.why: One half of the read-in gate described by Chairwoman Luna
us-house.note: HASC leadership approval is required, together with HAC-D leadership, for a non-committee member to view specific program material.

us-house.label: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
us-house.why: Committee that took the 2023 and 2024 public UAP testimony
us-house.note: House Oversight held the 26 July 2023 hearing and the 13 November 2024 hearing, and its Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets held the 9 September 2025 hearing.

us-house.label: The HASC/HAC-D special access program read-in gate
us-house.why: HASC and HAC-D leadership control member access to program material
us-house.note: The gate is described on the record by the chair of the investigating task force; the two committees controlling it are not the committee conducting the inquiry.

us-house.label: Tom Cole
us-house.why: Representative, Oklahoma 4th district; Chairman of Appropriations from April 2024
us-house.note: The House Appropriations chairmanship is one of only two House seats in the section 119 group that sit on the money side; the other is the Defense Subcommittee chair held by Ken Calvert.

us-house.label: William B. Adkins
us-house.why: House Appropriations Defense subcommittee staff overseeing NRO/NSA/NGA
us-house.note: Before becoming PDDNRO he 'served on the professional staff of the House Appropriations Committee, Subcommittee on Defense, where he led the subcommittee's oversight and legislative responsibility for the NRO, U.S. Space Force, U.S. Space Command, National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, National Security Agency, and U.S. Cyber Command' - the panel that writes the classified defense appropriations annex.

us-house.label: 509th Bomb Group
us-house.why: Congressionally requested GAO search of 509th and RAAF records
us-house.note: At the request of Rep. Steven H. Schiff, GAO searched for records of the units assigned to RAAF in 1947, including the 509th Bomb Group. It found that RAAF administrative records (Mar 1945-Dec 1949) and RAAF outgoing messages (Oct 1946-Dec 1949) had been destroyed, with the disposition form failing to record who destroyed them, when, or under what authority.

us-house.label: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
us-house.why: Committee of jurisdiction for IC controlled access programs
us-house.note: Programs carried in the IC SAP control enterprise are reported, if at all, to the intelligence committees rather than to the defense committees.

us-house.label: John M. McHugh
us-house.why: Representative, New York 23rd district, until 21 September 2009
us-house.note: McHugh remained a member of the House for three months after leaving the ranking seat, which is why the resignation date and the 119(e)(2) succession date are not the same. Conflating them would attribute mid-2009 waived-SAP notifications to the wrong member.

isoo.label: ODNI Controlled Access Program Coordination Office (CAPCO)
isoo.why: ISOO requests about IC controlled access programs are routed through CAPCO
isoo.note: ICD 906 section D.9.c makes CAPCO responsible for coordinating 'requests from the Information Security Oversight Office' about CAPs.

isoo.label: Program structure and organisational mapping
isoo.why: the office charged with counting the classification system, and therefore the boundary of the public map
isoo.note: ISOO is housed at the National Archives and is responsible to the President for policy and oversight of the government-wide security classification system and the National Industrial Security Program, under Executive Orders 13526 and 13556. Where ISOO's annual reporting stops is where this domain's open-source organisational mapping has to switch to inference.

isoo.label: Executive Order 13526 — Classified National Security Information
isoo.why: ISOO access to SAPs is granted and simultaneously conditioned
isoo.note: Section 4.3(b) affords the ISOO Director access to special access programs 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President' - a defeasible right.

isoo.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (Record Group 615)
isoo.why: Both are components of the National Archives
isoo.note: NARA hosts both the statutory UAP collection and the Information Security Oversight Office, the body responsible to the President for the classification system.

isoo.label: Waived Unacknowledged SAP (waived USAP) — the mechanism
isoo.why: The only external body with a claim of access, and the claim is conditional
isoo.note: E.O. 13526 sec. 4.3(b) affords the ISOO Director access to SAPs 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President'.

isoo.label: CAP Registry / CAPCO Register of control systems, compartments and sub-compartments
isoo.why: ISOO advises the working group that produces the marking standard
isoo.note: The CAPCO Register v5.1 lists NARA/Information Security Oversight Office among the IC Classification Markings Implementation Working Group advisors.

isoo.label: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)
isoo.why: NISP oversight is the only government-wide window on contractor-held classified work
isoo.note: ISOO is 'responsible to the President for policy and oversight of the Government-wide security classification system and the National Industrial Security Program'. A contractor-held program with no government sponsor of record would be visible, if anywhere, through NISP - and ISOO has never been directed at the UAP question.

gao.label: GAO High-Risk List: DOD Financial Management
gao.note: The High-Risk List is a GAO product, updated at the start of each Congress. Attested by GAO.

gao.label: Roswell Incident
gao.why: Found Roswell AAF outgoing messages 1945-1949 destroyed without authorisation
gao.note: GAO reported that the outgoing message traffic for March 1945 to December 1949 had been destroyed and that no destruction certificate authorising it could be located.

gao.label: Steven H. Schiff
gao.why: GAO conducted the Roswell records search at Rep. Schiff's request
gao.note: Schiff turned to GAO after the Air Force declined to answer him directly; GAO/NSIAD-95-187 is the result.

sffas-56.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
sffas-56.why: DoD identified the need for the standard in August 2016
sffas-56.note: The Statement records that the Department of Defense identified the need in August 2016, citing conflict between GAAP and classification obligations under Executive Order 13526. Attested by SFFAS 56's own basis for conclusions.

sffas-56.label: Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board (FASAB)
sffas-56.note: The standard is a FASAB pronouncement, effective for periods beginning after 30 September 2018. Attested by the Statement itself.

sffas-56.label: DoD Agency-Wide Financial Statement Audit (FY2018-present)
sffas-56.why: Authorises modification of the same public financial reports the audit examines
sffas-56.note: SFFAS 56 became effective for periods beginning after 30 September 2018 - the first period after the Department's first full-scope audit - and permits amounts to be presented in a different line item without narrative explanation. Attested by the Statement and by the FY2018 Agency Financial Report.

sffas-56.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
sffas-56.why: Accounting-side and appropriations-side concealment of the same activity
sffas-56.note: The classified annex conceals what was appropriated; SFFAS 56 permits the resulting spending to be reported in the wrong line of the public financial statement with no note. The inference is that the two together close the loop between authorisation and reporting; no document links them.

fasab.label: SFFAS 56 - Classified Activities (FASAB, 4 October 2018)
fasab.note: The standard is a FASAB pronouncement, effective for periods beginning after 30 September 2018. Attested by the Statement itself.

fasab.label: Terry K. Patton
fasab.why: Chairs the Board that owns SFFAS 56 since April 2026
fasab.note: FASAB's board members page identifies Terry K. Patton as Chair since April 2026. Attested by FASAB.

skidmore-fitts-report.label: Catherine Austin Fitts
skidmore-fitts-report.note: Fitts co-authored the summary report and the Missing Money archive that hosts it and its supporting documentation. Attested by the report and the Solari archive.

skidmore-fitts-report.label: DODIG-2016-113 - Army General Fund Adjustments Not Adequately Documented or Supported
skidmore-fitts-report.why: The single largest figure in the $21 trillion compilation comes from this report
skidmore-fitts-report.note: The Skidmore-Fitts compilation draws on published OIG reports including DODIG-2016-113, whose $6.5 trillion year-end unsupported adjustment figure is the largest single component. Attested by the authors' own supporting documentation index.

skidmore-fitts-report.label: Mark Skidmore
skidmore-fitts-report.note: Skidmore compiled the OIG and GAO unsupported-adjustment figures for FY1998-FY2015 and co-authored the September 2017 summary report. Attested by the report and by his own publication list.

nip.label: The Classified Schedule of Authorizations (Intelligence Authorization Act)
nip.why: The Schedule is the instrument by which the entire NIP is authorised
nip.note: Section 6102(a) of the FY2026 Intelligence Authorization Act provides that the amounts authorised for intelligence activities 'are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations prepared to accompany this division'. Attested by the statute itself.

nip.label: Funding Channels
nip.why: one of the two named channels through which US intelligence money is appropriated
nip.note: The National Intelligence Program is the DNI-controlled channel. Since FY2007, sec. 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act (P.L. 110-53) has required disclosure of the aggregate appropriated amount, and ODNI publishes request and appropriated toplines annually. Aggregate-only disclosure is precisely what makes it a channel this board can name but not itemise.

nip.label: 50 U.S.C. 3510 - CIA unvouchered funds (CIA Act of 1949, sec. 8)
nip.why: Unvouchered CIA spending sits inside the NIP and outside all expenditure law
nip.note: 50 U.S.C. 3510(b) permits Agency sums to be expended without regard to laws and regulations governing expenditure of government funds, accounted for solely on the Director's certificate. The CIA is funded within the National Intelligence Program. Attested by the statute.

nip.label: Military Intelligence Program (MIP)
nip.why: The two-programme split that divides intelligence money between DNI and SECDEF control
nip.note: The NIP is controlled by the Director of National Intelligence and the MIP by the Secretary of Defense; both are published only as annual aggregates. Attested by ODNI's own budget page and the FAS compilation.

nip.label: National Intelligence Program Summary for FY2013 (excerpts) - the 2013 black budget disclosure
nip.why: The only public view of the interior of the National Intelligence Program
nip.note: The FY2013 NIP Summary excerpts, classified TS/SI/TK/NOFORN, were released via the Washington Post in August 2013 and are hosted by FAS; the officially disclosed figure for the same year was a single aggregate. Attested by the FAS document index.

nip.label: IAA FY2024 Section 7343 - Funding Limitations Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena
nip.why: Binds funds authorised by the intelligence division
nip.note: Section 7343(b) bars use of funds authorised by Division F for UAP activity under special or restricted access limitation absent DNI disclosure to six committees and congressional leadership. Attested by the statute.

mip.label: Funding Channels
mip.why: the second named channel, under SECDEF and USD(I&S) rather than the DNI
mip.note: The Military Intelligence Program is the defence-side counterpart to the NIP, managed by the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. DoD has disclosed a MIP appropriated topline annually since 2010 and request figures since 2012; the DoD Financial Management Regulation Vol. 2B Ch. 16 governs how intelligence programmes are budgeted and displayed. Topline-only disclosure is the same structural property as the NIP.

mip.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
mip.why: The two-programme split that divides intelligence money between DNI and SECDEF control
mip.note: The NIP is controlled by the Director of National Intelligence and the MIP by the Secretary of Defense; both are published only as annual aggregates. Attested by ODNI's own budget page and the FAS compilation.

mip.label: Line item 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' / Program Element 9999999999
mip.why: Published classified line items are where MIP and NIP money physically sits in the defense budget
mip.note: The FY2026 funding tables carry roughly $95.9 billion in rows titled only 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS'; the published MIP request for FY2026 is $33.6 billion and the NIP request $81.9 billion, neither of which appears as a named line anywhere. The inference is that the classified rows are the appropriation vehicle. No document states the mapping.

classified-annex.label: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
classified-annex.why: DoDI 5205.11 para. 7.2.h - waived-programme justification materials go only to committee staff directors
classified-annex.note: DoDI 5205.11 para. 7.2.h, 'Congressional Budget Justification Materials': 'The DoD will conform to all congressional reporting requirements. The DoD will submit to the congressional defense and intelligence committees such additional materials as are requested by the committees and are within the jurisdiction of each committee. Justification materials for waived programs will be presented only to the committee staff directors.' This is the best available primary evidence that DoD continued to route waived-programme justification material to the defense committees after the 31 December 2021 termination of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) - but note that it routes that material to staff directors rather than through the 119(e)(2) chair-and-ranking channel, and it rests on committee request rather than on a standing statutory reporting duty.

classified-annex.label: Section 8084 - NIP reprogramming notification against classified annex levels
classified-annex.why: NIP reprogramming is measured against levels that exist only in the annex
classified-annex.note: Section 8084(b) conditions NIP reprogramming notice on cumulative change to 'the levels specified in the classified annex accompanying the Act' - a public statute making the unpublished annex the operative baseline. Attested by the enacted text.

classified-annex.label: Section 1001 General Transfer Authority (annual NDAA)
classified-annex.why: Funding-table amounts, including the annex, do not count against the section 1001 ceiling
classified-annex.note: Section 4001(c) of the FY2026 NDAA states transfers or reprogrammings of funding-table amounts shall not count against the section 1001 ceiling unless funds move between appropriation accounts; section 4001(d) applies the section to any classified annex. Attested by the enacted text.

classified-annex.label: Section 8005 Transfer Authority (annual DoD Appropriations Act)
classified-annex.why: Annex tables are exempted from the section 8005 transfer ceiling
classified-annex.note: Section 8006(b) of the FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act provides that amounts in the classified annex tables are not subdivisions of appropriations for section 8005 purposes; section 8005 applies only to movements between appropriation accounts. Attested by the enacted statutory text.

classified-annex.label: Line item 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' / Program Element 9999999999
classified-annex.why: The one-word line item is the public face of the annex table
classified-annex.note: Section 4001 authorises obligation of amounts in the funding tables and applies to any classified annex accompanying the Act; the printed tables show only 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' and a number, the annex shows the programme detail. Attested by the enacted text.

classified-annex.label: Waived SAP Notification Group
classified-annex.why: four of the twelve seats are appropriations leadership
classified-annex.note: The chair and ranking of both Appropriations Committees and both Defense Subcommittees sit in the 119(e)(2) group. This is the structural feature that distinguishes it from the Gang of Eight, which contains no appropriators, and it means the group's sight of a waived programme includes the money as well as the report.

classified-annex.label: Michael Powers
classified-annex.note: The Under Secretary (Comptroller)/CFO is the official responsible for execution of appropriated funds including those directed by the classified annex tables under section 8006(a). Reasoned inference from the office's statutory functions; no document names the incumbent in connection with the annex.

classified-annex.label: SFFAS 56 - Classified Activities (FASAB, 4 October 2018)
classified-annex.why: Accounting-side and appropriations-side concealment of the same activity
classified-annex.note: The classified annex conceals what was appropriated; SFFAS 56 permits the resulting spending to be reported in the wrong line of the public financial statement with no note. The inference is that the two together close the loop between authorisation and reporting; no document links them.

classified-schedule-authorizations.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
classified-schedule-authorizations.why: The Schedule is the instrument by which the entire NIP is authorised
classified-schedule-authorizations.note: Section 6102(a) of the FY2026 Intelligence Authorization Act provides that the amounts authorised for intelligence activities 'are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations prepared to accompany this division'. Attested by the statute itself.

classified-schedule-authorizations.label: 50 U.S.C. 3306 - Public disclosure of NIP aggregate amounts
classified-schedule-authorizations.why: Section 3306(a) is the sole affirmative exception to the bar on disclosing the Schedule
classified-schedule-authorizations.note: Section 6102(b)(3)(A) names 50 U.S.C. 3306(a) as the one statutory route by which any portion of the classified Schedule may be publicly disclosed. Attested by the enacted text.

classified-schedule-authorizations.label: National Intelligence Program Summary for FY2013 (excerpts) - the 2013 black budget disclosure
classified-schedule-authorizations.why: What the Schedule of Authorizations looks like from the inside
classified-schedule-authorizations.note: The FY2013 excerpts show agency, programme and objective-level detail of the kind that section 6102 of the Intelligence Authorization Act keeps in the classified Schedule. The inference that the two documents describe the same structure is reasoned; no source states it.

sec-8005-transfer.label: Reprogramming of DoD Appropriated Funds (DoD FMR Volume 3, Chapter 6; DD Form 1415 series)
sec-8005-transfer.why: The administrative layer beneath the statutory transfer authority
sec-8005-transfer.note: DoD FMR Volume 3 Chapter 6 implements reprogramming and transfer actions, including Below-Threshold Reprogramming which requires no approval or notification. Attested by the regulation.

sec-8005-transfer.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
sec-8005-transfer.why: Annex tables are exempted from the section 8005 transfer ceiling
sec-8005-transfer.note: Section 8006(b) of the FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act provides that amounts in the classified annex tables are not subdivisions of appropriations for section 8005 purposes; section 8005 applies only to movements between appropriation accounts. Attested by the enacted statutory text.

sec-1001-gta.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
sec-1001-gta.why: Funding-table amounts, including the annex, do not count against the section 1001 ceiling
sec-1001-gta.note: Section 4001(c) of the FY2026 NDAA states transfers or reprogrammings of funding-table amounts shall not count against the section 1001 ceiling unless funds move between appropriation accounts; section 4001(d) applies the section to any classified annex. Attested by the enacted text.

irad-mechanism.label: NDAA FY2024 Section 1687 - Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs
irad-mechanism.why: Statutory bar on UAP-related IR&D as an allowable indirect cost
irad-mechanism.note: Section 1687(b) provides that IR&D funding relating to UAP shall not be allowable as an indirect expense for contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless disclosed to the appropriate committees and leadership. Attested by the enacted statute.

irad-mechanism.label: Section 8009 - 30-day advance notice before initiating or materially modifying a special access program
irad-mechanism.why: IR&D reimbursement is not an appropriation and does not trigger SAP notification
irad-mechanism.note: Section 8009 attaches to funds appropriated by the Act; contractor IR&D is reimbursed as an allowable indirect cost across a contract portfolio rather than appropriated to a programme. Reasoned inference from the structure of both instruments.

irad-mechanism.label: The misappropriation allegation: Grusch's ICIG complaint and sworn testimony
irad-mechanism.why: The allegation of illegal contracting and the statute that names IR&D
irad-mechanism.note: Grusch's on-the-record formulation was 'illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations'; six months later Congress barred UAP-related IR&D from being an allowable indirect cost. The inference that the two describe the same mechanism is reasoned, not documented: no source states that section 1687(b) was drafted in response to Grusch.

usc-50-3510.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
usc-50-3510.why: Unvouchered CIA spending sits inside the NIP and outside all expenditure law
usc-50-3510.note: 50 U.S.C. 3510(b) permits Agency sums to be expended without regard to laws and regulations governing expenditure of government funds, accounted for solely on the Director's certificate. The CIA is funded within the National Intelligence Program. Attested by the statute.

usc-50-3510.label: Section 8009 - 30-day advance notice before initiating or materially modifying a special access program
usc-50-3510.why: An activity funded from unvouchered CIA money never touches the appropriations SAP tripwire
usc-50-3510.note: Section 8009 binds only funds appropriated by the annual Defense Appropriations Act; unvouchered Agency spending under 50 U.S.C. 3510 is neither DoD appropriated funds nor subject to normal expenditure law. Reasoned inference from the two texts; no document asserts this has occurred.

usc-50-3306.label: The Classified Schedule of Authorizations (Intelligence Authorization Act)
usc-50-3306.why: Section 3306(a) is the sole affirmative exception to the bar on disclosing the Schedule
usc-50-3306.note: Section 6102(b)(3)(A) names 50 U.S.C. 3306(a) as the one statutory route by which any portion of the classified Schedule may be publicly disclosed. Attested by the enacted text.

usc-50-3306.label: The intelligence budget disclosure record, FY1997-FY2026
usc-50-3306.why: The statute that produced the second segment of the disclosure record
usc-50-3306.note: Section 601 of P.L. 110-53, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3306, compels the annual aggregate NIP disclosures that resumed with FY2007 after a nine-year gap. Attested by the statute and by the ODNI and FAS compilations.

classified-programs-line.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
classified-programs-line.why: The Department is the account holder for every published classified line
classified-programs-line.note: All 25 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' rows in the FY2026 funding tables sit in Department of Defense appropriation accounts - Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, Defense-Wide and Special Operations. Attested by the enacted funding tables.

classified-programs-line.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
classified-programs-line.why: The one-word line item is the public face of the annex table
classified-programs-line.note: Section 4001 authorises obligation of amounts in the funding tables and applies to any classified annex accompanying the Act; the printed tables show only 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' and a number, the annex shows the programme detail. Attested by the enacted text.

classified-programs-line.label: Military Intelligence Program (MIP)
classified-programs-line.why: Published classified line items are where MIP and NIP money physically sits in the defense budget
classified-programs-line.note: The FY2026 funding tables carry roughly $95.9 billion in rows titled only 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS'; the published MIP request for FY2026 is $33.6 billion and the NIP request $81.9 billion, neither of which appears as a named line anywhere. The inference is that the classified rows are the appropriation vehicle. No document states the mapping.

classified-programs-line.label: National Reconnaissance Office
classified-programs-line.why: The $26.9 billion Other Procurement, Air Force classified line is the historical pass-through
classified-programs-line.note: FY2026 line 077A carries $26,920,092 thousand in Other Procurement, Air Force, an account long understood by budget analysts to carry national reconnaissance funding that the Air Force does not control. Inference from the size of the line, the account's history, and the Air Force's own repeated public complaints about a pass-through of this magnitude; no document confirms the recipient.

sec-8009-sap-notice.label: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
sec-8009-sap-notice.why: The appropriations tripwire on initiating or modifying a special access programme
sec-8009-sap-notice.note: Section 8009 of the FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act bars use of that Act's funds to initiate or materially modify the scope of a SAP without 30 days advance notice to the congressional defense committees; DoD SAPCO is the office that administers the SAP enterprise under the Deputy Secretary. Attested by the statute.

sec-8009-sap-notice.label: Independent Research and Development (IR&D) as a funding channel
sec-8009-sap-notice.why: IR&D reimbursement is not an appropriation and does not trigger SAP notification
sec-8009-sap-notice.note: Section 8009 attaches to funds appropriated by the Act; contractor IR&D is reimbursed as an allowable indirect cost across a contract portfolio rather than appropriated to a programme. Reasoned inference from the structure of both instruments.

sec-8009-sap-notice.label: 50 U.S.C. 3510 - CIA unvouchered funds (CIA Act of 1949, sec. 8)
sec-8009-sap-notice.why: An activity funded from unvouchered CIA money never touches the appropriations SAP tripwire
sec-8009-sap-notice.note: Section 8009 binds only funds appropriated by the annual Defense Appropriations Act; unvouchered Agency spending under 50 U.S.C. 3510 is neither DoD appropriated funds nor subject to normal expenditure law. Reasoned inference from the two texts; no document asserts this has occurred.

sec-8084-nip-reprogramming.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
sec-8084-nip-reprogramming.why: NIP reprogramming is measured against levels that exist only in the annex
sec-8084-nip-reprogramming.note: Section 8084(b) conditions NIP reprogramming notice on cumulative change to 'the levels specified in the classified annex accompanying the Act' - a public statute making the unpublished annex the operative baseline. Attested by the enacted text.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.why: AARO's reports address the retrieval claims and say nothing about the funding claims
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.note: The AARO Historical Record Report Volume I (March 2024) and the FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report contain no discussion of misappropriated funds, illegal contracting, IR&D or contractor financial arrangements. The absence is attested by the reports themselves.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.label: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.why: Sworn testimony before the committee, 26 July 2023
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.note: Grusch testified with Ryan Graves and David Fravor at 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'. Attested by the committee's own hearing page.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.label: Irvin Charles McCullough III
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.why: Counsel who filed the ICIG disclosure of urgent concern
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.note: McCullough, himself a former Intelligence Community Inspector General, filed the Disclosure of Urgent Concern(s) and Complaint of Reprisal on Grusch's behalf in May 2022. Attested by The Debrief.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.label: David Charles Grusch
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.why: The named complainant, under oath and under an IG complaint
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.note: Grusch filed the ICIG urgent-concern complaint in May 2022 through counsel, was found credible and urgent in July 2022, went on the record in June 2023 and testified under oath on 26 July 2023. Attested by The Debrief reporting and the House Oversight hearing record.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.label: Independent Research and Development (IR&D) as a funding channel
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.why: The allegation of illegal contracting and the statute that names IR&D
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.note: Grusch's on-the-record formulation was 'illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations'; six months later Congress barred UAP-related IR&D from being an allowable indirect cost. The inference that the two describe the same mechanism is reasoned, not documented: no source states that section 1687(b) was drafted in response to Grusch.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.label: DoD Agency-Wide Financial Statement Audit (FY2018-present)
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.why: An unauditable ledger cannot disprove the allegation
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.note: The Department's standing 'Universe of Transactions' material weakness means the complete population of its transactions is not established; no search of that population can therefore establish that funds did not flow to an undisclosed activity. Reasoned inference from the auditor's own definition of the weakness.

gao-high-risk-dod-fm.label: Government Accountability Office
gao-high-risk-dod-fm.note: The High-Risk List is a GAO product, updated at the start of each Congress. Attested by GAO.

gao-high-risk-dod-fm.label: DoD Agency-Wide Financial Statement Audit (FY2018-present)
gao-high-risk-dod-fm.why: Thirty years of Comptroller General certification that the books cannot produce reliable information
gao-high-risk-dod-fm.note: DOD Financial Management remains on GAO's 2025 High-Risk List with status maintained, alongside four other DoD entries. Attested by GAO's own list.

intel-budget-disclosure-record.label: Steven Aftergood
intel-budget-disclosure-record.why: Created the first segment of the record by litigation
intel-budget-disclosure-record.note: Aftergood was the plaintiff in the 1997 FAS FOIA suit against the CIA that forced the first release of the total intelligence budget in fifty years, $26.6 billion for FY1997. Attested by FAS and by the FAS Intelligence Resource Program budget page.

intel-budget-disclosure-record.label: 50 U.S.C. 3306 - Public disclosure of NIP aggregate amounts
intel-budget-disclosure-record.why: The statute that produced the second segment of the disclosure record
intel-budget-disclosure-record.note: Section 601 of P.L. 110-53, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3306, compels the annual aggregate NIP disclosures that resumed with FY2007 after a nine-year gap. Attested by the statute and by the ODNI and FAS compilations.

fas.label: National Intelligence Program Summary for FY2013 (excerpts) - the 2013 black budget disclosure
fas.why: FAS hosts the excerpts and the redacted FOIA budget justifications
fas.note: The FAS Intelligence Resource Program budget page indexes the FY2013 NIP Summary excerpts alongside redacted Congressional Budget Justifications for ODNI, NRO, NGA and the MIP. Attested by the page itself.

fas.label: Steven Aftergood
fas.why: Directed the Project on Government Secrecy 1991-2021
fas.note: Aftergood joined FAS in 1989 and directed the Project on Government Secrecy from 1991 to 2021. Attested by the FAS expert page.

fas.label: National Reconnaissance Office
fas.why: 2006 FOIA suit forced release of unclassified NRO budget records
fas.note: Aftergood, for FAS, won a FOIA suit against the National Reconnaissance Office securing release of unclassified budget records. Attested by the FAS expert page.

michigan-state.label: Mark Skidmore
michigan-state.why: Morris Chair in State and Local Government Finance and Policy
michigan-state.note: Skidmore holds the Morris Chair and is Professor of Economics at Michigan State University. Attested by his own site.

solari.label: Catherine Austin Fitts
solari.note: Fitts is founder and president of Solari, Inc., publisher of the Solari Report and the Missing Money archive. Attested by Solari's own biography page.

boston-university.label: Laurence J. Kotlikoff
boston-university.note: Kotlikoff is Professor of Economics at Boston University. Attested by the co-authored publication record.

nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.label: Federation of American Scientists
nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.why: FAS hosts the excerpts and the redacted FOIA budget justifications
nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.note: The FAS Intelligence Resource Program budget page indexes the FY2013 NIP Summary excerpts alongside redacted Congressional Budget Justifications for ODNI, NRO, NGA and the MIP. Attested by the page itself.

nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.why: The only public view of the interior of the National Intelligence Program
nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.note: The FY2013 NIP Summary excerpts, classified TS/SI/TK/NOFORN, were released via the Washington Post in August 2013 and are hosted by FAS; the officially disclosed figure for the same year was a single aggregate. Attested by the FAS document index.

nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.label: The Classified Schedule of Authorizations (Intelligence Authorization Act)
nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.why: What the Schedule of Authorizations looks like from the inside
nip-fy2013-summary-disclosure.note: The FY2013 excerpts show agency, programme and objective-level detail of the kind that section 6102 of the Intelligence Authorization Act keeps in the classified Schedule. The inference that the two documents describe the same structure is reasoned; no source states it.

uk-mod-ufo-desk.label: DI55 - Defence Intelligence Staff, Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence
uk-mod-ufo-desk.why: public desk fed the intelligence section's database
uk-mod-ufo-desk.note: Condign's database was built from approximately 10,000 reports accumulated by DI55 from the reporting stream the desk handled.

uk-mod-ufo-desk.label: Nick Pope
uk-mod-ufo-desk.note: Sky HISTORY, the broadcaster he worked for, records that he joined the MoD in 1985 and 'boarded its UFO programme in 1991', staying three years.

uk-mod-ufo-desk.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
uk-mod-ufo-desk.why: the two opposite answers to the same problem
uk-mod-ufo-desk.note: France put the file in a civil science agency with a public archive and it is still running; Britain kept it in a defence secretariat with no project name and closed it. Reasoning: contrasting institutional siting and survival of the two arrangements over the same period.

uk-di55.label: Ministry of Defence UFO Desk (Secretariat (Air Staff) / Directorate of Air Staff)
uk-di55.why: public desk fed the intelligence section's database
uk-di55.note: Condign's database was built from approximately 10,000 reports accumulated by DI55 from the reporting stream the desk handled.

uk-di55.label: Project Condign
uk-di55.why: study commissioned by and reporting on DI55
uk-di55.note: The product was issued as DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00 and its key recommendation was addressed to DI55's own tasking.

project-condign.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region (DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00)
project-condign.note: Project Condign's output is 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region'.

project-condign.label: DI55 - Defence Intelligence Staff, Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence
project-condign.why: study commissioned by and reporting on DI55
project-condign.note: The product was issued as DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00 and its key recommendation was addressed to DI55's own tasking.

doc-condign-report.label: Project Condign Volume 3 - Potential for Exploitation of UAP-Associated Effects / UAP Work in Other Countries
doc-condign-report.why: Volume 3 holds the material excluded from the RESTRICTED summary
doc-condign-report.note: Volume 3's own opening states that it 'primarily deals with sensitive matters associated with the UAP study which could not be placed in the RESTRICTED Executive Summary'.

doc-condign-report.label: London, United Kingdom
doc-condign-report.why: produced at Whitehall, released via TNA at Kew
doc-condign-report.note: Both ends of the Condign story sit in London: the report was held at the MoD Main Building in Whitehall, and the MoD's historical UFO files were transferred to The National Archives at Kew between 2008 and 2013 after the reporting desk closed in December 2009.

doc-condign-report.label: United Kingdom
doc-condign-report.why: UK-commissioned study of its own air defence region
doc-condign-report.note: Condign drew on approximately 10,000 sightings and reports gathered by DI55 within the UK Air Defence Region, making it a state-commissioned assessment of the phenomenon over British territory with no American equivalent released to the public.

doc-condign-report.label: Ministry of Defence Main Building, Whitehall, London
doc-condign-report.why: Condign report held at MoD Main Building
doc-condign-report.note: Project Condign was run by the Defence Intelligence Staff branch DI55 between 1997 and 2000; the resulting three-volume, 463-page report 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region' was held at the Ministry of Defence Main Building in Whitehall.

doc-condign-report.label: Dr David Clarke
doc-condign-report.why: FOI request that forced the release
doc-condign-report.note: Clarke and Gary Anthony filed the September 2005 FOI request; the MoD released the report on 15 May 2006 and logged an internal review in its own disclosure log.

doc-condign-report.label: Project Condign
doc-condign-report.note: Project Condign's output is 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region'.

doc-condign-report.label: Gary Anthony
doc-condign-report.note: Named with Clarke as co-requester in the report's release history and in contemporaneous BBC and Guardian coverage.

doc-condign-report.label: Closure of the MoD UFO Desk, 1 December 2009
doc-condign-report.why: key recommendation executed nine years later
doc-condign-report.note: Condign's single key recommendation was that DI55 should no longer be required to monitor UAP reports and that the database should not be maintained; the desk that fed it closed in 2009 on the same stated ground.

doc-condign-report.label: Project Magnet (Canada)
doc-condign-report.why: 1952 recommendation to acquire the technology prefigures Condign's redacted 'Related Military Applications'
doc-condign-report.note: Smith's 1952 report recommends 'acquisition of as much as possible of this technology'; Condign's own paragraph 7, 'Related Military Applications', is redacted in full under the defence exemption. Reasoning: both are government documents whose exploitation sections are the point at which the record becomes either explicit or withheld.

doc-condign-vol3.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region (DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00)
doc-condign-vol3.why: Volume 3 holds the material excluded from the RESTRICTED summary
doc-condign-vol3.note: Volume 3's own opening states that it 'primarily deals with sensitive matters associated with the UAP study which could not be placed in the RESTRICTED Executive Summary'.

doc-condign-vol3.label: United Kingdom Ministry of Defence
doc-condign-vol3.why: records a flat denial of any US/Canada exchange, then redacts four lines
doc-condign-vol3.note: Volume 3 para 12: 'There is no intelligence exchange or access or collaboration of any sort on the topic of UFOs' - followed by approximately four redacted lines.

doc-condign-vol3.label: SETKA-AN / SETKA-MO (later Galaktika, then Gorizont) - Soviet state anomalous phenomena programme
doc-condign-vol3.why: assessed the Soviet programme as exploitation-driven
doc-condign-vol3.note: Condign Volume 3 chapter 4 states that Soviet study of UAP 'may well be related to a programme of understanding and exploiting certain UAP-related natural phenomena, such as plasmas'.

doc-condign-vol3.label: SOYUZUFOTSENTR - USSR Inter-Industry Ufology Research Centre
doc-condign-vol3.why: Condign's Former Soviet Union chapter names, dates and assesses SOYUZUFOTSENTR
doc-condign-vol3.note: This is the reason the node exists at all. SOYUZUFOTSENTR reaches this board not through Russian ufology literature but through a UK SECRET UK EYES ONLY Defence Intelligence Staff assessment, which places the centre inside a paragraph opening 'It[s] clear that the Former Soviet Union has taken the study of UAPs seriously and th[a]t this may well be related to a programme of understanding and exploiting certain UAP-related natural phenomena, such as plasmas.' The same chapter runs on to Popovich's 1990 All Union Ufology Association at the Air Force Academy, General of Aviation Igor Maltsev's 1990 release of pilot reports, Vsevolod Troitsky of the Russian Academy of Sciences chairing a Commission for the Study of Anomalous Propagation and Phenomena, and Sokolov's account of Soviet aircraft incidents. Condign treats the public centre and the state effort as one national picture. Verified line by line against the released OCR.

doc-condign-vol3.label: Spanish Ministry of Defence UFO file declassification
doc-condign-vol3.why: records the Spanish release and DI55's non-access
doc-condign-vol3.note: 'Sixty six files have reportedly been released to the public. DI 55 Staff have not seen these files.'

doc-condign-vol3.label: Vladimir Georgievich Azhazha
doc-condign-vol3.why: names Azhazha as head of SOYUZUFOTSENTR
doc-condign-vol3.note: Condign identifies 'V.G. AZAHAZHA (or AZHAZHA) an eminent researcher and former naval submariner' as head of the 1990 inter-industry ufology research centre.

tna-ufo-release.label: Release of the Rendlesham Forest files, August 2009 (DEFE 24/1948)
tna-ufo-release.why: the August 2009 tranche carried the Rendlesham material
tna-ufo-release.note: The National Archives itself billed the tranche as containing 'Britain's very own Roswell - Rendlesham Forest in Suffolk'.

tna-ufo-release.label: DEFE 24 and DEFE 31 - MoD UFO record series, The National Archives, Kew
tna-ufo-release.why: released files placed in DEFE 24 and DEFE 31
tna-ufo-release.note: Every tranche page lists the piece numbers transferred; the final June 2013 tranche is DEFE 24/2448-2465 and 2623-2629.

tna-ufo-release.label: Dr David Clarke
tna-ufo-release.why: wrote the highlights guide for every tranche
tna-ufo-release.note: Each National Archives UFO release page credits Dr David Clarke's guide and carries his videocast or podcast.

tna-ufo-release.label: Nick Pope
tna-ufo-release.why: fronted the publicity for the file releases
tna-ufo-release.note: The MoD approached Pope to help with the publicity drive when it decided to declassify and release the files; he became, in the broadcaster's phrase, the face of the Ministry's new-found transparency.

uk-defe24.label: The National Archives / MoD UFO File Release Programme (2008-2013)
uk-defe24.why: released files placed in DEFE 24 and DEFE 31
uk-defe24.note: Every tranche page lists the piece numbers transferred; the final June 2013 tranche is DEFE 24/2448-2465 and 2623-2629.

ev-uk-ufo-desk-closure.label: Nick Pope
ev-uk-ufo-desk-closure.why: principal public critic of the 2009 closure
ev-uk-ufo-desk-closure.note: The National Archives records that the closure sparked a disclosure campaign; Pope was its most prominent voice and the only former desk officer speaking publicly.

ev-uk-ufo-desk-closure.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region (DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00)
ev-uk-ufo-desk-closure.why: key recommendation executed nine years later
ev-uk-ufo-desk-closure.note: Condign's single key recommendation was that DI55 should no longer be required to monitor UAP reports and that the database should not be maintained; the desk that fed it closed in 2009 on the same stated ground.

uk-fs-working-party.label: United Kingdom Ministry of Defence
uk-fs-working-party.why: first British body on the question, 1950-1951
uk-fs-working-party.note: The Flying Saucer Working Party precedes the UFO desk and reached the same self-terminating conclusion Condign would reach fifty years later.

cometa.label: France
cometa.note: COMETA operated informally from 1996 and was registered as a non-profit association under the French law of 1901 on 24 February 1999; its membership was drawn almost entirely from French flag officers, weapons engineers and IHEDN auditors.

cometa.label: Professeur André Lebeau
cometa.why: former CNES chairman; wrote the forward
cometa.note: Letty states that without Norlain and Lebeau 'COMETA would not have been born'.

cometa.label: Général Bernard Norlain
cometa.why: IHEDN director who sponsored the project
cometa.note: Norlain's own preface records that Letty came to his IHEDN office in March 1995 and that he referred the project to the Auditors Association, which backed it.

cometa.label: Général Denis Letty
cometa.note: Letty signs the report's foreword as chairman of the association and names the members and contributors himself.

cometa.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
cometa.why: shared IHEDN lineage; SEPRA head contributed
cometa.note: COMETA's introduction states that GEPAN was created on the recommendations of a 1976 IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, and Jean-Jacques Velasco, then head of SEPRA at CNES, is named among the report's contributors. COMETA also recommended 'developing the actions of SEPRA'.

cometa.label: Les OVNI et la Défense: à quoi doit-on se préparer? (COMETA report, July 1999)
cometa.note: Published as a special issue of VSD in July 1999 and delivered to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.

cometa.label: Project Blue Book
cometa.note: COMETA chapter 7.2 states that the strangest category D cases 'are generally labeled CE3s (close encounters of the third kind) according to the classification proposed by Professor A. Hynek, an astronomer and consultant to the USAF, within the context of the Blue Book Project'. Chapter 9 of the report separately surveys the organisation of research abroad.

cometa.label: Roswell Incident
cometa.why: dedicated appendix on Roswell and disinformation
cometa.note: COMETA's appendix 5 is titled 'The Roswell Affair - Disinformation'. A committee of retired French flag officers treating Roswell as a subject requiring an appendix in a defence study is itself part of what makes the document unusual.

cometa.label: Jean-Jacques Velasco
cometa.why: serving head of SEPRA contributed to the report
cometa.note: Letty names 'Jean-Jacques Velasco, Head of SEPRA at CNES' among those who gave testimony or contributed.

cometa.label: Paris, France
cometa.why: IHEDN origin; delivered to the Prime Minister
cometa.note: General Letty took the project to General Norlain at his IHEDN office in March 1995, and the report was subsequently delivered to the head of the French government. Robert Roussel, citing Jospin's chief of staff Olivier Schrameck, states the Prime Minister read and annotated it 'to mark his interest'. The handover route is not established from any primary document, hence tier 3.

cometa.label: SETKA-AN / SETKA-MO (later Galaktika, then Gorizont) - Soviet state anomalous phenomena programme
cometa.why: cites Soviet statistical distributions as comparable
cometa.note: COMETA chapter 7.3 records that 'statistical studies in the USSR yielded distributions comparable to those determined by Claude Poher, the first head of GEPAN, from some 200 French cases, or 1,000 cases worldwide'. The report does not name SETKA, and the identification of the Soviet studies with the SETKA programme is inference rather than citation - hence tier 3. [Re-pointed from the collapsed duplicate `setka`, 14 Aug 2026.]

doc-cometa-report.label: SEPRA - Service d'Expertise des Phénomènes de Rentrée Atmosphérique / Phénomènes Rares Aérospatiaux
doc-cometa-report.why: recommended boosting SEPRA's resources and foreign relations status
doc-cometa-report.note: Recommendation 2 asks the French state to expand the very office whose serving head had contributed to the report.

doc-cometa-report.label: COMETA - Comité d'Études Approfondies
doc-cometa-report.note: Published as a special issue of VSD in July 1999 and delivered to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.

doc-cometa-report.label: Aerolíneas Argentinas flight AR 674, San Carlos de Bariloche, 31 July 1995
doc-cometa-report.why: the US 2026 release cites COMETA as a source on the Argentine case
doc-cometa-report.note: The Buenos Aires Times reports that the released file sits in a section on investigations conducted outside the United States and 'references a report produced by COMETA'.

gepan.label: Dr Claude Poher
gepan.note: The NSA-held contemporaneous assessment records GEPAN's creation in 1977 under Poher and his resignation.

gepan.label: Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale (IHEDN)
gepan.note: COMETA's own introduction: a 1976 IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale opened the file and its recommendations produced GEPAN.

gepan.label: National Security Agency
gepan.why: US NSA holds a contemporaneous assessment of GEPAN's 1978 report

intl-uap-office-model.note: SEFAA sits inside the DGAC, publishes monthly resolved-case bulletins and archives cases by year back to 2018.

intl-uap-office-model.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
intl-uap-office-model.why: the reference implementation of a civil state UAP office
intl-uap-office-model.note: Published classification, published case conclusions, national police feed, three full-time staff and twenty-plus trained volunteers.

intl-uap-office-model.label: Sky Canada Project - Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada
intl-uap-office-model.why: the report is the source of the three-office model
intl-uap-office-model.note: This is the first time a G7 government has publicly named which other countries' arrangements it would copy.

cnes.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
cnes.why: GEIPAN is a unit of CNES at Toulouse
cnes.note: The French office has been hosted inside the national space agency continuously since 1977, an arrangement Norlain called unique in the world.

l-wright-patterson.label: The Pentacle Memorandum
l-wright-patterson.why: Addressed to Miles E. Goll at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
l-wright-patterson.note: No signed original has ever been produced by the Air Force or by Battelle.

l-wright-patterson.label: Bolender Memorandum
l-wright-patterson.why: The Bolender memo closed the base's public reporting channel while conceding another existed
l-wright-patterson.note: Brig. Gen. Carroll Bolender's 1969 memorandum recommended Blue Book's termination and stated that reports which could affect national security were never part of the Blue Book system - a statement about this base's own reporting architecture.

l-wright-patterson.label: Air Technical Intelligence Center
l-wright-patterson.why: ATIC and its successors were and are headquartered at Wright-Patterson
l-wright-patterson.note: The Air Technical Intelligence Center, formed in 1951 from Air Materiel Command's T-2 intelligence organisation at Wright Field, became the Foreign Technology Division in 1961 and NASIC in 1993, which remains at the base. Attested by USAF unit histories.

l-wright-patterson.label: Air Technical Intelligence Center
l-wright-patterson.why: ATIC and every legacy UFO project were located at Wright-Patterson
l-wright-patterson.note: SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book were all headquartered at Wright-Patterson AFB, the site of the Air Force's foreign materiel exploitation organisation and its successors.

l-wright-patterson.label: National Air and Space Intelligence Center
l-wright-patterson.why: NASIC is the current tenant institution at Wright-Patterson
l-wright-patterson.note: The National Air and Space Intelligence Center is a Wright-Patterson tenant and the direct institutional heir to ATIC/FTD's foreign materiel exploitation mission.

l-wright-patterson.label: Nathan F. Twining
l-wright-patterson.why: Twining wrote the 1947 AMC assessment from this command
l-wright-patterson.note: Lt. Gen. Nathan Twining signed 'AMC Opinion Concerning Flying Discs' on 23 September 1947 as commander of Air Materiel Command, headquartered at Wright Field.

l-wright-patterson.label: New Jersey and East Coast Drone Wave (Nov-Dec 2024)
l-wright-patterson.why: Wright-Patterson closed its airspace for nearly four hours during the wave
l-wright-patterson.note: The 14-15 December 2024 airspace closure over unauthorized drone activity occurred days before the federal statement that nothing anomalous had been identified.

l-wright-patterson.label: Project Blue Book
l-wright-patterson.why: Blue Book was hosted at Wright-Patterson from 1952 to 1969
l-wright-patterson.note: Project Blue Book, like SIGN and GRUDGE before it, was hosted at this base under ATIC. Of 12,618 sightings studied, 701 remained unexplained at closure. Attested by USAF fact sheets.

l-wright-patterson.label: Battelle Memorial Institute
l-wright-patterson.note: The research lineage from which nitinol shape-memory alloy emerged; researchers including Anthony Bragalia allege the corresponding reports are missing from both Air Force and Battelle archives.

l-wright-patterson.label: William Neil McCasland
l-wright-patterson.why: Commanded the Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson
l-wright-patterson.note: AFRL at Wright-Patterson is the single installation most persistently named in the legacy recovery literature.

l-wright-patterson.label: David Charles Grusch
l-wright-patterson.why: Corroborating NASIC officer sits at the installation at the center of the legacy custody claims
l-wright-patterson.note: Grusch testified he knows the exact locations of held material and provided them to the Inspector General; the one corroborator whose duty station is public serves at NASIC, Wright-Patterson. Reasoning: the geography is suggestive and no document places Grusch's locations at Wright-Patterson.

l-wright-patterson.label: Operation BLUE FLY
l-wright-patterson.why: Recovered material routed to Air Force technical intelligence at Wright-Patterson
l-wright-patterson.note: Foreign Technology Division at Wright-Patterson was the designated technical exploitation centre; the Air Force felt it necessary in its January 1985 public fact sheet to deny that extraterrestrial equipment had ever been there.

l-kirtland.label: AFOSI Kirtland AFB UFO File (1980-1983)
l-kirtland.why: The AFOSI Kirtland file is the documentary residue of the Bennewitz operation
l-kirtland.note: The AFOSI documents concerning the 1980 Kirtland incidents are the only contemporaneous official records of the observations that triggered the campaign against Bennewitz.

l-kirtland.label: Albuquerque, New Mexico
l-kirtland.why: Kirtland AFB lies inside the Albuquerque city limits
l-kirtland.note: The base occupies 51,558 acres in the southeast quadrant of Albuquerque and shares runways with the Albuquerque International Sunport.

l-kirtland.label: Sandia National Laboratories
l-kirtland.why: Sandia National Laboratories is adjacent to Kirtland AFB
l-kirtland.note: Sandia, descended from the Manhattan Project's Z Division, sits adjacent to Kirtland; Bennewitz licensed his humidity sensor technology from Sandia in 1966.

l-kirtland.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
l-kirtland.why: nuclear-adjacent installations named in AARO's own unresolved allegations
l-kirtland.note: Volume I page 30 records interviews with five former Air Force officers who served at Malmstrom, Ellsworth, Vandenberg and Minot between 1966 and 1977 and defers the unresolved allegations to Volume II.

l-kirtland.label: AFOSI Kirtland AFB UFO File (1980-1983)
l-kirtland.why: AFOSI District 17 file generated at Kirtland AFB
l-kirtland.note: The 10 November 1980 record concerns observations by Kirtland security police over Coyote Canyon and the Manzano storage area.

l-kirtland.label: Kirtland AFB / Manzano Weapons Storage Area incident
l-kirtland.why: Occurred at the Manzano Weapons Storage Area and Coyote Canyon
l-kirtland.note: Manzano is a nuclear weapons storage area on the Kirtland footprint shared with Sandia National Laboratories.

l-kirtland.label: Paul Frederick Bennewitz
l-kirtland.why: Bennewitz's 1979-1980 observations were of the Manzano area of Kirtland AFB
l-kirtland.note: Bennewitz dated his personally funded study to July 1979, filmed lights and recorded signals over the base, contacted Kirtland on 24 October 1980 and briefed base officials on 10 November 1980. Attested by his own correspondence and contemporary press.

l-kirtland.label: Richard C. Doty
l-kirtland.why: Doty's AFOSI detachment ran the Bennewitz deception from Kirtland
l-kirtland.note: Richard C. Doty, an AFOSI special agent at Kirtland, has said publicly he was tasked in the 1980s with hoaxing documents and feeding false information to UFO researchers including Bennewitz. A 1992 article held in the CIA library names Doty and William Moore.

l-kirtland.label: YANKEE BLUE (alleged AFOSI indoctrination program)
l-kirtland.why: reported in the lineage of Air Force UFO deception operations centred on Kirtland/AFOSI
l-kirtland.note: Yankee Blue sits in the same documented Air Force practice of manufacturing UFO belief for security purposes as the Kirtland AFB/AFOSI operations against Paul Bennewitz. The connection is thematic and institutional; no released document ties Yankee Blue administratively to Kirtland.

l-albuquerque.label: Kirtland Air Force Base and Albuquerque, New Mexico
l-albuquerque.why: Kirtland AFB lies inside the Albuquerque city limits
l-albuquerque.note: The base occupies 51,558 acres in the southeast quadrant of Albuquerque and shares runways with the Albuquerque International Sunport.

l-albuquerque.label: Steven H. Schiff
l-albuquerque.why: Schiff's New Mexico district inquiry produced the GAO Roswell audit
l-albuquerque.note: Rep. Steven H. Schiff of New Mexico asked GAO to search federal records after the Defense Department declined to answer his Roswell inquiries, producing GAO/NSIAD-95-187.

l-albuquerque.label: Lincoln LaPaz
l-albuquerque.why: LaPaz investigated the green fireballs from the University of New Mexico
l-albuquerque.note: Lincoln LaPaz, the UNM meteoriticist retained by the Air Force, conducted the green fireball investigation from Albuquerque and attended the 16 February 1949 Los Alamos conference.

l-roswell.label: Roswell Incident
l-roswell.why: The 1947 recovery was executed by Roswell Army Air Field
l-roswell.note: Maj. Jesse Marcel of the 509th Bomb Group intelligence office and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps were dispatched from RAAF to the Foster Ranch. Attested by the 1947 press record and the Air Force's own reports.

l-roswell.label: Roswell Incident
l-roswell.why: The 509th Bomb Group at Roswell AAF was the only atomic-armed unit in the world
l-roswell.note: The recovery, the announcement and the destroyed records all belong to a single installation with the most restrictive information discipline in the US military.

l-roswell.label: GAO/NSIAD-95-187, Government Records: Results of a Search for Records Concerning the 1947 Crash Near Roswell, New Mexico
l-roswell.why: GAO found the relevant RAAF records destroyed with no recorded authority
l-roswell.note: RAAF administrative records March 1945-December 1949 and outgoing messages October 1946-December 1949 were destroyed; the disposition form records neither who destroyed them nor under what authority.

l-roswell.label: White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico
l-roswell.why: Roswell sits inside the 1947 New Mexico nuclear and rocketry complex
l-roswell.note: The Foster Ranch debris field, White Sands Proving Ground, the Alamogordo Mogul launch site, Los Alamos, Sandia and Kirtland all lie within a few hundred miles. Reasoning: geographic proximity is the reason a materiel recovery there fell inside multiple classified security envelopes at once.

l-groom-lake.label: Area 51 (Homey Airport / Groom Lake operating location)
l-groom-lake.why: Area 51 is the named facility on the Groom Lake shore
l-groom-lake.note: The operating location is carried on charts as Homey Airport and sits on the southwest shore of the Groom Lake salt flat inside R-4808N.

l-groom-lake.label: Presidential Determinations on the Air Force's Operating Location Near Groom Lake
l-groom-lake.why: Annual presidential determinations exempt the Groom Lake operating location from environmental disclosure
l-groom-lake.note: Published in the Federal Register every year since 1995, the determinations never name the facility or describe its contents - the cleanest documentary proof of a contractor-operated site legally exempted from statutory disclosure.

l-groom-lake.label: Edwards Air Force Base, California
l-groom-lake.why: Edwards defines the acknowledged-testing boundary that Groom Lake was built to escape
l-groom-lake.note: Groom Lake exists because the U-2 could not be tested at Edwards. The pair therefore mark the boundary between the acknowledged and unacknowledged US flight test enterprise.

l-groom-lake.label: Nellis Air Force Base and the Nevada Test and Training Range
l-groom-lake.why: Groom Lake was administratively carried as part of the Nellis complex
l-groom-lake.note: Until the 1995 presidential determination, the official position was that Groom Lake was simply another part of the Nellis Air Force Base complex.

l-groom-lake.label: Tonopah Test Range, Nevada
l-groom-lake.why: Programmes matured from Groom Lake to operational basing at Tonopah
l-groom-lake.note: HAVE IDEA moved to Tonopah in May 1973; the 4450th Tactical Group moved from Groom Lake to Tonopah beginning 17 May 1982 to operate the F-117A.

l-groom-lake.label: Lockheed Martin Advanced Development Programs (Skunk Works)
l-groom-lake.why: Skunk Works aircraft were tested at Groom Lake because they could not be tested at Edwards
l-groom-lake.note: The CIA's own history records that U-2 flight test and pilot training could not be conducted at Edwards or Palmdale given the secrecy of the project. The U-2, A-12, HAVE BLUE and F-117 all flew first at Groom.

l-groom-lake.label: EG&G (Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier)
l-groom-lake.why: EG&G provided the classified site services and personnel transport for the Groom Lake operating location
l-groom-lake.note: The relationship is documented indirectly through the Groom Lake worker litigation and the annual presidential environmental exemptions rather than through any acknowledgment of the facility.

l-groom-lake.label: Las Vegas, Nevada
l-groom-lake.why: The Groom and Tonopah workforce commutes from Las Vegas
l-groom-lake.note: The unmarked JANET fleet operates from a dedicated terminal at the Las Vegas airport. Reasoning: publicly observable daily operations; no primary personnel or contract record has been obtained.

l-groom-lake.label: STAR GATE and predecessor remote viewing programs, 1970-1995
l-groom-lake.why: Both are demonstrations of decades-long concealment ending in bulk declassification
l-groom-lake.note: Groom Lake ran 58 years to specific acknowledgement via FOIA; STAR GATE ran 25 years to bulk CREST publication in 2017. Reasoning: structural comparison of two documented concealment lifecycles.

l-area51.label: Groom Lake, Nevada
