l-ames.label: National Aeronautics and Space Administration
l-ames.why: NASA field centre at Moffett Field
l-ames.note: Ames Research Center at Moffett Field, Mountain View, California is one of ten NASA field centres, selected as NACA's second aeronautical research laboratory on 20 December 1939 and absorbed into NASA in 1958.

l-stockholm.label: Astronomy & Astrophysics
l-stockholm.note: Villarroel's Stockholm-based VASCO project produced the October 2025 Scientific Reports correlation between POSS-I transients, nuclear testing and UAP reports.

l-fort-worth-tx.label: Roswell
l-fort-worth-tx.why: Where the disc became a balloon
l-fort-worth-tx.note: The Roswell debris was flown to Eighth Air Force headquarters at Fort Worth, where it was presented to the press as a weather balloon the same day.

l-virginia.label: National Reconnaissance Office
l-virginia.note: Since 1995 the National Reconnaissance Office has occupied a 68-acre compound at the Westfields International Center in Chantilly, Virginia, part of the Northern Virginia intelligence corridor this node stands for.

l-uk.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region (DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00)
l-uk.why: UK-commissioned study of its own air defence region
l-uk.note: Condign drew on approximately 10,000 sightings and reports gathered by DI55 within the UK Air Defence Region, making it a state-commissioned assessment of the phenomenon over British territory with no American equivalent released to the public.

l-uk.label: Rendlesham Forest Incident, RAF Woodbridge/Bentwaters
l-uk.note: The December 1980 reports were made by USAF personnel stationed at RAF Woodbridge and RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk, England. That the reports were made at this location is documented in the MoD file; the nature of what was seen remains unresolved.

l-france.label: COMETA - Comité d'Études Approfondies
l-france.note: COMETA operated informally from 1996 and was registered as a non-profit association under the French law of 1901 on 24 February 1999; its membership was drawn almost entirely from French flag officers, weapons engineers and IHEDN auditors.

l-france.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
l-france.why: French national UAP office, CNES Toulouse
l-france.note: GEIPAN is a technical department of CNES attached to the deputy directorate of the Toulouse Space Centre, with jurisdiction over sightings on French territory. CNES lists its location as Toulouse and its status as 'In operation' with an indefinite lifetime.

l-brazil.note: São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Goiás. A national-scale event, which is why it reads as a state posture rather than a local incident. l-brazil.why: Operação Prato was run on Colares, Pará, in northern Brazil
l-brazil.note: Pratt's file: intelligence agents 'from the Air Force base in Belém in northern Brazil interviewed hundreds of witnesses in Colares and about thirty other villages north of Belém'.

l-paris.label: COMETA - Comité d'Études Approfondies
l-paris.why: IHEDN origin; delivered to the Prime Minister
l-paris.note: General Letty took the project to General Norlain at his IHEDN office in March 1995, and the report was subsequently delivered to the head of the French government. Robert Roussel, citing Jospin's chief of staff Olivier Schrameck, states the Prime Minister read and annotated it 'to mark his interest'. The handover route is not established from any primary document, hence tier 3.

l-london.label: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region (DIS Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00)
l-london.why: produced at Whitehall, released via TNA at Kew
l-london.note: Both ends of the Condign story sit in London: the report was held at the MoD Main Building in Whitehall, and the MoD's historical UFO files were transferred to The National Archives at Kew between 2008 and 2013 after the reporting desk closed in December 2009.

l-ottawa.label: Sky Canada Project - Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada
l-ottawa.why: Office of the Chief Science Advisor, Ottawa
l-ottawa.note: The Sky Canada Project is run by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada, seated in Ottawa. Its report reviewed how UAP reports are handled in Canada and recommended the creation of a federal office to collect and investigate them.

l-santiago.label: CEFAA / SEFAA - Chilean anomalous aerial phenomena office, Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
l-santiago.note: Established at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in the Quinta Normal aeronautical complex, Santiago, the same site where Chile's 1968-1975 predecessor commission had operated out of the Oficina Meteorológica. SEFAA is now at Av. Pedro Aguirre Cerda 5100, Cerrillos, Santiago.

l-moscow.label: SETKA-AN / SETKA-MO (later Galaktika, then Gorizont) - Soviet state anomalous phenomena programme
l-moscow.why: run from Moscow: Kremlin decision, MoD institute, IZMIRAN
l-moscow.note: The founding Scientific and Technical Council meeting of the Military-Industrial Commission was held in the Kremlin in October 1977; the lead military executor was 'one of the central military research institutes in the Moscow region'; and the academic branch was run from IZMIRAN, also in the Moscow region. [Re-pointed from the collapsed duplicate `setka`, 14 Aug 2026.]

l-lasvegas.label: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)
l-lasvegas.why: AAWSAP contract performed from Las Vegas
l-lasvegas.note: Performance on DIA contract HHM402-08-C-0072 began 22 September 2008 with an initial value of $10 million; the work was carried out by BAASS in Nevada, making Las Vegas the operational centre of the AAWSAP effort rather than Washington.

l-lasvegas.label: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS), LLC
l-lasvegas.note: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, the sole bidder on DIA solicitation HHM402-08-R-0211 and holder of contract HHM402-08-C-0072, operated from Robert Bigelow's Las Vegas, Nevada base.

l-lasvegas.label: National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDS)
l-lasvegas.note: The National Institute for Discovery Science was a privately financed research organisation based in Las Vegas, Nevada, founded by Robert Bigelow in 1995 and disbanded in October 2004. It is the direct institutional predecessor of the BAASS staffing that later executed AAWSAP.

l-lasvegas.label: Harry M. Reid
l-lasvegas.why: Reid's Nevada base; earmark performed by a Las Vegas constituent
l-lasvegas.note: This is not merely a home-town link: Senator Harry Reid of Nevada secured the appropriation with Senators Inouye and Stevens, and the money was performed by Robert Bigelow, a Las Vegas constituent. The constituent relationship is the reported mechanism connecting the earmark to the contractor.

l-cambridge-ma.label: Abraham 'Avi' Loeb
l-cambridge-ma.why: Loeb's Harvard base; launched the project from here
l-cambridge-ma.note: Avi Loeb is a Harvard astrophysicist and launched the Galileo Project in 2021 from Cambridge, Massachusetts. Unlike the other academic locations on this board, the institution here hosts the actual detection hardware.

l-cambridge-ma.label: The Galileo Project
l-cambridge-ma.why: first Galileo Observatory, Harvard College Observatory roof
l-cambridge-ma.note: The Galileo Project's first all-sky observatory is on the roof of the Harvard College Observatory in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It is the physical instrument site for the project's instrumented search, not merely an administrative address.

waived-sap-notification-group.note: Luna is not listed among the members of the House Armed Services Committee and does not hold a chair or ranking seat on any of the six bodies named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g).

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Betty McCollum
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 12 of 12 - Ranking Member, House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Was vice chair of the same subcommittee in 2020, which is not one of the twelve seats.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Howard P. "Buck" McKeon
waived-sap-notification-group.why: Ranking Member then Chairman, House Armed Services Committee
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Entered the twelve-member group on his election as ranking member, announced by the committee chairman on 16 June 2009, and remained in it as chairman through the 112th and 113th Congresses to January 2015. Longest continuous House Armed Services occupancy of a 119(e)(2) seat in the 2009-2015 window the board's current-holder roster does not cover.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Christopher A. Coons
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 6 of 12 - Ranking Member, Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Congressional UAP Caucus
waived-sap-notification-group.why: caucus membership confers no statutory access
waived-sap-notification-group.note: A congressional caucus is not a committee and appears nowhere in 10 U.S.C. 119(g). Caucus members acquire no entitlement to waived-SAP notification, which is why UAP advocacy in Congress has consistently sought to legislate new access rather than to invoke existing access.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Program structure and organisational mapping
waived-sap-notification-group.why: the four-member channel that 10 U.S.C. 119(e) substitutes for committee reporting
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Sec. 119(e)(2) directs that where the Secretary exercises the waiver, the information and the justification go jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees - the Armed Services and Appropriations committees of both chambers. Attaching this node to the structural domain is what stops the two channels being conflated. [Corrected 14 Aug 2026: 10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as SIX bodies including both Appropriations Defense subcommittees, so notification runs to twelve seats, not eight. Section 119 uses its own definition, not 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16).]

waived-sap-notification-group.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)
waived-sap-notification-group.why: Secretary of Defense is the notifying authority under 119(e)
waived-sap-notification-group.note: The waiver decision under 119(e)(1) belongs to the Secretary of Defense personally and must be made case by case on a determination that inclusion would adversely affect the national security. The statute prescribes no review of that determination.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
waived-sap-notification-group.why: DoDI 5205.11 para. 7.2.a(3) - waived-SAP access limited to chair, ranking member, staff directors and one security manager
waived-sap-notification-group.note: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs,' effective 12 September 2024, para. 7.2.a(3): 'Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' This is materially wider than 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) on two axes: it admits committee staff directors and a security manager, and it extends to the intelligence committees, which have no entitlement under section 119. Any board text asserting that the twelve have no staff who can read the material should be corrected against this paragraph. Para. 7.2.b confirms that ordinary members of the defense and intelligence committees are authorised access to all DoD SAPs in their jurisdiction 'except for waived programs.'

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Eric Burlison
waived-sap-notification-group.why: no statutory entitlement; not a defense committee chair or ranking member
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Burlison is not listed among the members of the House Armed Services Committee and does not hold a chair or ranking seat on any of the six bodies named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g). His UAP oversight work therefore proceeds without any section 119 entitlement.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Harry M. Reid
waived-sap-notification-group.why: Senate Majority Leader in 2009 - in the Gang of Eight, not in the 119(e)(2) group
waived-sap-notification-group.note: This is the cleanest demonstration that the two small groups are different sets. 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) includes the majority and minority leaders of the Senate. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and 119(g) do not; they reach only committee and subcommittee chairs and ranking members. A Senate Majority Leader has no statutory entitlement to waived DoD SAP notification by virtue of that office. In 2009 the Senate armed services and appropriations seats were held by Levin, McCain, Inouye and Cochran.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
waived-sap-notification-group.why: not a defense committee; receives nothing under 10 U.S.C. 119
waived-sap-notification-group.note: The July 2023 Grusch testimony was taken by a House Oversight subcommittee. That committee has no entitlement under section 119(e)(2) and no statutory route to compel waived-SAP material, which is a structural reason why the hearing could establish allegation but not access.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: John F. Reed
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 2 of 12 - Ranking Member, Senate Armed Services
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Continuously in the group across 2020 (ranking), 2023 (chairman) and August 2026 (ranking).

waived-sap-notification-group.label: John M. McHugh
waived-sap-notification-group.why: Ranking Member, House Armed Services Committee
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Held a 119(e)(2) seat from January 2009 until his replacement by McKeon in June 2009. The committee chairman's 2 June 2009 statement records that McHugh 'took the reins as Ranking Member ... in January'; the 16 June 2009 statement records McKeon in the seat. The start date is given as the convening of the 111th Congress; the exact day of the Republican Conference vote that seated McKeon is not stated in the committee record, so the end date is the date of the committee statement announcing it.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Ken Calvert
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 11 of 12 - Chair, House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee
waived-sap-notification-group.note: In the group in 2020 as ranking member and from 2023 as chair.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Mike Rogers (Alabama)
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 7 of 12 - Chairman, House Armed Services
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Distinct from Mike Rogers of Michigan, former House Intelligence chairman, whose committee holds no section 119 entitlement.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Mitch McConnell
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 5 of 12 - Chair, Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Previously a Gang of Eight member by virtue of Senate leadership office; now in the 119(e)(2) group by virtue of a subcommittee gavel. The two entitlements are disjoint.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Nancy Ruth Mace
waived-sap-notification-group.why: House Armed Services member but not chair or ranking - no 119(e)(2) entitlement
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Mace sits on the House Armed Services Committee, one of the six defense committees, yet receives nothing under section 119(e)(2), which names only the chairman and ranking minority member. She would also not be told under section 119 that a waiver had been exercised at all. This is the clearest single illustration of how narrow the aperture is even inside a defense committee.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Congressional oversight of special access programs
waived-sap-notification-group.why: the narrow aperture through which Congress sees waived DoD SAPs
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Section 119 contains no analogue to 50 U.S.C. 3093(g), which requires that the rest of the committee be told a limited notification occurred. Members of the defense committees outside the twelve are not informed that a waiver has been exercised.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Patty Murray
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 4 of 12 - Vice Chair (ranking minority member), Senate Appropriations
waived-sap-notification-group.note: The Senate Appropriations Committee styles its ranking minority member 'Vice Chair'. The title does not change the 119(e)(2) entitlement.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Roger F. Wicker
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 1 of 12 - Chairman, Senate Armed Services
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Also held a 119(e)(2) seat as Ranking Member during the 118th Congress.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Rosa L. DeLauro
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 10 of 12 - Ranking Member, House Appropriations
waived-sap-notification-group.note: In the group continuously across the 118th and 119th Congresses.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Senate Armed Services Committee

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Susan M. Collins
waived-sap-notification-group.why: seat 3 of 12 - Chair, Senate Appropriations
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Held two of the twelve seats simultaneously in the 118th Congress as ranking member of both the full committee and its Defense Subcommittee.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Waived Unacknowledged SAP (waived USAP) — the mechanism
waived-sap-notification-group.why: sole statutory recipient of waived-SAP notification
waived-sap-notification-group.note: The waiver mechanism at 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) does not eliminate reporting; it redirects it. Whatever the Secretary withholds from the report goes instead to these twelve members under 119(e)(2), together with the justification for withholding.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: 10 U.S.C. 119 — Special Access Programs: Congressional Oversight
waived-sap-notification-group.why: created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and defined by 119(g)
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Section 119 was added by Pub. L. 100-180 div. A title XI sec. 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987. Subsection (e)(2) directs waived-SAP information and the waiver justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each defense committee; subsection (g) supplies the six-body definition of 'defense committees' used by the section.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)
waived-sap-notification-group.why: the twelve members with statutory sight of a waived programme
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Entitlement is bounded by characterisation: section 119 reaches only activity the Department treats as a DoD special access program. Activity held outside that characterisation is outside the group's statutory sight line entirely.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
waived-sap-notification-group.why: four of the twelve seats are appropriations leadership
waived-sap-notification-group.note: The chair and ranking of both Appropriations Committees and both Defense Subcommittees sit in the 119(e)(2) group. This is the structural feature that distinguishes it from the Gang of Eight, which contains no appropriators, and it means the group's sight of a waived programme includes the money as well as the report.

waived-sap-notification-group.label: David Charles Grusch
waived-sap-notification-group.why: allegations of a programme withheld from the statutory notification channel
waived-sap-notification-group.note: Grusch's 26 July 2023 testimony was given to a House Oversight subcommittee, which holds no entitlement under section 119. The twelve members who did hold 119(e)(2) seats on that date were Reed, Wicker, Murray, Collins, Tester, Rogers of Alabama, Smith, Granger, DeLauro, Calvert and McCollum - eleven distinct individuals, because Collins held both Senate appropriations seats. None has made a public statement about what, if anything, was notified to them under section 119.

fab.whatItIs: The Forca Aerea Brasileira (FAB), the air arm of the Comando da Aeronautica, formerly the Ministerio da Aeronautica, which existed as a cabinet ministry from 1941 until the Ministry of Defence absorbed it in 1999. It is the Brazilian state organ that holds the air-defence radar picture, controls civil and military air traffic through CINDACTA and COMDABRA/COMAE, and receives pilot and controller reports of unidentified aerial objects. Since 2010 it has operated under a published administrative rule requiring it to register those reports and forward them to a civilian national archive.
fab.whyImplicated: The FAB is the board's control case. It is a mid-sized air force inside a country that spent 1964 to 1985 under a military dictatorship, which means it had every institutional reason to behave like the US Air Force did after 1947, and for a period it did: SIOANI in 1969, Operacao Prato in 1977 under a named captain, and an air-defence scramble in 1986 that it initially treated as a security event. What it then did is what makes it load-bearing. It did not build a permanent denial apparatus around the subject; it built a filing pipeline out of it. Portaria do Comando da Aeronautica no 551/GC3 of 9 August 2010 does not classify unidentified aerial phenomena reports, it routes them to the Arquivo Nacional for public consultation, and the FAB says on the record that everything it holds from 1952 to 2025 has gone there. Every structural argument the US posture rests on (national security, sources and methods, the danger of public panic, the need to protect radar performance data) was equally available to a Cold War military government in Brasilia, and Brasilia declined to use it.
fab.narrative:
The Brazilian Air Force arrives on this board not as a suspected participant in a legacy recovery programme but as the measuring stick against which the US posture is read. Its value is that it controls for almost every variable the US concealment argument depends on. Brazil had an air force with a genuine air-defence mission, a real radar network, supersonic interceptors, a military intelligence service (the SNI), and, for twenty-one years, a military government answerable to nobody. If the argument for permanent secrecy about anomalous aerial objects were driven by the intrinsic sensitivity of the subject, the FAB should look like the most closed institution on the map. Instead it is the most open, and the openness is administrative rather than rhetorical, which is what makes it hard to dismiss.

The institutional history runs in three phases. The first is investigative. In 1969 the FAB stood up the Sistema de Investigacao de Objetos Aereos Nao Identificados, SIOANI, inside the 4a Zona Aerea in Sao Paulo, the command later renamed IV COMAR. SIOANI ran for roughly three years before ceasing operations quietly in 1972, and left behind a documentary residue that is now in the Arquivo Nacional. The second and best known phase is Operacao Prato, the field operation the FAB mounted in Para in 1977 and 1978 under Capitao Uyrange Hollanda, which put uniformed personnel into riverine villages with cameras and orders to observe. The third is the 19 May 1986 night, when CINDACTA and civil radar produced returns the FAB could not reconcile, five fighters were launched, and the Minister of Aeronautics stood in front of the press four days later and said the Air Force had no technical explanation.

What happened after 1986 is the part that matters most for comparison. The FAB did not sustain a public debunking programme. It did not issue a terminal report closing the file the way Project Blue Book was closed in 1969 with the Condon Committee as its warrant. Its posture, as characterised in the Brazilian Senate's own record, was discretion without denial: reticent when unasked, non-denying when asked. Then, in stages between 2007 and 2010, it converted the material into an archival stream. From 2007 the Aeronautica began sending its ufological papers to the Arquivo Nacional in Brasilia. In April 2009 CENDOC, the Air Force's documentation and history centre, sent across the first tranche relating to the Para operation. In August 2010 the Comando da Aeronautica published Portaria no 551/GC3 in the Diario Oficial da Uniao, formalising the pipeline: reports of aerial phenomena received by the aerospace operations command are received, registered, catalogued and forwarded to the Arquivo Nacional, where they are made available for consultation.

That rule is the single most consequential artefact in this dossier, because it inverts the default. Under 551/GC3 the resting state of a Brazilian military UAP report is public. There is no analytic gate, no adjudication of credibility before release, no requirement that the object be resolved before the paperwork moves. A LATAM captain reporting lights over Guarulhos in September 2025 and a Londrina tower controller reporting an intermittent radar-and-visual target in November 2025 both end up as scanned forms a citizen can pull down. In August 2026 the FAB restated the position in a written note to CNN Brasil: all documents, videos, photographs and reports available within the Comando da Aeronautica concerning unidentified aerial phenomena for the period 1952 to 2025 have already been transferred to the Arquivo Nacional, where they are in the public domain.

The limits are real and should be stated. The transfer was one service only. The Senate record is explicit that from 2007 it was the Aeronautica, and not the Army and not the Navy, that sent its papers to the Arquivo Nacional, and a 2013 approach to the Ministry of Defence by Brazilian researchers was aimed specifically at prying loose the Army and Navy holdings. So Brazil is not a case of total disclosure. It is a case of one service unilaterally choosing custody-with-publication while its sister services did not, which is itself an argument that the choice was institutional rather than physically compelled by the nature of the material. Nothing in the FAB record establishes retrieval of a craft or reverse-engineering activity, and nothing here should be read as claiming otherwise. What it establishes is narrower and sharper: a military that scrambled interceptors against unresolved radar contacts, said so at a podium, and then put the file in a civilian archive did not find that any of those three acts destabilised the state. The US argument that it cannot do the first two, let alone the third, is therefore not a claim about the subject matter. It is a claim about the US institution.

fab.denialPosture: The FAB does not deny; it defers to the archive. Its standing public answer, restated in a written note in August 2026, is that everything it holds from 1952 to 2025 is already in the Arquivo Nacional and in the public domain, which converts every substantive question into a records query rather than a security refusal. That posture is itself the artefact: an air force that treats the subject as a filing matter has decided the subject is not a secret.
connections: Ran Operacao Prato (operacao-prato) in Para in 1977-78 under Capitao Uyrange Hollanda, and ran SIOANI at IV COMAR from 1969 to 1972.
Scrambled the interceptors in the 19 May 1986 event (ev-noite-ovnis-1986); its minister, Brigadeiro Octavio Julio Moreira Lima, gave the 23 May 1986 press conference.
Is the producing body of the Arquivo Nacional's Fundo OVNI (arquivo-nacional-ufo), reference BR DFANBSB ARX, via CENDOC and COMDABRA/COMAE.
Named repeatedly in Senado Federal RQS 193/2022 (senado-brasil) as the state organ that opened the files while the Army and Navy did not.
Structural counterpart to the US Air Force's Project Sign / Grudge / Blue Book lineage and to AARO: same problem, opposite disposal.
Worked alongside the Servico Nacional de Informacoes (SNI) on the Para operation; SNI holdings on the case were later released by the Gabinete de Seguranca Institucional.
openQuestions: The full text of Portaria no 551/GC3 of 9 August 2010 as published in the Diario Oficial da Uniao has not been retrieved directly; the date and content are attested by the FAB's own note and by the Senate record, not yet by the DOU page itself.

The Senate record spells the 2010 FAB commander as 'Junichi Saito'; the commander of the Aeronautica in that period is conventionally rendered Juniti Saito. The discrepancy has not been resolved against a primary FAB or DOU source.

The FAB says it has transferred everything through 2025, but the Arquivo Nacional's own description of the fund gives the most recent occurrence as 2016. Whether this reflects a lag in accessioning, a separate accrual series, or a genuine gap is unresolved.
No document has been located establishing why the Aeronautica transferred and the Exercito and Marinha did not, or what the Army and Navy holdings contain.

Nothing in the FAB record located here speaks to material recovery, custody of hardware, or reverse-engineering. Absence of such records in an otherwise open service is itself a datum but is not evidence either way.

operacao-prato.whatItIs: Operacao Prato, literally Operation Plate and usually rendered Operation Saucer, was a field operation mounted by the Forca Aerea Brasileira in the state of Para in 1977 and 1978, centred on Colares and neighbouring riverine communities on the Atlantic coast of the Amazon delta. It was commanded by Capitao Uyrange Bolivar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima, who named it, and ran under I COMAR with involvement from the Servico Nacional de Informacoes. Its stated object was to investigate a wave of reports of luminous objects that residents said projected beams of light at them, a phenomenon locals called the chupa-chupa.
operacao-prato.whyImplicated: Operacao Prato is the specific thing the United States has never produced: a military UAP field operation with a name, a commanding officer identified by rank and full name, a defined area of operations, dated phases, a case count, a written final report, and a paper trail that a member of the public can now request from a civilian archive. The US analogue would be if Project Blue Book had deployed officers into a county for two months with cameras, and the resulting negatives, logs and the captain's signed report were downloadable from NARA. Everything about the operation that would in the American context be cited as a reason for permanent classification, that it was run under a military dictatorship, that it involved a domestic intelligence service, that it concerned civilians who claimed physical injury, and that it produced imagery, turned out not to prevent release. That is the contrast. The concealment argument in the US rests on the proposition that this class of record cannot be released; Brazil released this class of record, and the state did not fall.
operacao-prato.narrative:
In the second half of 1977 the coastal and riverine municipalities of Para began generating a volume of reports that local authorities could not absorb. Residents described luminous objects hovering over houses at night and directing narrow beams of light at people, and a hospital in Colares filled with patients presenting with burns, puncture-like marks and profound weakness. The mayor of Colares appealed for help. What the Brazilian state did next is what puts this node on the board: it sent the air force.

Operacao Prato was organised out of I COMAR, the First Regional Air Command in Belem, and placed under Capitao Uyrange Hollanda. It ran in phases across the last months of 1977 and into 1978, with a team on the ground carrying cameras and observation logs, and it operated in coordination with the Servico Nacional de Informacoes, the dictatorship's civilian intelligence service. Case counts in the surviving documentation are substantial. Material now in the Arquivo Nacional includes a compilation described as Registros de Observacoes de OVNI, drawn up from data gathered by I COMAR on the recommendation of the Minister of Aeronautics, forwarding 130 OVNI records catalogued between 2 September 1977 and 28 November 1978. Alongside the paper there are photographs and drawings, and elsewhere in the same fund the archive holds audio recordings of exchanges between pilots and control tower operators.

The written product of the operation was a report signed by Hollanda that recorded no evidence of extraterrestrials. That report is the operation's official position and, on the board's own method, it is the document that must be handled as an artefact rather than as an answer. It is dated, it is signed, it is attributable, and it was produced by an officer inside a chain of command under a military government. Twenty years later Hollanda repudiated it. In August 1997, at Cabo Frio in Rio de Janeiro state, he gave a long interview to the researchers A. J. Gevaerd and Marco Petit for Revista UFO in which he described what he said the team had actually encountered in the field, including close-quarters encounters, and described unexplained phenomena in his own home afterwards. On 2 October 1997 he was found dead in his apartment at Cabo Frio. The coroner recorded death by asphyxiation due to hanging and the death was ruled suicide.

The temptation with a witness who recants a signed military report and dies weeks later is obvious, and the record does not support taking it. Gevaerd, who had spent the hours of the interview with him and who has every professional incentive to say otherwise, has stated flatly that no one 'suicided' him for talking, that Hollanda acted for his own reasons, and that Hollanda had disclosed a previous attempt on his own life, a fall from the fourth floor of a building. The honest formulation is that the board has a commanding officer who signed a negative report, publicly contradicted it two decades later, and died by his own hand within weeks, and that the person best placed to allege foul play declines to. That is a knot, not a proof, and it belongs in the open questions.

The archival afterlife is where the contrast with the US becomes concrete. In April 2009 the Air Force's documentation centre, CENDOC, sent the first tranche of Operacao Prato material to the Arquivo Nacional. Later in 2009 the Gabinete de Seguranca Institucional of the Presidency released dozens of pages of former SNI documents on the same operation. The two streams converged into the collection coded BR DFANBSB ARX, the Fundo OVNI, where they sit digitised and searchable through SIAN, the Arquivo Nacional's online information system. The mechanism that made this routine was administrative rather than political: Portaria no 551/GC3 of August 2010 established that the Aeronautica registers and forwards, and the archive publishes.

What Operacao Prato does not do is establish recovery or reverse-engineering. There is no crash, no hardware, no custody chain in the released material. Its evidentiary function on this board is different and arguably stronger: it is a fully documented instance of a state deciding that objects it could not identify were interfering with its citizens, tasking a named officer to go and look, and then, three decades on, handing the whole file to the reading public. Every element of that sequence has a missing US counterpart, and the absence of the counterpart is the finding.

operacao-prato.denialPosture: The operation's own final report, signed by its commanding officer, is a negative finding: no signs of extraterrestrials at Colares. That report is the denial, and it is exactly the kind of denial this board catalogues rather than accepts, because it is dated, signed and attributable, and because the signatory publicly repudiated it twenty years later before dying by suicide within weeks. The FAB has never withdrawn or reaffirmed the report; it has simply released the file.
connections: Run by the Forca Aerea Brasileira (fab) through I COMAR, with participation by the Servico Nacional de Informacoes.
Its records form part of the Arquivo Nacional's Fundo OVNI (arquivo-nacional-ufo), reference BR DFANBSB ARX, released via CENDOC in 2009 and via GSI for the SNI material.
Named explicitly in Senado Federal RQS 193/2022 (senado-brasil) as an official Brazilian government UFO research programme.

Capitao Uyrange Hollanda is the named-officer counterpart the US legacy-programme record lacks; his 1997 recantation and death sit adjacent on the board to other late-life disclosures by uniformed personnel.
A. J. Gevaerd, who took the 1997 interview, later testified in the Brazilian Senate's 24 June 2022 special session.
Structural counterpart to Project Blue Book's field investigations and to the Condon Committee's negative finding.
openQuestions: The precise phase dates of the operation vary by source. One commonly cited framing gives two phases, 20 October to 11 November 1977 and 25 November to 5 December 1977, while other accounts extend the operation into 1978 and the archive compilation covers 2 September 1977 to 28 November 1978. No primary FAB order fixing the phases has been retrieved.
The identity and archival citation of Hollanda's signed final report inside BR DFANBSB ARX have not been pinned to a specific SIAN item number in this pass.
The attribution of the ARX 184 compilation to a report signed by Brigadeiro Jose Pessoa Cavalcanti de Albuquerque rests on a secondary blog account and has not been verified against the archive item.
Whether the Colares hospital admissions were medically documented in the military file, and whether those medical records were transferred with the rest, is unresolved.

The circumstances of Hollanda's death are recorded as suicide and the principal interviewer rejects foul play. The board should not treat the sequence of recantation followed by death as evidentiary without a document that has not been produced.
No released Operacao Prato material speaks to recovery of material, custody of hardware, or reverse-engineering.

ev-noite-ovnis-1986.whatItIs: The 'Noite Oficial dos OVNIs', the Official Night of the UFOs, is the night of 19 May 1986, when Brazilian civil and military radar tracked multiple unidentified returns across several states in the country's south-east and centre-west and the Forca Aerea Brasileira launched interceptors against them. Five fighters, a mix of F-5E and Mirage aircraft, were scrambled from Santa Cruz air base in Sao Paulo state and Anapolis air base in Goias. Four days later the Minister of Aeronautics, Brigadeiro Octavio Julio Moreira Lima, held a press conference at the ministry in Brasilia, presented controllers and pilots involved, and said the air force had no technical explanation.
ev-noite-ovnis-1986.whyImplicated: This is the single most important comparison point on the board, because it is the event the United States has never had and, on the concealment thesis, cannot have. A cabinet-rank defence official stood at a podium four days after a multi-aircraft intercept mission against radar-confirmed unidentified objects, named the mission, produced the aircrew and the controllers, and stated on the record that the state could not explain what it had chased. Nothing about Brazil's position in 1986 made this cheap: the country was two years out of military rule, the air force ministry was a serving-officer institution, and the radar and intercept performance data at issue were exactly the sort of material the US cites as the reason such events cannot be discussed. The 1986 night therefore converts the US argument from a claim about the sensitivity of the phenomenon into a claim about the sensitivity of the institution. It also carries its own lag, which is the honest half of the story: the minister promised a written document within thirty days and the report did not reach the public until September 2009, twenty-three years later.
ev-noite-ovnis-1986.narrative:
The evening of 19 May 1986 produced a cascade rather than a single sighting. Radar returns began appearing on civil scopes serving Sao Paulo airports and on the military picture held by CINDACTA, the Integrated Air Defence and Air Traffic Control Centre, and the objects were also acquired visually from the air. Among the airborne witnesses was Ozires Silva, at the time president of Petrobras and one of the most consequential figures in Brazilian aviation as the founder of Embraer, who was flying in an executive Xingu and who, with his pilot, pursued lights for roughly twenty-five minutes. The reported speeds spanned a wide band, from a few hundred kilometres per hour to well over a thousand, which is itself a characteristic of the case: the objects were not behaving like a single misidentified class of target.

The air force treated it as an air defence problem. Five interceptors went up, two F-5E from Santa Cruz in Sao Paulo state and three Mirage from Anapolis in Goias. Pilots reported acquisitions and losses, and the objects did not resolve into anything the crews could identify. In the Brazilian Senate's own later account of the night, twenty-one objects were involved and were pursued for hours.

What makes the date load-bearing is 23 May, not 19 May. The scale of the press coverage forced a response, and the response was a press conference at the Ministry of Aeronautics in Brasilia at which Moreira Lima appeared with air traffic controllers and air force pilots from the mission. He confirmed that five FAB fighters had pursued unidentified objects over Brazilian territory and, asked to account for them, said that technically he would tell them there was no explanation. Contemporary and retrospective Brazilian reporting has treated the phrase as the moment the state conceded, in public, at ministerial level, that its air defence system had engaged something it could not name. Documents later associated with the case describe the objects as solid bodies displaying intelligent behaviour, including formation flight and the ability to track aircraft.

The US comparison is not close. The nearest American analogue in kind, the Washington DC overflights of July 1952, produced a press conference that went the opposite way: the Air Force convened the largest such briefing since the Second World War in order to deliver an explanation, temperature inversion, and to close the matter. In 1986 Brasilia did not reach for an explanation because it did not have one, and said so. Nothing in the subsequent four decades suggests the admission harmed Brazilian air defence, deterrence, or public order. That absence of consequence is the evidence.

The concealment element sits in the timeline afterwards. The minister undertook to produce a written document on the incident and to release it within thirty days. That did not happen. The report became public only in September 2009, which places it inside the same window as the FAB's initial transfers to the Arquivo Nacional and just ahead of Portaria 551/GC3 in August 2010. So the correct reading of the 1986 night is two-part. The verbal disclosure was immediate, unqualified and at cabinet level. The documentary disclosure took twenty-three years and arrived only once the Aeronautica had built an archival pipeline that made release the default. A board tracking concealment should treat that gap as the ordinary metabolism of a defence bureaucracy, and should note that even a system with a twenty-three year documentary lag still ended in publication, which the US system has not.

Today the material sits in the Arquivo Nacional's Fundo OVNI. The archive itself flags 1986 as one of the best known cases in the collection, with around twenty-one unidentified objects detected on 19 May, and the fund includes audio recordings of exchanges between pilots and control tower operators alongside the written reports. In May and June 2026 the fortieth anniversary drew substantial Brazilian press coverage, including detailed reconstructions in the military press, which is a measure of how thoroughly the event has become part of the country's public record rather than its classified one. The comparison the board is built to make is therefore not rhetorical. It is a specific, dated, documented sequence in one country against a specific, dated, documented absence in another.

arquivo-nacional-ufo.whatItIs: The Fundo Objeto Voador Nao Identificado (OVNI), reference code BR DFANBSB ARX, is a discrete archival collection held by Brazil's Arquivo Nacional, the national archives, and produced by the Comando da Aeronautica. It contains reports, occurrence questionnaires, correspondence, photographs, drawings, video, audio and press clippings concerning objects observed in Brazilian skies. It is open to the public and searchable online through SIAN, the Arquivo Nacional's information system.
arquivo-nacional-ufo.whyImplicated: This is the physical answer to the question the US disclosure fight keeps asking in the abstract: what does it actually look like when a state moves its military UAP holdings into civilian custody and publishes them. It looks like a reference code, a finding aid, a login page and a holding count. The archive is the endpoint of the pipeline the FAB built through Portaria 551/GC3, and its existence dismantles the premise that this material is intrinsically unreleasable, because a NATO-adjacent air force with a real air defence mission released it and continues to accession into it annually. It is also honest about its own limits, and the board should be too: the collection covers one service, the Aeronautica, and not the Army or the Navy, and its holding count is reported differently by the archive and by the Senate. Those limits do not weaken the comparison. They sharpen it, because even a partial, imperfect, single-service release is more than the United States has produced in seventy-nine years.
arquivo-nacional-ufo.narrative:
Brazil's national archive holds the world's most accessible body of military records on unidentified aerial objects, and it holds them under an ordinary archival reference code with an ordinary finding aid, which is precisely what makes it remarkable. The Arquivo Nacional describes the collection plainly on its own website: the Fundo Objeto Voador Nao Identificado, BR DFANBSB ARX, produced by the Comando da Aeronautica do Brasil and held in the archive's custody, composed of 743 registros comprising reports, occurrence questionnaires, correspondence, photographs, drawings, videos, audio and clippings from newspapers and magazines about objects seen in Brazilian skies over the years. The earliest occurrence in the fund dates from 1952 and, per the archive's own description, the most recent from 2016. Access runs through SIAN, the Sistema de Informacoes do Arquivo Nacional, and a curated image set is published on the archive's Pinterest account, which is not a detail one expects from a body of military intelligence records.

The holding count is contested and the board should present both figures rather than pick one. The Arquivo Nacional says 743 registros. The Brazilian Senate's own record, in the justification to RQS 193/2022, says that searching the term OVNI alone returns 137 records but that entering the specific reference code BR DFANBSB ARX returns 758 documents. These are almost certainly counting different things, registros as archival units versus digitised items as retrieved by a code search, and the gap may also reflect accruals between the two dates. Neither figure is wrong and neither is authoritative for the other's purpose. Both are cited here. Layered on top, the ufologist A. J. Gevaerd told the Senate plenary in June 2022 that the Brazilian government and the Aeronautica had released more than 20,000 pages, which is a page count rather than an item count and is not in conflict with either.

The collection's provenance runs through the FAB's documentation and archival machinery rather than through litigation or leak. From 2007 the Aeronautica began sending its papers to the archive. In April 2009 CENDOC forwarded the first Operacao Prato material. In August 2010 Portaria no 551/GC3 formalised the flow, making the archive the default destination for reports received through the aerospace operations command. The consequence is that the fund is not a historical dump frozen at a cut-off date but a live series. In August 2026 Brazilian media reporting off documents released through the archive identified at least eighteen unidentified-object cases reported in Brazil during 2025 by pilots, controllers and other aviation personnel, with five clustered at Londrina in Parana and four in Ceara, including a LATAM captain's report near Guarulhos on 1 September 2025 and a Londrina tower controller's 23 November 2025 report of a white, round object that appeared and disappeared on the traffic display. A citizen can read the form.

The archive is not an advocate, and its framing is worth cataloguing precisely because it is not. Its public page carries an explicit caveat that OVNI does not necessarily mean flying saucers or extraterrestrials, and that the term designates any flying object whose origin was not immediately identified, which may include satellites, drones, balloons or natural phenomena. On this board that sentence is an artefact rather than a rebuttal: it is the institutional hedge a records body attaches when it publishes material a defence ministry produced, and its presence tells you the archive expected the material to be read as more than administrative residue. The important thing is that the hedge is attached to published records rather than used as a reason not to publish.

The boundary of the collection is the sharpest single fact in this dossier. The Senate record states without qualification that from 2007 it was the Aeronautica, and not the Exercito and not the Marinha, that sent its papers. Brazilian researchers went to the Ministry of Defence in April 2013, at the invitation of then Foreign Minister Celso Amorim and before the service commanders, specifically to press for the Army and Navy holdings. Those holdings have not been released. So the Fundo OVNI is a one-service archive, which means Brazil's disclosure is real but partial, and means the comparison with the United States should be drawn carefully: Brazil is not a state that opened everything, it is a state where one armed service unilaterally chose publication as its default and the other two did not. That variance is the most useful thing about it, because it isolates the decision. The material did not force the outcome. The institution chose it. And in the United States, no service has chosen it, at any point, in any decade, for any category of this material.

arquivo-nacional-ufo.denialPosture: The archive itself does not deny; it disclaims. Its public description states that OVNI does not necessarily mean flying saucers or extraterrestrials and that the label covers satellites, drones, balloons and natural phenomena. That is a records body inoculating itself against the reading its own holdings invite, and it is catalogued here as an institutional hedge attached to published material rather than as a reason for withholding it.
connections: Custodian of the records produced by the Forca Aerea Brasileira (fab) through CENDOC and COMDABRA/COMAE under Portaria 551/GC3.
Holds the Operacao Prato (operacao-prato) file, including the 2009 CENDOC transfer and the GSI release of former SNI documents.
Holds the 1986 Noite Oficial dos OVNIs (ev-noite-ovnis-1986) documentation and audio of pilot and control tower exchanges.
Its reference code BR DFANBSB ARX and its holding count of 758 documents are cited verbatim in Senado Federal RQS 193/2022 (senado-brasil).
Subordinate to the Ministerio da Justica e Seguranca Publica, which places custody of the records outside the defence establishment.
The structural counterpart the United States lacks: there is no NARA record group equivalent for a live, annually accruing US military UAP reporting series.
openQuestions: The 743 versus 758 discrepancy has not been reconciled. The two figures come from different bodies, are counting differently (archival registros versus documents returned by a reference-code search), and are separated in time. No authoritative reconciliation exists in the sources located.

Whether any material was withheld, redacted or reclassified during the transfers from CENDOC and GSI is not addressed in any located source.
Whether the fund contains any material relating to physical residue, recovered objects or materials analysis has not been established from the finding aid.

senado-brasil.whatItIs: The Senado Federal is the upper chamber of Brazil's National Congress. On 16 March 2022 it received Requerimento no 193, de 2022 (RQS 193/2022), tabled by Senator Eduardo Girao (PODEMOS/CE) with seven co-signatories, and approved it the same day; the resulting special plenary session was held on 24 June 2022. The requerimento's stated purpose was to hold a special session commemorating the 75th anniversary of World Ufology Day, and its justificacao entered into the Senate's permanent record a detailed account of Brazil's official UFO programmes and archive holdings.
senado-brasil.whyImplicated: The Senate node is where the correction lives, and correcting it makes the comparison stronger rather than weaker. RQS 193/2022 is not a records-production instrument. Its ementa is a request for a commemorative special session under Article 199 of the Senate's internal rules, and its disposition reads 'Aprovada pelo Plenario' followed by 'SESSAO REALIZADA'. What it did instead is arguably more useful to this board: it wrote into the permanent legislative record of a G20 state, over eight senators' names, that the Aeronautica ran Operacao Prato and SIOANI, that FAB fighters chased 21 objects in 1986, that from 2007 the air force but not the army and not the navy transferred its files, and that the archive reference code BR DFANBSB ARX returns 758 documents. No US congressional instrument has ever put an equivalent set of specifics into the record as settled institutional history. The contrast is not that Brazil compelled disclosure through legislation. It is that Brazil did not have to, because the executive had already published, and the legislature's role was to hold a session about it in the plenary chamber with foreign witnesses at the rostrum.
senado-brasil.narrative:
The premise that most needs correcting before this node is usable is the shape of the instrument. RQS 193/2022 is a requerimento, a procedural request, filed under Article 199 of the Regimento Interno do Senado Federal, asking for a special session at an appropriate date to commemorate 75 years of World Ufology Day. It carries the signatures of Eduardo Girao (PODEMOS/CE), Eliziane Gama (CIDADANIA/MA), Alessandro Vieira (CIDADANIA/SE), Izalci Lucas (PSDB/DF), Jorge Kajuru (PODEMOS/GO), Marcos do Val (PODEMOS/ES), Paulo Rocha (PT/PA) and Reguffe (PODEMOS/DF), which is a cross-party spread from left to right. It was read and approved on 16 March 2022, published in the Diario do Senado Federal no 32 of 17 March 2022 at pages 269 to 275 and page 62, the session was held on 24 June 2022 and published in DSF no 99 of 25 June 2022 at pages 7 to 67, and the matter was closed and sent to the archive coordination on 29 June 2022. It compelled nothing and produced no documents. Any claim on this board that the Senate passed an instrument seeking UAP records must be retired.

What survives, and what makes the node worth keeping, is the justificacao. Brazilian requerimentos carry a reasoning section that enters the permanent record with the instrument, and Girao's runs to several pages of institutional history. It states that Brazil was the first nation to officially admit that OVNIs exist and have extraterrestrial provenance, at a 1954 session at the Escola Superior de Guerra in Rio at which the then Aeronautica captain Joao Adil de Oliveira spoke to officers, civilians and press, and that France followed only in 1976. It states that since 1954 the Brazilian government has created several official UFO research programmes through the Aeronautica, naming Operacao Prato in 1977, SIOANI in 1969 at the IV Comando Aereo Regional in Sao Paulo, and the 1986 night in which 21 spherical objects, each given as 100 metres in diameter, were pursued for hours by Brazilian jet fighters. It states that the Aeronautica was always discreet about these facts but never denied them when asked. It states that from 2007 the Aeronautica, and expressly not the Exercito and not the Marinha, began sending its papers to the Arquivo Nacional, and that the total now exceeds 20,000 pages. It records that in August 2010 the then FAB commander determined by an instrument published in the Diario Oficial da Uniao that all OVNI cases across the force be concentrated at COMDABRA for onward transmission. It records the April 2013 meeting at the Ministry of Defence, convened at the invitation of then Foreign Minister Celso Amorim and held before the service commanders, at which researchers pressed for the Army and Navy files. And it gives the archive arithmetic directly: searching OVNI alone yields 137 registros, but the reference code BR DFANBSB ARX yields 758 documents, some of them more than 70 years old.

The justificacao also turns outward, and that is where the comparison it enables becomes explicit. It notes that at least 30 nations established research commissions, that the 2021 Pentagon UAP preliminary assessment examined 144 sighting cases of which only one was explained, and that on 15 March 2022 President Biden signed an omnibus funding bill including 782.5 billion dollars for defence with resources reserved for unexplained aerial phenomena research legislated within the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act. Brazil, in other words, put the American record into its own legislative record while noting that its own files were already open.

The session itself, on 24 June 2022, was held in the Senate plenary and is documented in the Senate's own file with individual presentation documents lodged for each invited speaker: Rony Vernet, Ademar Jose, Gary Heseltine, Geraldo Lemos Neto, Inajar Antonio Kurowski, Jackson Luiz Camargo, Robert Lambert Salas and Thiago Ticchetti. Agencia Senado's report of the session records Gevaerd calling the opening incomplete but fruitful, Robert Salas, a former US Air Force officer, describing unidentified objects disabling ten nuclear weapons at a launch facility he commanded, and the delivery to Girao at the close of a document the participants called the Carta de Brasilia, recommending creation of a permanent joint civil and military commission to enable organised research on the subject.

One error must be named and buried. A previous pass on this board asserted that Senator Girao brought the 1996 Varginha case to Capitol Hill in 2026. Nothing in the reporting located supports that. Girao's verified, documented action is RQS 193/2022 and the 24 June 2022 special session, and the board should carry that and nothing beyond it.

senado-brasil.denialPosture: None on the part of the Senate. The chamber's posture is the inverse of denial: it approved a plenary session on the subject unanimously enough to be recorded simply as 'Aprovada pelo Plenario', gave the floor to foreign and domestic witnesses including a former US Air Force officer, and entered into its permanent Diario the specific archive reference code under which its own military's files can be retrieved.
connections: RQS 193/2022 documents the Forca Aerea Brasileira's programmes (fab), naming SIOANI, Operacao Prato (operacao-prato) and the 1986 night (ev-noite-ovnis-1986).
Cites the Arquivo Nacional's OVNI holdings (arquivo-nacional-ufo) by reference code BR DFANBSB ARX and by document count.

Its justificacao explicitly frames the Brazilian record against the US record, citing the 2021 Pentagon UAP preliminary assessment and FY2022 NDAA UAP funding, which places it directly alongside the nip node.
Robert Salas, a witness at the 24 June 2022 session, connects the Brazilian legislative record to the US nuclear-facility incident testimony stream.
A. J. Gevaerd, who interviewed Capitao Uyrange Hollanda in 1997, testified at the same session, linking the Operacao Prato node to the Senate node through a single individual.
The Carta de Brasilia's proposal of a permanent joint civil-military commission is the Brazilian counterpart to the US push for a UAP Records Review Board.
openQuestions: A previous research pass asserted that Senator Girao brought the 1996 Varginha case to Capitol Hill in 2026. No source located supports this. It should be treated as retracted unless a primary record is produced.

No Brazilian legislative instrument has been located that compels production of Army or Navy holdings, establishes a records review board, or creates the permanent joint commission proposed in the Carta de Brasilia.
The text of the Carta de Brasilia itself has not been retrieved; its content is known only through Agencia Senado's summary.
Whether any of the eight co-signatory senators pursued follow-on action after the session closed on 29 June 2022 is not established.

The full stenographic record of the 24 June 2022 session is published in DSF no 99, pages 7 to 67, but has not been read in this pass; individual statements beyond those summarised by Agencia Senado are unverified.

Several factual assertions inside the justificacao, notably the 100-metre diameter figure for the 1986 objects and the primacy claim for Brazil in 1954, are the author's assertions entered into the record, not independently verified findings.

nip.whatItIs: The National Intelligence Program (NIP) is the aggregate budget covering the intelligence activities of the United States Intelligence Community that fall under the Director of National Intelligence's authority, as distinct from the Military Intelligence Program (MIP), which the Department of Defense, since 2025 styled the Department of War, funds and discloses separately. Every year the DNI publicly discloses a single figure: the NIP topline, either the requested appropriation or the enacted one. That single number, and nothing beneath it, is the totality of what the United States tells the public about how much it spends on intelligence.
nip.whyImplicated: The NIP is the board's measuring instrument rather than a suspect. It is the one intelligence quantity the US government is statutorily obliged to publish, which makes it the only fixed point in an otherwise unmeasurable field, and the disclosure comes bolted to an explicit statement of what will not follow. The DNI's own language is the artefact: beyond the topline figure, there will be no other disclosures of currently classified NIP budget information, the only exceptions being unclassified appropriations. The Department of War's parallel MIP release says the same thing in its own words. So the United States publishes a number in the tens of billions and simultaneously certifies that the composition of that number is not subject to public accounting. For a board premised on a concealed recovery and reverse-engineering effort, this is the structural fact that makes concealment financially unremarkable rather than extraordinary: a programme costing a rounding error against 81.9 billion dollars would not disturb the only figure anyone outside the compartment ever sees. It is also the exact inverse of the Brazilian nodes, where the state published the contents and never had to publish a price.
nip.narrative:
The NIP topline exists as a public number because Congress made it one. Section 601 of the Implementing the Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007, Public Law 110-53, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3306, requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate amount of appropriations requested for, and appropriated to, the National Intelligence Program. Before that statute the topline was itself classified, contested in litigation and estimated by outsiders from budget residue. The 9/11 Commission's reasoning was that a single aggregate number tells an adversary nothing operationally useful while giving the public a minimal handhold on scale. That reasoning is worth holding onto, because it is precisely the reasoning that has never been applied one level down.

The current figures are these. On 21 April 2026 the DNI disclosed an aggregate request of 81.9 billion dollars for the fiscal year 2027 NIP, in ODNI News Release No. 07-26. The same day the Department of War released the MIP topline request for FY2027 at 50.0 billion dollars. Taken together the disclosed US intelligence request for FY2027 is 131.9 billion dollars. The prior year's NIP request, disclosed on 4 June 2025, was also 81.9 billion. For FY2025 the requested figure was 73.4 billion and the appropriated figure, disclosed on 31 October 2025 in ODNI News Release No. 39-25, was 73.3 billion including supplemental funding. The FY2026 to FY2027 step from the low seventies to 81.9 billion is a substantial real increase, and no public account exists of where inside the NIP it went.

What the disclosure statute does not do is the point. The ODNI release states in terms that beyond the topline there will be no other disclosures of currently classified NIP budget information, with the sole exception of unclassified appropriations. The Department of War release mirrors it: the department determined that releasing the top line does not jeopardise any classified activities within the MIP, and no other MIP budget figures or programme details will be released, as they remain classified for national security reasons. Both of those sentences are dated, signed institutional statements, and on this board's method they are catalogued as such. Each is a public certification that the composition of a nine-figure-per-day expenditure is outside public accountability, issued by the same government that says nothing is being concealed about anomalous aerial phenomena.

The structural consequence for the legacy-programme thesis is arithmetic. The NIP and MIP toplines are aggregates over eighteen IC organisations plus the defence services, spanning collection, analysis, counterintelligence, acquisition and personnel. A special access programme, however sensitive, appears in that aggregate as an undifferentiated increment. Move a few hundred million dollars, or a few billion, between elements and the topline moves by a fraction of a percent, well inside the year-to-year variance the public figures already exhibit without explanation. There is no external mechanism that would detect it, because the statute that produces the only public number simultaneously certifies that nothing beneath it will be produced. That is not an allegation about where the money went. It is a statement about what the disclosure regime is capable of showing, which is nothing at the resolution the question requires.

The further complication is that the NIP is not the only channel. Programmes can sit in the MIP rather than the NIP, in service acquisition accounts outside both, in the Department of Energy's weapons complex, or in contractor-held independent research and development recovered through overhead rates on unrelated contracts. A programme domiciled outside the NIP would not appear even as an increment in the one number the public gets. The disclosure regime, in other words, is not a partial window onto the whole. It is a complete window onto one selected pane.

Set against the Brazilian nodes the asymmetry is stark and inverted. Brazil published the substance and never had to publish a price: the Fundo OVNI gives a citizen the report forms, the photographs and the audio, and there is no Brazilian equivalent of an annually disclosed intelligence topline. The United States publishes the price and none of the substance. A citizen of Brazil can read what an air force captain wrote in Para in 1977. A citizen of the United States can learn that 81.9 billion dollars was requested for intelligence in fiscal 2027 and is told, in the same paragraph, that they will learn nothing else. Both governments made a choice about what to make legible. Only one of them chose the part that answers a question.
