nip.denialPosture: The NIP disclosure is a denial wrapped around a concession. The DNI publishes one number and states in the same release that no other currently classified NIP budget information will be disclosed; the Department of War publishes its own number and states that no other MIP budget figures or programme details will be released because they remain classified. Both statements are dated and attributable, and both certify that the composition of the amounts disclosed is placed permanently outside public accounting.
connections: Funds the eighteen IC organisations listed by ODNI, including CIA, DIA, NSA, NGA and NRO, any of which could domicile a special access programme invisible at topline resolution.
Paired with the Military Intelligence Program, disclosed the same day by the Department of War, which uses the same no-further-disclosure formula.
Statutorily rooted in section 601 of P.L. 110-53 (50 U.S.C. 3306), which is the only affirmative US intelligence transparency obligation of its kind and covers scale alone, never composition.
The direct inverse of the Brazilian archival nodes (arquivo-nacional-ufo, fab): Brazil published the substance without a price, the US publishes the price without the substance.
Cited indirectly in Senado Federal RQS 193/2022 (senado-brasil), which entered the US defence and UAP funding posture into the Brazilian legislative record.
The measurement baseline against which unfunded-liability arguments about legacy programme costs, contractor IR&D recovery, and off-NIP domiciling must be assessed.
openQuestions: The FY2026 and FY2025 figures rest on ODNI press-release URLs whose live pages now redirect to the current ODNI newsroom; the figures were confirmed via indexed search results rather than by direct retrieval of the archived release text in this pass.
No public source establishes the internal composition of the NIP at any level below the topline, by agency, by discipline, or by programme, for any fiscal year.

Whether any UAP-related activity is funded within the NIP, within the MIP, within service acquisition accounts outside both, or within Department of Energy accounts is not determinable from any disclosed figure.

The 8.5 billion dollar step from the FY2025 request to the FY2026 and FY2027 requests is unexplained in the public record; whether it reflects inflation, a new mission area, a transfer from MIP, or a programme start is unknown.
The first year in which the NIP topline was disclosed under section 601, and the figure disclosed, have not been verified against a primary ODNI record in this pass.

Contractor independent research and development recovered through overhead on unrelated government contracts is not captured by either the NIP or the MIP topline, and its scale relative to these figures is not established.

doc-condign-vol3.whatItIs: Volume 3 of the UK Ministry of Defence Defence Intelligence Staff study "Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region", issued as Scientific & Technical Memorandum 55/2/00 by DI55 within DI(ST) from the Old War Office Building, Whitehall, and titled on its own contents page "MISCELLANEOUS RELATED STUDIES". Its preface is dated February 2000 and states plainly: "This is the third volume of a three-part report on the information held in DI55 on the subject of UAP." Every page is header- and footer-stamped UK SECRET / UK EYES ONLY, and the volume was released to the public on 15 May 2006 under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 with redactions under sections 26, 27 and 40.
doc-condign-vol3.whyImplicated: Volume 3 is the volume where a NATO ally's defence intelligence staff wrote down, in a classified assessment, the two things the United States has spent seventy years insisting do not exist: a chapter titled "POTENTIAL FOR EXPLOITATION OF UAP-ASSOCIATED EFFECTS" and a chapter titled "UAP WORK IN OTHER COUNTRIES". Chapter 3 opens by stating that one of the reasons for analysing UAP reports at all "was that of identifying any phenomena which could be robustly generated and provide a military advantage" - and the fourteen lines that follow that sentence are blacked out under Section 26 (Defence), as is the entire body of the page listing what DI55 called "three possible related potential applications". Chapter 4 then catalogues what other states were doing, naming Russian institutions, scientists, cosmonauts, laboratories and a research centre by name, and confirming in the Executive Summary that "DI55 does not have access to any other Government's classified reports, as there is no formal intelligence exchange on this topic." That last sentence is the load-bearing one for the board: the UK's own defence intelligence organisation, an ally inside the closest intelligence-sharing arrangement on earth, records that it was locked out of everyone else's UAP files - including, by necessary implication, Washington's. And the countries DI55 named as having staff active on the subject were redacted not under Defence but under Section 27, International Relations.
doc-condign-vol3.narrative:
The Condign report is usually reduced to a single soundbite - the plasma hypothesis - and Volume 3 is the volume that shows why that reduction is a mistake. Volume 1 carried the statistical analysis and the public-facing conclusions. Volume 2 carried the working papers. Volume 3 carried the material the study's author explicitly said "could not be placed in the RESTRICTED Executive Summary". Its own preface concedes the reason it is stamped SECRET is narrow and technical - it "contains performance values of the UKADR radars" - but then adds that the volume is "also a convenient place-holder for several other related findings" arising "out of earlier DI55 interest in any reliable information connected with this topic and focusing upon the potential technologies involved and their possible future military uses." That is an intelligence organisation stating on paper that it had a standing interest in the technology question.

Chapter 3 is the exploitation chapter. Its first paragraph states the purpose without hedging: to identify "any phenomena which could be robustly generated and provide a military advantage." What follows is redacted. Paragraph 2, "Exotic Vehicles", is remarkable for what a defence intelligence analyst was willing to commit to a classified page in 2000. It records that "the possibility of some sort of exotic vehicle, either terrestrial or from space could not be ruled out until all available evidence had been examined", that "the possibility of technologies beyond the scope of human engineering and conception could not initially be ruled out", and - critically - that had extra-terrestrial technology been proven, "then (possibly) recommendations could be made as to the way ahead." It goes further, sketching what would be required: propulsion "by the use of anti-matter, gravitational or torsion fields or of particle phenomena and fields or waves which are not currently known in science or technology", and reported performance that "appears to imply the negation of inertia". The chapter's stated conclusion is negative - "there is no indication that craft of extra-terrestrial origin exist" - but the surrounding architecture is that of a reverse-engineering feasibility study, and the section headed POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS, which announces "three possible related potential applications", has its entire page body struck out under Section 26 and remains struck out today.

Chapter 4 is the foreign-programmes chapter, and it is where the board's Soviet thread anchors. Paragraph 1 states: "It is clear that the Former Soviet Union has taken the study of UAPs seriously and that this may well be related to a programme of understanding and exploiting certain UAP-related natural phenomena, such as plasmas. A 'UFO' Commission was created under the USSR Union of Scientific and Engineering Societies in 1989, together in 1990 with an Inter-Industry Ufology Research Centre (SOYUZUFOSENTR) to co-ordinate records. This Centre had the rights of an Institute under the USSR Academy of Sciences, and was headed by V.G. AZAHAZHA (or AZHAZHA) an eminent researcher and former naval submariner." The paragraph goes on to record a ten-week school whose terms of reference were to study "ufology as a science of unidentified flying objects and their inter-relations with the universe and, in particular, with the biotechnosphere of the earth".

The chapter keeps naming things. Paragraph 2 identifies V.V. Alexandrov and cosmonaut Y.N. Glazov of the Cosmonaut Training Centre and the Scientific Production Association (Geophysics), and a supporting laboratory at Akhtubisk on the Volga. Paragraph 3, "Plasma Research", records that two Russian scientific papers summarised at Annex A appear to show "20-30 scientists have pursued research for the prevention of air target detection" - plasma stealth - and everything after that sentence is redacted under Section 26. Paragraph 5, "Near Field Effects", reports 1991 Russian soil sampling at alleged landing sites where "in all cases a local field developed over a period of three hours" and "impairment of human senses were reportedly observed in every person studied who had been 'in the field'". The DI55 analyst's own bracketed comment is the most telling line in the volume: "It is possible, and confirmed from some other data that russian scientists may have discovered some new field types."

The Executive Summary makes the intelligence posture explicit. Under "Foreign Military Interest", paragraph 9 records that UAP "are by no means confined to UK airspace", that "Other NATO nations, China, Russia and elsewhere frequently report the most extreme and puzzling incidents in the open press", and that DI55 had no access to any other government's classified reports. The identities of the countries known "to have at least one member of staff active in this area" are withheld under Section 27 - the international-relations exemption, not the defence one. Paragraph 10 adds that "Several governments have also been sufficiently concerned to set up Commissions and Institutes to examine the phenomena." The bullets on the following page state that Russian, Former Soviet Republic and Chinese authorities "have made a co-ordinated effort to understand the UAP topic", that "Several aircraft have been destroyed and at least four pilots have been killed 'chasing UFOs'", and that "Russian investigators have measured (or at least detected) 'fields', which are reported to have caused human effects when they are located close to the phenomena."

The redaction fight that followed is itself part of the record. The MoD's internal-review correspondence, held at The National Archives as DEFE 24/2090/1 and digitised, shows Clarke and Anthony challenging specific Volume 3 withholdings paragraph by paragraph, including Chapter 4 page 3 paragraph 12, where the reviewer notes that "information regarding DIS, the CIA desk officer and DI51 must remain redacted" while conceding that the Society for Scientific Exploration statement in the same sentence was already public. A CIA desk officer appears in the UK's classified UAP chapter on foreign programmes, and his existence is still redacted. That is the shape of the concealment, drawn from the inside.

university-at-albany.whatItIs: The University at Albany (SUNY), a public research university at 1400 Washington Avenue, Albany, New York, and specifically its Department of Physics. The department houses an established dark matter group working on the LZ (LUX-ZEPLIN) experiment and the Snowball Chamber, and it is the institutional home of Professor Kevin H. Knuth, Associate Professor Matthew Szydagis and Associate Professor Cecilia Levy. As of November 2025 it also hosts UAlbany Project X (UAPx), an endowed academic collaboration devoted solely to the scientific study of unidentified anomalous phenomena.
university-at-albany.whyImplicated: The standard defence of the concealment is that no serious scientist will touch the subject, therefore the absence of scientific data proves there is nothing there. UAlbany is the counter-example, and it is institutional rather than biographical: Matthew Szydagis's official departmental faculty page lists his research interests as "Experimental astroparticle physics, in particular direct detection of dark matter WIMPs ... and general detector development for rare event searches, neutron activation, and Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" - a state university publishing UAP as a declared faculty research interest on a .edu page alongside dark matter. In June 2025 the department placed two peer-reviewed UAP papers in Progress in Aerospace Sciences, one of them a 34-author historical review led by Knuth. In November 2025 the university accepted a named endowment gift specifically to fund UAP research in perpetuity and announced the launch of UAlbany Project X. And in the same announcement Knuth confirmed that physicist Eric W. Davis had joined the physics department as visiting adjunct faculty - placing one of the most heavily implicated figures in the legacy-program record inside a public university physics department, on the record, in a university press release.
university-at-albany.narrative:
The University at Albany physics department is a small, instrument-heavy group whose day job is looking for signals that are rare, faint and easy to confuse with noise. That is exactly the skill set the UAP problem has always lacked. Cecilia Levy and Matthew Szydagis both work on LZ, the multi-tonne xenon time-projection chamber operating a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota; Szydagis wrote NEST, the Noble Element Simulation Technique package the wider noble-liquid detector community depends on. Levy's second research line is the Snowball Chamber, a supercooled-water low-mass dark matter technology unique to the UAlbany group. Kevin Knuth came from a different direction: a PhD in physics from Minnesota, brain-imaging work at the Nathan Kline Institute and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, then four years as a GS-14 Research Scientist in the Intelligent Systems Division at NASA Ames Research Center from 2001 to 2005, designing inference algorithms for astrophysical data. He joined UAlbany as an Assistant Professor in 2005, was promoted to Associate in 2009 and to full Professor in 2023, and has been Editor-in-Chief of the MDPI journal Entropy since 2012.

Knuth's route into the phenomenon ran through the numbers. His 2019 paper with SCU collaborators, "Estimating Flight Characteristics of Anomalous Unidentified Aerial Vehicles", published in Entropy, worked out minimum speeds and accelerations for several documented cases including the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter off southern California. The Nimitz case is what drove the fieldwork: in July 2021 Knuth, Szydagis and Levy joined the non-profit UAPx for a week-long expedition to the Catalina Channel - the same water where the Nimitz strike group's aircrew recorded the Tic Tac - deploying visible-light and infrared cameras, Cosmic Watch scintillation-based radiation detectors, and National Weather Service Doppler radar data.

What came out of that expedition is the part that matters institutionally. It was not a conference talk or a preprint that died on arXiv. It was two papers in a June 2025 special edition of Progress in Aerospace Sciences, an Elsevier review journal with no prior history of publishing on this subject. Szydagis was lead author of "Initial results from the first field expedition of UAPx to study unidentified anomalous phenomena" (DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2025.101099), with Knuth, Benjamin Kugielsky and Levy. The paper reports approximately one hour of triggered visible and night-vision video, over 600 hours of untriggered far-infrared video, and 55 hours of background radiation measurement. The team plausibly explained all but one candidate anomaly: a dark spot in the visible/near-IR camera captured at roughly 4am Pacific on Friday 16 July 2021, possibly coincident with ionizing radiation, which has resisted prosaic explanation. Szydagis built a new analysis tool for the work, the Custom Target Analysis Protocol (C-TAP), applying pixel-by-pixel frame-differencing with AI assistance and human verification - the same logic used to separate a dark-matter recoil from detector noise.

The companion paper, "The new science of Unidentified Aerospace-Undersea Phenomena (UAP)" (DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2025.101097), had Knuth as lead author and, per the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies, thirty-four authors in total. It reviews roughly twenty historical government studies from 1933 to the present across Scandinavia, wartime Europe, the US, Canada, France, Russia and China, plus private studies in France, the UK and the US, and current instrumented research programmes in Ireland, Germany, Norway, Sweden and the US. Its stated purpose is to demonstrate that UAP "can be, and have been, scientifically investigated" and to dispel the misconception that this is an American phenomenon. Project Condign sits inside that review as one of the government studies catalogued - the two nodes on this board touch directly through that paper.

On 27 June 2025 SCU announced that Knuth had received its inaugural Distinguished Scholar Award, presented at SCU's Sixth Annual Conference at the Von Braun Center in Huntsville, Alabama, on 6-8 June 2025. The distinction worth preserving is that Knuth is an award recipient and paper author, not an SCU officer: the SCU release identifies Rich Hoffman as the Executive Board member who presented the award and describes Knuth only as a University at Albany professor and former NASA research scientist. Knuth does hold a science-and-technology role at UAPx, but that is a separate organisation.

The institutional consolidation came on 5 November 2025. UAlbany announced an endowment gift from Albany businessman Tony Gorman, formerly a principal owner of the Gorman Group highway construction and materials firm, who had seen a local news segment about the physicists' work. Knuth told The Debrief the gift funds the team for five years and "sets up an endowment that funds us in perpetuity." The gift launched UAlbany Project X, which absorbs the mission of the non-profit UAPx co-founded by Navy veterans Kevin Day and Gary Voorhis - both connected to the 2004 Nimitz encounter. The university's own release positions the group alongside academic UAP efforts in Sweden, Germany and at Harvard. Planned instrumentation includes diffraction gratings for spectroscopy, magnetic and electric field sensors, and portable multi-camera sky-monitoring arrays - categories Knuth notes are "often omitted from study".

Buried in Knuth's quote in that release is the sentence that puts UAlbany on this board rather than merely in a science-news roundup: "the physics department's UAP research base grows, with the recent addition of physicist Dr. Eric W. Davis as visiting adjunct faculty. Dr. Davis has cooperated with recent congressional UAP hearings." Davis is a central figure in the legacy-program record. A public university has just given him a faculty affiliation, and said so in its own press release.

What makes the node durable is that the team is deflationary about its own data: Szydagis's public line is that "we did not find evidence indicating that UAP have anything to do with non-human intelligence." That is what instrumented science looks like, and it is the thing the concealment has always been able to point to as absent. It is no longer absent. It is endowed, it is on a .edu faculty page, and it now has Eric Davis in the building.

aaro.whatItIs: The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office is the Pentagon body designated in July 2022 as the Department's authoritative office for unidentified anomalous phenomena. It was created under section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, sits under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, and absorbed the Navy's Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. It publishes the statutory annual UAP report, runs a secure reporting mechanism for current and former government personnel, and produced the Historical Record Report.
aaro.whyImplicated: AARO is the single point through which every UAP record, contract and data holding in the Department of Defense was ordered to flow, which makes it either the instrument of disclosure or the instrument of consolidation, and the record supports the second reading. The office was given, by its own account, unrestricted statutory access to compartmented and special access material, then used that access to produce a report clearing the Department of every allegation made against it. Its own numbers show what the reporting channel actually does: of 262 people who came forward in a single year, 255 were declared out of scope and 7 were judged worth interviewing. Witnesses under oath before the House Oversight Committee have described being targeted after providing classified testimony, and one described a session he understood to be with AARO leadership as an effort to attack the credibility of UAP witnesses. AARO is on this map not as an arbiter but as a party: it holds the custody, it wrote the exoneration, and it decides who counts as a witness.
aaro.narrative:
AARO exists because Congress forced it into existence. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA required the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to stand up an office with a scope broader than the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group that the Deputy Secretary had created in November 2021. On 15 July 2022 Deputy Secretary Kathleen Hicks signed the memorandum that renamed and expanded AOIMSG into AARO. That memorandum is the founding document and it is worth reading for what it actually does. It makes AARO the authoritative office for UAP and UAP-related activities for the whole Department. It orders the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data, analysis and other relevant material. And it contains the sentence that matters most for this board: any DoD Component acting on behalf of the UAPTF, or who has data, analysis, contracts, or other material related to UAP, will immediately synchronize their efforts with the AARO.

That is a consolidation order. In a Department where the argument is that recovered material and its associated paperwork have been dispersed across contractors and unacknowledged compartments, an instruction that all UAP data, analysis and contracts route to a single office under USD(I&S) is the sort of instruction that can be read two ways. It is the necessary precondition for an honest accounting. It is also the necessary precondition for a controlled one.

AARO's first director was Sean Kirkpatrick, previously chief scientist at the Defense Intelligence Agency's Missile and Space Intelligence Center. He retired on 1 December 2023 having largely completed the Historical Record Report that his office published the following March. He publicly characterised David Grusch's allegations while, by his own later account, never having interviewed him. Grusch's position is that AARO never contacted him. Whichever account is correct, the resulting document is an investigation of a whistleblower's claims conducted without the whistleblower. Jon Kosloski, from the National Security Agency, took over in late 2024.

The office's own annual reporting is the best evidence about how the reporting channel functions. Under section 3373b of title 50, AARO hosts a secure mechanism for people claiming first-hand knowledge of a US Government UAP-related programme dating back to 1945. In the FY2025 report AARO discloses that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals used it. AARO determined 255 were out of scope. Seven warranted a request for a follow-on interview. That is a 97 percent rejection rate applied by the office whose own conduct is the subject of many of the allegations. The same report states, in language AARO chose, that the office is authorised by law to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs, and that generally no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving it. AARO therefore claims the access and simultaneously reports that almost nobody who comes to it has anything worth hearing.

The FY2025 report contains a second internal tension that a hostile reader should sit with. It states flatly that to date no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. Two sentences later it states that AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG, drawing on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for the nothing it has found.

The performance record is poor by the Department's own inspector general's measure. DODIG-2023-109, whose unclassified summary was released on 24 January 2024, found the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP, had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan, and had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands. The Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report.

The delivery record is worse. Volume II of the Historical Record Report, covering interviews and research from 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024, was promised in Volume I under a deadline set in section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. By late February 2026 it had not appeared, the FY2025 annual report had not appeared, the deputy director post was vacant, and Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough, asked why AARO had not published or briefed in over a year, told DefenseScoop the office had nothing to announce at this time. Gough did confirm that AARO had been examining over 2,000 UAP cases, roughly 1,000 of which lacked sufficient data and sat in an active archive. When the FY2025 report finally issued, it carried document number 26-P-0880 and a Department of War letterhead, with an information cut-off of 30 May 2025.

The strongest single item against AARO is in its own Volume I. The report concedes that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and that the programme was later disestablished for lack of merit. AARO's framing is that the compartment was unwarranted and empty. The fact remains that a compartment was stood up to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and the office that told us so is the office that closed it.

aaro-historical-record-vol1.whatItIs: The Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, Volume I, is a 63-page unclassified report published by AARO on 8 March 2024 under a congressional mandate to document the US Government's UAP record back to 1945. It covers the period from 1945 to 31 October 2023 and was largely prepared under director Sean Kirkpatrick before his retirement on 1 December 2023. A Volume II covering 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024 was promised and has not appeared.
aaro-historical-record-vol1.whyImplicated: Volume I is the government's formal written denial that a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering programme exists, and as such it is the central artifact of the concealment argument rather than a rebuttal to it. It is an investigation of roughly thirty interviewees conducted without interviewing the most prominent complainant, written by the office whose own conduct several of the allegations concern, and published by the same office that decides which claims are in scope. Its own text concedes that an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program had its scope expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering, which is the single most consequential sentence any US government UAP document has ever contained. It disposes of the rest of the record by attributing it to circular reporting among a group of people who worked on a real, congressionally funded Defense Intelligence Agency programme. Volume I is on this map because it is the document a concealment effort would have to produce, and because the promised second half has never arrived.
aaro-historical-record-vol1.narrative:
The FY2023 NDAA, enacted December 2022, required AARO to produce a written report on the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena going back to 1 January 1945. AARO split the deliverable. Volume I would carry findings from 1945 to 31 October 2023. Volume II would carry anything derived from interviews and research completed between 1 November 2023 and 15 April 2024, on a date set by section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. Volume I went to Congress in the first week of March 2024 and to the public on 8 March. Volume II has not been published.

The methodology is stated plainly in the report and is the first thing a hostile reader should notice. AARO reviewed official investigatory efforts since 1945, researched classified and unclassified archives, partnered with IC and DoD officials responsible for controlled and special access programme oversight, and conducted approximately 30 interviews. Thirty interviews is the entire human-source basis for a report covering seventy-eight years. AARO categorised the interviewees into tiers, with Tier 1 being those referred to AARO after speaking with Members of Congress or congressional staff. The report then states that none of the interviewees had firsthand knowledge of these programmes, that they were not approved for access and did not work on these efforts, and that this likely resulted in misinterpretation.

The findings are absolute in tone. AARO found no evidence that any USG investigation, academic-sponsored research, or official review panel has confirmed that any sighting of a UAP represented extraterrestrial technology. AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology. AARO has found no evidence of any authentic UAP-related NDA or other evidence threatening death or violence for disclosing UAP information. AARO has found no evidence that U.S. companies ever possessed off-world technology; the report says executives, scientists and chief technology officers of named companies met the Director of AARO and denied on the record ever having recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered such technology. A metal sample obtained from a private UAP investigating organisation and the US Army is assessed as a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with trace elements including lead.

Against that, the report contains admissions its authors evidently regarded as harmless. It states that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, that the programme never recovered or reverse-engineered anything, and that it was disestablished for lack of merit. It states that KONA BLUE was a Prospective Special Access Program proposed to the Department of Homeland Security, never approved, whose supporters never provided empirical evidence. It states that on 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III asking that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program and that Lynn declined on the recommendation of Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper. It states that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he had managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which means AARO went to that official and obtained a denial rather than a record. It states that an alleged 1961 Special National Intelligence Estimate circulating online is inauthentic.

The report's explanatory theory is that the modern allegations are, in large part, the result of circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case despite the lack of any evidence, and that these individuals have been involved in various UAP-related endeavours since at least 2009, many of them connected to the cancelled DIA programme and the failed attempt to re-establish it under DHS as KONA BLUE. This is a genetic argument. It explains the allegations by the identity of the people making them rather than by testing what they allege, and it does so while conceding that the DIA programme was real, congressionally funded, and terminated over the objections of a sitting Senate Majority Leader.

The report also records lines of effort that are useful to this board regardless of its conclusions. AARO partnered with the archives of the Defense Intelligence Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the National Security Agency, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the Services and the Combatant Commands, and with the US National Archives on locating UAP data. It interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and other sites regarding a narrative of UAP over nuclear facilities. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites.

One correction this board has already logged belongs here permanently. A full-text search of the released Volume I returns no occurrence of the term YANKEE BLUE. The widely repeated claim that AARO conceded that programme in Volume I does not survive a check of the document.

Volume I should be read as a primary record of what the United States Government said in March 2024, which is exactly the tier at which it belongs. It is not a primary record of the facts it asserts, and its authors have never produced the second half.

aaro-historical-record-vol1.denialPosture: Volume I is itself the denial. dod.whatItIs: The Department of Defense, renamed the Department of War by executive action in 2025, is the cabinet department that has run every official US government UAP investigation from Project SIGN in December 1947 to AARO today. It holds the special access programme architecture, the counterintelligence organisations that respond to incursions on military installations, and the security review office that clears what its personnel may say in public. It is the institution against which the legacy programme allegation is principally made.
dod.whyImplicated: The Department has controlled every official UAP investigation for seventy-nine years and, by its own inspector general's finding, still had no coordinated approach and no comprehensive response plan eighteen months after Congress ordered it to build one. Its structure gives it the two things a concealed recovery programme requires: an unacknowledged special access programme system whose existence need not be disclosed, and counterintelligence organisations designated as the first responders to any anomalous incursion on any installation or range. Congress has twice legislated as though it believes unreported UAP compartments exist, first by giving AARO statutory access notwithstanding all access controls, then by forbidding the expenditure of funds on UAP-related special access activity not reported to the intelligence committees. A former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council testified under oath that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies and that the effort is hidden from elected representatives. The Department's own Historical Record Report concedes that a controlled access compartment was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.
dod.narrative:
The Department's UAP history is documented by its own inspector general. The first official DoD UAP activity was PROJECT SIGN, established by the Air Force Chief of Staff in December 1947. From 1947 to 1949 Air Force personnel investigated 243 reported sightings. In 1952 the Air Force Director of Intelligence initiated PROJECT BLUE BOOK, which investigated more than 12,000 sightings before its termination in 1969. Then, in the inspector general's own words, the DoD did not officially look at UAP again until mid-2000, when select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme to study UAP under the direction of the Defense Intelligence Agency. That sentence is worth pausing on. The Department's own watchdog records that the resumption of UAP work was not a Departmental decision at all. It was a congressional earmark inserted over the Department's disinterest, and when the Senate Majority Leader asked for it to be made a Special Access Program in June 2009 the Deputy Secretary of Defense declined on the advice of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

That forty-year gap is the load-bearing claim of the official account and the weakest point in it. The Department asks the public to accept that between BLUE BOOK's closure in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 it did nothing on the subject at all, in the same period in which it was operating an unacknowledged special access programme architecture whose whole purpose is that its contents cannot be inferred from budget documents or organisation charts.

Congress does not appear to accept it. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA forced the creation of an office. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the creation of a reporting mechanism usable notwithstanding non-disclosure agreements and free from reprisal. Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the historical report. Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA went further and prohibited the use of authorised funds for any special access or restricted access programme activity relating to UAP that has not been reported to the congressional committees by the Director of National Intelligence, and extended the restriction to contractor Independent Research and Development. Legislators do not write funding prohibitions against activities they believe do not exist.

The Deputy Secretary's July 2022 establishment memorandum is the Department's own consolidation instrument. It made AARO the authoritative office for all UAP and UAP-related activities, disestablished the Navy task force, and directed every DoD component holding UAP data, analysis, contracts or other material to synchronise immediately with AARO. If material and paperwork from a legacy programme existed anywhere in the Department, that memorandum is the order that would have moved it, and it moved it into an office reporting to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security.

The inspector general's evaluation, DODIG-2023-109, is the best independent measure of the Department's conduct. Its unclassified summary, released 24 January 2024, found that the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP; that DoD components had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands, the organisations actually responsible for detecting and preventing threats against the United States; that components had developed varying informal processes; and that the Department had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan. The evaluation notes that the Military Services and counterintelligence organisations had sent some UAP incident reports to AARO but that the Department does not formally require them to do so. It also records that the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report. That is three of the Department's most senior officials refusing to go on the record with the inspector general on this subject.

The response architecture matters as much as the analytic one. AARO's FY2025 report states that the military Services' counterintelligence, law enforcement and security agencies are the cognizant authorities responsible for responding to UAP incidents and incursions on all installations and ranges, and that AARO aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025. The doctrine governing what the United States military does when an anomalous object comes down on its property is classified, and the organisations that would execute it are Army Counterintelligence, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. Those are the same organisations that, in the concealment argument, would administer the silence.

Luis Elizondo, who told the House Oversight Committee in November 2024 that in his last government position he managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council, testified in writing that UAP are real, that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies, and that the country is in the midst of a multi-decade secretive arms race funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from elected representatives and oversight bodies. He testified that a small cadre within the government has created a culture of suppression and intimidation including unwarranted criminal investigations and harassment, and that the Pentagon's public affairs office employs a professional psychological operations officer as the single point of contact for UAP inquiries from citizens and the media.

The Department's posture since February 2026 has been transparency by executive channel. Secretary Hegseth committed to full compliance with a presidential disclosure directive, and a War Department official told DefenseScoop that AARO was working in close coordination with the White House to consolidate existing UAP records collections and facilitate the expeditious release of never-before-seen UAP information. The releases run through a departmental website rather than through the statutory National Archives collection, which puts the pace and the redactions back inside the Department.

openQuestions: No public accounting exists of unacknowledged special access programmes reviewed under section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA, nor any report from the Director of National Intelligence identifying which UAP-related SAPs were reported to the congressional committees and which were not.

The forty-year gap the Department claims between BLUE BOOK's termination in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 rests on the absence of a record, not on a record of absence, and has never been tested against the Department's SAP inventory for that period.

The Department has not published which components held UAP 'data, analysis, contracts, or other material' that were synchronised to AARO under the July 2022 memorandum, nor an inventory of what was transferred.
Whether the DOPSR prepublication review process has been used to suppress UAP-related disclosures by cleared personnel is undocumented on this board and is a Wave 5 target.

dia.whatItIs: The Defense Intelligence Agency is the Department of Defense combat support agency responsible for foreign military intelligence. Between 2008 and 2012 it managed the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, the congressionally earmarked effort that produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on advanced propulsion, materials and related subjects, executed under contract by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies. AARO has confirmed that the material generated by that programme remains in DIA's archived holdings.
dia.whyImplicated: DIA is the only agency the United States Government has formally admitted ran a modern programme that commissioned studies on how one would build and detect craft with capabilities no terrestrial system possesses, and it is the acknowledged custodian of that archive today. Its programme manager approved a contractor's UAP field investigations that were not in the statement of work, including proposals to stand up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials, which is a documented plan for a materials exploitation capability inside a defence intelligence contract. When the Senate Majority Leader asked in June 2009 that the programme be raised to Special Access Program status, the Department refused; when DIA cancelled it, its participants immediately proposed reconstituting it under Homeland Security as a compartment explicitly justified by claims that relevant material existed. AARO's own explanation for the entire modern disclosure movement traces it back to this DIA programme and its people. DIA is therefore the acknowledged root of the modern record, the custodian of its archive, and absent from the National Archives UAP collection.
dia.narrative:
In 2008 DIA posted a solicitation and awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace for what became the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program. The money came from Senate-directed appropriations rather than a Departmental requirement, a point the DoD Inspector General records plainly when it notes that the Department did not officially look at UAP again after Blue Book until select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme under DIA's direction. The programme ran from 2008 through 2012 in its various forms and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents covering advanced propulsion, warp drive metrics, traversable wormholes, metamaterials, invisibility cloaking, high energy laser weapons, and biological effects of anomalous exposure. DIA transmitted the list of titles and principal authors to Congress in January 2018.

AARO's own account of AAWSAP, in Historical Record Report Volume I and in its standalone KONA BLUE paper, is more useful to this board than AARO seems to have realised. It confirms the programme was managed by DIA from 2009 to 2012 and funded through congressional earmarks with Bigelow Aerospace as prime contractor. It confirms the stated purpose was investigating next-generation aerospace technologies across twelve specific areas including advanced lift, propulsion, unconventional materials and controls, and signature reduction. It then states that although investigating UFO or UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organisation conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA programme manager, and that this research included reviewing new cases and older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.

That sentence is the whole argument in miniature. A defence intelligence agency programme, funded outside the normal requirements process, with a programme manager who authorised his contractor to run field investigation teams and to propose materials exploitation laboratories for recovered UFO material. AARO's framing is that DIA did not seek nor specifically authorise this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract, which is an attempt to place the agency at arm's length from its own programme manager. It does not work. A contract managed by an agency employee, funded by an agency line, delivering to an agency archive, is the agency's programme.

The escalation attempt is documented. On 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Lynn declined on the recommendation of then Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper, who advised that the designation was not justified. Read against the concealment thesis, a request for SAP status is a request for a compartment in which recovered material could lawfully be held without disclosure, and the refusal is the point at which the effort had to find another home.

It found one, briefly. AARO's KONA BLUE paper states that when DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP, several individuals involved advocated that the Department of Homeland Security take the effort over and fund a new version under the code name KONA BLUE. In 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology established KONA BLUE as a Prospective Special Access Program based on claims that relevant information and material existed and required this level of protection. Six months later the Deputy Secretary of DHS disapproved it and directed immediate termination. AARO's insistence that no data or material was ever transferred to DHS is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that a Presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Under Secretary stood up a prospective compartment on the strength of a representation that material existed.

The custody question is settled by AARO's own words. Its KONA BLUE paper states that information associated with the activities conducted under the auspices of AAWSAP/AATIP remains within DIA's archived holdings. Whatever the thirty-eight reference documents, the field investigation files, the debriefing records and the case reviews amount to, DIA has them. That makes DIA a custody node on this map regardless of what one concludes about the underlying phenomenon.

The people matter. James T. Lacatski, a career DIA propulsion and missile intelligence specialist, was the programme manager who brought the subject to Senator Reid and who converted the contractor's deliverables into Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. He co-authored Skinwalkers at the Pentagon with Colm Kelleher, the biochemist who ran the contractor's field science effort, and George Knapp, the investigative reporter who first obtained and published the DIRD title list. AARO's Volume I addresses that body of work by describing the contractor's Utah property investigations, its interest in shadow figures, creatures, remote viewing and human consciousness anomalies, and its plan to hire psychics. AARO presents this as evidence the programme lacked merit. It is equally evidence that a defence intelligence agency programme was pursuing lines of inquiry it would never have funded without something driving it.

One further fact belongs on the board. AARO states that it partnered with DIA's archives for the historical review. Yet as of the National Archives Record Group 615 page's review date of 22 May 2026, DIA does not appear among the agencies with a UAP records transmittal to the National Archives. The agency that holds the acknowledged archive of the acknowledged programme has not, on the public record, delivered it to the statutory collection.

cia.whatItIs: The Central Intelligence Agency is the United States civilian foreign intelligence service. Its documented involvement with the UFO question runs from the Office of Scientific Intelligence study group of 1952 through its convening of the Robertson Panel in January 1953 to its management of the U-2 and OXCART cover stories through the 1950s and 1960s. Its own in-house historian published a detailed account of that record in Studies in Intelligence in 1997.
cia.whyImplicated: The CIA is the only agency in this dossier set that has published, in its own classified-origin journal, a first-person institutional admission that it directed the government to debunk UFO reports, concealed its sponsorship of the panel that recommended doing so, and knowingly allowed the Air Force to issue misleading and deceptive statements about more than half of all UFO reports for over a decade. That is not an allegation; it is the CIA's own historian describing the machinery of a UFO cover story and calling it by name. Once an agency has demonstrably run one UFO cover story for a real classified programme, the argument that it would not run a second for a different one loses its force. The Agency also sits at the point in the concealment argument where a recovery capability would have to live if the operations occurred on foreign soil, and it has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
cia.narrative:
The primary document here is Gerald K. Haines, CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90, published in Studies in Intelligence in 1997 and posted on the Agency's own website. Haines was a government historian with access to Agency files. What he wrote is more damaging to the Agency's credibility on this subject than anything a critic has written.

The Robertson Panel convened in January 1953 at CIA's instigation, following a recommendation from the Intelligence Advisory Committee to enlist selected scientists to review and appraise the available evidence in light of pertinent scientific theories. The panellists had expertise in nuclear physics, high-energy physics, radar, electronics and geophysics. Their formal conclusion was that there was no evidence of a direct threat to national security and no evidence of extraterrestrial visitation. Their operational recommendation was something else entirely. Haines writes that to meet these problems, the panel recommended that the National Security Council debunk UFO reports and institute a policy of public education to reassure the public of the lack of evidence behind UFOs. It suggested using the mass media, advertising, business clubs, schools, and even the Disney corporation to get the message across. In the same breath, reporting at the height of McCarthyism, it recommended that private UFO groups including the Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators in Los Angeles and the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization be monitored for subversive activities.

That is a US intelligence agency recommending, at national security council level, a domestic public-opinion management campaign on a scientific subject and the surveillance of American civil society organisations that took an interest in it. The Agency then concealed its own role. When public pressure built for release of the panel report in 1956, Philip Strong, Deputy Assistant Director of the Office of Scientific Intelligence, refused to declassify it and declined to disclose CIA sponsorship of the panel. Haines records that the Agency instead prepared a sanitized version which deleted any reference to CIA and avoided mention of any psychological warfare potential in the UFO controversy. When Donald Keyhoe told Mike Wallace on CBS in March 1958 that the CIA was deeply involved and had sponsored the panel, the Agency held firm to its policy of not revealing its role in UFO investigations and refused to declassify the full report.

The U-2 passage is the strongest single piece of documentary evidence anywhere in the official record that the United States Government has deliberately generated false explanations for aerial phenomena and sustained them for years. Haines writes that Air Force BLUE BOOK investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights tried to explain away such sightings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and temperature inversions, that by checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in Washington they were able to attribute many UFO sightings to U-2 flights, and that they were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public. He then reports that according to later estimates from CIA officials who worked on the U-2 and OXCART projects, over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s were accounted for by manned reconnaissance flights, namely the U-2, over the United States, and that this led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily sensitive national security project. Haines adds that while perhaps justified, this deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup controversy of the 1970s.

The Agency also drafted, and then abandoned, a National Security Council Intelligence Directive on UFOs following the Robertson Panel findings. A directive of that class would have assigned standing intelligence community responsibility for the subject. That it was drafted at all establishes that the Agency treated UFOs as a candidate for permanent national intelligence tasking in 1953.

The modern allegations against the Agency are thinner and must be marked as such. Journalist Ross Coulthart has reported, on the basis of David Grusch and other sources, that an office within CIA has coordinated crash retrievals on foreign soil for many years. No document supporting that has been released, no named official has confirmed it on the record, and this board carries it at Tier 3 as a research direction rather than a finding. AARO's Volume I addresses a related allegation and reports that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which is an on-the-record denial obtained by an interested party rather than a document from the period.

What can be said cleanly is this. AARO states it partnered with CIA archives for the historical review, so the Agency's UAP holdings were at least nominally opened to the office writing the government's history. Yet as of 22 May 2026 the CIA does not appear among the seven organisations with a transmittal in the National Archives UAP Records Collection. Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, named the CIA first among the agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading in his words to unchecked power and corruption. An agency with a published institutional history of running UFO cover stories, no statutory records transmittal, and a named place in sworn whistleblower testimony belongs on this map.

doe.whatItIs: The Department of Energy is the successor to the Atomic Energy Commission and the custodian of the United States nuclear weapons complex, including Los Alamos, Sandia, Lawrence Livermore and the Pantex assembly and disassembly plant, operated through the National Nuclear Security Administration. Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 it holds a government-wide classification authority, Restricted Data, that exists entirely outside the executive order classification system and is not subject to automatic declassification.
doe.whyImplicated: DOE holds the one classification authority in the United States government that a legacy programme could hide behind indefinitely, because Restricted Data is created by statute rather than by executive order, applies government-wide, and never automatically declassifies. Its facilities are also the physical centre of gravity of the phenomenon's own documented history: the green fireball wave of 1948 to 1951 concentrated over Los Alamos and Sandia, Project GRUDGE recorded case clusters in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area and at Oak Ridge, and Congress now requires AARO to report annually on incidents at nuclear weapons production, transportation and storage facilities. In the most recent reporting year the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman sent AARO fifty incident reports, a 177.8 percent increase over the prior year, every one of which AARO records as not reported as UAP. A former DoD official named DOE under oath as one of the agencies with a role and no accountability. DOE has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
doe.narrative:
The reason DOE belongs on a map of concealment has nothing to do with what anyone alleges and everything to do with statute. Restricted Data is defined by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and covers all data concerning the design, manufacture or utilisation of atomic weapons, the production of special nuclear material, and the use of special nuclear material in the production of energy. It is classified under the Act, not under an executive order. Everything else in the national security classification system flows from a presidential order, currently the 13526 lineage, and is therefore subject to automatic declassification at twenty-five years unless exempted. Restricted Data is not. It requires affirmative review before declassification, it cannot be declassified by an agency that did not originate it, and the authority is government-wide. DOE's implementing regulation is 10 CFR Part 1045, most recently overhauled by a final rule published in the Federal Register on 21 December 2018.

The practical consequence is that if a UAP incident occurred over a weapons production facility, a storage igloo, a transport convoy or a laboratory working on weapons physics, the record of it could be created as Restricted Data from the moment of its generation and would then be permanently outside the reach of the executive order declassification machinery that every UAP disclosure statute has assumed. The FY2024 NDAA's records collection provisions operate on federal records generally. They do not amend the Atomic Energy Act.

The history is dense. From late November 1948 through early 1951 a wave of green luminous objects was reported over New Mexico, concentrated near Los Alamos and Sandia and over other sensitive installations. On 16 February 1949 a conference at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory brought together laboratory director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller, Frederick Reines, representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the military, and Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico Institute of Meteoritics, who had personally observed the objects. LaPaz, after interviewing more than a hundred witnesses, advised the military and the AEC that the fireballs were most likely either unconventional defensive devices being tested by the United States or Soviet reconnaissance devices. The Air Force ran Project Twinkle from 1949 to 1951 to instrument the phenomenon, never fully implemented it, and concluded the objects were probably natural.

AARO's own Volume I preserves the pattern independently. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites. It records that AARO interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and elsewhere in connection with a narrative that UAP sightings near nuclear facilities resulted in malfunctioning missiles and a destroyed test reentry vehicle. It records that AARO continues to investigate these cases because of their potential impact on the readiness of the US nuclear programme. And it lists DOE among the agency archives AARO partnered with.

Congress has legislated the nuclear connection into permanent statutory reporting. Section 3373(k) of title 50 requires AARO's annual report to include the number and description of incidents of UAP associated with military nuclear assets, and separately the results of consultation with the Administrator for Nuclear Security regarding incidents at facilities or assets associated with the production, transportation or storage of nuclear weapons or their components, and with the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding nuclear power stations and fuel storage sites. That is a standing legal obligation on the nuclear weapons enterprise to account, annually, for anomalous objects over its facilities.

The FY2025 report is the most recent execution of it and the number is striking. AARO received fifty reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the NRC Chairman regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near US nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, a 177.8 percent increase over the eighteen reported the previous year. Forty-seven of the fifty occurred between 1700 and 0500 local. Five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours. AARO then adds the sentence that carries all the weight: none of these incidents were reported as UAP. The nuclear complex is reporting a rising volume of unexplained aerial activity over the most sensitive sites in the country and categorising all of it, in advance, as drones.

The 2015 Pantex incident is the clearest recent case. A Department of Energy report describes security personnel at the nuclear weapons assembly and disassembly plant near Amarillo observing a diamond-shaped object in September 2015, hovering and moving in a northerly trajectory at roughly ten to fifteen miles per hour, described by witnesses as around four feet tall and two feet wide at the base and thinner at the top, with conflicting colour descriptions. The object was tracked by ground radar and photographed from a nearby radar tower, and the imagery was analysed by DOE's Sandia National Laboratories. The report was released in more complete form during the 2026 executive-branch disclosure tranches after earlier heavily redacted releases.

Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, listed the Department of Energy among the White House, CIA, NASA and the Pentagon as agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading to unchecked power and corruption. As of the National Archives collection page's 22 May 2026 review, DOE had no transmittal listed in Record Group 615.
