No released document establishes whether any UAP-related record has ever been classified as Restricted Data or Formerly Restricted Data. If one has, the FY2024 NDAA collection is structurally incomplete.

AARO reports 50 incidents near nuclear weapons infrastructure from NNSA and NRC in a single year and states none were reported as UAP. The criteria by which the reporting agency classifies an unresolved object as an unmanned aerial system rather than a UAP have not been published.
The Sandia National Laboratories imagery analysis of the 2015 Pantex object has not been released in full, and it is not known whether Sandia reached a conclusion on the object's identity.

The complete record of the 16 February 1949 Los Alamos conference, the LaPaz interviews and the Project Twinkle instrument data has never been released as a set, and it is unclear which portions sit in DOE holdings versus Air Force holdings.

nara-uap-collection.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection is a statutory records collection at the National Archives and Records Administration, created by sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act and codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note. NARA established it as Record Group 615. Every federal agency was required to review, identify and organise its UAP records for disclosure and transmission, and to transfer publicly releasable digital copies in advance of 30 September 2025.
nara-uap-collection.whyImplicated: The collection is the concealment argument reduced to an inventory problem, and the inventory is nearly empty. Congress wrote a statutory definition that expressly reaches records concerning technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence, which is a legislature drafting for the existence of the thing rather than the possibility of it. It then stripped out the two provisions that would have given the statute teeth, the eminent domain power over privately held recovered material and the independent Review Board modelled on the JFK Act, leaving agencies to grade their own homework. What arrived is the measure of what compliance is worth: as of May 2026 the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations, and the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the Defense Intelligence Agency, NASA and the military departments are not among them. A parallel executive-branch release channel opened in 2026 that routes disclosures around the statutory collection entirely.
nara-uap-collection.narrative:
The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, sponsored by Senators Schumer and Rounds, passed the Senate in July 2023 as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA. In its Senate form it would have created an independent Review Board with authority over agency withholding decisions, and it would have directed the federal government to exercise eminent domain over any recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private persons or entities. Neither survived conference. What was enacted in Public Law 118-31 on 22 December 2023 was the records collection framework alone.

What survived is still remarkable as legislative drafting. The statute directs NARA to build a collection consisting of copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence, or equivalent subjects by any other name, with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects. Congress wrote three categories into federal records law. Unidentified anomalous phenomena is the neutral one. Technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence are not neutral at all; they are the categories a legacy recovery programme would generate. The clause about equivalent subjects by any other name is anti-evasion drafting aimed at codeword renaming. The exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects is there to keep routine drone and balloon traffic out. Legislatures do not build statutory taxonomies for things they believe do not exist.

NARA implemented it. It established Record Group 615, issued guidance to agencies through memoranda AC 26.2024 and AC 04.2025, and set the mechanics: agencies identify all UAP records in any format, make digital copies, attach prescribed metadata, and transfer. NARA accepts only digital versions. Agencies were to complete identification and organisation by 20 October 2024 and to initiate transfer in advance of 30 September 2025. One provision deserves particular attention. Where a publicly releasable record includes redactions, the agency must simultaneously transfer redacted and unredacted copies to NARA. The National Archives therefore holds unredacted originals of redacted UAP records that it does not publish, which makes NARA itself a custody node with material it is sitting on.

The results are the story. As of the Record Group 615 page's stated review date of 22 May 2026, the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. That list is as notable for its absences as its contents. The Central Intelligence Agency, whose own historian documented decades of UFO cover story management, is absent. The Department of Energy, which holds the nuclear complex and the Restricted Data authority, is absent. The Defense Intelligence Agency, which AARO has confirmed holds the AAWSAP archive, is absent. NASA is absent. The Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force are absent, which means the services that ran Project SIGN, Project GRUDGE, Project Blue Book and Project Moon Dust have not appeared in the collection created to hold that history. AARO itself, whose Volume I lists partnering with the National Archives on locating UAP data as one of its four lines of effort, appears only through OSD.

The statutory architecture explains why. The Act imposes an obligation on agencies to identify their own records and to decide what is publicly releasable. There is no Review Board, no independent adjudicator of withholding, and no penalty for a null return. Independent tracking of the transfer deadline found that most agencies approached with records requests either produced nothing or did not respond at all. A statute that asks the holders of a secret to declare it, and provides no mechanism when they do not, produces exactly the collection that exists.

The 2026 development compounds rather than fixes this. A presidential directive in February 2026 launched a multiagency effort to identify, review, declassify and publicly release UAP records, with a centralised repository opened in May 2026 on the Department of War's own website and material issued in periodic tranches. The releases have included previously unseen material, including a Department of Energy report on a 2015 incident over the Pantex nuclear weapons plant. But the channel is executive, discretionary, and controlled by the departments whose compliance with the statutory channel was the problem. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation made the point directly in February 2026, noting that Congress had already passed laws establishing a public UAP records collection at the National Archives and that the existing statutory framework gave the administration a path it was not using, while warning that classification nuances could produce misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.

The collection is therefore best understood on this board as an instrument that works and a compliance record that does not. The statute is the strongest UAP disclosure law ever enacted and it names the categories precisely. Record Group 615 is real, it is growing, and NARA is holding unredacted copies the public cannot see. Seven agencies have delivered. The agencies at the centre of the argument have not.

claims.text: Sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, require NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and require each federal agency to review, identify and organise each UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission to the National Archives.

The statutory scope is 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).'
NARA established Record Group 615 as the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and will accept only digital copies of UAP records from agencies.

Agencies were required to identify and organise UAP records by 20 October 2024 and to initiate transfer of publicly releasable records in advance of 30 September 2025, with metadata prescribed by NARA guidance in memorandum AC 26.2024.

Where a publicly releasable record includes redactions, agencies must simultaneously transfer both redacted and unredacted copies to NARA, meaning the National Archives holds unredacted originals of redacted UAP records that it does not publish.

As of the Record Group 615 page's stated review date of 22 May 2026, the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the Defense Intelligence Agency, NASA and the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force do not appear among the organisations with transmittals listed in Record Group 615 as of 22 May 2026.

The eminent domain mandate over privately held recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence, and the independent Review Board, were contained in the Senate-passed UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 but were removed in conference and are not part of Public Law 118-31.
AARO lists 'Partner with the U.S. National Archives on locating UAP data, refining requests based on the discovery of new leads' as one of its four stated lines of effort for the historical review.
claims.source: AARO Historical Record Report Volume I, March 2024, Scope and Methodology; https://media.defense.gov/2024/Mar/08/2003409233/-1/-1/0/DOPSR-CLEARED-508-COMPLIANT-HRRV1-08-MAR-2024-FINAL.PDF

claims.text: NARA maintains a bulk catalog download facility for UAP records alongside the Record Group 615 series listings, allowing the collection's contents to be enumerated independently of NARA's own summaries.

In February 2026 a War Department official stated that AARO 'has made progress to make UAP information available and transfer those records to the National Archives in accordance with federal law,' while AARO's own historical and annual reports remained unpublished and overdue.

Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation, stated in February 2026 that 'Congress already has passed laws establishing a public UAP records collection at the National Archives' and that the existing statutory framework provided the administration a path it was not using, while warning that classification nuances risked misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.

A presidential directive issued in February 2026 established a multiagency UAP records release effort with a centralised repository on the Department of War website, releasing material in periodic tranches beginning May 2026, operating alongside and outside the statutory National Archives collection.
NARA's guidance to agencies on identifying, preparing and transferring UAP records is published as a records management guidance page and in agency memoranda AC 26.2024 and AC 04.2025.

nara-uap-collection.denialPosture: NARA has made no substantive claim about the phenomenon and issues no denials; it is a records custodian executing a statute. Its published position is procedural, that it receives records from agencies on a rolling basis and will add to Record Group 615 as they are transferred. The absence of denial is itself significant: NARA has never stated that any agency has certified it holds no UAP records, and it publishes no compliance register.
openQuestions: NARA publishes no register of which agencies have certified compliance, which have made null returns, and which have not responded at all. Without it, the seven listed transmittals cannot be distinguished from a near total failure of compliance.
The statutory transfer deadline of 30 September 2025 has passed. No enforcement action, referral or public accounting of non-compliance has been identified.
NARA holds unredacted copies of redacted UAP records under the simultaneous transfer requirement. The volume of that unpublished holding is not disclosed anywhere.

Whether records classified as Restricted Data under the Atomic Energy Act are treated as within or outside the transfer obligation has never been addressed by NARA guidance, which matters directly for DOE and the nuclear weapons complex.

The relationship between the statutory Record Group 615 collection and the 2026 executive-branch release channel is undefined. It is not established whether material released through the executive channel is also being accessioned into RG 615, or whether it substitutes for it.
The Senate-passed Review Board and eminent domain provisions have not been reintroduced and enacted. Whether any subsequent NDAA restores them is a live tracking item.

mitre-corporation.whatItIs: The MITRE Corporation is a private not-for-profit spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1958 that operates exclusively as a manager of federally funded research and development centers. It runs six FFRDCs on behalf of the Department of Defense, the Federal Aviation Administration, Treasury and the IRS, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Health and Human Services, and NIST. It is headquartered in McLean, Virginia, and also provides the administrative home for JASON, the government's standing outside scientific advisory panel.
mitre-corporation.whyImplicated: MITRE is on this map because of the legal mechanism it embodies, not because a witness has named it as a custodian of material. An FFRDC is granted, by regulation, access to government and contractor data 'beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship' - including sensitive and proprietary data, installations, equipment and real property - and its sponsoring agreement gives the sponsor's Executive Agent approval authority over the classification, publication and distribution of its output. That combination produces a private organisation holding federal program records under a disclosure obligation that runs to a sponsoring agency rather than to Congress or to the public, and whose corporate files are not agency records for FOIA purposes. The DHS sponsoring agreement goes further: MITRE's own staff sign non-disclosure agreements that expressly preserve the right to report substantial violations of law to Congress, but subcontractors and consultants are required to sign the same NDA with that whistleblower carve-back removed. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison put this exact structure in writing, telling MITRE that FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records' and demanding a search back to 1 January 1930.
mitre-corporation.narrative:
MITRE occupies a category that exists nowhere else in the federal enterprise. It manufactures nothing, competes for nothing, and sells nothing. It exists to hold institutional memory and technical judgement on behalf of government sponsors, and the Federal Acquisition Regulation builds that role out of a single privilege: an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.' That sentence, FAR 35.017(a)(2), is the load-bearing beam of this dossier. Everything a prime contractor knows about its own black programmes, and everything the government knows about the prime, can lawfully sit inside the FFRDC that sits between them.

MITRE currently operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for DoD; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and the IRS, co-sponsored by Veterans Affairs, the Social Security Administration and Commerce; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC for NIST. Its own fact sheet notes there are only forty-two FFRDCs in total and that operating six of them is 'a high honor.' The relevant point for this board is not prestige but coverage: one nonprofit sits inside the defence establishment, the intelligence-adjacent national security enterprise, and the civil aviation regulator that owns the primary radar picture of American airspace.

The governing document that shows how this works in practice is the FY2009 sponsoring agreement between DHS and MITRE for HS SEDI, signed by MITRE's president and by the Acting Under Secretary for Science and Technology on 13 March 2009. It is worth reading as a specification for exactly the kind of custody problem this board is mapping. Section 3 states that SEDI's work 'will often require privileged access to information, including sensitive Government information and industry proprietary data not normally available to non-Government organizations.' Section 5(h) obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data.' Section 6(c)(9) records the routine practice: 'Ordinarily, sponsors release classified, privileged, no-contractor, and other sensitive material directly to SEDI.' Section 5(a) states plainly that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects.'

Then the agreement closes the loop on disclosure. Section 6(b)(9) gives the DHS Executive Agent authority to review and approve 'the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications.' Section 9(g) defines 'Privileged Information' so broadly that it captures every deliverable, note, lab record, test result and analysis MITRE produces for the sponsor, and forbids disclosure except as required by law or 'as expressly authorized in writing by the DHS Executive Agent.' Section 9(g)(2) then carves back the whistleblower statutes, stating that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.' That is the protective clause. And Section 5(j)(iv) requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2).' The people at the outer edge of the work - the ones brought in for specialised expertise MITRE does not hold in-house - are contractually bound by the secrecy terms without the clause that preserves their right to tell Congress.

This is the structural argument, and on 22 May 2026 a member of Congress made it out loud. Rep. Eric Burlison, of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, sent a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE's president Mark Peters and its general counsel Christopher Land. The relevant time period is 'January 1, 1930, to the present.' The definitions section reaches every MITRE-operated FFRDC, every subcontractor, and any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, or equivalent terms.'

The interrogatories are targeted at exactly the mechanism described above. Section III demands identification of every Special Access Program, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword and DOE SIGMA category MITRE participated in or supported in connection with UAP records, and asks whether each 'was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks MITRE to identify any classification guide, NDA, access roster or sponsor communication that instructed personnel to avoid using the terms UAP, UFO, crash retrieval or reverse engineering in records. Section VIII asks for every NDA or indoctrination instrument 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress.' Section IX asks MITRE to identify any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems or Bigelow Aerospace. Section X asks whether responsive funding was routed through a cover programme 'whose public description differed materially from the responsive work performed.' The letter warns that concealment or destruction may implicate 18 U.S.C. sections 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519 and 2071.

MITRE's reply, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was a single sentence from a spokesperson: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That answer is not evasive so much as accurate. It restates the architecture the letter was written to expose. An FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor. Congress asks MITRE; MITRE asks the sponsor; the sponsor is the same authority that classified the work. What the record does not contain, as of this writing, is the certification of search methodology, the records-location index, the preservation hold, or any production - all of which the letter demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks.

claims.text: Federal Acquisition Regulation 35.017(a)(2) states that an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.'

MITRE operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center (DoD), the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development (FAA), the Center for Enterprise Modernization (Treasury/IRS, co-sponsored by VA, SSA and Commerce), the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute (DHS), the Health FFRDC (HHS), and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC (NIST).

The DHS-MITRE sponsoring agreement for HS SEDI obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data ... including that which is not normally available to non-government organizations' (Section 5(h)).

Under Section 6(b)(9) of the same agreement, the DHS Executive Agent 'Reviews and approves the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications' - meaning the sponsoring agency, not MITRE, controls whether MITRE's work product can be released.

Section 5(j)(iv) of the same agreement requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) secrecy terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2)' - the clause that preserves the right to make disclosures to Congress essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.

Section 9(g)(2) of the same agreement states that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law' - a protection extended to MITRE's own personnel but expressly withheld from its subcontractors and consultants.

Section 5(a) of the same agreement states that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects and shall strictly comply with the provisions of the National Industrial Security Program ... as set forth in DOD Directive 5220.22-M as amended.'

On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison transmitted a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE president Mark Peters and general counsel Christopher Land, setting the relevant search period as 'January 1, 1930, to the present.'

The Burlison interrogatories demand that MITRE identify all Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, Managed-Need-To-Know codewords and DOE SIGMA categories it participated in or supported in connection with UAP-related records, and state for each 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify any nondisclosure agreement, indoctrination record or sponsor communication 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress, Inspectors General, AARO, NARA, federal law enforcement, or appropriate cleared oversight officials.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify 'any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems, Bigelow Aerospace or its successors/affiliates.'

Burlison's accompanying statement of 26 May 2026 says FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records - especially records Congress has directed to be identified, preserved, reviewed, and transferred for public release.'

MITRE's public response, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets'; a member of Burlison's staff told the same outlet that the letter was informed by 'advice from many whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations, and those working at FFRDCs.'

MITRE's certification of search methodology, records-location index, preservation hold and production of unclassified responsive records - all demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks from 22 May 2026 - have not been placed on the public record.

mitre-corporation.denialPosture: MITRE has not denied holding UAP-related records. Its only public statement on the Burlison inquiry, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was that it was reviewing its archives and that 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' No certification, denial of possession, or records-location index has been made public.
openQuestions: Did MITRE issue the preservation hold demanded within ten business days, and if so, which systems, archives and air-gapped environments does it cover?

Whether the subcontractor/consultant NDA construction found in the DHS HS SEDI sponsoring agreement - Section 9(g) secrecy terms without the Section 9(g)(2) congressional-disclosure carve-back - also appears in the sponsoring agreements for MITRE's DoD, FAA, Treasury, HHS and NIST FFRDCs, which are not public in comparable form.
Which federal sponsor would have to authorise release of any responsive MITRE record, and whether any sponsor has been asked.

Whether MITRE's National Security Engineering Center or its work for the FAA ever handled UAP sensor, radar or anomaly-detection data, which Section V of the interrogatories asks about directly and which has not been answered publicly.
MITRE's role in administering JASON, and whether JASON was ever tasked on UAP or anomalous materials questions, is not addressed anywhere in the public record reviewed here.

lockheed-martin.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Corporation is the largest single recipient of United States defense contract obligations, formed by the 1995 merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta. It operates cleared facilities accredited for Special Access Program work and runs the Advanced Development Programs organisation, the Skunk Works, which has built the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 among other classified aircraft. It is the only corporation named on the record, by a sworn witness in a congressional hearing, as a holder of recovered non-terrestrial material.
lockheed-martin.whyImplicated: Lockheed Martin sits at the intersection of the two conditions this board treats as necessary for a legacy programme to survive without congressional visibility: a company with the industrial capacity to store and work on recovered material, and a legal regime that can lift normal industrial security oversight off it. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of National Industrial Security Program oversight for DoD special access programs whenever the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves a carve-out provision. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee or consultant may provide SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. Two sworn witnesses - George Knapp in September 2025 and Luis Elizondo in November 2024 - have testified to a specific, dated, blocked transaction in which material collected in the 1950s and held at a California facility was to move from a corporation to Bigelow's BAASS, and did not. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of that sworn testimony.
lockheed-martin.narrative:
The Lockheed Martin allegation is unusual on this board because it is the one that has been made under oath, in a hearing room, with a company name attached. On 9 September 2025, before the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, George Knapp told the committee: 'It has been widely reported and suspected that Lockheed Martin is one of the contractors - the defense contractors, that has held this stuff, stored it away in secrecy, and tried to figure out how it works.' He then went further and put his own reporting on the record: 'I have confirmed on the record that Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.' Later in the same hearing Rep. Tim Burchett asked which corporations hold the material. Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.' He added a line that is, for the purposes of this map, more revealing than the accusation itself: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Ten months earlier, on 13 November 2024, Luis Elizondo had testified to the same transaction from inside the government side of it. Asked by Rep. Burlison whether the government or defence contractors possess technology, Elizondo said one reason his predecessor programme AAWSAP was trying to collect material of unknown origin was that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material ... that was collected in the 1950s. Unfortunately, that did not actually occur.' Burlison then put the Christopher Sharp reporting to him directly - a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace, and a CIA block - and Elizondo answered: 'What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.' He described the missing instrument: 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

The official record does not name the company, but it does record the allegation. AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, logs an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.' A separate entry logs a claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly intact, under a CIA partnership that ended in 1989. AARO says it found no empirical evidence for either. AARO's denial is procedurally notable in its own right: 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, on what date, and describes no verification step beyond the meeting itself. Under this board's sourcing rule, that is an artefact of a statement, not evidence of the fact asserted.

What makes the allegation structurally survivable rather than merely unproven is the regulatory architecture around a company like Lockheed Martin. Industrial security oversight of cleared contractors is normally exercised by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency under the National Industrial Security Program. But 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.' A carve-out programme is therefore a cleared contractor facility from which the government's own standing industrial security inspector has been formally removed by name, at the direction of the second-ranking official in the Department.

The congressional side is narrowed by the same directive. DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' That is a standing prior-restraint on contractor-to-Congress disclosure inside the SAP world, in an unclassified, publicly posted directive. The statutory reporting channel is narrower still: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content of any SAP report to the defence committees on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - eight people, not four committees.

So the record on Lockheed Martin has an unusual shape. Two witnesses under oath, one of them a former Pentagon official, describing the same blocked transfer with the same missing Secretary of the Air Force memorandum. An official report that catalogues the allegation, does not name the company, and reports an unverified denial from unnamed executives. A statutory and regulatory framework that would make exactly this kind of holding invisible to the ordinary inspection and reporting machinery. And, on the other side of the ledger, no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no inventory, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record statement from Lockheed Martin responding to sworn testimony that named it.

That material was not made here.'
Asked by Rep. Tim Burchett at the same hearing to name the corporations holding the material, Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.'
Knapp added at the same hearing: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE list Lockheed Martin first among the entities whose UAP-related work MITRE must identify, placing the company's name in a formal congressional production request rather than only in testimony.

No contract, facility designation, transfer or shipping document, inventory record, subpoena, inspection report, or on-the-record corporate response from Lockheed Martin to the sworn testimony naming it has been placed in the public record.

lockheed-martin.denialPosture: Lockheed Martin has issued no public, on-the-record rebuttal of the sworn testimony of September 2025 naming it. The only denial in the documentary record is AARO's summary statement in its 2024 Historical Record Report that unnamed 'executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees' met the Director of AARO and denied ever having recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered extraterrestrial technology.
openQuestions: Whether any Lockheed Martin facility has ever operated under a Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense-approved carve-out relieving DCSA of industrial security oversight, and if so for which programmes and over what period. Carve-out approvals are not published.
The identity of the 'facility in California' described in Knapp's sworn testimony, and whether it is a company-owned site or leased space on a government-owned installation.
Whether the Secretary of the Air Force memorandum Elizondo described as necessary and never issued exists in draft, and in whose files.
Whether Lockheed Martin executives were among those AARO says met its Director, and on what date - AARO names neither the companies nor the individuals.

Lockheed Martin's SEC filings report results attributable to classified programmes without identifying them; whether any of those programmes intersect the custody allegation cannot be tested from the public filings and is a line of research, not a claim.

ttsa.whatItIs: To The Stars Academy of Arts and Science Inc. was a Delaware public benefit corporation incorporated in 2017 and registered with the SEC under Commission File Number 024-10728, CIK 1710274, EIN 82-0601064. Its directors were Tom DeLonge, former CIA Directorate of Operations officer Jim Semivan, and physicist Harold Puthoff; Lockheed Skunk Works veteran Steve Justice and former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo were listed as significant employees. It raised money through a Regulation A offering, hosted the first officially released US military UAP videos, and signed a research agreement with the US Army before winding down its aerospace work and reverting to entertainment as To The Stars Inc.
ttsa.whyImplicated: TTSA matters to this map not as a research institution but as a legal vehicle. For roughly three years it was the corporate person through which men carrying intelligence, special-access and black-aerospace careers could act in public, hold material, sign agreements with the government, and speak to Congress and the press without a government employer's prepublication apparatus sitting on top of every sentence. Its SEC filings are the single richest primary record on this board of who those people were, what clearances and career histories they carried, and what the venture was actually organised to do. In October 2019 it converted that standing into a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering 'material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage' - a government laboratory relationship with a private company that held claimed anomalous material. AARO's own history records the same personnel network attempting to reconstitute the AAWSAP effort inside the Department of Homeland Security as the prospective special access programme KONA BLUE.
ttsa.narrative:
To The Stars Academy is the most thoroughly documented entity on this board, for a reason that has nothing to do with UAP: it sold securities. A company that offers stock under Regulation A must file with the SEC, and the filings are public, dated, signed and auditable. The FY2017 Form 1-K is therefore the closest thing this subject has to a sworn organisational chart.

What it shows is a very small company with a very unusual staff. Officers and directors were Tom DeLonge as president and interim chief executive; Jim Semivan as vice president of operations and director; and Harold E. Puthoff as vice president of science and technology and director. The filing states that Semivan 'retired from the Central Intelligence Agency's Directorate of Operations after 25 years working as an operations officer both overseas and domestically,' that he 'was a member of the CIA's Senior Intelligence Service,' and that he 'currently holds Top Secret Clearances.' It states that Puthoff is president and chief executive of EarthTech International and director of the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin. Two significant employees are listed: Steve Justice, Director of Advanced Programs and Technology, part-time at twenty hours a week, whose industry background the filing ties to the Lockheed organisation 'known as the "Skunk Works"'; and Luis Elizondo, Chief of Security and Special Programs, full-time, described as a career intelligence officer. As of 31 December 2017 the company had eleven employees.

The financial picture in the same filing is stark. Revenues for 2017 were $1,376,215 against cost of revenues of $750,932, producing gross profit of $625,283 - essentially a merchandise and music business. The net loss for 2017 was $30,665,436, against $422,670 the prior year, almost entirely non-cash stock compensation. Gravity Holdings LLC, whose sole member is the DeLonge Family Trust, held 60,000,000 Class A shares, 85.7 per cent of the class. This was not a research budget. It was a capital structure wrapped around a founder and a small group of named individuals.

What the company did with that structure is the part that belongs on this map. It became, as the filing puts it, 'the very first company to obtain official U.S. Government footage of unidentified aerial phenomena ("UAP") that had gone through the declassification process and been approved for public release,' publishing the footage through its online Community of Interest. The videos that entered the mainstream through the New York Times in December 2017 - the material now known as FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast - reached the public through a private securities issuer, not through a Pentagon press release. That routing is itself a finding. A declassification review was completed and the product was handed to a company in which a serving-until-recently Pentagon official was chief of security and special programs.

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command 'to advance TTSA's materiel and technology innovations in order to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles.' The announcement described the technology set as leveraging 'developments in material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage,' and set out the exchange: 'TTSA will share its discoveries with Ground Vehicle System Center (GVSC) and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection (GVSP) and the U.S. Army shall provide laboratories, expertise, support, and resources to help characterize the technologies and its applications.' Dr Joseph Cannon of US Army Futures Command called the partnership 'an exciting, non-traditional source for novel materials and transformational technologies.' Steve Justice, by then TTSA's chief operating officer and aerospace division director, said the agreement brought 'additional, critically important expertise that is necessary to advance the state-of-the-art in both our near and long-term technology areas of study.'

Read against the rest of this board, the CRADA is the important document. A private company holding material it described as anomalous obtained access to Army laboratories to characterise it, under an instrument that is not a procurement contract and does not require the government to pay. A CRADA moves capability and data across the government-private boundary in both directions with far less contractual and oversight furniture than a prime contract, and it does so without a competitive solicitation. Whether or not anything anomalous was ever in those laboratories, the mechanism is precisely the kind of low-visibility government-private research channel this board is built to map.

The network did not begin with TTSA and did not end with it. AARO's Historical Record Report records that after AAWSAP was terminated, 'its supporters unsuccessfully attempted to convince DHS to support a new version of this effort dubbed KONA BLUE,' which AARO characterises as 'a UAP-related Prospective Special Access Program (PSAP) called KONA BLUE that was proposed to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and supported by individuals who believed the USG was hiding off-world technology,' and which 'was never approved by DHS.' The same people, in sequence: a DIA contract, a proposed DHS special access programme, a Delaware public benefit corporation, a congressional hearing.

Elizondo, Christopher Mellon and Justice departed in December 2020, the aerospace and materials work wound down, and the entity renamed itself To The Stars Inc. and returned to entertainment. What it leaves behind is a documentary trail that is unusually hard to argue with, because it was filed under penalty of securities law: names, ages, clearances, prior employers, share counts, losses, and an executed agreement with a US Army laboratory command.

The nearest thing in the record is AARO's 2024 finding that a sample it acquired 'from a private UAP investigating organization and the U.S. Army' is a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with no exceptional qualities, and its characterisation of KONA BLUE - proposed by the same personnel network - as a prospective special access programme that DHS never approved and whose supporters 'never provided empirical evidence to support their claims.'

What happened to TTSA's materials holdings when the aerospace and science divisions wound down in 2020-2022, and who holds them now.

Whether any TTSA principal was under a live nondisclosure or special-access indoctrination instrument at the time of the company's public statements, and whether DoD SAPCO approval under DoDD 5205.07 Section 3.1.g was sought or given for any briefing to Congress.

sol-foundation.whatItIs: The Sol Foundation is a private non-profit co-founded by Stanford pathology professor Garry Nolan and anthropologist Peter Skafish that describes its work as science, policy and public education for what it calls the post-UAP world. It runs observational and analytical research projects, publishes a numbered white-paper and policy-briefing series, and holds an annual conference. In June 2026 five people connected to it - both co-founders, a senior adviser, an advisory board member and its production lead - were named to the US government's UAP Science Advisory Council.
sol-foundation.whyImplicated: Sol is the institution that converted the private technical layer into a policy actor with standing inside government. Its published output is not popular advocacy; it is a policy programme aimed squarely at the concealment mechanism, including a November 2024 paper by its own executive director on executive-branch UAP secrecy and the harm to Congress, a May 2025 paper by retired Colonel Karl Nell calling for US government disclosure, and an April 2026 briefing by its senior legislative affairs officer - a 37-year Senate Armed Services Committee staffer - proposing a whistleblower restitution fund to incentivise disclosures to Congress. Within under three years of formation, that programme placed a plurality of the members of the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject. The single largest gap in the Sol record is that it names no donors, and the board treats an unfunded map of a funding question as an open problem rather than a settled one.
sol-foundation.narrative:
The Sol Foundation is the closest thing the modern disclosure effort has to a think tank, and the useful way to read it is by its bibliography rather than its press. Its publication series is numbered, dated and authored, and the sequence tells you what the organisation actually decided to work on.

The first tranche in 2024 was scoping work. Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, US Navy retired, published 'Beneath the Surface: We May Learn More about UAP by Looking in the Ocean' in March 2024, arguing that transmedium UAP and unidentified submersible objects are the overlooked domain. The foundation itself published 'UAP in Crowded Skies' in the same month and 'Anomalous Health Threats: Health Security Considerations for UAP' in July. Helen McCaw wrote on UK policy implications in May 2024. Paul Thigpen wrote on the Catholic Church's likely response in July.

Then in November 2024 Peter Skafish, the foundation's executive director and co-founder, published 'The Prospect of Executive Branch Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Secrecy: The Harm to Congress and Potential Remedies.' That is the pivot. The subject is no longer whether UAP are anomalous; it is whether an executive-branch secrecy regime has concealed decades of knowledge, research programmes and potentially retrieved technologies from Congress itself, and what remedies exist. In May 2025 the series published Colonel Karl E. Nell, retired, on 'The UFO Enigma: A Call for US Government Disclosure,' framed around the effort to revive the UAP Disclosure Act.

By 2026 the series had become numbered Science and Policy Briefings and had acquired an author who is the point of the whole exercise. Briefing No. 2, April 2026, is 'UAP Whistleblower Restitution Fund Would Incentivize Disclosures to Congress,' by Kirk McConnell. McConnell is Sol's senior legislative affairs officer and spent thirty-seven years on the staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. The paper's premise is stated at the top: individuals considering disclosing information about classified executive-branch UAP programmes to Congress face significant retaliation, including immediate loss of livelihood, and several senators have said so. That is a former SASC staffer, writing under a foundation's imprint, designing a financial instrument to overcome the deterrent that the special-access architecture places on contractor and government employees who might talk to his old committee. Briefings No. 1 and No. 3, both by Marik von Rennenkampff, cover Beatriz Villarroel's pre-satellite-era night-sky plate work and what the foundation describes as the first peer-reviewed scientific analysis of possible UAP materials, involving Garry Nolan.

That combination - a Stanford immunologist doing materials and biological analysis, a career Senate Armed Services staffer doing legislative design, an anthropologist doing the theory of secrecy - is why Sol belongs on this map. It is not a UFO group. It is a small institution that identified the mechanism, staffed against it, and published a remedy.

The consequence arrived in June 2026. Following what the foundation calls 'historic releases of government records about UAP encounters,' the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the support of the FBI, announced a UAP Science Advisory Council led by Avi Loeb, who sits on Sol's own advisory board. The foundation's announcement states that among the fourteen scientists and experts named were Sol co-founders Garry Nolan and Peter Skafish; Sol senior adviser Tim Gallaudet; and Sol advisory board member Jacob Haqq-Misra. Ross Howard, who leads production for the foundation, would lead communications for the council. The council reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board, 'an interagency body coordinating across military, law enforcement, and intelligence community agencies,' and 'All data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The foundation's own framing is unambiguous about what it thinks happened: 'The appointment of Sol's co-founders, Admiral (ret.) Gallaudet and Dr. Jacob Haqq-Misra to the government's scientific advisory body is a fulfillment of its founding mission. Sol can now share its insight to the highest levels of government deliberation about disclosure, amplifying our impact.'

Two things about that are worth holding separately. The first is a genuine institutional achievement: a private foundation went from formation to supplying a plurality of the government's outside scientific advisers on this subject in under three years. The second is a caution the board should apply without softening it: the council those people joined is, on the government's own description, unclassified-only. A body with no access to classified material cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a carve-out special access programme, and cannot compel anything. Sol's own executive director wrote the paper explaining exactly why that matters. The organisation that best articulated the executive-branch secrecy problem has now placed its people inside a body that has been constituted on the far side of the secrecy line.

The last thing to say about Sol is the thing it does not say about itself. Its site solicits membership and donations. It names no donors, no foundations and no corporate supporters. For an entity on a board whose organising question is who pays, that is the largest single documentary gap in its record, and it is not resolved by anything published as of this writing. There is also a small unresolved inconsistency in its own account of its founding date - the June 2026 announcement says the foundation 'was established in 2023,' which does not match every version the organisation has published.

claims.text: The Sol Foundation publishes a numbered white-paper and policy-briefing series whose authors include Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet (US Navy, ret.), Colonel Karl E. Nell (ret.), Peter Skafish, Kirk McConnell, Helen McCaw, Rizwan Virk, Paul Thigpen and Marik von Rennenkampff.

Sol's Vol. 1 No. 6 paper of November 2024, by co-founder and executive director Peter Skafish, is titled 'The Prospect of Executive Branch Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Secrecy: The Harm to Congress and Potential Remedies' and argues that long-standing executive-branch secrecy may have concealed decades of UAP knowledge, research programmes and potentially retrieved technologies from Congress.

Sol published Colonel Karl E. Nell (retired), 'The UFO Enigma: A Call for US Government Disclosure,' in May 2025, framed around the effort to revive the UAP Disclosure Act in 2025 and establish an independent review body.

Sol Science and Policy Briefing No. 2, April 2026, is 'UAP Whistleblower Restitution Fund Would Incentivize Disclosures to Congress' by Kirk McConnell, and states that individuals considering disclosing information about classified executive-branch UAP programmes to Congress face significant retaliation including immediate loss of livelihood.

Sol Science and Policy Briefing No. 3, April 2026, describes the first peer-reviewed analysis of physical materials associated with a multi-witness UAP event, conducted by Stanford immunologist Garry P. Nolan and colleagues using atomic and isotopic analysis techniques.

Sol Science and Policy Briefing No. 1, January 2026, covers Beatriz Villarroel's finding that night-sky survey photographs taken between 1949 and 1957, before the satellite era, contain large numbers of temporary star-like points of light.

The Sol Foundation states that the UAP Science Advisory Council was announced by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence 'with the support of the FBI' and is led by Avi Loeb, a member of Sol's own advisory board.

Sol states that among the fourteen people named to the council were its co-founders Garry Nolan and Peter Skafish, its senior adviser Tim Gallaudet, and its advisory board member Jacob Haqq-Misra, and that Ross Howard, who leads production for the foundation, would lead communications for the council.

Sol states that the council 'reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board, an interagency body coordinating across military, law enforcement, and intelligence community agencies' and that 'All data shared with the council will be unclassified.'

Sol characterises the appointments as 'a fulfillment of its founding mission,' adding that 'Sol can now share its insight to the highest levels of government deliberation about disclosure, amplifying our impact.'

The Skeptics Society's independent announcement of the council's formation names Garry Nolan and Peter Skafish as Sol Foundation co-founders and Tim Gallaudet as an appointee, corroborating Sol's own account of the membership.

Sol's June 2026 announcement states that the foundation 'was established in 2023 by Dr. Nolan and Dr. Skafish,' which conflicts with founding-year information the organisation has published elsewhere.
The Sol Foundation solicits membership and donations on its own site but names no donors, foundations or corporate supporters anywhere in its published material.

openQuestions: Who funds the Sol Foundation. No donor, foundation or corporate supporter is named in any published Sol material, and there is no public filing reviewed here that discloses its revenue sources.

The foundation's own founding date is inconsistent across its publications (2022 in some material, 'established in 2023' in the June 2026 council announcement); the incorporation record has not been checked.
Whether any Sol principal or adviser holds or has held a security clearance or special-access indoctrination that would constrain what they can say about the concealment thesis they publish on.
Whether the McConnell whistleblower restitution fund proposal has been introduced in any legislative vehicle, and by whom.

What relationship, if any, exists between Sol and the government bodies its people now advise beyond the individual appointments - whether any contract, agreement, data-sharing arrangement or funding flows between the foundation and ODNI, AARO or the FBI.

uap-science-advisory-council.whatItIs: The UAP Science Advisory Council is an outside scientific advisory body assembled in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the FBI and other agencies, and chaired by Harvard theoretical physicist Avi Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board that met for the first time in mid-June 2026. All data shared with the council is unclassified.
uap-science-advisory-council.whyImplicated: This is the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject, which makes the terms on which it was convened the most informative thing about it. Its chair has stated in writing that 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' A body with no clearances and no access to classified holdings cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a special access programme operating under a DCSA carve-out, cannot compel testimony, and cannot verify a negative. Its function, on the record as constituted, is to apply scientific method to the portion of the record that nobody disputes and that the executive branch has already chosen to release. Its membership was drawn almost entirely from the private technical and advocacy layer - the Sol Foundation and the Galileo Project - rather than from the federal laboratories, FFRDCs or prime contractors where the custody allegations point, and the published membership lists changed three times in seventeen days.
uap-science-advisory-council.narrative:
The council is best understood as a boundary object: an institution created at the seam between a declassification programme and a scientific community, whose terms of reference tell you exactly where the executive branch has decided that seam sits.

The origin story is not disputed by anyone involved. The Skeptics Society announcement of 15 June 2026 says the council was 'formed at the request of the White House and in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and other agencies.' Avi Loeb's own account, published on Medium and dated by the platform to 13 June 2026, says: 'Over the past week, I was tasked by the above organizations to create a research team of young scientists who will serve on this council,' naming the White House, AARO, ODNI, the FBI and all Intelligence Community members. The Sol Foundation's account says ODNI, with the support of the FBI, announced it. DefenseScoop obtained confirmation from an ODNI official that ODNI, alongside the FBI and DoD, established the UAP Governance Board 'to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies,' and that the board 'met for the first time yesterday' as of Wednesday 17 June 2026, without identifying the participants.

The membership is where the record becomes genuinely strange, and the board should record the instability rather than smoothing it into a single roster. Loeb's first post named a core research team of five: Richard Cloete, Regina Sarmiento, Matthew Szydagis, Devesh Nandal and Omer Eldadi. The Skeptics Society, two days later, published an alphabetised list of eleven, adding Tim Gallaudet, Garry Nolan, Michael Shermer, Peter Skafish and Jennice Vilhauer, and identifying Loeb as chair. The Sol Foundation described a fourteen-member council and additionally named Jacob Haqq-Misra and Ross Howard. Loeb's list supplied to DefenseScoop on 17 June named twelve and introduced Carol Cleland and Ben Lamm while dropping Sarmiento. His second Medium post, dated by the platform to 29 June, listed fifteen and added Liberty Vittert Capito, Robin Hanson and Kevin Knuth while restoring none of the dropped names. Four published lists in seventeen days, none of them identical, none of them issued by the government that convened the body. There is no charter, no Federal Advisory Committee Act notice, and no agency-published membership roster in the record reviewed here.

The operative constraint is stated by the chair himself, twice, in plain language: 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The Sol Foundation repeats it. DefenseScoop reports that Loeb 'confirmed that all of the data shared with the newly installed team will be unclassified.' Loeb also told DefenseScoop that the meeting cadence has not been decided, and closed with a formulation that is worth quoting exactly because it is candid about the position: 'We will make the best lemonade out of the lemons we are given.'

Set that against what the council would need in order to test the central allegation on this board. The custody claims concern material held at contractor facilities under special access protection. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), the Director of DCSA can be relieved of industrial security oversight of exactly such a facility by a Deputy Secretary of Defense-approved carve-out. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee may hand SAP material to a member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. A council with no clearances is on the outside of both of those doors. It cannot look at a carve-out programme, cannot subpoena a contractor, cannot inspect material, and cannot verify that the archival material it is given is complete. Its chair says the council's purpose is to advise on how to resolve the nature of UAP and, in support of the Governance Board, to 'assist in the timely coordination of declassification of UAP-related information, in accordance with Executive Order 13526.' That is a real function. It is also, structurally, an advisory role over the release of material that the classification authorities have already decided to release.

The second structural observation is about where the people came from. Loeb chairs the Galileo Project at Harvard; Cloete and Sarmiento are described in the Skeptics Society announcement as Galileo Project researchers. Nolan and Skafish co-founded the Sol Foundation; Gallaudet is a Sol senior adviser; Haqq-Misra sits on Sol's advisory board; Ross Howard leads Sol's production and was named to lead the council's communications. Nobody named to the council in any published list is identified as coming from a federal weapons laboratory, an FFRDC, a University Affiliated Research Center, or a prime contractor's advanced development organisation. The council is staffed from the community that has been asking the questions, not from the institutions that would hold the answers.

None of that is a criticism of the individuals, several of whom have argued publicly for exactly the kind of instrumentation and data quality that would move this subject forward. It is a statement about the shape of the instrument. The government convened an outside body, gave it distinguished members and a reporting line to an interagency board, and drew the boundary of its access at the classification line - the same line on the far side of which every substantive allegation this board catalogues is alleged to sit.

claims.text: The UAP Science Advisory Council was, per the Skeptics Society announcement of 15 June 2026, 'formed at the request of the White House and in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and other agencies.'

Avi Loeb wrote that 'Over the past week, I was tasked by the above organizations to create a research team of young scientists who will serve on this council,' identifying the White House, AARO, ODNI, the FBI and all Intelligence Community members.
Loeb states in writing that 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.'

The council reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board whose mission, per Loeb, is 'to serve as an interagency body that can use each member's capabilities and unique authorities to cohesively address national security threats posed by UAP' and which 'will assist in the timely coordination of declassification of UAP-related information, in accordance with Executive Order 13526.'

An ODNI official told DefenseScoop that ODNI, alongside the FBI and DoD, established the UAP Governance Board 'to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies,' and that the board met for the first time on 16 June 2026, without identifying the participants.

The Skeptics Society published an alphabetised list of eleven appointees on 15 June 2026: Cloete, Gallaudet, Nandal, Nolan, Eldadi, Loeb (chair), Sarmiento, Shermer, Skafish, Szydagis and Vilhauer.

The list Loeb supplied to DefenseScoop on 17 June 2026 named twelve people, introducing Carol Cleland (anomaly identification), Ben Lamm (oceanography and biology) and Ross Howard (communication), and omitting Regina Sarmiento.

No charter, Federal Advisory Committee Act notice, agency-published membership roster, or terms of reference for the UAP Science Advisory Council or the UAP Governance Board has been located in the public record.

uap-science-advisory-council.denialPosture: The council itself has issued no denial. Its chair has repeatedly and publicly stated its principal limitation rather than concealing it: all data shared with the council is unclassified. AARO, one of the convening agencies, maintains in its published reporting that no US government investigation has found a case of UAP representing off-world technology, and that all authentic programmes referenced by whistleblowers were properly notified and reported to the congressional defence and intelligence committees.
openQuestions: Whether the council has a charter, terms of reference, or FACA status, and whether its membership has ever been published by a government agency rather than by members and third parties.
The definitive membership. Four published lists in seventeen days disagree; the government has published none.
Whether any council member holds a security clearance in another capacity, and whether that creates an asymmetry inside a body constituted to work on unclassified material only.
The identity of the participants in the UAP Governance Board, which ODNI declined to share, and the board's own authorities over declassification decisions.

Whether the council has any mechanism to determine that the archival material it receives is complete, or is dependent on the classification authorities whose conduct is the subject of the underlying allegations.

aawsap.whatItIs: The Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program was a Defense Intelligence Agency effort solicited publicly on 18 August 2008 as HHM402-08-R-0211 by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity and awarded on 22 September 2008 as firm-fixed-price contract HHM402-08-C-0072 to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, LLC of Las Vegas. Its stated objective was to understand the physics and engineering of breakthrough aerospace weapon system applications out to the year 2050 across twelve technical areas. It ran to 2012 and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents plus a much larger body of work that has never been released.
aawsap.whyImplicated: AAWSAP is the only documented instance in the modern record of the United States government funding a private company to study the physics of observed anomalous flight performance, and its own procurement file shows the seams through which such work escapes normal visibility. The solicitation was posted as a total small business set-aside under a classification code meaning 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' place of performance was the contractor's own facility, and the Top Secret facility clearance requirement was formally amended so that it was not required prior to contract implementation. The statement of work provides that any accountable property the contractor acquires with government funds becomes government-owned property and must be inventoried and returned within sixty days of contract end - a custody provision whose closeout has never been publicly documented. Senator Harry Reid asked the Deputy Secretary of Defense to convert the effort into a special access program on 24 June 2009 and was refused. The unreleased output of this contract, which its own government manager has described as running to more than a hundred detailed reports, is the largest identified block of missing documentary material in the modern record.
aawsap.narrative:
AAWSAP is the best-documented UAP effort in the history of the United States government, and the reason is mundane: it was a competed commercial-items procurement, so it left a paper trail that the Freedom of Information Act could reach.

The solicitation went up on FedBizOpps as a combined synopsis/solicitation on 18 August 2008 under number HHM402-08-R-0211, issued by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity at Bolling AFB, with responses due 5 September 2008. It was coded B, 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' under NAICS 541330, Engineering Services, and it was 'solicited as a total small business set aside' with a size standard of twenty-five million dollars. The Statement of Objectives, dated 18 July 2008, is unambiguous about what was wanted: 'The objective of this program is to understand the physics and engineering of these applications as they apply to the foreign threat out to the far term, i.e., from now through the year 2050. Primary focus is on breakthrough technologies and applications that create discontinuities in currently evolving technology trends. The focus is not on extrapolations of current aerospace technology.' Twelve technical areas were named, covering lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament including directed energy, and other peripheral areas.

The qualification language is the tell. Offerors were asked to 'provide examples, conducted within the past 7 years, of having performed, as a prime contractor, the analysis, design, construction, and flight testing of high performance aircraft and/or satellites,' with the note that 'Success in this program is dependent upon this capability and experience.' The government was not shopping for a literature review.

The award document, Standard Form 1449, records contract HHM402-08-C-0072, awarded 22 September 2008 to BIGELOW AEROSPACE ADVANCED SPACE STUDIES, LLC, 4640 S Eastern Ave, Las Vegas NV, CAGE 54JU7, DUNS 827037768, with a total award amount of $21,948,810.00 and a base year of 22 September 2008 to 29 September 2009 followed by option years. The solicitation had anticipated 'a base year of 12 months from date of award plus four (4) 12 month option years' running to 30 September 2013. Deliverable line items were status reports, a project management plan for tasks 3.a.1 through 3.a.12, research reports for the same tasks, a Comprehensive Integrated Threat Assessment, travel and other direct costs.

Three provisions in the statement of work matter more than the money. First, security: 'The contractor shall comply with the terms and conditions of the DD-254 BEFORE initiating any classified effort,' and 'Contractor shall provide a work facility (including unclassified information systems) with a Top Secret Facility Clearance granted by the Defense Security Service (DSS).' But an amendment posted with the solicitation changed DD Form 254 Block 13 from 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE GRANTED BY THE DEFENSE SECURITY SERVICE (DSS) PRIOR CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION' to 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL NOT BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE ... PRIOR TO CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION. HOWEVER, IT MUST BE OBTAINED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE DURING THE INITIAL YEAR OF THE CONTRACT.' The facility-clearance bar was lowered before award.

Second, place of performance: 'The work under this contract shall be performed at the Contractor's facility.' Third, and most consequential for this board, property: 'Any accountable property acquired by the contractor with government funds during the execution of this contract shall become government owned property. ... This property must be inventoried and returned to the government not more than 60 days after the end of the contract.' There is, in the released file, no closeout inventory.

What the contractor actually did is not seriously in dispute, and AARO concedes it. AARO's Historical Record Report states: 'Although investigating UFO/UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organization conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager. This research included: reviewing new cases and much older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.' AARO adds that 'DIA did not seek, nor specifically authorize, this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract with the private sector organization,' and that the effort also investigated an alleged hotspot of UAP and paranormal activity at a Utah property then owned by the head of the contractor.

The special access question is the hinge. AARO records that 'On 24 June 2009, Senator Reid sent a letter to then Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Deputy Secretary Lynn declined to do so based on the recommendation of then-Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, James R. Clapper, Jr., that such a designation was not justified.' That refusal is documented in the FOIA record alongside DIA talking papers prepared for Reid's visits to the Director of DIA in January and May 2009 and an eighteen-page packet presented to the Deputy Secretary in November 2009.

AARO's account and the contractor's account of what the programme produced differ by an order of magnitude. AARO says the contract 'produced exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed,' and that it 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work.' The releasable record contains thirty-seven of thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. What is not in the record is the 494-page BAASS Ten Month Report, the Utah ranch investigation report, the personnel roster, obligation-by-year funding data, and the balance of the material that the government programme manager has described as running past a hundred reports. Under this board's sourcing rule, AARO's characterisation is a Tier 2 record of what AARO said, not a Tier 1 record of what exists.
