condon-committee.denialPosture: Condon's Section I contains one of the two most consequential official denials in the record: "We have no evidence of secrecy concerning UFO reports." It was issued by a body that had explicitly declined to evaluate the defense question, that acknowledged its access to classified missile and radar material was limited by the contracting agency, and whose project coordinator had described the public framing as a trick two months before the contract was signed. The Air Force's January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet supplies the companion denial about physical custody.
connections: Robertson Panel — a sanitized version of the panel report was published as Appendix Y of the Condon Report; Thornton Page sat on the Robertson Panel and later criticized Condon's statistical logic in the American Journal of Physics (vol. 37 no. 10, October 1969).

J. Allen Hynek — proposed the review that led to the O'Brien Committee, was rejected as a host institution, and became the report's leading critic, writing that the committee could not explain more than a quarter of the cases examined.
James E. McDonald (University of Arizona) — surfaced the Low memo in July 1967 and published "Science in Default" on 27 December 1969; he is a named node for the board's researcher-fate thread.

Air Force Office of Scientific Research — the contracting activity; Dr. J. Thomas Ratchford and AFOSR executive director Dr. William Price are the named officials who recruited Colorado in July-August 1966.
Brian O'Brien and the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board — the mechanism by which the Air Force generated the recommendation it then used to retire its own program.
National Academy of Sciences panel under Gerald M. Clemence — the independent validator, retained by the Air Force before the report was complete.
Project Blue Book / Wright-Patterson AFB — terminated on the strength of this report; its records went to NARA as microfilm publication T-1206, 94 rolls.
Air Force Regulation 80-17, reproduced as Appendix B, is the base-level UFO reporting procedure the same review created and the Air Force rescinded on Blue Book's closure.
AARO — the first federal UFO office since Condon recommended against creating one; the fifty-three-year gap between the two is the concealment window this board examines.
openQuestions: The report states the Air Force assured the project that no information would be withheld. No document memorializing that assurance, and no accounting of what classified missile or radar material was in fact withheld, has been produced.
Was the Colorado project given access to anything outside the Blue Book file series — ATIC's Battelle-era holdings, foreign technology division files, or any compartmented program?

Condon stated in a January 1967 lecture that he thought the government should not study UFOs because the subject was nonsense, "but I'm not supposed to reach that conclusion for another year." Who, if anyone, in the Air Force knew of that statement at the time?
The GAO declined Rep. Roush's request to investigate the project. On what stated grounds, and does a written GAO declination exist?
Fifty-nine case studies were published with their locations altered "for legal reasons." The key mapping location-to-case has never been released.
Low resigned in May 1968; no further contemporaneous account of the August 1966 memo's audience or purpose has surfaced.
Why did the Air Force commission an NAS review of the report before the report was finished?

carve-out.whatItIs: A "carve-out" is the regulatory provision under which the Director of the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency is relieved of industrial security oversight for a Department of Defense special access program. It is codified at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) — the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule — and exercised in accordance with DoD Directive 5205.07, DoD Special Access Program Policy. Approval authority rests with exactly two officials: the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense.
carve-out.whyImplicated: The carve-out is the mechanism that makes a concealed program administratively possible, and it is written down in the Code of Federal Regulations. Every cleared contractor facility in the United States is subject to DCSA oversight under the NISP; the carve-out is the single lawful exception, and once approved, DCSA retains cognizance only over the baseline facility clearance and not over the program. That means the government's own industrial security inspectorate — the body that would otherwise know which contractor holds what, in which vault, under which contract — is by design blind to the program. DoDD 5205.07 layers a second control on top: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval." A contractor holding carve-out material therefore faces an affirmative regulatory prohibition on telling Congress, enforced by an office whose director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. And the statutory backstop weakened rather than strengthened: the annual special access program reports to the defense committees required by 10 U.S.C. § 119(a) and (b) terminated by operation of law effective 31 December 2021. This is the load-bearing structural claim of the entire board — not that concealment is possible in principle, but that the specific regulatory instruments exist, are named, are current, and route around both DCSA and Congress by design.
carve-out.narrative:
Start with the ordinary case. Under Executive Order 12829 and 32 CFR Part 117, the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security acts as the Cognizant Security Agency for the Department of Defense, and DCSA serves as the DoD Cognizant Security Office. Section 117.6(b)(3) assigns DCSA the duty to "provide security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO on behalf of DoD components and those non-DoD executive branch agencies who enter into agreements with DoD." Then comes the exception, in the same sentence-pair: "The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, 'DoD SAP Policy.'"

The operative definition is not in the CFR; it is in the instructions to DD Form 254, the Contract Security Classification Specification that accompanies every classified contract. Item 10f: "A 'carve-out' is a classified contract awarded by the GCA in connection with a SAP for which DCSA has been relieved of security and/or oversight responsibility by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense." The instructions add two operationally decisive notes. First: "Check block 15 'Yes' if the contract is performed at the contractor facility and DCSA will be relieved of security cognizance (a carve-out), and identify the CSO for the SAP as it is responsible for inspection of the SAP. NOTE: DCSA does retain oversight responsibility for the baseline FCL at which there is an approved carve-out." Second: "Not all SAPs are 'carve-outs' because, in some instances, the program or supporting SAP Security Office will allow the DCSA CSO to retain inspection responsibility." Read together: at a carved-out facility, DCSA still validates the company's baseline clearance but has no visibility into the program, and the program's own security office designates the inspecting authority. The inspector is chosen by the inspected.

DoDD 5205.07 was reissued on 12 September 2024, approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It cancels the July 1, 2010 directive and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform," 11 July 2023. Its governance architecture is a closed loop. The DoD SAP Central Office director sits under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense and reports directly to him or her; is Executive Secretary of the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, which the Deputy Secretary chairs; is Executive Secretary of the Senior Review Group; chairs the SAP Senior Working Group; is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for purposes of issuing security classification guides; accredits congressional SAP facilities; and maintains the records of what SAP information Congress has been given. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments "will be by exception," and establishment of SAPs to protect new and novel critical program information "at all tiers of the SAP architecture requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval."

DCSA's residual role under the same directive is limited to two lines in section 2.7: develop SAP-related training courses and maintain a cadre of proficient personnel, and support professional development and certification of SAP security professionals. The agency that oversees industrial security for the rest of the defense industrial base is, inside the SAP enterprise, a training provider.

The congressional-notification provision is the one that converts an administrative arrangement into a concealment mechanism. Section 3.2.g of DoDD 5205.07 requires all personnel accessed to DoD SAPs to notify the SAPCO director when briefing or providing SAP material to a member of Congress or staff, and then states flatly: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval." A contractor employee at a carved-out facility who believes a program has been improperly withheld from Congress is, by this directive, prohibited from doing anything about it without permission from the office nearest the Deputy Secretary.

Statute does less work here than most people assume. 10 U.S.C. § 119 required annual reports on special access programs to the defense committees under subsections (a) and (b) — but a note to the section records that those reporting requirements terminated effective 31 December 2021 pursuant to section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. Subsection (e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive inclusion of specified information in a report on national security grounds, in which case the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — a set of eight members across four committees. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse; there is no enforcement provision, no penalty, and no auditing body outside the executive branch positioned to detect a program that was never notified. 10 U.S.C. § 119a governs the parallel category of alternative compensatory control measures.

One loose thread in the directive itself is worth flagging to a downstream analyst. Section 2.1.a(6) makes the SAPCO director "Executive Secretary of the Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee pursuant to the November 21, 2020 Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum," while the directive's own reference list names that memorandum "Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee (STAOC) Charter," 21 November 2020. The body is named twice, differently, in a single 2024 directive. That committee's charter has not been released.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides: "The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, 'DoD SAP Policy.'"

The operative definition is in the DD Form 254 Instructions: "A 'carve-out' is a classified contract awarded by the GCA in connection with a SAP for which DCSA has been relieved of security and/or oversight responsibility by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense (DoDD 5205.07, 'Special Access Program (SAP) Policy')."

At a carved-out facility DCSA's residual visibility is limited to the baseline facility clearance: "NOTE: DCSA does retain oversight responsibility for the baseline FCL at which there is an approved carve-out." Inspection of the SAP itself is performed by a CSO identified by the SAP.

Carve-out status is discretionary and program-controlled: "Not all SAPs are 'carve-outs' because, in some instances, the program or supporting SAP Security Office will allow the DCSA CSO to retain inspection responsibility."

DoDD 5205.07 was reissued effective 12 September 2024, approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks; it reissues and cancels DoDD 5205.07 of 1 July 2010 as amended, and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform," 11 July 2023.

DoDD 5205.07 section 3.2.g provides: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval."

The Director, DoD SAPCO, is under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, reports directly to the Deputy Secretary, serves as Executive Secretary of the SAP Oversight Committee (which the Deputy Secretary chairs) and of the Senior Review Group, and chairs the SAP Senior Working Group.

The Director, DoD SAPCO "has jurisdiction over the protection of information contained within DoD SAPs and is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for purposes of issuing SAP security classification guides," and separately "accredits congressional SAPFs" and "maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress."

DoDD 5205.07 §3.1.d provides that "Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments will be by exception. Establishment of SAPs to protect new and novel CPI at all tiers of the SAP architecture requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval."

Under DoDD 5205.07 §2.7 the Director, DCSA has only two SAP responsibilities: developing SAP-related training courses and maintaining a proficient cadre, and supporting professional development and certification of SAP security professionals. DCSA has no inspection or oversight function assigned in the directive.

10 U.S.C. § 119(e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive inclusion of information in SAP reports on national security grounds on a case-by-case basis, in which case the information and justification are provided "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — that is, to eight members across the Senate and House Armed Services and Appropriations Committees.

The annual special access program reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. § 119(a) and (b) terminated effective 31 December 2021 pursuant to section 1061 of Public Law 114-328, per the Termination of Reporting Requirements note to the section.

10 U.S.C. § 119(f) provides that a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse; the statute prescribes no penalty for non-notification and assigns no external auditor.

DoDD 5205.07 names the same oversight body inconsistently within a single document: §2.1.a(6) calls it the "Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee" while the References section cites the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum, "Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee (STAOC) Charter," 21 November 2020.

carve-out.denialPosture: There is no denial here, and that is the point: the carve-out is publicly promulgated regulation, published on the Directives Division website and cleared for public release. The Department has never had to deny the existence of a mechanism that relieves its own security inspectorate of oversight, because the mechanism is printed in the Code of Federal Regulations and in the instructions to a form every classified contract carries.
connections: DCSA (formerly the Defense Security Service, renamed 20 June 2020) is the agency relieved; USD(I&S) is the Cognizant Security Agency for DoD and DCSA's chain of authority.

DoD SAPCO and its director, reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, is the single node through which SAP information reaches Congress and through which contractors must seek permission to speak to Congress.
Kathleen H. Hicks signed the current DoDD 5205.07 on 12 September 2024 as Deputy Secretary of Defense — the office that is also one of the two carve-out approval authorities.
Executive Order 13526 and Executive Order 12829 are the classification and industrial-security foundations; 32 CFR Part 2001 and 32 CFR Part 2004 are the implementing ISOO rules.
The Special/Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee, chartered by DepSecDef memorandum of 21 November 2020, is the least-documented body named in the directive.

Integrated Joint Special Technical Operations (IJSTO), run by the CJCS with USD(P) oversight, is the process by which SAP-protected capabilities are apportioned to combatant commands — the operational half of the architecture.
USD(C)/CFO "leads all budget and execution reviews for DoD-funded capabilities and information activities protected by DoD SAPs" — the funding node for any carve-out program.
DD Form 254 is the artifact a FOIA or subpoena would seek: block 10f and block 15 on a specific contract would reveal whether a facility is carved out and who inspects it.
Battelle-operated national laboratories, and any prime with SAP facilities, are the population to which carve-out designations would attach.

AARO's FY2025 report claims statutory authority to receive UAP information "regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs" — an assertion that runs directly against the DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g prohibition on contractors providing SAP material without SAPCO approval.
openQuestions: How many DoD SAPs currently hold approved carve-out provisions? The number has never been published, and 32 CFR 117.6 imposes no counting or reporting requirement.
Who are the Cognizant Security Offices designated to inspect carved-out programs in lieu of DCSA, and are any of them staffed by the contractor's own personnel?
The DepSecDef memorandum chartering the Special/Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee (21 November 2020) has not been publicly released. What does it cover?
What replaced the 10 U.S.C. § 119(a)-(b) annual SAP reports after they terminated on 31 December 2021, if anything?
Does any statute or directive require notification to Congress of the approval of a carve-out provision itself, as distinct from establishment of the underlying SAP?

DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g prohibits contractors from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval. How is that provision reconciled with whistleblower protections and with AARO's claimed statutory access?
Is there any record of a carve-out provision ever being denied or revoked by a Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense?

Which office audits whether a program that should have been notified under § 119(f) actually was? The Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Privacy, Civil Liberties, and Transparency is assigned audit functions under DoDD 5148.13, but the scope is not specified in 5205.07.

nids.whatItIs: The National Institute for Discovery Science was a privately financed research organization based in Las Vegas, Nevada, formed by real-estate developer Robert Bigelow in October 1995 and disbanded in October 2004. It bought the 480-acre Sherman ranch in the Uinta Basin near Fort Duchesne, Utah — the property later known as Skinwalker Ranch — in 1996 and staffed it around the clock with scientists and a veterinarian. It was the direct organizational and personnel predecessor to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, the contractor that executed the Defense Intelligence Agency's AAWSAP contract from 2008.
nids.whyImplicated: NIDS is the point at which anomaly research moved into private hands under conditions of contractual secrecy, and it is the documented bridge from that private effort into a DIA-funded government program. Within weeks of buying the ranch Bigelow had the previous owner, Terry Sherman, working for him under a nondisclosure agreement that Sherman told the Las Vegas Sun prevented him from discussing what happened on the property — a private-sector information control instrument doing exactly the work a security classification would do, without any of the accountability. NIDS drew its personnel directly from the national security research establishment: John B. Alexander, the former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratory, was the institute's public voice from its Las Vegas offices in 1996. And the continuity to government is not inferential: Rice University's published biography of Colm Kelleher states that he led the NIDS team on Skinwalker Ranch from 1996 to 2004 and that "in 2008, Kelleher became deputy administrator of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) where he led the day-to-day operations in executing the AAWSAP contract with Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)." NIDS is where the government's later program acquired its methodology, its site, its database concept and its senior staff.
nids.narrative:
The sequence is tight and dated. In July 1996 the Sherman family broke years of silence and went public in the Deseret News and on national radio with accounts of strange lights, lights emerging from circular "doorways" that appeared in mid-air, three cows mutilated, several others vanished, unusual soil impressions and circles of flattened grass. Several weeks later Robert Bigelow met the Shermans and negotiated to buy the 480-acre ranch for about $200,000. By 23 October 1996, when the Las Vegas Sun published its account, Bigelow had erected an observation building, moved in a pair of scientists and a veterinarian, and had someone on the property twenty-four hours a day recording anything out of the ordinary. The Shermans relocated fifteen miles away. Terry Sherman stayed on as ranch caretaker, employed by Bigelow, and told the Sun he could no longer discuss the activity because of a nondisclosure agreement Bigelow had him sign. He also said he had been offered more money by a Colorado family and a local hunting club but did not want to put anyone at risk. His summary: "It's just been a bad deal all the way around. All that's really redeeming is that you have some knowledge that a lot of people don't have, for what it's worth."

The institutional framing was scientific and the operating posture was closed. Officially the research was conducted by the National Institute for Discovery Science, which Bigelow had formed the previous October. John B. Alexander — described in the same article as "former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratories in New Mexico" — spoke for the institute and articulated the public mission: "Our approach is to do good, high-quality research using a standard scientific approach and do what we can to get hard data. One of the missions of the institute is to make information widely available." He said results would be published in scientific journals and on the institute's web page. Bigelow declined to be interviewed. Alexander would not provide details of how or why the research was being conducted. Outside researchers, including Chris O'Brien, who had visited the ranch in July before Bigelow's involvement and called it "the most impressive case I've ever personally investigated," objected that "it should be public knowledge."

The cattle-mutilation program was built deliberately. Bigelow met Roosevelt, Utah veterinarian Dan Dennis on 15 October 1996 to ask for assistance performing necropsies on any animals whose deaths or mutilations might be tied to UFO or paranormal phenomena, and planned to write to area ranchers requesting notification of unusual animal deaths. From 1999 NIDS ran a public hotline; over five thousand reports arrived by phone and email, many later attributed to missile test launches and meteors. NIDS's stated research areas were cattle mutilation and black triangle reports. Colm Kelleher, deputy administrator, framed the scope: "We don't study aliens, we study anomalies. They're the same thing in a lot of people's minds, but not in our minds." NIDS disbanded in October 2004.

What matters for this board is what happened next. Kelleher went from NIDS to Prosetta in San Francisco from 2004 to 2008, where he was laboratory director executing Department of Defense contracts to discover drugs against Ebola virus and other viruses of interest to DoD — a four-year interval inside the DoD contracting system. Then, per Rice University's published biography, "in 2008, Kelleher became deputy administrator of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) where he led the day-to-day operations in executing the AAWSAP contract with Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)." Rice lists his affiliation on that page as "Program Manager, Advanced Aerospace System Weapons Application Program (AAWSAP) Contractor, Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)." From 2012 to 2020 he ran the Environmental Control and Life Support Systems department at Bigelow Aerospace, building life-support systems for expandable spacecraft. He co-authored Hunt for the Skinwalker (2005) with George Knapp and Skinwalkers at the Pentagon (2021) with James Lacatski and Knapp.

The archival record now treats NIDS and BAASS as a continuous object. The finding aid for the Jacques F. Vallee UFO and paranormal phenomena papers at Rice describes the collection as containing "field notes and press documents about related topics such as cattle mutilations, and face-to-face meetings of NIDS and BAASS, as well as various research proposals." Vallee — one of the reported NIDS science advisory board members — is thus the custodian of documentation on the meetings that connect the private institute to the DIA contractor, and that documentation sits in a collection restricted until 2028 and 2031.

The analytic significance of NIDS is not that it proved anything. None of the NIDS work was published in a peer-reviewed journal despite Alexander's 1996 commitment. The significance is structural. NIDS demonstrated that a private individual with sufficient capital could stand up an anomaly-research operation staffed by former national-laboratory and intelligence-community personnel, acquire physical custody of a site of interest, impose nondisclosure obligations on witnesses, collect data outside any government records system, and then — twelve years later — sell that same capability, that same site, that same database concept and that same staff back to the Defense Intelligence Agency under a contract. Whatever NIDS collected between 1996 and 2004 was never subject to FOIA, never subject to congressional oversight, and was never in a federal recordkeeping system. That is a concealment architecture built out of contract law rather than classification, and it is the model the AAWSAP era inherited.

claims.text: NIDS was formed by Robert Bigelow in October 1995; the Las Vegas Sun reported on 23 October 1996 that the ranch research was "being conducted by the National Institute for Discovery Science, which Bigelow formed last October."

Bigelow negotiated to buy the Shermans' 480-acre ranch for about $200,000 several weeks after the family went public in July 1996 with accounts of lights emerging from circular "doorways" appearing in mid-air, three mutilated cows, several missing cattle, unusual soil impressions and circles of flattened grass.

By October 1996 Bigelow had erected an observation building on the property, installed a pair of scientists and a veterinarian, and maintained someone on the property twenty-four hours a day recording anything out of the ordinary.
Terry Sherman, retained by Bigelow to maintain the ranch, told the Las Vegas Sun he could no longer discuss the activity because of a nondisclosure agreement Bigelow had him sign.

John B. Alexander, described as "former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratories in New Mexico," was among the scientists involved and spoke for NIDS from its Las Vegas offices, stating that "one of the missions of the institute is to make information widely available" and that results would be published in scientific journals and on the institute's web page.

Bigelow met Roosevelt, Utah veterinarian Dan Dennis on 15 October 1996 to request assistance performing necropsies on animals whose deaths or mutilations might be tied to UFO or paranormal phenomena, and planned to write area ranchers requesting notification of unusual animal deaths.

Bigelow declined to be interviewed and Alexander would not provide details of how or why the research was being conducted; outside researchers including Chris O'Brien, who had visited the ranch in July 1996, objected that the case "should be public knowledge."
NIDS operated from 1995 to 2004 and was disbanded in October 2004; its research areas were cattle mutilation and black triangle reports.
NIDS established a hotline in 1999 to receive reports of odd occurrences and received over 5,000 reports by phone and email; officials said many were explained as missile test launches and meteors.
Deputy Administrator Colm Kelleher characterized the institute's scope as: "We don't study aliens, we study anomalies. They're the same thing in a lot of people's minds, but not in our minds."

Rice University's published biography of Colm A. Kelleher states: "From 1996-2004, he led the National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDS) team on Skinwalker Ranch as well as multiple other NIDS projects."

The same Rice biography states: "In 2008, Kelleher became deputy administrator of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) where he led the day-to day operations in executing the AAWSAP contract with Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)," and lists his affiliation as "Program Manager, Advanced Aerospace System Weapons Application Program (AAWSAP) Contractor, Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)."

Between the NIDS and BAASS periods, from 2004 to 2008, Kelleher served as laboratory director at San Francisco biotechnology company Prosetta, leading teams executing Department of Defense contracts to discover drugs against Ebola virus and other viruses of interest to DoD.

The finding aid for the Jacques F. Vallee UFO and paranormal phenomena papers (MS 0672, Woodson Research Center, Rice University) states the collection contains "field notes and press documents about related topics such as cattle mutilations, and face-to-face meetings of NIDS and BAASS, as well as various research proposals"; the collection is restricted, with Series I and II opening 24 January 2028 and Series III case files 1 January 2031.

nids.denialPosture: NIDS did not deny; it declined. Bigelow refused interviews, Alexander refused to explain how or why the research was being conducted, and the previous owner was placed under a nondisclosure agreement within weeks of the sale. Alexander's 1996 public commitment that results would appear in scientific journals was not fulfilled — no NIDS finding was published in a peer-reviewed journal in the institute's nine-year existence.
connections: Robert Bigelow — founder and sole financier; later founder of Bigelow Aerospace and Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, the AAWSAP prime contractor, and of the Bigelow Institute for Consciousness Studies.

Colm A. Kelleher — the load-bearing personnel link: NIDS Skinwalker team lead 1996-2004, DoD contract laboratory director 2004-2008, BAASS deputy administrator and AAWSAP day-to-day manager from 2008, Bigelow Aerospace ECLSS department head 2012-2020.
John B. Alexander — former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratory, a Battelle-co-managed facility, and the public voice of NIDS in 1996.

George Knapp — the KLAS-TV journalist whose 1996 reporting brought the ranch to Bigelow's attention; later co-author with Kelleher of Hunt for the Skinwalker (2005) and, with Kelleher and James Lacatski, Skinwalkers at the Pentagon (2021).
Jacques Vallee — reported NIDS advisory board member and the archival custodian of NIDS-BAASS meeting documentation now held at Rice under restriction.
James Lacatski — the DIA official associated with AAWSAP's creation and Kelleher's later co-author.
Defense Intelligence Agency — the government customer that in 2008 contracted with BAASS for AAWSAP, importing the NIDS methodology and staff into a federal program.
Terry and Gwen Sherman — the witnesses whose testimony was placed under a private nondisclosure agreement, and the Deseret News, the outlet that first published it in July 1996.

Los Alamos National Laboratory — Alexander's prior employer, operated by Triad National Security LLC of which Battelle is a member; the same installation the Robertson Panel identified in 1953 as an unexplained sighting cluster.

Christopher "Kit" Green, Hal Puthoff and John Schuessler are reported in secondary accounts to have served on the NIDS science advisory board alongside Vallee and Alexander; this roster is not established by any primary source located here.
openQuestions: The full NIDS science advisory board roster, its meeting minutes and its charter have never been published. Secondary accounts name Kit Green as chairman with Hal Puthoff, John B. Alexander, Jacques Vallee, John Schuessler, Edgar Mitchell and Harrison Schmitt among the participants; no primary document confirms this.
What became of the NIDS data holdings when the institute disbanded in October 2004? Were they transferred to Bigelow Aerospace, to BAASS in 2008, or destroyed?
The terms and scope of the Sherman nondisclosure agreement have never been disclosed. Is it still in force, and how many other witnesses signed comparable instruments?
Did any federal agency fund, task or receive NIDS product between 1995 and 2004, before the 2008 DIA contract?
NIDS ran a hotline receiving over 5,000 reports. Where is that report corpus now, and did any of it enter the AAWSAP database?
Alexander committed publicly in 1996 to journal publication. Was that commitment abandoned by choice, by the absence of results, or by an internal restriction?
Vallee's papers document face-to-face meetings between NIDS and BAASS. Who attended, when, and what was transferred? The files are restricted until 2028-2031.

The AAWSAP solicitation and contract numbers reported in secondary accounts (solicitation HHM402-08-R-0211; contract HHM402-08-C-0072, performance beginning 22 September 2008) have not been verified here against a primary contracting record.

aaro-fy2025-annual-report.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena is the fourteen-page statutory report submitted by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office under 50 U.S.C. § 3373(k), covering UAP events from 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025, bearing the clearance number 26-P-0880 and issued under the letterhead "Department of War." It was publicly released on 21 July 2026, months after the annual reporting cycle Congress contemplated. It records 319 new reports, 370 total resolutions, and no unexplained residue attributed to advanced foreign or non-human capability.
aaro-fy2025-annual-report.whyImplicated: This is the current, dated instrument of official denial, and it is therefore the most useful single artifact on the board. Its flat assertion — "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials" — is immediately followed by the statement that AARO "is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG," a process AARO says draws on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for it. The report also claims an access authority that collides directly with standing DoD regulation: AARO states it is authorized to receive UAP information "regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs," while DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g simultaneously forbids any DoD contractor employee from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval and 32 CFR 117.6 removes DCSA visibility from carved-out programs entirely. Claiming access is not the same as exercising it. And the report is internally inconsistent on its headline finding: §IV.C states AARO resolved 44 events as satellite flaring during the reporting period while §VI states the new capability "enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring."
aaro-fy2025-annual-report.narrative:
The arithmetic is the place to start, because the report's own numbers do not reconcile cleanly and the discrepancy runs through its most-promoted achievement. AARO received 319 reports between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025: 284 events inside the window and 35 from 2010 to 2024 not previously reported. Of the 319, AARO resolved 114 and additionally resolved 256 cases from prior periods, for 370 resolutions in the reporting period. Case holdings totaled 1,870 as of 30 May 2025. By domain, 274 were airborne, 44 space, one maritime. Of the 319, 191 were transferred to the "active archive" — the category for cases with insufficient data to assess whether performance characteristics are consistent with natural phenomena or exceed the known state of the art. Nine reports were identified as meriting further analysis by intelligence community and science-and-technology partners. Two case files were merged.

Now the flaring numbers. Section III.A states that all 44 space-domain reports were assessed as satellite flaring, of which 42 came from FAA civilian pilot reports and two from ground-based U.S. Space Command sensors — and notes, pointedly, that "none of AARO's space-domain case assessments originated from space-based sensors." Section IV.C states: "AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period." Section VI states: "This capability, consisting of advanced three-dimensional modeling and simulation applications, enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring." The executive summary uses 238. Gillibrand's press release uses 238. The 238 figure only coheres if it spans the 256 previously reported cases as well as the current-period 44, which the report never states and which would mean the office's flagship analytic advance was applied overwhelmingly to a backlog rather than to new reporting. A downstream analyst should treat the 238/44 gap as an unresolved presentation problem in a fourteen-page document.

The substantive denials come in Section IV.G and Section IV.H. On materials: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel." On health: "To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects associated with their experience." Both are negative claims about AARO's own holdings, not about the world. The report never asserts that no such program or materials exist; it asserts that no evidence of them has reached this office.

The access claim in Section V.C is the report's strongest institutional assertion and its most testable: "AARO is authorized by law to receive all UAP-related information, including any classified national security information involving military or intelligence related activities, at any level of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs. Generally, no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority within the DoW, the IC, or any other USG department or agency." Note the hedge: "Generally." Note also what the sentence does not say — it describes a right to receive, not an exercised capability to compel, and it does not state that AARO has audited any carved-out special access program. Against that, 262 individuals used the secure reporting mechanism in the period; AARO determined 255 were out of scope and identified seven for follow-on interview. A 97 percent out-of-scope rate is either an accurate measure of noise or a measure of a scoping filter, and the report gives no criteria by which to tell.

Two passages cut against the report's own framing. Section IV.E: "AARO received and analyzed several reports describing UAP in or near national security sites or critical infrastructure. Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector." And Section III.A, the sole maritime case: a report from U.S. Navy assets operating off the coast of Virginia describing "approximately 100 airborne UAP and two, likely uncrewed, surface systems," which AARO says it is actively investigating. An office reporting no flight-safety concerns and no anomalous residue is simultaneously reporting an unmitigated threat vector and a hundred-object maritime event under investigation.

Section IV.F is the nuclear line. AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites — a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 in the FY2024 report. "None of these incidents were reported as UAP." Forty-seven of the 50 occurred between 1700 and 0500 local; five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours; 33 involved a single system, 17 involved between two and seven. The categorical exclusion of all 50 from UAP status is a classification decision made by the reporting agencies, not an analytic finding by AARO, and the report does not say who made it.

On process: the report was released 21 July 2026 under a statute requiring submission "not later than 180 days after December 23, 2022, and annually thereafter for four years." The FY2024 report was published in November 2024 and documented 757 reports against FY2025's 319. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who created AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and secured the FY2024 NDAA declassification language, issued a same-day statement calling the report "another crucial step forward" and AARO "the most comprehensive government effort on UAPs to date," and framed the arithmetic as 319 received, 114 explained, "leaving 205 unresolved." The report's own foreign-engagement section names exactly one activity for the year: AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London.

claims.text: The report is titled "Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena," is issued under "Department of War / All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office" letterhead, carries clearance number 26-P-0880, states an information cut-off of 30 May 2025, and runs 14 pages.

AARO reports receiving 319 UAP reports between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025 (284 in-period, 35 from events between 2010 and 2024), resolving 114 of them plus 256 cases from prior periods for 370 total resolutions, with case holdings of 1,870 reports as of 30 May 2025.

The report states in §IV.C that "AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period," while §VI and the Executive Summary state that a new capability "enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring" — an unexplained discrepancy within a 14-page document.

AARO states: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel."

AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP-related information, including any classified national security information involving military or intelligence related activities, at any level of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs," and that "generally, no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving UAP-related information."

Between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals contacted AARO through the secure reporting mechanism for persons claiming first-hand knowledge of a USG UAP-related program or activity dating back to 1945; AARO determined 255 were out of scope and identified 7 warranting a follow-on interview request.

On reports near national security sites the report states: "Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector."

The single maritime-domain case of the reporting period was a report from U.S. Navy assets operating off the coast of Virginia describing "approximately 100 airborne UAP and two, likely uncrewed, surface systems"; AARO states it "is actively investigating this event in coordination with the reporting unit."

AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding UAS incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites — a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 reported in FY2024 — and states "None of these incidents were reported as UAP." Forty-seven of 50 occurred between 1700 and 0500 local time; five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours.

AARO transferred 191 of the 319 reports to its "active archive" for insufficient data, and identified nine reports meriting further analysis by intelligence community and science-and-technology partners.

None of AARO's 44 space-domain case assessments originated from space-based sensors: 42 came from civilian pilot reports via the FAA and two from ground-based U.S. Space Command sensors. FAA reports from civilian aviators constituted 21 percent of AARO's incoming reporting.

The report's sole named foreign-partner engagement for the year is that "AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London, United Kingdom." AARO states it "aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025."
The report was released on 21 July 2026, well after the statutory annual cycle; the FY2024 report was published in November 2024, and the FY2024 report documented 757 reports against FY2025's 319.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who created AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and secured FY2024 NDAA language requiring declassification of UAP records, issued a same-day statement on 21 July 2026 calling the report "another crucial step forward," describing AARO as "the most comprehensive government effort on UAPs to date," and characterizing the numbers as 319 received and 114 explained, "leaving 205 unresolved."

aaro-fy2025-annual-report.denialPosture: The report issues two categorical denials and one implicit one. On materials: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials." On health: "To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects." On adversary technology: "None of the cases AARO resolved indicate advanced foreign adversarial capabilities or breakthrough technologies in any domain." Each is scoped to what has reached AARO rather than to what exists, and each is undercut within the same document by the unmitigated-threat-vector language, the hundred-object Virginia maritime case, and the fact that AARO is building a materials custody process for materials it says do not exist.
connections: The carve-out mechanism at 32 CFR 117.6 and DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g is the direct structural rebuttal to AARO's claimed unrestricted access: a contractor at a carved-out facility is regulatorily barred from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval, and DCSA has no oversight visibility into the program at all.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand — statutory author of AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and of the FY2024 NDAA declassification language; the office's principal congressional patron and the first responder to each annual report.
AARO Director Dr. Jon Kosloski, named in §VI as having participated in multiple on-camera interviews with national-level audiences during the reporting period.
50 U.S.C. § 3373 is the enabling statute; § 3373b establishes the authorized reporting mechanism through which the 262 first-hand claimants contacted the office.
The Condon Report's 1969 recommendation against establishing a federal UFO agency held until AARO's creation in 2022 — a fifty-three-year gap that is itself the concealment window.

The Robertson Panel's 1953 conclusion of "no residuum of cases" attributable to artifacts is the direct ancestor of AARO's "none of the cases AARO resolved indicate advanced foreign adversarial capabilities or breakthrough technologies in any domain."
The Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN of February 2025 is named but not described; it is the operative DoD-wide reporting order and has not been released.
The National Nuclear Security Administration and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission are the reporting sources for the 50 nuclear-adjacent UAS incidents that AARO excludes from UAP status.

The FY2024 report (757 reports) and the FY2025 report (319) together show a 58 percent drop in incoming volume in a single cycle, which the report attributes to the FY2024 FAA backlog rather than to any change in reporting behavior.
openQuestions: Why does §IV.C state 44 satellite-flaring resolutions for the reporting period while §VI and the Executive Summary state 238? The report never reconciles the figures or states which case population the 238 spans.
Who decided that all 50 nuclear-adjacent UAS incidents were "not reported as UAP" — the reporting agencies or AARO — and against what criteria?
What are the scoping criteria by which 255 of 262 first-hand claimants were ruled out of scope? None are published.
AARO says it is building a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials "by an appropriate line organization." Which organization, under what authority, and with what facility?
AARO claims access regardless of special access controls. Has AARO ever invoked that authority against a specific carved-out SAP, and if so, was access granted or refused?
The February 2025 Joint Staff UAP GENADMIN remains classified. What does it direct, and does it reach contractor personnel?
The Virginia maritime case describes approximately 100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems. What sensors recorded it, and what is the current status of the investigation?

Two reports described electronic or avionic interference near operational aircraft; AARO says it has "not yet rendered a determination." What is the determination timeline, and which airframes were involved?
The report was released roughly eight months later than the prior year's. What accounts for the delay, and was the report submitted to Congress on time even if released late?

stargate-program.whatItIs: STAR GATE was the final code name for a U.S. government psychic-intelligence effort that ran from roughly 1970 to 1995 under a rotating series of names and host agencies: SCANATE (CIA-funded, from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM Detachment G at Fort Meade, 1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, 1985), and STAR GATE (DIA with SAIC as prime contractor, 1991). It combined an operational collection unit that tasked trained remote viewers against real intelligence targets with a separately maintained contract research program run out of Stanford Research Institute. It was terminated in 1995 after a Congressionally Directed Action moved it to CIA and CIA declined to keep it.
stargate-program.whyImplicated: STAR GATE is the board's cleanest declassified proof-of-concept for the exact institutional pattern the legacy program is alleged to follow: a real, funded, operational, compartmented effort into a phenomenon the government publicly treated as nonsense, sustained across two decades and at least four host organizations by serial renaming, moved between Army, DIA and CIA in a way that defeats continuity of oversight, and run through a cleared contractor (SRI, then SAIC) rather than in-house. The 1995 CIA program-status memorandum shows the disposal mechanics with unusual clarity: CIA and DIA had already made 'plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' before any evaluation was complete, and the memo's author recommended asking Congress to agree the program should NOT transfer to CIA before the contracted review had even begun. That is a decision to terminate reached in advance of the evidence, followed by a curated declassification, which means the archive the public got is the residue of a deliberate sorting operation rather than a data dump. The program also demonstrates that a phenomenon-adjacent effort could be carried in the black for twenty-five years while officials denied its existence, and that its closure could be framed publicly as a scientific verdict rather than a bureaucratic one. Finally, STAR GATE is a personnel bridge: the scientists, contractors and case officers it credentialed are the same names that reappear in the NIDS, AAWSAP and To The Stars-era record, giving the board a documented lineage from Cold War compartmented research to the 2017-2026 disclosure fight.
stargate-program.narrative:
The origin story is threat-mirroring. Between 1969 and 1971, U.S. intelligence concluded the Soviet Union was investing seriously in what it called psychotronics, with estimates running to 60 million rubles per year by 1970 and over 300 million by 1975. Whether or not the Soviets had anything, the money itself was treated as evidence, and CIA opened a research line in 1970 under the name SCANATE. In 1972 the research moved to Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, where Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff ran it, initially around a small set of gifted individuals including the artist Ingo Swann. The client requirement, per the FAS program file, was a minimum accuracy of 65 percent.

The operational side grew separately out of the Army. GONDOLA WISH, a 1977 Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence effort under the Systems Exploitation Detachment, was chartered to evaluate potential adversary applications of remote viewing. It became a collection project in mid-1978 as GRILL FLAME, INSCOM 'Detachment G,' housed in buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, Maryland. The SRI research was folded into GRILL FLAME in early 1979, and hundreds of experiments were run at SRI through 1986. Renamed the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project in 1983, the unit adopted a written methodology developed by Swann and Puthoff meant to make the capability trainable rather than innate. Its existence surfaced publicly when columnist Jack Anderson reported on it in April 1984. That same year the National Academy of Sciences' National Research Council evaluated remote viewing for the Army Research Institute and returned an unfavorable verdict. When Army funding ended in late 1985, the unit did not die; it was redesignated SUN STREAK and moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate under office code DT-S. In 1991 the contract moved to Science Applications International Corporation and the program became STAR GATE, downgraded from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS, limited dissemination, program. Edwin May presided over roughly 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of data collection. Over two decades the effort consumed on the order of $20 million, with about $11 million spent from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, and involved more than forty personnel including about twenty-three remote viewers.

The end is where the concealment mechanics are legible. The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed transfer to CIA and directed CIA to conduct a retrospective review. What happened next is documented in a SECRET memorandum, 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction,' now in the CIA reading room as CIA-RDP96-00791R000100160001-0. The Executive Director approved CIA's approach in late January 1995; it was transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the Senate Appropriations Committee staff on 27 March 1995. CIA transferred funds to the Army Research Institute to make it executive agent for a National Research Council blue-ribbon review. In parallel, and this is the sentence that matters for the board, CIA was 'working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate' and had 'made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program.' The sorting of what the public would eventually see was underway before the verdict was in.

NRC declined the review by letter dated 5 May 1995, citing its own 1988 report and quoting its conclusion that the case for remote viewing was 'not just very weak, but virtually nonexistent.' NRC referred CIA to Dr. David Goslin, president of the American Institutes for Research. The memo's author then recommended skipping the review entirely: 'in view of the strong position taken by the NRC... I want to propose at this point that we strongly consider the option of going back to Congress with the recommendation not to accept the Star Gate program from DIA,' adding that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.' He also recorded that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and deferred any decision about the operational personnel still at DIA. The recommendation was explicit: 'ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA.'

AIR did the review anyway. Its final report is dated 29 September 1995 and was released publicly on 28 November 1995. It contained two irreconcilable assessments, statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect and psychologist Ray Hyman finding none, and a single recommendation to terminate. CIA's public line was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations. The program had been sustained politically for years by Senator Claiborne Pell of Rhode Island and Representative Charles Rose of North Carolina; with the program dead, the constituency dissolved.

What the board should take from STAR GATE is not whether remote viewing worked. It is the demonstrated administrative repertoire: serial renaming across host commands, movement between Army, DIA and CIA, SAP-to-LIMDIS reclassification, contractor intermediation, a pre-cooked termination decision, a curated declassification, and a public verdict framed in the language of science rather than of budget politics. Every one of those moves is available to any program that wants to disappear while remaining funded, and every one is documented here in the government's own paper.

claims.text: A SECRET CIA memorandum titled 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction' records that a Congressionally Directed Action transferred the STAR GATE program to CIA, that the Executive Director approved CIA's recommended approach in late January 1995, and that the approach was 'formally transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the SAC staff on 27 March 1995.'

The same CIA memorandum states that CIA 'have been working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate and have made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' - meaning the scope of the eventual public release was decided before the outside evaluation was performed.

The same CIA memorandum records that the National Research Council declined to perform the evaluation by letter dated 5 May 1995, and that CIA was then referred to Dr. David Goslin, President of the American Institutes for Research.

The same CIA memorandum recommends terminating before the review is performed: 'I recommend we adopt this alternative plan and ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA,' noting that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.'

The same CIA memorandum states that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and that a decision on the operational personnel then at DIA was deferred pending the blue-ribbon panel assessment.

The American Institutes for Research final report, 'An Evaluation of Remote Viewing: Research and Applications,' is dated 29 September 1995 and was released to the public on 28 November 1995; its final recommendation was to terminate the STAR GATE effort.

STAR GATE was the last in a chain of renamed programs: SCANATE (CIA-funded from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI Systems Exploitation Detachment, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM 'Detachment G,' buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, mid-1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE Project (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, late 1985), STAR GATE (1991).

In 1991 the program transitioned to Science Applications International Corporation (SAIC) and was changed from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS (limited dissemination) program; Edwin May presided over 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of the program's data collection.

Remote viewing research began in 1972 at Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California, conducted by Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff, initially focused on a small number of individuals including Ingo Swann.

Over more than two decades roughly $20 million was spent on STAR GATE and related activities, with about $11 million budgeted from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s; over forty personnel served in the program at various times, including about twenty-three remote viewers.
The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed that the program be transferred to CIA and that CIA conduct a retrospective review of it.
The program's political survival depended on two named legislators: Senator Claiborne Pell (D-RI) and Representative Charles Rose (D-NC).

The existence of the then-highly-classified program was publicly reported by columnist Jack Anderson in April 1984; a 1984 National Academy of Sciences / National Research Council evaluation performed for the Army Research Institute returned unfavorable results.

The AIR evaluation contained a positive assessment by statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect, offset by a negative assessment by psychologist Ray Hyman; CIA's public conclusion was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations.

Next research step: establish the exact volume and cut-off criteria of the STAR GATE material released into CIA's electronic reading room through the January 2017 CREST expansion, and identify what categories of record are absent from it, against the 1995 decision to withhold 'the most sensitive aspects of the program.'

The 1995 internal memorandum shows that position was arrived at before the evaluation was contracted, and that the declassification package was scoped in parallel by CIA and DIA to exclude 'the most sensitive aspects of the program.'

DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate (DT-S) hosted the program from 1985 to 1991; DIA is the same agency that later hosted AAWSAP, making DIA the most persistent institutional host across both threads.

American Institutes for Research and its president David Goslin are the named third-party validators used to close the program, the same 'independent review' device later used with the NASA 2023 UAP study panel and AARO's Historical Record Report.

odni-preliminary-assessment-2021.whatItIs: A nine-page unclassified intelligence product titled 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' issued by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence on 25 June 2021 in response to a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. It was drafted by the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from sixteen named agencies and components, and prepared for the Congressional Intelligence and Armed Services Committees. It reviewed 144 U.S. Government UAP reports from November 2004 to March 2021 and resolved exactly one.
odni-preliminary-assessment-2021.whyImplicated: This is the document in which the U.S. Intelligence Community, in writing and on the record, declined to attribute a single one of 143 unresolved incidents to American classified programs, and admitted it could not confirm that its own developmental programs accounted for any of them. That admission cuts both ways and the board should hold both edges. If the objects are not U.S. black programs, the IC has just conceded 143 unexplained penetrations of restricted airspace, many near nuclear-capable and test infrastructure. If they are U.S. black programs, then the DNI's own coordinating body was denied read-in access to them, which is the definition of the concealment the board asserts. The assessment further records that UAP cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds and near facilities carrying the most advanced sensor systems, that in eighteen incidents observers reported unusual flight characteristics, that military aircraft systems processed radio-frequency energy associated with sightings, and that the task force holds data appearing to show acceleration or signature management. It is also a concealment artifact in its own right: it names the accountable official only by title, ships the substance to a classified annex, and defines the problem as a data-collection deficiency rather than an access deficiency, converting a question about who is hiding what into a request for better forms and more money.
odni-preliminary-assessment-2021.narrative:
The assessment exists because of a paragraph in a Senate committee report, not because of an executive decision to inform the public. Senate Report 116-233, submitted by Senator Marco Rubio from the Select Committee on Intelligence on 17 June 2020 to accompany S. 3905, directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to submit an intelligence assessment of the threat posed by UAP and of the progress the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force had made. Appendix B of the resulting product reprints the eight specific things the Senate asked for. Two of them are worth memorizing. Item 4 demanded 'a detailed description of an interagency process for ensuring timely data collection and centralized analysis of all UAP reporting for the Federal Government, regardless of which service or agency acquired the information.' Item 5 demanded 'Identification of an official accountable for the process described in paragraph 4.' The Senate was asking, in oversight language, who owns the file. ODNI's answer, in the Scope section, is a title with no name attached: 'The Director, UAPTF, is the accountable official for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP.'

The drafting coalition is itself a finding. The report was written by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Navy/ONI, DARPA, FAA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI's National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and the National Intelligence Council. The Department of Energy is not on the list. Neither is CIA. Neither is any Special Access Program Central Office. For a document whose central unresolved question is whether the objects are American, the absence of the organizations that would custody the most sensitive American aerospace and nuclear-adjacent programs is the shape of the hole.

The numbers are small and precise. One hundred forty-four reports originated from USG sources. Eighty of those involved observation with multiple sensors: radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, visual. One was identified with high confidence, 'a large, deflating balloon.' The rest, 143, 'remain unexplained.' In eighteen incidents, described across twenty-one reports, observers reported unusual movement or flight characteristics: objects that appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, maneuver abruptly, or travel at considerable speed 'without discernable means of propulsion.' In a small number of cases 'military aircraft systems processed radio frequency (RF) energy associated with UAP sightings.' The UAPTF 'holds a small amount of data that appear to show UAP demonstrating acceleration or a degree of signature management,' with further analysis promised. Eleven documented near misses were on file.

The five-bin taxonomy, airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other,' is where the board plants its flag. Under the third bin the report says: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to developments and classified programs by U.S. entities. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' That is not a denial that such programs exist. It is a statement that the drafters could not obtain confirmation. An intelligence assessment written by the DNI's aviation manager and coordinated across sixteen organizations was unable to check its own government's classified aerospace inventory against its own government's unexplained-object file. Either no such inventory exists, or access to it was refused, or the query was never seriously pressed. Each possibility is load-bearing.

The geographic finding is handled the same way. UAP sightings 'tended to cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds,' and 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems.' The report immediately neutralizes this as probable collection bias: more sensors, greater expectation, standing guidance to report anomalies. That may be true. It is also exactly the explanation one would offer to avoid the alternative reading, which is that the objects are interested in specific American infrastructure, the same pattern documented at Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot and Falconbridge in October and November 1975.

The remedies proposed are all inputs, never access. Standardize reporting. Consolidate data. Employ artificial intelligence and machine learning to cluster features. Search historical radar archives with advanced algorithms. Update the interagency collection strategy. Increase R&D investment guided by a UAP Collection Strategy, a UAP R&D Technical Roadmap, and a UAP Program Plan. Not one recommendation asks any agency to disclose what it already holds. The report also records, candidly, that no standardized reporting mechanism existed anywhere in the U.S. military until the Navy created one in March 2019 and the Air Force adopted it in November 2020, meaning that for the entire post-Blue Book era the United States operated with no formal channel by which a military aviator could report an object over a nuclear or test facility. That is not an accident of bureaucracy; it is a design decision with a fifty-year half-life. The report is equally candid about the human cost: aviators and analysts 'describe disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues.'

The institutional sequel followed within six months. Section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 117-81, signed 27 December 2021, directed establishment of a successor office. The Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group was stood up and then superseded; the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was formally established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum published 20 July 2022, designating AARO the authoritative DoD focal point for UAP and placing it under USD(I&S), one of the very components that had contributed to this assessment. The task force that could not confirm whether American programs accounted for any of its own 144 cases was thereby replaced by an office that would go on to assert that no such programs ever existed. The 2021 assessment is the last moment the U.S. government's written position was uncertainty rather than denial, which is precisely why it is the most useful single document in the modern record.

The assessment was mandated by a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 and was prepared for the Congressional Intelligence and Armed Services Committees; Senate Report 116-233 was submitted by Senator Marco Rubio from the Select Committee on Intelligence on 17 June 2020 to accompany S. 3905.

Every recommendation in the assessment concerns increasing collection, standardization, analytic tooling and funding; none directs any U.S. agency to disclose UAP-related holdings it already possesses.

The successor office was created by statute within six months: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (Public Law 117-81, enacted 27 December 2021) directed establishment of a UAP office, and the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was formally established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum published 20 July 2022 designating it the authoritative DoD focal point for UAP and UAP-related activities.

odni-preliminary-assessment-2021.denialPosture: The assessment does not deny that a U.S. legacy program exists; it declines to confirm one, in the specific formulation 'We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' That is a sourcing statement about the drafters' own access, not a factual finding about the U.S. inventory, and it is signed institutionally by ODNI rather than by any named individual.

DARPA, NRO, NGA and NSA are listed contributors; the Department of Energy and CIA are not, which is the negative-space finding for the custody thread.
