aaro-fy2024-annual-report.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, produced by the Department of Defense All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) with an information cut-off of 1 June 2024 and released 14 November 2024. It is submitted to Congress under a statutory requirement at 50 U.S.C. 3373(k) and covers UAP reports from 1 May 2023 to 1 June 2024 plus all prior-period reports not previously reported. It was drafted in coordination with more than two dozen named organisations including ODNI, the Service intelligence centres, NRO, NGA, NSA, DIA, FBI, NCIS, DoE, NASA, the NNSA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
aaro-fy2024-annual-report.whyImplicated: AARO is not a neutral authority here; it is the office the Department created to be the answer to the question, and this report is the instrument by which it discharges its obligation to Congress. What makes it load-bearing is not its denials but the specific admissions embedded in them. Section IV.G is headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP" and its entire body is a single sentence stating that AARO is working with mission partners "to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured" - meaning that as of mid-2024 no such process existed anywhere the office could see. Section VI.C confirms that Oak Ridge National Laboratory analysed "a material claimed to be from a UAP." Section VI.D confirms AARO posted historical documents on KONA BLUE, a prospective and unapproved Special Access Program that interviewees described as a DHS compartment to cover up "the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" And the report concedes that 444 of the 757 reports lacked sufficient data for any analysis and that AARO received zero UAP reporting through national GEOINT, SIGINT or MASINT platforms during the entire period - the national technical means that would find a concealed program were not pointed at the problem at all.
aaro-fy2024-annual-report.narrative:
Read as a compliance document, the FY2024 report is a study in what a statutory reporting requirement can and cannot compel. 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1)(B) enumerates roughly fifteen mandatory content items, and the report walks them in order: events in period, events out of period, analysis by intelligence discipline, incidents over restricted airspace, threats, foreign attribution, breakthrough foreign capability, allied consultation, capture-or-exploitation efforts, health effects, nuclear-asset association, NNSA and NRC consultation, designated line organisations, and a summary of authorised reporting. The statute is well drafted. The answers are mostly negative, and the negatives are the interesting part.

The numbers: 757 reports received, of which 485 occurred in the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were only reported now. Cumulative holdings as of 24 October 2024 were 1,652 reports. Of the 757, 392 - more than half - came from the FAA, and consisted of the entire FAA UAP reporting log since June 2021. By domain: 708 air, 49 space, zero maritime, zero transmedium; and AARO notes that none of the space-domain reports came from space-based sensors, all being pilot or ground-observer accounts of objects estimated above 100 kilometres. AARO resolved 49 cases in-period, recommended 243 more for closure, judged 21 to merit further analysis by intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners, and consigned 444 to an 'Active Archive' for lack of data. By publication, the office reported 118 resolved and a further 174 finalised, all to prosaic objects.

The key sentence for anyone tracking concealment is buried in Section III.B: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms." Every input was pilot report, post-mission full-motion video, or FAA log. AARO can search IC databases case-by-case, but nothing was tasked. Whatever else the report establishes, it establishes that the collection architecture of the United States was not being used to answer this question during the period covered.

The second key passage is the nuclear-infrastructure section. AARO received eighteen reports from the NNSA Administrator and the NRC Chairman regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all of which those agencies categorised as unmanned aircraft systems. Two involved incursions of 53 minutes and one hour 57 minutes. On 3 August 2023 security at the D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant recovered a crashed UAS and turned it over to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement; AARO states flatly that it "has no further information about the crashed UAS." A recovered object over a nuclear facility left the federal system entirely and the office statutorily charged with anomaly resolution never got it back. Separately, the BWXT Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia experienced UAS overflights on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

The third is the authorities language. AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," with "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority." This is the exact authority whose absence is the subject of the Wilson-Davis memo - a Deputy Director of DIA being told by a contractor committee that his tickets and statutory authority were not sufficient. The FY2024 report asserts the authority exists. It does not report ever having exercised it against a waived or unacknowledged SAP, nor does it report a single instance of an access denial.

The science-and-technology section names the partner set: Oak Ridge National Laboratory for physics-relevant case analysis and the UAP-material analysis; the Air Force Research Laboratory for propulsion, stealth and sensing assessments; the Georgia Tech Research Institute, which built the GREMLIN sensor architecture that demonstrated functionality in a March 2024 test and was slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection "at a site of national security"; MIT Lincoln Laboratory, building prototype processing to recover objects currently filtered out of FAA and National Weather Service radar; and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source work. That is a real, funded, technically competent architecture, and its existence should be weighed against the report's own admission that the office cannot resolve most of its caseload.

Finally, the strategic communications section records that AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, characterising it as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" AARO's framing is dismissive. But the disclosure itself confirms that a UAP-linked prospective SAP was drafted, staffed toward DHS, and documented well enough that its papers could be posted eight months later.

claims.text: The report is submitted under a requirement established in 50 U.S.C. 3373(k), which directs the Director of the Office to report to the appropriate congressional committees not later than 180 days after enactment of the FY2023 Intelligence Authorization Act and annually thereafter for four years.

AARO received 757 UAP reports during the period 1 May 2023 - 1 June 2024; 485 occurred in period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were not previously reported. As of 24 October 2024 AARO held 1,652 reports in total.

Of the 757 reports, 392 came from the FAA and consisted of all of the FAA's UAP reports since 2021; 708 occurred in the air domain, 49 in the space domain, and none in the maritime or transmedium domains.

AARO determined 21 cases merit further analysis by its intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners; 444 cases lacked sufficient data to facilitate analysis and were placed in the Active Archive.
The report states verbatim: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms."

Section IV.G, headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP," consists in its entirety of the statement that "AARO is working with mission partners to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured, drawing on current USG capabilities and operating procedures" - an admission that no such process existed as of the cut-off date.
The report states: "It is important to underscore that, to date, AARO has discovered no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology."

AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," and that there is "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority."

Oak Ridge National Laboratory "provided analysis for a material claimed to be from a UAP," and AARO S&T, in coordination with ORNL, wrote a materials-analysis report and posted it on AARO's website, with supplemental data promised.

AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, described in the report as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'"

AARO received 18 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all categorised by those agencies as UAS; two incursions lasted 53 minutes and 1 hour 57 minutes respectively.

On 3 August 2023 D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant security recovered a crashed UAS which was given to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement, and "AARO has no further information about the crashed UAS." Separately, the BWXT (formerly Babcock and Wilcox Nuclear Energy) Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia observed UAS flyovers on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

In May 2023 the Joint Staff issued a UAP GENADMIN message directing Combatant Commands and Services to report all UAP incidents, incursions and engagements to Combatant Command Joint Operations Centers, Service Watch Centers, and respective counterintelligence elements no later than 96 hours after the event.

AARO's named science-and-technology partners are Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Georgia Tech Research Institute (developer of the GREMLIN sensor architecture, tested March 2024 and slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection at a site of national security), MIT Lincoln Laboratory (prototype processing for FAA and National Weather Service radar), and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source analysis.

aaro-fy2024-annual-report.denialPosture: Categorical and repeated: no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity or technology; no data indicating the capture or exploitation of UAP; no confirmation of foreign adversarial attribution. The denials are consistently framed as statements about what AARO possesses or has discovered rather than about what exists, which preserves deniability if material is held in a compartment AARO has not in fact penetrated.

wilson-davis-memo.whatItIs: A 15-page document consisting of meeting notes attributed to Dr. Eric W. Davis, headed "Eric Davis Meeting with Adm. Wilson" and dated 10/16/02, purporting to record an approximately seventy-minute conversation with recently retired Vice Adm. Thomas R. Wilson - former Deputy Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency and Assistant Joint Chief of Staff J-2, and Director of DIA from 1999 until July 2002. The notes place the conversation in Wilson's parked car behind the EG&G Special Projects building at Grier and Paradise in Las Vegas. The document is said to have surfaced from the estate of Apollo 14 astronaut Edgar Mitchell following his death in February 2016 and circulated online from 2019. Its provenance is contested and Wilson has denied the meeting on the record. Critical handling note: the version in general circulation is an annotated PDF prepared by an anonymous third party, and the marginal identifications of Lockheed Martin as the unnamed contractor and of Noel Longuemare Jr. as the Senior Review Group chairman are the annotator's inferences, not statements attributed to Wilson anywhere in the notes.
wilson-davis-memo.whyImplicated: If authentic, this is the single most operationally specific description in the open record of how a legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering effort would be insulated from oversight - and it is specific in ways that are checkable. It describes a special projects record group inside the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Technology that sat outside the SAP divisions William Perry reorganised in 1994. It names the officials Wilson allegedly worked through: Perry, Under Secretary Paul Kaminski, Brig. Gen. Michael Kostelnik as director of special programs and SAPCO director and executive secretary to SAPOC, Maj. Gen. H. Marshal Ward, Judith Daly at OUSD(A&T), and Jacques Gansler on arrival in December 1997. It describes a contractor-side committee of program director, security director and corporate attorney - calling itself "the watch committee" - administering access criteria that overrode a serving three-star's statutory need-to-know, and a bigot list dated 1990 and updated 1993 covering 400 to 800 workers containing no politicians, no White House names and no congressional staffers. And it describes the enforcement mechanism: the SAPOC Senior Review Group sustaining the contractor and warning Wilson he would lose his promotion and one or two stars. If it is a fabrication, that is equally load-bearing, because the fabricator understood SAP governance vocabulary well enough that the document was later entered into a congressional hearing record.
wilson-davis-memo.narrative:
The document must be handled as three separable things: an artifact with a physical history, a set of assertions about 1997, and a contested attribution. Keeping them separate is what makes it usable.

As an artifact, its most consequential fact is institutional. The Internet Archive copy of the annotated memo cites, as its provenance, the congressional document HHRG-117-IG05-20220517-SD001 posted at congress.gov under the 17 May 2022 hearing of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Subcommittee on Counterterrorism, Counterintelligence and Counterproliferation - the first open congressional UAP hearing in over fifty years. Reporting indicates Rep. Mike Gallagher raised the document with the Pentagon witnesses and obtained unanimous consent to enter it into the record. Whatever its authenticity, it is now a document in a congressional hearing file, and its assertions are therefore assertions Congress has formally received and not adjudicated.

As a set of assertions, the notes describe a search rather than a revelation. Wilson, then Deputy Director of DIA and Assistant JCS J-2, is depicted as acting after an April 1997 Pentagon conference-room briefing given by Steven Greer, Cmdr. Willard Miller and Edgar Mitchell, at which Adm. Mike Crawford and Wilson's superior Lt. Gen. Patrick Hughes were present. Wilson and Miller then spoke privately for two hours about, in the memo's phrasing, UFOs, MJ-12, Roswell, crashed UFOs and alien bodies. Wilson is described as already knowing of intelligence on US military and foreign government close encounters. Over roughly forty-five days he made calls, was pointed by Maj. Gen. Ward and by Perry toward the records groups in OUSD(A&T), located what he describes as a special projects record group that did not belong to the usual SAP divisions as organised by Perry in 1994, and read the index abstracts. He is described as being told by Kostelnik that program security costs ran two to three times the program budget and at times six to seven times core budget, that Perry had wanted an investigation of that ratio and was told to drop it, and that Judith Daly explained the discrepancy as a records-keeping artifact of cumulative versus annual reporting.

What follows is the part that is genuinely novel in the UFO literature, because it is not about a craft. It is about jurisdiction. Wilson is described as making three calls to the program manager, one a conference call with a security director and a corporate attorney, and then flying out ten days later to meet the same three in a secure vault. They call themselves "the watch committee" or gatekeepers, and explain that they formed after an earlier audit investigation nearly exposed them, following which a formal agreement was struck with SAPOC establishing special access criteria administered by the contractor committee rather than by the government, such that no USG personnel gain access unless the contractor's criteria are met "irregardless of the tickets and position USG personnel possessed." Wilson's regulatory and statutory authority as Deputy Director DIA is declared not relevant to their program. He is shown a bigot list several pages long, dated 1990 and updated 1993, mostly program employees, civilians, with a handful of recognisable Pentagon names from OUSD(A&T), one from another department, and one at the NSC who was a Pentagon SES employee. No politicians. No White House. No Congress.

Only then does the substance appear, and it is brief: the program manager states they are not a weapons, intelligence, special operations or logistics program; that they are a reverse engineering program; that something was recovered years ago; that they have an intact craft they believe could fly; that it did not come from overseas and could not have; that they did not know where it was from; that it was "technology that was not of this Earth - not made by man - not by human hands"; that progress had been agonisingly slow with painful lack of outside collaboration; and that the bigot-list workforce ran about 400 to 800 people varying with funding. On Roswell, Holloman, MJ-12 and Zamora and Bentwaters, they declined to discuss. Wilson threatened to escalate to SAPOC, did so, and the Senior Review Group sustained the contractor twice, told him to drop it, and - per the memo - the chairman warned he would not see the DIA director promotion, would get early retirement, and would lose one or two stars. In January 1998 Wilson is described as raising his June 1997 meetings with the new Under Secretary Jacques Gansler, who had somehow been briefed, and who said: "UFOs are real, so-called 'alien abductions' not real."

As a contested attribution, the record is unambiguous on one side and silent on the other. Wilson has denied it directly, telling a reporter it is all fiction, that he would not know Eric Davis if he walked in, and that he did not sit in a car with him in Las Vegas for an hour; he says he told both a Senate staffer and AARO that Davis is making it up. Davis has declined to comment publicly on the document since it appeared. Individuals identified in the memo as arranging the meeting are reported to have denied knowing Wilson. And AARO's own Historical Record Report Volume 1, the government's most extensive published treatment of exactly these allegations, does not contain the name Wilson anywhere in its 1,500-plus lines of text - it disposes of the entire category by asserting that claims involving specific people, locations, tests and documents are inaccurate and largely the product of circular reporting, without engaging this document at all. A critical handling note: the widely circulated PDF is an annotated version, and the marginal identification of Lockheed Martin as the unnamed contractor is the anonymous annotator's inference, not anything attributed to Wilson in the notes.

Reporting indicates Rep. Mike Gallagher raised the document at that hearing and obtained unanimous consent to enter it into the record as SD001.

claims.text: The memo records the contractor program manager stating the program was "a reverse engineering program," that "They had a craft - an intact craft they believed could fly," and that "it was technology that was not of this Earth - not made by man - not by human hands."

The memo names Maj. Gen. H. Marshal Ward and Secretary William Perry as the sources of the suggestion to search records-group files in OUSD(A&T), and identifies Paul Kaminski as Under Secretary of Defense (Acquisition and Technology) and Brig. Gen. Michael Kostelnik as director of special programs in OUSD(A&T), director of the Special Access Programs Coordination Office (SAPCO), executive secretary to the Special Access Programs Oversight Committee (SAPOC), and a member of the Senior Review Group. The memo states that what Wilson found there was "a special projects record group not belonging to usual SAP - a special subset of the unacknowledged/carve-outs/waived programs - not belonging to usual SAP divisions as organized in '94 by Perry himself - set apart from rest but buried/covered by conventional SAPs."

The memo records that program security spending ran "like 2-3 times the program budget, but there were times when it went as high as 6-7 times core budget," that Perry wanted an investigation of the ratio and "was told to drop it," and names Judith Daly, Assistant Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Advanced Development, OUSD(A&T), as the official who explained the figures as cumulative rather than annual security budget reporting.

The memo describes three contractor officials - a program director, a security director identified as NSA-retired and a counterintelligence expert, and a corporate attorney - who "Called themselves 'the watch committee,' or gate keepers," and who told Wilson that access criteria were "to be administered by contractor committee... irregardless of the tickets and position USG personnel possessed," and that "Regulatory and statutory authority as Deputy Director DIA not relevant or pertinent to nature of their program."

The memo records a bigot list "several pages long - dated 1990, updated 1993," comprising mostly civilian program employees, containing no politicians, no White House names, no President, no Congressional people and no Congressional staffers, but including "a handful of names" of Pentagon individuals Wilson recognised - some from OUSD(A&T), one from another department and one at the National Security Council who was a Pentagon SES employee - and a workforce of "about 400-800 (bigot list count) workers varying in number with funding or personnel changes."

The memo records Wilson identifying the holder only as "An aerospace technology contractor - one of the top ones in US," "the best one of them," with intelligence "In their corporate portfolio," and refusing to name it, the program compartment or the code name, each time on the grounds that it was a "core secret."

The memo records that after Wilson complained to the SAPOC Senior Review Group, its members sustained the contractor's access denial twice, told him "to immediately drop the matter and let it go," and that the Senior Review Group chairman warned that if he did not comply he "would not see Director DIA promotion, get early retirement, lose 1 or 2 stars along the way."

The memo records Wilson quoting incoming Under Secretary of Defense (Acquisition and Technology) Jacques Gansler, in a January 1998 conversation about the June 1997 meetings, as saying "UFOs are real, so-called 'alien abductions' not real," and then telling Wilson to drop the matter.

The memo package includes an attached letter from Cmdr. Willard 'Will' Miller dated 25 April 2002, addressed to "Dr. Eric W. Davis, CEO, Warp Drive Metrics, 4849 San Rafael Ave., Las Vegas, NV 89120," offering to supply "A list of civilian government contractors who, by virtue of their past and current highly classified work... most likely have current involvement in and knowledge of USG work in alien-derived technologies, crashes, landing, and associated events" at "$180 per straight-time hour."
claims.source: Miller to Davis, 25 April 2002, reproduced in the Wilson-Davis memo package, pp.3-5; https://archive.org/stream/annotated_wilson_memo/annotated_wilson_memo_djvu.txt

afosi.whatItIs: The Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI) is the Department of the Air Force's federal law enforcement and counterintelligence agency, established 1 August 1948 and operating as a Field Operating Agency under the Secretary of the Air Force Inspector General. Its first commander was Special Agent Joseph F. Carroll, a senior FBI official and assistant to Director J. Edgar Hoover, who in 1961 became the first Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency. AFOSI is currently chartered by Air Force Mission Directive 39, dated 12 February 2024.
afosi.whyImplicated: AFOSI sits on both sides of the concealment problem simultaneously, and its own charter says so. Under AFMD 39 paragraph 3.16 it "Executes independent special access program CI and LE investigations, operations, specialized investigative activities, compliance inspections, integrated technology protection, and program security responsibilities for all DAF special access programs, and non-DAF special access programs where the DAF has been assigned responsibility." That is the security envelope around Air Force black programs, held by one agency. Under paragraph 3.3 it is the Department's sole counterintelligence agency, and under 3.2 its investigations supersede any other Air Force entity's inquiry. Historically, AFOSI took over UFO investigation from Air Materiel Command shortly after its 1948 creation under the name Project Grudge, ran most of those investigations out of District 17 at Kirtland AFB in New Mexico - the district co-located with Sandia, Los Alamos and the Manzano weapons storage area - and in 1967 sent a piece of an alleged UFO to the FBI Crime Laboratory. And the single best-documented instance of a US counterintelligence element manufacturing UFO belief, the campaign run against Albuquerque physicist Paul Bennewitz in the late 1970s and 1980s, was run by an AFOSI special agent at Kirtland.
afosi.narrative:
Start with the charter, because it is unclassified and it is decisive. Air Force Mission Directive 39, signed 12 February 2024 by Lt. Gen. Stephen L. Davis as The Inspector General, states AFOSI's mission as identifying, exploiting, investigating, disrupting and neutralising criminal, terrorist and intelligence threats across all domains. Paragraph 3.3 designates AFOSI, by the Secretary of the Air Force, as the Department's counterintelligence component and its sole agency for counterintelligence investigations, collections, operations and analysis. Paragraph 3.2 gives it primary investigative authority over everything in its jurisdiction and provides that its investigations "will supersede any other DAF entity's investigation or inquiry." Paragraph 3.7 gives it counterintelligence responsibility for cleared contractor facilities under the National Industrial Security Program. Paragraph 3.8 gives it counterintelligence support to critical DoD research and development under DoDI-O 5240.24. Paragraph 3.16 gives it program security responsibility for all Department of the Air Force special access programs and for non-DAF SAPs where the DAF has been assigned responsibility, under AFPD 16-7 and AFI 16-701. And paragraph 2.2 requires the commander to notify the Secretary in writing of any instance in which a commander or any other Air Force official attempts to impede an investigation - an obligation that exists precisely because the situation arises.

Set that against the historical record published by AFOSI's own command historian, Dr. Deborah Kidwell, in August 2020. Her account states that at the inception of Project Sign, Air Force Materiel Command held responsibility for UFO reports, but that shortly after AFOSI's creation in 1948 it took over that responsibility under the name Project Grudge. Most investigations were run by District 17 at Kirtland AFB, New Mexico. The 1948 green fireball investigations drew in a University of New Mexico meteoriticist; District 17 briefed Sandia Base, Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, the University of California Geophysics Institute, the Atomic Energy Commission and the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project in early 1949. On the recommendation of an Air Force Scientific Advisory Board member in April 1949, District 17 established an observation post on the crest of the Sandia Mountains northeast of Albuquerque where agents manned spectrographic photo surveillance equipment twenty-four hours a day. The results were collected under OSI Letter Number 85: Unconventional Aircraft-Special Inquiry, classified file designation 24-185.

Two items in that same account matter disproportionately. First: "In 1967, agents briefed a scientific group on Neutron Activity analysis and sent a piece of an alleged UFO to the FBI Crime Laboratory. The lab concluded that while the item was unusual, there was no evidence that it belonged to an alien craft." This is an official, on-the-record acknowledgement of AFOSI custody and forensic routing of purported UAP material, and it is the same workflow that runs today through Oak Ridge. Second: AFOSI declassified its UFO investigative files in late 1975 and sent them to the National Archives, and Kidwell writes that "The National Archives has been unable to locate any documentation among the Blue Book records that discuss the incident in Roswell." The service whose district office covered New Mexico transferred its New Mexico UFO files to NARA and none of them mention Roswell - which sits alongside the GAO's separate finding that Roswell Army Air Field's outgoing messages for 1946-1949 were destroyed without recorded authority.

Then there is Kirtland in 1980. On 9 August 1980 security personnel at the Manzano Weapons Storage Area adjacent to Kirtland reported a bright light descending in a restricted area, and a report was filed with AFOSI at Kirtland. The investigating agent was Special Agent Richard C. Doty. In the same period Doty became the primary AFOSI contact for Paul Bennewitz, an Albuquerque physicist and businessman who had been filming and intercepting signals around Kirtland and Manzano. Rather than being turned away, Bennewitz was fed. Doty has since publicly acknowledged participating in counterintelligence disinformation directed at the UFO research community, and both Doty and documentary producer Linda Moulton Howe state they met at Kirtland AFB in April 1983. Bennewitz's mental deterioration is the documented outcome.

The reason this matters to a board about a legacy program is not that Doty's stories were true. It is that they were false, deliberately, and produced under colour of federal counterintelligence authority at the base where the Air Force's New Mexico UFO files, its nuclear weapons storage and its special access program security responsibilities all converged. Disinformation is expensive and is not deployed to protect nothing. AFOSI's own charter tells you what it protects at Kirtland: special access programs and nuclear surety. Whether the thing being screened was a conventional black program, a nuclear security vulnerability, or the retrieval architecture itself is exactly the question - and AFOSI is the agency whose files would settle it.

AFOSI remains inside the current reporting architecture. The May 2023 Joint Staff GENADMIN reproduced in AARO's FY2024 annual report directs Combatant Commands and Services to report all UAP incidents, incursions and engagements to Joint Operations Centers, Service Watch Centers, and respective counterintelligence elements within 96 hours. For the Department of the Air Force, per AFMD 39 paragraph 3.3, that counterintelligence element is AFOSI and only AFOSI.

galileo-project.whatItIs: The Galileo Project for the Systematic Scientific Search for Evidence of Extraterrestrial Technological Artifacts is a Harvard-hosted, cross-institutional research programme launched in July 2021 and co-founded by Avi Loeb, the Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science at Harvard, and Frank Laukien, chairman, president and CEO of the scientific instrument manufacturer Bruker Corporation. It operates three branches: the study of interstellar objects near Earth, the search for unidentified aerial phenomena using multimodal ground-based observatories, and the study of interstellar meteors. It is funded entirely by private donation.
galileo-project.whyImplicated: Galileo is the control experiment for this entire board. Every version of the legacy-program hypothesis and every official denial of it reduce to claims about physical evidence held under classification. The only structural way to break that is an independent, uncleared, publishing instrument capable of producing calibrated data on the same phenomena - data that is not subject to prepublication classification review because it was never collected on government money or on government sensors. Galileo is the first serious institutional attempt to build one, and its funding structure is the mechanism: $1.755 million raised in the first two weeks from named private donors, which means its outputs go to arXiv rather than to a DOPSR queue. Its director also co-authored a March 2023 draft paper with Sean Kirkpatrick, the sitting Director of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office - the only documented instance of a joint technical product between the Pentagon's UAP office and an independent academic programme. And its IM1 interstellar meteor work is the most instructive public failure mode on the board: a physical-recovery campaign that produced material, published it, and could not establish a chain from the material to the event, generating a citation war that maps precisely onto the epistemics of the whole subject.
galileo-project.narrative:
Loeb's framing paper, "Overview of the Galileo Project," was posted to arXiv on 2 August 2022 as arXiv:2209.02479 and published in a special issue of the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation in 2023. Its abstract describes the project as "the first systematic scientific research program in search for potential astro-archaeological artifacts or remnants of extraterrestrial technological civilizations (ETCs) or potentially active equipment near Earth," and characterises the approach as taking a path not taken and conceivably picking low-hanging fruit. That is a statement about method, and the method is the point: Galileo's premise is that the subject has been starved of instrumented, calibrated, continuous data, not of anecdotes.

The UAP branch built to that premise. Wesley Watters and colleagues published "The Scientific Investigation of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Using Multimodal Ground-Based Observatories" in the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation, volume 12, article 2340006 (2023), laying out the sensor architecture: synchronised optical, infrared, radio, magnetometric and acoustic channels producing a continuous census of everything above an observation site, so that anomaly is defined by exclusion from a measured baseline rather than by the surprise of an observer. The first instrument came online at Harvard. Commissioning results for the all-sky infrared camera array were posted as arXiv:2411.07956, and a system architecture paper followed as arXiv:2506.00125. Loeb has publicly discussed commissioning data covering roughly half a million objects. No Galileo detection has been shown to be non-human technology, and the project has not claimed otherwise.

The interstellar meteor branch is where the project collided with the discipline. CNEOS 2014-01-08, designated IM1, is a bolide detected over the western Pacific whose inferred velocity implied a hyperbolic, interstellar trajectory. In summer 2023 Galileo mounted an ocean expedition off Papua New Guinea, dragging a magnetic sled across a roughly ten-kilometre region around the fireball localisation across twenty-six runs and recovering approximately 700 sub-millimetre spherules. Loeb and colleagues reported that a subset had a distinctive composition rich in beryllium, lanthanum and uranium - the 'BeLaU' type - which they argued was inconsistent with solar-system materials. The chemical classification work was eventually published in Chemical Geology (2024), with the preprint at arXiv:2401.09882.

The response was immediate and formal, and it is worth cataloguing precisely because it is the model of how a materials claim gets adjudicated in the open. Steve Desch and Alan Jackson published a direct critique, arXiv:2311.07699, arguing among other things that the spherules plot on or extremely near a terrestrial fractionation line and that a body entering at the assumed IM1 velocity would have been essentially vaporised, so that recovered iron spherules cannot be attributed to that event. A separate paper, arXiv:2403.05161, proposed the BeLaU signature as microtektites of terrestrial laterites. Most damaging to the localisation, Fernando and colleagues published "Seismic and acoustic signals from the 2014 'interstellar meteor'" in Geophysical Journal International, volume 238, issue 2 (2024), concluding that the seismic signal used to pin the impact site changed direction over time in a way that matched a road running past the seismometer - a truck, not a bolide. Galileo replied with "Peak-Brightness Localization of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Fireball," arXiv:2403.07696, arguing that the search region was set by the NASA/JPL CNEOS localisation box - 11.112 km on a side, centred at 1.3 degrees south, 147.6 degrees east - and not by the seismic data at all.

Whichever way that dispute resolves, its structure is the finding. A privately funded team recovered candidate material, published composition data, and could not establish provenance linking material to event; independent groups published falsifying analyses within months; the original team responded in the same channel. This is exactly the adjudication process that has never been available for any material alleged to be in government custody, and the contrast is the argument. The Nolan-Vallee 2022 paper faces the same problem from the other direction - a sample with a documented same-night recovery but a forty-four-year custody gap.

The most direct institutional connection on the board is the Loeb-Kirkpatrick paper. Dated 7 March 2023 and titled "Physical Constraints on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena," it derives physical constraints on interpretations of highly manoeuvrable UAP from standard physics and known forms of matter and radiation, and it is co-authored by the serving Director of AARO. The draft circulated publicly, drew criticism from multiple directions, and was never formally issued as an AARO product. It nonetheless establishes that the Pentagon's UAP office and Galileo were in direct technical collaboration during Kirkpatrick's tenure, which bears on how one reads AARO's later categorical statements and on what data, if any, moved in either direction.

For an analyst, Galileo's value is threefold. It produces a public, timestamped, instrumented baseline that any future disclosure has to be consistent with. Its funding graph - Eugene Jhong, Vinny Jain, Teddy Jones, Eric Keto, the Laukien Science Foundation, Joerg Laukien, William A. Linton, Adnan Sen, the Brinson Foundation - identifies the private capital willing to underwrite the question outside the appropriations system. And through Laukien and Bruker it sits one step from the mass-spectrometry instrument industry whose products define what any materials claim, government or otherwise, can actually be tested with.

uap-science-advisory-council-2026.whatItIs: An external scientific advisory body stood up in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, ODNI, the FBI and the wider Intelligence Community, chaired by Harvard astrophysicist Abraham (Avi) Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board co-established by ODNI, the FBI and the Department of War, which held its first meeting on 16 June 2026. Every dataset the council is given is unclassified by design.
uap-science-advisory-council-2026.whyImplicated: The council is the scientific-legitimacy layer bolted onto the 2026 disclosure architecture, and its terms of reference are the tell. It exists to advise on the coordinated declassification of UAP information under Executive Order 13526, yet its own members are restricted to unclassified data — a body chartered to resolve the mystery is structurally barred from the evidence that would resolve it. Its membership includes Rear Admiral (ret.) Tim Gallaudet, whose account of a 2015 SIPRNET email titled "Urgent safety of flight issue" being deleted overnight from a flag officer's classified system is one of the most concrete public allegations of a special access program reaching into fleet communications; and Prof. Garry Nolan, whose laboratory work on claimed anomalous materials is the closest civilian science has come to the custody question. The council therefore places people with direct knowledge of concealment inside the advisory apparatus while denying them access to the compartments. Loeb's own public framing — that the "down-to-Earth interpretation" is adversary technology and compromised espionage defence — supplies the administration with an alarm-raising narrative that never touches the legacy retrieval question.
uap-science-advisory-council-2026.narrative:
On 16 June 2026, Avi Loeb published a Medium post announcing that he had been "tasked by the White House, the Pentagon's All Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and the Intelligence Community, to assemble a 'UAP Science Advisory Council'." The following day DefenseScoop's Brandi Vincent confirmed the arrangement with an ODNI official, who described the parent UAP Governance Board as an interagency body created "to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies," and confirmed that it had met for the first time the previous day. The ODNI official declined to identify the board's original participants — the body that will control declassification sequencing is itself anonymous.

The council's composition is the most analytically useful fact about it, and the two authoritative lists do not match. Loeb's own 16 June account names fifteen members: Prof. Liberty Vittert Capito (data analysis and statistics), Prof. Carol Cleland (anomaly identification), Dr. Richard Cloete (data analysis and AI tools), Dr. Omer Eldadi (data management, AI, human psychology), Dr. Tim Gallaudet (oceanography), Prof. Robin Hanson (statistics and economics), Ross Howard (communication), Dr. Kevin Knuth (physics and instrumentation), Ben Lamm (oceanography and biology), Dr. Devesh Nandal (numerical analysis and astrophysics), Prof. Garry Nolan (molecular biology and materials science), Dr. Michael Shermer (the study of anomalies), Dr. Peter Skafish (anthropology), Prof. Matthew Szydagis (instrumentation and data collection), and Dr. Jennice Vilhauer (quantitative psychology). The list Loeb supplied to DefenseScoop one day later drops Vittert Capito, Hanson and Knuth — three of the four quantitative-methods seats — and is otherwise identical. Whether that is editorial compression or a roster in flux within twenty-four hours is unresolved, but it is a documented discrepancy between two dated statements by the same source.

Loeb is explicit about the design intent behind Shermer's inclusion: "Including at least one member with a skeptical perspective (or a designated 'devil's advocate') in every committee is highly important. The skeptic prevents blind spots, reduces cognitive biases, and actively protects groups from disastrous decision-making as a result of groupthink." Read against the stance of this board, a council that pre-installs its own debunker and pre-commits to unclassified-only inputs has been engineered for a specific class of output: methodological recommendations, sensor procurement advice, and the repeated observation that better data is needed. It cannot produce a finding about custody, because it will never see a custody record.

The council's first substantive engagement with government product illustrates the boundary. Loeb pointed to an AARO report dated 5 June 2026, signed by AARO Director Dr. Jon Kosloski and posted in the third PURSUE tranche as DOW-UAP-D077, "Unresolved Case Analysis Update — Western United States Event." Loeb's summary: during two days in October 2023, law enforcement officials observed anomalous phenomena including an orange "mother" orb launching smaller red orbs, and about 40 percent of the reported phenomena lack a reasonable explanation and remain unresolved. That is the council's raw material — a published, unresolved case file, offered to outside scientists after AARO has already declined to resolve it.

The personnel overlaps are where the network becomes legible. Gallaudet is the former Oceanographer of the Navy, former commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, and former Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere. He is also an advisor to Ryan Graves's Americans for Safe Aerospace, and it was through Graves's sworn July 2023 testimony that his account of the deleted Fleet Forces Command email entered the congressional record. The man whose story is the strongest public evidence that a special access program suppressed a safety-of-flight warning about the very encounters that produced the GO FAST video now sits on the government's own science council — advising on declassification, with unclassified data only.

Loeb's institutional history matters too. He served on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) in 2019-2020, chaired Harvard's Astronomy department 2011-2020, chaired the National Academies' Board on Physics and Astronomy 2018-2021, and has run the Galileo Project since roughly 2021, which now operates three observatories scanning for objects outside the performance envelope of human technology. He is, in short, exactly the kind of credentialed outsider whose participation converts a political disclosure exercise into something that reads as science — and whose access constraints guarantee it will remain an exercise. The sequencing underlines the point: three PURSUE tranches had already gone public before the council was constituted, so the scientific advisory body was assembled after the declassification pipeline was already running.

odni-memo-es-2026-00818.whatItIs: An Office of the Director of National Intelligence memorandum titled "Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver," bearing control number ES 2026-00818, dated 31 July 2026, from the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence to the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency and other IC element heads. It directs the Department of War and the Intelligence Community to build a process by which current and former employees and contractors may disclose UAP information to AARO or to designated representatives of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) Task Force notwithstanding existing non-disclosure agreements, agreements, oaths or commitments.
odni-memo-es-2026-00818.whyImplicated: The memo is an admission written in the form of a remedy. No government waives non-disclosure obligations for a subject about which nothing is being withheld. Its most consequential sentence is the one instructing the IC to make its workforce aware that any NDA prohibiting disclosure to the President, the PURSUE Task Force or other designees is no longer in force — an instruction that only makes sense if such instruments exist, and DLA Piper's government contracts practice notes that an NDA barring disclosure to the President "would be unusual if not unlawful" because the President is the ultimate classification authority. It was not published by ODNI. The administration authorised the House office of Rep. Eric Burlison, a founding member of the Congressional UAP Caucus, to distribute it — routing an IC-wide directive through the oversight bloc rather than dni.gov. And it is materially narrower than the statute it purports to implement: 50 U.S.C. § 3373b already authorises disclosure to AARO notwithstanding Executive Order 13526, the Atomic Energy Act, and Section 798 of the Espionage Act, while the memo reaches only contractual and oath-based restrictions.
odni-memo-es-2026-00818.narrative:
On 31 July 2026 the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence signed a memorandum, numbered ES 2026-00818, addressed to the Director of the CIA and the heads of the other Intelligence Community elements. Two days later Rep. Eric Burlison (MO-07) posted it on his House website, noting that "the administration authorized Congressman Burlison's office to publicly distribute the memorandum." That single procedural fact deserves more attention than the memo's contents. The executive branch chose, as the public release channel for a national-level intelligence directive, the congressional office of a member who had spent three years accusing the executive branch of hiding UAP records — and who ten days earlier, on 21 July 2026, had publicly invited anyone who believed the President's directive applied to them to contact his office for help navigating the process. Burlison's office was, in effect, standing up a parallel intake channel for whistleblowers while the official one was still being written.

What the memo does: it directs the Department of War and the IC to implement a process ensuring that current and former governmental employees and contractors holding alleged UAP information may disclose it to designated government representatives in AARO or the PURSUE Task Force notwithstanding contravening NDAs, agreements, oaths or commitments. It instructs every IC element, within thirty days of receipt, to coordinate with ODNI to establish a PURSUE designee and to "inform their workforce of the President's order." It states that NDAs prohibiting disclosure to the President, to PURSUE or to other designees are no longer in force. And it flags two further tranches of guidance to come — implementing guidance for the preliminary guidance itself, and a separate ODNI/DoW package for the broader PURSUE transparency project.

What the memo does not do is the more informative half. It does not authorise public disclosure of classified information. It does not authorise disclosure to Congress other than through AARO or existing channels — a striking limitation given that the standard ODNI classified information nondisclosure agreement, Standard Form 312, already contemplates disclosure to Congress in some form. It does not tell government contractors, as distinct from IC employees, how to make an authorised disclosure at all, even though the FY2023 NDAA's anti-retaliation protection expressly extends to any "contractor, subcontractor, grantee, subgrantee, or personal services contractor" of a covered department or agency. For an entity board built on the premise that the retrieval and reverse-engineering work sits inside cleared private industry, that omission is the operative fact: the memo waives the secrecy instruments of the government workforce while leaving the contractor workforce — the population most likely to hold the material — without a documented route.

The memo is also narrower than the law. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. No. 117-263, 136 Stat. 2959-62, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373b(b)(1)) authorises disclosure to AARO notwithstanding not merely NDAs but any regulation or order issued under Executive Order 13526, anything under the Atomic Energy Act, Section 798 of the Espionage Act, and any other "provision of law relating to the disclosure of information." ES 2026-00818 speaks only to "[NDAs], agreements, oaths, or commitments." As agency guidance it is not binding law, and DLA Piper's alert notes that it "does not, by itself, confer legal rights with respect to making authorized disclosures beyond those established by statute." A person weighing whether to come forward is therefore being handed a document that sounds like permission and is legally less protective than the statute already on the books — and told that the real guidance is still being drafted. That is a structure that produces delay.

The scale problem is visible in AARO's own reporting. Its Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report states that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, seven individuals contacted AARO with UAP-related claims that AARO judged warranted a request for a follow-on interview. Seven. The same report asserts that AARO is legally authorised to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs. Those two statements coexisting is the concealment argument in miniature: an office with unlimited statutory reach and a single-digit annual intake.

Context matters for dating. The PURSUE Task Force was launched by the Department of War on 1 May 2026 following President Trump's 19 February 2026 Truth Social directive; the first tranche of records went public on 8 May 2026, with further tranches on 22 May, 12 June, 10 July and 7 August 2026. ES 2026-00818 arrives at the end of that sequence, nearly three months into a rolling public release — the NDA waiver follows the file dumps rather than preceding them, which means the population best able to contextualise those files was still under contractual gag while the files were being published.

One further structural note. AARO sits inside the Department of War but reports to ODNI on operational and security matters under 50 U.S.C. § 3373(b)(3)(B)(ii). ES 2026-00818 was issued by ODNI, while the FY2023 NDAA assigns the establishment of the secure disclosure mechanism to the Secretary of War acting through the head of AARO in consultation with the DNI. The guidance therefore comes from the consulted party rather than the responsible one — a jurisdictional wrinkle that any contractor's counsel will find, and that gives every recipient a colourable argument that the instrument binding them has not yet been properly issued.

dird-collection.whatItIs: A set of 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents (DIRDs) produced between roughly 2008 and 2010 as deliverables of the Defense Intelligence Agency's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP), later known as the Advanced Aviation Threat Identification Program (AATIP), contracted to Robert Bigelow's Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS). The titles and authors were compiled by DIA at the request of the offices of Senators John McCain and Jack Reed and released to the Federation of American Scientists under FOIA on 16 January 2019; 37 of the 38 documents themselves were released by DIA under FOIA in 2022.
dird-collection.whyImplicated: The DIRD list is the closest thing in the public record to a published requirements document for a reverse-engineering effort. A conventional foreign-threat forecasting portfolio does not commission papers on traversable wormholes, stargates and negative energy, warp drive and the manipulation of extra dimensions, invisibility cloaking, antigravity for aerospace applications and metamaterials. That is a menu of observed capabilities in search of a physics, written by a tight network around Bigelow — Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis of EarthTech International, Kit Green, George Hathaway, Paul Czysz — and paid for out of a roughly $22 million defense intelligence line between 2008 and 2012. DIA's own framing in the cover letter to the Senate Armed Services Committee, that "the purpose of AATIP was to investigate foreign advanced aerospace weapons threats from the present out to the next 40 years," is itself the artifact of concealment: it recasts stargates as threat forecasting. The classification pattern reinforces it. Thirty-seven of the 38 carry only "For Official Use Only"; exactly one was produced in two versions, the second classified Secret with a foreign-national release restriction. A single deliverable set with a two-tier publication scheme is where the applied work hides.
dird-collection.narrative:
The DIRDs exist in the public record because two Senate offices asked a question. DIA compiled the list of every product produced under the AATIP contract at the request of the offices of Senator John McCain, then Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Senator Jack Reed, its ranking Democrat. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists' Project on Government Secrecy obtained the five-page document under FOIA on 16 January 2019, and Nick Pope obtained the same package the same month; George Knapp's I-Team at Las Vegas CBS affiliate KLAS had already published a near-complete list of titles and authors in July 2018. The cover letter's operative sentence reads: "Based on interest from your staff regarding the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)'s role in the Advanced Aviation Threat Identification Program (AATIP) please find attached a list of all products produced under the AATIP contract for DIA to publish."

The program's origin is documented but blurred by three names for one thing. It began in 2007 as the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications program (AAWSA/AAWSAP), was contracted to BAASS under a DIA solicitation, and came to be known publicly as AATIP after December 2017. DIA spent approximately $22 million between 2008 and 2012 and produced 38 reports. The technical papers commissioned by BAASS were converted into Defense Intelligence Reference Documents by DIA's James T. Lacatski — the individual who is also, by his own later account, the government official who conceived and championed the program. AATIP sat inside DIA's Defense Warning Office, a unit created in 2002 to monitor threats to U.S. interests in critical regions, which is the bureaucratic camouflage: an office whose remit is strategic surprise is exactly where you park a program about technologies nobody can explain.

The authorship concentration is the analytically load-bearing fact. Puthoff and Davis of EarthTech International in Austin, Texas were primary authors on six of the 38 between them, and Davis is a co-author on a seventh from independent consultant Richard Obousy. Because the DIA list records only the primary author, the true EarthTech footprint is unknowable from the document. Both men have prior ties to Bigelow's National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDSci). Puthoff went on to To The Stars Academy alongside Luis Elizondo, the DoD official who publicly identified himself as running AATIP — meaning the research network, the government program office and the 2017 disclosure vehicle share personnel across all three layers. Other named contributors are more conventional: Ulf Leonhardt of the University of St Andrews wrote "Invisibility Cloaking" and is a genuine authority on transformation optics; Lockheed Martin supplied three reports including one on fusion power and one titled "Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications"; Directed Technologies, Inc. of Virginia supplied the high energy laser weapon work. More than half of the 38 came from authors at academic institutions including UNLV, the University of Nevada-Reno, Ohio State and St Andrews. Marc Millis, the former NASA propulsion engineer who founded the Tau Zero Foundation, is among the authors — a direct thread between the DIRD collection and NASA's institutional periphery.

One procurement decision inside the set is indefensible on its face and therefore diagnostic. Robert Baker's company GravWave supplied a report on high-frequency gravitational waves. In 2008 the JASON advisory group had reviewed separate HFGW work Baker had done for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and concluded: "The proposed applications of the science of HFGW are fundamentally wrong" and "No foreign threat in HFGW is credible." DIA funded the topic anyway. Either the program office did not read the JASON review — implausible for a defense intelligence element — or topic selection was driven by something other than technical merit review. The second possibility is the interesting one: a portfolio assembled to cover a hypothesis space rather than to assess adversary capability.

The classification arithmetic completes the picture. Of the 38, the high energy laser weapon report was published in two versions, one of them classified Secret with instructions not to release it to foreign nationals. Every other product is marked For Official Use Only. When DIA released the collection under FOIA in 2022 it produced 37 of the 38; the missing document is the classified version of one of the others. DIA's release posture treats these as unclassified basic science surveys. That posture is exactly what you would adopt if the classified, applied, compartmented work were being conducted under a different program element with a different contract vehicle — which is the entire question the Senate offices were circling and never got answered.

The work did not stop with the reports. In 2025 Booz Allen Hamilton briefly advertised a TS/SCI "Counterintelligence and HUMINT Operations Officer, Senior" position requiring "Experience conducting comprehensive records reviews of U.S. government agencies, including archived and classified materials, for information about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) activities," the ability to "assess, plan, and execute site surveys of government facilities, archives, and locations linked to alleged historical UAP activity," and the ability to prepare input for "congressionally mandated reports such as the Historical Record Report." The posting was live for under a week. Whoever the client was, the same structure persists seventeen years after AAWSAP: the government's historical UAP records work is executed by cleared contractors, interviewing cleared contractors, about facilities that are themselves contractor-operated.

roosevelt-2014-2015.whatItIs: The sustained series of unidentified object encounters reported by U.S. Navy aircrews operating with Carrier Air Wing One and the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group off the U.S. East Coast from roughly the summer of 2014 through the Roosevelt's 2015 deployment work-ups. The episode produced the two ATFLIR infrared videos known publicly as GIMBAL and GOFAST, both of which the Navy has officially dated to 21 January 2015.
roosevelt-2014-2015.whyImplicated: This is the case in which a U.S. Navy fighter squadron documented an unidentified object corridor over an active training range for months, and the institutional response was to erase the paperwork rather than identify the objects. Ryan Graves testified under oath that after a near-collision at the W-72 entry point his squadron submitted a safety report and there was "no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings." The stronger allegation, entered into the same congressional record, comes from Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet: a 2015 SIPRNET email from the Fleet Forces operations commander to all one- and two-star admirals, titled "Urgent safety of flight issue" and attaching the GO FAST video, was removed from his and his deputy's classified systems the next day and never discussed — which he attributes to a classified special access program. That is a documented instance of a compartmented program reaching into a flag officer's classified mail to delete a safety-of-flight warning. Meanwhile the Navy's own on-record position is that it "considers the phenomena contained/depicted in those 3 videos as unidentified" and will provide "no details on individual reports."
roosevelt-2014-2015.narrative:
In 2014, Lieutenant Ryan Graves was flying F/A-18F Super Hornets with Strike Fighter Squadron 11 out of the Virginia Beach area. Following an upgrade to the squadron's radar, aircrews began detecting unknown objects in their operating airspace. The tracks were initially dismissed as software glitches until they were corroborated with infrared sensors, at which point, in Graves's words, the sightings "became an open secret among our aircrew" and "were so frequent that they became part of daily briefs."

The pivotal incident occurred in Warning Area W-72, a block of restricted airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach through which all traffic enters at a single GPS point and set altitude. Graves testified: "Just at the moment the two jets crossed the threshold, one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere — motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. The jets, only 100 feet apart, were forced to take evasive action. They terminated the mission immediately and returned to base. Our squadron submitted a safety report, but there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings." His description of the objects' performance is specific and falsifiable: they "could accelerate at speeds up to Mach 1, hold their position against hurricane-force winds, and outlast our fighter jets, operating continuously throughout the day," with "no visible means of lift, control surfaces or propulsion."

The cover-up allegation is Gallaudet's, and Graves put it in the record. While serving as an admiral at Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from his boss, the Operations Commander, addressed to all one- and two-star admiral subordinates. The subject line was "Urgent safety of flight issue." Attached was the GO FAST video from a Navy F/A-18. The email asked whether anyone knew the objects' origin, expressed concern about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach — the same airspace as Graves's encounters — and raised the possibility of shutting down the exercise for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was gone from both their systems. Despite routine in-person meetings of that same group, no one ever discussed it. Gallaudet presumes it was removed in connection with a classified special access program, and has stated publicly that after seeing the report he did not believe the objects represented any known human technology.

The Navy's public position is a study in minimal concession. In September 2019, Joseph Gradisher, official spokesperson for the Deputy Chief of Naval Operations for Information Warfare, told The Black Vault that the Navy's official identifiers for the videos do not match the TTSA names FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast — the Navy identifies them by the dates of the observations — and then supplied the dates: "[The] dates are 14 November 2004 for 'FLIR1' and 21 January 2015 for both 'Gimbal' and 'GoFast.'" That single sentence established for the first time that GIMBAL and GOFAST were recorded on the same day and may be two aspects of a single event. Gradisher went on: "The Navy has not publicly released characterizations or descriptions, nor released any hypothesis or conclusions, in regard to the objects contained in the referenced videos," while conceding that "The Navy considers the phenomena contained/depicted in those 3 videos as unidentified." Asked for the location, the answer was: "We will not be providing any details on individual reports." The Navy also confirmed the footage had never been cleared for public release when To The Stars Academy published it in December 2017 and March 2018.

Geography can be reconstructed anyway. Filmmaker Dave Beaty worked the deck logs of USS Normandy, the cruiser escorting the Roosevelt, and placed her on 21 January 2015 slightly more than 100 miles east, roughly equidistant between Jacksonville and Savannah — the JAX operating area. A cruiser stays with the carrier during operations, so the deck log fixes the approximate position of the encounter that the Navy declined to disclose.

What happened afterward is the concealment argument's second half. Graves testified that "all UAP videos since 2021 are classified Secret or above, which prevents the American people and even some Members of Congress from seeing UAP videos like the full GIMBAL video recorded by my squadron." The 2021 UAP Task Force preliminary assessment reported eleven near misses with UAP; Graves said he understood the number had grown. In April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia had experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. Graves founded Americans for Safe Aerospace, which by July 2023 had nearly 5,000 members and was working with more than 30 UAP witnesses, most of whom refuse to speak publicly for fear of professional consequences; he also chairs the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics' UAP Integration and Outreach Committee with roughly 80 volunteer PhDs and aerospace engineers. In his testimony he noted that among the accounts reaching ASA, "in several, sensor data was escalated for analysis and there were profound irregularities in how the data was handled" — the same signature as the deleted email, reported independently by other witnesses.

The loop closes in June 2026. Gallaudet — the flag officer whose deleted email is the strongest public evidence that a special access program suppressed a UAP safety warning about this exact airspace — was named to the government's new UAP Science Advisory Council, seated for oceanography, and restricted to unclassified data.

congressional-uap-caucus.whatItIs: A bipartisan House caucus launched by Rep. Tim Burchett (TN-02) in August 2023 and co-chaired with Rep. Jared Moskowitz (FL-23). Its founding cohort — the six members who signed its first act, a letter to the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community — were Burchett, Moskowitz, Anna Paulina Luna (FL-13), Nancy Mace (SC-01), Eric Burlison (MO-07) and Andy Ogles (TN-05).
congressional-uap-caucus.whyImplicated: The caucus is the only organised bloc in Congress whose founding premise is that UAP crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programs exist and have been concealed from the committees of jurisdiction. Its very first act, less than a month after David Grusch's July 2023 testimony, was to demand from the IC Inspector General the names of the people and the identities of the facilities involved in those programs. Its members subsequently drove the FY2024 NDAA's UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, the House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, the September 2025 whistleblower hearing, and the UAP Disclosure Act amendment adopted into the House FY2027 NDAA on 22 July 2026 with its eminent domain provision intact — a provision that would order the government to seize recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private entities. In August 2026 the relationship inverted: the executive branch authorised Burlison's House office to publish ODNI memo ES 2026-00818, making the oversight bloc the administration's distribution channel for its own IC directive.
congressional-uap-caucus.narrative:
On 26 July 2023 the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs held the first public UAP hearing to take testimony from military pilots and whistleblowers. David Grusch, a former intelligence officer, testified that he could not provide specific details regarding UAP crash retrieval or reverse engineering programs because those details are classified, but that he had provided them to the Office of the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community. Twenty-seven days later, on 22 August 2023, Tim Burchett announced that he had launched the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Caucus and had led five colleagues in a letter to IC IG Thomas A. Monheim asking for follow-up on Grusch's testimony — specifically, in the caucus's own words, "information from the Intelligence Community Inspector General regarding which people and facilities are involved with UAP crash retrieval programs and reverse engineering programs."

That question has never been publicly answered. The caucus's subsequent trajectory is best read as successive attempts to answer it by other means.

The statutory route came first. The FY2022 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-81, § 1683, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373) created AARO. The FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-263, § 1673, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373b) required a secure channel for authorised disclosure of UAP information relating to any government or contractor activity, notwithstanding NDAs, EO 13526, the Atomic Energy Act and Section 798 of the Espionage Act, and prohibited retaliation by agencies and by contractors, subcontractors, grantees and subgrantees. The FY2024 NDAA (Pub. L. 118-31, § 1841) then created the UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, defining covered records as any "Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence." That statutory phrase — "technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence" — is now U.S. public law, drafted by a Congress that would not have needed the category if nothing occupied it.

The FY2024 NDAA also contained the sharpest instrument the caucus era produced and the one that quietly died: sections 1687 and 7343 prohibited the use of FY2024 funds for any UAP-related secret program until the Secretary of Defense or the Director of National Intelligence fully disclosed the relevant details to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership. Those funding limitations were not renewed in subsequent enactments. Whoever allowed that lapse removed the only appropriations-side leverage Congress had ever applied to the question.

The Senate route was the UAP Disclosure Act, which passed the Senate in 2023 as Division G of S. 2226 by unanimous-consent incorporation of Amendment No. 935 and would have created an independent review board empowered to advise the President on declassification and release of UAP records. Its most aggressive clause orders the government to "exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good." It was stripped in conference. On 22 July 2026 the House adopted its own version — including the eminent domain provision — as an amendment to the FY2027 NDAA, recorded as Amendment No. 315 at H.R. Rep. 119-755, pages 419-442. The named sponsors are Burlison of Missouri, Crane of Arizona, Carson of Indiana, Luna of Florida, Moskowitz of Florida and Begich of Alaska: three of the six are caucus founders, and Crane, Carson and Begich extend the coalition. The House bloc carried into law-adjacent text the provision the Senate had been unable to protect.

The hearing route continued through the 119th Congress. Luna chairs the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, which held a hearing on 9 September 2025 titled "Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection," taking testimony from Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland. That task force also runs the JFK files declassification work — the same members, the same theory of the case, applied to two record sets.

The most revealing development is procedural rather than legislative. On 21 July 2026 Burlison publicly invited anyone covered by President Trump's UAP NDA directive to contact his office for help navigating the process — a member of Congress standing up an informal whistleblower intake because the official one did not yet exist. Eleven days later, ODNI signed memorandum ES 2026-00818. On 1 August 2026 Burlison released it, noting that "the administration authorized Congressman Burlison's office to publicly distribute the memorandum." A national-level Intelligence Community directive to the Director of the CIA and the heads of every IC element reached the public through the website of a backbench House member from southwest Missouri who had spent three years accusing that same community of concealment. Whether that is co-option or capitulation is the open question; either way it is the clearest measure of the caucus's leverage in 2026. It is also worth noting what the memo Burlison distributed does not give him: it forecloses disclosure to Congress outside AARO, meaning the caucus published an instrument that routes around itself.

One cataloguing caution for downstream analysis: the domain uapcaucus.com belongs to a private advocacy organisation, not to the congressional caucus, and the House caucus has never published an official membership roster.
