nasa.whatItIs: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the U.S. civil space agency. Since 2022 it has been a formal participant in the government's UAP effort through a commissioned Independent Study Team, whose final report it published on 14 September 2023 alongside the appointment of a Director of UAP Research. Since 2026 it has been a contributing agency to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, supplying Apollo- and Gemini-era imagery and astronaut accounts.
nasa.whyImplicated: NASA's role in the concealment architecture is not custody; it is certification. It is the civilian, scientifically credentialed institution that repeatedly states there is no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while holding, by its own design choices, no access to the compartmented material where the question would actually be settled — its Independent Study Team used unclassified data only, and its charter expressly excluded review of past incidents. The sharper fact is a custody claim. In 2025 NASA's Office of Communications told a records researcher that it has no UAP records qualifying for transfer to the National Archives under the FY2024 NDAA because "any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That single sentence removes NASA's UAP holdings from the statutory records regime by attributing ownership to the department least likely to release them. Ten months later NASA's own Administrator publicly identified NASA-provided Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 lunar-surface imagery as "some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure." Both statements cannot sit comfortably together: an agency with nothing to transfer, holding the most interesting data.
nasa.narrative:
NASA entered the modern UAP file formally in 2022, when it commissioned an outside Independent Study Team to advise on how the agency might contribute. The team's final report was published on 14 September 2023 under NASA release 23-106, chaired by David Spergel, president of the Simons Foundation, with sixteen members. Its overall recommendation was that NASA play a prominent role in the whole-of-government effort by using its open-source resources, technological expertise, data analysis techniques, federal and commercial partnerships, and Earth-observing assets to curate a better dataset for understanding future UAP. The report explicitly is not a review or assessment of previous UAP incidents. That boundary is the point: NASA's charter for the study excluded the historical record, which is where the legacy program question lives.

Spergel described the methodological constraint as a virtue: "Using unclassified data was essential for our team's fact-finding, open-communication collaboration, and for upholding scientific rigor to produce this report for NASA." The team reported that there are currently a limited number of high-quality observations of UAP, which make it impossible to draw firm scientific conclusions about their nature. The same architecture reappears three years later in the UAP Science Advisory Council chaired by Avi Loeb — unclassified data only, chartered to recommend how to get better data, structurally incapable of reaching a custody finding. NASA built the template.

With the report NASA named Mark McInerney its Director of UAP Research. McInerney had previously served as NASA's liaison to the Department of Defense "covering limited UAP activities for the agency" — meaning the agency's UAP function had already existed as a DoD liaison billet before it was given a public title. Administrator Bill Nelson framed the role in terms of instrumentation and analytics: the director would apply "artificial intelligence and machine learning to search the skies for anomalies," and "NASA will do this work transparently for the benefit of humanity." McInerney's career runs through NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, NOAA and the National Hurricane Center since 1996 — a NOAA lineage he shares with Tim Gallaudet, the retired admiral now on the 2026 UAP Science Advisory Council.

Then came the records question, and with it the most consequential NASA statement in the public record. The FY2024 NDAA, sections 1841-1842, required federal agencies to identify and transfer UAP records to a new collection at the National Archives, with digital transfers due by 30 September 2025. Record Group 615 was created to hold them. Over the course of 2025 the FAA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the National Security Agency, ODNI and the Office of the Secretary of Defense transferred records into the online catalog. NASA did not. Asked why, NASA's Office of Communications replied: "Per the requirements in Section 1841-1842 of the Fiscal Year 2024 National Defense Authorization Act for handling records related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), NASA does not have any records that meet the requirements to submit records to the National Archives. Any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That is not a denial of possession. It is an assertion of foreign ownership over material NASA holds — a jurisdictional argument that keeps agency UAP records outside a statutory public-release regime by routing their custody back into the Department of War.

The 2026 disclosure wave then produced the contradiction. On 27 May 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that the newly declassified files show "real unexplained phenomena" but no recovered craft: "What's being surfaced isn't crashed ships or alien bodies, but real unexplained phenomena," and "There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships." Note the construction — personal awareness, from a political appointee without read-in to the compartments where such material would be held. In the same interview Isaacman said agencies "really didn't take this quite as seriously in the past until President Trump put out the tweet, basically giving an order to government agencies and going out and saying, look, this time you better go through the files, you better start searching your databases and bring things up" — a sitting NASA Administrator stating that federal agencies did not conduct records searches for UAP material until a presidential post compelled them.

And on NASA's own contribution: "I would say that some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure was taken on the surface of the moon from Apollo 12 and 17. You can't be a moon landing denier and also believe that those photos captured unexplained phenomenon." Fox News reported that the PURSUE material includes astronaut and NASA-related accounts from the Apollo and Gemini eras describing strange lights and unidentified objects observed in space, alongside 2023 infrared footage of an F-16 engaging a diamond-shaped object over Lake Huron and reports from military operations in Iran, Syria, Iraq and Greece. Set against the 2025 Office of Communications statement — NASA has no qualifying records because DoD owns them — the position is that NASA's most interesting UAP data was released through the Department of War's website rather than deposited in the National Archives collection Congress created for exactly that purpose. One route is statutory, permanent and indexed; the other is a rolling, discretionary web publication controlled by the Secretary of War. NASA's material went down the second.

A loose thread worth pulling: on the war.gov PURSUE page, the Release 05 slideshow of 7 August 2026 carries an image described as "A photograph of an unidentified object in low-Earth orbit, taken from Space Shuttle Columbia in 1996," while the underlying file is named DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953.jpg. A 1996 Columbia photograph filed under a 1953 film analysis is either a metadata error or an indexing artifact, and either way it is a checkable discrepancy in the government's own release. The Columbia 1996 imagery in question is almost certainly from STS-75, the tethered satellite mission whose downlink footage has been argued over for thirty years — meaning the 2026 disclosure has quietly placed a long-contested NASA video into an official unresolved-case release.

nasa.denialPosture: NASA's denial operates in three layers, each with an escape hatch. The 2023 Independent Study Team found no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while working exclusively from unclassified data and explicitly excluding past incidents from its charter. The 2025 Office of Communications statement denies possession of transferable records by asserting DoD ownership rather than absence — a custody argument, not a factual one. And Administrator Isaacman's 2026 formulation, 'There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships,' limits the denial to the personal knowledge of an appointee with no read-in to the compartments in question. Each is technically defensible and none touches the underlying question.

aaro-historical-record-vol2.whatItIs: Volume II of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office's Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena — the sequel that Volume I (cleared for public release March 2024) explicitly promised. As of August 2026 no Volume II has been published, and AARO has also not issued its 2025 annual report. The entity is therefore a documented promise and a documented non-delivery rather than a document.
aaro-historical-record-vol2.whyImplicated: Volume I did not close its own investigation; it closed the public phase of it. AARO named a Department of Homeland Security prospective special access program (KONA BLUE), disclosed that an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program had its scope expanded in 2021 "to protect UAP reverse-engineering" and was then disestablished, and asserted that every alleged reverse-engineering program it examined either did not exist, was a misidentified authentic sensitive program, or resolved to "an unwarranted and disestablished program." Each of those three outcomes is an admission that named, real, compartmented activity exists behind the denial. Volume I then deferred everything unresolved to a Volume II that never came. The non-publication is the finding: the office that was granted, by its own account, "full, unrestricted access by all organizations" produced one volume of conclusions and no volume of the remaining work. A promised second volume that never appears converts a partial exculpation into a permanent one, because there is no dated deliverable against which anyone can measure what was left out.
aaro-historical-record-vol2.narrative:
The statutory hook is Section 6802 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117-263, enacted 23 December 2022), which rewrote the 2021 UAP framework, codified much of it at 50 U.S.C. 3373, and directed AARO to conduct a historical review of all U.S. Government UAP activity from 1 January 1945 forward, reporting no later than 540 days after enactment — roughly 15 June 2024. The statute reached the exact material a legacy program would generate: any program or activity protected by restricted access that had not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress, and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect information about UAP. Congress also directed the Comptroller General to monitor the review's progress and brief designated members.

AARO answered in March 2024 with a document titled Volume I. The title itself is the tell. A single report was due; AARO delivered a first installment, front-loaded the conclusions, and moved the unfinished work into a second installment. Volume I states that AARO "remains open to additional, verifiable information that may alter the conclusions rendered in Volume I and will note any changes to the findings in this report in Volume II," and elsewhere commits to publishing Volume II in accordance with the Section 6802 date while confining it to information acquired after Volume I's publication. That construction is load-bearing: the statutory deadline is satisfied by Volume I, and Volume II inherits no independent enforceable date of its own. Nothing in the record obliges anyone to produce it, and nobody has.

What Volume I left on the table is specific. AARO disclosed KONA BLUE, a UAP-related Prospective Special Access Program pitched to DHS and "supported by individuals who believed the USG was hiding off-world technology," which DHS never approved. It disclosed that in 2021, "without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering," and that the program "was disestablished due to its lack of merit." AARO does not name the IC program, does not name the original classification authority that expanded it, does not say who requested the expansion, and does not say what the program's pre-2021 scope was. It disclosed a materials analysis resolving a sample to magnesium "and bismuth with some other trace elements, such as lead," based on materials characterization. It attributed the reverse-engineering allegations to "circular reporting from a group of individuals" who "have been involved in various UAP-related endeavors since at least 2009," and tied many of them to "a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE" — an unmistakable reference to AAWSAP/BAASS and the Bigelow-Puthoff-Davis network, named by function rather than by name.

Every one of those threads is a live investigative lead, and each was left dangling. Who inside the IC expanded a Controlled Access Program to cover reverse-engineering in 2021, and on what asserted basis, is exactly the question Congress wrote Section 6802 to answer. AARO's own framing concedes that at least one compartment did, for some period, formally exist to protect UAP reverse-engineering. Whether it protected a real capability or a phantom, someone signed the security classification guide.

The delivery record since then is thin. DefenseScoop reported on 25 February 2026 that AARO had published neither its 2025 annual report nor a second volume of the historical review, while its caseload exceeded 2,000 cases. The FY2026 NDAA (P.L. 119-60, signed 18 December 2025) added three new AARO obligations — NORTHCOM/NORAD intercept briefings, an accounting of UAP-related security classification guides, and consolidation of duplicative reporting — but did not compel Volume II. Congress layered new demands on top of an unfulfilled old one without noticing, or without minding, that the old one had lapsed.

Read as an artifact of the concealment effort, Volume I is an unusually well-executed document. It is signed, dated, sourced, and comprehensive in tone; it names two compartmented programs, concedes access to a third, and asserts that AARO went everywhere and found nothing. Its most consequential feature is structural rather than substantive: by splitting the report, AARO produced an authoritative-sounding public verdict while retaining the ability never to publish the working papers behind it. Two and a half years on, that is precisely what has happened.

ndaa-fy2026.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, S. 2296 of the 119th Congress, signed into law on 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60. It carries three UAP-related provisions affecting AARO. It does not carry the UAP Disclosure Act, which was excluded for the third consecutive year.
ndaa-fy2026.whyImplicated: The FY2026 NDAA is the clearest available measurement of what Congress can and cannot pass on this subject. What survived is procedural: briefings, an inventory of classification guides, and reporting consolidation. What died — again — was every provision with teeth: records preservation, an independent Review Board, eminent domain over privately held recovered material, and mandatory declassification timelines. The pattern is now three cycles deep and consistent in kind: the disclosure architecture is introduced in the Senate with bipartisan leadership sponsorship, and it is removed in or around conference. One surviving provision is unusually revealing on its own terms — a directive that AARO account for the UAP-related security classification guides governing its own reports and investigations. A classification guide is a written instrument with an author, a date, and an original classification authority. Congress asking for an inventory of them is Congress conceding it does not know how many exist or who wrote them.
ndaa-fy2026.narrative:
S. 2296 passed the Senate on 10 October 2025 and became P.L. 119-60 on 18 December 2025. Three UAP provisions made the conferenced text, all of them modifications to the existing AARO framework rather than new authorities.

The first amends the AARO mandate to require the director to supply Congress with briefings and data on UAP intercepts conducted by U.S. Northern Command and the North American Aerospace Defense Command going back to 2004 — specifically the "number, location, and nature" of such intercepts, together with the procedures and protocols followed, "including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts." The 2004 start date is not arbitrary; it is the year of the USS Nimitz/USS Princeton encounters off southern California. That a statutory obligation was needed in 2025 to get NORTHCOM and NORAD intercept data in front of Congress establishes that, for twenty-one years, the commands responsible for defending North American airspace were not routinely providing it — not to Congress, not to AARO, and not to the scientific community. Christopher Mellon, the former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence who now chairs the Disclosure Foundation's board, has made precisely that point publicly: the United States operates some of the world's most advanced sensor systems, and what those systems capture about anomalous incursions has not been reaching oversight.

The second provision directs AARO to account for the UAP-related security classification guides that apply to information used in reports and investigations of the phenomena. This is the provision an analyst should mine. Security classification guides are the operative documents of concealment: they are what tells a program office which facts are classified at what level and for how long, and they are signed by an original classification authority. Disclosure Foundation officials, Mellon among them, have argued in public that DoD classification guides have been applied inconsistently with executive order standards and have been used to suppress material that was previously unclassified. An accounting of those guides would produce a list of instruments, custodians and dates. Whether AARO produces it, and whether the accounting is delivered classified, is the next measurable event.

The third provision consolidates duplicative reporting requirements and streamlines how federal agencies provide data and information to the Pentagon for AARO's investigations. Streamlining is double-edged: it reduces friction for AARO, and it reduces the number of separate documents Congress receives.

Against that, consider what was excluded. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) submitted the UAP Disclosure Act of 2025 as an amendment to the FY2026 NDAA in late August 2025. It would have prohibited the destruction or alteration of UAP records, created a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, established an independent UAP Records Review Board, and required public disclosure of UAP records within twenty-five years absent a presidential certification of a clear national security reason for delay. It failed in the House. On the Senate side the same architecture was offered as S.Amdt. 3111 to S. 2296. Neither survived. The UAP Disclosure Act has now been excluded from three consecutive defense authorization bills despite bipartisan Senate backing associated with Schumer, Rounds and Gillibrand, and Liberation Times has reported that sources attribute the FY2026 failure specifically to Senator Mitch McConnell.

The records-destruction prohibition is the provision whose repeated exclusion should be read hardest. It is cheap, non-controversial on its face, and imposes no disclosure burden — it merely freezes the evidentiary record in place. Its removal, three cycles running, from a bill that Congress has enacted for more than six decades without fail, is a fact about the removers. The precedent for why it matters is documentary and sixty years old: GAO found in 1995 that the administrative records and outgoing message traffic of Roswell Army Air Field for the relevant period were destroyed with no indication of by whom or under what authority (see gao-nsiad-95-187). A statutory bar on destruction is the one measure that would prevent the 1995 finding from recurring, and it is the measure that keeps not passing.

Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation — the rebranded UAP Disclosure Fund — characterized the three enacted provisions as "a meaningful, if incremental, step toward transparency and oversight," and noted that two of them mirror recommendations Mellon and his team had promoted for years. That is the accurate reading: the FY2026 NDAA moved the oversight perimeter a few feet and left the custody question untouched.

iaa-fy2024-sec-1102.whatItIs: The contractor turn-in provision of the Fiscal Year 2024 Intelligence Authorization Act: a Gillibrand amendment adopted unanimously by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 14 June 2023, which required any person currently or formerly under federal contract holding government-derived UAP material to notify AARO within 60 days and, within 180 days, to hand over "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" for assessment, analysis and inspection. It carried a safe harbor, a sweeping funding ban on unreported UAP special access programs, and a Sense of Congress. It was numbered Sec. 1104 in S. 2103 as reported on 22 June 2023, renumbered as the bill moved, and was enacted in drastically narrowed form as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 on 22 December 2023.
iaa-fy2024-sec-1102.whyImplicated: This is the single most important statutory hook on the board because it is the only text Congress has ever voted out of committee that presumes, on its face, that private contractors are holding non-earth-origin material derived from federal programs and that treats getting it back as an administrative problem with a deadline. A safe harbor is not written for a hypothetical. Congress does not draft immunity from criminal and civil action "for receiving" material unless someone plausibly received it. The definition of covered activities is equally load-bearing: it contemplates government or contractor personnel with "a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft," and it defines the reverse-engineering perimeter as work on "any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Seventeen senators on the Intelligence Committee voted this text out. Then it was cut in conference.
iaa-fy2024-sec-1102.narrative:
On 14 June 2023, nine days after The Debrief published David Grusch's allegations, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence adopted by voice vote a UAP amendment sponsored by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and cosponsored by Senators Mike Rounds (R-SD), John Cornyn (R-TX) and Marco Rubio (R-FL). The committee then approved the underlying Intelligence Authorization Act unanimously. The bill was filed and numbered on 22 June 2023 as S. 2103; the UAP text appeared as Section 1104, titled "Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena." Section 1102 of that same reported text was an unrelated provision on defense sensitive support; the board's identifier tracks a later renumbering as the IAA moved into the NDAA vehicle, and the substance — not the number — is what matters.

The operative mechanism had three parts.

First, a notification and turn-in mandate. The text reached "any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access." Such persons had 60 days from enactment to notify the AARO director, and 180 days to provide "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" in their possession and to make it available to the director for "assessment, analysis, and inspection." The AARO director then had 30 days to notify designated congressional committees and leaders of any notification, information or material received. That last clause is the accountability trigger: it would have created a dated congressional paper trail for each turn-in.

Second, a safe harbor: "No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving" the covered material or information, contingent on meeting the deadlines. Douglas Johnson, who first reported the text, read this as implying that a private entity holding non-human technology outside democratic oversight — and possibly profiting from it — would otherwise be in a legally tenuous position, and that the provision functioned as a time-limited amnesty to smooth an orderly return. Nothing in the provision created new criminal offenses, and nothing immunized threats, violence or perjury.

Third, a funding ban. No future federal funds, directly or indirectly, for any UAP-related special access program activity unless the program had been "formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified to the appropriate committees of Congress, congressional leadership, and the Director" of AARO. The designated recipients were the intelligence, armed services and appropriations committees of both chambers plus the Speaker, House minority leader, and Senate majority and minority leaders — 58 senators and 137 House members in total. The categories of covered activity were drafted in six expansive paragraphs and included recruiting, employing, training, equipping, operating and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a retrieval mission; managing and providing security for activities and information relating to UAP "from disclosure"; and reverse-engineering work reaching any aerospace craft using propulsion other than chemical propellants, solar power and electric ion thrust.

The Sense of Congress attached to the provision is the most candid language Congress has produced on the subject. It asserted that "due to the increasing potential for technology surprise from foreign adversaries and to ensure sufficient integration across the United States industrial base and avoid technology and security stovepipes... the Federal Government must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes." Read plainly: the government previously provided exotic technology antecedents to industry for R&D, secrecy has stovepiped that work, and the stovepiping is now a national security liability. Whether or not one accepts the premise, the drafters wrote it into a bill that a Senate committee approved unanimously.

The legislative arc from there is the concealment story in miniature. The Senate Armed Services Committee carried parallel but non-identical language at Section 1546 of S. 2226, without the safe harbor and without the Sense of Congress, and with the funding limitation confined to FY2024 DoD programs. On 20 July 2023 SSCI Chairman Mark Warner filed a revised version, SA 994, narrowing the IAA's funding limitation to FY2024 as well. The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence approved its own FY2024 IAA (H.R. 3932) on 13 July 2023 containing no UAP provisions at all, and the House Rules Committee blocked a floor vote on Rep. Mike Gallagher's parallel amendment to the House NDAA — reportedly because of objections from HPSCI leadership, whose chairman Michael Turner and ranking member Jim Himes had made dismissive public comments about secret alien technology on 6 June 2023. The Senate passed a combined NDAA-IAA on 27 July 2023. In conference, the turn-in mandate and safe harbor did not survive. What was enacted on 22 December 2023 as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 is a funding limitation only, conditioned on the Director of National Intelligence providing program details to the appropriate committees and leadership — which the Intelligence chairmen explained "provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area."

The deletion is the finding. A unanimous committee wrote a hand-back-the-material provision with an amnesty clause, and the amnesty and the hand-back both vanished behind closed doors.

earthtech-international.whatItIs: EarthTech International, Inc. is a private research company in Austin, Texas, incorporated in 1991 as the corporate vehicle for the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin, which Harold E. Puthoff founded in 1985. Its declared research program covers spacetime and gravitation theory, the quantum vacuum and zero-point energy, modifications to standard electrodynamics, interstellar flight science, and SETI, framed as inputs to innovative space propulsion and energy generation. Puthoff is president, CEO and board chairman; Eric W. Davis is chief science officer.
earthtech-international.whyImplicated: EarthTech is the intellectual clearinghouse where the legacy program's technical vocabulary was written down and then sold back to the government as reference literature. Under the Defense Intelligence Agency's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, EarthTech was subcontracted through Robert Bigelow's BAASS, and Puthoff and Davis commissioned the set of expert studies that DIA published as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on traversable wormholes, antigravity, metamaterials and invisibility cloaking. That output supplied the exact conceptual frame — non-chemical propulsion, spacetime metric engineering, exotic materials — that Congress later wrote into statute as the boundary of a covered reverse-engineering program. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I aims squarely at this network without naming it, attributing the reverse-engineering allegations to a group involved in UAP endeavors "since at least 2009" and tied to "a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE." AARO's own account therefore places these people at the center of both the DIA program and its DHS successor attempt, while insisting nothing was ever recovered.
earthtech-international.narrative:
Harold E. Puthoff earned his PhD at Stanford in 1967 as a theoretical and experimental physicist working on lasers, and spent the 1970s running the SRI International parapsychology program with Russell Targ under intelligence-community sponsorship — the lineage that became Project STARGATE. In 1985 he founded the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin; in 1991 it was incorporated under EarthTech International, Inc. Both remain co-located in Austin. Eric W. Davis, whose declared specializations include breakthrough propulsion physics, beamed energy propulsion, directed energy weapons, general relativity, quantum field theory, quantum gravity and what he calls SETI-xenoarchaeology, is chief science officer of both entities.

The institutional significance is not the physics. It is that EarthTech occupied, for four decades, a specific structural position: a small, privately held, security-cleared research house with no shareholders to answer to, no publication obligations, and a standing relationship with the parts of the defense and intelligence enterprise that buy speculative propulsion analysis. That is precisely the shape of entity a legacy program would need — small enough to compartment, technical enough to be credible, private enough to sit outside the FOIA perimeter.

The documented engagement is AAWSAP. In 2008 the Defense Intelligence Agency awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, reported at up to $22 million over five years, to assess advanced aerospace threats. Puthoff served as the program's chief scientist on the BAASS side, and EarthTech was subcontracted to produce the written product. Puthoff and Davis commissioned a series of thirty-eight expert studies, which DIA then issued as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. The subjects released into the public record include traversable wormholes and negative energy, antigravity, metamaterials for aerospace applications, and invisibility cloaking. Whatever one makes of the science, the procurement fact is unambiguous: a U.S. intelligence agency paid, through a contractor and a subcontractor, for a reference library on how one would build and analyze a craft that violates the propulsion assumptions of every acquisition program in the department. Fifteen years later Congress drafted the covered-activity definition for UAP reverse-engineering as any aerospace craft using "propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust" — the DIRD library's subject matter, rendered as statutory text.

Davis is also the pivot of the two most consequential unofficial documents in the modern record. In October 2002 he met with retired Vice Admiral Thomas Ray Wilson, former director of DIA; the handwritten notes of that conversation, describing a special access program under contractor control that had denied access to a senior flag officer, surfaced publicly in 2019 as the Wilson-Davis memo. In July 2020 the New York Times reported that Davis, then a contractor for Aerospace Corporation, had briefed a Defense Department agency in October 2019 and Senate Armed Services Committee staff about retrievals from "off-world vehicles not made on this earth." Both items are contested; neither is invented. Both were produced by the chief science officer of EarthTech International.

The AARO response is where this entity becomes central rather than peripheral. Volume I never names EarthTech, Puthoff, Davis or Bigelow. It does not need to. It states that the modern reverse-engineering claims stem "largely" from "a consistent group of individuals who have been involved in various UAP-related endeavors since at least 2009," and that many of them were "involved in or supportive of a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE." The cancelled DIA program is AAWSAP. AARO's rebuttal is therefore built on the same population that AARO concedes staffed a real, funded DIA program and then attempted, unsuccessfully, to stand up a DHS prospective special access program to continue it. AARO also reports resolving a claimed anomalous material sample to magnesium "and bismuth with some other trace elements, such as lead" by materials characterization — the layered magnesium-bismuth specimen that has circulated through this network for decades and been analyzed by parties associated with it.

The network extends forward. Davis appears on the team roster of the Disclosure Foundation, the organization chaired by former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Christopher Mellon, whose published recommendations two of the three FY2026 NDAA UAP provisions mirror. So the same technical population that wrote the DIA reference library, that AARO identifies as the source of the circular reporting, and that pitched KONA BLUE to DHS, is also inside the advocacy apparatus that now shapes what Congress writes into the defense authorization act. That is not a contradiction. It is what a closed technical community looks like when the subject matter has no other constituency.

rand-corporation.whatItIs: The RAND Corporation is a nonprofit research institution created by the U.S. Army Air Forces in 1946 as Project RAND, operating under contract to the Douglas Aircraft Company, and spun out as an independent California nonprofit in 1948 with initial capital from the Ford Foundation. It operates federally funded research and development centers for the Department of Defense, including Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute and the Army Research Division, and has published on unidentified aerial phenomena in both 1968 and 2023.
rand-corporation.whyImplicated: RAND is the original defense-contractor-adjacent think tank, born inside an airframe manufacturer and chartered to think about things the Air Force could not think about in uniform. It sat at the center of the 1946-1968 window in which any recovery and exploitation effort would have needed exactly RAND's product: threat framing, capability assessment, and analytic cover. Its 1968 internal draft "UFOs: What To Do?" states flatly that the phenomenon is "unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms" — a judgment produced inside the Air Force's own analytic arm during the same period the Condon Committee was preparing to declare the subject scientifically barren. RAND stamped that document for internal use only and reportedly refused to acknowledge its existence for thirty-two years. Fifty-five years later, RAND published an OSD-sponsored study whose central finding is that public UAP reports cluster around military operations areas — analytically useful, and also the most institutionally comfortable finding available, since it relocates the phenomenon inside U.S. military activity without ever addressing recovery or custody.
rand-corporation.narrative:
Project RAND was created in 1946 under contract between the Army Air Forces and the Douglas Aircraft Company, expressly to retain the civilian scientific talent that had won the war. Its first assignment, delivered on a three-week deadline, was the design of a world-circling spaceship; the resulting "Preliminary Design of an Experimental World-Circling Spaceship" was released in May 1946. The organization incorporated as a California nonprofit on 14 May 1948, and on 1 November 1948 the Project RAND contract was formally transferred from Douglas Aircraft to the RAND Corporation, with the Ford Foundation supplying the initial capital for the spin-off.

That founding sequence is the point. RAND was a defense contractor's internal analysis shop that became a national institution by changing its corporate wrapper without changing its customer. The July 1947 Roswell events fall squarely inside the Douglas-contract period; the FBI teletype GAO later recovered records that the recovered disc and balloon were "being sent to Wright Field... for examination" — Wright Field being Air Materiel Command, the same enterprise for which Project RAND was doing its earliest work on exotic aerospace concepts. GAO in 1995 could find no Air Materiel Command records from 1947-1950 mentioning the crash or any examination of debris.

RAND's documented engagement with the phenomenon comes in two widely separated bursts.

The first is DRU-1571, "UFOs: What To Do?", by George Kocher, 1968, forty-three pages. RAND's own abstract for the document is unusually direct: "Since World War II, however, there seems to have been a drastic increase in the number of sightings. We have enough data — both visual and photographic — on some of these sightings to know that the phenomenon is unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms." Kocher examines UFO brightness, size and maneuvers, discusses the frequency and location of sightings, and closes by proposing standardized reporting so that times and locations of appearances may be anticipated and objective data obtained. He recommended going beyond a national collection to worldwide data with intensive investigation of the most interesting reports. The document is dated 27 November 1968 and was stamped for RAND use only, with instructions not to quote or cite externally; researchers report that RAND did not acknowledge the paper's existence and authenticity until 2000. RAND now files it in a series it describes as unrestricted drafts that "were not usually formally edited or peer reviewed" — a retrospective classification that softens a document written by its own staff during the exact months the Air Force was preparing to shut down Project Blue Book on the strength of the Condon report.

The timing is the finding. In late 1968 the Air Force's analytic contractor produced an internal paper saying the phenomenon was real, extraordinary and inexplicable, and recommending a global standardized collection architecture. In January 1969 the Condon report was released and Blue Book was terminated. The Kocher draft was suppressed for a generation.

The second burst is 2023. RAND published "Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America," report number RR-A2475-1, by Marek N. Posard, Ashley Gromis and Mary Lee. The research was sponsored by the Office of the Secretary of Defense and conducted within the Acquisition and Technology Policy Program of the RAND National Security Research Division. The authors analyzed 101,151 public UAP reports across 12,783 U.S. Census Bureau locations. The headline result is that reports cluster near Military Operations Areas — designated blocks of airspace for military training and maneuvering, not necessarily near airbases. RAND completed the report in May 2023, sent it to the Department of Defense for review, and published it on 25 July 2023 — the day before the House Oversight Committee's UAP hearing at which David Grusch testified.

For an analyst, the 2023 study is a two-edged artifact. Its finding is genuinely useful: whatever is being reported, it is being reported disproportionately where the military flies. That is consistent with misidentification of military activity, and it is equally consistent with the phenomenon exhibiting interest in military activity — the correlation does not discriminate. What the study does not do, and was not scoped to do, is ask a single question about recovery, custody, materials, or program structure. An OSD-sponsored study, reviewed by the Department before release, published the day before the most consequential UAP hearing in fifty years, framing the entire subject as a geography-of-misidentification problem, is exactly the deliverable a concealment posture would commission. That does not make the analysis wrong. It makes the timing and the scoping evidence about the sponsor.

RAND's structural position remains what it was in 1946: an FFRDC operator with continuous classified access across Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute and the Army Research Division, publishing an unclassified fraction of its output and disclaiming that its publications "do not necessarily reflect the opinions of its research clients and sponsors." Between 1968 and 2023 the public record shows nothing. Fifty-five years of an FFRDC's silence on a subject its own analyst called unambiguously extraordinary is itself a data point.

gao-nsiad-95-187.whatItIs: GAO/NSIAD-95-187, B-262046, "Government Records: Results of a Search for Records Concerning the 1947 Crash Near Roswell, New Mexico" — a General Accounting Office letter report issued 28 July 1995 to Representative Steven H. Schiff of New Mexico. It documents a fifteen-month government-wide search for records on the Roswell events, conducted March 1994 to June 1995 across NARA, the National Personnel Records Center, the FBI, CIA, NSA, DoD, DOE, the National Security Council and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
gao-nsiad-95-187.whyImplicated: This is the single strongest tier-one document on the board, because it is a congressional audit agency reporting, in its own voice and under its own signature, that the primary records of the unit at the center of the founding incident were destroyed and that nobody can say who destroyed them or under what authority. GAO found the administrative records of Roswell Army Air Field for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing message traffic for October 1946 through December 1949 gone, with a disposition form that "does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed." It found that in 1947 Army regulations required air accident reports to be maintained permanently. It found no regulation governing the handling of the debris the FBI recorded as en route to Wright Field, and no Air Materiel Command record of that debris ever arriving or being examined. It found the records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) — the security unit — never retired to the records center at all. Every element of a documentary cover is present in a 1995 GAO letter report, and it has been sitting in the public record for thirty-one years.
gao-nsiad-95-187.narrative:
Representative Steven H. Schiff (R-NM) asked GAO for this work because, in GAO's own framing, he was "Concerned that the Department of Defense (DOD) may not have provided you with all available information on the crash." That sentence, in a GAO letter report, is a member of Congress on the record stating that he did not believe the Pentagon's answers about Roswell. GAO's mandate was narrow — determine the reporting requirements for air accidents like the Roswell crash, and identify any government records concerning it — and GAO answered both.

On requirements: "In 1947, Army regulations required that air accident reports be maintained permanently." GAO identified four air accidents reported by the Army Air Forces in New Mexico during July 1947, all involving military fighter or cargo aircraft, and all occurring after 8 July 1947 — the date the RAAF public information office announced the recovery of a flying disc. The Navy reported none. Air Force officials told GAO that under the record-keeping requirements then in effect, there was no requirement to prepare a report on the crash of a weather balloon. That is the pivot on which the official account rests: reclassify the object as a balloon and the permanent-retention requirement evaporates.

On records: GAO went to the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis and obtained documentation showing that RAAF administrative records covering finance and accounting, supplies, buildings and grounds and other general administrative matters from March 1945 through December 1949, and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949, were destroyed. GAO's finding on authority is stated twice, in two forms, and both are unambiguous. In Results in Brief: "The document disposition form does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed." In the body, attributed to the Center's Chief Archivist: "the document disposition form did not properly indicate the authority under which the disposal action was taken." The Chief Archivist added, from personal experience, "that many of the Air Force organizational records covering this time period were destroyed without entering a citation for the governing disposition authority," and GAO's own review of records control forms for other destroyed material — including outgoing RAAF messages for 1950 — supported that view.

That last detail deserves an analyst's attention, because it cuts both ways and should be handled honestly. GAO and the Chief Archivist offer a systemic explanation: sloppy Air Force records management across the whole period, not targeted destruction. But a systemic practice of destroying records without citing disposition authority is precisely the environment in which a targeted destruction becomes undetectable. GAO does not, and cannot, distinguish between the two. The report establishes that the records are gone and that the paper trail for their destruction is defective. It does not establish intent, and it does not need to for the record to be load-bearing.

GAO further reports that document disposition forms show the Walker Air Force Base records officer transferred unit histories to the Army's Kansas City depository in 1953 — the 509th Bomb Group and RAAF for February to October 1947, the 1st Air Transport Unit for July 1946 to June 1947, the 427th Army Air Force Base Unit for January 1946 to February 1947. But: "We could not locate any documentation indicating that records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) were ever retired to the National Personnel Records Center or its predecessor depositories." The military police company at the field where the recovery was announced has no retirement record at all.

GAO's entire yield from 1947 was two documents. The July 1947 combined 509th Bomb Group/RAAF history states the public information office "was kept quite busy . . . answering inquiries on the 'flying disc,' which was reported to be in [the] possession of the 509th Bomb Group. The object turned out to be a radar tracking balloon," certified by the commanding officer's signature as a complete and accurate account. And an FBI teletype of 8 July 1947 from the Dallas field office reporting that an Eighth Air Force headquarters official had telephonically advised of the recovery near Roswell of "a hexagonal-shaped disc suspended from a large balloon by cable," that the recovered object resembled a high-altitude weather balloon with a radar reflector, and that "the disc and balloon were being sent to Wright Field . . . for examination." The FBI conducted no further investigation.

GAO then followed the debris. "Because the FBI message reported that debris from the Roswell crash was being transported to Wright Field for examination, we attempted to determine whether military regulations existed for handling such debris. We were unable to locate any applicable regulation." And: GAO reviewed Air Materiel Command records from 1947 to 1950 and "found no records mentioning the Roswell crash or the examination by Air Materiel Command personnel of any debris recovered from the crash." Material was documented as shipped to Wright Field. There is no governing regulation for how such material is handled, and no record at Wright Field that it arrived, was examined, or was disposed of. That is a custody gap of exactly the shape a legacy program requires at its origin.

The agency responses complete the picture. The NSC, OSTP and Department of Energy said they held nothing. DoD said the July 1994 Air Force Roswell report was the extent of its records, and offered no comments on GAO's draft. The CIA's Executive Director told GAO in March 1995 that "it was unclear whether the CIA had ever conducted a search for records specifically relating to Roswell" — forty-eight years after the event — and then ordered one; on 30 May 1995 he reported no documents. GAO's methodology section concedes the environment: "Our search of government records was complicated by the fact that some records we wanted to review were missing and there was not always an explanation."

The FBI teletype of 8 July 1947 from the Dallas office recorded that an Eighth Air Force headquarters official telephonically reported the recovery near Roswell of "a hexagonal-shaped disc suspended from a large balloon by cable," and that "the disc and balloon were being sent to Wright Field . . . for examination"; the FBI conducted no further investigation.
GAO states: "we attempted to determine whether military regulations existed for handling such debris. We were unable to locate any applicable regulation."

GAO reviewed Air Materiel Command (Wright Field) records from 1947 to 1950 and "found no records mentioning the Roswell crash or the examination by Air Materiel Command personnel of any debris recovered from the crash."

In March 1995 the CIA's Executive Director told GAO that it was "unclear whether the CIA had ever conducted a search for records specifically relating to Roswell," then directed a comprehensive search; on 30 May 1995 he reported that a search of the term "Roswell, New Mexico" across all CIA databases produced no documents related to the crash.

DoD told GAO that the July 1994 Report of Air Force Research Regarding the Roswell Incident represented the extent of DoD records or information on the crash, and DoD "offered no comments or suggested changes to the report" when given GAO's draft. GAO's methodology section states: "Our search of government records was complicated by the fact that some records we wanted to review were missing and there was not always an explanation."
claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-95-187, 28 July 1995, Agency Comments and Scope and Methodology, https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-95-187.pdf

gao-nsiad-95-187.denialPosture: The Department of Defense's position, recorded in GAO's report, is that the July 1994 Report of Air Force Research Regarding the Roswell Incident — attributing the debris to a Project MOGUL balloon train — constitutes the entirety of the department's records and information on the subject, and DoD declined to comment on GAO's draft at all. The Air Force's 1994 report did not dispute that something happened near Roswell. The National Security Council, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the Department of Energy each certified they held nothing. The CIA's denial is the most revealing: forty-eight years after the event its own Executive Director could not confirm that any Roswell-specific records search had ever been performed.
connections: Rep. Steven H. Schiff (R-NM) — requester; the member who told GAO in writing that he doubted DoD had given him everything. Schiff died in 1998.
Richard Davis, GAO Director, National Security Analysis, and Gary K. Weeter, Assistant Director — the named GAO officials responsible for the report.

Roswell Army Air Field / Walker Air Force Base, 509th Bomb Group, 1st Air Transport Unit, 427th AAF Base Unit, 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) — the units whose records were destroyed, transferred, or never retired.

Wright Field / Air Materiel Command (later Wright-Patterson AFB) — documented destination of the recovered disc and balloon per the FBI teletype, with no corresponding receipt or examination record 1947-1950. The historical anchor for every subsequent claim about Wright-Patterson as a custody node.
Eighth Air Force headquarters, Fort Worth — source of the telephonic report to the FBI and of the same-day balloon retraction.
FBI Dallas and Cincinnati field offices — originator and addressee of the only surviving contemporaneous federal record outside the unit history.
Project MOGUL — the classified balloon program invoked in the Air Force's 1994 report as the explanation.
National Personnel Records Center, St. Louis — custodian of the disposition forms that fail to cite destruction authority.
ndaa-fy2026 — the records-destruction prohibition repeatedly stripped from the UAP Disclosure Act is the direct legislative remedy for the condition GAO documented in 1995.
aaro-historical-record-vol2 — AARO's Section 6802 historical review covers 1 January 1945 forward, i.e., the same period whose primary records GAO found destroyed.
openQuestions: Who destroyed the RAAF administrative records and outgoing messages, when, and under what claimed authority — the disposition form does not say and GAO could not determine it.
Whether the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) records were destroyed, misfiled, retained elsewhere, or never created; GAO found no retirement documentation of any kind.
Whether any Air Materiel Command receiving record for the shipment described in the 8 July 1947 FBI teletype exists in any classification or in any non-AMC file series.
Why no military regulation governed the handling of recovered airborne debris in 1947, and whether a classified handling instruction existed outside the regulation system.
What the Eighth Air Force official's name was, and whether the FBI's Dallas office recorded it; GAO does not name him.
Whether GAO's underlying working papers for NSIAD-95-187 survive and are obtainable, including the classified documents GAO says it examined.
Whether Rep. Schiff received any classified supplement or briefing beyond the public letter report.

Whether the systemic non-citation of disposition authority the Chief Archivist described is documented anywhere as an Air Force records-management finding, or whether it exists only as his personal characterization to GAO.

classified-annex.whatItIs: The classified addenda -- variously called annexes, schedules, appendices and supplements -- attached to the three annual national security statutes (Intelligence Authorization Act, National Defense Authorization Act, Department of Defense Appropriations Act) and to the committee reports that accompany them. Together with the classified notification channels of 10 U.S.C. 119, they are the legal machinery by which Congress appropriates money and issues binding direction to programs whose existence is not public. No classified annex has ever been published, in any form, redacted or otherwise.
classified-annex.whyImplicated: If a legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering effort has been funded for eight decades, the money moved through this channel, because there is no other channel that both carries the force of law and never surfaces. The annex system is not a leak in oversight; it is a purpose-built container that gives classified direction "the legal status of public law" while keeping it in a safe in a secure room that few members ever enter. Layered on top of it, 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense strip specified content out of the Special Access Program reports entirely and deliver it to only eight people -- the chair and ranking member of four committees. And the statutory backbone that forced annual SAP disclosure at all, 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b), was terminated effective December 31, 2021 by a sunset provision Congress itself enacted. David Grusch's sworn answer to the funding question -- "misappropriation of funds and self-fund" -- describes an abuse that this architecture is uniquely well designed to conceal, because the annex records what Congress intended to buy but the public record cannot be reconciled against it.
classified-annex.narrative:
The classified annex is the least glamorous object on this board and the most important. It is the mechanism that makes the rest of the question -- who, where, under what authority, paid for how -- answerable in principle and unanswerable in practice.

Dakota Rudesill, a former Senate Budget Committee staffer and Intelligence Community official, published the only serious empirical study of the practice. His finding: over thirty-six years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda the force of law, and produced at least 271 committee reports carrying classified addenda since 1977. About half of the 124 were incorporation provisions -- statutory text whose entire operative content is a pointer to a document nobody outside the compartment will ever see. The standard formulation appears at Section 102 of virtually every Intelligence Authorization Act: the amounts authorized and the personnel ceilings "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations." Accompanying report language routinely states that the Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law." The Intelligence Community's own top lawyer has agreed with that characterization.

Rudesill is careful, and his carefulness is itself evidence. He notes that nothing is publicly known about the length of any annex -- "An individual addendum could be two pages long, or 20, or 200" -- and that each committee invites members to read the addenda in a secure room, but "few do." He also records that the practice accelerated: Congress wrote more force-of-law annex provisions in 2011-2015 than in the first eight Congresses of the practice combined, from 1977 to 1992. This is the shape of a mechanism that grew because it worked.

The second layer is statutory rather than procedural. 10 U.S.C. 119 is the SAP oversight statute. Subsection (a) requires an annual March 1 report to the four defense committees listing every DoD special access program, with descriptions, milestones, actual costs by year, and estimated costs across a six-year horizon. Subsection (b) requires a February 1 notice and justification for every new SAP. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. On its face this is real oversight.

Subsection (e) is the escape hatch. The Secretary of Defense "may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report" upon determining that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security." When he does, the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- eight members of Congress, no staff specified. DoD Instruction 5205.11 builds the corresponding category into doctrine: a waived SAP is "An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

The third layer is the one almost nobody has noticed. The U.S. Code note appended to Section 119 reads: "For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328." The annual SAP report and the new-SAP notice -- the two provisions that produced a written, dated, comprehensive inventory of the black budget's program structure -- were swept away by a generic reporting-burden sunset enacted in the FY2017 NDAA. The subsection (e) waiver survives; the reports it was designed to abridge do not.

Against that background, Congress in December 2022 legislated a tell. 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) -- Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA -- requires the Secretary of Defense, within 72 hours, to report to the defense and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership any authorized UAP disclosure that relates to "a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees." Congress does not write 72-hour tripwires for hypotheticals. The statute is a signed, dated legislative acknowledgment that unreported access programs are a live possibility.

AARO has since conceded, in its own words, one instance: "In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering." AARO adds that the program never recovered or reverse-engineered anything and was disestablished for lack of merit. Set aside the exculpatory half. The admitted half is that a controlled access program was expanded without sufficient justification, in 2021, specifically to protect UAP reverse-engineering -- which is precisely the nesting behavior Grusch described when he said agencies were "nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities."

Finally, the annex logic reappears in the disclosure statute itself. Under Section 1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, a UAP record may be withheld from the National Archives collection when "the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence" of enumerated harms. The original classification authority is the agency holding the record. The annex principle -- the withholder judges the withholding -- survived into the law written to end it.

claims.text: Over 36 years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda legal force; about half were full or partial incorporation provisions. Counting committee reports, Congress has produced at least 271 reports with classified addenda since 1977.

Virtually all annual Intelligence Authorization Acts stipulate at Section 102 that funding authorizations and personnel levels "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations," and accompanying report language states that the classified Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law."

Congress has used annex-incorporation provisions to earmark specific sums invisibly, including $4.8 billion for "classified programs, described...in the classified annex" at the height of the Iraq war.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive any requirement under subsections (a), (b) or (c) that certain information be included in a special access program report if the Secretary determines that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security," on a case-by-case basis.

When the Secretary of Defense exercises the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver, the withheld information and the waiver justification go only "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- eight members of Congress.

The annual DoD special access program report (10 U.S.C. 119(a)) and the annual new-SAP notice and justification (10 U.S.C. 119(b)) were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328, the FY2017 NDAA.

classified-annex.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue here, because the mechanism is openly documented in statute and doctrine and defended on its merits: the Intelligence Community's chief lawyer has publicly agreed that classified schedules carry the legal status of public law. The concealment is not denied; it is legislated.
connections: 10 U.S.C. 119 is the statutory hinge shared with dodi-5205-11: DoDI 5205.11 implements Section 119, and its 'waived SAP' category exists only because Section 119(e) authorizes the waiver.

Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA (50 U.S.C. 3373b), drafted with input from David Grusch while he was in government, created the 72-hour tripwire for programs not reported to the defense or intelligence committees -- the direct legislative counterpart to grusch-misappropriation-allegation.
Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA (nara-rg615) transplant the annex logic into the disclosure regime by leaving postponement to the original classification authority.

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer's UAP Disclosure Amendment, quoted at the July 26, 2023 hearing for the phrase 'technologies of unknown origins, non-human intelligence, and unexplainable phenomena,' was the legislative attempt to break the annex model.
AARO's admitted 2021 expansion of an IC Controlled Access Program 'to protect UAP reverse-engineering' links this mechanism directly to manhattan-project-2 and to the AAWSAP/AATIP-KONA BLUE lineage.

Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, arranged the first congressional staff briefings on retrievals (Senate Armed Services staff, October 21, 2019; Senate Intelligence staff two days later), working the same committee channel the annexes flow through.
openQuestions: Whether any classified annex from 1944 to the present contains a line item, program identifier or nickname corresponding to a materials-retrieval or exploitation effort -- no annex has ever been released.
Which specific SAPs, if any, have had 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waivers applied to them, and how many waivers have been issued in total; the statute requires no public accounting.
Whether the December 31, 2021 termination of the 119(a) and 119(b) reporting requirements was substantively debated or was a drafting artifact of a generic reporting-burden sunset.
Whether the DoD or IC has ever complied with the 72-hour notification requirement of 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B), and how many such notifications have been made.
The identity of the IC Controlled Access Program whose scope AARO says was expanded in 2021 'without sufficient justification' to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and who authorized the expansion.

grusch-misappropriation-allegation.whatItIs: A protected whistleblower complaint and subsequent sworn congressional testimony by David Charles Grusch, a former Air Force officer, National Reconnaissance Office senior intelligence officer and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency co-lead for UAP analysis, alleging that a multi-decade U.S. crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering program exists, is concealed from Congress, and is sustained by the misappropriation of appropriated funds. The complaint was filed with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022 by Charles McCullough III, the first Senate-confirmed ICIG.
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.whyImplicated: This is the only allegation of its kind that has passed through a statutory inspector-general channel, been assessed as credible and urgent, been transmitted to the Director of National Intelligence and both intelligence committees, and then been repeated under oath in open session with the penalty of perjury attached. The specific charge is not that craft exist; it is a financial-crimes charge -- that money appropriated by Congress for other purposes was diverted, and that the diversion was the concealment method. That reframes the question from metaphysics to auditability. Grusch's counsel is the man who built the ICIG whistleblower system, which means the filing was engineered to survive procedurally. And Grusch's own hand appears in the FY2023 NDAA UAP language, so the statutory tripwires now on the books were drafted by the complainant against the mechanism he was complaining about.
grusch-misappropriation-allegation.narrative:
Precision matters more here than anywhere else on the board, because the allegation has been repeatedly restated in forms Grusch never used.

What he filed: in May 2022, Charles McCullough III -- senior partner at Compass Rose Legal Group, and the original Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, confirmed by the Senate in 2011 under DNI James Clapper -- filed on Grusch's behalf a "Disclosure of Urgent Concern(s); Complaint of Reprisal" with the ICIG. The complaint concerned information Grusch had gathered beginning in 2019 while working with the UAP Task Force. All testimony Grusch provided for the classified complaint was given under oath, and the document closed with his signed affirmation: "I do solemnly affirm under the penalties of perjury that the contents of the foregoing paper are true and correct to the best of my knowledge."

What the unclassified version of the complaint says: that Grusch has direct knowledge that UAP-related classified information has been withheld and concealed from Congress by "elements" of the intelligence community "to purposely and intentionally thwart legitimate Congressional oversight of the UAP Program." Note the construction -- withheld from Congress, intentionally, to defeat oversight. That is an allegation about a crime against the legislature, not about biology.

What the ICIG did: found the complaint "credible and urgent" in July 2022. This is a procedural determination under the urgent-concern statute -- it means the complaint met the threshold for transmission, not that its substance was adjudicated true. Per Grusch, a summary went immediately to DNI Avril Haines, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. A whistleblower reprisal investigation was opened. Several current members of the alleged recovery program spoke to the Inspector General's office and, per reporting, corroborated information Grusch had provided.

What he said under oath on July 26, 2023, before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs. The core sentence: "I was informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program to which I was denied access to those additional read-ons when I requested it." Two things are asserted and one is not. Asserted: that he was officially informed such a program exists, and that he formally requested and was denied read-on. Not asserted: that he saw craft, materials or bodies himself. Every subsequent claim of first-hand observation attributed to him is a media artifact.

On funding, Representative Jared Moskowitz asked directly. Grusch: "I will give you generalities. I can get very specific in a closed session. But misappropriation of funds and self-fund." Two mechanisms, not one. Misappropriation -- money appropriated for a stated purpose spent on another. Self-fund -- the effort generating its own revenue, presumably through the commercial exploitation of derived technology, which would place private contractors inside the financial architecture rather than merely adjacent to it.

On sourcing, asked whether he had met people with direct knowledge of non-human origin craft, he answered: "Yes. I personally interviewed those individuals." On timeline, asked when contact first occurred: "I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's." On the campaign against public knowledge, in response to Representative Anna Paulina Luna, he referred to "a multi-decade, you know, campaign to disenfranchise public interest."

His pre-hearing DOPSR-cleared statements go further on the contracting angle: "Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia." He also characterized the effort as a "publicly unknown Cold War for recovered and exploited physical material -- a competition with near-peer adversaries over the years to identify UAP crashes/landings and retrieve the material for exploitation/reverse engineering to garner asymmetric national defense advantages."

The corroboration that matters is Karl E. Nell's, because Nell put his name to it while identifying himself by his official role. Nell, the Army's liaison to the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, said: "His assertion concerning the existence of a terrestrial arms race occurring sub-rosa over the past eighty years focused on reverse engineering technologies of unknown origin is fundamentally correct, as is the indisputable realization that at least some of these technologies of unknown origin derive from non-human intelligence." Nell also called Grusch "beyond reproach."

The institutional counter-position arrived in 2024. AARO's historical review concluded: "AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology," and attributed the narrative "in large part" to "circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case." AARO further asserts that "all the authentic programs have been properly notified and reported to Congress through the congressional defense and/or intelligence committees." That last sentence is a testable claim, and it is testable only against the classified annex.

As of 2026 the legal obstacle Grusch cited has formally been removed. On July 31, 2026, Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas issued memorandum ES 2026-00818 directing that prior nondisclosure agreements, oaths and commitments are waived for current and former employees and contractors speaking to AARO or to the PURSUE Task Force. The corroboration Grusch said existed in closed session is now, on paper, free to speak.

All testimony Grusch provided for the classified complaint was given under oath, and the complaint closed with his signature attached to the statement "I do solemnly affirm under the penalties of perjury that the contents of the foregoing paper are true and correct to the best of my knowledge."

claims.text: Asked by Rep. Jared Moskowitz how such a program is funded, Grusch testified: "I will give you generalities. I can get very specific in a closed session. But misappropriation of funds and self-fund."

Asked whether he had met people with direct knowledge of non-human origin craft, Grusch testified: "Yes. I personally interviewed those individuals." He did not testify to first-hand observation of craft or materials.

Asked when U.S. contact with non-human intelligence first occurred, Grusch testified: "I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's."

In statements cleared for open publication by the DoD Office of Prepublication and Security Review on April 4 and 6, 2023, Grusch alleged "illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia."

Grusch served as the National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAP Task Force from 2019 to 2021 and as the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency's co-lead for UAP analysis and task force representative from late 2021 to July 2022, as a GS-15 cleared at TS/SCI; he left government on April 7, 2023.

Grusch helped draft the UAP language in the FY2023 National Defense Authorization Act, spearheaded by Senators Kirsten Gillibrand and Marco Rubio and signed into law in December 2022 -- the provisions now codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373b.

Retired Army Colonel Karl E. Nell, the Army's liaison to the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, stated on the record: "His assertion concerning the existence of a terrestrial arms race occurring sub-rosa over the past eighty years focused on reverse engineering technologies of unknown origin is fundamentally correct, as is the indisputable realization that at least some of these technologies of unknown origin derive from non-human intelligence."

50 U.S.C. 3373b(b)(1)(A) provides that an authorized disclosure "shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure," and 3373b(b)(2)(A) prohibits reprisal including revocation or suspension of security clearances.
