grusch-misappropriation-allegation.denialPosture: Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough stated that the Department had not discovered "any verifiable information to substantiate claims that any programs regarding the possession or reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial materials have existed in the past or exist currently," and separately that it had "no information that any individual has been harmed or killed as a result of providing information." AARO's 2024 historical review states it "found no empirical evidence" for reverse-engineering claims and attributes them to "circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case." Both are dated, attributable statements from institutions Grusch named as concealing; neither addresses the misappropriation-of-funds charge on its own terms.
connections: Charles McCullough III designed and ran the ICIG whistleblower channel he later used on Grusch's behalf -- the complainant's counsel is the architect of the mechanism.
Karl E. Nell corroborated Grusch on the record and appears again in manhattan-project-2 as the proponent of a state-scale reverse-engineering effort.

Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, said he had received detailed information from well-placed officials about the alleged program including 'the history, governing documents and the location where a craft was allegedly abandoned and recovered.'

Jonathan Grey of the National Air and Space Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson AFB went on the record in the same June 5, 2023 report asserting the existence of 'complex historical programs involving the coordinated retrieval and study of exotic materials, dating back to the early 20th century.'
The funding mechanism Grusch alleges is the one described in classified-annex; the program-structure mechanism is the one described in dodi-5205-11.
AARO's KONA BLUE disclosure is the Department's competing origin story for the same allegation set, tracing it to AAWSAP/AATIP, DIA and Bigelow Aerospace rather than to a legacy program.

rendlesham-1980.whatItIs: A series of encounters in and around Rendlesham Forest, Suffolk, England, in late December 1980, between the twin USAF bases RAF Bentwaters and RAF Woodbridge, in which USAF security police and, on a later night, the deputy base commander reported an unexplained illuminated object described as metallic and triangular, together with ground depressions and elevated radiation readings. The primary document is a one-page unclassified memorandum from Lt Col Charles I. Halt to the UK Ministry of Defence dated 13 January 1981 and headed "Unexplained Lights."
rendlesham-1980.whyImplicated: Rendlesham is the cleanest specimen on the board of an official, contemporaneous, signed U.S. military document describing a landed object of unknown origin at a nuclear-capable forward base -- and of the institutional machinery that made it go away. The memo was never classified, which is itself the tell: a document that is not secret cannot be leaked, and a document that is not investigated cannot generate a record. The USAF then threw away its own copy and had to obtain another from the British MoD when a FOIA requester asked for it in 1983. On the British side, a defence minister's briefing paper concluded in writing that "no additional action was required," reasoning from Halt's two-week reporting delay and "relatively low-key manner" rather than from the physical evidence the memo describes. Rendlesham is therefore the paper trail of a non-investigation: everything that would have been generated by taking it seriously is absent, and the absence is documented.
rendlesham-1980.narrative:
The Halt memo is short enough to quote nearly in full, and its brevity is part of the case.

Paragraph 1: "Early in the morning of 27 Dec 80 (approximately 0300L) two USAF security police patrolmen saw unusual lights outside the back gate at RAF Woodbridge. Thinking an aircraft might have crashed or been forced down, they called for permission to go outside the gate to investigate. The on-duty flight chief responded and allowed three patrolmen to proceed on foot. The individuals reported seeing a strange glowing object in the forest. The object was described as being metallic in appearance and triangular in shape, approximately two to three meters across the base and approximately two meters high. It illuminated the entire forest with a white light. The object itself had a pulsing red light on top and a bank(s) of blue lights underneath. The object was hovering or on legs. As the patrolmen approached the object, it maneuvered through the trees and disappeared. At this time the animals on a nearby farm went into a frenzy. The object was briefly sighted approximately an hour later near the back gate."

Paragraph 2: "The next day, three depressions 1.5 inches deep and 7 inches in diameter were found where the object had been sighted on the ground. The following night (29 Dec 80) the area was checked for radiation. Beta/gamma readings of 0.1 milliroentgens were recorded with peak readings in the three depressions and near the center of the triangle formed by the depressions. A nearby tree had moderate (0.05-0.07) readings on the side of the tree toward the depressions."

Paragraph 3 describes the third night: a "red sun-like light" that "appeared to throw off glowing particles and then broke into five separate white objects," then three star-like objects at about ten degrees elevation, two north and one south, moving "in sharp, angular movements" and displaying red, green and blue lights, the southern object "visible for two or three hours" and beaming "down a stream of light from time to time." Halt closes: "Numerous individuals, including the undersigned, witnessed the activities in paragraphs 2 and 3." Signed, Charles I. Halt, Lt Col, USAF, Deputy Base Commander.

This is a deputy base commander of a major forward USAF installation putting his name to a report of a landed object, physical ground traces, radiological readings taken with an instrument, and multiple military witnesses including himself. The memo was written on official USAF letterhead and was not classified in any way. It went to the British MoD. It was released under the U.S. Freedom of Information Act in June 1983 to Robert Todd of Citizens Against UFO Secrecy -- and the covering letter to Todd explains that the USAF had discarded its own copy and had to obtain another from the British MoD to satisfy the request. A U.S. Air Force base commander's report of a landed unknown craft was, by the institution's own account, not worth keeping.

The British disposition is documented with equal precision. In October 1985 the defence minister Lord David Trefgarne held a private, off-the-record meeting with Lord Peter Hill-Norton, the former Chief of the Defence Staff, who had been pressing the MoD on the case. The briefing paper prepared for Trefgarne survives as pages 115-116 of file DEFE 24/1925 at The National Archives, released in May 2008. Trefgarne's recorded view: "Our own view also was that no additional action was required. We believe that the fact that Col. Halt did not report these occurrences to MoD for almost two weeks after the event, together with the relatively low-key manner in which he handled the matter, are indicative of the degree of importance in defence terms which should be attached to the incident." The reasoning is worth isolating: the MoD assessed the significance of a reported landing not from the reported facts but from the reporter's delay and demeanour. Trefgarne wrote "Oh, dear" at the top of Hill-Norton's letter of 26 July 1985, which survives at pages 208-210 of the same file and in duplicate at pages 259-261 and 280-282 of DEFE 31/174.

Simon Weeden, the MoD desk officer who received the Halt memo, later described the disposition to journalist David Clarke: "once we had been through all the basic checks and found there was nothing seen on radar, no obvious explanation, no obvious threat to air defence, we decided no further action was needed." No witness was interviewed. No further official report was made or action taken by the U.S. or U.K. authorities beyond the memo.

In June 2010 Halt wrote and signed a two-page notarised affidavit committing his then-current memory to paper. It goes materially beyond the memo. It says one of the objects moved overhead and sent a laser-like beam down to their feet; that the same object then moved back toward Bentwaters and sent beams of light down into the Weapons Storage Area; and that several airmen present reported seeing the beams. Neither the beam-to-their-feet event nor the Weapons Storage Area beams appear in the 1981 memo or on Halt's contemporaneous field tape.

The denials attached to the affidavit are themselves catalogued artifacts. Airman Tim Egercic, on duty at the Bentwaters Weapons Storage Area, has specifically denied that any beams came down into the WSA. Halt's superior officer Col Ted Conrad, who says he was watching from outside his quarters at Woodbridge and saw nothing resembling Halt's descriptions, said of him: "He should be ashamed and embarrassed by his allegation that his country and England both conspired to deceive their citizens over this issue. He knows better." Conrad's statement is a dated, attributable denial by a named commanding officer -- which makes it evidence about the chain of command's posture, whatever it establishes about the lights.

rendlesham-1980.denialPosture: The British position, set out in the Trefgarne briefing paper of October 1985 (DEFE 24/1925 pp. 115-116) and defended for decades as the MoD's 'no defence significance' line, is that no additional action was required and that the incident's importance should be inferred from Halt's reporting delay and low-key handling. The U.S. position is expressed by omission: the Air Force generated no further report, took no further action, and did not retain its own copy of the memo. Col Ted Conrad's on-the-record repudiation of Halt supplies a named commanding officer's denial dated decades after the event.
connections: Rendlesham is the archetype for the 'documented event, undocumented follow-through' pattern that Grusch describes at programme scale in grusch-misappropriation-allegation.

The Halt memo and the DEFE 24 files are exactly the class of record that Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA sweep into nara-rg615 -- records already publicly disclosed in unredacted form, which section 1842(a)(2)(B) forbids from being re-withheld or reclassified.

Lord Peter Hill-Norton, former Chief of the Defence Staff and Chairman of the NATO Military Committee, is the highest-ranking serving-officer-turned-critic in the case file and pressed the MoD again in 2001 correspondence released under FOI in 2007.

Robert Todd and Citizens Against UFO Secrecy obtained the memo through the U.S. FOIA in June 1983, establishing the FOIA route as the operative disclosure channel four decades before the UAP Records Collection Act.
Charles Halt has remained a public claimant into the disclosure era, making his 2010 affidavit a bridge between the 1980 record and the 2023-2026 congressional cycle.
The Weapons Storage Area at RAF Bentwaters, named in Halt's affidavit, ties the case to the recurring pattern of reported UAP activity over weapons-storage and nuclear infrastructure.

manhattan-project-2.whatItIs: An alleged secrecy and industrial architecture -- not an established one -- in which a legacy U.S. materials-retrieval and reverse-engineering effort is said to have been run since the 1940s on the organisational model of the Manhattan Project: extreme compartmentalisation, industrial-scale contractor execution, and funding and reporting arrangements that keep the effort outside normal congressional visibility. The label is used descriptively by named proponents, chiefly retired Army Colonel Karl E. Nell, who has publicly called for an open 'Manhattan project' to reverse engineer recovered UAP precisely because he asserts a closed one already exists.
manhattan-project-2.whyImplicated: This is the organising hypothesis that makes the rest of the board cohere, and it must be tiered honestly: the architecture's existence is a Tier 3 allegation carried by named, credentialed proponents, not a documented fact. What raises it above rumour is the specificity and the seniority of who says it. Nell was the Army's liaison officer to the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022 and later Modernization Advisor to the Vice Chief of Staff of the Army; he asserted on the record that an eighty-year sub-rosa arms race focused on reverse engineering technologies of unknown origin is 'fundamentally correct,' and he presented a dated campaign plan with an October 1, 2030 disclosure target and the explicit objective of restoring 'proper Federal government oversight over all UAP legacy (and ongoing) program efforts.' A serving-adjacent officer does not build a slide deck to restore oversight over programs he believes are imaginary. The Department's own rebuttal, meanwhile, concedes the shape of the thing while denying its content: AARO acknowledges a prospective DHS special access program built to protect the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics,' and a 2021 IC controlled access program expanded without sufficient justification to protect UAP reverse-engineering.
manhattan-project-2.narrative:
The name is an analogy, and the analogy is doing analytical work, so it is worth stating precisely what is being claimed and what is not.

What is not claimed: that a document exists bearing the title 'Manhattan Project II.' No such document has been produced. The phrase circulates in independent investigative work and podcasting, and its use there does not constitute evidence.

What is claimed, by named individuals with attributable positions: that the United States has run, since roughly the 1940s, a compartmented effort to recover and exploit materials of non-human origin, structured to be invisible to ordinary oversight, and that the Manhattan Project is the correct organisational template for understanding it. The template matters because the Manhattan Project is the canonical American precedent for a state-scale industrial programme conducted in total secrecy -- AARO's own historical review notes that in 1942 'the USG started the Manhattan Project. This program operated in secrecy and led to the establishment of several "secret cities" across the United States to support the development of the nuclear bomb.' That is the model: not a hidden filing cabinet but a hidden industrial base.

Karl E. Nell is the central named proponent. At the first symposium of the Sol Foundation, held at Stanford in November 2023, Nell called for a 'campaign plan' to force greater transparency and a 'Manhattan project' to reverse engineer recovered UAP. His presented slides set a disclosure target of October 1, 2030, acknowledged schedule risk, and listed the intended outcomes: 'Proper Oversight Restored,' 'Catastrophic Disclosure Avoid[ed],' and 'Scientific Understanding Advanced.' The operative line is his advocacy for 'restoration of proper Federal government oversight over all UAP legacy (and ongoing) program efforts.' The word 'restoration' presupposes that oversight was lost. The words 'legacy (and ongoing)' presuppose a continuous programme lineage.

Nell's credentials are not in dispute. He was the Army's liaison for the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, working alongside Grusch. Lieutenant General Laura A. Potter, Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence, Headquarters, Department of the Army, described him in a 2022 performance evaluation as 'an officer with the strongest possible moral compass.' His most recent listed position was Modernization Advisor to the Vice Chief of Staff of the Army.

The second proponent is Hal Puthoff, the former CIA-affiliated physicist, who told the same Stanford symposium that in 2004 a CIA think tank, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the Pentagon broadly agreed that information about UFOs should not be declassified, deeming the societal risks too great. This is a reported claim about an unproduced 2004 decision, and it is tiered accordingly -- but note its structural role: it supplies a mechanism and a date for the maintenance of secrecy in the modern era rather than its origin.

The third is Grusch, who framed the same object financially and temporally: a 'publicly unknown Cold War for recovered and exploited physical material,' an 'eighty-year arms race' whose continuation in secrecy 'further inhibits the world populace to be prepared for an unexpected, non-human intelligence contact scenario.' The fourth is Jonathan Grey of the National Air and Space Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, who said on the record that 'the existence of complex historical programs involving the coordinated retrieval and study of exotic materials, dating back to the early 20th century, should no longer remain a secret.' The fifth is Christopher Mellon, who said officials had shared with him 'insights into the history, governing documents and the location where a craft was allegedly abandoned and recovered' -- governing documents being the phrase an analyst should mark.

The Department's counter-narrative is the KONA BLUE file, and it deserves close reading because it concedes more than it intends. AARO reports that multiple interviewees identified KONA BLUE as 'a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sensitive compartment established to protect the retrieval and exploitation of "non-human biologics."' AARO's correction is that KONA BLUE was a Prospective Special Access Program proposed to DHS leadership, never approved, never funded, never in receipt of material. But AARO also states that in 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology did establish KONA BLUE as a PSAP, citing claims that relevant information and material existed and required that level of protection, and citing congressional interest and possible homeland security impacts; and that six months later the Deputy Secretary of DHS disapproved it as a SAP and directed immediate termination over the adequacy of justification and the sufficiency of information including personnel and budget requirements. So: a Cabinet department stood up a protective compartment on the represented existence of retrieved non-human material, and a Deputy Secretary killed it. That is an architecture attempting to form and being caught mid-formation.

AARO traces the proposal's lineage to AAWSAP/AATIP, managed by DIA from 2009 to 2012, funded through congressional earmarks, with Bigelow Aerospace of Nevada as prime contractor. And AARO separately concedes: 'In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering.'

AARO's overall verdict is flat: 'AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology,' the narrative being 'in large part, the result of circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case,' and 'all the authentic programs have been properly notified and reported to Congress.' AARO also reports that executives, scientists and chief technology officers of the named companies met the Director of AARO and 'denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' Those denials are artifacts with dates and signatories, and they are the most specific corporate denials on the record.

nara-rg615.whatItIs: Record Group 615, the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the U.S. National Archives, created by Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act (Public Law 118-31, div. A, title XVIII, subtitle C, December 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 699). It is the statutory destination for record copies of all Government, Government-provided or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.
nara-rg615.whyImplicated: RG 615 is the first time Congress has created a records collection whose statutory scope explicitly includes 'technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.' A legislature does not write a records-collection statute around a category it believes to be empty; the statutory text is itself a congressional finding that such records are believed to exist and to be held by federal agencies. But the enforcement architecture was hollowed. The Senate-origin design contemplated an independent review board to push postponed records toward disclosure; the enacted subtitle contains none. Postponement is decided by 'the original classification authority' -- the agency holding the record -- and postponed records physically remain with the originating body until NARA stands up a security programme. So the collection that was supposed to break the compartment is, for the withheld portion, still inside the compartment. What has actually arrived at RG 615 by 2026 is the readily releasable material from FAA, NRC, ODNI, OSD, NSA, State and FBI.
nara-rg615.narrative:
Read the statute rather than the coverage.

Section 1841(a)(1)(A) required the Archivist to commence establishing the collection within 60 days of enactment. Section 1841(a)(1)(C) defines its contents with unusual reach: 'record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).' Three features of that sentence are load-bearing. First, 'Government-funded' reaches contractor holdings. Second, 'or equivalent subjects by any other name' is an anti-euphemism clause -- a direct legislative anticipation that the material will be filed under cover terminology. Third, the sole carve-out is for temporarily non-attributed objects, i.e. drones and balloons, which is Congress saying the collection is not about the prosaic.

Section 1841(a)(1)(D) requires the Archivist to 'prepare and publish a subject guidebook and index to the Collection.' Section 1841(b) requires that transmitted records be available for inspection and copying at the National Archives within 30 days of transmission and digitally within not more than 180 days thereafter. Section 1841(e) assigns continuing oversight jurisdiction to Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services and Intelligence, and to House Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services and Intelligence.

Section 1842 governs the agencies. Subsection (c)(1) gave each head of a Government office 300 days from December 22, 2023 to review, identify and organise every UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission. Subsection (a)(2)(A) is absolute: 'No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way.' Subsection (a)(2)(B) forbids withholding, redacting, postponing or reclassifying any UAP record already made available or disclosed to the public before enactment -- a retroactive lock on the existing public record, including documents like the Halt memo. Subsection (a)(2)(C) extends the same protection to records created by persons or entities outside the federal government.

Subsection (c)(2)(G) sets priorities, and the priority order is revealing. Agencies must give precedence first to records not already public; second to 'all records that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence'; third to records already in FOIA litigation; fourth to earliest-provenance records. Congress wrote a triage rule that puts the most explicitly non-human material at the front of the queue.

Then the gate. Section 1843(a) permits postponement 'if the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' that the threat to military defence, intelligence operations or foreign relations 'is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure' and that disclosure would reveal a currently protected agent, a currently used source or method, or 'any other matter currently relating to the military defense, intelligence operations, or conduct of foreign relations of the United States, the disclosure of which would demonstrably and substantially impair the national security.' Additional grounds cover the Privacy Act, unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, and confidentiality understandings with cooperating individuals.

'Clear and convincing evidence' is a demanding standard on paper. The problem is who applies it. The original classification authority is an official of the agency that owns the record and, on the allegations at issue, may be the same institutional actor accused of the concealment. There is no independent adjudicator in the enacted text. This is the JFK Records Act model with the Assassination Records Review Board removed.

Section 1842(g) supplies the only ongoing pressure. Postponed records must be reviewed periodically by the originating agency and the Archivist. Every continued postponement 'shall require an unclassified written description of the reason for such continued postponement relevant to these specific records,' provided to the Archivist and published in the Federal Register. And section 1842(g)(2)(D) sets the backstop: each record must be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation, unless the President personally certifies that continued postponement is necessitated by an identifiable harm of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest. On a 25-year rule, anything created before 2001 is already past due absent a presidential certification.

Section 1841(d)(2) and section 1842(f) together create the physical bottleneck. NARA's National Security Program Office, with the Information Security Oversight Office, must establish a programme to secure the postponed and classified portion of the collection -- and until that programme exists, postponed records are 'held for reasons of security and preservation by the originating body.' The withheld material does not move.

What has actually landed is documented on NARA's RG 615 page, last reviewed May 22, 2026: series from the Federal Aviation Administration (National Archives Identifier 493468575), the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (488808322), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (493468579), the Office of the Secretary of Defense (493468580), the National Security Agency (580103959), the Department of State (608806625), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (580705010). NARA issued AC Memo 04.2025 to agencies on the transfer of publicly releasable UAP records, and describes transfers as arriving on a rolling basis.

By 2026 a parallel executive channel has opened alongside the statutory one. Following a presidential order to disclose collected UAP records, the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters -- the PURSUE Task Force -- released a fourth tranche of records on July 10, 2026, published at war.gov/ufo, and ODNI issued memorandum ES 2026-00818 on July 31, 2026 waiving nondisclosure agreements for anyone speaking to PURSUE or AARO. The analytically important question is whether PURSUE releases are being routed into RG 615 as section 1842(e) requires, or are accumulating in a separate executive-branch publication stream outside the Archivist's custody and outside the Federal Register accountability of section 1842(g)(2)(B).

nara-rg615.denialPosture: No agency has publicly asserted that it holds no UAP records; the posture is instead procedural. Agencies transfer 'publicly releasable' material under AC Memo 04.2025 while postponement determinations remain with each originating agency's own original classification authority under section 1843(a), and postponed records stay physically in agency custody under section 1842(f) pending a NARA security programme. The result is that the withholding is never articulated as a denial -- it is expressed as a classification determination made by the withholder.
connections: RG 615 is the disclosure end-state of the same statutory sequence that begins with 50 U.S.C. 3373b (FY2023 NDAA sec. 1673), which Grusch helped draft.
Section 1843's 'original classification authority' gate imports the self-adjudication principle described in classified-annex.
Records like the Halt memo and the DEFE 24 files bearing on rendlesham-1980 fall under section 1842(a)(2)(B)'s bar on re-withholding already-public UAP records.

AARO is named in sections 1842(c)(2)(E), (F) and (3) as an office that other agencies must make records available to -- giving the office accused of being non-neutral a statutory role in the records pipeline.
The KONA BLUE and AAWSAP/AATIP documents released by DoD and DHS in partnership are precisely the class of record section 1842 was written to capture.
The 2026 PURSUE Task Force and ODNI memorandum ES 2026-00818 (Aaron Lukas, July 31, 2026) run alongside RG 615 and raise the question of dual custody.
Presidential libraries and archival depositories under 44 U.S.C. 2112 are given expedited-review priority by section 1842(c)(3), reaching back into the 1944-1970 period this board covers.
openQuestions: Whether the subject guidebook and index required by section 1841(a)(1)(D) has been prepared or published.

How many records have been postponed under section 1843, by which agencies, and whether any unclassified written descriptions of continued postponement have been published in the Federal Register as section 1842(g)(2)(B) requires.
Whether NARA's National Security Program Office has stood up the security programme required by section 1841(d)(2) -- until it does, no postponed record can leave agency custody.
Whether any President has issued a certification under section 1842(g)(2)(D) to continue postponing records older than 25 years, and how many records are past that deadline without one.

Whether any agency has certified completion of the section 1842(c)(1) 300-day review, and whether the Department of Energy, CIA, DIA, NRO, NGA and the military departments have transferred anything into RG 615.
Whether contractor-held records are being captured under the 'Government-funded' clause of section 1841(a)(1)(C), and whether any contractor has been served a records demand.
Whether PURSUE tranche releases at war.gov are also being transmitted to the Archivist for inclusion in RG 615, or are a parallel channel outside the statutory accountability structure.

dodi-5205-11.whatItIs: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs (SAPs),' signed by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and effective February 6, 2013, cancelling the classified DoDI 0-5205.11 of July 1, 1997. It is the unclassified, publicly releasable rulebook for how the Department creates, nests, staffs, reports, waives reporting on, and disestablishes special access programs, and it implements the congressional oversight statute at 10 U.S.C. 119.
dodi-5205-11.whyImplicated: This is the machine's operating manual, published in the open, and it describes every capability a concealed legacy programme would need. It defines the unacknowledged SAP, whose very existence is not acknowledged to anyone not cleared for it. It defines the waived SAP, for which the Secretary of Defense has set aside the reporting Congress imposed. It builds a four-level nesting hierarchy -- umbrella, compartment, sub-compartment, project -- and expressly contemplates unacknowledged waived sub-elements added underneath a non-waived umbrella, which is a documented mechanism for hiding a black effort inside a program Congress has already been told about. It authorises 'carve-out' proposals to relieve the Defense Security Service of industrial security oversight over contractor performance. And it conditions access not merely on need-to-know and clearance but on a determination that the individual 'will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' -- the discretionary gate through which David Grusch's read-on request was denied.
dodi-5205-11.narrative:
The most useful thing about DoDI 5205.11 is that it is unclassified and approved for public release with unlimited releasability. The Department published its own concealment architecture and nobody read it.

Start with the vocabulary, because the Glossary is where the load is carried. An 'unacknowledged SAP' is 'A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A 'waived SAP' is 'A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting ... following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' A 'waiver' more generally is 'A decision that provides an approved exception to or deviation from a SAP security standard.' Two of the three definitions describe subtraction from the oversight baseline.

The waiver traces to statute. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) lets the Secretary of Defense waive any requirement that certain information be included in a SAP report where inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' case by case; 119(e)(2) routes the withheld content and the justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Eight members. No staff named. That is the entire congressional footprint of a waived SAP.

The governance layer is three committees stacked above the Deputy Secretary: the SAP Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG), and the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), which 'advise and assist the SecDef and DepSecDef in the management, administration, and oversight of DoD SAPs.' The SRG 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and provides recommendations to the SAPOC 'concerning continued waived status.' There is, in other words, an internal annual re-authorisation cycle for programmes Congress cannot see -- run entirely by the Department.

Establishment is the part that looks like oversight. The SAPOC reviews the package and submits it to the Deputy Secretary of Defense for decision. 'If approved, the DepSecDef will submit formal notification letters to Congress that the SAP has been established.' And: 'The SAP may not be initiated until the congressional defense committees are notified of the program and a period of 30 days has elapsed after such notification is received.' That mirrors 10 U.S.C. 119(f). The Instruction also fixes the annual reporting calendar: SAP Listing on February 1, SAP Annual Report on March 1, forwarded to the congressional defense committees by the DoD SAPCO. Those dates correspond to 10 U.S.C. 119(b) and 119(a) respectively -- and both of those statutory reporting requirements were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The Instruction's reporting calendar survives on paper; the statutory obligation behind it does not.

Now the nesting. Enclosure 5 sets out the SAP hierarchy: a SAP is called an 'umbrella' if it has subordinate elements, which in descending order are compartments, sub-compartments, and projects. A person accessed to a compartment is also accessed to all subordinate elements 'unless an exception is specifically approved by the CA SAPCO.' Subordinate elements 'will be presumed to be within the same type unless' otherwise designated -- and the Instruction expressly addresses the case of unacknowledged waived sub-elements added under a non-waived umbrella, requiring specific SAPCO action. Read that as an analyst: the doctrine anticipates, and provides procedure for, burying a waived unacknowledged effort inside a programme that has been properly reported. This is the documented, unclassified mechanism corresponding exactly to Grusch's charge of 'nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities.'

Enclosure 6 lists what a Cognizant Authority SAPCO must notify the Director, DoD SAPCO of in writing. The list is a taxonomy of the moves available: change of category (acquisition, intelligence, operations and support); 'Change of type (acknowledged, unacknowledged)'; 'Alteration of scope'; IJSTO apportionment or deapportionment; disestablishment by termination, cancellation or transition; 'Support of non-DoD SAPs'; 'Addition, deletion, or changes of compartments, sub-compartments, and projects'; 'Proposals to relieve DSS of NISP security oversight responsibilities (carve-out) when required'; 'Change of nickname, codeword, PID'; and 'Foreign involvement.' Every one of these is an entry point for an analyst. Nickname and codeword changes break longitudinal tracking. Carve-outs remove the Defense Security Service from contractor facilities. 'Support of non-DoD SAPs' is the doctrinal bridge to DHS, DOE and IC compartments -- the category KONA BLUE would have occupied had it been approved.

Access is the human gate. 'Access to a SAP will be strictly limited to the minimum number of personnel necessary for execution of the program. Granting access to a SAP will be based solely upon a determination that the individual has a valid NTK, has the requisite security clearance, meets approved personnel prerequisites, and will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program.' The final clause is a subjective judgment reserved to the programme, and it is the clause that answers Grusch's testimony that he was 'denied access to those additional read-ons when I requested it.' Under this Instruction, a person conducting oversight can be lawfully excluded on the programme's own determination that he would not materially contribute to it.

Two further details reward attention. Sample SAP approval documentation reproduced in the Instruction's appendices uses a notional unacknowledged operations-and-support SAP designated GTE, with planned unacknowledged sub-compartments including LEAF BARK (LBK) and a recommendation line reading 'That you approve GTE as an unacknowledged SAP and authorize' -- a published template showing exactly how a sub-compartment request is written and approved. And the Instruction carries its own expiry: it 'Must be reissued, cancelled, or certified current within 5 years of its publication ... If not it will expire effective February 6, 2023.'

claims.text: The Instruction defines an unacknowledged SAP as 'A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.'

The Instruction defines a waived SAP as 'A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting ... following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.'

The SAP governance structure consists of the SAP Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG) and the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), which 'advise and assist the SecDef and DepSecDef in the management, administration, and oversight of DoD SAPs'; the SRG 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and recommends to the SAPOC on continued waived status.

The Instruction provides that a SAP 'may not be initiated until the congressional defense committees are notified of the program and a period of 30 days has elapsed after such notification is received,' and that upon approval 'the DepSecDef will submit formal notification letters to Congress that the SAP has been established.'

The statutory obligations behind that calendar -- the annual SAP report at 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and the new-SAP notice and justification at 10 U.S.C. 119(b) -- were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328.

Access is conditioned on a determination that the individual 'has a valid NTK, has the requisite security clearance, meets approved personnel prerequisites, and will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' -- a discretionary gate held by the programme.

Whenever a SAP's classification is to change or SAP information is to be declassified and made public, the DoD SAPCO must give the congressional defense committees a report describing the proposed changes, the reasons, and notice of any planned public announcement.

claims.text: A SAP disestablishment plan must address contracting, fiscal, audit, property disposition, classified material disposition, training, public affairs, legal, logistics and technical actions, and the CA SAPCO must provide the termination plan to the DoD SAPCO for SSWG review of potential impact on other programs.

The Instruction contains a self-expiry clause: it 'Must be reissued, cancelled, or certified current within 5 years of its publication in accordance with DoDI 5025.01. If not it will expire effective February 6, 2023 and be removed from the DoD Issuances Website.'

dodi-5205-11.denialPosture: None. DoDI 5205.11 asserts nothing about UAP and denies nothing; it is a procedural issuance published with unlimited releasability. Its evidentiary value is that the Department has openly documented, in its own doctrine, every structural capability -- unacknowledged type, waived reporting, nested waived sub-elements under reported umbrellas, industrial-security carve-outs, and discretionary denial of oversight read-ons -- that a concealed legacy programme would require.
connections: Implements 10 U.S.C. 119, the statute whose subsection (e) waiver and December 31, 2021 reporting termination are the core of classified-annex.
The 'will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' access gate is the doctrinal basis for the read-on denial David Grusch testified to on July 26, 2023.

'Support of non-DoD SAPs' is the doctrinal bridge to the DHS compartment KONA BLUE would have become, and to the IC Controlled Access Program AARO says was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.

The carve-out provision relieving the Defense Security Service of National Industrial Security Program oversight is the mechanism by which contractor facilities performing SAP work fall outside routine DoD industrial security inspection.
'Change of nickname, codeword, PID' is the doctrinal answer to why a legacy effort would be untrackable across decades even to cleared reviewers.
The February 1 SAP Listing and March 1 SAP Annual Report are the documents that, if they still existed, would settle whether an unreported UAP materials programme is inside the DoD SAP inventory.
Deputy Secretary of Defense signature authority makes the DepSecDef, not the SecDef, the approving official for SAP establishment -- a specific office to interrogate for any given programme's origin.
openQuestions: Whether DoDI 5205.11 was reissued, cancelled or certified current before its stated February 6, 2023 expiry, and what issuance governs DoD SAPs now.
How many DoD SAPs are currently designated waived, and whether that number has ever been disclosed even to the eight members who receive 119(e) material.

Whether any unacknowledged waived sub-element has ever been added under a non-waived umbrella in a manner that kept it out of the congressional notification stream, and what the SAPCO record of such additions shows.
Which contractor facilities currently operate under NISP carve-outs, and who inspects them.
Whether the SAP Listing and SAP Annual Report continued to be produced after the December 31, 2021 statutory termination, and if so whether they are still transmitted to Congress.
Whether GTE and LEAF BARK are purely notional or were drawn from real program nomenclature for the published sample.
Whether the SAPOC, SRG or SSWG has ever reviewed a programme relating to materials of unknown origin, and whether their minutes exist as records subject to section 1842 of the FY2024 NDAA.

dod-sapco-arch.whatItIs: The DoD Special Access Program Central Office (SAPCO) and the governance stack built around it — the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG), the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), and the Cognizant Authority SAPCOs inside each Component — is the machinery that creates, names, compartments, funds, audits and reports every DoD Special Access Program. It is defined by DoD Directive 5205.07, DoD Instruction 5205.11 (12 September 2024), and DoD Manual 5205.07 (17 January 2025). The Director, DoD SAPCO sits directly under the Deputy Secretary of Defense and is the Department's single point of congressional liaison for SAPs.
dod-sapco-arch.whyImplicated: If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort has been carried inside the Department of Defense since the 1940s, this is the architecture that would hold it, and this is the architecture that would keep Congress from seeing it. DoDI 5205.11 states in plain text that the Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when standard congressional reporting 'would adversely affect national security' — a category whose existence is admitted, whose contents are not. The same office that decides what is waived is the office through which every congressional inquiry about SAPs must pass; it is simultaneously the gatekeeper and the answering service. Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna reported in September 2025 that DoD told Oversight Committee staff that only HASC and HAC-D members could be read into UAP-relevant SAP material at all, meaning the committee actually investigating concealment was structurally locked out by the concealment architecture. And Congress's own annual SAP report requirement under 10 U.S.C. 119(a)-(b) terminated by operation of law on 31 December 2021 — the year before AARO was stood up.
dod-sapco-arch.narrative:
The Special Access Program is the American government's designed answer to a question nobody asked out loud: how do you run a program that no one is allowed to know exists, and still call it lawful? The answer is a tiered architecture with a central clearinghouse, and that clearinghouse is the DoD Special Access Program Central Office.

The structure is documented, and the documentation is more revealing than any leak. DoD Instruction 5205.11, reissued 12 September 2024, assigns oversight authority over DoD SAPs to four Principal Staff Assistants: the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, and the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. Those four offices map with uncomfortable precision onto the four functions a recovery-and-exploitation effort would require: science, procurement, policy cover, and security. Below them sit Cognizant Authority SAPCOs inside each Component, each with its own security director, access approval authority, and classification guide annexes.

Above them sits the Director, DoD SAPCO, who under DoDM 5205.07 operates 'Under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense' — not the Secretary, not the Under Secretary for Intelligence and Security, but the Deputy. That reporting line matters. It means SAP governance runs through the Department's chief operating officer, the official who signs the memoranda establishing and terminating programs, and the official who convenes the SAPOC and the SRG. The Deputy Secretary is the single human node through which the entire waived-program universe passes.

The most quotable sentence in the entire corpus is DoDI 5205.11's own description of waiver: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.' The second sentence is the tell. It is an assertion of a conclusion, not a description of a mechanism. The mechanism is in 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2): when the Secretary waives, the information and the justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Subsection (g) defines the defense committees as the Armed Services and Appropriations committees of both chambers plus their defense subcommittees. Chairman plus ranking member of four committees equals eight members of Congress — for the most sensitive programs in the Department, out of 535.

That is the theory. In practice it is worse. The termination note attached to 10 U.S.C. 119 records that the annual SAP report to the defense committees under subsections (a) and (b) — the report enumerating every SAP, its cost history and its milestones — was terminated effective 31 December 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The single most comprehensive recurring window Congress had into the SAP portfolio closed by statute the year before the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was created, and eleven months before the Intelligence Authorization Act rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373 to demand a historical accounting of exactly the sort of program that report would have listed.

The SAPOC's annual review, per DoDI 5205.11, expressly includes assessment of 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' Somebody, once a year, reads a list of the programs Congress is not told about and decides whether to keep not telling Congress. That list exists. It has a custodian. Its custodian answers to the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

Two further mechanisms deserve analyst attention. First, 'carve out': DoDI 5205.11 authorizes Component heads to initiate actions replacing Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency security cognizance at contractor facilities, and to notify DCSA that it is 'relieved from inspection authority.' Carve-out removes the government's default industrial-security inspector from a contractor site. Whatever is inside a carved-out facility is inspected only by the program's own security apparatus. Second, the DoD SAPCO 'Functions as the DoD single point of congressional liaison concerning SAPs' and verifies that congressional offices approved to store SAP information implement DoD's own security requirements — meaning the Department also sets the terms on which the legislature may hold what the Department gives it.

Representative Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE attack this architecture directly. He asks MITRE to identify every SAP, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword, DOE Restricted Data compartment and SIGMA category it touched in connection with UAP records, and for each one to state 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' That question only has to be asked if the answer might be no.

oversight-congress.whatItIs: The congressional oversight apparatus for the legacy program question spans four venues with mismatched authorities: the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (broad jurisdiction, no SAP access), the House and Senate Armed Services and Appropriations committees (SAP access, narrow appetite), the two intelligence committees (Controlled Access Program access), and the eight-member chairman-and-ranking-member channel through which waived Special Access Programs are reported under 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Since 2021 Congress has legislated repeatedly and specifically against concealment, and has been told, repeatedly and specifically, that there is nothing to conceal.
oversight-congress.whyImplicated: Congress is not a bystander in this record; it is the party that wrote into permanent law the demand that the Executive account for 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.' That sentence exists in the United States Code because members with access to classified briefings concluded such programs might exist. Congress then legislated that AARO must enumerate every instance in which data was withheld from it on classification grounds, barred contractors from charging UAP-related independent research and development to overhead unless the material is furnished to Congress, and created a statutory UAP Records Collection at the National Archives. Each of those provisions is a countermeasure, and countermeasures are designed against something. What Congress has not obtained is compliance: the eminent-domain and Review Board provisions were stripped in conference, the annual SAP report requirement lapsed on 31 December 2021, and in September 2025 the chairwoman of the investigating task force told the public that DoD would not read her members in at all.
oversight-congress.narrative:
Congressional oversight of the legacy program problem has a structural defect that no amount of legislative will has cured: the committees with the appetite lack the access, and the committees with the access lack the appetite.

The modern sequence begins on 26 July 2023, when the House Oversight Committee's National Security subcommittee convened 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency.' Former National Reconnaissance Office and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency officer David Grusch testified under oath alongside former Navy pilot Ryan Graves and retired Navy Commander David Fravor. Grusch alleged a decades-long crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering effort, recovery of non-human biologics, and misappropriation of funds to evade congressional oversight, and said the specifics required a classified setting. The hearing produced a printed transcript, a legislative wave, and no records.

The legislative wave crested in the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act. Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds had drafted the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, which passed the Senate with three teeth: a presidentially appointed nine-member Review Board, a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan, and federal eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private parties. Conference removed all three. What survived became sections 1841 through 1843 of Public Law 118-31, codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note: a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, populated by 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence,' housed by NARA in Record Group 615. The eminent domain provision — the only clause that would have compelled a private contractor to surrender physical material — was the one the private contractors did not have to face.

What survived elsewhere in the same law is less discussed and arguably sharper. Section 1687(b) of P.L. 118-31 provides that, consistent with DoDI 3204.01, 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses' on covered contracts 'unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Congress legislated, in the FY2024 NDAA, against a specific accounting mechanism by which a defense contractor could fund UAP work with taxpayer money routed through overhead and owe nobody an explanation. That provision is a fingerprint.

The permanent statute carries more. 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4) requires the AARO Director, every briefing period, to give the chairs and ranking members of the Armed Services and Intelligence committees 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.' Congress anticipated that its own office would be stonewalled by other parts of the Executive and built a tripwire. Section 3373(j) requires the Historical Record Report to reach back to 1 January 1945 and to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' together with 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information.' The Comptroller General was directed by section 6803 of P.L. 117-263 to audit that very report process with cleared GAO personnel and to brief Congress semiannually on it.

Congress kept legislating. Public Law 119-60, enacted 18 December 2025, amended 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) so that the data-sharing mandate binds every component of the Department of Defense, not merely elements of the intelligence community — an amendment that would be pointless unless DoD components had been withholding under the old text. The same act added subsection (l)(5), requiring briefings to include details of NORAD and USNORTHCOM intercepts of UAP, with the first post-enactment briefing to reach back to 1 January 2004. Section 1673(a) ordered the AARO Director to make, within 180 days, 'an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena.' Congress is now demanding an inventory of the classification instruments themselves.

Against all of this stands the access problem. On 11 February 2025 Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets under Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, authorized for six months under Committee Rules. On 9 September 2025 Luna told the public that DoD had informed her staff that only HASC and HAC-D members could be read into the relevant SAPs, and that any other Member required the approval of the chairman and ranking member of both. She added: 'Independent SAP oversight has presented a consistent problem for Congress as the program's budgets are classified.' That is the architecture of 10 U.S.C. 119 operating exactly as designed, against the committee investigating it.
