ndaa-fy2022-sec-1683.whatItIs: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-81, enacted 27 December 2021 at 135 Stat. 2118, is the statute that created the office lineage running from the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force through the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and was rewritten wholesale a year later by section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 (Public Law 117-263), and amended again in 2023 and 2025.
ndaa-fy2022-sec-1683.whyImplicated: This is the only place in the United States Code where Congress wrote down, in operative statutory language, that programs concerning unidentified anomalous phenomena may have been 'protected by restricted access' and 'not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' and demanded an accounting of them going back to 1 January 1945. It is also the only statute that directs the Secretary of Defense to designate line organizations for 'the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models' relating to UAP, and to run a science plan whose stated purpose includes providing 'the foundation for potential future investments to replicate' anomalous performance characteristics. Congress did not merely authorize a reporting office; it authorized materials testing, medical study of exposed personnel, and replication research — the exact functional description of a reverse-engineering enterprise — and then required that any prior version of the same enterprise be disclosed. The statute's subsequent amendment history is a record of the Executive branch failing to comply.
ndaa-fy2022-sec-1683.narrative:
Section 1683 began as a modest reorganization and became, through two rewrites, the sharpest disclosure instrument in federal law. Read it as a chronology of what Congress learned.

The original enactment on 27 December 2021 stood up an office to absorb the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, in the wake of the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment. A year later, section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 amended the section generally — replacing it in full — and section 1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever the word appeared. That single-word substitution is not cosmetic. It extended the statute's reach from aircraft to transmedium objects and submerged objects, a definitional move that matters if what is at issue includes things recovered from water.

The rewritten statute names the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office and hardwires a dual chain of command. The Director is appointed by the Secretary of Defense in consultation with the DNI; the Deputy Director is appointed by the DNI in coordination with the Secretary. The Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence — and, separately, 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters.' That administrative reporting line runs to the same office that is a SAP Oversight Authority under DoDI 5205.11 and the DoD interface to the DNI's Controlled Access Program Central Office. The office chartered to find concealed compartments is administratively subordinate, in part, to the office that manages compartments.

Subsection (j) is the load-bearing clause. Within 540 days of 23 December 2022, the Director was to deliver to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership a written report on 'the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' drawn from intelligence community records, oral history interviews, open source analysis, interviews of current and former officials, and classified and unclassified national archives. It must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945. And it must include 'a compilation and itemization of the key historical record of the involvement of the intelligence community with unidentified anomalous phenomena, including — (I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.' Subsection (j)(2) obliges the Archivist of the United States to make classified NARA holdings available to the office for that purpose.

Subsections (e) and (g) are where the statute stops sounding like transparency legislation and starts sounding like a program charter. Under (e)(1), the Secretary of Defense in coordination with the DNI 'shall designate one or more line organizations that will be primarily responsible for scientific, technical, and operational analysis of data gathered by field investigations... including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.' Under (e)(2), both officials must issue directives ensuring those line organizations 'has authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.' Under (g), the science plan must account for performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation,' and 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.' Congress wrote replication into the law. Subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) then requires each annual report to include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

Definitions matter here too. Subsection (n)(6) defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense — pushing materials testing and medical studies out to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories, and therefore out to contractor-operated facilities. Subsection (n)(7) defines transmedium objects as those observed transitioning between space and atmosphere, or atmosphere and water.

The amendment history is the compliance record. In December 2023, P.L. 118-31 §7341 moved the annual report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly onto the AARO Director alone. In December 2025, P.L. 119-60 §1672(b) rewrote subsection (f)(1)(A) so the data-availability mandate binds 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' — the prior text covered only IC elements. Congress had to amend the statute to reach the Department of Defense's own components. Section 1671 added the NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept requirement with a 2004 lookback, and section 1673(a) demanded an accounting of the security classification guides themselves. Each amendment closes a door someone had walked through.

claims.text: Section 1683 was enacted as Pub. L. 117-81, div. A, title XVI, §1683, on 27 December 2021, at 135 Stat. 2118, and is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373.

Pub. L. 117-263 §6802(a) (23 December 2022) amended section 1683 generally, replacing its text, and §1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever appearing, extending the statute's definitional reach to transmedium and submerged objects.

The AARO Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, and reports 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters of the Office.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii) requires the historical record report to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.'

The same subsection requires itemization of 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

The historical record report must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945, and the Archivist of the United States must make available to AARO NARA holdings 'including classified information' as the Director considers necessary.

50 U.S.C. 3373(e)(1) directs the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, to designate one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(g) requires a science plan to account for characteristics 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.'
Each AARO annual report must include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

The statute defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense, pushing designated materials-testing and medical-study responsibility outward to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories.

Annual reports must name 'the line organizations that have been designated to perform the specific functions under subsections (d) and (e), and the specific functions for which each such line organization has been assigned primary responsibility.'
Subsection (m) required the Secretary of Defense to terminate the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force no later than the date the new office was established.

Public Law 119-60 §1672(b) (18 December 2025) rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to bind 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense'; the prior text reached only IC elements.

AARO published Volume I of its historical record report on 8 March 2024, asserting no verifiable evidence that any UAP sighting represented extraterrestrial activity and no verifiable evidence that the U.S. government or private industry has ever had access to extraterrestrial technology, and characterizing interviewees as having 'mistakenly associated' authentic classified programs with alien activity.
claims.source: AARO, 'Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), Volume I,' 8 March 2024 — https://media.defense.gov/2024/Mar/08/2003409233/-1/-1/0/DOPSR-2024-0263-AARO-HISTORICAL-RECORD-REPORT-VOLUME-1-2024.PDF

ndaa-fy2022-sec-1683.denialPosture: The statute contains no denial; the office it created does. AARO's Volume I historical record report (8 March 2024) states it found no verifiable evidence that the U.S. government or private industry has ever had access to extraterrestrial technology, and attributes whistleblower accounts to misidentification of authentic classified programs. That formulation concedes the existence of authentic classified programs proximate to the allegations while denying their nature, and it is the denial Chairwoman Luna attacked on the record on 9 September 2025.
connections: AARO and its first Director, Sean Kirkpatrick — the office created by this section; Kirkpatrick reported to the NASA UAP Independent Study Team's 31 May 2023 public meeting that AARO had collected more than 800 events.
Deputy Secretary of Defense and USD(I&S) — the reporting lines written into 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3), which run into the same offices that control the DoD SAP architecture under DoDI 5205.11.

NARA and the Archivist of the United States — obligated by subsection (j)(2) to open classified holdings to AARO; separately the statutory custodian of the UAP Records Collection created by the FY2024 NDAA.
NASA — named in subsection (c)(6) as a required coordination partner; NASA's own Independent Study Team reported in September 2023 with no access to the classified data this section covers.
GAO / Comptroller General — assigned by P.L. 117-263 §6803 to audit the historical record report process with cleared personnel.
David Grusch — his 2023 allegation of a program 'protected by restricted access' not reported to Congress tracks the exact statutory language of subsection (j)(1)(B)(ii)(I).

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories — Section II.4 demands identification of MITRE work performed for AARO, the UAP Task Force, AATIP and AAWSAP, connecting the statutory office lineage to contractor custody.
Pub. L. 118-31 §1687(b) — the companion prohibition on charging UAP-related IRAD to contract overhead without congressional disclosure.
openQuestions: Which line organizations were designated under subsections (d) and (e), and for which functions? The statute requires them to be named in annual reports; no unclassified naming has been published.
Was the science plan required by subsection (g) ever produced, and does it contain a replication program element as the statute contemplates?
Has any annual report actually addressed subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) — efforts 'to capture or exploit' discovered UAP — and what was said?
Did the Archivist open classified NARA holdings to AARO under subsection (j)(2), and what accession records document that transfer?
Why did Congress need to amend subsection (f)(1)(A) in December 2025 to reach DoD components — which components had withheld data under the prior text?

The original 27 December 2021 text of section 1683 differs materially from the 2022 rewrite; what provisions in the original were dropped, and at whose request? The Code preserves only a summary amendment note.
Has the AARO Director delivered the accounting of security classification guides required within 180 days of 18 December 2025, and does it list any guide covering recovered materials?

nasa-uap-ist.whatItIs: The NASA Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Independent Study Team was a 16-member external panel convened by NASA in 2022 under the Earth Science Advisory Committee, chaired by astrophysicist David Spergel of the Simons Foundation, with Dr. Daniel Evans of NASA Headquarters as Designated Federal Official. It held a single public meeting on 31 May 2023 and delivered its final report on 14 September 2023. On the same day NASA created a Director of UAP Research position and initially declined to name the appointee.
nasa-uap-ist.whyImplicated: The panel is a study in the shape of a hole. It was chartered to advise NASA on UAP using only unclassified civilian, commercial and open-source data, and it says so plainly — which means the one body assembled to bring scientific rigor to the question was structurally barred from the classified holdings where the question actually lives. Its report says the quiet part in print: military and intelligence sensor data are classified 'often because of what the imagery could reveal about U.S. technical capabilities to our adversaries, and not because of what is actually in the images,' and that these classified observations 'enhance the sense of mystery and conspiracy surrounding UAP, and they present an obstacle to scientific inquiry.' That is a federally chartered panel, in an official NASA publication, stating that classification is generating the appearance of concealment. Three of its sixteen members came from commercial remote-sensing, space-hardware and private-equity defense firms — Maxar, Redwire and AE Industrial Partners — and two from the FAA, making the panel a map of who holds the civilian sensor data that would matter. And the harassment record around the panel and the withheld name of NASA's UAP research director are themselves artifacts: the cost of association was high enough that the agency initially treated the identity of a civil servant as a security matter.
nasa-uap-ist.narrative:
NASA's Independent Study Team was born of a specific institutional bet: that the agency with the most public trust and the least security baggage could drag UAP into normal science. The bet was placed by Administrator Bill Nelson and executed by the Science Mission Directorate under Nicola Fox, following her predecessor Thomas Zurbuchen, with the activity graciously hosted, in the report's own words, by NASA's Earth Science Division under the Earth Science Advisory Committee. That administrative placement is worth pausing on: a panel about unidentified objects in the airspace was parked in the division that studies the planet's surface and atmosphere. It kept the activity out of astrophysics and out of anything that would have implied a search for technology.

The roster reads as a deliberate coalition of civilian instrumentation. Chair David Spergel of the Simons Foundation. Anamaria Berea of George Mason, Federica Bianco of Delaware, Paula Bontempi of Rhode Island, Jennifer Buss of the Potomac Institute for Policy Studies, science journalist Nadia Drake, David Grinspoon of the Planetary Science Institute, retired astronaut Captain Scott Kelly, Matt Mountain of AURA, Joshua Semeter of Boston University, and Shelley Wright of UC San Diego. Then the operators: Warren Randolph and Karlin Toner from the Federal Aviation Administration, Walter Scott from Maxar Technologies, Mike Gold from Redwire Space, and Reggie Brothers from AE Industrial Partners. Two FAA officials, one commercial satellite imaging executive, one space infrastructure executive, and one defense-focused private equity operator who had previously been Under Secretary for Science and Technology at DHS. If the panel's recommendations pointed anywhere, they pointed at data these institutions own.

And they did. The report recommends NASA leverage its Earth-observing assets to probe local environmental conditions associated with UAP detected by other means, and 'explore enhancing collaborations with the U.S. commercial remote-sensing industry, which offer powerful constellations of high-resolution Earth-observing satellites.' It recommends multispectral and hyperspectral acquisition, AI and machine learning applied to anomaly detection, a crowdsourcing system built on open-source smartphone apps, and better leveraging of the Aviation Safety Reporting System, which NASA operates for the FAA, as 'a critical database for the whole-of-government effort.' Every one of those recommendations routes future UAP data through civilian and commercial channels rather than military ones. Read charitably, that is a strategy for building an evidentiary base outside the classification perimeter. Read uncharitably, it is a strategy for building an evidentiary base that will never intersect the classification perimeter.

The panel's own frustration surfaces in the passage that matters most. Discussing why existing observations cannot resolve UAP, the report states: 'In addition, much of the data collected by military sensors or intelligence satellites are classified—often because of what the imagery could reveal about U.S. technical capabilities to our adversaries, and not because of what is actually in the images. While essential for security, these classified observations enhance the sense of mystery and conspiracy surrounding UAP, and they present an obstacle to scientific inquiry.' A federal advisory panel wrote, in a public report, that the government's classification practice is manufacturing the appearance of a cover-up and blocking the science that would dispel it. That sentence is a finding about the concealment architecture, delivered by scientists who could not see inside it.

On the evidence question the report is careful and narrow: 'To date, in the peer-reviewed scientific literature, there is no conclusive evidence suggesting an extraterrestrial origin for UAP.' The qualifier is doing work — peer-reviewed literature is precisely the corpus from which classified holdings are absent. The panel also recorded that then-AARO Director Sean Kirkpatrick reported at its 31 May 2023 public meeting that AARO had collected more than 800 reported events, against 263 reports filed in the 17 years before March 2021.

The cost of participation is documented in the report itself: team members received hate mail from colleagues, were ridiculed and criticized on social media, and had firsthand knowledge of colleagues warned away from technosignature research on the grounds that it could damage scientific credibility and promotion prospects. On 14 September 2023 NASA announced the creation of a Director of UAP Research and Administrator Nelson said the identity would be withheld to prevent harassment. NASA reversed within hours and named Mark McInerney, a former NASA liaison to the Department of Defense on UAP matters. The reversal is instructive twice over: it shows the agency's first instinct was concealment framed as protection, and it shows how quickly that instinct collapsed under press pressure — which is not how the Department of Defense's instances of the same instinct have behaved.

The statutory tie is direct. 50 U.S.C. 3373(c)(6) requires AARO to coordinate with NASA, among other agencies. Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories demand identification of all UAP-related work MITRE performed for or with NASA. NASA sits inside the legal architecture of the program question while its own expert panel sat outside the data.

nasa-uap-ist.denialPosture: NASA's posture is not denial but bounded agnosticism: the report asserts only that the peer-reviewed literature contains no conclusive evidence of extraterrestrial origin, while simultaneously stating that the relevant military and intelligence data are classified and inaccessible. NASA's initial decision to withhold the name of its own UAP research director, reversed within hours, is a concealment artifact in its own right.

openQuestions: Did any panel member hold clearances permitting review of AARO or SAP-controlled material, or was the entire panel unclassified? The report describes unclassified sourcing but does not state member clearance status.
Who selected the sixteen members, and against what criteria did three commercial space and defense-investment executives and two FAA officials join a scientific advisory panel?
What did NASA's Terms of Reference — the eight charge elements the report responds to — actually say? The full Terms of Reference text is not reproduced in the public report summary.
Which colleagues warned other scientists away from technosignature research, and were any of those warnings institutional rather than personal?
Has NASA implemented any of the panel's recommendations — commercial remote-sensing collaboration, crowdsourced smartphone data, ASRS integration — and with what budget line?
What UAP-related work, if any, has MITRE or another FFRDC performed for NASA? Burlison asked; no answer is public.
Who made the initial decision to withhold the UAP research director's name, and on what threat assessment?

task-force-declassification-federal-secr.whatItIs: The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets is a panel of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, established by Chairman James Comer on 11 February 2025 and chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL), authorized for six months under Committee Rules. Its announced portfolio spans the Kennedy, Robert Kennedy and King assassination records, UAP and USO, the Epstein files, COVID-19 origins and the 9/11 files. It has become the principal congressional venue for the legacy program question since 2025.
task-force-declassification-federal-secr.whyImplicated: This is the first congressional body to run at the concealment architecture rather than at the phenomenon. Its members subpoena-adjacent letters go to contractors and federally funded research and development centers rather than to the Pentagon press office, on the theory that the records are in private hands under federal sponsorship. Its chairwoman has stated on the record that the Department of Defense refused to read her members into the relevant special access programs, naming HASC and HAC-D as the only committees with access — which converts a suspicion about compartmentation into a documented, dated institutional fact. Its member Eric Burlison has converted that finding into legislative interrogatories to MIT Lincoln Laboratory and The MITRE Corporation demanding enumeration of SAPs, ACCMs, cover programs, hidden funding and instructions to avoid certain vocabulary. And its chairwoman has used her opening statement to attack the credibility of the former AARO director by name, making the government's own denial instrument a subject of the investigation.
task-force-declassification-federal-secr.narrative:
The Task Force exists because a different theory of the problem won an internal argument. For four years the congressional approach to UAP was to demand better reports from the Executive branch. The Task Force's approach is to demand records from whoever physically holds them, and to treat classification as a claim to be adjudicated rather than an answer to be accepted.

It was created on 11 February 2025 when Chairman James Comer announced the panel and named Rep. Anna Paulina Luna to lead it, following President Trump's 23 January 2025 executive order on declassification of records concerning the assassinations of President Kennedy, Senator Robert Kennedy and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Comer framed it in institution-repair language: 'This secrecy has sowed distrust in our institutions.' Luna's own statement laid out a portfolio nobody expected a single panel to carry: 'We will also investigate UAPs/USOs, the Epstein client list, COVID-19 origins, and the 9/11 files.' The Task Force was authorized for six months pursuant to Committee Rules, and Comer and Luna transmitted eleven letters the same day. Its first hearing addressed the JFK files; Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) was initially the ranking member, and by the September 2025 UAP hearing Luna was yielding to Ranking Member Crockett.

The 9 September 2025 hearing, 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection,' is the panel's substantive turn. Four witnesses testified: Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp, and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland. Luna's opening statement is the single most useful congressional document on the access problem. She described following a lead from active-duty Air Force pilot whistleblowers alleging a cover-up of UAP activity at Eglin Air Force Base, pursued with former Rep. Matt Gaetz and Rep. Tim Burchett. She said pilots decline to come forward out of fear for their flight status and careers. And then she stated the mechanism: 'In preparation for previous UAP hearings, the Committee repeatedly asked DoD to allow Members to view videos and files relating to UAP incidents. Unfortunately, DoD notified Committee staff that due to the Department's special access program (SAP) rules, only members of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) and the Defense Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee (HAC-D) were allowed to be "read in" on such programs. For a non-committee Member to be allowed to view these documents and videos, individual Members must be approved by the Chairman and Ranking Member of both HASC and HAC-D.' She added that 'Independent SAP oversight has presented a consistent problem for Congress as the program's budgets are classified.'

That is 10 U.S.C. 119 operating as designed, quoted from the receiving end by a committee chairwoman. It also identifies precisely four people — the chairs and ranking members of HASC and HAC-D — as the gatekeepers for any Oversight Committee member seeking access.

Luna also went after AARO directly, calling former director Sean Kirkpatrick 'a documented liar' and questioning 'what his purpose at AARO really was if it was not to follow up on investigations and disclose his findings to Members of Congress.' She entered into the record former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Chris Mellon's characterization of an AARO report as 'the most error-ridden and unsatisfactory government report I can recall reading during or after decades of government service,' noting Mellon's claims that it was the first AARO report submitted to Congress without the DNI's sign-off, that it omitted agencies with known UAP investigations, and that it omitted any discussion of efforts to hide information — including at U.S. Customs and Border Protection. A congressional task force treating the government's own investigative office as a suspect witness is a meaningful shift in posture.

The Task Force's method matured into contractor-directed process in 2026. On 7 May 2026 Burlison wrote to MIT Lincoln Laboratory about a reel-to-reel recording catalogued as 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52' from the Beacon Hill Study, labeled 'flying saucer talk,' with Edward J. Ruppelt as briefer. On 22 May 2026 he transmitted ten pages of legislative interrogatories to MITRE, copied to Luna, Comer, and Information Security Oversight Office Director Michael D. Thomas. Both letters run on the same statutory theory: sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, create a UAP Records Collection at NARA in Record Group 615 that encompasses government-funded records, and contractor custody does not defeat it. Burlison's framing in the accompanying release is the Task Force's thesis in one sentence: FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records.'

The backdrop by 2026 is a Trump administration declassification push. Following a 19 February 2026 Trump directive, the Department of War began publishing declassified UAP files in May 2026 under the banner PURSUE — Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters — at war.gov/ufo. Burlison's press release places his MITRE inquiry explicitly inside that effort, testing whether agencies, contractors, FFRDCs and laboratories are actually complying.

burlison-mitre-letter-2026.whatItIs: A ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests dated 22 May 2026, sent by Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO-07) to Dr. Mark Peters, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Christopher Land, Senior Vice President and General Counsel, of The MITRE Corporation at 7525 Colshire Drive, McLean, Virginia. Copied to Task Force Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna, Oversight Chairman James Comer, and Michael D. Thomas, Director of the Information Security Oversight Office at NARA. The enclosure runs eleven numbered sections and more than forty specific requests, with a relevant time period beginning 1 January 1930.
burlison-mitre-letter-2026.whyImplicated: This is the first congressional instrument that treats a federally funded research and development center as a potential custodian of the legacy program's paper. It does not ask MITRE whether UAP are real. It asks MITRE which Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, Managed-Need-To-Know codewords, DOE Restricted Data compartments and SIGMA categories it participated in touching UAP subject matter, and for each one, 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks for any classification guide, nondisclosure agreement or sponsor communication that instructed MITRE personnel to avoid the words UAP, UFO, USO, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, technology of unknown origin or non-human intelligence in their records. It asks for funding routed through 'a cover program' whose 'public description differed materially from the responsive work performed,' and for funding MITRE understood to be 'hidden from, not briefed to, or not readily visible to ordinary sponsor budget channels.' And it names twelve companies by name. The letter is a map of the concealment hypothesis rendered as a document request.
burlison-mitre-letter-2026.narrative:
Burlison's MITRE package is the moment the congressional inquiry stopped asking the Pentagon and started asking the people who hold the Pentagon's files.

The premise is stated in the cover letter's second paragraph. MITRE operates multiple FFRDCs, and 'By design, FFRDCs often receive special access to government facilities, data, sponsor requirements, and sensitive technical information that ordinary private contractors may not receive. This special public-trust role makes records stewardship, sponsor accountability, and congressional visibility especially important.' The statutory hook is sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA and NARA's Record Group 615: if government-funded UAP records sit in a contractor's archive, the statute reaches them, and MITRE's status as a nonprofit operator does not create a safe harbor. DefenseScoop reported that FFRDCs are largely shielded from public disclosure by FOIA exemptions, and that some officials have warned this lets them hold government information the public has a right to see.

The scope is deliberately enormous. 'Unless otherwise specified, the relevant time period is January 1, 1930, to the present.' MITRE was incorporated in 1958; the 1930 start date is a trap for inherited archives, telling MITRE that if it contends the request is overbroad for a legacy period it must 'identify the earliest date for which MITRE can search reliably, the reason older records cannot be searched, and the custodian or sponsor most likely to hold the older records.' The definition of 'UAP-related' extends to any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving' UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, 'or equivalent terms.' Euphemism is named as a category of evidence.

The deadlines are tight and sequenced. Within five business days, designate a vice-president-level officer to coordinate. Within ten business days, issue and confirm a written preservation hold covering 'restricted systems, air-gapped environments, classified repositories, personal workspaces used for official business, archived systems, email, collaboration platforms, backup media, contractor/subcontractor systems, and offsite storage.' Within fourteen days, contact the office to coordinate a classified briefing for Task Force Members and cleared Committee staff at 'the appropriate TS/SCI/SAP level.' Within thirty days, written answers plus a records-location index naming repositories, custodians, contract vehicles, sponsors, classification authorities and record schedules. Within forty-five days, production of all unclassified responsive records in native electronic format with complete metadata, plus a segregated classified annex and a privilege and classification log. The letter warns that 'False statements, concealment, alteration, destruction, or obstruction in connection with this inquiry may implicate federal law, including but not limited to 18 U.S.C. §§ 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519, and 2071.'

The eleven enclosure sections read as a taxonomy of how a program stays hidden. Section I demands an accounting of records destroyed, degaussed, sanitized, reclassified, moved to a restricted system or 'placed under sponsor control,' with the authority and the responsible personnel named. Section II demands identification of every contract, IDIQ, GWAC, BPA, OTA and CRADA under which MITRE touched UAP information, and every individual involved with 'their specific functions and duties' — and names AARO, the UAP Task Force, AATIP, AAWSAP, DIA, CIA, NSA, NRO, NGA, ONI, NRL, DARPA, IARPA and DOE laboratories, 'or any successor, predecessor, cover, compartment, or renamed activity.' Section II.6 asks whether MITRE 'provided cover' for another entity's UAP work.

Section III is the compartmentation audit already described. Section IV asks what MITRE has and has not sent to NARA under the UAP Records Collection. Section V asks for sensor work across radar, optical, infrared, acoustic and undersea domains, expressly including 'SOSUS/IUSS-related' systems and 'unidentified submerged objects.' Section VI asks about recovered anomalous materials, isotope ratios, chain of custody, metamaterials, propulsion and 'cognitive interface systems' — and, in VI.4, about 'biological material, biological samples, human physiological effects, medical monitoring, occupational exposure, anomalous injury, cognitive or neurological effects, or environmental hazards associated with UAP-related materials, objects, fields, occupants, or events,' with the careful caveat that the request 'seeks records and safety documentation only and does not presume the validity of any particular biological claim.' The word 'occupants' is doing a great deal of work in a congressional document.

Section VII asks for SCIFs, SAPFs, vaults and 'material-containment work.' Section VIII asks for internal disclosures, retaliation, and nondisclosure instruments 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations' that restricted personnel from reporting to Congress, IGs, AARO, NARA or law enforcement. Section IX names Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace or its successors. Section X goes at the money. Section XI demands a certified response signed by a responsible MITRE officer and counsel.

MITRE's answer, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was custodial rather than responsive: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That is a statement that anything found goes back to the sponsor, not to Congress. A member of Burlison's staff told DefenseScoop the letter was informed by 'advice from many whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations, and those working at FFRDCs.'

The MITRE package was not the first shot. On 7 May 2026 Burlison had written to MIT Lincoln Laboratory Director Melissa G. Choi and counsel David A. Suski about a single object: a reel-to-reel recording catalogued as 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52' from the Beacon Hill Study, labeled 'flying saucer talk,' with Edward J. Ruppelt — then head of Project Blue Book — listed as the briefer. That letter demanded the laboratory determine whether the recording is extant, preserve it, digitize it to preservation grade, and transmit it with metadata to NARA for Record Group 615. It also instructed the laboratory to coordinate with the cognizant sponsor, the original classification authority, ISOO and the Public Interest Declassification Board if an active Security Classification Guide still applies to a 1952 tape.

gerb-mitre-investigation.whatItIs: An open-source investigation by the pseudonymous researcher known as UAP Gerb into The MITRE Corporation and the wider federally funded research and development center (FFRDC) layer as custodians of UAP-related material, which in 2026 converged with a formal congressional records demand. On May 22, 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison (MO-07) transmitted ten pages of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE covering its possible custody, control, analysis, transfer, destruction or withholding of records on UAP, recovered materials, technologies of unknown origin and alleged legacy crash-retrieval or reverse-engineering programs. MITRE confirmed publicly that it is reviewing its archives.
gerb-mitre-investigation.whyImplicated: The FFRDC is the structural blind spot in the whole concealment architecture: it holds government-funded records, sits inside classified programs, and is largely shielded from FOIA. Burlison's letter names the exact mechanism the record has always lacked a demand for, asking MITRE to identify Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, activities under Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, classification guides, nondisclosure instruments, contractor-held federal records, budgetary mechanisms and internal retaliation complaints. It asks for records back to 1930, which is a date choice that only makes sense if the requester believes the paper trail predates Roswell. It explicitly asks MITRE to describe UAP-related work conducted with Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace or its successors, which converts the letter into a map of the suspected contractor network. And a member of Burlison's own staff told DefenseScoop the letter was informed by advice from whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations and people working at FFRDCs, meaning an independent researcher's target list has been laundered into a congressional production request.
gerb-mitre-investigation.narrative:
The investigation has two halves that need to be tiered separately, because they are not equally evidenced.

The first half is the independent research. UAP Gerb is a pseudonymous researcher and documentarian who produces multi-hour, heavily sourced video investigations into crash retrieval, reverse-engineering facilities and the contractor and laboratory network around them. His signature thesis is not about craft at all but about legal architecture: that the Department of Energy, not the Pentagon, is the load-bearing custodian, that the Nuclear Emergency Support Team has a classified retrieval mission alongside its public one, and that the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 supplies the classification vehicle by designating recovered material as trans-classified foreign nuclear material, a category that sits outside the reach of the congressional intelligence committees. In his August 2025 Danny Jones Podcast appearance he put it directly: the DOE NEST had authority under the 1954 Atomic Energy Act, which also governs how UFO materials are classified as transclassified foreign nuclear materials. This matters because it is a falsifiable structural claim about statute, not a witness anecdote, and because it explains a specific documented behavior, namely why UAP disclosure amendments keep naming the 1954 Act as an obstacle.

The second, and more consequential, half of the investigation is Gerb's January 2026 attack on the AARO to Oak Ridge to Battelle circuit. As reported by IBTimes UK on January 17, 2026, Gerb alleges that in 2024 AARO contracted Oak Ridge National Laboratory to examine a metallic specimen recovered from private land in Ohio; that AARO subsequently issued a brief statement suggesting the sample was ordinary while the full Oak Ridge analysis was never released; that former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick left government in December 2023 to become Chief Technology Officer for Defense and Intelligence Programs at Oak Ridge, the same laboratory that received material he had previously decided to send out for analysis; that Oak Ridge subsequently removed the webpage announcing his appointment and that he did not list the position on his public CV; and that former Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security Ronald Moultrie removed his prior Battelle board service from his official biography. The structural point behind the personnel allegations is the one that survives regardless of motive: Oak Ridge is operated by UT-Battelle, a Battelle entity, and Battelle is the same institution that performed the statistical analysis published as Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 in 1955. The organization that wrote the government's foundational public assessment of the phenomenon in the 1950s operates the laboratory that assessed its recovered material in the 2020s. That is not a coincidence anyone has been asked to explain on the record.

The third half, the one that turns research into leverage, is Burlison. Reports in the research community indicate Burlison invited Gerb to dinner, and by May 2026 Burlison had transmitted to MITRE a document whose enclosure lists more than forty specific requests. The letter instructs MITRE to designate a senior official, issue a preservation hold, provide a records-location index, produce unclassified responsive records in native electronic format with complete metadata within 45 days, identify classified or sponsor-controlled material, and coordinate a classified briefing for cleared committee staff. It asks MITRE to identify all work involving detection, tracking, correlation, characterization, data fusion, anomaly detection or attribution of UAP-related signatures across air, space, maritime, undersea, cyber, electromagnetic, acoustic, radar, optical, infrared, nuclear, biological, chemical or multi-intelligence domains. And it includes the trapdoor clause: if no responsive records exist, MITRE must certify the search methodology, repositories searched, custodians contacted, search terms used, date ranges and the responsible MITRE official who supervised the search. That converts a null answer into an attributable, signed, falsifiable statement by a named person, which is exactly the property that a denial needs in order to become evidence.

The MITRE demand did not arrive alone. Burlison's press release states it builds on his earlier letter to MIT Lincoln Laboratory concerning historical UAP records associated with the Beacon Hill Study and a reel-to-reel recording identified as AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52. A film reel identified by an Air Technical Intelligence Center designator and a March 1952 date, held at an MIT laboratory rather than at the National Archives, is the single most specific artifact anyone in Congress has publicly named in this line of inquiry.

What the record does not yet contain is any MITRE production. As of the reporting, MITRE has said only that insiders are reviewing archives and that if relevant material is found it will coordinate with the responsible federal agencies. That is a conditional, agency-deferring non-answer, which is the standard posture of a contractor that intends to route any responsive material back through the classification authority that created it.

us-house.whatItIs: The United States House of Representatives, and specifically the three bodies within it that have repeatedly touched the legacy program question: the Committee on Armed Services, which held the first open congressional UFO hearing in 1966; the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, which has run the modern public hearings since 2023; and that committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna. The House is also the chamber whose FY2024 NDAA conference product created the statutory UAP Records Collection at the National Archives.
us-house.whyImplicated: The House is not a bystander in this record; it is the institution that has been lied to, and periodically the institution that catches the lie. Its 1966 Armed Services hearing extracted the Air Force's official position on the record from a sitting Secretary and simultaneously put J. Allen Hynek's dissent into the Congressional record. Its Oversight Committee in 2023 put a former Navy pilot and other witnesses in front of cameras under oath. Its members have since gone after the contractor layer directly, issuing legislative interrogatories to The MITRE Corporation and MIT Lincoln Laboratory rather than to executive agencies, which is a deliberate move around the FOIA exemptions and classification authorities that block agency requests. And the House is where the funding lever sits: FY2024 NDAA section 1687 makes UAP-related independent research and development costs unallowable as indirect expenses unless the underlying material is made available to the defense and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership.
us-house.narrative:
The House's involvement runs on a sixty-year cycle of the same three moves: hearing, denial, statute.

Move one, 1966. On April 5, 1966 the Committee on Armed Services of the House of Representatives, 89th Congress, second session, held a hearing on Unidentified Flying Objects, convened after pressure from House Minority Leader Gerald Ford. The Air Force sent Secretary Harold Brown, and Project Blue Book sent Major Hector Quintanilla, its serving chief, and Dr. J. Allen Hynek, its scientific consultant. Brown put the Air Force position on the record: no evidence that UFOs threatened national security or were extraterrestrial. Hynek used the same hearing to place on the record that the Air Force's practice of assigning conventional explanations to every report was a poverty of hypotheses, and to call for an independent civilian scientific panel. The Air Force's response was to fund the Condon study at the University of Colorado, which is the template: a congressional hearing produces not disclosure but an outsourced study whose public summary can be written to a conclusion. That is exactly what had already been done with Battelle and Special Report No. 14 eleven years earlier.

Move two, 2023 to 2026. On July 26, 2023 the Oversight Committee's Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, chaired by Rep. Glenn Grothman with Rep. Robert Garcia as ranking member, and driven by Reps. Tim Burchett and Anna Paulina Luna, held the first public hearing to take testimony from military pilots and whistleblowers. Ryan Graves's written statement placed three institutional claims into the record: that UAP in U.S. airspace are grossly underreported; that stigma is itself a national security problem; and that excessive classification is hiding what the government knows, with all UAP video classified secret or above since 2021. Graves also entered a specific, dated, attributable account of information suppression: his advisor Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue' attaching the GO FAST video, and the following day the email was removed from Gallaudet's system and from his deputy's, with no one ever discussing it again. Gallaudet's own stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That single paragraph in a House witness statement is the cleanest documented instance of a UAP record being pulled out of an official system.

By 2025 the House had institutionalized the effort. Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets and named Luna to chair it, with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member and Republican members Nancy Mace, Tim Burchett, Lauren Boebert, Eric Burlison, Eli Crane and Brandon Gill, and Democratic members Stephen Lynch, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Dave Min. On September 9, 2025 the task force held a hearing on restoring public trust through UAP transparency and whistleblower protection, taking testimony from Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland.

Move three, statute. The FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, sections 1841 through 1843, directed NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and required every federal agency to review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by October 20, 2024. The statutory definition of what belongs in the collection is the tell: copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence. Congress wrote non-human intelligence into a records statute. NARA's implementing metadata schema then required a mandatory Special Controls field populated with SAP, SCI, RD/FRD and FGI markings, and required the Department of Energy to be entered as a referral agency whenever a file contains Restricted Data or Formerly Restricted Data. The Archives built its intake to receive special-access and nuclear-classified UAP material before anyone had produced any. Separately, section 1687(b) of the same law made UAP-related independent research and development funding unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and the four congressional leaders. That provision exists because someone in Congress concluded that contractors were charging the taxpayer for UAP work through overhead while reporting nothing.

By 2026 the House had pivoted to attacking the contractor and FFRDC layer directly. Burlison's May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE, and his earlier letter to MIT Lincoln Laboratory, assert that a nonprofit FFRDC cannot become a private vault for federal records. On August 1, 2026 Burlison released, with administration authorization, preliminary implementation guidance for President Trump's directive on nondisclosure agreements binding current and former government employees and contractors with UAP information, and invited anyone who believes the directive applies to them to contact his office. That is a sitting member of the House offering himself as the intake channel for people whose NDAs may have just been waived. Running alongside it, and not through it, the administration began posting declassified interagency UAP files in May 2026 on war.gov/ufo, an executive release track that answers to no congressional deadline.

On September 9, 2025 the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets held a hearing on UAP transparency and whistleblower protection with witnesses Jeffrey Nuccetelli (U.S. Air Force veteran), Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp, and Dylan Borland (U.S. Air Force veteran).

The FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, sections 1841-1843, requires NARA to establish the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection' and required each federal agency to review, identify and organize each UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission to the National Archives by October 20, 2024.

The statutory scope of the UAP Records Collection is 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).'

NARA's metadata requirements for UAP records include a mandatory 'Special Controls' field to be populated with access or handling restrictions such as SAP, SCI, RD/FRD and FGI, and require the Department of Energy to be entered as a referral agency whenever a file contains Restricted Data or Formerly Restricted Data.

Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 (Dec. 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 621) provides that independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena 'shall not be allowable as indirect expenses' for covered contracts under DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless such material and information is made available to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.

Rep. Eric Burlison, a member of both the Oversight Committee and the Task Force, transmitted legislative interrogatories to The MITRE Corporation on May 22, 2026 and had previously sent a records demand to MIT Lincoln Laboratory concerning the Beacon Hill Study and the recording 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52'.

On August 1, 2026 Rep. Burlison publicly released, with administration authorization, preliminary implementation guidance for President Trump's directive on nondisclosure agreements covering current and former government employees and contractors with UAP-related information, following his July 21, 2026 statement inviting affected individuals to contact his office.

The Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 (118th Congress), introduced by the Chairman and Ranking Member of the House Oversight National Security Subcommittee, would allow civilian pilots to report UAP through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System, provide protection against retaliation, and make all UAP reports publicly available.

In May 2026 the administration began posting declassified interagency UAP files as part of President Trump's disclosure initiative, with the first tranche published on war.gov/ufo, an executive-branch release running parallel to, rather than through, the congressional records process.

blue-book-special-report-14.whatItIs: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, formally titled 'Analysis of Reports of Unidentified Aerial Objects,' dated 5 May 1955, is the largest statistical study of UFO reports the U.S. government has ever produced. The analysis was performed under contract by Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus, Ohio, under a project designation reported as Project STORK, using 3,201 cases with an information cut-off of the end of 1952. It was released publicly on October 25, 1955 through Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55.
blue-book-special-report-14.whyImplicated: The gap between what the study found and what the government said it found is the cleanest documented instance of deliberate framing in the entire record, and it is verifiable from two documents that were published together. The press release and Secretary of the Air Force Donald Quarles's accompanying statement told the public that the unknowns amounted to three per cent, a figure drawn from 131 sightings in the first four months of 1955, not from the 3,201-case study sample the report actually analyzed. The report body shows unknowns running far higher, and highest precisely where witness reliability was rated Excellent. The release also declined to name Battelle, describing the analysis only as the work of a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio. The full 316-page report was then not distributed, on stated grounds of printing cost, until a private citizen reprinted it. Every element of a concealment operation is present and dated: a suppressed dataset, a substituted statistic, an unnamed contractor, and a restricted distribution.
blue-book-special-report-14.narrative:
Start with what the report says about itself. Its own Summary states that the special study started in 1953, that to provide the study group with a complete set of files the information cut-off date was established as of the end of 1952, and that in these charts, 3201 cases have been used. It describes a three-part analytic method: a systematic attempt to find distinguishing characteristics in the data, a study of any trend or pattern, and an attempt to determine the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS represented observations of technological developments not known to this country. On the first of these it records a genuinely load-bearing finding: 'The first step in the analysis of the data revealed the existence of certain apparent similarities between cases of objects definitely identified and those not identified. Statistical methods of testing when applied indicated a low probability that these apparent similarities were significant.' Read plainly, Battelle tested whether the unknowns looked like the knowns and found that the resemblance did not hold up. That is the opposite of the conclusion the public was handed. The report then walks it back through re-evaluation, concluding that the probability the unknowns represented unknown technology was very small.

Now the release. Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55, dated October 25, 1955 and headlined 'AIR FORCE RELEASES STUDY ON UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL OBJECTS', opens with the flat assertion that no evidence of the existence of the popularly-termed flying saucers was found. It attributes the work to a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio, and never says the word Battelle. It then executes the substitution: since the instigation of the investigation more than seven years ago, methods and procedures have been so refined that of the 131 sightings reported during the first four months of 1955 only three per cent were listed as unknown. Secretary Quarles then attaches his name to that number: 'On the basis of this study we believe that no objects such as those popularly described as flying saucers have overflown the United States. I feel certain that even the unknown three per cent could have been explained as conventional phenomena or illusions if more complete observational data had been available.' The phrase on the basis of this study is doing enormous work. The study is the 3,201-case Battelle analysis. The three per cent is from a 131-case sample the study did not analyze, collected three years after the study's own cut-off date. The two are welded together in a single sentence and a Cabinet-level official signs it.

The attached Summary makes the substitution visible in its own numbers. For cases received before the end of 1952 it gives Unknown at 9 per cent; for the more recent tranche it gives Unknown at 3 per cent. Neither figure is the rate for the 3,201 cases whose charts and tables make up the report.

The body tells a different story, which is why the body was hard to get. Leon Davidson, a chemical engineer who had worked at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory and who reprinted the report photographically beginning in 1956, wrote in his publisher's analysis that the key to the answer is contained in Fig. 8 (orig. p. 24) and Tables A1, A2, and A3 (orig. pp. 107 and 108); that Fig. 8 shows Unknown sightings constitute 33.3 per cent of all the object sightings for which the reliability of the sighting is considered Excellent; and that Tables A1 through A3 agree, with the percentage of Unknown sightings not less than about 20 per cent even when sightings of lesser reliability are included. The distribution runs the wrong way for the official framing: the better the witness, the more likely the object stayed unidentified.

Distribution was the second layer of the concealment. Davidson reproduces a letter from Air Force Secretary Donald A. Quarles dated July 5, 1956 stating that it has been estimated that the cost of printing enough copies for distribution to the public through such outlets as libraries and academic institutions would be between $10 and $15 per copy. The 316-page full report was therefore never distributed. The non-availability became a matter of congressional record at the House Subcommittee on Government Information under Rep. John E. Moss on November 15, 1956. Davidson's privately financed edition, reproduced photographically page by page with the main text intact, is why the document exists in public hands at all.

One further anomaly sits in the photographic reproduction. Davidson points to original page 295, where the codes for Final Identification carry typewritten strikeovers: the category originally called Rockets and Missiles in the early analytic work was changed to read Insufficient Information, and the category originally called Electromagnetic Phenomenon was changed to read Unknown. If that reading of the page is correct, then the report's residual category was not an empty bin for the unexplained. It was a renamed bin for a hypothesis.

Battelle is the connective tissue. The same institute later formed UT-Battelle, the operator of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which per contemporary allegations received AARO's 2024 material analysis work. Battelle is also one of the entities Rep. Burlison named in his May 2026 MITRE interrogatories, alongside Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace. The organization that wrote the government's founding public statistical assessment of the phenomenon has never left the file.

waived-usap.whatItIs: A waived unacknowledged special access program is the most tightly held category in the Department of Defense classification system. Department of Defense training doctrine defines it in one sentence: 'Waived SAPs are unacknowledged SAPs for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting requirements under Section 119, Title 10 U.S. Code.' The waiver authority is 10 U.S.C. 119(e), under which the Secretary may withhold specified information from the statutory reports to Congress if he determines that including it would adversely affect national security, and must then provide the information and the justification for the waiver only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.
waived-usap.whyImplicated: This is the mechanism. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering program exists and has been concealed from Congress, waived SAP status is the lawful instrument by which that concealment is accomplished, and no unlawful act is required to sustain it. The statute permits an entire program's existence, cost, milestones and technology to disappear from the reports Congress wrote to keep itself informed, on the unilateral written determination of a single official. The population read in on the legislative side collapses to eight members and, per DoD policy, their staff directors. Everyone else in Congress, including every member of both intelligence committees who is not chair or ranking, can hold a Top Secret clearance and still be told nothing exists. The system is designed to produce truthful denials from officials who genuinely do not know, which is the precise pathology alleged across every UAP whistleblower account since 2017.
waived-usap.narrative:
The architecture has four layers, and each one narrows the audience.

Layer one is the baseline reporting duty. 10 U.S.C. 119, added by Public Law 100-180 section 1132(a)(1) on December 4, 1987, required the Secretary of Defense to submit to the defense committees an annual report on special access programs by March 1 of each year, setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP, a brief description, its major milestones, its actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and its estimated total cost across the current year, the budget year and four succeeding years. Subsection (b) required a separate annual report by February 1 giving notice and justification for each new SAP designation, with the current total program cost estimate and an identification of existing programs or technologies similar in technology or mission to the one being hidden. Subsection (f), added by Public Law 101-510 section 1482(a)(2) in November 1990, added the hard gate: a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

Layer two is the waiver. Subsection (e)(1) provides that the Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security, with each waiver made on a case-by-case basis. Subsection (e)(2) then routes the withheld information and the justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists put the practical result plainly: waived SAPs are exempted by statute (10 USC 119e) from normal congressional notification requirements, and in such cases only eight senior members of the congressional defense committees may be advised of the program.

Layer three is DoD policy, which is more restrictive than the statute. Under the pre-2024 SAP policy framework, only the chair, the ranking minority member and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's oversight role, absent approval by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary. The currently effective directive, DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued September 12, 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, adds a provision that is the operational choke point for whistleblowers: no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval. The people most likely to hold the evidence are contractors, and the directive forbids them from handing it to Congress without permission from the office that runs the SAP system.

Layer four is the quiet erosion of the reporting baseline itself. The U.S. Code note under section 119 records that for termination, effective December 31, 2021, of the provisions in subsections (a) and (b) requiring submittal of an annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notification report, the two instruments the 1987 Congress built, were sunset by a general reporting-requirement cull. And the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 does not define waived SAP anywhere in its glossary. It defines SAP, SAP architecture, SAP umbrella, SAP compartment, SAP sub-compartment, Joint Force Integration SAP and Strategic Enabler SAP. The acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy that appears in DoD's own training material has been replaced in the public directive by a vocabulary that does not distinguish between programs Congress is told about and programs it is not. Whether that is reform or relabeling, the public governing document no longer names the category.

The rest of the directive maps the custody chain. All DoD SAPs are assigned to an oversight authority drawn from USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), USD(I&S) and the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. The Director of DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, holds delegated Top Secret original classification authority for all DoD SAP information, publishes and maintains the security classification guides for every SAP umbrella, accredits congressional SAP facilities, and maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is by exception and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. The senior governing body, the SAP Oversight Committee, is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. Approximately 75 to 80 per cent of all DoD SAPs are acquisition SAPs, which is the category that would cover a materials exploitation or reverse-engineering effort.

Congress has attacked the funding side rather than the classification side. FY2024 NDAA section 1687(b) makes independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material and information is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. That is an admission on the face of the statute that Congress believed UAP work was being charged to the taxpayer through contractor overhead and reported to no one. It is also a route around the waiver, because IR&D allowability is an accounting question, not a classification question.

waived-usap.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue, because the Department has never publicly acknowledged any individual waived SAP; acknowledging one would defeat the category. What is on the record instead is a quieter act: the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoD Directive 5205.07 removed the acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy from the public policy document entirely, while DoD's own unclassified training material continues to teach it. The public governing directive no longer names the category by which programs are lawfully hidden from Congress.
