americans-for-safe-aerospace.whatItIs: Americans for Safe Aerospace (ASA) is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2023 by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18F pilot from strike fighter squadron VFA-11. It operates a confidential intake channel through which military and commercial aircrew report UAP encounters, and it functions as the principal non-governmental witness pipeline into Congress. Headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC, it describes itself as the world's largest UAP advocacy community and reported more than 30,000 members as of 2026, up from roughly 4,000 at its founding.
americans-for-safe-aerospace.whyImplicated: ASA is the institution that solved the collection problem the government created. Because there is no protected, non-stigmatizing reporting route for commercial pilots, and because military witnesses face a confusing internal process, the observational data that would test the phenomenon has never been aggregated by the state. ASA aggregates it privately and then feeds it to Congress, which is why its founder's July 2023 testimony landed as the first public congressional hearing to take military pilot and whistleblower evidence. More importantly for a concealment map, ASA is where several people who were inside the classified system have landed: Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force; Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence; Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former head of NOAA and Oceanographer of the Navy; and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. That roster means ASA holds institutional memory of both the task force that collected the data and the committee staff that wrote the oversight statutes. It is a private organization staffed with the government's own former custodians.
americans-for-safe-aerospace.narrative:
ASA's origin is a specific failure of the reporting system. Graves joined the Navy in 2009 and by 2014 was flying with VFA-11 near Virginia Beach when a radar upgrade began producing unknown tracks that were initially dismissed as software glitches and then corroborated on infrared, confirming their physical presence. The sightings became routine enough to appear in daily briefs. The pivotal event was in Warning Area W-72, an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach where all traffic enters through a single GPS point at a set altitude. As two jets crossed the threshold one hundred feet apart, one pilot saw a dark gray cube inside a clear sphere, motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. Both aircraft took evasive action and terminated the mission. The squadron filed a safety report. There was no official acknowledgement and no mechanism to report further sightings. Graves founded ASA to build the mechanism that did not exist.

The organization scaled faster than anyone planned. Its July 18, 2023 launch release for the UAP Witness Campaign stated that more than 30 commercial aircrew and military witnesses had already approached it and that ASA had more than 4,000 members. Eight days later, in written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, Graves reported nearly 5,000 members and more than 30 UAP witnesses being actively worked. By 2026 the public membership figure is over 30,000. The witness profile is itself a finding: the majority are commercial pilots at major airlines, often veterans with decades of experience, and their reports frequently open with an apology, in Graves's phrasing, 'I apologize, I realize this will sound crazy.' They describe objects at altitudes apparently above 40,000 feet, potentially in low earth orbit or in the grey zone below the Karman line, executing right-hand turns, retrograde orbits and j-hooks, with recurring clusters north of Hawaii and in the North Atlantic. They are adamant these are not Starlink flares.

ASA's process is deliberately witness-controlled. A pilot or veteran contacts the organization confidentially with an outline, ASA conducts an interview, brings in an advisor with relevant expertise for evaluation, and only then, and only with the witness's explicit permission, are next steps taken, which can include meetings with congressional staff and Members or with AARO. Most witnesses do not want to speak publicly and fear professional consequences; they want their account added to the data set. That design is a direct response to the retaliation problem that runs through the whole file.

The advisory bench is what makes ASA structurally significant rather than merely large. Its pilots include David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, the first former Navy pilots to meet with Congress about their UAP encounter, plus Michael Greene and Sam Fletcher. Its national security advisors are Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force, Christopher Mellon, Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff on the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is the committee that wrote the AARO statutes and whose chair and ranking member sit inside the eight-member waived-SAP notification group. Its policy advisors include Susan McCue, former chief of staff to Senator Harry Reid, and Bryan Bender, former defense editor at Politico, plus Mike Gold of the NASA UAP Independent Study Team and David Radzanowski, former CFO and Chief of Staff at NASA. Its science bench includes Avi Loeb of Harvard, Garry Nolan of Stanford, Robin Hanson of George Mason and Ravi Starzl of Carnegie Mellon.

The single most operationally important thing ASA has put on the congressional record came through Gallaudet. Graves testified that while serving as an Admiral with Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from the Operations Commander to all one- and two-star subordinates, titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue', attaching the GO FAST video and raising concerns about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach, with a note that the exercise might be shut down for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was removed from both of their systems, and despite routine in-person meetings with that group, no one ever discussed it again. Gallaudet's stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That is a flag officer, on the record through a congressional witness, describing the retroactive deletion of a safety-of-flight communication.

Graves also entered two hard data points into the House record: that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 there had been eleven near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment of June 25, 2021, and that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. He also flagged an unexplained reversal by AARO's director, who told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview shortly before the hearing that he had what he needed.

On policy, ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 in the 118th Congress, which would let civilian pilots report through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System with anti-retaliation protection and public release of all reports, a mechanism recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team. ASA's July 2023 release also documents the organization's read of the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023, sponsored by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, whose central mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena UAP witnesses and documents.

claims.text: Americans for Safe Aerospace is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy lieutenant and F/A-18 pilot, headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC 20006; Graves is Founder and Executive Director.

As of 2026 ASA publicly reports more than 30,000 members and describes itself as 'the world's largest UAP advocacy community dedicated to pilot support, aerospace safety, data-driven research, and analysis of UAP.'

At launch of its UAP Witness Campaign on July 18, 2023, ASA stated that 'More than 30 commercial aircrew and military witnesses have already approached ASA to share their accounts' and that the organization had more than 4,000 members.

In written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs on July 26, 2023, Graves stated ASA had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses who have approached us.'

Graves testified that ASA advisor Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former head of NOAA and Oceanographer of the Navy, received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 while serving with Fleet Forces Command, titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue', attaching the GO FAST video and citing multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP off Virginia Beach; the email was removed from Gallaudet's system and his deputy's the next day and was never discussed, and Gallaudet 'presumes the email was removed in connection with a classified special access program.'

Graves testified to the W-72 incident: two F/A-18s entering Warning Area W-72 ten miles east of Virginia Beach through a single GPS entry point, one hundred feet apart, when a pilot saw 'a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere, motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point'; the jets took evasive action, terminated the mission, and the squadron's safety report received no official acknowledgement and no further reporting mechanism.
Graves testified that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 that there were 11 near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment on UAP dated June 25, 2021.

Graves testified that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operation managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP.

ASA's national security advisory bench includes Jay Stratton (former Director, UAP Task Force), Christopher Mellon (former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence), Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet (former head of NOAA), and Kirk McConnell (former professional staff, Senate Armed Services Committee).

ASA's aircrew leadership includes David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, the first former Navy pilots to meet with Congress about their UAP encounter, plus Michael Greene (former U.S. Marines F/A-18 weapons system officer) and Sam Fletcher (former U.S. Navy F/A-18 weapons system officer).

ASA's policy and science advisors include Susan McCue (former chief of staff to Senator Harry Reid), Bryan Bender (former defense editor, Politico), Mike Gold (former NASA UAP Independent Study Team member), David Radzanowski (former CFO and Chief of Staff, NASA), Avi Loeb (Harvard), Garry Nolan (Stanford), Robin Hanson (George Mason) and Ravi Starzl (Carnegie Mellon).

ASA's witness process is witness-controlled: confidential outline, ASA interview, evaluation with a subject-matter advisor, then referral to congressional staff, Members, or AARO 'only at the explicit permission and willingness of the UAP witness.'

ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 (118th Congress), which would allow civilian pilots to report UAP through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System, provide protection against retaliation, and make all UAP reports publicly available; the mechanism was recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team.

ASA documented that the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 was proposed by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, and that its key mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to 'hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena [UAP] witnesses and documents' in connection with declassifying UAP documents for public distribution.

Its posture toward the government's own position is captured in Graves's testimony noting that AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview a week before the hearing that he had what he needed, a reversal Graves flagged on the record as unexplained.

senate-armed-services.whatItIs: The Committee on Armed Services of the United States Senate, one of the four congressional defense committees named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g), and therefore one of the bodies whose chairman and ranking minority member sit inside the eight-member group that may be advised of a waived special access program. SASC is also the drafting venue for the annual National Defense Authorization Act provisions that created the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, defined unidentified anomalous phenomena in statute, and progressively tightened the reporting obligations attached to them.
senate-armed-services.whyImplicated: SASC occupies the structural pinch point: it is simultaneously the committee that is supposed to receive notification of the most closely held programs and the committee that keeps writing new statutes because it apparently is not receiving it. The language it has enacted is an admission. 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) requires AARO's historical record report to itemize any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress, and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about UAP. Congress does not write that sentence about a subject on which it believes it has been told the truth. Subsection (l)(4) goes further, requiring the AARO Director to hand the SASC and SSCI chair and ranking member an enumeration of every instance in which UAP data was withheld from AARO because of classification restrictions or for any other reason, which is a statutory acknowledgment that data is being withheld from the office created to collect it. And in December 2025 Congress had to amend the statute again to extend the immediate data-availability requirement beyond intelligence community elements to Department of Defense components, meaning that for three years the mandate did not reach the department that owns the special access program system.
senate-armed-services.narrative:
Follow the statutory ratchet, because it is a record of what did not work.

In December 2021, section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, 135 Stat. 2118, created the office structure and authorities to address what were then called unidentified aerial phenomena. Twelve months later, in December 2022, Public Law 117-263 rewrote the section twice over: section 1673(c) of the NDAA substituted anomalous for aerial throughout and added congressional leadership to the notification list, while section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act amended the section generally, standing up the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office proper. The Senate-side drive came from SASC members, principally Senator Kirsten Gillibrand working with Senator Marco Rubio.

What the rewritten section actually demands is the interesting part. AARO's duties include developing procedures to synchronize and standardize the collection, reporting and analysis of UAP incidents, including adverse physiological effects, across the entire Department of Defense and intelligence community. The Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence must jointly designate an official responsible for ensuring the expertise, authorities, accesses, data, systems, platforms and capabilities exist for rapid response to and support for field investigations, and must designate one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of data, including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models. Congress wrote materials testing and medical studies into the statute. It also required that each designated line organization have authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the federal government with appropriate security clearances, and it listed the Department of Energy among the elements that may detail personnel to be physically located at the office.

The historical record report in subsection (j) is the closest thing to a congressional charge sheet in U.S. law. It requires a written report to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership covering the period beginning January 1, 1945, compiling the key historical record of intelligence community involvement with UAP, and specifically itemizing three things: any restricted-access program or activity not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track UAP; and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect information, classified or unclassified. The Archivist of the United States is directed to make NARA holdings, including classified holdings, available to AARO for that purpose. Congress then attached an auditor: section 6803 of Public Law 117-263 required the Comptroller General to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the historical record report process, to conduct work on site as appropriate, and to brief the intelligence committees, the defense committees and congressional leadership semiannually on AARO's progress and its compliance with legislative requirements. That requirement was extended by Public Law 118-159 section 6802 in December 2024.

The FY2024 NDAA added the money lever. Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 made independent research and development funding relating to UAP unallowable as an indirect expense on contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. This is the appropriations-side answer to the classification-side problem, and its existence implies a belief that contractors were recovering UAP-related costs through overhead.

The FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60, enacted December 18, 2025, shows what still was not working. Section 1671 added a new subsection (l)(5) requiring every semiannual briefing to include details on any UAP intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or United States Northern Command, including the number, location and nature of the intercepts and a description of the procedures and protocols followed, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts, and requiring the AARO Director to inform Congress of any failure by NORAD or NORTHCOM to provide timely information. Section 1671(b) reached backward, requiring the first briefing after enactment to cover intercepts not previously reported going back to January 1, 2004. Section 1673(a) gave the AARO Director 180 days to produce an accounting of the security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, with discretionary authority to issue a consolidated security classification matrix. Section 1672(b) rewrote the data-availability clause so that the immediate-production requirement now binds each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with UAP data, where the prior text bound only intelligence community elements.

That last amendment is the single most damning line in the sequence. From December 2022 to December 2025, the statutory command to hand UAP data over immediately did not reach Department of Defense components as such. The department that operates the special access program system, that houses DoD SAPCO, and that owns the classification guides sat outside the mandate for three years, and it took an act of Congress in December 2025 to close it.

What SASC has not delivered is the enforcement architecture. The UAP Disclosure Act, offered by Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds as an NDAA amendment and modeled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act, would have created a nine-member presidentially appointed civilian Review Board with subpoena power and would have asserted federal eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private entities. The Review Board and the eminent domain provision were stripped in conference in FY2024, and the Act was excluded again from the FY2026 NDAA. What survived was a records collection with no independent adjudicator. The one provision that would have reached into contractor custody, eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin, is the one that has never made it into law.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1) names the Committee on Armed Services of the Senate as one of the 'defense committees' entitled to special access program notification, making its chairman and ranking minority member two of the eight members who may be advised of a waived SAP under section 119(e)(2).

The statutory basis for AARO originates in section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, division A, title XVI, December 27, 2021, 135 Stat. 2118, and was amended generally by Public Law 117-263 section 1673(c) and Intelligence Authorization Act section 6802(a) on December 23, 2022.

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(III) requires the report to include 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

Section 1672(b) of the FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 (December 18, 2025, 139 Stat. 1202), amended 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to require that 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' with UAP data make it immediately available to AARO; the prior text bound only intelligence community elements.

Section 1671(a) of Public Law 119-60 added 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(5), requiring each semiannual briefing to detail any UAP intercepts conducted by NORAD or U.S. Northern Command, including 'the number, location, and nature of such intercepts' and 'a description of the procedures and protocols followed during the intercepts, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts', and requiring notice to Congress of any failure by NORAD or NORTHCOM to provide timely information.

50 U.S.C. 3373(i) lists the Department of Energy among the elements that may provide detailees to be physically located at AARO, alongside CIA, DIA, NSA, NGA, the service intelligence elements and DHS.

Section 6803 of Public Law 117-263 required the Comptroller General to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the AARO historical record report process, including on-site work, and to brief the intelligence committees, defense committees and congressional leadership semiannually on AARO's progress and compliance with legislative requirements; the requirement was extended by Public Law 118-159 section 6802 (December 23, 2024).

Section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA, Public Law 118-31 (137 Stat. 621), bars UAP-related independent research and development funding from being allowable as an indirect expense on contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, HPSCI, SSCI and the four congressional leaders.

The UAP Disclosure Act, offered by Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA and modeled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act, would have created a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths and subpoena witnesses and documents, and would have asserted eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private entities; the Review Board and eminent domain provisions were stripped in conference and the Act was again excluded from the FY2026 NDAA.

uapda-fy2027-house-adopted.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act as adopted by the U.S. House of Representatives on 22 July 2026 as an amendment to the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (H.R. 8800, 119th Congress). It would create a permanent UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, stand up an independent Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority, and extend disclosure obligations to covered government contractors. It is the first time the full JFK-Act-style disclosure architecture has cleared a chamber of Congress since the original Schumer-Rounds text was gutted in conference in December 2023.
uapda-fy2027-house-adopted.whyImplicated: The amendment is written on the assumption that UAP records exist outside the reach of ordinary congressional oversight, in agency holdings and in contractor holdings, and that the agencies holding them will not surrender them voluntarily. Three design choices give that away: the records collection is compulsory and on a statutory timeline rather than voluntary; the review board is given subpoena power rather than a request authority; and disclosure obligations are extended to 'covered government contractors,' which is meaningless unless Congress believes private firms hold federal UAP records. Burlison's own framing, that records have 'remained scattered across agencies and outside meaningful oversight,' is a sitting member of Congress stating on the record that the existing oversight architecture does not reach the material. The amendment also explicitly positions itself as statutory backstop to a presidential declassification effort (PURSUE), which is an admission that executive-branch goodwill is not considered durable. Every one of those features is a legislative inference about the concealment structure, drawn by people with access to classified briefings.
uapda-fy2027-house-adopted.narrative:
The Burlison amendment is the third act of a five-year legislative arc, and the arc itself is the evidence.

Act one was July 2023, when Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds introduced the UAP Disclosure Act as Senate Amendment 797 to S.2226, the FY2024 NDAA, explicitly modeled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992. That text carried a presumption of immediate disclosure, an independent review board, presidential authority to overturn board determinations, a hard 25-year outer deadline, and — the provision that made the defense industry move — federal eminent domain over 'recovered technologies of unknown origin' and biological evidence held by private persons. The Senate adopted it 84 to 0. An eminent domain clause is not written into a defense bill as an abstraction. It is written because the drafters believe there is specific property, in specific private hands, that the government cannot presently compel.

Act two was December 2023. In conference with the House, the review board, the eminent domain provision and the presidential certification mechanism were stripped. What survived became Sections 1841 through 1843 of Public Law 118-31, which directed the Archivist to establish a UAP Records Collection at NARA and required agencies to identify, organize and begin transmitting UAP records. The surviving language was the filing cabinet without the locksmith: a collection with no independent body empowered to second-guess an agency's decision to withhold, and no reach into contractor vaults. Agencies were left as the sole judges of what constituted a covered record.

Act three is 2025-2026. Burlison, a Missouri Republican on the House Oversight Committee, reintroduced the disclosure act as an NDAA amendment during FY2026 consideration; it did not reach a floor vote. He came back for FY2027. On 22 July 2026 the House adopted his amendment to H.R. 8800, and later that day passed the underlying bill 216 to 212 on Roll Call 278. The press release from his office is precise about what the amendment restores: 'a permanent UAP Records Collection at the National Archives,' 'an independent, Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority to review records, hear testimony, and determine whether information should remain protected under standards established by law,' and extension of disclosure requirements 'to covered government contractors.' The review board is back. The contractor reach is back. Eminent domain is not mentioned.

The contractor clause is the load-bearing provision for anyone mapping the legacy program. Under the existing FY2024 architecture, a record physically held by a prime or a subcontractor under an IRAD-funded or SAP-funded effort is not obviously a 'federal record' subject to transmission. The FY2023 statutory scheme had already tried to grip this problem from a different angle: 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(1)(B) protects authorized disclosure of any activity 'by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency' relating to UAP including 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering,' and 3373b(b)(3)(A) ordered federal agencies and their contractors to conduct comprehensive searches of records relating to UAP nondisclosure orders and hand copies to AARO. A subpoena-armed review board with contractor jurisdiction is the enforcement mechanism those provisions never had.

The PURSUE relationship is the other tell. The press release says the amendment would 'support President Trump's Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE)' by 'bolstering in law authorities for carrying out disclosure.' PURSUE is a Department of War declassification and release effort standing at war.gov/ufo, running on rolling tranches. A legislator who trusted an executive declassification program to be complete and permanent would not spend a year of floor strategy building a Senate-confirmed board with subpoena power to sit alongside it. The amendment is insurance against the possibility that PURSUE releases what the executive branch chooses to release and stops there.

What happens next is a conference fight. The FY2027 NDAA moved to the Senate; the House-passed disclosure architecture will meet whatever the Senate produces, and the 2023 precedent is that the strongest provisions die quietly in conference without a recorded vote. Conference is where the concealment structure has historically been most effective, because it is the one stage of the legislative process with no roll call, no floor debate and no public amendment text.

isoo.whatItIs: The Information Security Oversight Office, a component of the National Archives and Records Administration, established by Section 5.2 of Executive Order 13526 to develop implementing directives for the national security classification system, oversee agency compliance, and report at least annually to the President. Its Director is appointed by the Archivist of the United States subject to the approval of the President; the current Director is Michael D. Thomas, successor to Mark A. Bradley. ISOO is, on paper, the only government-wide civilian oversight body for classified information.
isoo.whyImplicated: ISOO is implicated by absence, not by action. In fifty years of annual reports to the President, ISOO has never reported the existence of a program engaged in the recovery or exploitation of non-human craft — and the reason is that the Executive Order that created ISOO also built the trapdoor through which such a program would fall. Section 4.3(b)(3) of E.O. 13526 says the ISOO Director 'shall be afforded access' to special access programs, then immediately permits an agency head to limit that access to the Director plus one employee, or, for programs deemed 'extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable,' to the Director alone. Section 5.2(b)(4) goes further: an agency head who believes ISOO access would pose 'an exceptional national security risk' may recommend denial to the President through the National Security Advisor, and 'Access shall be denied pending the response.' The denial is self-executing. ISOO's oversight is therefore contingent on the consent of the agency being overseen. Every ISOO annual report is an accounting of the classification system that a concealed waived SAP would not appear in, and ISOO would not know it was missing.
isoo.narrative:
ISOO is the institution people point to when they say the classification system has oversight. Read the authorities and the picture inverts: ISOO is the institution that documents the boundary of what oversight cannot see.

The charter is Executive Order 13526, signed 29 December 2009. Section 5.2(a) places ISOO inside the National Archives and gives the Archivist the appointment power over its Director, subject to presidential approval. Section 5.2(b) lists nine functions: develop directives, oversee agency compliance, approve agency implementing regulations, conduct on-site reviews, review requests for original classification authority, take action on complaints, standardize forms, report annually to the President, and chair interagency meetings. Section 5.1(a) makes ISOO directives 'binding on the agencies.' On its face this is real authority.

Then come the carve-outs, and they are written with unusual care.

Section 5.2(b)(4) grants ISOO the authority to conduct on-site reviews of any agency program 'and to require of each agency those reports and information and other cooperation that may be necessary to fulfill its responsibilities.' The very next sentence is the trapdoor: 'If granting access to specific categories of classified information would pose an exceptional national security risk, the affected agency head or the senior agency official shall submit a written justification recommending the denial of access to the President through the National Security Advisor within 60 days of the request for access. Access shall be denied pending the response.' An agency head who wants to keep ISOO out of a compartment does not need to win an argument. He needs to file a paper and wait. Access is denied by default during the pendency, and the order sets no deadline for the President to respond.

Section 4.3 is where the structure becomes specific to special access programs. Only six officials may create a SAP — the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each. Section 4.3(b)(2) requires each agency head to 'establish and maintain a system of accounting for special access programs' — note that the accounting system is the agency's, not ISOO's. Section 4.3(b)(3) provides ISOO access, then caps it: 'An agency head may limit access to a special access program to the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.' A single human being, with no staff, no analysts, and no ability to delegate, is the entire oversight footprint for the most sensitive category of American secrecy.

And then Section 4.3(c), one sentence, easy to skip: 'Nothing in this order shall supersede any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119.' Section 119 of Title 10 is the congressional SAP oversight statute. It requires annual reports to the defense committees identifying each SAP, its cost history, and its milestones — and subsection (e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content requirement 'if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security,' delivering the information instead only 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' That is the statutory birth certificate of the waived SAP: a program known to four members of Congress and to no one else on the Hill. E.O. 13526 does not disturb it.

The oversight picture then gets worse, not better. The Office of Law Revision Counsel's note to 10 U.S.C. 119 records that the annual reporting requirements in subsections (a) and (b) — the SAP inventory and the new-program notification — were terminated effective 31 December 2021 by Section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The one recurring, statutory, cross-committee accounting of DoD special access programs sunset four years ago, in the same window in which Congress was writing UAP oversight law on the assumption that unreported restricted-access programs existed.

So the analytical position is this. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort is carried as a waived unacknowledged SAP or under a non-DoD authority such as an Atomic Energy Act restricted-data compartment, ISOO would have no independent way to detect it. It has no access it cannot be denied, no staff it can bring, no inventory it maintains itself, and no statutory partner report to cross-check against since 2021. ISOO's annual report to the President — the FY2024 edition was transmitted in early August 2025 and publicly issued on 18 September 2025 by Director Michael D. Thomas, the first of his tenure, restructured around four areas of action — is an honest accounting of the classification system as agencies choose to describe it to ISOO.

That is the argument. ISOO is not a participant in concealment. ISOO is the measuring instrument that was built with a blind spot exactly the shape of the thing being hidden, and the blind spot was written into the order by the same executive branch that would be operating in it.

claims.text: The Information Security Oversight Office is established within the National Archives by Section 5.2(a) of Executive Order 13526, and its Director is appointed by the Archivist of the United States subject to the approval of the President.

E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(b)(3) permits an agency head to limit ISOO's access to a special access program to 'the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.'

E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.2(b)(4) provides that where an agency head recommends denial of ISOO access on grounds of 'exceptional national security risk,' the written justification goes to the President through the National Security Advisor within 60 days and 'Access shall be denied pending the response.'
Under E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(b)(2), the system of accounting for special access programs is maintained by each agency head, not by ISOO.

Only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program absent separate presidential authorization.

E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3(c) states in full: 'Nothing in this order shall supersede any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119,' preserving the statutory SAP reporting regime and its waiver mechanism intact against the classification order.

10 U.S.C. 119(e) authorizes the Secretary of Defense to waive, case by case, any requirement that specified information be included in a SAP report to the defense committees where inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' and to provide that information and the waiver justification only 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

The annual SAP reporting requirements in 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) were terminated effective 31 December 2021 by Section 1061 of Public Law 114-328, eliminating the recurring statutory inventory of DoD special access programs delivered to the defense committees.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) bars initiation of a special access program until the defense committees are notified and 30 days elapse — a notification requirement that survives the 2021 termination of the annual reports.

ISOO directives issued under E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.1(a) are 'binding on the agencies,' and Sec. 5.2(b)(8) requires the Director to report at least annually to the President on implementation of the order.

ISOO transmitted its Fiscal Year 2024 Annual Report to the President in early August 2025 and publicly issued it on 18 September 2025; it was the first annual report of Director Michael D. Thomas's tenure and restructured ISOO's mission into four areas: Oversight and Compliance, Guidance and Implementation, Data Collection and Analysis, and Administration and Engagement.

ISOO's published annual reports run back to 1979, providing a continuous forty-five-year government-wide accounting of the classification system in which no recovery or exploitation program for non-human technology has been reported.
claims.source: https://www.archives.gov/isoo/reports/annual-report-archive.html ; see also https://isoo-overview.blogs.archives.gov/2025/09/18/announcing-the-publication-of-isoos-fiscal-year-2024-annual-report-to-the-president/ ('I studied our prior releases, dating all the way back to 1979')

claims.text: Under E.O. 13526 Sec. 5.2(b)(6), ISOO is required to 'consider and take action on complaints and suggestions from persons within or outside the Government' regarding administration of the classification program, providing a standing external channel that has not, on the public record, produced a UAP-related classification finding.

ISOO sits inside the same agency, NARA, that the FY2024 NDAA designated as custodian of the UAP Records Collection and that the FY2027 Burlison amendment would make the permanent home of that collection.

isoo.denialPosture: ISOO does not deny the existence of a legacy program; it has never made an affirmative public statement on the subject either way. Its posture is structural silence — an annual report to the President that accounts for the classification system as agencies self-report it, produced by an office that E.O. 13526 permits any of six agency heads to lock out of the relevant compartment with a single memorandum to the National Security Advisor.

It owns DoD security policy, counterintelligence, and the department's interface with the DoD Special Access Program Central Office. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B)(i), the Director of AARO reports to the USD(I&S) on all administrative matters of the office.
ousdi.whyImplicated: OUSD(I&S) is the office that produced the paper trail of the Elizondo counter-narrative, and that paper trail is the cleanest documentary evidence in the entire record of a deliberate, dated, signed effort by a defense component to control the public account of a UAP program. Its Director for Defense Intelligence, Garry Reid, wrote a memorandum for record in late December 2017 — within a week of the New York Times AATIP story — asserting that Luis Elizondo had 'aggrandized his role' and that to the best of Reid's knowledge Elizondo 'had no job responsibilities related to the AATIP,' while simultaneously initiating an AFOSI inquiry into Elizondo's handling of classified material. The Pentagon then sat on that determination for eighteen months before deploying it publicly through spokesman Christopher Sherwood in June 2019, and afterwards quietly amended the wording from 'no responsibilities' to 'no assigned responsibilities.' The same office holds administrative authority over AARO, the body Congress created to investigate the concealment, and it is the department's SAP security-policy owner. The entity that ran the counter-narrative also holds the keys to the compartments and supervises the investigators.
ousdi.narrative:
OUSD(I&S) is where the security state's plumbing and its press strategy meet, and the December 2017 file shows both running at once.

The charter first. DoD Directive 5143.01, reissued 24 October 2014 and updated by Change 2 on 6 April 2020, sets the USD(I&S)'s responsibilities, functions, relationships and authorities pursuant to 10 U.S.C. 113 and 137, 50 U.S.C. 3001 et seq., Public Law 108-458, and Executive Orders 12333, 13470 and 13869. The 'and Security' in the title was added in 2019-2020 and is the whole point: this office does not merely produce intelligence, it writes the rules for who may know things. It coordinates with the Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office on SAP matters involving ODNI and the intelligence community, and it runs the department's counterintelligence, law enforcement and security enterprise. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B)(i), enacted by Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA, the Director of AARO 'shall report... to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters of the Office.' Operational and security matters go to the Deputy Secretary and the Principal Deputy DNI; administration — staffing, funding, personnel, facilities — goes to OUSD(I&S). Congress placed the investigative body's housekeeping under the office whose predecessor had spent five years managing the Elizondo problem.

Now the file. Records obtained by The Black Vault under FOIA establish the sequence.

3 October 2017: Elizondo submits a resignation letter, received by his direct supervisor John Garrity III. A second, differently worded resignation letter — the one public since 2018 — is later characterized in Reid's memo as having 'uncertain provenance' and as never delivered to the Secretary of Defense.

12 October 2017: Reid learns of the To The Stars Academy launch, at which Elizondo appears as Director of Global Security and Special Programs one week after leaving DoD and states that TTSA plans to provide 'never-before-released footage from real U.S. government systems.' Reid contacts the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. AFOSI finds no 'tangible indicators' of misconduct and declines to open a case.

7 December 2017: The New York Times contacts DoD about AATIP and Elizondo.

15 December 2017: The OUSD(I) Security Officer is notified that Elizondo may have 'misused government systems' and 'may intend to release [U.S. government] footage or information that he obtained during his employment with OUSD(I).'

16 December 2017: 'Glowing Auras and Black Money' publishes, carrying the FLIR1 and Gimbal videos captioned as released by AATIP and courtesy of the Department of Defense. The same two videos appear on TTSA's YouTube channel.

18 December 2017: OUSD(I) discovers a classified email Elizondo sent to a Navy civilian in August 2017 requesting assistance getting videos declassified, with the same videos attached.

21 December 2017: Reid meets AFOSI agents to initiate a formal inquiry into Elizondo's possible mishandling of classified materials. AFOSI concludes the investigation in April 2018. No charges are known to have followed.

23 December 2017: A copy of Reid's memorandum for record carries handwritten marginal notes and initials dated '12/23' believed to be those of Secretary of Defense James N. Mattis, including a question whether Elizondo's 'sudden departure' was a 'counter-intelligence alarm?'

The two propositions in that file cannot both be casually true. If Elizondo had no job responsibilities related to AATIP, the department's own security office had no reason to fear that he would release government footage 'obtained during his employment with OUSD(I),' and Reid had no reason to open a counterintelligence inquiry about material he possessed. The counter-narrative and the counterintelligence action are internally inconsistent, and both were produced by the same office in the same week.

The eighteen-month gap is the other artifact. The determination was reached in December 2017. It was not made public until June 2019, when spokesman Christopher Sherwood told The Intercept that Elizondo 'had no responsibilities with regard to the AATIP program while he worked in OUSDI... up until the time he resigned effective 10/4/2017.' That formulation was later revised to 'no assigned responsibilities' — a lawyer's edit, narrowing a claim about what a man did to a claim about what was written in his position description. Departments do not narrow their own denials unless the broader version is indefensible.

Reid himself was removed in April 2022, following a nearly two-year investigation by The Debrief; the stated cause was an inappropriate relationship and favoritism with a colleague, not the Elizondo matter, and sources described him as the person most directly responsible for preventing further UAP video releases and for retaliating against Elizondo. The office continued. Bradley Hansell was confirmed as USD(I&S) by the Senate 61-35 and took office 25 July 2025, succeeding acting Under Secretary Dustin Gard-Weiss.

For an analyst the significance is structural rather than personal. The record shows that when a UAP disclosure event occurred, the response was generated inside OUSD(I&S) by the Director for Defense Intelligence, coordinated with a service investigative agency, briefed to the Secretary of Defense within a week, and held in reserve for eighteen months before public deployment. That is not confusion. That is an information operation run through a security-policy office — and the same office now holds administrative authority over AARO and coordination authority over DoD SAPs.

michels-gerb-structural-episode.whatItIs: The long-form interview 'The Hidden UFO Program Is Real - Here's How It Works! (ft. UAPGerb),' published 11 January 2026 on American Alchemy with Jesse Michels, running three hours and fifty-four minutes. In it the pseudonymous open-source researcher UAPGerb walks Michels through a claimed organizational map of the legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort: the contractor hierarchy, the administering agencies, the facilities, and the named individuals. It is the most detailed publicly available attempt to render the concealment structure as an org chart rather than an anecdote.
michels-gerb-structural-episode.whyImplicated: This episode matters not as testimony but as a hypothesis document. Its published chapter structure is itself a claim about how the program is organized — 'Legacy Programs,' 'The Pyramid of Contractors,' 'Modern Majestic 12,' 'The Administrators of Secrecy,' 'The Office of Global Access,' 'The Role of MITRE,' 'The DOE NEST,' 'The 1954 Atomic Energy Agreement,' 'The Y-12 Complex,' 'Underground Military Bases' — asserting that the effort is administered through a layered contractor pyramid with Department of Energy and federally funded research and development center involvement rather than through a single DoD program office. That is a falsifiable structural model, and it is the one an analyst can test against procurement records, facility clearances and statutory authorities. The episode also names individuals and cases as nodes — Jonathan Wagan, J. Andrew Kistner, Eric Henry Wang, Marconi — converting rumor into a checkable list. Its evidentiary weight is low; its investigative value as a target list is high.
michels-gerb-structural-episode.narrative:
There is a difference between a witness and a cartographer. Most UAP media is witness content: a person describes what he saw or was told, and the audience is asked to weigh his credibility. The Michels-Gerb episode is cartography. UAPGerb is not claiming personal access; he is claiming that the public record, read carefully enough and cross-indexed hard enough, discloses the shape of the thing. That makes the episode assessable in a way testimony is not, because a map can be checked against the terrain.

The episode published on 11 January 2026 at 7:15 PM UTC on Jesse Michels's American Alchemy, running 3 hours 54 minutes. The chapter list published with it is the closest thing the open record has to a table of contents for the concealment hypothesis, and it is worth reading as a document in itself.

The first movement is structural. 'Legacy Programs' at 6:00, then 'The Pyramid of Contractors' at 12:03, then 'Whistleblowers and Leaks' at 16:46 and 'Modern Majestic 12' at 23:50. The claim embedded in that ordering is that the program's continuity lives in the contractor layer rather than in any government office — that government offices rotate, get renamed, get terminated by statute, while the corporate custodians and their facility clearances persist. This is the single most consequential structural assertion in the episode, because it is the one that explains how a program survives the abolition of the Aerial Phenomena Task Force, the creation of AARO, and forty years of reorganizations. It is also the assertion that makes the 'covered government contractors' clause of the Burlison FY2027 amendment the operative provision rather than a throwaway.

The second movement is administrative. 'Exploring the IPU Docs' at 27:10 reaches back to the 1947 Interplanetary Phenomenon Unit; 'The Administrators of Secrecy' at 32:24 and 'Individuals in the Shadows' at 37:38 name people; 'The Office of Global Access' at 43:04 and 'The Conflict of Interest' at 49:48 lead into 'The Role of MITRE' at 51:28. MITRE operates federally funded research and development centers — organizations that hold government facility clearances and perform government work while sitting outside both the civil service and ordinary contractor competition. In the legacy-program hypothesis the FFRDC is the ideal custodian: it has continuity, clearances, and a relationship to government that is neither employment nor procurement in the ordinary sense.

The third movement is nuclear. 'The DOE NEST' at 1:22:01, 'The 1954 Atomic Energy Agreement' at 1:30:25, 'The GAO Audit' at 1:31:55, 'The Y-12 Complex' at 1:32:56. The Department of Energy thread is analytically the strongest part of the map, for a reason that has nothing to do with anyone's testimony: Restricted Data under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 is classified by statute at birth, sits outside the Executive Order 13526 classification system entirely, and is therefore outside the reach of the Information Security Oversight Office's oversight authority. Congress noticed this. When it drafted the UAP authorized-disclosure protections at 50 U.S.C. 3373b(b)(1)(B), it wrote that an authorized disclosure 'shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under the authority of Executive Order 13526... or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954.' Legislators do not immunize disclosures against the Atomic Energy Act unless they have reason to think the Atomic Energy Act is being used.

The fourth movement is geographic and biographical: 'Underground Military Bases' at 1:44:25, 'Covert Operations and Facilities' at 1:52:44, 'Marconi's Involvement' at 2:04:48, 'The Legacy of Eric Henry Wang' at 2:07:16, and named witness segments for Jonathan Wagan at 1:15:47 and J. Andrew Kistner at 1:31:35. The fifth is meta: 'Controlled Disclosure Dynamics' at 2:28:42, 'The Shadow Government' at 2:38:42, 'The Role of Psyops' at 2:51:34 — Gerb arguing that disclosure itself is being managed, which is a claim about the current period rather than the historical one.

On sourcing discipline, this dossier draws a hard line. The episode's existence, date, duration, host, guest and published chapter structure are verifiable primary metadata. Every substantive assertion inside it — that MITRE holds a custodial role, that an 'Office of Global Access' exists, that Y-12 is implicated, that a 1954 atomic energy agreement bears on the subject — is UAPGerb's claim, unverified here, and is catalogued as such at tier 3. The correct use of this episode by a downstream analyst is as a query list: take each named entity, each facility, each individual, and test it against procurement data, FOIA releases, clearance records and statutory authority. The episode's value is that it is specific enough to be wrong.

The relationship to the broader board is that Gerb's structural model and Congress's legislative behaviour have converged without either citing the other. Gerb says the continuity lives in the contractor pyramid. Congress, in the FY2023 authorized-disclosure statute and again in the FY2027 House-adopted disclosure amendment, keeps writing provisions that reach contractors, contractor nondisclosure agreements, and contractor-held records. Two independent processes arriving at the same load-bearing assumption is the kind of convergence worth flagging.

ndaa-fy2023-sec-6802.whatItIs: Section 6802 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, Public Law 117-263, Division F (the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023), Title LXVIII, enacted 23 December 2022, 136 Stat. 3586. Section 6802(a) amended 50 U.S.C. 3373 in its entirety, replacing the FY2022 Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group language with the statutory charter of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. It is the provision that put a congressional demand for the concealment history into permanent federal law.
ndaa-fy2023-sec-6802.whyImplicated: Section 6802 is the moment Congress wrote its suspicion into the United States Code. The historical record report it mandates at 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) does not ask whether UAP are real; it orders the Director of AARO to compile and itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress' and 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities,' from 1 January 1945 forward. Those are not the words of a legislature seeking information about aerial objects. They are the words of a legislature accusing the executive branch of running unreported compartmented programs and conducting a disinformation effort, and then ordering the executive branch to write the indictment itself. Section 6802 also created the material-testing and propulsion-science machinery at 50 U.S.C. 3373(e) and (g), and Section 6803 attached a Comptroller General audit to the historical record report because Congress did not trust the self-investigation it had just commissioned.
ndaa-fy2023-sec-6802.narrative:
Read Section 6802 the way a prosecutor reads a charging document and the picture is unmistakable.

The mechanics first, because the citation matters and is commonly muddled. Public Law 117-263 is the FY2023 NDAA. Division F of that act is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023. Section 6802(a) of Division F, Title LXVIII, amended 50 U.S.C. 3373 generally, at 136 Stat. 3586. That is the AARO charter. A separate provision, Section 1673 of Division A, Title XVI, at 136 Stat. 2959, created 50 U.S.C. 3373b, the authorized-disclosure mechanism, and it is Section 1673 rather than Section 6802 that carries the phrase 'reverse engineering.' An analyst tracing statutory authority needs both, and needs to keep them distinct: 6802 built the office, 1673 built the whistleblower channel, and Section 6803 built the audit.

Now the language. Subsection (j)(1)(A) requires the Director of AARO, within 540 days of 23 December 2022, to submit to the congressional defense committees, the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership 'a written report detailing the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' drawing on intelligence community records and documents, oral history interviews, open source analysis, interviews of current and former Government officials, and 'classified and unclassified national archives including any records any third party obtained pursuant to section 552 of title 5.' Subsection (j)(1)(B)(i) sets the period: 'beginning on January 1, 1945' and running to completion.

Then (j)(1)(B)(ii), the operative demand. The report shall 'include a compilation and itemization of the key historical record of the involvement of the intelligence community with unidentified anomalous phenomena, including — (I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

Subparagraph (I) is a statutory recognition that unreported restricted-access programs may exist — which is precisely the waived-SAP and Restricted Data territory that the Information Security Oversight Office cannot independently inventory and that the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver channel narrows to four members of Congress. Subparagraph (III) is a statutory recognition that a disinformation effort may exist, and it uses the word 'obfuscate' and the phrase 'manipulate public opinion' in the United States Code. Congress does not legislate against hypotheticals in these terms.

Subsection (j)(2) removed the obvious dodge in advance: 'The Archivist of the United States shall make available to the Office such information maintained by the National Archives and Records Administration, including classified information, as the Director of the Office considers necessary.' No classification barrier at the Archives.

Section 6802 also built the technical apparatus. Subsection (e)(1) directs the Secretary of Defense, coordinating with the DNI, to designate 'one or more line organizations' primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of field-investigation data and data from other sources, 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.' Subsection (e)(2) requires directives ensuring each designated line organization has authority 'to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.' Subsection (g) orders a science plan to develop and test theories accounting for 'characteristics and performance of unidentified anomalous phenomena that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation,' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.' Replicate. The statute contemplates replication of performance exceeding the known state of the art. Subsection (n)(6) then defines 'line organization' in a way that excludes any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense — pushing the material testing out to service labs, national labs and agencies where the work would actually be done.

The reporting architecture around it is equally telling. Subsection (l)(4) requires the Director to give the Armed Services and Intelligence committee leadership, every briefing period, 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.' Congress built a running log of refusals into the statute. And Section 6803 of the same public law, at 136 Stat. 3594, required the Comptroller General within 90 days to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the historical record report process, with on-site work as appropriate, quarterly findings to AARO, and semiannual verbal briefings to the intelligence committees, the defense committees and congressional leadership.

That is a statute that funds an office, orders it to investigate its own department's concealment history back to 1945, strips the classification defense at the Archives, requires it to log every time it is refused data, and puts an independent auditor over its shoulder. Later Congresses kept tightening: Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60, enacted 18 December 2025, ordered the AARO Director within 180 days to make 'an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena,' and Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 barred UAP-related independent research and development costs from being allowable as indirect contract expenses unless the material is made available to the defense and intelligence committees and congressional leadership — a direct strike at the mechanism by which contractor-held UAP work could be billed to the taxpayer without congressional visibility.

Section 6802 is the hook because everything downstream hangs from it: AARO's existence, the historical record report, the line-organization material testing, the classification-guide accounting, and the statutory vocabulary — 'restricted access,' 'not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' 'obfuscate' — that the rest of the disclosure fight is conducted in.

ndaa-fy2023-sec-6802.denialPosture: Section 6802 contains no denial; it is the instrument that compels one. Its significance for the concealment record is that any AARO historical record report issued under 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) that fails to itemize unreported restricted-access programs or obfuscation efforts is a dated, signed statutory filing by a named Director, made under a mandate that expressly contemplated finding both — which converts a null finding from an absence of evidence into an attributable representation to Congress.
connections: Creates the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office; AARO's Director reports to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI on operational and security matters and to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B).

Companion to Section 1673 of the same public law, which created 50 U.S.C. 3373b — the authorized-disclosure channel, the reverse-engineering enumeration, the anti-reprisal protections and the government-wide and contractor-wide sweep of UAP nondisclosure orders.
Section 6803 attaches Government Accountability Office audit oversight to the historical record report; the Comptroller General is the only independent auditor in the scheme.

The 'restricted access... not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress' formulation directly implicates the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waived-SAP channel and the E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3 special access program structure that ISOO cannot independently inventory.
The Atomic Energy Act immunity in 3373b(b)(1)(B) ties the statutory scheme to Department of Energy Restricted Data authorities outside the E.O. 13526 system.

The Archivist of the United States is made a compelled source under 3373(j)(2), the same official who holds the UAP Records Collection under the FY2024 NDAA and would hold the permanent collection under the Burlison FY2027 amendment.
Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 targets contractor independent research and development billing, the funding mechanism most often alleged for contractor-held UAP work.

Later amendments by Public Law 118-31 Sec. 7341, Public Law 118-159 Sec. 1089, and Public Law 119-60 Secs. 1671 and 1672 progressively tightened reporting, added NORAD and NORTHCOM intercept reporting back to 1 January 2004, and required the classification guide accounting.
openQuestions: Whether the historical record report required by 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) was delivered within the 540-day statutory deadline and in how many volumes; the delivery record was not examined for this dossier.

Which 'line organizations' were designated under 50 U.S.C. 3373(e)(1) for material testing, medical studies and theoretical modelling — the names are required to be reported under 3373(k)(1)(B)(xvi) but have not been verified here.
How many enumerations of withheld data have been provided to the committees under 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4), and what they contain.
What the Comptroller General's Section 6803 audit found, and whether any of the semiannual verbal briefings produced a written product.
Whether the nondisclosure order sweep required by 50 U.S.C. 3373b(b)(3)(A) was in fact conducted by all covered agencies and contractors, and how many instruments were produced to AARO.
How many 72-hour congressional notifications under 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) have been made — each one would be a formal statement that an unreported restricted-access program was implicated.
Whether any contractor has had UAP-related IRAD costs disallowed under Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31, which would be a documented dollar figure attached to contractor UAP work.

Whether the security classification guide accounting required by Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60 was completed by its June 2026 deadline and whether a consolidated classification matrix was issued.

aztec-1948.whatItIs: A retrieval story with no retrieval behind it: the documented history is a Denver oil-fraud scheme
aztec-1948.whyImplicated: Aztec is on this board for one reason, and it is not that a saucer came down in Hart Canyon. It is the earliest fully traceable example of a crash-retrieval narrative whose entire provenance can be reconstructed end to end - source, motive, transmission, monetisation, exposure, conviction, and revival - and that makes it the control case against which every other retrieval claim on this board has to be measured. Everything the story needed to survive it had: named military witnesses, a specific canyon, a specific craft diameter, a specific body count, a bestselling book, a metal sample, and a federal-sounding cover-up. What it did not have was a crash.
aztec-1948.narrative:
Aztec is on this board for one reason, and it is not that a saucer came down in Hart Canyon. It is the earliest fully traceable example of a crash-retrieval narrative whose entire provenance can be reconstructed end to end - source, motive, transmission, monetisation, exposure, conviction, and revival - and that makes it the control case against which every other retrieval claim on this board has to be measured. Everything the story needed to survive it had: named military witnesses, a specific canyon, a specific craft diameter, a specific body count, a bestselling book, a metal sample, and a federal-sounding cover-up. What it did not have was a crash.

The chain begins with Silas Mason Newton, a Denver oil promoter whose name first reached the FBI on 24 September 1938 on a suspected wire-fraud referral, and Leo (Leonard) A. GeBauer, a Phoenix electronics merchant who appears in the literature under the pseudonym 'Dr. Gee', the 'magnetologist'. On 8 March 1950 Newton, billed only as 'Mr. X' or 'Scientist X', lectured a room of science students at the University of Denver. He told them he had seen two recovered flying saucers held in a secret government facility; one had come down near Aztec, New Mexico, brought down by a 'magnetic fault line', the other near Durango, Colorado. The occupants of the first had been burned dark brown when a porthole blew out; the crew of the second had suffocated from a change in atmosphere. He described the beings as between 38 and 42 inches tall, dressed in cloth that could not be torn, probably from Venus, flying on magnetic propulsion at twice the speed of light.

Frank Scully, a Variety columnist, had already begun retailing the story in his 1949 columns. In 1950 Henry Holt published 'Behind the Flying Saucers', which turned Newton's lecture into a bestseller and into the template. Scully's version put the event in March 1948, a 99-foot craft - the largest UFO reported to that date - containing sixteen humanoid bodies, recovered by the military after a controlled landing in Hart Canyon roughly twelve miles northeast of Aztec, and hauled away for secret research. Scully added that the craft ran on 'magnetic principles', that the crew carried concentrated food wafers and heavy water, and that every dimension of the vehicle was divisible by nine. Martin Gardner, in 'Fads and Fallacies in the Name of Science', took the book apart as 'wild imaginings' and 'scientific howlers'.

The monetisation is the part that matters. Through the late 1940s and early 1950s Newton and GeBauer were travelling the Four Corners selling 'doodlebugs' - devices that in the oil business claim to locate deposits by remote sensing - and their sales pitch was that the doodlebug was built from, or reverse-engineered out of, the alien technology recovered at Aztec. Herman A. Flader, a Denver industrialist, put in $50,000 for a partnership in GeBauer's Colorado Geophysics & Development company, on the represented understanding that each unit cost around $800,000 to build. Dr. Alfred D. Kleyhauer, a Denver optometrist, lost $15,000. When investigators opened the devices they found surplus military radio parts; the estimated build cost was about $3.50 each. When J. P. Cahn of the San Francisco Chronicle demanded a sample of the miracle metal, the sample tested as ordinary aluminium. Cahn published the exposure in True magazine in September 1952 and returned in August 1956 with a second piece cataloguing further victims. Flader pressed charges. Newton and GeBauer were convicted of fraud in 1953 and also faced federal charges for moving the proceeds across state lines. Neither did jail time; the Denver Public Library's account records Newton still on probation and in violation of its terms by June 1955, and on 30 April 1969 he pleaded guilty again, this time to salting the Buckhorn Mine at Silver City, New Mexico. He died in 1972, probably still on probation.

The story should have died in 1956 and did, for about fifteen years - through the mid-1950s to the early 1970s most ufologists treated it as radioactive. It came back because the surrounding mythology gave it somewhere to live. In 1974 Robert Spencer Carr publicly claimed alien bodies recovered near Aztec were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, drawing official Air Force denials. Leonard Stringfield in the late 1970s went further, arguing the craft was one of many the US military had captured and stored. From there the Aztec details - the small burned bodies, the intact hull, the fast military sanitisation of the site - migrated wholesale into later allegedly first-hand accounts of Roswell, which is the single most important structural fact in this dossier: a documented hoax became a donor of detail to the case that the modern disclosure argument rests on.

It also acquired a paper artefact that will not go away. On 22 March 1950, two weeks after Newton's Denver lecture, Guy Hottel, special agent in charge of the FBI's Washington Field Office, filed a one-page memo relaying a third-party account of three recovered circular craft in New Mexico, 'approximately 50 feet in diameter', each holding three bodies 'only three feet tall' in 'metallic cloth', allegedly downed by high-powered radar. The memo ends 'No further evaluation was attempted'. When the FBI launched The Vault in April 2011 the Hottel memo became its most-viewed document, and in March 2013 the Bureau published a statement that it 'does not prove the existence of UFOs; it is simply a second- or third-hand claim that we never investigated', adding that some believe it simply repeats a hoax then in circulation.

Revisionism continues. Aztec's public library ran an annual UFO Symposium as a library fundraiser from 1997 to 2011. Scott and Suzanne Ramsey, with journalism professor Frank Thayer, spent three decades on the case and published 'The Aztec Incident: Recovery at Hart Canyon' (2012) and 'The Aztec UFO Incident' (2016), arguing the crash was real and independently witnessed; Ramsey placed a commemorative plaque at the canyon site in 2007. Nothing in that body of work has displaced the trial record. Tier it accordingly: the fraud is documented, the retrieval is not.
