geipan.whatItIs: France has run a state UAP office inside its space agency continuously since 1977 and publishes the case files
geipan.whyImplicated: GEIPAN is the answer to the question the US posture keeps deflecting: what does it actually look like when a government decides that unidentified aerospace phenomena are a normal object of public administration. The answer is a two- or three-person office in a space agency, a volunteer investigator corps, a steering committee of police, gendarmes, air force, meteorologists and scientists, a published four-tier classification, and a searchable public archive of every closed case. It has run without interruption since 1977 under three names.
geipan.narrative:
GEIPAN is the answer to the question the US posture keeps deflecting: what does it actually look like when a government decides that unidentified aerospace phenomena are a normal object of public administration. The answer is a two- or three-person office in a space agency, a volunteer investigator corps, a steering committee of police, gendarmes, air force, meteorologists and scientists, a published four-tier classification, and a searchable public archive of every closed case. It has run without interruption since 1977 under three names.

CNES states plainly on its own site that it has studied unidentified aerospace phenomena since 1977, the year GEPAN - the Groupe d'Étude des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés - was created. Its origin was not a scandal or a leak but a recommendation: a 1976 Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale committee, chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, opened the UFO file with the explicit objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection, and GEPAN was created on the back of that committee's recommendations. That lineage is stated in the COMETA report's own introduction. Claude Poher directed GEPAN at its inception. In 1988 GEPAN was replaced by SEPRA, the Service d'Études des Phénomènes de Rentrées Atmosphériques, which absorbed the UAP function into a unit whose principal job was routine monitoring of orbital debris and re-entry risk objects. At the end of 2001 the CNES Direction Générale commissioned an audit to decide the activity's future. The 2005 outcome was restructuring rather than closure: GEIPAN replaced SEPRA, and the audit carried what CNES calls 'une recommandation importante d'informer le public en toute transparence' - an important recommendation to inform the public in complete transparency. That recommendation is embedded in the acronym; the added 'I' stands for Information. It was implemented starting in 2007 with the online publication of GEIPAN's archives and case files.

The structure is worth stating precisely because it is the operational counter-model. GEIPAN sits under the deputy directorate of the Toulouse Space Centre. It is steered by a comité de pilotage (COPEIPAN) chaired by a recognised figure from the aerospace world and composed of representatives of the country's civil and military authorities - Gendarmerie nationale, civil aviation, meteorology, the Air and Space Force, scientific research - plus CNES. That committee's job is to analyse GEIPAN's results and make recommendations to CNES on its direction. Beneath it sits a collège d'experts of roughly thirty multidisciplinary volunteers who take the hardest cases, and a corps of volunteer field investigators across France who are mandated case by case and work to the methods set out in GEIPAN's investigator guide. GEIPAN holds standing conventions with the Gendarmerie, the Air Force, civil aviation, the Navy and Météo France for rapid access to hard data, and works with CNRS and the CEA. The permanent staff, per GEIPAN's own history page, is two full-time CNES agents - the head and an assistant - supported by external contractors for case analysis, statistics, anonymisation and archiving. Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor, surveying the office in 2025, counted three full-time employees and over 20 trained volunteer investigators. Funding comes out of the general public-service subsidy CNES receives; there is no separate UAP line item. Frederic Courtade has headed GEIPAN since January 2024.

The classification is what makes the archive usable. Each case is scored on two axes - consistency (C), the product of the quantity and reliability of data, and residual strangeness (E) after comparison against known-phenomenon hypotheses - then filed as A (perfectly identified), B (probably identified), C (unidentified for lack of data) or D (unidentified after investigation). Cases in C and D can be reopened if new information arrives. As of the site statistics dated 11 August 2026, 3,381 published classified cases break down as 950 class A (28.1%), 1,310 class B (38.7%), 1,015 class C (30.0%) and 106 class D (3.1%). Canada's report, working from the 2025 figures, recorded 3,188 cases with 3.2% unidentified after investigation and 31.4% unexplained for insufficient data. The residual is small, it is stable, and it is public.

GEIPAN is also unusually explicit about what it is not. Its FAQ states that it is not an independent structure but a technical department of CNES; that it carries no national-security, space-surveillance or alert mission; and that, 'contrary to popular belief', it is not a research group on UFOs, extraterrestrial life or other paranormal phenomena. It uses only recognised scientific knowledge, 'without speculation or unverified hypotheses'. That disclaimer is not evasion - it is the price of the archive, and it is precisely the trade the US system has refused to make.

The substantive work is on the record. In June 1978 GEPAN presented its scientific council with a five-volume, roughly 500-page report on the first semester of 1978; a contemporaneous English-language summary of that report, held in the NSA's public UFO document collection, records that eleven high-credibility, high-strangeness cases were studied in detail, that only one proved to have a conventional explanation, that in ten of the eleven the conclusion was that witnesses had seen a material phenomenon explicable as neither a natural phenomenon nor a human device, and that the report concluded there was behind the phenomenon a 'flying machine. . . whose modes of sustenance and propulsion are beyond our knowledge'. The same summary judges that the care taken with distances, angles and psychological factors 'makes the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison'. GEPAN's most cited physical-trace investigation, the Trans-en-Provence landing of 8 January 1981, was published as Note Technique n° 16, 'Analyse d'une trace', issued by CNES in Toulouse on 1 March 1983 and still hosted on the GEIPAN site.

The office's standing outside France is the argument in compressed form. When Canada's Chief Science Advisor set out to design a national UAP reporting system in 2025, GEIPAN was the model it described in the most detail, the example it explicitly told Canada to consider when establishing a dedicated service, and one of only four international bodies - alongside AARO, NASA and Chile's SEFAA - that it recommended Canada partner with.

claims.text: 'Le CNES étudie les PAN depuis 1977, date de la création du GEPAN (Groupe d'Étude des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés). En 1988, le GEPAN est remplacé par le SEPRA (Service d'Études des Phénomènes de Rentrées Atmosphériques).'

'Fin 2001, la Direction générale du CNES commande un audit pour statuer sur l'avenir de l'activité. En 2005, à la suite d'un audit, le Président du CNES décide la restructuration de l'activité et le GEIPAN ... se substitue au SEPRA, avec une recommandation importante d'informer le public en toute transparence.' The 'I' in GEIPAN stands for Information, and the recommendation was implemented through publication of the archives 'entamée en 2007'.

GEIPAN is steered by a comité de pilotage 'composé de représentants des autorités civiles et militaires du pays (Gendarmerie nationale, Aviation civile, Météo, Armée de l'air, Recherche scientifique) et du CNES', supported by a collège d'experts of 'une trentaine de bénévoles' and volunteer field investigators across France.

'L'équipe du GEIPAN est constituée de deux agents CNES à temps plein: le responsable et son assistante', with external support for case study, statistics, anonymisation and archiving; its budget comes from the general public-service subsidy received by CNES rather than a dedicated allocation.

Classification is by consistency (C) and residual strangeness (E), producing categories A (perfectly identified), B (probably identified), C (unidentified due to lack of data) and D (unidentified after investigation); C and D cases may be revisited if new information is supplied.
Published statistics dated 11/08/2026 cover 3,381 classified cases: 950 class A (28.1%), 1,310 class B (38.7%), 1,015 class C (30.0%), 106 class D (3.1%).

GEIPAN's FAQ states it is 'a technical department of CNES', that it 'does not involve in a security topic nor a sky and space awareness or alert service', and that 'contrary to popular belief, GEIPAN is not a research group on UFOs and extraterrestrial life, or other paranormal phenomena', using 'only recognized scientific knowledge, without speculation or unverified hypotheses'.

CNES lists GEIPAN's inception as 1977, its location as CNES Toulouse, its lifetime as 'Indefinite' and its status as 'In operation', with partners Gendarmerie, Police, Air and Space Force, CNRS and Meteo France; 'Currently headed by Frédéric Courtade since January 2024, GEIPAN is overseen by COPEIPAN, a steering committee'.

Key milestones per CNES: '2008: GEIPAN website created and UAP archives transferred to it; 2005: GEIPAN replaces SEPRA; 1988: GEPAN replaced by SEPRA, the permanent unit at CNES responsible for routine monitoring of orbital debris and risk objects; 1977: Inception of GEPAN'.

GEPAN's June 1978 five-volume report to its scientific council studied eleven high-credibility, high-strangeness cases; 'only one proved to have a conventional explanation'. 'In 10 of the 11 cases, the conclusion was that the witnesses had witnessed a material phenomenon that could not be explained as a natural phenomenon or a human device', and the report concluded that behind the phenomenon there is a 'flying machine. . . whose modes of sustenance and propulsion are beyond our knowledge'.
claims.source: 'French Government UFO Study', contemporaneous English-language summary submitted by Ron Westrum, held in the NSA public document collection - https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/ufo/french_gov_ufo_study.pdf

claims.text: The same summary states that in GEPAN's investigations 'the care with which distances, angles, and psychological factors were evaluated makes the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison', and that each case was worked by a four-person team including a psychologist.

GEPAN's investigation of the Trans-en-Provence physical-trace case of 8 January 1981 was published as Note Technique n° 16, 'Analyse d'une trace', CNES Toulouse, and remains hosted on the GEIPAN site.

cometa.whatItIs: Retired French generals, admirals and IHEDN auditors put the defence question in writing and named the extraterrestrial hypothesis
cometa.whyImplicated: COMETA is the document that has no American equivalent. A committee of retired French flag officers - an air force general in the chair, a vice-admiral, a weapons engineer general, a chief of police from the Interior Ministry, a research director from ONERA - spent close to three years reviewing UAP case material, wrote ninety pages under the title 'UFOs and Defense: What Should We Prepare For?', concluded that the extraterrestrial hypothesis could not be excluded and was the most credible of the available explanations, and put their names on it. cometa.narrative:
COMETA is the document that has no American equivalent. A committee of retired French flag officers - an air force general in the chair, a vice-admiral, a weapons engineer general, a chief of police from the Interior Ministry, a research director from ONERA - spent close to three years reviewing UAP case material, wrote ninety pages under the title 'UFOs and Defense: What Should We Prepare For?', concluded that the extraterrestrial hypothesis could not be excluded and was the most credible of the available explanations, and put their names on it. It was not commissioned by the French state, and its authors are careful about that. But it was written by people the French state had trained to think about national defence, using material from the French state's own UAP office, and it reads as a defence staff study rather than a polemic.

The committee's institutional centre of gravity is the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale. Almost every named member is an IHEDN auditor, identified by promotion number: Michel Algrin, doctor of political science and attorney-at-law (AA 35); Pierre Bescond, Weapons Engineer General, 2nd Section (AA 48); Denis Blancher, Chief of Police, Police Nationale, Ministry of the Interior; Jean Dunglas, honorary engineer general (AR 48); Bruno Le Moine, Air Force General, 2nd Section (AA 41); Françoise Lepine of the Fondation pour les Études de Défense (AA 33); Christian Marchal, research director at ONERA; Marc Merlo, Admiral, 2nd Section (AA 35); and Alain Orszag, Weapons Engineer General, 2nd Section. General Denis Letty, Air Force, 2nd Section (AA 35), chaired it. The report carries a foreword by Professor André Lebeau, former chairman of CNES, and one by General Bernard Norlain, former director of IHEDN, whom Letty visited at IHEDN in March 1995 to explain the project. Letty thanks both, saying that without them 'COMETA would not have been born'.

The report's own account of its lineage matters for this board because it closes a loop back to GEIPAN. COMETA's introduction states that in 1976 an IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale opened the unidentified flying objects file with the objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection, that 'the goal was achieved, because the recommendations of this committee were followed in the creation of' GEPAN, and that twenty years later it seemed useful to take stock again. In other words the same institution produced both the French state's UAP office and, two decades on, the committee that reviewed its output.

The evidentiary base is the French official record. Contributors included Jean-Jacques Velasco, then head of SEPRA at CNES; François Louange, chief executive of the image-analysis firm Fleximage; the pilots Jean-Charles Duboc, Jean-Pierre Fartek and René Giraud; Edmond Campagnac, former technical director of Air France at Antananarivo; Squadron Commander Michel Perrier of the Gendarmerie Nationale; an official of the DGAC; and Air Force General Joseph Domange. Letty specifically thanks the commander of the Air Force Air Operations Command Center for its participation in the investigation into Air France flight AF 3532 of 28 January 1994.

On substance, COMETA reproduces GEPAN/SEPRA's four-category scheme and then states the number that the whole document turns on: 'Category D UAPs represent 4 to 5% of the cases and are called UAP Ds.' Category D means unidentified despite the abundance and quality of the data - not unidentified for want of it. The report's position is that a residue of that size, often attested by consistent testimony and by visual sightings coupled with radar, can no longer be filed as no action: 'if there had only been ten or so UAP D [sightings], this ambiguous file could just have been classified as "no action," but we are no longer at that point and are far beyond that. Thus we are forced to seek plausible explanations.' It records around one hundred GEPAN/SEPRA investigations, several of which 'demonstrated, in the end, the physical presence of a phenomenon the nature and origin of which remain unknown', singling out Trans-en-Provence (8 January 1981) and 'Amaranth' (21 October 1982), documented in GEPAN technical memoranda 16 and 17. On aeronautical cases it records twelve French cases, only three or four of them category D; the first, in 1951, involving Vampire aircraft near Orange; and AF 3532 on 28 January 1994 as the first French case of a visual sighting correlated with radar over fifty seconds. It also draws on Dominique Weinstein's enumeration of 489 well-documented aeronautical UAP D cases worldwide since 1942, most from official sources.

COMETA is structured in three parts - facts and testimonies, the extent of current knowledge, and UFOs and defence - plus a conclusion and seven appendices, among them 'Radar Detection in France', 'Life in the Universe', 'Colonization of Space' and 'The Roswell Affair - Disinformation'. Its recommendations are set out in the introduction: give civilian and military pilots enough information to adopt adapted conduct when faced with these phenomena, and inform the public and decision-makers more generally; develop the actions of SEPRA and promote supplemental scientific monitoring and research; and consider the strategic, political and religious consequences of a possible confirmation of the extraterrestrial hypothesis, 'the bizarre connotation of which it is advisable to eliminate here and now'. Letty's own framing, in the foreword, is the sentence most often quoted from the document and is verbatim: 'The accumulation of well-documented sightings made by credible witnesses forces us to consider from now on all of the hypotheses regarding the origin of unidentified flying objects, or UFOs, and the extraterrestrial hypothesis, in particular.'

COMETA the association was registered under the French law of 1901 on 24 February 1999, having operated informally since 1996, and went dormant around 2006. The report appeared in July 1999 in a special issue of VSD, was reissued by Éditions du Rocher in 2003, and was not widely circulated in its original form because of copyright restrictions. According to Robert Roussel, citing Olivier Schrameck, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin read and annotated it 'to mark his interest'. There was no formal government response beyond that. GEIPAN made an archive of the report public in 2007.

cefaa.whatItIs: A civil aviation regulator that has treated UAP as a flight-safety problem, on the record, since 1997
cefaa.whyImplicated: Chile's UAP office exists because pilots kept reporting things and a civil aviation authority decided that was an aviation-safety matter rather than an embarrassment. That framing - not disclosure, not exobiology, but the safety of air operations in 32 million square kilometres of airspace - is what has kept it alive for nearly thirty years and what makes it the South American counterweight on this board.
cefaa.narrative:
Chile's UAP office exists because pilots kept reporting things and a civil aviation authority decided that was an aviation-safety matter rather than an embarrassment. That framing - not disclosure, not exobiology, but the safety of air operations in 32 million square kilometres of airspace - is what has kept it alive for nearly thirty years and what makes it the South American counterweight on this board.

The prehistory runs back to 1968. Anomalous aerial phenomena were first reported officially in Chile at the old Oficina Meteorológica de Chile in the Quinta Normal aeronautical complex in Santiago, where the director, Aviation Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores, began collecting reports and led the Comisión Chilena para Estudios de Fenómenos Espaciales No Identificados, formed with the support of the Sociedad Científica de Chile. Bravo's first act, on 9 July 1968, was to circulate 43 aeronautical installations from Arica to the Chilean Antarctic asking for reports. The commission - a meteorologist from Línea Aérea Nacional, an engineer, a physician, a doctor of physical and mathematical sciences, a Chilean Air Force lieutenant seconded to the aeronautics directorate, and several engineers - stated its object as establishing 'with all seriousness the true causes' of the matter. In seven years it gathered around a dozen reports, some of which were forwarded to the University of Colorado, where the panel later known as the Condon Committee was at work. It wound up in 1975 when Bravo retired.

The modern office was created twenty-two years later. A wave of sightings reported over Arica in the last days of March and first days of April 1997, together with the expressed interest of the former Commander-in-Chief of the Chilean Air Force, General del Aire Ramón Vega Hidalgo, moved the Director General of Civil Aeronautics, Aviation General Gonzalo Miranda Aguirre, to create the Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos on 3 October 1997, by Resolución Exenta N° 01599. The resolution sited the committee at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in Quinta Normal, Santiago, and on 14 October 1997 the school's director, Colonel Enzo Di Nocera García, set out its organisation and operating basis and named its members: himself as head, air traffic controller Gustavo Rodríguez Navarro, and the heads of the air traffic and meteorology areas as consultants, with ETA specialists and external organisations convened as needed. In practice Rodríguez Navarro carried the office's work through its early years.

The institutional history is not a straight line, and the dossier is stronger for saying so. Di Nocera led the committee until 1998, when Air Brigade General Ricardo Bermúdez Sanhueza took over the ETA and with it CEFAA, running it to February 2002. Air Brigade General Hernán Henríquez Cobaise took the directorship in March 2002 and held it to 31 March 2008, and the DGAC's own account describes the period from March 2002 to March 2008 as 'una etapa de latencia' - a dormancy. On 15 December 2009, by Resolución N° 02/0/01937, Director General José Huepe Pérez ordered the committee to operate from 1 January 2010 reporting directly to the Secretaría General, detaching it from the ETA and putting its members on permanent, exclusively investigative postings. Bermúdez returned to the directorship in 2009 and served to 2016; Hugo Camus Palacios succeeded him. On 18 October 2021, Resolución Exenta N° 04/3/0113/1385 repealed the 1997 resolution and renamed the office the Sección de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos, moving it under the DGAC's Subdepartamento Comunicacional. It is now based at Av. Pedro Aguirre Cerda 5100, Cerrillos, Santiago.

Its remit is defined by airspace, not by belief. SEFAA's mission is to support the safety of air operations in the national territory and in the airspace of DGAC responsibility, which extends across 32 million square kilometres from Arica in the north, between 120° and 131° west, to the South Pole. Its principal source is pilot reports - military, commercial, private, sport and institutional - supplemented by public reports, and it explicitly reserves the right to select which material is investigable. Investigations are grounded in the scientific method and depend heavily on audiovisual records. A digital case database was created in 2018; by September 2021 the office had received 1,675 cases in total, with 362 arriving in 2020 alone, nearly a 300% jump on prior years, and 300 more by September 2021. Since 2020 investigated and resolved cases have been published on the office's website, with reports made available to the public quarterly, and resolved-case pages remain live by year through 2026. The permanent staff is small - in 2018 the committee comprised its director and two investigators - but it draws on an external research committee of astronomers, geographers, physicists, psychologists, a nuclear chemist, aerospace medicine specialists, air traffic controllers, a meteorologist, aeronautical investigators, inspector pilots, aeronautical engineers, image analysts and armed forces representatives. On its 24th anniversary the DGAC described CEFAA as 'uno de los organismos públicos más antiguos del continente' and as leading a transparency model comparable, allowing for the difference in human and budgetary resources, to a European government body.

Its most visible case is the Chilean Navy footage of 11 November 2014, in which an Airbus Cougar AS-532 helicopter crew recorded roughly ten minutes of infrared video of an object off the coast west of Santiago. CEFAA investigated for over two years and released the footage with an official report in January 2017; Bermúdez, who had directed the investigation, summarised the outcome as knowing what it was not rather than what it was. The case is also the clearest documented instance of European-South American technical cooperation on UAP: photo and video analysts in France, including François Louange, were brought in through GEIPAN, and GEIPAN's analysts proposed a mundane explanation - a medium-haul aircraft venting - that CEFAA rejected. Independent analysts subsequently matched the timestamps and geometry to scheduled flights. The disagreement is the point: two state UAP offices on different continents worked the same tape, reached different conclusions, and both published.

That visibility is now institutional. Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor, designing a national UAP reporting system in 2025, described SEFAA as one of only three national models worth examining alongside the United States and France, and recommended that Canada's lead organisation establish partnerships with AARO and NASA, GEIPAN and SEFAA.

claims.text: 'El 3 de octubre de 1997 se creó el Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos (CEFAA), a través de la Resolución Exenta N° 01599. Sin embargo, el 18 de octubre de 2021 la mencionada Resolución fue derogada, y por Resolución Exenta N° 04 / 3 / 0113 / 1385 el nombre de la oficina fue cambiado a Sección de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos (SEFAA), pasando a depender del Subdepartamento Comunicacional de la DGAC.'

The creating resolution was 'firmada por el Director General de Aeronáutica Civil, General de Aviación, Gonzalo Miranda', and sited the committee at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in Quinta Normal, Santiago; on 14 October 1997 ETA director Enzo Di Nocera 'estableció la organización y las bases de su funcionamiento' and named its members.

The creation was prompted by 'una serie de avistamientos reportados en la ciudad de Arica en los últimos días de marzo y primeros de abril de 1997' together with 'el interés manifestado por el ex Comandante en Jefe de la Fuerza Aérea de Chile, General del Aire Ramón Vega Hidalgo'.

Predecessor body: from 1968 Aviation Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores, director of the Oficina Meteorológica de Chile, led the Comisión Chilena para Estudios de Fenómenos Espaciales No Identificados, formed with support of the Sociedad Científica de Chile. On 9 July 1968 he circulated 43 aeronautical installations requesting reports; the commission ran to 1975 and some of its dozen or so reports were sent to the University of Colorado, 'en donde la una comisión de académicos (bautizada posteriormente como Comisión Condon) realizaba un detallado estudio'.

Directorship chronology per DGAC: Di Nocera to 1998; Ricardo Bermúdez 1998 to February 2002; Hernán Henríquez Cobaise from March 2002 to 31 March 2008, during which period 'el CEFAA entró en una etapa de latencia'; reactivated by Resolución N° 02/0/01937 of 15 December 2009 under Director General José Huepe Pérez, operating from 1 January 2010 under the Secretaría General; Bermúdez again from 2009 to 2016; then Hugo Camus Palacios.

Remit: 'Apoyar la seguridad de las operaciones aéreas en el territorio nacional, y en el espacio aéreo de responsabilidad de la Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil de Chile', an airspace that 'se extiende por 32 millones de kilómetros cuadrados, desde Arica, por el norte, entre los 120º y los 131º grados oeste, hasta el Polo Sur.'

Caseload as of September 2021: 'ha recepcionado un total de 1675 casos'; 'El año 2020 llegaron 362 casos, superando en casi un 300% las cifras que se venían registrando en años anteriores'; 300 further reports to September 2021; supported by 'una Base de Datos Digital creada el año 2018'.

Publication practice: 'Desde el año 2020, se publican en el sitio www.cefaa.gob.cl los casos investigados y resueltos. Esos informes están a disposición del público trimestralmente y entregan una completa descripción de los fenómenos reportados y la conclusión a la que se llegó.' Resolved-case indexes remain published by year from 2018 through 2026.

On its 24th anniversary the DGAC described CEFAA as 'uno de los organismos públicos más antiguos del continente' and stated that, 'Comparable a un organismo gubernamental europeo -guardando las proporciones en cuanto a recursos humanos y presupuestarios- el CEFAA lidera un modelo de transparencia respecto a sus investigaciones.'

As of October 2018 CEFAA comprised 'su Director, Hugo Camus Palacios y dos investigadores', supported by an external research committee of astronomers, geographers, physicists, psychologists, a nuclear chemist, aerospace medicine professionals, air traffic controllers, a meteorologist, aeronautical investigators, inspector pilots, aeronautical engineers, image analysts and armed forces representatives.

Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor: 'In Chile, the SEFAA ... serves as the official body responsible for collecting, analyzing and scientifically studying UAPs. It operates within the General Directorate of Civil Aeronautics.' It adds that 'SEFAA publishes monthly reports detailing the cases it has received, investigated, and closed'.

The Chilean Navy case: an Airbus Cougar AS-532 helicopter with an infrared camera recorded roughly ten minutes of footage of an unidentified object off the coast west of Santiago on 11 November 2014; CEFAA released the footage with an official report in January 2017. Director Ricardo Bermúdez summarised the finding as 'We do not know what it was, but we do know what it was not.'

setka-program.whatItIs: Twin USSR Academy of Sciences and Ministry of Defence programmes, 1978-1990. The Soviet Union turned its entire army into a standing UAP sensor network for thirteen years, and then published
setka-program.whyImplicated: SETKA is the largest state UAP data-collection effort ever run, and almost nothing about it looks like the American arrangement. It was created by a bureaucratic decision minuted at the Kremlin, funded out of nobody's budget, executed by fewer than a dozen people, mandated in writing to every Soviet serviceman, and - the part that matters here - written up afterwards by the two men who ran it and published in the Academy of Sciences' own journal.
setka-program.narrative:
SETKA is the largest state UAP data-collection effort ever run, and almost nothing about it looks like the American arrangement. It was created by a bureaucratic decision minuted at the Kremlin, funded out of nobody's budget, executed by fewer than a dozen people, mandated in writing to every Soviet serviceman, and - the part that matters here - written up afterwards by the two men who ran it and published in the Academy of Sciences' own journal.

The trigger was the Petrozavodsk phenomenon of 20 September 1977, a large-scale luminous event seen across the north-west USSR and into Finland by ambulance crews, militia, dockers, military personnel and airport staff, and reported in Izvestia three days later under the headline 'The Unidentified natural phenomenon'. Local authorities asked the Presidium of the Academy of Sciences to explain it; letters arrived from northern European governments asking whether the effects came from military-technical experiments and endangered the environment. Under that pressure the President of the Academy of Sciences, Academician Anatoly Aleksandrov, wrote to L. Smirnov, Vice-President of the government and Chairman of the Military-Industrial Commission, asking that a complex research programme on anomalous phenomena be started with Ministry of Defence and war-industry involvement. The MIC Scientific and Technical Council met in the Kremlin in October 1977 under Lieutenant-General B. A. Kijasov. Members noted that reports of extraordinary phenomena also reached Ministry of Defence organisations from servicemen, and had sometimes coincided with equipment failures.

The meeting recommended, and the MIC under the Council of Ministers adopted, the inclusion of two topics in the 1978 state plan of defence research: 'Setka MO' (Ministry of Defence) - 'Research of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena and their influence on the operation of military technical equipment and personnel' - and 'Setka AS' (Academy of Sciences) - 'Research of a physical nature and mechanisms of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena'. The programme ran without interruption for thirteen years, to 1990, and was re-approved in the five-year defence research plans of 1981 and 1986. Platov and Sokolov note that the October 1977 STC meeting 'was the first and last measure with a so high official level of the participants engaged in the problem'.

The execution was tiny. The military branch was led from one of the central military research institutes in the Moscow region, with its chief V. Balashov - an expert on radiation and other damaging factors on military equipment - as scientific head, and four to five specialists doing the collection, processing and analysis. Around fifteen further Ministry of Defence and war-industry organisations participated voluntarily and very limitedly. The academic branch was led by Academician V. Migulin, director of IZMIRAN, which was designated head institute; the working group there, also four to five people, was headed by Yu. Platov. Budget financing covered salaries and travel, drawn from the executing organisations' own budgets, with no special allocation - 'the most inexpensive one, if not the cheapest, among the scientific works on defensive subjects'.

The instrument that made it work was a document authorised by the Chief of the General Staff in January 1980 and distributed to the troops as a General Staff Directive. It designated the central military research institute as the collection, processing and analysis centre for all UAP information obtained by the military; named the research institutes responsible in all five arms; set the procedure by which the centre could obtain identification data, above all launch data for military aerospace systems; and fixed the rules for documenting detections and the reporting order by urgency. The authors' own summary is the sentence worth having verbatim: the directive 'for 13 years put the army into the on-duty regime of observation of the paranormal phenomena in the places of the army dislocation, i.e. practically on the whole territory of the USSR'. Every serviceman became, as they put it, 'without knowing it' a potential participant, obliged to report any inexplicable phenomenon in writing.

The work was classified for three stated reasons: it sat inside the classified defence research plan; a military-technical origin for the effects was thought likely at the outset; and there was a possible military application of properties such as absence of radar contrast and high manoeuvrability. The word 'UFO' was not used in official documents, which said 'anomalous phenomenon' instead - partly because it fitted the observations better, partly to keep clear of popular agitation about aliens arriving on flying saucers.

The results are what a large sensor network with a small analysis cell produces. Over thirteen years about three thousand messages arrived, describing more than 400 distinct events after mass-observation reports were consolidated. More than 90% were resolved as effects accompanying rocket and space launches - sunlight scattered off gas-and-dust clouds from rocket exhaust, visible over hundreds of kilometres in twilight geometry - or as high-altitude balloons, which accounted for 10-12% of messages. The Petrozavodsk event itself was attributed to the launch of Kosmos 955 from Plesetsk. Notably, reports did not come in from units at or near test ranges, where such effects were familiar. The 1984-87 series of flight emergencies at the Borisoglebsk air unit in Voronezh region, where unknown objects appeared on radar and were seen by pilots, the authors leave explicitly unidentified.

And then the finding that makes the programme worth a node rather than a footnote. Across thirteen years of compulsory reporting spanning roughly a sixth of the Earth's land surface, the programme received no report of a landing, no report of contact with occupants, and no report of an abduction. Platov and Sokolov put the conclusion as a fork: either the USSR was closed to alien visitation for at least thirteen years, or the extraterrestrial-origin hypothesis is inconsistent. They also dismiss the 1990s wave of claims about 'KGB secret files' and 'classified capture of UFO' as absurd. Whatever one makes of the conclusions, the contrast with the American record is the point: the Soviet state ran the collection openly enough inside its own system to mandate it army-wide, and its coordinators published the account under their own names in Vestnik Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk in 2000.

Verbatim: 'One can say that the noted directive for 13 years put the army into the on-duty regime of observation of the paranormal phenomena in the places of the army dislocation, i.e. practically on the whole territory of the USSR, and this means, anyway, approximately 1/6 of the Earth territory.' Each serviceman 'became (without knowing it) a potential participant of the program'.

The research was classified for three stated reasons: it formally entered the classified defence plan; a military-technical origin for the effects was thought likely at the outset; and there was 'a capability of a military use of some probable properties of the UFO ... absence of a radar contrast, high manoeuvrability, etc.' In official documents 'the use of an abbreviation "UFO" was not accepted, instead of it the term "paranormal phenomenon" was used.'

'During the work on the program (for 13 years) about three thousand of messages reporting about extraordinary phenomena have been obtained ... on the whole, more than 400 events were registered and identified as extraordinary or paranormal.' Over 90% were resolved as rocket-launch effects or high-altitude balloons, the balloon class accounting for 10-12% of messages. The Petrozavodsk phenomenon itself was attributed to 'the launch of an artificial Earth satellite "Kosmos 955" from the space range in Plesetsk'. Reports 'did not practically come' from units at or near test ranges, where such effects were familiar.

Across the whole programme there was no message about a UFO landing, no message about contact with UFO occupants, and no message about abductions. The authors state the conclusion as a fork: 'either the territory of the USSR was, due to any reasons, closed for alien visitations during, at least, 13 years or that the hypothesis of an extraterrestrial origin of "UFO" is inconsistent.'

The series of flight emergencies in 1984-87 at the Borisoglebsk air unit in Voronezh region, characterised by unknown objects on radar and visually observed by pilots in emergency zones, is left explicitly unresolved: 'So far there is no consensus of opinion as to the role played in these emergencies by the mysterious objects observed in the zone of flight, and we shall interpret these events as unidentified.'
Secondary accounts state that the SETKA designations were changed to 'Galaktika' (MO and AN) in 1981 and to 'Gorizont' (MO and AN) in 1986.

langley-2023-incursions.whatItIs: A sustained wave of unidentified aerial incursions over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Hampton, Virginia, beginning the evening of 6 December 2023 and running for roughly seventeen nights into late December. The objects overflew the home of the 1st Fighter Wing and the headquarters of Air Combat Command, the East Coast's principal F-22 Raptor base and a linchpin of the NORAD air-defense mission for Washington, D.C. Neither the Air Force, NORTHCOM, the FBI, nor the Pentagon's UAP office has ever publicly identified what the objects were, who operated them, or where they launched from.
langley-2023-incursions.whyImplicated: This is the cleanest modern test case of the board's central proposition: that the United States government maintains a category of aerial object it will not name, and that its institutional response to encountering one is to reach for a label rather than an answer. For seventeen consecutive nights, objects that a four-star general watched from a rooftop transited restricted airspace over the most defended fighter base on the Atlantic seaboard, and the response was to move the F-22s, call in a NASA high-altitude imaging aircraft, hold two weeks of interagency meetings, and then say nothing for three months until a trade publication forced the acknowledgment. The objects were classified as 'uncrewed aerial systems' without a single one being downed, captured, tracked to a launch point, or attributed to any operator, and the Pentagon's own anomaly office told a reporter in May 2024 that it had never received a report on the incident at all. The government therefore produced, in the same event, a defense failure it could not explain and a taxonomy it could not justify: a 'drone' with no drone attached to it. Langley is the node where the concealment apparatus and the air-defense apparatus become visibly the same apparatus, because the thing that stopped the inquiry was not an absence of sensors but an official noun.
langley-2023-incursions.narrative:
The incursions began after dark on 6 December 2023. A Langley Air Force Base spokesperson, responding to The War Zone three months later, confirmed the outline in language that has never been amended: the installation 'first observed UAS activities the evening of December 6' and 'experienced multiple incursions throughout the month of December,' with the number of objects fluctuating and their size and configuration varying. The same statement declined to discuss impacts to operations or force protection measures, and noted only that the FAA had been made aware.

What that statement omitted was the scale of the response. Flight-tracking hobbyists watching Newport News in mid-December saw F-16s flying what looked like combat air patrols with tanker support around 12 December. The following week, one of NASA's three WB-57F high-altitude research jets, civil registration N927NA, flew circular orbits with Langley at their center. NASA's own public airborne-science calendar listed N927NA as tasked with 'Imagery Support' on 18 and 19 December 2023. Asked about it, NASA's Langley Research Center said the aircraft had been on the East Coast to image the SpaceX CRS-29 capsule's return and that 'while in the area, the aircraft provided additional imaging support in Virginia.' A NORAD/NORTHCOM spokesperson told The War Zone in December that NORTHCOM 'has been coordinating with [the] FBI' and referred further questions to the Bureau. The FBI declined to comment then and declined again in March 2024.

The senior officer on the ground was Gen. Mark Kelly, then commander of Air Combat Command, headquartered at Langley. He went to the roof of a squadron building for an unobstructed view. His account, given to 60 Minutes in March 2025, is the most detailed first-person military description on the record: 'The reports were coming in 20-to-30 sightings, same time every evening, 30-to-45 minutes after sunset.' The objects varied in size, altitude, and speed. 'The smallest, you know you're talking about a commercial-size quadcopter. And then the largest ones are probably size what I would call a bass boat or a small car.' The Wall Street Journal, reporting in October 2024, had one object at roughly twenty feet long, moving at more than 100 miles an hour at 3,000 to 4,000 feet, with others following one by one and sounding at distance like a parade of lawn mowers.

Gen. Glen VanHerck was the NORAD and NORTHCOM commander at the time. He provided fighters, AWACS, and helicopters to try to characterize the objects, and could not. NORAD's radars, built to see high-altitude bombers and missiles, could not see things a person could see with the naked eye. Asked by CBS whether he could rule out hobbyists, VanHerck said no: 'It would be my assessment they weren't hobbyists because of the magnitude of the events, the sizes of some of the drones, and the duration.' He added the sentence the board treats as load-bearing: 'It certainly could have a foreign nexus, a threat nexus.' A senior official in the Biden White House told 60 Minutes, anonymously, that it was likely the work of hobbyists. Both statements describe the same seventeen nights. Only one of them is attributable.

The first public official acknowledgment came on 14 March 2024, when VanHerck's successor, Gen. Gregory Guillot, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that counter-UAS had dominated his first month in command, that he 'wasn't prepared for the number of incursions,' and that he had 'gone into the events at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, and I'm using that as the centerpiece of my 90-day assessment.' The War Zone published its investigation the next day. Everything the public knows about Langley therefore entered the record either through a reporter's persistence or through a general's aside at a budget hearing, never through an announcement.

The subsequent posture is instructive. In October 2024 Guillot told reporters at Peterson Space Force Base that 'the only thing I can tell you about the Langley drones is roughly the number and roughly the altitude,' that he did not know whether they had been tracked to a recovery point or launched from a vessel offshore, and that he knew of no 'organized or unorganized foreign nexus.' That same month, Langley's 633rd Contracting Squadron posted a sources-sought notice for counter-drone netting to be draped over up to 42 open-ended aircraft sunshades: a base that could not identify what flew over it buying nets to catch it. In February 2025 Guillot told the SASC there had been 350 drone detections at 100 different military installations in 2024, and that only about half of U.S. installations even qualify as 'covered installations' with authority to act under 10 U.S.C. 130i.

Then came New Jersey. Beginning November 2024, thousands of sightings across the Northeast produced a joint DHS/FBI/FAA/DoD statement on 16 December 2024 asserting that the agencies had 'not identified anything anomalous.' The statement is the concealment posture in its purest form: an assurance issued about a phenomenon the same document concedes generated more than 5,000 tips and roughly 100 open leads. Langley is what that assurance is built on top of, and Langley was never solved.

VanHerck, retired and unconstrained, closed the loop in August 2026 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium. 'There were no surprises, at least for myself and the team at NORAD/NORTHCOM and others,' he said of learning about the incursions. He had told Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin on 16 December 2021, two years to the week before Langley, that he lacked the domain awareness to do his mission, and that 'we're not set up to fight in and from our own land.' Installation commanders, he said, 'really felt a lack of trust' about whether they would be covered if they shot at something. The record therefore shows an air-defense system that knew it was blind, wrote it down, briefed it upward, and then watched seventeen nights of objects it could not name pass over its own F-22s.

langley-2023-incursions.denialPosture: The government's Langley posture is not denial of the event but denial of its significance, executed through a taxonomy: the objects were declared 'uncrewed aerial systems' without a single one being recovered, downed, tracked, or attributed, which converts an unexplained penetration of restricted airspace into a routine force-protection problem. That posture has four dated, attributable artifacts - the Air Force's 'none of the incursions appeared to exhibit hostile intent' (March 2024), Gen. Guillot's 'I do not know of any organized or unorganized foreign nexus' (October 2024), an unnamed Biden White House official's characterization to 60 Minutes of the affair as likely hobbyists, and the 16 December 2024 four-agency joint statement's 'we have not identified anything anomalous.' It is contradicted on the record by VanHerck, who commanded the response and who says magnitude, size, and duration rule hobbyists out. AARO's May 2024 statement that it had 'not yet received a report or any information on this incident' is the strangest artifact of the set: the office chartered to resolve unidentified objects was, by its own account, never told about the largest unresolved domestic airspace event in decades.
connections: Gen. Glen VanHerck - NORAD/NORTHCOM commander during the incursions; ordered the F-22 shootdown of the Chinese surveillance balloon ten months earlier; the only four-star to publicly reject the hobbyist explanation; his 16 December 2021 warning to SecDef Lloyd Austin about lack of domain awareness predates Langley by two years and establishes documented foreknowledge of the vulnerability.

Gen. Gregory Guillot - VanHerck's successor from February 2024; made the first public acknowledgment before the Senate Armed Services Committee on 14 March 2024 and made Langley the centerpiece of his 90-day assessment; directed in November 2024 to serve as DoD's synchronizer, integrator and coordinator of counter-small-UAS activity within the continental United States and Alaska; the official through whom nearly all subsequent government characterization of Langley flows.

Gen. Mark Kelly - commander of Air Combat Command, headquartered at Langley; the senior military eyewitness and the source for the WSJ's physical description. Distinct from Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), SASC and Intelligence Committee member, who separately told reporter Matt Laslo that some base incursions are 'very likely to be foreign nationals that are doing surveillance with low-cost systems that are somewhat expendable.'

AARO (All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office) - reported to have joined two weeks of interagency meetings on Langley, yet told Liberation Times in May 2024 it had received no report; Guillot separately said in October 2024 that he 'coordinates frequently' with AARO. Connects Langley to the board's AARO node and to the pattern of service-level withholding from AARO also alleged of the Navy.

FBI - held jurisdiction outside the base perimeter, received witness video from civilian eyewitness Jonathan Butner, and has declined comment on the investigation since December 2023; the agency in whose files the primary evidentiary record most plausibly sits.

FAA - notified of the incursions; later a signatory to the December 2024 joint statement; the agency whose airspace authority creates the jurisdictional seam VanHerck describes as ending 'at the fence line.'

NASA - the WB-57F N927NA orbits over Langley on 18-19 December 2023 place a civilian science agency's high-altitude imaging asset inside a military anomaly response, with NASA's public explanation (SpaceX CRS-29 support, plus 'additional imaging support in Virginia') covering the tasking.

Chinese surveillance balloon (February 2023) - shot down by an F-22 flown from Langley; the immediately preceding demonstration that NORAD's radar clutter gates were misconfigured for non-traditional aerial objects, and the precedent Guillot cites for 'lessons learned.'

New Jersey / Picatinny Arsenal drone wave (November 2024 onward) - the mass-sighting event that forced the four-agency joint statement and generated the congressional pressure Langley alone had not; the Army confirmed 11 drone sightings over Picatinny Arsenal beginning in November 2024.

Prior and parallel incursion nodes - Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station (2019), the Colorado plains ICBM-field drone reports (winter 2019-2020), the USS Paul Hamilton and other warships off Southern California (2019), Air Force Plant 42 in Palmdale (2024), the Energy Department's Nevada National Security Site nuclear-weapons experiment facility (October 2023), Wright-Patterson AFB, Guam's THAAD battery, and the RAF Lakenheath/Mildenhall/Feltwell cluster in the UK (November 2024).

10 U.S.C. 130i and the 'covered installation' regime - the statutory bottleneck that made non-engagement lawful; Sens. Tom Cotton and Kirsten Gillibrand pushed expansion legislation, and the later Safer Skies Act extended limited mitigation authority to DHS, DOJ, and certain state, local and tribal agencies.

Sen. Roger Wicker - SASC chairman; the ranking legislator to state on camera that the incursions have a military intelligence dimension and that the executive branch remains mystified despite top-level classified briefings.

House Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs (Chairman William Timmons, Ranking Member Suhas Subramanyam) - the 29 April 2025 'Securing the Skies' hearing, the closest thing to a dedicated congressional examination of the base-incursion pattern.

Fengyun Shi prosecution - the only criminal case to emerge from Hampton Roads airspace in that window, involving a separate January 2024 flight over Newport News Shipbuilding; frequently conflated with the December incursions in secondary coverage and useful chiefly as a control case demonstrating what identification, attribution and prosecution look like when they actually occur.

Joint Base Langley-Eustis ISR units - the 363rd and 480th Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Wings are based at JBLE, meaning the incursions occurred over an installation hosting national-level ISR analytic capability.
Falcon Peak (2024, 2025) - the NORTHCOM-led counter-small-UAS demonstration series at Fort Carson, Colorado, created as a direct downstream product of the Langley assessment.

Ross Coulthart and Liberation Times - the disclosure-side journalists who pressed the eyewitness account and the AARO non-receipt statement into the record; Coulthart has publicly flagged the classification problem, noting that if no craft were ever recovered, the word 'drones' is doing unearned work.
openQuestions: No launch or recovery point was ever identified. Guillot stated in October 2024 that he did not know whether the objects were tracked to a recovery point or whether they could have been launched from a vessel offshore, leaving the maritime-launch hypothesis neither confirmed nor excluded.

On what basis were the objects classified as 'uncrewed aerial systems'? None was downed, captured, or attributed. The Air Force has never disclosed the identification methodology, and the 'UAS' label is the single act that removed the event from the anomaly-resolution track.

Why does AARO say it received no report when other reporting places AARO personnel in two weeks of interagency meetings on the incident? Either the office was excluded from a case squarely within its charter, or its public statement is incomplete. Both readings are consequential.

What did the NASA WB-57F N927NA record on 18-19 December 2023? No imagery, sensor tasking order, or product from those flights has been released, and NASA's public explanation attributes the deployment to a spacecraft-reentry imaging mission.

The FBI investigative file remains unreleased and the Bureau has declined comment continuously since December 2023. It is not publicly known whether the investigation was closed, and if so on what finding.

What did Langley's own counter-UAS equipment register? Security Forces are equipped with handheld Dronebuster-type detection and jamming devices, yet seventeen nights of activity produced no publicly acknowledged operator geolocation or radio-frequency signature.
Whether Gen. Guillot's 90-day NORAD/NORTHCOM assessment, of which Langley was the stated centerpiece, contains a Langley-specific annex, and whether any portion of it is releasable.

Civilian eyewitness Jonathan Butner described orb-shaped objects and a separate low-flying saucer-form object, and provided his video to the FBI. Whether any government entity analyzed that footage and what it concluded is unestablished; his morphological description and the official 'UAS' classification have never been reconciled.
Which specific F-22 airframes were relocated, to which base, and under whose order. The relocation is confirmed by 60 Minutes and VanHerck but no unit-level movement record has surfaced.

Whether the October 2023 drone overflights of the Energy Department's Nevada National Security Site, reported by the Wall Street Journal two months before Langley, are operationally connected to the Virginia events or merely contemporaneous.

Whether any classified session of the Senate or House Armed Services Committees produced a finding on Langley attribution, and whether such a finding, if it exists, differs from the public 'no known foreign nexus' posture Wicker's 'still mystified' remark implicitly denies.

Whether the F-16 combat air patrols observed over southeastern Virginia around 12 December 2023 were flown in direct response to the incursions, and whether any airborne sensor track of the objects exists from those sorties or from the AWACS and helicopter assets VanHerck says he provided.

wayne-state-university.whatItIs: Wayne State University is a public research university in midtown Detroit whose School of Medicine operates jointly with the Detroit Medical Center, a large urban academic hospital system. Inside that medical school sat a small, defense- and intelligence-facing neuroscience unit called the Emergent Technology Research Division, built around functional neuroimaging and cognitive-workload measurement. That division, not the university's public research portfolio, is the reason Wayne State appears on this board.
wayne-state-university.whyImplicated: Four of the thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents commissioned under the DIA's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications program are attributed on the government-derived DIRD list to two Wayne State men: Christopher C. "Kit" Green and Richard J. Genik II. Green is a career CIA analyst (1969-1985) who came to Wayne State as executive director for emergent technology research for the School of Medicine and Detroit Medical Center, and then as assistant dean; Genik directed the Emergent Technology Research Division that Green's role had seeded, and the two had already co-authored on "cognitive avionics" for spaceflight crews in 2005. Green's DIRD is the human-effects paper, the single AAWSAP deliverable about injured bodies rather than propulsion, and it states outright that clinical diagnosis of injured witnesses can be used to reverse-engineer the craft that hurt them. That makes a named academic medical centre in Detroit a node in the custody chain for injury data on people harmed by anomalous craft, and it makes the university's silence about that work the relevant fact. Wayne State has never issued any public acknowledgement of the DIA contract deliverables written by its faculty, and Green himself has since recast the entire enterprise as private consulting done outside any institutional review structure.
wayne-state-university.narrative:
The program reached into universities, and Wayne State is where it reached into a hospital.

The entry point is Christopher C. Green. His career is the point: senior division analyst and assistant national intelligence officer for science and technology at CIA from 1969 to 1985, then General Motors, then Wayne State. The National Research Council's own 2008 biography of him, published while he chaired a committee on military and intelligence methodology for emergent neurophysiological research, records that immediately prior to becoming assistant dean he was "executive director for emergent technology research for the SOM/DMC" and that he held clinical appointments in the Departments of Diagnostic Radiology and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurosciences of the School of Medicine and the Detroit Medical Center. Note what that means. A former CIA science-and-technology officer was running the emergent-technology research function of a large American medical school, with hospital-side appointments in the two departments that give access to brain imaging and to psychiatric case material.

By 2009 the unit had a name and a successor. Wayne State's own School of Medicine news office described Richard J. Genik II as "director of the Emergent Technology Research Division and assistant professor of the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurosciences," announcing that the U.S. Army had picked him as one of fifteen experts to direct two decades of Army neuroscience investment, and that he briefed the Pentagon, the Board of Army Science and Technology, the Army Research Lab and Training and Doctrine Command. The university publicised that. It has never publicised what came next.

What came next was AAWSAP. The DIRD list attributes to Genik three papers and to Green one. Genik's three are all verifiable in the released record: "Technological Approaches to Controlling External Devices in the Absence of Limb-Operated Interfaces" (DIA-08-1003-012, 23 March 2010), "Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft" (DIA-08-1101-001, 15 December 2010, ICOD 8 September 2010, issued in the "Defense Futures" series), and a quantum-computing paper dated 10 December 2010. Read together they are not miscellaneous: brain-machine control of external devices, cognitive ceilings on piloting multiple craft at once, and molecular computing. That is a specification sheet for operating something you do not fly with your hands.

Green's contribution is the one that matters most. "Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues," dated 11 March 2010 with an information cut-off of 1 December 2009, produced under the FY 2009 AAWSA program in the "Acquisition Threat Support" series, opens with three antenna engineers who suffered erythema, fever, hair loss, blood dyscrasia and, in one case, "signs of malignant transformations" after a near-field exposure centred at about 785 MHz. Its summary is the load-bearing sentence in the whole DIRD corpus: the paper "relates, summarizes, and analyzes evidence of unintended injury to human observers by anomalous advanced aerospace systems," and argues "that the subsequent work can inform (e.g., reverse engineer), through clinical diagnoses, certain physical characteristics of possible future advanced aerospace systems from unknown provenance." Later it states: "It is our contention that characteristics of the fields or mechanisms associated with close encounters with anomalous craft can even sometimes carefully be gleaned from archival records where effects on human physiology have been carefully reported." Its appendices draw on the Schuessler catalog of UFO-related human physiological effects and on Vallee's close-encounter typology. The internal references cite "Green C. 2009 & 1983 (Unpublished Personal Archives)" and "Green, CC 2001, 2009 Unpublished HIPPA files" — a defence intelligence reference document resting, in part, on one physician's private patient archive.

The custody problem is exactly there. The released PDFs redact every author name under FOIA exemption (b)(6); the attribution to Wayne State comes from the DIRD list, not from the documents. Green, interviewed in April 2022, said he was a consultant to AAWSAP facilitated by BAASS, that there were no control groups and no institutional review board because he was doing "case studies" and not research, that a client gave him a grant he would not name, and that DIA reviewers objected to his use of the word UFO and had him change the wording. So the human-effects paper commissioned by a defence intelligence agency was written by a Wayne State assistant dean, drew on patient material he holds personally, passed through no university IRB, and was scrubbed of the word that described what it was about. The institution's name is on the government's list; the institution's oversight machinery never touched the work; and the institution has said nothing since. That is not an accident of paperwork. It is how the program used a university: for the credential and the clinical access, not for the accountability.

wayne-state-university.denialPosture: Wayne State University has issued no public acknowledgement of the DIA/AAWSAP deliverables written by its School of Medicine personnel; no press release, statement or research disclosure naming the contract has been located, in contrast to the university's 2009 publicity for Genik's Army neuroscience work. Green's own posture is displacement rather than denial: he characterises the human-effects paper as private consulting and personal case studies conducted outside any university review structure, and declines to name the funder. The DIA's standing line that DIRDs are contractor-produced theoretical papers that do not represent agency positions performs the same function for the government side.
connections: Christopher C. "Kit" Green — CIA science and technology analyst 1969-1985, Wayne State assistant dean and clinical appointee, author of the AAWSAP human-effects DIRD; the person through whom the intelligence community entered the medical school.

Richard J. Genik II — director of Wayne State's Emergent Technology Research Division, author of three AAWSAP DIRDs on brain-machine control, cognitive limits of multi-vehicle piloting, and molecular/quantum computing; Green's 2005 co-author.
Detroit Medical Center / Harper University Hospital — the clinical side of the joint appointments, and the imaging and psychiatric infrastructure that made human-effects work possible.
AAWSAP / AATIP — the DIA program under which all four Wayne State papers were commissioned, in the FY 2009 "Acquisition Threat Support" and FY 2010 "Defense Futures" series.
Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) — the prime contractor that, by Green's own account, facilitated his consultancy and collected the DIRDs.
Defense Intelligence Agency — the commissioning agency; AAWSA Program Manager, Bldg 6000, Washington DC 20340-5100 per each DIRD's administrative note.
John Schuessler and Jacques Vallee — whose UFO physiological-effects catalogues and close-encounter typology supply the appendices of the Wayne State human-effects paper.

National Research Council / National Academies — Green chaired the 2008 committee on military and intelligence methodology for emergent neurophysiological research; Genik chaired the technology group of the 2009 Army neuroscience study, placing both inside the national-security science advisory system.
EarthTech International, University of Nevada, University of Arizona, Lockheed Martin and the other DIRD performers — the peer set of institutions the program contracted through.
openQuestions: No evidence was found that Green ever held a named or endowed chair at Wayne State. The verifiable titles are assistant dean, adjunct/clinical professorial appointments in Diagnostic Radiology and Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurosciences, and earlier executive director for emergent technology research. Any claim of a 'chair' for anomalous-exposure research should be treated as unsupported until a Wayne State appointment letter or catalogue entry surfaces.

The exact start and end dates of Green's Wayne State appointments are not established in the sourced record; the 2008 NRC biography is the firm anchor, and his status in 2009-2010 when the DIRD was written is inferred rather than documented.

Whether any part of the AAWSAP work flowed through Wayne State accounts, contracts, facilities or the Emergent Technology Research Division's budget is unresolved. Green describes personal consulting; no subcontract, subaward or effort-reporting document has surfaced either way.

Whether Genik's three DIRDs were written under university affiliation or, like Green's, as private consulting is not established. He is attributed to Wayne State on the DIRD list, but no contract instrument has been located.

The document number on the human-effects DIRD is illegible in the released scan, so the paper is cited here by title and date only. The quantum-computing DIRD's number OCRs ambiguously and is likewise cited by date.
Whether Wayne State's institutional review board ever reviewed, or was ever asked to review, any of the clinical or imaging work Green describes conducting on 'experiencers' in later years.
The identity of 'Morris' in the DIRD's Appendix B 'Green/Morris' ICD-coding exercise, and whether that collaborator was a Wayne State colleague.
Whether the Emergent Technology Research Division still exists at Wayne State, when it was wound down or renamed, and where its records went.
Whether Wayne State has ever received a FOIA, records request or press inquiry about the DIA work, and what it said in response.

waived-sap-notification-group.narrative: The group that receives notification of a WAIVED Department of Defense special access program is not the Gang of Eight, and conflating the two is the single most common error in public argument about how a legacy programme could be hidden. The waived-SAP channel is created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Subsection (e)(1) provides: 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Subsection (e)(2) then specifies where the withheld material goes instead: 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' The term 'defense committees' is defined not by the general Title 10 definition but by section 119's own subsection (g): 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate' and 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six bodies, each contributing a chairman and a ranking minority member: twelve members of Congress. This is deliberately narrower than a full committee and deliberately wider than eight. Note that 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines a different, similar-sounding term, 'congressional defense committees,' as only the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of the two chambers - four bodies, eight chairs and rankings. Section 119 does not use that definition; it uses its own, which adds the two Defense Appropriations Subcommittees. A board that cites 101(a)(16) for the waived-SAP group would be naming the wrong set. The Gang of Eight is a separate creature governing covert action, not DoD SAPs. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2), where the President determines that it is essential to limit access to a covert action finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, 'the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Different committees (intelligence, not armed services or appropriations), different people (the four party leaders sit in the Gang of Eight and are absent from the 119(e) group; the appropriators sit in the 119(e) group and are absent from the Gang of Eight), and different subject matter. The structural comparison is where the argument actually lives, and it cuts against the covert-action statute being the tighter one. Title 50 contains two escape valves that Title 10 does not. First, 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) imposes a 180-day clock: within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limiting access, the President must either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a fresh statement of reasons for continuing to withhold. Section 119(e) contains no sunset, no periodic re-justification, and no mechanism that ever widens the circle. A waiver, once made, is permanent as to that report. Second, 50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires the President to tell all members of the intelligence committee that a limited notification occurred and to give them a general description of it. Section 119 has no analogue: the members of the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees who are not chair or ranking are never told that a waiver happened at all. They cannot ask about what they do not know exists. That asymmetry - no sunset, no notice of bypass - is the load-bearing limit on congressional oversight of a waived programme, and it is a limit written into the statute rather than an abuse of it. What the twelve can see is also bounded. They receive the withheld report content and the Secretary's justification. They do not thereby acquire subpoena power over the programme, staff who can read the material, or any statutory right to share it with colleagues. What they cannot see is anything the Department declines to characterise as a DoD special access program at all - the recurring allegation in the UAP context being that recovery and reverse-engineering activity was moved into contractor-held or non-DoD structures where section 119 does not reach. Finally, the mechanism's present scope is narrower than it was. Pub. L. 114-328 section 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among the reporting requirements it terminates, and section 1061(b)(1) provides that each such report still required as of December 31, 2021 'shall no longer be required to be submitted to Congress after that date.' The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries this as a Termination of Reporting Requirements note under section 119. The annual SAP budget report and the annual new-SAP designation-and-justification report are therefore gone. Because 119(e)(1) can only waive a requirement 'under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' the waiver authority now has live operation only as to subsection (c), the report on a planned change in classification or a planned declassification and public announcement. Subsections (d), (f) and (g) survive and are not waivable at all - notably 119(f), which bars initiating any SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) directs waived-SAP information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve members, given the six bodies listed in 119(g).

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' for this section as the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senate Appropriations Committee, Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, House Armed Services Committee, House Appropriations Committee, and House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee.

10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines the different term 'congressional defense committees' as only '(A) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate; and (B) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the House of Representatives' - four bodies, not the six used by section 119.

The Gang of Eight under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) consists of 'the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' It governs covert action findings, not DoD special access programs.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) forces re-justification or widened access within 180 days of a limited covert-action notification. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) contains no sunset and no re-justification requirement, so a SAP reporting waiver is permanent as to that report.

50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires that all members of the intelligence committee be told a limited notification occurred and be given a general description of it. Section 119 imposes no equivalent duty, so non-leadership members of the defense committees are never informed that a waiver has been exercised.

Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among terminated reporting requirements, and sec. 1061(b)(1) ends them after 31 December 2021. The OLRC note under section 119 records the termination as effective 31 December 2021.

Because 119(e)(1) reaches only 'a requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' and (a) and (b) terminated on 31 December 2021, the waiver authority retains live operation only as to subsection (c) - reports of a planned classification change or declassification. This is an inference from the statutory text, not a statement carried in the statute itself.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) bars initiating a special access program until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. Subsection (f) is outside the reach of the 119(e)(1) waiver, which by its terms covers only subsections (a), (b) and (c).
