dossier.denialPosture: AARO has denied, in Volume I of its Historical Record Report and in every annual report since, that any US Government or private entity has recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered non-human technology, that any authentic UAP-related non-disclosure agreement exists, and that any UAP-derived material has ever been captured or exploited. Its FY2025 report states there is no evidence any entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials while simultaneously reporting that AARO is building a handling process for such materials. Its FY2024 and FY2025 reports assert that every resolved case is attributable to prosaic objects.
openQuestions: Volume II of the Historical Record Report, statutorily promised under section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA and covering 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024, had not been published as of the last confirmed reporting in February 2026. Its current status is unresolved on this board.

The identity of the IC Controlled Access Program whose scope AARO says was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering is not disclosed in Volume I, nor is the authority that expanded it or the authority that disestablished it.
AARO reports 255 of 262 secure-mechanism contacts as out of scope but publishes no breakdown of the scope test applied, no appeal route, and no record of which claims were referred elsewhere.

Whether AARO's claimed unrestricted access extended to unacknowledged SAPs and to contractor-held Independent Research and Development compartments, or only to programmes DoD and IC security officials volunteered, is not established by any released document.

l0.label: ODNI Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (25 June 2021)

dossier.whatItIs: A nine-page unclassified intelligence product titled 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' issued by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence on 25 June 2021 in response to a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. It was drafted by the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from sixteen named agencies and components, and prepared for the Congressional Intelligence and Armed Services Committees. It reviewed 144 U.S. Government UAP reports from November 2004 to March 2021 and resolved exactly one.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the document in which the U.S. Intelligence Community, in writing and on the record, declined to attribute a single one of 143 unresolved incidents to American classified programs, and admitted it could not confirm that its own developmental programs accounted for any of them. That admission cuts both ways and the board should hold both edges. If the objects are not U.S. black programs, the IC has just conceded 143 unexplained penetrations of restricted airspace, many near nuclear-capable and test infrastructure. If they are U.S. black programs, then the DNI's own coordinating body was denied read-in access to them, which is the definition of the concealment the board asserts. The assessment further records that UAP cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds and near facilities carrying the most advanced sensor systems, that in eighteen incidents observers reported unusual flight characteristics, that military aircraft systems processed radio-frequency energy associated with sightings, and that the task force holds data appearing to show acceleration or signature management. It is also a concealment artifact in its own right: it names the accountable official only by title, ships the substance to a classified annex, and defines the problem as a data-collection deficiency rather than an access deficiency, converting a question about who is hiding what into a request for better forms and more money.
dossier.narrative:
The assessment exists because of a paragraph in a Senate committee report, not because of an executive decision to inform the public. Senate Report 116-233, submitted by Senator Marco Rubio from the Select Committee on Intelligence on 17 June 2020 to accompany S. 3905, directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to submit an intelligence assessment of the threat posed by UAP and of the progress the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force had made. Appendix B of the resulting product reprints the eight specific things the Senate asked for. Two of them are worth memorizing. Item 4 demanded 'a detailed description of an interagency process for ensuring timely data collection and centralized analysis of all UAP reporting for the Federal Government, regardless of which service or agency acquired the information.' Item 5 demanded 'Identification of an official accountable for the process described in paragraph 4.' The Senate was asking, in oversight language, who owns the file. ODNI's answer, in the Scope section, is a title with no name attached: 'The Director, UAPTF, is the accountable official for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP.'

The drafting coalition is itself a finding. The report was written by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Navy/ONI, DARPA, FAA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI's National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and the National Intelligence Council. The Department of Energy is not on the list. Neither is CIA. Neither is any Special Access Program Central Office. For a document whose central unresolved question is whether the objects are American, the absence of the organizations that would custody the most sensitive American aerospace and nuclear-adjacent programs is the shape of the hole.

The numbers are small and precise. One hundred forty-four reports originated from USG sources. Eighty of those involved observation with multiple sensors: radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, visual. One was identified with high confidence, 'a large, deflating balloon.' The rest, 143, 'remain unexplained.' In eighteen incidents, described across twenty-one reports, observers reported unusual movement or flight characteristics: objects that appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, maneuver abruptly, or travel at considerable speed 'without discernable means of propulsion.' In a small number of cases 'military aircraft systems processed radio frequency (RF) energy associated with UAP sightings.' The UAPTF 'holds a small amount of data that appear to show UAP demonstrating acceleration or a degree of signature management,' with further analysis promised. Eleven documented near misses were on file.

The five-bin taxonomy, airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other,' is where the board plants its flag. Under the third bin the report says: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to developments and classified programs by U.S. entities. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' That is not a denial that such programs exist. It is a statement that the drafters could not obtain confirmation. An intelligence assessment written by the DNI's aviation manager and coordinated across sixteen organizations was unable to check its own government's classified aerospace inventory against its own government's unexplained-object file. Either no such inventory exists, or access to it was refused, or the query was never seriously pressed. Each possibility is load-bearing.

The geographic finding is handled the same way. UAP sightings 'tended to cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds,' and 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems.' The report immediately neutralizes this as probable collection bias: more sensors, greater expectation, standing guidance to report anomalies. That may be true. It is also exactly the explanation one would offer to avoid the alternative reading, which is that the objects are interested in specific American infrastructure, the same pattern documented at Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot and Falconbridge in October and November 1975.

The remedies proposed are all inputs, never access. Standardize reporting. Consolidate data. Employ artificial intelligence and machine learning to cluster features. Search historical radar archives with advanced algorithms. Update the interagency collection strategy. Increase R&D investment guided by a UAP Collection Strategy, a UAP R&D Technical Roadmap, and a UAP Program Plan. Not one recommendation asks any agency to disclose what it already holds. The report also records, candidly, that no standardized reporting mechanism existed anywhere in the U.S. military until the Navy created one in March 2019 and the Air Force adopted it in November 2020, meaning that for the entire post-Blue Book era the United States operated with no formal channel by which a military aviator could report an object over a nuclear or test facility. That is not an accident of bureaucracy; it is a design decision with a fifty-year half-life. The report is equally candid about the human cost: aviators and analysts 'describe disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues.'

The institutional sequel followed within six months. Section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 117-81, signed 27 December 2021, directed establishment of a successor office. The Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group was stood up and then superseded; the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was formally established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum published 20 July 2022, designating AARO the authoritative DoD focal point for UAP and placing it under USD(I&S), one of the very components that had contributed to this assessment. The task force that could not confirm whether American programs accounted for any of its own 144 cases was thereby replaced by an office that would go on to assert that no such programs ever existed. The 2021 assessment is the last moment the U.S. government's written position was uncertainty rather than denial, which is precisely why it is the most useful single document in the modern record.

claims.text: The assessment states that '144 reports originated from USG sources. Of these, 80 reports involved observation with multiple sensors,' that one UAP was identified with high confidence as 'a large, deflating balloon,' and that 'The others remain unexplained.'
claims.source: https://www.dni.gov/files/ODNI/documents/assessments/Prelimary-Assessment-UAP-20210625.pdf (ODNI, Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, 25 June 2021, p. 4)

claims.text: On the possibility that the objects are American, the assessment states: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to developments and classified programs by U.S. entities. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.'
The dataset is 'currently limited primarily to U.S. Government reporting of incidents occurring from November 2004 to March 2021.'

'In 18 incidents, described in 21 reports, observers reported unusual UAP movement patterns or flight characteristics,' including objects that appeared to 'remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, maneuver abruptly, or move at considerable speed, without discernable means of propulsion.'

'In a small number of cases, military aircraft systems processed radio frequency (RF) energy associated with UAP sightings,' and 'The UAPTF holds a small amount of data that appear to show UAP demonstrating acceleration or a degree of signature management.'

The report was drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Navy/ONI, DARPA, FAA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and the ODNI National Intelligence Council. The Department of Energy and CIA are not listed among contributors.

The Senate directive reprinted at Appendix B item 5 required 'Identification of an official accountable for the process' of centralized federal UAP data collection; the assessment identifies that official only by title, 'The Director, UAPTF,' and never by name.

'No standardized reporting mechanism existed until the Navy established one in March 2019. The Air Force subsequently adopted that mechanism in November 2020, but it remains limited to USG reporting.'

'UAP sightings also tended to cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds,' and 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems' - both attributed by the drafters to probable collection bias.
'The UAPTF has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.'

The assessment records institutional stigma as an active suppressant: 'Narratives from aviators in the operational community and analysts from the military and IC describe disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues.'

The assessment was mandated by a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 and was prepared for the Congressional Intelligence and Armed Services Committees; Senate Report 116-233 was submitted by Senator Marco Rubio from the Select Committee on Intelligence on 17 June 2020 to accompany S. 3905.

Every recommendation in the assessment concerns increasing collection, standardization, analytic tooling and funding; none directs any U.S. agency to disclose UAP-related holdings it already possesses.

The successor office was created by statute within six months: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (Public Law 117-81, enacted 27 December 2021) directed establishment of a UAP office, and the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was formally established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum published 20 July 2022 designating it the authoritative DoD focal point for UAP and UAP-related activities.

dossier.denialPosture: The assessment does not deny that a U.S. legacy program exists; it declines to confirm one, in the specific formulation 'We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' That is a sourcing statement about the drafters' own access, not a factual finding about the U.S. inventory, and it is signed institutionally by ODNI rather than by any named individual.
connections: Senator Marco Rubio, as Senate Select Committee on Intelligence chairman, is the named originator of the reporting requirement via S. Rept. 116-233; item 5 of that requirement, name the accountable official, is the direct ancestor of later legislative attempts to establish custody and eminent-domain provisions over recovered material.

The Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force is the operational predecessor entity; its Director is the unnamed accountable official, and identifying that person by name is a discrete research target.

USD(I&S) is listed as a contributor and later becomes AARO's parent organization, the same office that both wrote into this report that it could not confirm U.S. program attribution and later asserted through AARO that no such programs existed.
DARPA, NRO, NGA and NSA are listed contributors; the Department of Energy and CIA are not, which is the negative-space finding for the custody thread.

The clustering finding is the modern echo of the October-November 1975 SAC overflights (sac-overflights-1975), where the objects concentrated on nuclear weapons storage areas and missile fields and NORAD likewise failed to identify them.

The Sky Canada Project report (sky-canada-project) cites this U.S. architecture as a model and recommends Canadian partnership with AARO and NASA, making the 2021 assessment the template exported to allied governments.

The report's call for 'additional investment' and a 'UAP Program Plan' connects to the funding thread: any such plan requires a budget line, and the DoD audit record (dod-agencywide-audit) is the environment in which such lines become unverifiable.
openQuestions: Who was the Director, UAPTF, on 25 June 2021, and why is that individual unnamed in a document responding to a Senate demand to name the accountable official?
What is in the classified annex, and which committees received it?
By what procedure did the UAPTF attempt to check the 144 reports against U.S. classified developmental programs, which offices were queried, and which declined?
Why are the Department of Energy and CIA absent from the contributor list on a report whose central unresolved bin is 'USG or industry developmental programs'?
What became of the promised 'further analysis' of the acceleration and signature-management data, and does a completed product exist?
Do FAA or NOAA holdings referenced in the report contain UAP data predating November 2004 that was excluded from the dataset by scoping rather than by absence?
Which of the 144 cases, if any, occurred over or near nuclear weapons storage, ICBM fields or nuclear-powered vessels, and was that variable ever coded?

l0.label: AARO FY2024 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
l0.short: AARO FY2024 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP

dossier.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, produced by the Department of Defense All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) with an information cut-off of 1 June 2024 and released 14 November 2024. It is submitted to Congress under a statutory requirement at 50 U.S.C. 3373(k) and covers UAP reports from 1 May 2023 to 1 June 2024 plus all prior-period reports not previously reported. It was drafted in coordination with more than two dozen named organisations including ODNI, the Service intelligence centres, NRO, NGA, NSA, DIA, FBI, NCIS, DoE, NASA, the NNSA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
dossier.whyImplicated: AARO is not a neutral authority here; it is the office the Department created to be the answer to the question, and this report is the instrument by which it discharges its obligation to Congress. What makes it load-bearing is not its denials but the specific admissions embedded in them. Section IV.G is headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP" and its entire body is a single sentence stating that AARO is working with mission partners "to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured" - meaning that as of mid-2024 no such process existed anywhere the office could see. Section VI.C confirms that Oak Ridge National Laboratory analysed "a material claimed to be from a UAP." Section VI.D confirms AARO posted historical documents on KONA BLUE, a prospective and unapproved Special Access Program that interviewees described as a DHS compartment to cover up "the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" And the report concedes that 444 of the 757 reports lacked sufficient data for any analysis and that AARO received zero UAP reporting through national GEOINT, SIGINT or MASINT platforms during the entire period - the national technical means that would find a concealed program were not pointed at the problem at all.
dossier.narrative:
Read as a compliance document, the FY2024 report is a study in what a statutory reporting requirement can and cannot compel. 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1)(B) enumerates roughly fifteen mandatory content items, and the report walks them in order: events in period, events out of period, analysis by intelligence discipline, incidents over restricted airspace, threats, foreign attribution, breakthrough foreign capability, allied consultation, capture-or-exploitation efforts, health effects, nuclear-asset association, NNSA and NRC consultation, designated line organisations, and a summary of authorised reporting. The statute is well drafted. The answers are mostly negative, and the negatives are the interesting part.

The numbers: 757 reports received, of which 485 occurred in the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were only reported now. Cumulative holdings as of 24 October 2024 were 1,652 reports. Of the 757, 392 - more than half - came from the FAA, and consisted of the entire FAA UAP reporting log since June 2021. By domain: 708 air, 49 space, zero maritime, zero transmedium; and AARO notes that none of the space-domain reports came from space-based sensors, all being pilot or ground-observer accounts of objects estimated above 100 kilometres. AARO resolved 49 cases in-period, recommended 243 more for closure, judged 21 to merit further analysis by intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners, and consigned 444 to an 'Active Archive' for lack of data. By publication, the office reported 118 resolved and a further 174 finalised, all to prosaic objects.

The key sentence for anyone tracking concealment is buried in Section III.B: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms." Every input was pilot report, post-mission full-motion video, or FAA log. AARO can search IC databases case-by-case, but nothing was tasked. Whatever else the report establishes, it establishes that the collection architecture of the United States was not being used to answer this question during the period covered.

The second key passage is the nuclear-infrastructure section. AARO received eighteen reports from the NNSA Administrator and the NRC Chairman regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all of which those agencies categorised as unmanned aircraft systems. Two involved incursions of 53 minutes and one hour 57 minutes. On 3 August 2023 security at the D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant recovered a crashed UAS and turned it over to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement; AARO states flatly that it "has no further information about the crashed UAS." A recovered object over a nuclear facility left the federal system entirely and the office statutorily charged with anomaly resolution never got it back. Separately, the BWXT Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia experienced UAS overflights on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

The third is the authorities language. AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," with "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority." This is the exact authority whose absence is the subject of the Wilson-Davis memo - a Deputy Director of DIA being told by a contractor committee that his tickets and statutory authority were not sufficient. The FY2024 report asserts the authority exists. It does not report ever having exercised it against a waived or unacknowledged SAP, nor does it report a single instance of an access denial.

The science-and-technology section names the partner set: Oak Ridge National Laboratory for physics-relevant case analysis and the UAP-material analysis; the Air Force Research Laboratory for propulsion, stealth and sensing assessments; the Georgia Tech Research Institute, which built the GREMLIN sensor architecture that demonstrated functionality in a March 2024 test and was slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection "at a site of national security"; MIT Lincoln Laboratory, building prototype processing to recover objects currently filtered out of FAA and National Weather Service radar; and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source work. That is a real, funded, technically competent architecture, and its existence should be weighed against the report's own admission that the office cannot resolve most of its caseload.

Finally, the strategic communications section records that AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, characterising it as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" AARO's framing is dismissive. But the disclosure itself confirms that a UAP-linked prospective SAP was drafted, staffed toward DHS, and documented well enough that its papers could be posted eight months later.

claims.text: The report is submitted under a requirement established in 50 U.S.C. 3373(k), which directs the Director of the Office to report to the appropriate congressional committees not later than 180 days after enactment of the FY2023 Intelligence Authorization Act and annually thereafter for four years.

AARO received 757 UAP reports during the period 1 May 2023 - 1 June 2024; 485 occurred in period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were not previously reported. As of 24 October 2024 AARO held 1,652 reports in total.

Of the 757 reports, 392 came from the FAA and consisted of all of the FAA's UAP reports since 2021; 708 occurred in the air domain, 49 in the space domain, and none in the maritime or transmedium domains.

AARO determined 21 cases merit further analysis by its intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners; 444 cases lacked sufficient data to facilitate analysis and were placed in the Active Archive.
The report states verbatim: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms."

Section IV.G, headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP," consists in its entirety of the statement that "AARO is working with mission partners to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured, drawing on current USG capabilities and operating procedures" - an admission that no such process existed as of the cut-off date.
The report states: "It is important to underscore that, to date, AARO has discovered no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology."

AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," and that there is "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority."

Oak Ridge National Laboratory "provided analysis for a material claimed to be from a UAP," and AARO S&T, in coordination with ORNL, wrote a materials-analysis report and posted it on AARO's website, with supplemental data promised.

AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, described in the report as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'"

AARO received 18 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all categorised by those agencies as UAS; two incursions lasted 53 minutes and 1 hour 57 minutes respectively.

On 3 August 2023 D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant security recovered a crashed UAS which was given to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement, and "AARO has no further information about the crashed UAS." Separately, the BWXT (formerly Babcock and Wilcox Nuclear Energy) Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia observed UAS flyovers on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

In May 2023 the Joint Staff issued a UAP GENADMIN message directing Combatant Commands and Services to report all UAP incidents, incursions and engagements to Combatant Command Joint Operations Centers, Service Watch Centers, and respective counterintelligence elements no later than 96 hours after the event.

AARO's named science-and-technology partners are Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Georgia Tech Research Institute (developer of the GREMLIN sensor architecture, tested March 2024 and slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection at a site of national security), MIT Lincoln Laboratory (prototype processing for FAA and National Weather Service radar), and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source analysis.

dossier.denialPosture: Categorical and repeated: no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity or technology; no data indicating the capture or exploitation of UAP; no confirmation of foreign adversarial attribution. The denials are consistently framed as statements about what AARO possesses or has discovered rather than about what exists, which preserves deniability if material is held in a compartment AARO has not in fact penetrated.
connections: 50 U.S.C. 3373 and 50 U.S.C. 3373b are the statutory hooks; 3373(k) creates the report and 3373b creates the secure mechanism for current and former USG employees and contractors to report knowledge of purported UAP programs dating back to 1945

AARO was established on 15 July 2022 by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, renaming and expanding the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group; Sean Kirkpatrick (first director, July 2022 - December 2023) to Tim Phillips (acting) to Jon Kosloski, previously of NSA, is the leadership chain across the report's drafting
Oak Ridge National Laboratory is the government-side materials-analysis node, directly parallel to the Nolan-Vallee 2022 protocol

KONA BLUE links AARO's disclosure to the AAWSAP/DIA lineage and to the Department of Homeland Security; AARO's own Historical Record Report Vol 1 ties KONA BLUE's supporters to the cancelled DIA program
Georgia Tech Research Institute (GREMLIN), MIT Lincoln Laboratory, AFRL and NASIC are the technical contractor and laboratory set now built around the UAP problem
The report was drafted in coordination with NRO, NGA, NSA, DIA, MSIC, NGIC, NASIC, NCIS, FBI, DoE, NNSA and NRC among others - the same institutional set named across the legacy-program allegations
The May 2023 Joint Staff GENADMIN routes UAP reporting through Service counterintelligence elements, which for the Department of the Air Force means AFOSI

Rep. Mike Gallagher's May 2022 House Intelligence subcommittee hearing, at which the Wilson-Davis memo was entered into the record, is the immediate legislative antecedent of the reporting regime this document satisfies
openQuestions: What the 21 cases judged to merit further analysis actually are, and what became of them
Whether AARO has ever exercised its asserted authority to compel access to a waived or unacknowledged special access program, and whether any access was refused
Which material was analysed by ORNL, who supplied it, and what the chain of custody was
Why no national GEOINT, SIGINT or MASINT collection was tasked against UAP during a full reporting year, and who makes that tasking decision
What happened to the UAS recovered at D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant on 3 August 2023 after it was handed to county law enforcement
The identity of the 'site of national security' selected for the GREMLIN 90-day pattern-of-life collection
Whether the report's zero maritime and zero transmedium counts reflect absence of events or absence of a reporting channel from the naval and undersea domains

l0.label: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
l0.short: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP

dossier.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena is the fourteen-page statutory report submitted by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office under 50 U.S.C. § 3373(k), covering UAP events from 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025, bearing the clearance number 26-P-0880 and issued under the letterhead "Department of War." It was publicly released on 21 July 2026, months after the annual reporting cycle Congress contemplated. It records 319 new reports, 370 total resolutions, and no unexplained residue attributed to advanced foreign or non-human capability.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the current, dated instrument of official denial, and it is therefore the most useful single artifact on the board. Its flat assertion — "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials" — is immediately followed by the statement that AARO "is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG," a process AARO says draws on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for it. The report also claims an access authority that collides directly with standing DoD regulation: AARO states it is authorized to receive UAP information "regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs," while DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g simultaneously forbids any DoD contractor employee from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval and 32 CFR 117.6 removes DCSA visibility from carved-out programs entirely. Claiming access is not the same as exercising it. And the report is internally inconsistent on its headline finding: §IV.C states AARO resolved 44 events as satellite flaring during the reporting period while §VI states the new capability "enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring."
dossier.narrative:
The arithmetic is the place to start, because the report's own numbers do not reconcile cleanly and the discrepancy runs through its most-promoted achievement. AARO received 319 reports between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025: 284 events inside the window and 35 from 2010 to 2024 not previously reported. Of the 319, AARO resolved 114 and additionally resolved 256 cases from prior periods, for 370 resolutions in the reporting period. Case holdings totaled 1,870 as of 30 May 2025. By domain, 274 were airborne, 44 space, one maritime. Of the 319, 191 were transferred to the "active archive" — the category for cases with insufficient data to assess whether performance characteristics are consistent with natural phenomena or exceed the known state of the art. Nine reports were identified as meriting further analysis by intelligence community and science-and-technology partners. Two case files were merged.

Now the flaring numbers. Section III.A states that all 44 space-domain reports were assessed as satellite flaring, of which 42 came from FAA civilian pilot reports and two from ground-based U.S. Space Command sensors — and notes, pointedly, that "none of AARO's space-domain case assessments originated from space-based sensors." Section IV.C states: "AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period." Section VI states: "This capability, consisting of advanced three-dimensional modeling and simulation applications, enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring." The executive summary uses 238. Gillibrand's press release uses 238. The 238 figure only coheres if it spans the 256 previously reported cases as well as the current-period 44, which the report never states and which would mean the office's flagship analytic advance was applied overwhelmingly to a backlog rather than to new reporting. A downstream analyst should treat the 238/44 gap as an unresolved presentation problem in a fourteen-page document.

The substantive denials come in Section IV.G and Section IV.H. On materials: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel." On health: "To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects associated with their experience." Both are negative claims about AARO's own holdings, not about the world. The report never asserts that no such program or materials exist; it asserts that no evidence of them has reached this office.

The access claim in Section V.C is the report's strongest institutional assertion and its most testable: "AARO is authorized by law to receive all UAP-related information, including any classified national security information involving military or intelligence related activities, at any level of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs. Generally, no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority within the DoW, the IC, or any other USG department or agency." Note the hedge: "Generally." Note also what the sentence does not say — it describes a right to receive, not an exercised capability to compel, and it does not state that AARO has audited any carved-out special access program. Against that, 262 individuals used the secure reporting mechanism in the period; AARO determined 255 were out of scope and identified seven for follow-on interview. A 97 percent out-of-scope rate is either an accurate measure of noise or a measure of a scoping filter, and the report gives no criteria by which to tell.

Two passages cut against the report's own framing. Section IV.E: "AARO received and analyzed several reports describing UAP in or near national security sites or critical infrastructure. Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector." And Section III.A, the sole maritime case: a report from U.S. Navy assets operating off the coast of Virginia describing "approximately 100 airborne UAP and two, likely uncrewed, surface systems," which AARO says it is actively investigating. An office reporting no flight-safety concerns and no anomalous residue is simultaneously reporting an unmitigated threat vector and a hundred-object maritime event under investigation.

Section IV.F is the nuclear line. AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites — a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 in the FY2024 report. "None of these incidents were reported as UAP." Forty-seven of the 50 occurred between 1700 and 0500 local; five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours; 33 involved a single system, 17 involved between two and seven. The categorical exclusion of all 50 from UAP status is a classification decision made by the reporting agencies, not an analytic finding by AARO, and the report does not say who made it.

On process: the report was released 21 July 2026 under a statute requiring submission "not later than 180 days after December 23, 2022, and annually thereafter for four years." The FY2024 report was published in November 2024 and documented 757 reports against FY2025's 319. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who created AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and secured the FY2024 NDAA declassification language, issued a same-day statement calling the report "another crucial step forward" and AARO "the most comprehensive government effort on UAPs to date," and framed the arithmetic as 319 received, 114 explained, "leaving 205 unresolved." The report's own foreign-engagement section names exactly one activity for the year: AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London.

claims.text: The report is titled "Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena," is issued under "Department of War / All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office" letterhead, carries clearance number 26-P-0880, states an information cut-off of 30 May 2025, and runs 14 pages.

AARO reports receiving 319 UAP reports between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025 (284 in-period, 35 from events between 2010 and 2024), resolving 114 of them plus 256 cases from prior periods for 370 total resolutions, with case holdings of 1,870 reports as of 30 May 2025.

The report states in §IV.C that "AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period," while §VI and the Executive Summary state that a new capability "enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring" — an unexplained discrepancy within a 14-page document.

AARO states: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel."

AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP-related information, including any classified national security information involving military or intelligence related activities, at any level of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs," and that "generally, no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving UAP-related information."

Between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals contacted AARO through the secure reporting mechanism for persons claiming first-hand knowledge of a USG UAP-related program or activity dating back to 1945; AARO determined 255 were out of scope and identified 7 warranting a follow-on interview request.

On reports near national security sites the report states: "Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector."

The single maritime-domain case of the reporting period was a report from U.S. Navy assets operating off the coast of Virginia describing "approximately 100 airborne UAP and two, likely uncrewed, surface systems"; AARO states it "is actively investigating this event in coordination with the reporting unit."

AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding UAS incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites — a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 reported in FY2024 — and states "None of these incidents were reported as UAP." Forty-seven of 50 occurred between 1700 and 0500 local time; five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours.

AARO transferred 191 of the 319 reports to its "active archive" for insufficient data, and identified nine reports meriting further analysis by intelligence community and science-and-technology partners.

None of AARO's 44 space-domain case assessments originated from space-based sensors: 42 came from civilian pilot reports via the FAA and two from ground-based U.S. Space Command sensors. FAA reports from civilian aviators constituted 21 percent of AARO's incoming reporting.

The report's sole named foreign-partner engagement for the year is that "AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London, United Kingdom." AARO states it "aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025."
The report was released on 21 July 2026, well after the statutory annual cycle; the FY2024 report was published in November 2024, and the FY2024 report documented 757 reports against FY2025's 319.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who created AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and secured FY2024 NDAA language requiring declassification of UAP records, issued a same-day statement on 21 July 2026 calling the report "another crucial step forward," describing AARO as "the most comprehensive government effort on UAPs to date," and characterizing the numbers as 319 received and 114 explained, "leaving 205 unresolved."

dossier.denialPosture: The report issues two categorical denials and one implicit one. On materials: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials." On health: "To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects." On adversary technology: "None of the cases AARO resolved indicate advanced foreign adversarial capabilities or breakthrough technologies in any domain." Each is scoped to what has reached AARO rather than to what exists, and each is undercut within the same document by the unmitigated-threat-vector language, the hundred-object Virginia maritime case, and the fact that AARO is building a materials custody process for materials it says do not exist.
connections: The carve-out mechanism at 32 CFR 117.6 and DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g is the direct structural rebuttal to AARO's claimed unrestricted access: a contractor at a carved-out facility is regulatorily barred from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval, and DCSA has no oversight visibility into the program at all.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand — statutory author of AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and of the FY2024 NDAA declassification language; the office's principal congressional patron and the first responder to each annual report.
AARO Director Dr. Jon Kosloski, named in §VI as having participated in multiple on-camera interviews with national-level audiences during the reporting period.
50 U.S.C. § 3373 is the enabling statute; § 3373b establishes the authorized reporting mechanism through which the 262 first-hand claimants contacted the office.
The Condon Report's 1969 recommendation against establishing a federal UFO agency held until AARO's creation in 2022 — a fifty-three-year gap that is itself the concealment window.

The Robertson Panel's 1953 conclusion of "no residuum of cases" attributable to artifacts is the direct ancestor of AARO's "none of the cases AARO resolved indicate advanced foreign adversarial capabilities or breakthrough technologies in any domain."
The Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN of February 2025 is named but not described; it is the operative DoD-wide reporting order and has not been released.
The National Nuclear Security Administration and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission are the reporting sources for the 50 nuclear-adjacent UAS incidents that AARO excludes from UAP status.

The FY2024 report (757 reports) and the FY2025 report (319) together show a 58 percent drop in incoming volume in a single cycle, which the report attributes to the FY2024 FAA backlog rather than to any change in reporting behavior.
openQuestions: Why does §IV.C state 44 satellite-flaring resolutions for the reporting period while §VI and the Executive Summary state 238? The report never reconciles the figures or states which case population the 238 spans.
Who decided that all 50 nuclear-adjacent UAS incidents were "not reported as UAP" — the reporting agencies or AARO — and against what criteria?
What are the scoping criteria by which 255 of 262 first-hand claimants were ruled out of scope? None are published.
AARO says it is building a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials "by an appropriate line organization." Which organization, under what authority, and with what facility?
AARO claims access regardless of special access controls. Has AARO ever invoked that authority against a specific carved-out SAP, and if so, was access granted or refused?
The February 2025 Joint Staff UAP GENADMIN remains classified. What does it direct, and does it reach contractor personnel?
The Virginia maritime case describes approximately 100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems. What sensors recorded it, and what is the current status of the investigation?

Two reports described electronic or avionic interference near operational aircraft; AARO says it has "not yet rendered a determination." What is the determination timeline, and which airframes were involved?
The report was released roughly eight months later than the prior year's. What accounts for the delay, and was the report submitted to Congress on time even if released late?

l0.label: YANKEE BLUE (alleged AFOSI indoctrination program)

dossier.whatItIs: YANKEE BLUE is an alleged United States Air Force practice in which personnel entering certain classified units were shown photographs of flying saucers and told they were being read on to a programme to reverse-engineer non-human craft, when no such programme existed. It was reported in June 2025 by The Wall Street Journal as a finding of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office under its first director, Sean Kirkpatrick, and was said to have been halted by a spring 2023 directive from the office of the Secretary of Defense. No primary document establishing the programme, the practice or the directive has been released.
dossier.whyImplicated: If documented, YANKEE BLUE would be the single strongest item in the concealment strand of this board, because it is the government manufacturing belief in a recovery and reverse-engineering programme inside its own ranks - which means that some fraction of insider testimony about that programme could be the product of a deliberate indoctrination rather than of access. It cuts both ways and it cuts hard, which is exactly why the tiering here has to be strict. What is documented is not the programme. What is documented is the Department's behaviour when asked for the paper: an Office of the Secretary of Defense FOIA search confined to a single correspondence office returning no records in September 2025, a Pentagon spokesperson on 1 October 2025 stating she could not confirm the memorandum with the word "alleged" underlined for emphasis, and an OSD appellate authority on 12 December 2025 overturning that search as inadequate and remanding for a new one. A department that cannot locate a Secretary-level directive from 2023 has either a records problem or a candour problem, and either is on the map.
dossier.narrative:
This entity is retained on the board with the allegation graded low and the negative findings graded high, and the distinction should be kept in front of the reader at all times. A negative primary finding is a documented fact. It is not a record of the thing.

The allegation entered the public record on 6 June 2025, when Joel Schectman and Aruna Viswanatha of The Wall Street Journal published "The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology." The reporting described a decades-long pattern in which the Air Force encouraged UFO belief to screen classified aviation programmes, and within that pattern a specific practice: personnel in certain classified units were briefed that they were being admitted to a programme called YANKEE BLUE concerned with reverse-engineering recovered non-human craft, shown photographs of saucers, bound by non-disclosure agreements, and in some accounts warned of extreme consequences for disclosure. The practice was said to have run from roughly the Cold War until 2023, when the office of the Secretary of Defense circulated a directive across the services ordering it to stop immediately. The finding was attributed to AARO's internal historical review under Sean Kirkpatrick.

Everything downstream of that article is either restatement or an attempt to find the paper. Popular Mechanics, VICE and the New York Post ran versions in June 2025; none produced independent documentation. The article itself, as researcher John Greenewald has noted, did not publish the memorandum, did not identify its date and did not describe its sourcing.

The documentary trail that does exist is a FOIA trail, and it is unusually clean because it has been published in full. On 17 June 2025 Greenewald's Black Vault filed a request with the Office of the Secretary of Defense for any directive issued in spring 2023 ordering a halt to YANKEE BLUE-related practices or to other activities involving fabricated claims of reverse-engineering non-human technology. OSD searched solely within its Correspondence Management Division and reported no responsive records. On 17 September 2025 an administrative appeal was filed arguing that a search confined to one office was not "reasonably calculated to uncover all relevant documents" under Oglesby v. U.S. Dep't of Army, 920 F.2d 57 (D.C. Cir. 1990), that a Secretary-level directive could reasonably reside in policy directorates or the OSD Executive Secretariat, and that agencies must pursue logical leads under Campbell v. DOJ, 164 F.3d 20 (D.C. Cir. 1998). The appeal also made the records-management point directly: any such 2023 memorandum would be subject to mandatory federal retention, so its absence is itself a finding.

On 1 October 2025, asked again about the WSJ claim, Pentagon spokesperson Susan Gough replied: "Regarding the alleged memo: I cannot confirm the existence of any department-level memo as described in the article. You may want to ask the Air Force or other military services whether they put out such a memo to their personnel." In the original email the word "alleged" was underlined. This is a carefully constructed sentence. It does not deny that the practice occurred. It denies confirmation of a department-level memorandum and redirects to the services. The Air Force did not respond to a request for comment.

On 12 December 2025 the Acting Chief of the OSD FOIA Division ruled on the appeal: "After carefully considering your appeal, and as a result of discussions between FOID personnel and this office, I am remanding your request to FOID for a search for responsive records." The appellate decision, released as case 25-A-3514-A1, does not establish that the memorandum exists. It establishes that the Department's own appellate authority found the Department's prior categorical no-records answer to rest on an inadequate search, and ordered it done again. As of the last published status the case remains open.

There is a second correction this board has already had to make about itself, and it belongs in the dossier. It has been widely repeated - including previously on this board - that AARO acknowledged YANKEE BLUE in its Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I, published 8 March 2024. It did not. A full-text check of the released 63-page volume returns no occurrence of the term, and it appears in none of the FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 consolidated annual reports. The board logged that correction on 12 August 2026. The only official gesture toward the subject is the Department's statement, made in the context of the June 2025 reporting, that it "is committed to releasing a second volume of its Historical Record Report, to include AARO's findings on reports of potential pranks and inauthentic materials," then expected in late 2025. No such volume was located in the sources available for this dossier, which means the sole official channel through which the finding was to be documented had not delivered as of the research cutoff.

So the honest state of the record is this. A major newspaper reported a specific, named, dated practice sourced to a Pentagon office's internal review. The Pentagon has neither confirmed nor denied the practice, has said it cannot confirm the memorandum, has failed one FOIA search on appeal, has been ordered to search again, has promised a report volume that would address it, and has not published that volume. Every one of those is an artifact of an institution's conduct and every one of them is dated and attributable. None of them is the programme. YANKEE BLUE stays on this board as a node about the Department's disclosure behaviour, and it should not be cited by anyone as established fact about what was done to Air Force personnel until a document with a signature block exists.

claims.text: The Wall Street Journal reported on 6 June 2025 that AARO, under its first director Sean Kirkpatrick, found that personnel in classified Air Force units had for decades been shown flying-saucer imagery and told they were being read on to a reverse-engineering programme called YANKEE BLUE that did not exist.
claims.source: Joel Schectman and Aruna Viswanatha, "The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology," The Wall Street Journal, 6 June 2025, https://www.wsj.com/politics/national-security/ufo-us-disinformation-45376f7e

claims.text: The Wall Street Journal reported that a directive from the office of the Secretary of Defense was circulated across the services in spring 2023 ordering the practice to stop immediately. The article did not publish the memorandum, identify its date or describe its sourcing, and no such document has surfaced publicly.

A FOIA request filed with the Office of the Secretary of Defense on 17 June 2025 sought any spring 2023 directive halting YANKEE BLUE-related practices; OSD searched solely within its Correspondence Management Division and reported no responsive records in September 2025.

Pentagon spokesperson Susan Gough stated on 1 October 2025: "Regarding the alleged memo: I cannot confirm the existence of any department-level memo as described in the article. You may want to ask the Air Force or other military services whether they put out such a memo to their personnel." In the original email the word "alleged" was underlined for emphasis.

On 12 December 2025 the Acting Chief of the OSD FOIA Division granted the administrative appeal and wrote: "After carefully considering your appeal, and as a result of discussions between FOID personnel and this office, I am remanding your request to FOID for a search for responsive records."

The appeal, filed 17 September 2025, argued that confining the search to the Correspondence Management Division was not "reasonably calculated to uncover all relevant documents" under Oglesby v. U.S. Dep't of Army, 920 F.2d 57 (D.C. Cir. 1990), and that agencies must pursue logical leads under Campbell v. DOJ, 164 F.3d 20 (D.C. Cir. 1998).
The Air Force did not respond to a request for comment on the alleged directive, and as of 15 December 2025 the FOIA case seeking information on the alleged YANKEE BLUE ritual remained open.

The term "Yankee Blue" does not appear anywhere in AARO's Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I (8 March 2024), nor in the FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 consolidated annual reports. The widely repeated claim that AARO conceded the programme in Volume I does not survive a full-text check.
