l0.label: Sec. 6802, James M. Inhofe NDAA for FY2023 (Pub. L. 117-263) - AARO establishment, Historical Record Report and annual reports
l0.short: Sec. 6802, James M. Inhofe NDAA for FY2023 (Pub. L. 117-263)

dossier.whatItIs: Section 6802 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, Public Law 117-263, Division F (the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023), Title LXVIII, enacted 23 December 2022, 136 Stat. 3586. Section 6802(a) amended 50 U.S.C. 3373 in its entirety, replacing the FY2022 Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group language with the statutory charter of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. It is the provision that put a congressional demand for the concealment history into permanent federal law.
dossier.whyImplicated: Section 6802 is the moment Congress wrote its suspicion into the United States Code. The historical record report it mandates at 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) does not ask whether UAP are real; it orders the Director of AARO to compile and itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress' and 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities,' from 1 January 1945 forward. Those are not the words of a legislature seeking information about aerial objects. They are the words of a legislature accusing the executive branch of running unreported compartmented programs and conducting a disinformation effort, and then ordering the executive branch to write the indictment itself. Section 6802 also created the material-testing and propulsion-science machinery at 50 U.S.C. 3373(e) and (g), and Section 6803 attached a Comptroller General audit to the historical record report because Congress did not trust the self-investigation it had just commissioned.
dossier.narrative:
Read Section 6802 the way a prosecutor reads a charging document and the picture is unmistakable.

The mechanics first, because the citation matters and is commonly muddled. Public Law 117-263 is the FY2023 NDAA. Division F of that act is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023. Section 6802(a) of Division F, Title LXVIII, amended 50 U.S.C. 3373 generally, at 136 Stat. 3586. That is the AARO charter. A separate provision, Section 1673 of Division A, Title XVI, at 136 Stat. 2959, created 50 U.S.C. 3373b, the authorized-disclosure mechanism, and it is Section 1673 rather than Section 6802 that carries the phrase 'reverse engineering.' An analyst tracing statutory authority needs both, and needs to keep them distinct: 6802 built the office, 1673 built the whistleblower channel, and Section 6803 built the audit.

Now the language. Subsection (j)(1)(A) requires the Director of AARO, within 540 days of 23 December 2022, to submit to the congressional defense committees, the congressional intelligence committees and congressional leadership 'a written report detailing the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' drawing on intelligence community records and documents, oral history interviews, open source analysis, interviews of current and former Government officials, and 'classified and unclassified national archives including any records any third party obtained pursuant to section 552 of title 5.' Subsection (j)(1)(B)(i) sets the period: 'beginning on January 1, 1945' and running to completion.

Then (j)(1)(B)(ii), the operative demand. The report shall 'include a compilation and itemization of the key historical record of the involvement of the intelligence community with unidentified anomalous phenomena, including — (I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

Subparagraph (I) is a statutory recognition that unreported restricted-access programs may exist — which is precisely the waived-SAP and Restricted Data territory that the Information Security Oversight Office cannot independently inventory and that the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver channel narrows to four members of Congress. Subparagraph (III) is a statutory recognition that a disinformation effort may exist, and it uses the word 'obfuscate' and the phrase 'manipulate public opinion' in the United States Code. Congress does not legislate against hypotheticals in these terms.

Subsection (j)(2) removed the obvious dodge in advance: 'The Archivist of the United States shall make available to the Office such information maintained by the National Archives and Records Administration, including classified information, as the Director of the Office considers necessary.' No classification barrier at the Archives.

Section 6802 also built the technical apparatus. Subsection (e)(1) directs the Secretary of Defense, coordinating with the DNI, to designate 'one or more line organizations' primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of field-investigation data and data from other sources, 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.' Subsection (e)(2) requires directives ensuring each designated line organization has authority 'to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.' Subsection (g) orders a science plan to develop and test theories accounting for 'characteristics and performance of unidentified anomalous phenomena that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation,' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.' Replicate. The statute contemplates replication of performance exceeding the known state of the art. Subsection (n)(6) then defines 'line organization' in a way that excludes any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense — pushing the material testing out to service labs, national labs and agencies where the work would actually be done.

The reporting architecture around it is equally telling. Subsection (l)(4) requires the Director to give the Armed Services and Intelligence committee leadership, every briefing period, 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.' Congress built a running log of refusals into the statute. And Section 6803 of the same public law, at 136 Stat. 3594, required the Comptroller General within 90 days to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the historical record report process, with on-site work as appropriate, quarterly findings to AARO, and semiannual verbal briefings to the intelligence committees, the defense committees and congressional leadership.

That is a statute that funds an office, orders it to investigate its own department's concealment history back to 1945, strips the classification defense at the Archives, requires it to log every time it is refused data, and puts an independent auditor over its shoulder. Later Congresses kept tightening: Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60, enacted 18 December 2025, ordered the AARO Director within 180 days to make 'an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena,' and Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 barred UAP-related independent research and development costs from being allowable as indirect contract expenses unless the material is made available to the defense and intelligence committees and congressional leadership — a direct strike at the mechanism by which contractor-held UAP work could be billed to the taxpayer without congressional visibility.

Section 6802 is the hook because everything downstream hangs from it: AARO's existence, the historical record report, the line-organization material testing, the classification-guide accounting, and the statutory vocabulary — 'restricted access,' 'not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' 'obfuscate' — that the rest of the disclosure fight is conducted in.

claims.text: Section 6802(a) of Public Law 117-263, Division F, Title LXVIII, enacted 23 December 2022 at 136 Stat. 3586, amended 50 U.S.C. 3373 in its entirety, establishing the statutory charter of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office.

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(I), as enacted by Section 6802, requires AARO's historical record report to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(III) requires the report to itemize 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

The historical record report was due not later than 540 days after 23 December 2022 and must focus on the period 'beginning on January 1, 1945,' running to the date the Director completes the activities.

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(2) requires the Archivist of the United States to make available to AARO 'such information maintained by the National Archives and Records Administration, including classified information, as the Director of the Office considers necessary' — removing classification as a basis for withholding at NARA.

50 U.S.C. 3373(e)(1) directs designation of one or more 'line organizations' primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of UAP data 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models'; subsection (n)(6) defines 'line organization' so as to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense.

50 U.S.C. 3373(g) requires a science plan to develop and test theories accounting for UAP 'characteristics and performance... that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4) requires the AARO Director each briefing period to provide the chairs and ranking members of the Armed Services and Intelligence committees 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.'

Section 6803 of Public Law 117-263, at 136 Stat. 3594, required the Comptroller General within 90 days of enactment to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the historical record report process, including on-site work, with quarterly findings provided to AARO and semiannual verbal briefings to the congressional intelligence committees, defense committees and congressional leadership.
claims.source: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3373&num=0&edition=prelim (Statutory Notes, 'Comptroller General of the United States Audits and Briefings on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Historical Record Report')

claims.text: The phrase 'reverse engineering' does not appear in Section 6802; it appears in the companion provision, Section 1673 of Public Law 117-263, Division A, Title XVI, 136 Stat. 2959, which created 50 U.S.C. 3373b and covers federal and contractor activity relating to UAP 'including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.'

50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) requires the Secretary, within 72 hours of determining that an authorized disclosure relates to a restricted access activity, special access program or compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the defense or intelligence committees, to report that disclosure to those committees and to congressional leadership.

50 U.S.C. 3373b(b)(1) provides that an authorized disclosure shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement, shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under Executive Order 13526 or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, and is not a violation of 18 U.S.C. 798 or other disclosure law.

Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31, enacted 22 December 2023, bars independent research and development funding relating to UAP from being allowable as indirect contract expenses under DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless such material and information is made available to the congressional defense committees, the House and Senate intelligence committees and congressional leadership.
claims.source: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3373&num=0&edition=prelim (Statutory Notes, 'Limitation Regarding Independent Research and Development')

claims.text: Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60, enacted 18 December 2025, requires the AARO Director within 180 days to make 'an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena' and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix for UAP-related programs.
claims.source: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3373&num=0&edition=prelim (Statutory Notes, 'Accounting of Security Classification Guides Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena')

dossier.denialPosture: Section 6802 contains no denial; it is the instrument that compels one. Its significance for the concealment record is that any AARO historical record report issued under 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) that fails to itemize unreported restricted-access programs or obfuscation efforts is a dated, signed statutory filing by a named Director, made under a mandate that expressly contemplated finding both — which converts a null finding from an absence of evidence into an attributable representation to Congress.
connections: Creates the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office; AARO's Director reports to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI on operational and security matters and to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B).

Companion to Section 1673 of the same public law, which created 50 U.S.C. 3373b — the authorized-disclosure channel, the reverse-engineering enumeration, the anti-reprisal protections and the government-wide and contractor-wide sweep of UAP nondisclosure orders.
Section 6803 attaches Government Accountability Office audit oversight to the historical record report; the Comptroller General is the only independent auditor in the scheme.

The 'restricted access... not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress' formulation directly implicates the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waived-SAP channel and the E.O. 13526 Sec. 4.3 special access program structure that ISOO cannot independently inventory.
The Atomic Energy Act immunity in 3373b(b)(1)(B) ties the statutory scheme to Department of Energy Restricted Data authorities outside the E.O. 13526 system.

The Archivist of the United States is made a compelled source under 3373(j)(2), the same official who holds the UAP Records Collection under the FY2024 NDAA and would hold the permanent collection under the Burlison FY2027 amendment.
Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 targets contractor independent research and development billing, the funding mechanism most often alleged for contractor-held UAP work.

Later amendments by Public Law 118-31 Sec. 7341, Public Law 118-159 Sec. 1089, and Public Law 119-60 Secs. 1671 and 1672 progressively tightened reporting, added NORAD and NORTHCOM intercept reporting back to 1 January 2004, and required the classification guide accounting.
openQuestions: Whether the historical record report required by 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) was delivered within the 540-day statutory deadline and in how many volumes; the delivery record was not examined for this dossier.

Which 'line organizations' were designated under 50 U.S.C. 3373(e)(1) for material testing, medical studies and theoretical modelling — the names are required to be reported under 3373(k)(1)(B)(xvi) but have not been verified here.
How many enumerations of withheld data have been provided to the committees under 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4), and what they contain.
What the Comptroller General's Section 6803 audit found, and whether any of the semiannual verbal briefings produced a written product.
Whether the nondisclosure order sweep required by 50 U.S.C. 3373b(b)(3)(A) was in fact conducted by all covered agencies and contractors, and how many instruments were produced to AARO.
How many 72-hour congressional notifications under 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) have been made — each one would be a formal statement that an unreported restricted-access program was implicated.
Whether any contractor has had UAP-related IRAD costs disallowed under Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31, which would be a documented dollar figure attached to contractor UAP work.

Whether the security classification guide accounting required by Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60 was completed by its June 2026 deadline and whether a consolidated classification matrix was issued.

l0.label: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)
l0.short: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program

dossier.whatItIs: The Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program was a Defense Intelligence Agency effort solicited publicly on 18 August 2008 as HHM402-08-R-0211 by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity and awarded on 22 September 2008 as firm-fixed-price contract HHM402-08-C-0072 to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, LLC of Las Vegas. Its stated objective was to understand the physics and engineering of breakthrough aerospace weapon system applications out to the year 2050 across twelve technical areas. It ran to 2012 and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents plus a much larger body of work that has never been released.
dossier.whyImplicated: AAWSAP is the only documented instance in the modern record of the United States government funding a private company to study the physics of observed anomalous flight performance, and its own procurement file shows the seams through which such work escapes normal visibility. The solicitation was posted as a total small business set-aside under a classification code meaning 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' place of performance was the contractor's own facility, and the Top Secret facility clearance requirement was formally amended so that it was not required prior to contract implementation. The statement of work provides that any accountable property the contractor acquires with government funds becomes government-owned property and must be inventoried and returned within sixty days of contract end - a custody provision whose closeout has never been publicly documented. Senator Harry Reid asked the Deputy Secretary of Defense to convert the effort into a special access program on 24 June 2009 and was refused. The unreleased output of this contract, which its own government manager has described as running to more than a hundred detailed reports, is the largest identified block of missing documentary material in the modern record.
dossier.narrative:
AAWSAP is the best-documented UAP effort in the history of the United States government, and the reason is mundane: it was a competed commercial-items procurement, so it left a paper trail that the Freedom of Information Act could reach.

The solicitation went up on FedBizOpps as a combined synopsis/solicitation on 18 August 2008 under number HHM402-08-R-0211, issued by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity at Bolling AFB, with responses due 5 September 2008. It was coded B, 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' under NAICS 541330, Engineering Services, and it was 'solicited as a total small business set aside' with a size standard of twenty-five million dollars. The Statement of Objectives, dated 18 July 2008, is unambiguous about what was wanted: 'The objective of this program is to understand the physics and engineering of these applications as they apply to the foreign threat out to the far term, i.e., from now through the year 2050. Primary focus is on breakthrough technologies and applications that create discontinuities in currently evolving technology trends. The focus is not on extrapolations of current aerospace technology.' Twelve technical areas were named, covering lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament including directed energy, and other peripheral areas.

The qualification language is the tell. Offerors were asked to 'provide examples, conducted within the past 7 years, of having performed, as a prime contractor, the analysis, design, construction, and flight testing of high performance aircraft and/or satellites,' with the note that 'Success in this program is dependent upon this capability and experience.' The government was not shopping for a literature review.

The award document, Standard Form 1449, records contract HHM402-08-C-0072, awarded 22 September 2008 to BIGELOW AEROSPACE ADVANCED SPACE STUDIES, LLC, 4640 S Eastern Ave, Las Vegas NV, CAGE 54JU7, DUNS 827037768, with a total award amount of $21,948,810.00 and a base year of 22 September 2008 to 29 September 2009 followed by option years. The solicitation had anticipated 'a base year of 12 months from date of award plus four (4) 12 month option years' running to 30 September 2013. Deliverable line items were status reports, a project management plan for tasks 3.a.1 through 3.a.12, research reports for the same tasks, a Comprehensive Integrated Threat Assessment, travel and other direct costs.

Three provisions in the statement of work matter more than the money. First, security: 'The contractor shall comply with the terms and conditions of the DD-254 BEFORE initiating any classified effort,' and 'Contractor shall provide a work facility (including unclassified information systems) with a Top Secret Facility Clearance granted by the Defense Security Service (DSS).' But an amendment posted with the solicitation changed DD Form 254 Block 13 from 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE GRANTED BY THE DEFENSE SECURITY SERVICE (DSS) PRIOR CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION' to 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL NOT BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE ... PRIOR TO CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION. HOWEVER, IT MUST BE OBTAINED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE DURING THE INITIAL YEAR OF THE CONTRACT.' The facility-clearance bar was lowered before award.

Second, place of performance: 'The work under this contract shall be performed at the Contractor's facility.' Third, and most consequential for this board, property: 'Any accountable property acquired by the contractor with government funds during the execution of this contract shall become government owned property. ... This property must be inventoried and returned to the government not more than 60 days after the end of the contract.' There is, in the released file, no closeout inventory.

What the contractor actually did is not seriously in dispute, and AARO concedes it. AARO's Historical Record Report states: 'Although investigating UFO/UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organization conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager. This research included: reviewing new cases and much older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.' AARO adds that 'DIA did not seek, nor specifically authorize, this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract with the private sector organization,' and that the effort also investigated an alleged hotspot of UAP and paranormal activity at a Utah property then owned by the head of the contractor.

The special access question is the hinge. AARO records that 'On 24 June 2009, Senator Reid sent a letter to then Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Deputy Secretary Lynn declined to do so based on the recommendation of then-Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, James R. Clapper, Jr., that such a designation was not justified.' That refusal is documented in the FOIA record alongside DIA talking papers prepared for Reid's visits to the Director of DIA in January and May 2009 and an eighteen-page packet presented to the Deputy Secretary in November 2009.

AARO's account and the contractor's account of what the programme produced differ by an order of magnitude. AARO says the contract 'produced exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed,' and that it 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work.' The releasable record contains thirty-seven of thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. What is not in the record is the 494-page BAASS Ten Month Report, the Utah ranch investigation report, the personnel roster, obligation-by-year funding data, and the balance of the material that the government programme manager has described as running past a hundred reports. Under this board's sourcing rule, AARO's characterisation is a Tier 2 record of what AARO said, not a Tier 1 record of what exists.

claims.text: AAWSAP was solicited as a combined synopsis/solicitation posted 18 August 2008 under solicitation number HHM402-08-R-0211 by the Defense Intelligence Agency's Virginia Contracting Activity, coded 'B -- Special studies and analysis - not R&D' under NAICS 541330, and 'solicited as a total small business set aside.'

The Statement of Objectives dated 18 July 2008 states: 'The objective of this program is to understand the physics and engineering of these applications as they apply to the foreign threat out to the far term, i.e., from now through the year 2050.'

The solicitation asked offerors to provide examples from the past seven years 'of having performed, as a prime contractor, the analysis, design, construction, and flight testing of high performance aircraft and/or satellites,' stating that 'Success in this program is dependent upon this capability and experience.'

An amendment to the solicitation changed DD Form 254 Block 13 from requiring a Top Secret Facility Clearance from the Defense Security Service prior to contract implementation to stating that the contractor 'WILL NOT BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE ... PRIOR TO CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION. HOWEVER, IT MUST BE OBTAINED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE DURING THE INITIAL YEAR OF THE CONTRACT.'

The statement of work provides that 'Any accountable property acquired by the contractor with government funds during the execution of this contract shall become government owned property' and 'must be inventoried and returned to the government not more than 60 days after the end of the contract.'
The statement of work provides that 'The work under this contract shall be performed at the Contractor's facility.'

Contract HHM402-08-C-0072 was awarded on 22 September 2008 to BIGELOW AEROSPACE ADVANCED SPACE STUDIES, LLC, 4640 S Eastern Ave, Las Vegas NV, CAGE 54JU7, DUNS 827037768, as a firm fixed price contract, with a total award amount of $21,948,810.00 recorded on the Standard Form 1449.

The award document records deliverable line items of status reports, a project management plan for tasks 3.a.1 through 3.a.12, research reports for the same tasks, a Comprehensive Integrated Threat Assessment, travel and other direct costs, with a base year of 22 September 2008 to 29 September 2009 and option-year line items running into 2010.

AARO states that 'Although investigating UFO/UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organization conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager,' including reviewing new and Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and 'proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.'
AARO states that 'DIA did not seek, nor specifically authorize, this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract with the private sector organization.'

AARO states that on 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program, and that 'Deputy Secretary Lynn declined to do so based on the recommendation of then-Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, James R. Clapper, Jr., that such a designation was not justified.'

AARO states that 'AAWSAP/AATIP was terminated in 2012 upon the completion of its deliverables due to DIA and DoD concerns about the project,' and that afterwards 'its supporters unsuccessfully attempted to convince DHS to support a new version of this effort dubbed KONA BLUE.'

The DIA FOIA release file for AAWSAP includes Reid's 24 June 2009 special access program request letter to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, DIA talking papers prepared for Reid's January and May 2009 visits, and contract status briefings dated December 2008, May 2009 and August 2009.

The BAASS Ten Month Report, the Utah property investigation report, the AAWSAP personnel roster, and obligation-by-year funding data have never been officially released, and no contract closeout property inventory required by the statement of work appears in the released record.

dossier.denialPosture: AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report concedes the UFO research but characterises AAWSAP as an unauthorised drift from an authorised aerospace threat study, states that DIA 'did not seek, nor specifically authorize' the UFO work, that the deliverables were 'exploratory papers' that were 'never thoroughly peer reviewed,' and that AARO 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work conducted by AAWSAP/AATIP.'
openQuestions: Whether the property inventory and return required within sixty days of contract end was ever performed, what was on it, and where that property is now. The statement of work made everything the contractor bought with government money government property.

The obligated funding by year. The Standard Form 1449 records a total award amount of $21,948,810.00, but the line-item prices are redacted under FOIA exemption (b)(4) and no year-by-year obligation data has been released.
The full deliverable inventory. Thirty-seven of thirty-eight DIRDs are public; the Ten Month Report, the Comprehensive Integrated Threat Assessment, and the monthly status reports are not.
Whether the Top Secret facility clearance the amended DD-254 required 'as soon as possible during the initial year of the contract' was ever granted, and on what date.
Who the DIA program manager's chain of command was, and what internal record exists of the decision not to stop the UFO work that AARO says DIA never authorised.

dossier.whatItIs: AATIP is the unclassified nickname attached to a Defense Intelligence Agency effort that ran on congressional earmarks from FY2008 through roughly 2012, executed under contract by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies LLC (BAASS) of North Las Vegas. Primary documents show the name used in at least three incompatible ways: as the DIA contract line (Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program), as the internal DIA program office designation (AAWSAP, the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program), and as a later OUSD(I) activity that Luis Elizondo says he ran and that DoD public affairs says never officially existed. The naming collision is not trivia; it is the seam along which the whole custody question runs.
dossier.whyImplicated: AATIP is the only publicly documented instance in which a sitting Senate Majority Leader wrote to a Deputy Secretary of Defense asking for a Restricted SAP with a Bigoted Access List to protect, in his own words, "the methodology used to identify, acquire, study, and engineer the advanced technologies associated with AATIP." Acquire and engineer are custody and reverse-engineering verbs, and Reid put them in a signed letter dated 24 June 2009 to William Lynn III. DIA's own December 2010 info memo from LTG Ronald Burgess to USD(AT&L) confirms the SAP request, confirms DIA refused it in November 2009 for lack of classification grounds, and then confirms Burgess told Reid the work "could be transitioned to another agency or component better suited to oversee the project." That single sentence is the hinge: it is DIA, in writing, describing the handoff that becomes KONA BLUE eighteen months later. Everything the Pentagon has said since 2017 about AATIP has been an argument about the name rather than a denial of the paper trail, and the paper trail is signed by Reid, Lynn, Burgess and Maples.
dossier.narrative:
The origin is documented to the appropriation. LTG Ronald L. Burgess Jr., Director of DIA, wrote to the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics in an info memo dated 3 December 2010 (U-10-2552/CE) that "The Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program was first sponsored in the Fiscal Year (FY) 2008 Defense Supplemental Appropriation Act by Senators Reid and Inouye with a $10 million add," for the purpose of investigating "foreign advanced aerospace weapon threats from the present out to the next 40 years" and to "build an infrastructure to house a center of expertise on advanced aerospace technologies." The FY2010 Defense Appropriations Act added $12 million more. DIA issued an RFP naming twelve technical areas: lift, propulsion, control, armament, signatures reduction, materials, configuration, power generation, temporal translation, human effects, human interface, and technology integration. The contract went to BAASS, which Burgess notes was "the only bid." A separate DHS memo dated 28 November 2011 puts the two-year total at $22M, the deliverables at 38 research papers, and describes "an active, searchable database (now with greater than 100,000+ entries)."

The procurement history in that DHS memo adds names the DoD record does not volunteer. In May 2008 Senators Reid, Inouye and Stevens invited a DIA program manager (name redacted in the release) to meet with them about a research program involving 'exotic sciences.' In July 2008 LTG Michael Maples, then Director of DIA, was briefed by Reid directly. The redacted program manager is widely identified in secondary literature as James Lacatski; the released document does not name him.

The Reid letter of 24 June 2009 to Deputy Secretary William Lynn III is the load-bearing artifact. Reid asks for a Restricted SAP with a Bigoted Access List for specific portions of AATIP, and enumerates what needs protecting. First, "The methodology used to identify, acquire, study, and engineer the advanced technologies associated with AATIP." Second, allocation of personnel, support and oversight, because "Protection of industry partnerships and participation is critical. Public awareness of an industry's AATIP affiliation may discourage that industry's further participation with the U.S. Government in this program." Third, "Application and engineering" — where Reid writes that "The nuanced manner in which some of these technologies will be collected, engineered and applied by the U.S. may require senior level government approval" and that access to "the 'big picture' or overall intent of the program" should be restricted to a strict Bigoted List. Attachment 1 to the letter designates SAP Category "Intelligence, DoD Acquisition," program length FY09-FY13, and lists a preliminary bigoted list beginning with Lynn, Reid, Inouye, and Robert T. Herbert of the U.S. Senate; the contractor list begins with BAASS.

DIA said no. Burgess writes that in November 2009, at the request of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, DIA reviewed the program and "determined that, based on classification levels of current and projected deliverables, insufficient grounds existed to classify the program, invoke an ACCM, or establish a restricted SAP." He and Lynn then met Reid in November 2009, "determined the reports were of limited value to DIA," and Burgess suggested transition to another agency. That is the documented push that lands at DHS as KONA BLUE in 2011.

The second life of the name begins in 2017. On 16 December 2017 the New York Times identified AATIP and Luis Elizondo, who had resigned from OUSD(I) effective 4 October 2017. From 2019 onward Pentagon spokeswoman Susan Gough has said Elizondo "had no assigned responsibilities for AATIP." In August 2024, after a three-year FOIA fight, The Black Vault obtained a 2017 draft memorandum authored by Elizondo and intended for issuance by Deputy Secretary Patrick Shanahan. The memo describes AATIP's strategic focus as "beyond next generation technologies in the areas of lift, propulsion, cloaking, and human effects," states that "DoD continues to consider AATIP a priority," and directs that "all DoD elements are hereby required to provide a courtesy copy of any data and information obtained from the field that related to unexplained or unknown aerial systems to the Director of Defense Intelligence for Technical Collection and Special Programs" — the position then held by Neill Tipton. DoD had told The Black Vault in December 2021 that no such records existed.

Who matters by name: Reid, Inouye, Stevens; Robert T. Herbert (Reid staff); Lynn; Maples; Burgess; Lacatski (per secondary sourcing); Robert Bigelow and BAASS; Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis as DIRD authors; Elizondo; Tipton; Shanahan; Gough. The record shows an earmarked, contractor-executed technology-exploitation effort whose sponsor asked in writing for engineering-grade compartmentation and was refused. The record does not show DIA ever taking custody of physical material under this contract, and does not resolve whether the OUSD(I) 'AATIP' Elizondo describes was the same activity or a successor riding the same nickname.

l0.short: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS), LLC

dossier.whatItIs: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) was the Las Vegas company, an arm of Robert Bigelow's aerospace operation, that held the Defense Intelligence Agency's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP) contract beginning in 2008. It staffed physicists, intelligence veterans and field investigators, produced the 38 technical papers that DIA later designated Defense Intelligence Reference Documents, and ran field investigations at Skinwalker Ranch and elsewhere. Funding is generally reported at $22 million across 2007-2012, with the DIA declining to renew in 2010.
dossier.whyImplicated: BAASS is the single best-documented instance of the US government routing intelligence money to a private aerospace contractor to study UAP and 'breakthrough technology applications employed in future aerospace weapon systems.' It is the exact structural shape the legacy-program hypothesis predicts: an intelligence agency sponsor, a cleared contractor with its own facilities in Nevada, cover stories for field investigators, and an explicit internal instruction that the sponsor's identity 'should NEVER be released or discussed in public.' Its deliverables are the government's own reverse-engineering reading list — warp metrics, traversable wormholes, metamaterials, invisibility cloaking. It also acquired custody of civilian-collected physical evidence by buying MUFON's case database, moving material from a public non-profit into a DIA-funded contractor without the reporting witnesses knowing who the ultimate sponsor was. Finally, the solicitation was written, by the sponsoring senator's own account, specifically to avoid the words UFO or UAP.
dossier.narrative:
The BAASS story begins with money and a Senate Majority Leader. In 2008 the Defense Intelligence Agency issued a solicitation for the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, whose stated purpose was to explore 'potential breakthrough technology applications employed in future aerospace weapon systems.' Harry Reid of Nevada has said publicly that he was behind the funding, and has explained the wording directly: 'The people putting out the bid thought it would be better that it didn't say flying saucers or unidentified flying objects. It was thought by many that it would just draw too much attention, and by it being phrased the way it was, we had somebody from the Defense Intelligence Agency draw out the specs of it. It covered that anyway.' Reid also stated flatly that Bigelow 'was not pre-selected' and that the award followed a competitive bid. The record shows the solicitation produced a single bidder, and the winner was a Nevada constituent of the senator who arranged the money. Steven Aftergood, writing for the Federation of American Scientists in January 2019, put it in a sentence: the program was 'apparently initiated at the behest of then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, with most of the funding directed to a Nevada constituent of his.'

What BAASS actually did splits into three streams, and the split matters for the board. The first is the technical literature. BAASS assembled a network of outside scientists — most prominently Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis — who produced 38 papers that DIA designated Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. DIA sent the title list to Senate Armed Services chairman John McCain and ranking member Jack Reed in January 2018, marked For Official Use Only, and released it publicly under FOIA on 16 January 2019. The titles include 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy' and papers on metamaterials, programmable matter, high-power microwave technology, metallic glasses and biological effects. Aftergood's summary is worth quoting because it is the government's own science-integrity problem stated plainly: many of the titles are 'highly conjectural and well beyond the boundaries of current science, engineering — or military intelligence.' For the board's purposes, the DIRD list is not evidence that any of this works. It is evidence of what an intelligence agency thought it needed to understand, and therefore of what it believed it might be looking at.

The second stream is field investigation. BAASS sent investigators to Utah's Uinta Basin and to Skinwalker Ranch — 512 acres owned by Bigelow personally until he sold it to Brandon Fugal in 2016. Internal BAASS documents obtained by The Debrief instructed investigators to pose as researchers from the local oil fields and never to reveal the names of 'BAASS, Robert Bigelow, Bigelow Aerospace…and most certainly [the] sponsors' identity should NEVER be released or discussed in public.' The ultimate sponsor was the DIA. The same documents record interviews about a bipedal 'dog-like creature' over six feet tall smelling of sulfur, 'little people' three to four feet tall, and a ghostly figure on a mesa. A progress report obtained separately by Tim McMillan indicated BAASS was attempting to establish communication with a non-human entity it believed occupied the ranch. A former team member told The Debrief that the actual job was to collect anything anomalous and work out 'how it could lead to new technology,' and that data quality was compromised because some ranch guards embellished incidents in hopes of a bonus.

The third stream, and the most under-analysed, is data and evidence acquisition. In 2009 BAASS funded the Mutual UFO Network and bought its entire reporting database — witness reports, witness identifying information, and collected evidence. James Carrion, MUFON's international director at the time, told The Debrief that all 'physical evidence that needed to be analyzed went to BAASS,' that he does not know whether any of it was returned, and that he himself did not know DIA was the sponsor when MUFON entered the agreement. Members of the public filing reports agreed only that their information might go to an unnamed 'third party.' BAASS also sought data from France's GEIPAN, approached Canadian researcher Chris Rutkowski for Canadian government cases, and sent a team to Brazil in 2009 to collect evidence from a recent event. That is a private contractor, funded by a US intelligence agency, systematically vacuuming up the international civilian UAP evidentiary base under a cover identity.

DIA declined to renew in 2010 and the investigative team was disbanded; a former employee described being told by phone that they no longer had a job. Some analysts held Secret clearances and were reportedly in the process of upgrading to Top Secret when terminated. What happened next is the pivot into AATIP under Luis Elizondo, and thence into the 2017 New York Times story. Elizondo has said he was not involved with BAASS but knew the individuals, and that they 'decided to cast a very wide net.' Michael Gold, testifying to House Oversight on 13 November 2024, gave AAWSAP a retrospective defence that is also a concession about how thin the official record is: 'If not for the work of the Advanced Aerospace Weapon Systems Applications Program (AAWSAP), Commander Dietrich's experience may have been lost to history.'

What the record does not establish: it does not show BAASS handling recovered non-human material, and no DIRD is a reverse-engineering report on a specific artefact. It does not resolve whether AAWSAP and AATIP were the same program under two names — the DoD has given conflicting accounts. And it does not account for what became of the MUFON physical evidence.

DIA released a list of 38 research titles funded by the program on 16 January 2019 under FOIA; the list, marked For Official Use Only, had previously been provided to Congress in January 2018.
One of the 38 titles is 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy,' prepared by Dr. Eric Davis.
The AAWSAP solicitation stated its purpose as exploring 'potential breakthrough technology applications employed in future aerospace weapon systems.'

Harry Reid told The Debrief: 'The people putting out the bid thought it would be better that it didn't say flying saucers or unidentified flying objects... we had somebody from the Defense Intelligence Agency draw out the specs of it. It covered that anyway.'

Asked whether Bigelow had been pre-selected because of his relationship with Reid and his public interest in UFOs, Reid said: 'No. It was like any other government contract... He was not pre-selected.'

Internal BAASS documents instructed field investigators to pose as researchers from nearby oil fields and stated that the names of 'BAASS, Robert Bigelow, Bigelow Aerospace…and most certainly [the] sponsors' identity should NEVER be released or discussed in public.' The sponsor was the Defense Intelligence Agency.

BAASS funded MUFON in 2009 in a deal that included the sale of all witness reports, witness information, collected evidence, and MUFON's entire reporting database; former MUFON international director James Carrion said all 'physical evidence that needed to be analyzed went to BAASS' and that he was unaware DIA was the sponsor at the time.

BAASS sought UAP data from France's GEIPAN via a former data analyst, contacted Canadian researcher Chris Rutkowski in 2009 for Canadian government cases, and sent investigators to Brazil around 2009 to collect evidence from a recent event.
Skinwalker Ranch is a 512-acre property owned by Robert Bigelow until his 2016 sale to Brandon Fugal; BAASS investigated it and the surrounding Uinta Basin under the DIA-funded contract.

A DIA FOIA Electronic Reading Room item is titled 'Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Contract,' with a companion item 'UNCLASSIFIED//P&S Aerospace Contract Status'; secondary reporting identifies the contract as HHM402-08-C-0072 with performance beginning 22 September 2008 and a single bid received.

Michael Gold testified to House Oversight on 13 November 2024 that 'If not for the work of the Advanced Aerospace Weapon Systems Applications Program (AAWSAP), Commander [Alex] Dietrich's experience may have been lost to history.'

Michael Shellenberger's written testimony states that 'From 2009 to 2017, the Pentagon had a program called Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)' and that 'AAWSAP reports ended in 2010 but ran through 2012, according to the DOD' — dates that conflict with the 2008 contract start and require reconciliation.

Colm Kelleher served as BAASS deputy administrator running day-to-day execution of the AAWSAP contract, and DIA officer James Lacatski originated the program; this is sourced to the participants' own book and to interested-party accounts rather than to a government record.
claims.source: James T. Lacatski, Colm A. Kelleher and George Knapp, 'Skinwalkers at the Pentagon' (2021); secondary summary at https://www.mysterywire.com/ufo/skinwalkers-inside-the-pentagon/

dossier.denialPosture: The Pentagon told The Debrief that DIA was not investigating UFOs, a position The Debrief noted is contradicted by the documentary record; the confusion is traceable to a solicitation that, by Harry Reid's own account, was deliberately written to omit the words UFO and UAP. Reid separately denied that Bigelow was pre-selected for the contract.
connections: Robert Bigelow to Harry Reid: the Senate Majority Leader who arranged the funding and the Nevada constituent who received it; Reid on the record denying pre-selection while confirming he arranged the money.

James Lacatski (DIA) is the named government originator; Colm Kelleher ran BAASS execution; both later co-authored a book with journalist George Knapp, making the primary participants also the primary secondary sources — a structural sourcing problem for the whole AAWSAP record.

Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis authored DIRDs and later appear across the To The Stars, AATIP and Grusch-adjacent networks; the DIRD list is the connective tissue between 2008-era DIA money and the post-2017 disclosure figures.

BAASS to MUFON to DIA: a chain of custody moving civilian-collected physical evidence and witness identities into an intelligence-funded contractor without witness knowledge — the clearest documented instance of private-sector evidence capture on the board.
BAASS to GEIPAN (CNES, France), to Canadian government case files via Chris Rutkowski, and to Brazil: an international collection footprint under commercial cover.
AAWSAP to AATIP to Luis Elizondo to the 16 December 2017 NYT article: the sequence by which contractor-era work surfaced publicly.
Skinwalker Ranch to Brandon Fugal (2016 purchase) and thence to commercial television; the site's evidentiary record is now controlled by a private owner.
Alex Dietrich's Nimitz encounter enters the record via AAWSAP, per Michael Gold's 2024 congressional testimony — linking BAASS directly to the 2004 Nimitz case and the 2017 videos.
openQuestions: Was $22 million the contract ceiling, the obligated amount, or the expended amount, and how much of the field-investigation work was funded from Bigelow's personal wealth rather than appropriated money?
What happened to the physical evidence transferred from MUFON to BAASS, and does any of it remain in private custody?
Did BAASS retain copies of the 38 DIRDs and the collected international case data after the contract lapsed in 2010, and were those holdings ever inventoried for the NARA UAP Records Collection?
Who else was on the AAWSAP distribution list, and which offices outside DIA received the DIRDs?
Are AAWSAP and AATIP the same program under two names, sequential programs, or a program and a successor counterintelligence portfolio? DoD has given inconsistent accounts.
Where did BAASS-cleared analysts go after the late-2010 terminations, and did any move to successor programs or to contractors named elsewhere on this board?

l0.label: The 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents (DIRDs)

dossier.whatItIs: The Defense Intelligence Reference Documents are a series of approximately thirty-eight unclassified technical survey papers commissioned from outside specialists under the AAWSAP contract and published by the Defense Intelligence Agency between roughly 2009 and 2011. They cover metamaterials, warp drive, traversable wormholes, antigravity, negative mass propulsion, quantum vacuum energy extraction, invisibility cloaking, high-frequency gravitational wave communications, and human biological effects of anomalous fields. Thirty-seven of the thirty-eight were released to The Black Vault by DIA on 25 March 2022 under FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018.
dossier.whyImplicated: The DIRDs are the most literal artefact on this board: a list, written by the United States government's own defence intelligence agency, of every theoretical route by which the observed flight performance of anomalous objects might be achieved. Read as a set, they are not a scattershot survey but a systematic decomposition of a capability - lift without visible propulsion, translation in space and time, signature reduction, materials that do not behave conventionally, and the effects such a craft would have on a human body standing near it. The government commissioned this taxonomy in 2008 and 2009 while the same contract was running field investigation teams and proposing laboratories to examine recovered material. One of the thirty-eight, the classified SECRET version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons,' has never been released and was not even acknowledged as withheld in the release letter, which is why the requester appealed on the adequacy of the search rather than on an exemption.
dossier.narrative:
There is a way of reading the DIRD series that makes it the single most informative document set on this board, and it is simply to read the titles in order and ask what question they collectively answer.

The released thirty-seven include 'Metallic Glasses - Status and Prospects for Aerospace Applications,' 'Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter,' 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms,' 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications' and 'Metallic Spintronics' - the materials question. They include 'Positron Aerospace Propulsion,' 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion,' 'Advanced Nuclear Propulsion For Manned Deep Space Missions,' 'Negative Mass Propulsion,' 'Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion,' 'Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion II,' 'MHD Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications' and 'Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites' - the propulsion question. They include 'Warp Drive, Dark Energy, and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions,' 'Advanced Space Propulsion Based on Vacuum (Spacetime Metric) Engineering,' 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy,' 'The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research,' 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications,' 'Concepts for Extracting Energy From the Quantum Vacuum' and 'Quantum Tomography of Negative Energy States in the Vacuum' - the physics-you-would-need question. They include 'Invisibility Cloaking - Theory and Experiments' and 'Detection and High Resolution Tracking of Vehicles at Hypersonic Velocities' - signature and detection. And they include 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues,' 'Biosensors and BioMEMS,' 'Biomaterials,' 'Technological Approaches to Controlling External Devices,' 'Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft' and 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' - the human question, which is to say, what happens to a person near one of these, and what would it be like to be inside one.

That is not a random reading list. It maps one to one onto the twelve technical areas in the AAWSAP statement of objectives: lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament, and peripheral areas. The DIRDs are the deliverable structure of the contract made visible. And two of the titles are difficult to explain by any framing other than the one this board starts from. 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues' is a medical paper about injury from proximity to something. 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' is a human factors paper about operating a vehicle that does not exist.

The release history is its own artefact. Eric Davis, who worked for Bigelow Aerospace and BAASS, said on Coast to Coast AM on 28 January 2018 that thirty-eight such reports had been produced under AAWSAP. Within forty-eight hours The Black Vault filed for all of them; the request became FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018. In January 2019 a listing breakdown of the reports arrived under a separate case, FOIA-0033-2019, though a slightly different version of the list had already leaked. DIA completed the main request more than four years later, on 25 March 2022, releasing thirty-seven of the thirty-eight. The one that did not come out was the SECRET-classified version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons.' Critically, it was not listed as withheld. The release letter did not reference it at all, which is why the appeal was filed on the adequacy of DIA's search rather than on the applicability of an exemption - a procedurally different and, for a board about concealment, a more interesting posture. An unclassified version of that same paper, DIRD 23, is in the released set at thirty-one pages.

The DIRDs also function as a personnel map. The authorship of the series connects the private technical layer catalogued elsewhere on this board directly to a DIA contract: the space-time metric engineering and quantum vacuum papers, the wormhole and warp drive papers, and the materials papers were written by named specialists who reappear later at To The Stars Academy, at EarthTech International, and in the disclosure hearings of 2023 to 2025. The government did not go to a federal laboratory or an FFRDC for this survey. It went to a small network of physicists with an existing interest in the subject, through a small business set-aside contract, performed at the contractor's own facility.

What the series does not contain is equally important and should be stated plainly. No DIRD reports an examination of recovered material. No DIRD describes a craft. They are literature surveys and theoretical assessments, and several of them conclude that the routes they examine are not presently achievable. AARO's characterisation is that they were 'exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed.' On the face of the documents, that is accurate.

The argument for their place on this map is therefore not that they contain the secret. It is that they define its shape. A government office that believed it was looking at nothing would not commission a paper on the acute and subacute effects of anomalous fields on human biological tissue. A programme whose only interest was foreign aerospace threat out to 2050 would not need a survey of traversable wormholes. The DIRDs are the negative space around an object: thirty-eight independent attempts to explain, from first principles, how something that had already been observed could possibly work.

claims.text: The Defense Intelligence Agency released thirty-seven of the thirty-eight AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Documents to The Black Vault on 25 March 2022, completing FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018, which had been filed on 31 January 2018.

The one report not released was the SECRET-classified version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons'; it was not referenced as withheld in the release documentation, so the administrative appeal was filed on the adequacy of DIA's search rather than on an exemption.

The released series includes 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' (DIRD 28, 57 pages), a human-factors assessment of operating a vehicle with capabilities beyond current aerospace technology.

The released series includes 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications' (DIRD 22), 'Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter' (DIRD 02), 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms' (DIRD 05), 'Metallic Glasses - Status and Prospects for Aerospace Applications' (DIRD 01) and 'Invisibility Cloaking - Theory and Experiments' (DIRD 07).

The subject coverage of the series maps onto the twelve technical areas specified in the AAWSAP Statement of Objectives of 18 July 2008: lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial/temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament, and peripheral areas.

AARO states that the DIRDs represent essentially the whole of what AAWSAP produced, that it 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work conducted by AAWSAP/AATIP,' and that the remainder of the effort consisted of case reviews, interviews of observers, and work on alleged paranormal activity at the contractor principal's Utah property.

No released DIRD reports the examination of recovered material or describes a recovered craft; the released series consists of literature surveys and theoretical assessments, several of which conclude the routes examined are not presently achievable.
The tasking record showing who inside DIA selected the thirty-eight DIRD topics, and on what basis each was chosen, has not been released.

dossier.denialPosture: DIA has not denied the existence of the series; it released thirty-seven of thirty-eight papers under FOIA in March 2022. Its release documentation made no reference to the classified SECRET version of the high-energy laser weapons report, neither producing it nor logging it as withheld. AARO's position is that the papers are unreviewed exploratory surveys tasked under the contract's stated aerospace-threat scope.
openQuestions: The status of the thirty-eighth document, the SECRET version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons,' and the outcome of the adequacy-of-search appeal.
The internal DIA tasking record: who chose the thirty-eight topics, when, and against what requirement. No topic-selection memorandum has been released.
Whether the DIRDs were circulated, cited or acted upon anywhere in DoD or the Intelligence Community after publication, or whether they were shelved on delivery.
Whether any of the DIRD authors held or were offered special-access read-ins in connection with the work, which would connect the unclassified series to a classified effort.

Whether the 'proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials' that AARO says the contractor made are documented anywhere alongside the DIRD tasking, and whether any DIRD topic was selected in support of such a laboratory.

l0.label: House Oversight joint hearing, 13 November 2024 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth'

dossier.whatItIs: A joint hearing of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability's Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation and its Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, titled 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth,' held 13 November 2024 at 11:30 a.m. in 2154 Rayburn House Office Building. The four witnesses were Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet USN (Ret.), Luis Elizondo, Michael Gold, and Michael Shellenberger. Written testimony from all four is published on the committee's website.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the hearing that entered the name of an alleged active Unacknowledged Special Access Program — IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION — into the congressional record, together with the sourced allegation that the program is controlled by the White House and executed by DoD specifically 'to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code.' It is also the hearing at which a retired flag officer testified under his own name that a UAP safety-of-flight email was deleted from Navy accounts overnight, and at which a former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program for the White House and NSC testified that 'the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies.' The same witness testified that the Pentagon's Public Affairs Office employs a psychological operations officer as the single point of contact for UAP inquiries, and another witness described being subjected to an hours-long influence operation by the then-acting AARO director. The hearing converts whistleblower assertions into dated, attributable, congressionally-published documents.
dossier.narrative:
The November 2024 hearing was the third in the House Oversight sequence that began with the July 2023 Grusch hearing, and it is the one that matters most structurally, because it moved the argument from 'there are unexplained objects' to 'there is a named program and a named legal evasion.'

Michael Shellenberger's written testimony carries the load. He reported that a current or former US government official acting as a whistleblower had written a report, provided to authorised committees of Congress and their staff, stating that 'the Executive Branch has been managing UAP/NHI issues without Congressional knowledge, oversight, or authorization for some time, quite possibly decades.' The report names an active DoD Unacknowledged Special Access Program, IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION, described by the document's source as a 'strategic intelligence program' that is part of the military's family of long-standing highly-sensitive programs dealing with aspects of the UAP problem. The report states that 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION serves as a central or parent USAP that consolidates observations' of UAP 'by both tasked and untasked collection platforms,' and that it 'includes high-quality Imagery Intelligence (IMINT) and Measurement and Signature Intelligence (MASINT) of UAPs,' sourced from a blend of directed and incidental collection in Low Earth Orbit, the upper atmosphere, aviation altitudes and maritime environments. The whistleblower alleges the USAP was created in 2017, after the New York Times published its AATIP story.

The program's stated function, as quoted in the testimony, is the concealment mechanism itself: 'the existence of IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION demonstrates the extant capability to detect, quarantine, and transfer UAP and RV [Reproduction Vehicle] collection incidents before they are observed and circulated within the Military Intelligence Enterprise, thus serving as a means of enforcing internal information security.' That is a claim about a filter operating upstream of the intelligence enterprise, and it is the single most consequential sentence in the hearing record.

The legal mechanism follows. DoD spokesperson Sue Gough issued a categorical denial: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION.' After publication, Shellenberger says a source told him the SAP 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code' — 'It is essentially a DOD Program, as the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.' A former IC official told him: 'That program is run out of SEC DEF. They don't want to acknowledge it's real.' Shellenberger also notes that AARO is housed within OUSD(I&S), so 'the office that Congress created to investigate unreported UAP programs is troublingly close to the organizations running the alleged programs.' A source warned him that merely printing the program name could trigger FISA surveillance of whoever published it.

The testimony also describes two incidents from the whistleblower's report. An F-22 'broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs,' with one holding station within twelve metres starboard of the cockpit, 'maintaining its exact position and orientation parallel with the F-22's cockpit despite multiple evasive rolls and maneuvers,' the aircraft then 'forced out of the mission area under the escort of the UAP formation.' Separately, an aircraft carrier's crew observed a 'small orange-red sphere' descend to 100-200 yards above the flight deck, emitting light that 'did not illuminate the ocean or the flight deck of the CVN despite the visual appearance of intense luminosity,' with a surface 'roiling like the surface of the sun.'

Tim Gallaudet's testimony supplies the institutional-deletion evidence. In January 2015, as Commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, he received an email on the Navy's secure network from the Fleet Forces Command operations officer, addressed to all subordinate commanders, subject line in capitals: 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE,' attaching what is now the 'Go Fast' video. 'The very next day, the email disappeared from my account and those of the other recipients without explanation,' and neither the Commander of Fleet Forces nor his operations officer ever raised it again. Gallaudet's inference is stated plainly: 'I concluded that the UAP information must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' He further testified that in 2024 he was the object of an hours-long influence operation by the then-acting AARO director and senior staff, aimed at validating AARO's historical records report, questioning the Nimitz tic tac case, and disparaging former officials who have spoken publicly. He told the committee that on 11 November 2024, two days before the hearing, Chris Mellon had asked for his help getting Congress details of a 2017 case involving satellite imagery of UAP 'that has still not been shared with Congress.'

Luis Elizondo's testimony is the shortest and the most direct: 'UAP are real. Advanced technologies not made by our Government — or any other government — are monitoring sensitive military installations around the globe. Furthermore, the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies, as are some of our adversaries. I believe we are in the midst of a multi-decade, secretive arms race — one funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from our elected representatives and oversight bodies.' He established his standing in the same paragraph: 'In my last position, I managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council.' He described a 'small cadre' inside government that has created 'a culture of suppression and intimidation,' including 'unwarranted criminal investigations, harassment, and efforts to destroy one's credibility,' and stated that many of his former colleagues have given classified testimony to the DoD and Intelligence Community Inspectors General and were subsequently targeted with threats to their careers, clearances 'and even our lives.'

Michael Gold's testimony is the counterweight in tone but not in direction: a former NASA associate administrator arguing that stigma, not evidence, is the binding constraint.

What the record does not settle: no committee has published the underlying Immaculate Constellation report, no dates or units are attached to the F-22 or carrier incidents, and the acting AARO director in Gallaudet's account is not named in his written testimony.
