l0.label: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)

dossier.whatItIs: A "carve-out" is the regulatory provision under which the Director of the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency is relieved of industrial security oversight for a Department of Defense special access program. It is codified at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) — the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule — and exercised in accordance with DoD Directive 5205.07, DoD Special Access Program Policy. Approval authority rests with exactly two officials: the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense.
dossier.whyImplicated: The carve-out is the mechanism that makes a concealed program administratively possible, and it is written down in the Code of Federal Regulations. Every cleared contractor facility in the United States is subject to DCSA oversight under the NISP; the carve-out is the single lawful exception, and once approved, DCSA retains cognizance only over the baseline facility clearance and not over the program. That means the government's own industrial security inspectorate — the body that would otherwise know which contractor holds what, in which vault, under which contract — is by design blind to the program. DoDD 5205.07 layers a second control on top: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval." A contractor holding carve-out material therefore faces an affirmative regulatory prohibition on telling Congress, enforced by an office whose director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. And the statutory backstop weakened rather than strengthened: the annual special access program reports to the defense committees required by 10 U.S.C. § 119(a) and (b) terminated by operation of law effective 31 December 2021. This is the load-bearing structural claim of the entire board — not that concealment is possible in principle, but that the specific regulatory instruments exist, are named, are current, and route around both DCSA and Congress by design.
dossier.narrative:
Start with the ordinary case. Under Executive Order 12829 and 32 CFR Part 117, the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security acts as the Cognizant Security Agency for the Department of Defense, and DCSA serves as the DoD Cognizant Security Office. Section 117.6(b)(3) assigns DCSA the duty to "provide security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO on behalf of DoD components and those non-DoD executive branch agencies who enter into agreements with DoD." Then comes the exception, in the same sentence-pair: "The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, 'DoD SAP Policy.'"

The operative definition is not in the CFR; it is in the instructions to DD Form 254, the Contract Security Classification Specification that accompanies every classified contract. Item 10f: "A 'carve-out' is a classified contract awarded by the GCA in connection with a SAP for which DCSA has been relieved of security and/or oversight responsibility by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense." The instructions add two operationally decisive notes. First: "Check block 15 'Yes' if the contract is performed at the contractor facility and DCSA will be relieved of security cognizance (a carve-out), and identify the CSO for the SAP as it is responsible for inspection of the SAP. NOTE: DCSA does retain oversight responsibility for the baseline FCL at which there is an approved carve-out." Second: "Not all SAPs are 'carve-outs' because, in some instances, the program or supporting SAP Security Office will allow the DCSA CSO to retain inspection responsibility." Read together: at a carved-out facility, DCSA still validates the company's baseline clearance but has no visibility into the program, and the program's own security office designates the inspecting authority. The inspector is chosen by the inspected.

DoDD 5205.07 was reissued on 12 September 2024, approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It cancels the July 1, 2010 directive and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform," 11 July 2023. Its governance architecture is a closed loop. The DoD SAP Central Office director sits under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense and reports directly to him or her; is Executive Secretary of the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, which the Deputy Secretary chairs; is Executive Secretary of the Senior Review Group; chairs the SAP Senior Working Group; is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for purposes of issuing security classification guides; accredits congressional SAP facilities; and maintains the records of what SAP information Congress has been given. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments "will be by exception," and establishment of SAPs to protect new and novel critical program information "at all tiers of the SAP architecture requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval."

DCSA's residual role under the same directive is limited to two lines in section 2.7: develop SAP-related training courses and maintain a cadre of proficient personnel, and support professional development and certification of SAP security professionals. The agency that oversees industrial security for the rest of the defense industrial base is, inside the SAP enterprise, a training provider.

The congressional-notification provision is the one that converts an administrative arrangement into a concealment mechanism. Section 3.2.g of DoDD 5205.07 requires all personnel accessed to DoD SAPs to notify the SAPCO director when briefing or providing SAP material to a member of Congress or staff, and then states flatly: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval." A contractor employee at a carved-out facility who believes a program has been improperly withheld from Congress is, by this directive, prohibited from doing anything about it without permission from the office nearest the Deputy Secretary.

Statute does less work here than most people assume. 10 U.S.C. § 119 required annual reports on special access programs to the defense committees under subsections (a) and (b) — but a note to the section records that those reporting requirements terminated effective 31 December 2021 pursuant to section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. Subsection (e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive inclusion of specified information in a report on national security grounds, in which case the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — a set of eight members across four committees. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse; there is no enforcement provision, no penalty, and no auditing body outside the executive branch positioned to detect a program that was never notified. 10 U.S.C. § 119a governs the parallel category of alternative compensatory control measures.

One loose thread in the directive itself is worth flagging to a downstream analyst. Section 2.1.a(6) makes the SAPCO director "Executive Secretary of the Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee pursuant to the November 21, 2020 Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum," while the directive's own reference list names that memorandum "Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee (STAOC) Charter," 21 November 2020. The body is named twice, differently, in a single 2024 directive. That committee's charter has not been released.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides: "The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, 'DoD SAP Policy.'"

The operative definition is in the DD Form 254 Instructions: "A 'carve-out' is a classified contract awarded by the GCA in connection with a SAP for which DCSA has been relieved of security and/or oversight responsibility by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense (DoDD 5205.07, 'Special Access Program (SAP) Policy')."

At a carved-out facility DCSA's residual visibility is limited to the baseline facility clearance: "NOTE: DCSA does retain oversight responsibility for the baseline FCL at which there is an approved carve-out." Inspection of the SAP itself is performed by a CSO identified by the SAP.

Carve-out status is discretionary and program-controlled: "Not all SAPs are 'carve-outs' because, in some instances, the program or supporting SAP Security Office will allow the DCSA CSO to retain inspection responsibility."

DoDD 5205.07 was reissued effective 12 September 2024, approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks; it reissues and cancels DoDD 5205.07 of 1 July 2010 as amended, and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform," 11 July 2023.

DoDD 5205.07 section 3.2.g provides: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval."

The Director, DoD SAPCO, is under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, reports directly to the Deputy Secretary, serves as Executive Secretary of the SAP Oversight Committee (which the Deputy Secretary chairs) and of the Senior Review Group, and chairs the SAP Senior Working Group.

The Director, DoD SAPCO "has jurisdiction over the protection of information contained within DoD SAPs and is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for purposes of issuing SAP security classification guides," and separately "accredits congressional SAPFs" and "maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress."

DoDD 5205.07 §3.1.d provides that "Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments will be by exception. Establishment of SAPs to protect new and novel CPI at all tiers of the SAP architecture requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval."

Under DoDD 5205.07 §2.7 the Director, DCSA has only two SAP responsibilities: developing SAP-related training courses and maintaining a proficient cadre, and supporting professional development and certification of SAP security professionals. DCSA has no inspection or oversight function assigned in the directive.

10 U.S.C. § 119(e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive inclusion of information in SAP reports on national security grounds on a case-by-case basis, in which case the information and justification are provided "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — that is, to eight members across the Senate and House Armed Services and Appropriations Committees.

The annual special access program reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. § 119(a) and (b) terminated effective 31 December 2021 pursuant to section 1061 of Public Law 114-328, per the Termination of Reporting Requirements note to the section.

10 U.S.C. § 119(f) provides that a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse; the statute prescribes no penalty for non-notification and assigns no external auditor.

DoDD 5205.07 names the same oversight body inconsistently within a single document: §2.1.a(6) calls it the "Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee" while the References section cites the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum, "Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee (STAOC) Charter," 21 November 2020.

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial here, and that is the point: the carve-out is publicly promulgated regulation, published on the Directives Division website and cleared for public release. The Department has never had to deny the existence of a mechanism that relieves its own security inspectorate of oversight, because the mechanism is printed in the Code of Federal Regulations and in the instructions to a form every classified contract carries.
connections: DCSA (formerly the Defense Security Service, renamed 20 June 2020) is the agency relieved; USD(I&S) is the Cognizant Security Agency for DoD and DCSA's chain of authority.

DoD SAPCO and its director, reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, is the single node through which SAP information reaches Congress and through which contractors must seek permission to speak to Congress.
Kathleen H. Hicks signed the current DoDD 5205.07 on 12 September 2024 as Deputy Secretary of Defense — the office that is also one of the two carve-out approval authorities.
Executive Order 13526 and Executive Order 12829 are the classification and industrial-security foundations; 32 CFR Part 2001 and 32 CFR Part 2004 are the implementing ISOO rules.
The Special/Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee, chartered by DepSecDef memorandum of 21 November 2020, is the least-documented body named in the directive.

Integrated Joint Special Technical Operations (IJSTO), run by the CJCS with USD(P) oversight, is the process by which SAP-protected capabilities are apportioned to combatant commands — the operational half of the architecture.
USD(C)/CFO "leads all budget and execution reviews for DoD-funded capabilities and information activities protected by DoD SAPs" — the funding node for any carve-out program.
DD Form 254 is the artifact a FOIA or subpoena would seek: block 10f and block 15 on a specific contract would reveal whether a facility is carved out and who inspects it.
Battelle-operated national laboratories, and any prime with SAP facilities, are the population to which carve-out designations would attach.

AARO's FY2025 report claims statutory authority to receive UAP information "regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs" — an assertion that runs directly against the DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g prohibition on contractors providing SAP material without SAPCO approval.
openQuestions: How many DoD SAPs currently hold approved carve-out provisions? The number has never been published, and 32 CFR 117.6 imposes no counting or reporting requirement.
Who are the Cognizant Security Offices designated to inspect carved-out programs in lieu of DCSA, and are any of them staffed by the contractor's own personnel?
The DepSecDef memorandum chartering the Special/Sensitive Technical Activities Oversight Committee (21 November 2020) has not been publicly released. What does it cover?
What replaced the 10 U.S.C. § 119(a)-(b) annual SAP reports after they terminated on 31 December 2021, if anything?
Does any statute or directive require notification to Congress of the approval of a carve-out provision itself, as distinct from establishment of the underlying SAP?

DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g prohibits contractors from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval. How is that provision reconciled with whistleblower protections and with AARO's claimed statutory access?
Is there any record of a carve-out provision ever being denied or revoked by a Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense?

Which office audits whether a program that should have been notified under § 119(f) actually was? The Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Privacy, Civil Liberties, and Transparency is assigned audit functions under DoDD 5148.13, but the scope is not specified in 5205.07.

dossier.whatItIs: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs (SAPs),' signed by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and effective February 6, 2013, cancelling the classified DoDI 0-5205.11 of July 1, 1997. It is the unclassified, publicly releasable rulebook for how the Department creates, nests, staffs, reports, waives reporting on, and disestablishes special access programs, and it implements the congressional oversight statute at 10 U.S.C. 119.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the machine's operating manual, published in the open, and it describes every capability a concealed legacy programme would need. It defines the unacknowledged SAP, whose very existence is not acknowledged to anyone not cleared for it. It defines the waived SAP, for which the Secretary of Defense has set aside the reporting Congress imposed. It builds a four-level nesting hierarchy -- umbrella, compartment, sub-compartment, project -- and expressly contemplates unacknowledged waived sub-elements added underneath a non-waived umbrella, which is a documented mechanism for hiding a black effort inside a program Congress has already been told about. It authorises 'carve-out' proposals to relieve the Defense Security Service of industrial security oversight over contractor performance. And it conditions access not merely on need-to-know and clearance but on a determination that the individual 'will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' -- the discretionary gate through which David Grusch's read-on request was denied.
dossier.narrative:
The most useful thing about DoDI 5205.11 is that it is unclassified and approved for public release with unlimited releasability. The Department published its own concealment architecture and nobody read it.

Start with the vocabulary, because the Glossary is where the load is carried. An 'unacknowledged SAP' is 'A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A 'waived SAP' is 'A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting ... following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' A 'waiver' more generally is 'A decision that provides an approved exception to or deviation from a SAP security standard.' Two of the three definitions describe subtraction from the oversight baseline.

The waiver traces to statute. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) lets the Secretary of Defense waive any requirement that certain information be included in a SAP report where inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' case by case; 119(e)(2) routes the withheld content and the justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Eight members. No staff named. That is the entire congressional footprint of a waived SAP.

The governance layer is three committees stacked above the Deputy Secretary: the SAP Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG), and the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), which 'advise and assist the SecDef and DepSecDef in the management, administration, and oversight of DoD SAPs.' The SRG 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and provides recommendations to the SAPOC 'concerning continued waived status.' There is, in other words, an internal annual re-authorisation cycle for programmes Congress cannot see -- run entirely by the Department.

Establishment is the part that looks like oversight. The SAPOC reviews the package and submits it to the Deputy Secretary of Defense for decision. 'If approved, the DepSecDef will submit formal notification letters to Congress that the SAP has been established.' And: 'The SAP may not be initiated until the congressional defense committees are notified of the program and a period of 30 days has elapsed after such notification is received.' That mirrors 10 U.S.C. 119(f). The Instruction also fixes the annual reporting calendar: SAP Listing on February 1, SAP Annual Report on March 1, forwarded to the congressional defense committees by the DoD SAPCO. Those dates correspond to 10 U.S.C. 119(b) and 119(a) respectively -- and both of those statutory reporting requirements were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The Instruction's reporting calendar survives on paper; the statutory obligation behind it does not.

Now the nesting. Enclosure 5 sets out the SAP hierarchy: a SAP is called an 'umbrella' if it has subordinate elements, which in descending order are compartments, sub-compartments, and projects. A person accessed to a compartment is also accessed to all subordinate elements 'unless an exception is specifically approved by the CA SAPCO.' Subordinate elements 'will be presumed to be within the same type unless' otherwise designated -- and the Instruction expressly addresses the case of unacknowledged waived sub-elements added under a non-waived umbrella, requiring specific SAPCO action. Read that as an analyst: the doctrine anticipates, and provides procedure for, burying a waived unacknowledged effort inside a programme that has been properly reported. This is the documented, unclassified mechanism corresponding exactly to Grusch's charge of 'nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities.'

Enclosure 6 lists what a Cognizant Authority SAPCO must notify the Director, DoD SAPCO of in writing. The list is a taxonomy of the moves available: change of category (acquisition, intelligence, operations and support); 'Change of type (acknowledged, unacknowledged)'; 'Alteration of scope'; IJSTO apportionment or deapportionment; disestablishment by termination, cancellation or transition; 'Support of non-DoD SAPs'; 'Addition, deletion, or changes of compartments, sub-compartments, and projects'; 'Proposals to relieve DSS of NISP security oversight responsibilities (carve-out) when required'; 'Change of nickname, codeword, PID'; and 'Foreign involvement.' Every one of these is an entry point for an analyst. Nickname and codeword changes break longitudinal tracking. Carve-outs remove the Defense Security Service from contractor facilities. 'Support of non-DoD SAPs' is the doctrinal bridge to DHS, DOE and IC compartments -- the category KONA BLUE would have occupied had it been approved.

Access is the human gate. 'Access to a SAP will be strictly limited to the minimum number of personnel necessary for execution of the program. Granting access to a SAP will be based solely upon a determination that the individual has a valid NTK, has the requisite security clearance, meets approved personnel prerequisites, and will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program.' The final clause is a subjective judgment reserved to the programme, and it is the clause that answers Grusch's testimony that he was 'denied access to those additional read-ons when I requested it.' Under this Instruction, a person conducting oversight can be lawfully excluded on the programme's own determination that he would not materially contribute to it.

Two further details reward attention. Sample SAP approval documentation reproduced in the Instruction's appendices uses a notional unacknowledged operations-and-support SAP designated GTE, with planned unacknowledged sub-compartments including LEAF BARK (LBK) and a recommendation line reading 'That you approve GTE as an unacknowledged SAP and authorize' -- a published template showing exactly how a sub-compartment request is written and approved. And the Instruction carries its own expiry: it 'Must be reissued, cancelled, or certified current within 5 years of its publication ... If not it will expire effective February 6, 2023.'

claims.text: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs (SAPs),' is effective February 6, 2013, is signed by the Deputy Secretary of Defense, cancels the classified DoDI 0-5205.11 of July 1, 1997, and carries releasability 'Unlimited.'

claims.text: The Instruction defines an unacknowledged SAP as 'A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.'

The Instruction defines a waived SAP as 'A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting ... following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.'

The SAP governance structure consists of the SAP Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG) and the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), which 'advise and assist the SecDef and DepSecDef in the management, administration, and oversight of DoD SAPs'; the SRG 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and recommends to the SAPOC on continued waived status.

The Instruction provides that a SAP 'may not be initiated until the congressional defense committees are notified of the program and a period of 30 days has elapsed after such notification is received,' and that upon approval 'the DepSecDef will submit formal notification letters to Congress that the SAP has been established.'

The Instruction sets the congressional reporting calendar as SAP Listing due February 1 and SAP Annual Report due March 1, forwarded to the congressional defense committees by the DoD SAPCO, and states that the SAP report 'is submitted to Congress in accordance with section 119 of Title 10, United States Code.'

The statutory obligations behind that calendar -- the annual SAP report at 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and the new-SAP notice and justification at 10 U.S.C. 119(b) -- were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328.

claims.text: The Instruction establishes a four-level hierarchy -- umbrella, compartment, sub-compartment, project -- in which a person accessed to a compartment is also accessed to all subordinate elements unless the CA SAPCO approves an exception, subordinate elements are presumed to be of the same type as the parent, and unacknowledged waived sub-elements added under a non-waived umbrella are expressly addressed as a distinct case requiring SAPCO action.

Cognizant Authority SAPCOs must notify the Director, DoD SAPCO in writing of proposals for change of category; 'Change of type (acknowledged, unacknowledged)'; 'Alteration of scope'; IJSTO apportionment or deapportionment; disestablishment (termination, cancellation, transition); 'Support of non-DoD SAPs'; addition, deletion or changes of compartments, sub-compartments and projects; 'Proposals to relieve DSS of NISP security oversight responsibilities (carve-out) when required'; 'Change of nickname, codeword, PID'; and 'Foreign involvement.'

Access is conditioned on a determination that the individual 'has a valid NTK, has the requisite security clearance, meets approved personnel prerequisites, and will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' -- a discretionary gate held by the programme.

Whenever a SAP's classification is to change or SAP information is to be declassified and made public, the DoD SAPCO must give the congressional defense committees a report describing the proposed changes, the reasons, and notice of any planned public announcement.

Sample SAP approval documentation reproduced in the Instruction uses a notional unacknowledged operations-and-support SAP designated GTE with planned unacknowledged sub-compartments including LEAF BARK (LBK), and a recommendation line reading 'That you approve GTE as an unacknowledged SAP and authorize.'
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, Enclosure 6 appendices (sample SAP approval memorandum), https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: A SAP disestablishment plan must address contracting, fiscal, audit, property disposition, classified material disposition, training, public affairs, legal, logistics and technical actions, and the CA SAPCO must provide the termination plan to the DoD SAPCO for SSWG review of potential impact on other programs.

The Instruction contains a self-expiry clause: it 'Must be reissued, cancelled, or certified current within 5 years of its publication in accordance with DoDI 5025.01. If not it will expire effective February 6, 2023 and be removed from the DoD Issuances Website.'

dossier.denialPosture: None. DoDI 5205.11 asserts nothing about UAP and denies nothing; it is a procedural issuance published with unlimited releasability. Its evidentiary value is that the Department has openly documented, in its own doctrine, every structural capability -- unacknowledged type, waived reporting, nested waived sub-elements under reported umbrellas, industrial-security carve-outs, and discretionary denial of oversight read-ons -- that a concealed legacy programme would require.
connections: Implements 10 U.S.C. 119, the statute whose subsection (e) waiver and December 31, 2021 reporting termination are the core of classified-annex.
The 'will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' access gate is the doctrinal basis for the read-on denial David Grusch testified to on July 26, 2023.

'Support of non-DoD SAPs' is the doctrinal bridge to the DHS compartment KONA BLUE would have become, and to the IC Controlled Access Program AARO says was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.

The carve-out provision relieving the Defense Security Service of National Industrial Security Program oversight is the mechanism by which contractor facilities performing SAP work fall outside routine DoD industrial security inspection.
'Change of nickname, codeword, PID' is the doctrinal answer to why a legacy effort would be untrackable across decades even to cleared reviewers.
The February 1 SAP Listing and March 1 SAP Annual Report are the documents that, if they still existed, would settle whether an unreported UAP materials programme is inside the DoD SAP inventory.
Deputy Secretary of Defense signature authority makes the DepSecDef, not the SecDef, the approving official for SAP establishment -- a specific office to interrogate for any given programme's origin.
openQuestions: Whether DoDI 5205.11 was reissued, cancelled or certified current before its stated February 6, 2023 expiry, and what issuance governs DoD SAPs now.
How many DoD SAPs are currently designated waived, and whether that number has ever been disclosed even to the eight members who receive 119(e) material.

Whether any unacknowledged waived sub-element has ever been added under a non-waived umbrella in a manner that kept it out of the congressional notification stream, and what the SAPCO record of such additions shows.
Which contractor facilities currently operate under NISP carve-outs, and who inspects them.
Whether the SAP Listing and SAP Annual Report continued to be produced after the December 31, 2021 statutory termination, and if so whether they are still transmitted to Congress.
Whether GTE and LEAF BARK are purely notional or were drawn from real program nomenclature for the published sample.
Whether the SAPOC, SRG or SSWG has ever reviewed a programme relating to materials of unknown origin, and whether their minutes exist as records subject to section 1842 of the FY2024 NDAA.

dossier.whatItIs: The Defense Intelligence Agency is the Department of Defense combat support agency responsible for foreign military intelligence. Between 2008 and 2012 it managed the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, the congressionally earmarked effort that produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on advanced propulsion, materials and related subjects, executed under contract by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies. AARO has confirmed that the material generated by that programme remains in DIA's archived holdings.
dossier.whyImplicated: DIA is the only agency the United States Government has formally admitted ran a modern programme that commissioned studies on how one would build and detect craft with capabilities no terrestrial system possesses, and it is the acknowledged custodian of that archive today. Its programme manager approved a contractor's UAP field investigations that were not in the statement of work, including proposals to stand up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials, which is a documented plan for a materials exploitation capability inside a defence intelligence contract. When the Senate Majority Leader asked in June 2009 that the programme be raised to Special Access Program status, the Department refused; when DIA cancelled it, its participants immediately proposed reconstituting it under Homeland Security as a compartment explicitly justified by claims that relevant material existed. AARO's own explanation for the entire modern disclosure movement traces it back to this DIA programme and its people. DIA is therefore the acknowledged root of the modern record, the custodian of its archive, and absent from the National Archives UAP collection.
dossier.narrative:
In 2008 DIA posted a solicitation and awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace for what became the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program. The money came from Senate-directed appropriations rather than a Departmental requirement, a point the DoD Inspector General records plainly when it notes that the Department did not officially look at UAP again after Blue Book until select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme under DIA's direction. The programme ran from 2008 through 2012 in its various forms and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents covering advanced propulsion, warp drive metrics, traversable wormholes, metamaterials, invisibility cloaking, high energy laser weapons, and biological effects of anomalous exposure. DIA transmitted the list of titles and principal authors to Congress in January 2018.

AARO's own account of AAWSAP, in Historical Record Report Volume I and in its standalone KONA BLUE paper, is more useful to this board than AARO seems to have realised. It confirms the programme was managed by DIA from 2009 to 2012 and funded through congressional earmarks with Bigelow Aerospace as prime contractor. It confirms the stated purpose was investigating next-generation aerospace technologies across twelve specific areas including advanced lift, propulsion, unconventional materials and controls, and signature reduction. It then states that although investigating UFO or UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organisation conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA programme manager, and that this research included reviewing new cases and older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.

That sentence is the whole argument in miniature. A defence intelligence agency programme, funded outside the normal requirements process, with a programme manager who authorised his contractor to run field investigation teams and to propose materials exploitation laboratories for recovered UFO material. AARO's framing is that DIA did not seek nor specifically authorise this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract, which is an attempt to place the agency at arm's length from its own programme manager. It does not work. A contract managed by an agency employee, funded by an agency line, delivering to an agency archive, is the agency's programme.

The escalation attempt is documented. On 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Lynn declined on the recommendation of then Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper, who advised that the designation was not justified. Read against the concealment thesis, a request for SAP status is a request for a compartment in which recovered material could lawfully be held without disclosure, and the refusal is the point at which the effort had to find another home.

It found one, briefly. AARO's KONA BLUE paper states that when DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP, several individuals involved advocated that the Department of Homeland Security take the effort over and fund a new version under the code name KONA BLUE. In 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology established KONA BLUE as a Prospective Special Access Program based on claims that relevant information and material existed and required this level of protection. Six months later the Deputy Secretary of DHS disapproved it and directed immediate termination. AARO's insistence that no data or material was ever transferred to DHS is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that a Presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Under Secretary stood up a prospective compartment on the strength of a representation that material existed.

The custody question is settled by AARO's own words. Its KONA BLUE paper states that information associated with the activities conducted under the auspices of AAWSAP/AATIP remains within DIA's archived holdings. Whatever the thirty-eight reference documents, the field investigation files, the debriefing records and the case reviews amount to, DIA has them. That makes DIA a custody node on this map regardless of what one concludes about the underlying phenomenon.

The people matter. James T. Lacatski, a career DIA propulsion and missile intelligence specialist, was the programme manager who brought the subject to Senator Reid and who converted the contractor's deliverables into Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. He co-authored Skinwalkers at the Pentagon with Colm Kelleher, the biochemist who ran the contractor's field science effort, and George Knapp, the investigative reporter who first obtained and published the DIRD title list. AARO's Volume I addresses that body of work by describing the contractor's Utah property investigations, its interest in shadow figures, creatures, remote viewing and human consciousness anomalies, and its plan to hire psychics. AARO presents this as evidence the programme lacked merit. It is equally evidence that a defence intelligence agency programme was pursuing lines of inquiry it would never have funded without something driving it.

One further fact belongs on the board. AARO states that it partnered with DIA's archives for the historical review. Yet as of the National Archives Record Group 615 page's review date of 22 May 2026, DIA does not appear among the agencies with a UAP records transmittal to the National Archives. The agency that holds the acknowledged archive of the acknowledged programme has not, on the public record, delivered it to the statutory collection.

l0.label: KONA BLUE

dossier.whatItIs: KONA BLUE was an unacknowledged, waived Prospective Special Access Program established inside the Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate by Under Secretary Dr. Tara O'Toole on 11 July 2011, and terminated by Deputy Secretary Jane Holl Lute effective 10 February 2012. Its stated purpose was "to investigate, identify and potentially exploit sensitive advanced aerospace-related technology and to prevent disclosure of scientific, technical and engineering data vital to the US." It was the direct successor proposal to the DIA AAWSAP/AATIP contract and was to be funded by a congressional add steered by Senators Reid and Lieberman.
dossier.whyImplicated: KONA BLUE is the best-documented attempt in the modern record to build a compartmented U.S. government home for exploitation of materials of claimed non-human origin, and the government declassified the paperwork itself in 2023-2024. The program's own approval memo states DHS proposed a SAP because "we have been informed that there is a body of previous work held by other entities that requires a SAP level classification to access it." That sentence is an admission, in a signed DHS action memo, that someone told the Under Secretary for Science and Technology that SAP-protected prior work existed and was held elsewhere. AARO's cover narrative asserts that interviewees identified KONA BLUE as "a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sensitive compartment established to protect the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics'" and then argues the program never got materials because it was never approved. Both can be true and the interesting question survives: who were the "other entities," and what was the "body of previous work"? The termination reason of record is not that the claims were false. Deputy Secretary Lute killed it over adequacy of threat/vulnerability justification and insufficiency of budget and personnel documentation.
dossier.narrative:
The declassified package released jointly by DoD and DHS is unusually complete: an establishment memo, a decision briefing, SAPOC minutes, an action memo, a termination memo, a memorandum for the record, and — folded into the same release — the underlying Reid letter and DIA info memo that explain where the program came from.

Establishment: on 11 July 2011 the Director of DHS S&T's Special Projects Office asked Dr. Tara O'Toole, Under Secretary for Science and Technology and an Original Classification Authority, to approve creation of KONA BLUE as a Prospective Special Access Program under DHS Instruction 140-04-001. The stated purpose was "to investigate, identify and analyze sensitive advanced materials and technologies and to assess potential emerging and/or disruptive scientific and technical data necessary in support of national security." O'Toole approved. Classification was TOP SECRET//KONA BLUE//NOFORN, HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY, classified under E.O. reason 1.4(e), with a declassification date of 25 April 2036. The DHS SAPCO decision briefing lists the program manager as Joel Wall, S&T Special Programs Division.

Scope: the proposal document describes four research centers — Data Collection and Analysis, Advanced Technology, Consciousness, and Technology Application/Integration — investigating "emerging and/or disruptive advanced materials and controls, alternative energy/power source/generation opportunities, temporal translation; human effects and interface, signature reduction and weaponry, as well as technology integration." That is the AAWSAP twelve-area list with a Consciousness Center bolted on. The Department's interest area is stated as "the scientific and technical investigation, threat analysis, and assessment of materials and data of unique origin, engineering, and purpose." Materials of unique origin. Written by DHS.

Money: the planned research objectives slide gives FY12 $12M, FY13 $25M, FY14 $35-50M, FY15-FY18 TBD. The SAPCO briefing gives "Expected amount for funding expected to be 12 to 15m" and flags a pending issue: a "Classified Line Item in CSO budget" and that the Under Secretary for Management "has concurred in the need to establish a Business/Administrative SAP to handle primarily 'unacknowledged' monies (e.g., KONA BLUE)." A dedicated financial vehicle for unacknowledged money was being stood up to receive it.

The politics are in the SAPOC minutes of 21 November 2011, chaired by Deputy Secretary Jane Holl Lute, with Caryn Wagner (U/S Intelligence and Analysis), Rafael Borras (U/S Management), Ivan Fong (General Counsel), Gregory Marshall (Chief Security Officer), Steven J. Cover (Chief SAPCO), security officers Michael Zawasky and Allen Olsen, and O'Toole. The minutes record that "The Deputy Secretary opened the meeting with an explanation of what caused this meeting to occur with some sense of urgency which was the impending transfer of funds to DHS from Senators Reid and Leiberman to conduct the KONA BLUE program." O'Toole "stated that the Senators were prepared to provide $10M for the execution of this program in the FY12 budget." She was asked why the FBI was not approached and answered that the FBI "had no organic capability to do research & development in the scientific arena." Wagner raised whether S&T even had collection authority, and whether KONA BLUE "is actually an intelligence program which DIA no longer had the authority to conduct per Executive Order 12333." Lute closed by tasking O'Toole and Cover with a 5-10 page paper documenting "how we got to where we are now with the KONA BLUE program, it's provenance (history) while at DIA, and exactly what science would be researched," adding that "S2 is still not certain of what the 'It' is in the program or otherwise what exactly we are researching."

The November action memo from O'Toole records that in October 2011 she met with Senator Lieberman, Chairman of Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and Senate Majority Leader Reid, to discuss program funding. It also states the operative custody claim: "A SAP is proposed as we have been informed that there is a body of previous work held by other entities that requires a SAP level classification to access it."

Death: a progress review was held 8 December 2011 in Lute's office with Fong, Wagner, Cover and Associate General Counsel Kronisch. O'Toole was invited but could not attend. Lute directed immediate termination. The termination memo is dated 12 December 2011 and Lute's signature block shows Disapprove dated 2-10-12. DHS's Acting Deputy Secretary Kristie Canegallo confirmed in a 5 February 2024 letter to Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks that the PSAP was "terminated on February 10, 2012." A memorandum for the record from Cover dated 5 June 2013 states that no security classification guide, SOP, facility accreditation or AIS plan was ever issued, that all briefed personnel would be administratively debriefed, and that "No other documentation or paperwork would be required."

AARO's framing, published in 2024, is that KONA BLUE "never received any materials or funding" and that "no data or material of any kind was ever transferred to or collected by DHS under the auspices of KONA BLUE." On the narrow question of DHS custody, the paperwork supports that. On the broader question the AARO narrative raises and does not answer: DHS believed material would be delivered, and DHS wrote that a body of prior work was held by other entities under SAP protection. AARO does not identify those entities.

l0.label: PURSUE - Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters

dossier.whatItIs: The PURSUE releases are the five dated tranches of UAP material published by the Department of War at war.gov/UFO between 8 May 2026 and 7 August 2026. Each tranche is posted as a paired download - a document bundle served from www.war.gov/medialink/ufo/ and a video bundle served from a CloudFront distribution - alongside a searchable database of individual records. The files carry originator-prefixed identifiers such as DOW-UAP-D###, DOW-UAP-PR## and FBI-UAP-D###, the first time the United States Government has issued UAP material under a single public numbering scheme.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the physical evidence of what the government chose to hand over when a President ordered it to hand something over. The ledger is therefore diagnostic in both directions. It confirms the archive: material spanning 1944 to 2026, FBI holdings, NASA crew audio, INDOPACOM reporting, all of it previously unavailable and now released without clearance. It also confirms the shape of the withholding: at least a hundred of the roughly 160 files in the first tranche carry redactions, and every serious analyst who examined them - Mellon, Graves, Gallaudet, Rojas - reported the same absence of coordinates, sensor parameters, altitude, timing and chain of custody, which are the precise fields that would permit independent verification. No tranche carries a manifest, an exemption citation, a FOIA case number or a provenance statement. The releases are the strongest available proof that the holdings exist and the strongest available proof that the release process was designed to be unauditable.
dossier.narrative:
Five tranches, over three months, from a Department web page. Release 01 on 8 May 2026, Release 02 on 22 May, Release 03 on 12 June, Release 04 on 10 July, Release 05 on 7 August. The portal states the sequence plainly: 'The Department of War just released the fifth tranche of records under PURSUE. The first tranche was released on May 8, 2026.'

The delivery mechanism is worth describing exactly, because it is not a records system. Each release offers two ZIP archives. The documents come from war.gov itself: Release 01 documents at 1.2gb, Release 02 at 70.1mb, Release 03 at 826mb, Release 04 at 227mb, Release 05 at 130mb. The videos come from a commercial content delivery network at d34w7g4gy10iej.cloudfront.net: 1.3gb, 5.6gb, 4.6gb, 1.4gb and 513mb respectively. There is no manifest file, no checksum, no metadata schema, no index of what was withheld. The portal offers a filterable database by agency, release, incident date, incident location and type - which is more structure than any prior US UAP release has had, and still less than any archivist would call a finding aid. At the time this dossier was compiled the portal's 'LATEST RELEASE' link still pointed to Release 04 while the banner above it announced Release 05, which tells you something about how the page is maintained.

The file identifiers are the most analytically useful artefact in the whole programme. Filenames visible on the portal include DOW-UAP-PR46-Unresolved-UAP-Report-INDOPACOM-2024, DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953, FBI-UAP-D025_Digital-Rendering_Airborne-Triangle_2002, FBI-UAP-D027_Digital-Rendering_Dark-Translucent-Triangle_2023, FBI-UAP-D031_Digital-Rendering_Large-Triangle-with-Red-Lights_2023 and FBI-UAP-D038 through D042, a run of digital renderings of multiple red lights dated 2026. Two things follow. First, the numbering is originator-prefixed, which means the tranches were assembled by pulling from multiple agencies' holdings under a single tasking rather than compiled from one department's files - a single-department dump would not need agency prefixes. Second, the Bureau is a substantial contributor, and its contributions run to the present: FBI-UAP-D038 through D042 are dated 2026, the year of release.

The imagery convention is itself a disclosure decision. A large share of the FBI material is published as 'Digital Rendering' - artists' reconstructions of witness accounts rather than sensor products. DefenseScoop's illustration caption for the first tranche describes an 'Actual site photo with FBI rendered graphic depicting corroborating eye witness reports from September 2023 of an apparent ellipsoid bronze metallic object materializing out of a bright light in the sky, 130-195 feet in length, and disappearing instantaneously.' A rendering cannot be independently analysed. It can only be believed or not.

On volume and redaction, the contemporaneous count is DefenseScoop's: 'The initial PURSUE tranche contained a little more than 160 files, with at least 100 of those including redactions, according to researchers and experts who are currently studying them.' Roughly five files in eight were released with material removed, in a programme whose stated purpose was to stop hiding material, and with no exemption citation attached to any redaction.

The substantive verdict from the people best placed to give one was delivered within a week and was unanimous on the technical point. Alejandro Rojas, whose Enigma Labs team was cross-referencing the drop against a database of over 200,000 public sightings: 'Although there is a lot of information here, there is little context. Case summaries without coordinates, sensor parameters, or altitude data make independent analysis very difficult.' Tim Gallaudet, who thought some of the videos showed genuinely anomalous behaviour including right-angle turns and formation flying: 'the ambiguity of the video content in particular is concerning as no metadata was included. Therefore, it is impossible to conclude that any of the objects were truly anomalous.' Ryan Graves, on what a useful release looks like: 'The real value is in records that include clear provenance, sensor context, metadata, chain of custody, date and location, and enough operational context to allow serious independent analysis. Ambiguous imagery without that surrounding data is hard for pilots, researchers, or the public to evaluate responsibly.'

Several of the same people noted that much of the first tranche was not new. The Australian researcher Grant Lavac: 'For those of us in the UAP research community, the newness of the data in this first tranche is underwhelming. Much of it is a compilation of documents that have been in the public domain for decades.' His countervailing point is the one this board accepts: 'the story here isn't necessarily the content, but the process of official acknowledgment.'

And there is a provenance problem that the releases themselves create. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation raised it in the first week: the US Government's own documented mid-century practice of manufacturing false UAP documents as cover for real weapons programmes means some of what is being published as authentic government UAP records may be disinformation artefacts. 'If some of what is now being released to the public as authentic government UAP records are in fact disinformation artifacts from that era, the public deserves to know. Transparency requires not just releasing files, but accounting for their provenance and integrity.' PURSUE publishes without provenance statements, which means it cannot distinguish a genuine 1953 film analysis from a 1953 cover story, and neither can anyone downstream.

What the ledger establishes is therefore narrower and harder than the headlines suggested. The archive exists and is large. The Department was able to produce material from at least six agencies within eleven weeks of a presidential post. The material released is the unresolved residue, stripped of the fields that would let anyone check it, with a third to two-thirds of it redacted and none of it assessed. That is not the record of a government that has nothing. It is the record of a government deciding, file by file, how much of what it has to show.

l0.label: ADAM Research Project (Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials)

dossier.whatItIs: The ADAM Research Project — Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials — is a private materials-analysis program launched in July 2018 by To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science, a Delaware public benefit corporation founded by Tom DeLonge. It acquires physical samples reportedly recovered from advanced aerospace vehicles of unknown origin and contracts laboratory analysis, principally through Hal Puthoff's EarthTech International in Austin, Texas. Its best-known holding is the magnesium-zinc-bismuth 'Art's Parts' sample purchased with an archive from journalist Linda Moulton Howe in July 2019.
dossier.whyImplicated: ADAM is the only publicly documented instance of claimed recovered material moving from private custody into a federal laboratory pipeline with a signed government agreement attached. In October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering material science, space-time metric engineering, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage. By 2024 the same magnesium-zinc-bismuth sample had been analyzed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory with AARO in the room, and Puthoff and Eric Davis — both of whom authored deliverables under the DIA AAWSAP contract a decade earlier — wrote the private counter-analysis. That is a closed loop: the same physicists who wrote the government's exotic-propulsion reference documents in 2009-2010 are the ones adjudicating a national laboratory's findings on a claimed recovered artifact in 2024. Whether or not the sample is exotic, the custody chain and the recurrence of the same named individuals across government and private roles is the finding.
dossier.narrative:
TTSA announced ADAM in July 2018 as an academic research program focused on the collection and scientific evaluation of material samples obtained through reported encounters with advanced aerospace vehicles of unknown origin. Analysis was contracted to EarthTech International, the Austin think tank run by Dr. Harold E. Puthoff, who was simultaneously TTSA's Vice President of Science and Technology and had been a senior adviser and subcontractor on the DIA-funded AAWSAP/AATIP work.

The acquisition that gave ADAM an object rather than a concept came on 25 July 2019. TTSA's press release states that it 'has acquired multiple pieces of metamaterials and an archive of initial analysis and research for their controversial ADAM Research Project,' materials 'previously retained and studied by investigative journalist Linda Moulton Howe and are reported to have come from an advanced aerospace vehicle of unknown origin.' Steve Justice — TTSA's COO and formerly head of Advanced Systems at Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works — is quoted: 'The structure and composition of these materials are not from any known existing military or commercial application.' He adds the crucial custody caveat in the same paragraph: 'They've been collected from sources with varying levels of chain-of-custody documentation, so we are focusing on verifiable facts and working to develop independent scientific proof of the materials' properties and attributes.' And a dating claim: 'In some cases, the manufacturing technology required to fabricate the material is only now becoming available, but the material has been in documented possession since the mid-1990's.' Justice explicitly frames the endgame as transition to capability: 'If the claims associated with these assets can be validated and substantiated, then we can initiate work to transition them from being a technology to commercial and military capabilities.'

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command, sharing its work with the Ground Vehicle Systems Center and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection, with the Army providing laboratories, expertise and resources. The announced technology areas were material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage. A CRADA is not a procurement; no money moved to TTSA and the Army acquired nothing. What it did establish is a formal, signed channel through which privately held claimed-exotic material could reach Army laboratories.

The analytic endgame arrived in 2024. Oak Ridge National Laboratory analyzed the magnesium-zinc-bismuth 'Art's Parts' sample; TTS posted the ORNL report in July of that year. A TTS-AARO-ORNL meeting was held on 27 August 2024. Puthoff and Eric W. Davis then produced their own analysis, submitted to the TTS Board of Directors on 27 September 2024 and published by TTS with a recommendation history attached. TTS's own summary of the outcome is unusually candid and is the single most useful sentence ADAM has produced: 'the Puthoff/Davis analysis (and the ORNL analysis) did not reveal any form of proof of exotic (Extraterrestrial, Ultra-terrestrial, or inter-dimensional) origin, but it did not absolutely rule it out either.' TTS adds that 'the actual purpose of the material, though clearly manufactured, still remains a bit of a mystery.'

AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 states more bluntly that a piece of metal alleged to be recovered from an off-world spacecraft was determined to be ordinary, of terrestrial origin, and to possess no exceptional qualities. Both statements can be reconciled: nothing exotic was demonstrated. What was demonstrated is process — a private entity holding claimed recovered material got it into a DOE national laboratory and into a room with the Pentagon's UAP office.

The scientific parallel track matters for method rather than result. Garry Nolan of Stanford, Jacques Vallée, Sizun Jiang and Larry Lemke published 'Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics' in Progress in Aerospace Sciences volume 128 in January 2022, DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2021.100788. That paper is the peer-reviewed statement of what a defensible analysis of a claimed anomalous sample would look like — isotopic ratio analysis, SIMS, and comparison against known terrestrial baselines — and it is the standard against which every ADAM claim should be measured.

Who matters by name: Tom DeLonge (founder), Steve Justice (COO, ex-Skunk Works Advanced Systems), Hal Puthoff (EarthTech, TTSA VP Science and Technology, AAWSAP DIRD author), Eric W. Davis (AAWSAP DIRD author, co-author of the 2024 counter-analysis), Linda Moulton Howe (prior custodian), Luis Elizondo and Chris Mellon (TTSA principals in the founding period), Garry Nolan and Jacques Vallée on the independent scientific track. What the record shows is a documented chain of private acquisition, a signed Army CRADA, a national-laboratory analysis, and a published negative-but-not-exclusionary result. What the record does not show is any chain of custody back to a recovery event.

The Schumer-Rounds eminent domain provision, stripped from the final FY2024 NDAA, would have compelled federal seizure of exactly the class of privately held material ADAM holds; its removal left ADAM's holdings in private hands.

l0.short: CRADA between U.S. Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center and To The Stars Academy

dossier.whatItIs: Cooperative Research and Development Agreement No. 19-15, titled 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation (NETE),' between To The Stars Academy of Arts and Science, Inc. and the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Ground Vehicle Systems Center at the Detroit Arsenal, Warren, Michigan. Executed under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a with a term of sixty months from the effective date, it committed TTSA to provide the Army with samples of metamaterial 'collected, obtained, or developed as part of its Field Operations' and the Army to provide laboratories, expertise and analysis, with no exchange of funds in either direction. TTSA's principal investigator of record was Luis Elizondo.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only publicly released, signed U.S. Government instrument in which a federal laboratory agrees to characterize material that the counterparty represented, in filings to the Securities and Exchange Commission, as coming from unidentified aerial phenomena. That makes it the board's hardest documentary bridge between the alleged recovery-and-exploitation enterprise and the ordinary federal technology-transfer system. The Joint Work Plan names the Government's actual interests, and the list is not generic materials science: 'inertial mass reduction, mechanical/structural metamaterials, electromagnetic metamaterial wave guides, quantum physics, quantum communications, and beamed energy propulsion.' Inertial mass reduction is not a ground-vehicle survivability requirement. The Collaborator principal investigator is Luis Elizondo, the former Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence official associated with AATIP who left DoD in 2017 alleging excessive secrecy, meaning the same individual who publicly accused the Pentagon of concealment is, two years later, the named point of contact delivering anomalous material back into an Army laboratory under an agreement whose supporting records the Department of Defense then withheld under national-defense FOIA exemptions. Finally, the CRADA form itself is the point: it moves technology and creates invention rights without appropriated funds, without a contract, without competition and without a reportable obligation, and it carries a statutory information shield. It is a legal channel for moving exploitable material into and out of the Government that leaves almost no financial footprint.
dossier.narrative:
On 17 October 2019 To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science issued a press release announcing a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles. The release was thin. The Army was not. Doug Halleaux, public affairs officer for CCDC's Ground Vehicle Systems Center, gave John Greenewald of The Black Vault the executed agreement, twenty-six pages, redacted only for phone numbers.

The document is CRADA No. 19-15, 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation (NETE),' between TTSA and CCDC Ground Vehicle Systems Center, 6501 E. 11 Mile Road, Warren, Michigan. The named administrators matter. On the Government side the principal investigators are Ben Soave and Dr. Joseph Cannon, both of Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection, mail stop 263b. The ORTA representative is Andrea Simon; Government legal counsel is Christina Dellmore, Chief of the Intellectual Property Law Division at US Army TACOM LCMC. On the Collaborator side, the principal investigator and preferred contact is Luis Elizondo, 'Director of Global Security and Special Programs,' Encinitas, California. Collaborator legal counsel is Heidy Vaquerano, Esq., of Wolf, Rifkin, Shapiro, Schulman & Rabkin, LLP, Los Angeles.

The Joint Work Plan is where the agreement stops sounding like armor research. The Government's stated interests are 'a variety of the Collaborator's technologies, such as, but not limited to inertial mass reduction, mechanical/structural metamaterials, electromagnetic metamaterial wave guides, quantum physics, quantum communications, and beamed energy propulsion.' The Collaborator's deliverables include, verbatim, 'Metamaterial: Samples of mechanical and EM sensitive metamaterial collected, obtained, or developed as part of its Field Operations,' plus written material analysis and quantum-communication research. 'Field Operations' is the operative euphemism; the CRADA does not define provenance, and the Army made a point of saying provenance was irrelevant to it.

The legal architecture is standard Federal Technology Transfer Act plumbing put to non-standard use. Information exchanged is protected under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a(c)(7), and every page carries a marking legend invoking it. Licenses to CRADA inventions run under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a(b)(2), with the Collaborator holding an option for an exclusive license that must be requested within six months of notification of an invention. The agreement automatically expires sixty months from the effective date under Article 4.2, and enters force on the date signed by the last authorized representative under Article 4.3.

TTSA's own SEC filings supply the numbers the CRADA does not. In its Regulation A offering circular the company states that on 10 October 2019 it entered into the CRADA with CCDC, that 'the purpose of the CRADA is to advance developments in material science (including testing of the metamaterials), space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage,' that the parties bear their own costs, that the total value of anticipated U.S. Government resources including personnel, services, intellectual property, facilities, equipment and reporting is 'estimated at $750,000,' that the total value of the company's participation is 'estimated at $1,000,000,' and that the agreement is terminable by mutual consent or unilaterally on thirty days' notice.

The same filing describes where the material came from. The ADAM Research Project, Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials, launched in July 2018, and 'within one year this division acquired a collection of material samples reported to come from advanced vehicles of unknown origin from all over the world.' In July 2019 the company 'purchased multiple pieces of metamaterials and an archive of initial analysis and research.' Elsewhere TTSA states flatly to the SEC: 'The exotic materials that were purchased come from unidentified aerial phenomenon and are anomalous in that they have a structure and composition that we believe are unknown to any existing commercial or military application.' By November 2019, per the filing, ETI had performed analysis pursuant to the SOW-MSSA showing 'a unique physical structure unknown to any past or current commercial or military application.' The filing also records that planned ADAM laboratory testing 'was paused.'

The Army's public framing was deliberately deflationary. Halleaux told The Black Vault that 'the Army is providing the expertise and facilities to analyze the materials, and TTSA is providing the materials themselves; both parties receive the results of the analysis,' and that 'just as there is no financial compensation to TTSA for the use of the materials, there is no financial compensation to the Army for the use of the facilities.' On provenance he was explicit: 'the Army's interest is in the potential for novel materials and exploring the edges of materials science, any speculation as to their origin is (pardon the pun) immaterial.' He also stressed that a CRADA is not an endorsement, offering the Army's fuel-cell CRADA with General Motors as the comparison.

Then the record closed. Individuals who had custody of pieces of the metamaterial before TTSA acquired them were placed under non-disclosure agreements; The Black Vault reached one such person, who declined comment citing an NDA. Some of the material was described in SEC filings as being 'on loan.' The Department of Defense invoked FOIA exemptions covering national defense and foreign policy to withhold CRADA-related documents. It took until October 2024, five years after execution and at the natural end of the sixty-month term, before the Army agreed to a rolling release under FOIA case FA-24-0006, with the first package released on 23 October 2024.

The analytic point for the board is the instrument, not the rock. A CRADA requires no appropriation, no competition, no contract file and no reportable obligation, and carries a statutory information shield. It creates a lawful, low-visibility conduit for moving materials of undeclared origin into a federal laboratory and moving analysis and invention rights back out, with the collaborator holding a first option on exclusive rights to anything invented. Whatever the metamaterial turns out to be, CRADA 19-15 is the working proof that the channel exists, is routine, and is FOIA-resistant by design.

l0.label: Battelle Memorial Institute

dossier.whatItIs: Battelle Memorial Institute is a Columbus, Ohio applied-science nonprofit founded in 1929 that describes itself as the world's largest independent nonprofit applied science organization. From late 1951 it held the classified Air Technical Intelligence Center contract code-named Project STORK, out of which came Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 (5 May 1955), the largest statistical study of UFO reports ever performed for the U.S. government. Today Battelle manages or co-manages eight U.S. national laboratories, including Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Idaho, Pacific Northwest and Savannah River.
dossier.whyImplicated: Battelle is the single institution that sits on both sides of the mid-century split: it produced the numbers that the public debunking campaign was built on, and it is the contract operator of the laboratory system where exotic-materials characterization would actually be performed. The Durant Report's own list of documentary evidence placed before the CIA's Robertson Panel names, as item 3, "Progress Reports of Project STORK (code name for Battelle Memorial Institute contract work supporting ATIC)" — meaning a private contractor's classified analysis was the evidentiary substrate for the panel that recommended a national "training and debunking" program. Battelle's own analysis found roughly 22 percent of about 3,200 cases were unknowns, and that the higher the case quality the more likely it was to be unknown; the Air Force publicized the study in October 1955 as proof that flying saucers did not exist and cited a 3 percent unknown rate. Five days before the Robertson Panel convened, a Battelle memorandum dated 9 January 1953 — the document Jacques Vallee found in J. Allen Hynek's files in 1967 and calls the "Pentacle memorandum" — is reported to have proposed that Battelle and ATIC agree in advance on what could and could not be said to the CIA panel. Battelle is therefore not a neutral statistical vendor; it is the earliest documented instance of the pattern this board tracks, a cleared contractor mediating between what the government knew and what a public-facing scientific body was permitted to see.
dossier.narrative:
The relationship began with an admission of institutional inadequacy. Captain Edward J. Ruppelt, running the Air Force's UFO desk at the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, concluded at the end of 1951 that the Air Force lacked the analytic capacity to do anything scientific with the report backlog. He went to Battelle Memorial Institute in Columbus, roughly a hundred and twenty miles away, and the resulting classified support contract was code-named Project STORK. Battelle built a standardized observer data sheet, encoded about thirty characteristics of each sighting onto IBM punched cards, and ran the first machine-assisted statistical analysis of the UFO corpus. It is important to hold the shape of this arrangement in view: the government's public UFO investigation had, from 1952 onward, a classified contractor layer underneath it that the public did not know existed and that Blue Book's own critics could not see.

The Robertson Panel is where that layer surfaces in the documentary record. F.C. Durant's 16 February 1953 memorandum to the CIA's Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence records that on Thursday morning, 15 January 1953, "The Project STORK support at Battelle Memorial Institute, Columbus, was described by Dr. Hynek." Tab B of the same document lists the STORK progress reports as evidence item 3, sitting alongside the Project GRUDGE and BLUE BOOK status reports, the Holloman Air Force Base sightings summary, Project TWINKLE, and Project POUNCE. The five-scientist panel that would recommend stripping UFOs "of the special status they have been given" was reading Battelle's work product.

The timing of the Pentacle memorandum is the part of this that will not settle. Vallee has stated for decades that in 1967, while organizing Hynek's files, he found a memorandum stamped SECRET dated 9 January 1953 — five days before the Robertson Panel's first session — written by Battelle's Howard C. Cross and addressed to Miles Goll at Wright-Patterson, and that it proposed agreement between Project Stork and ATIC on what could and could not be discussed in Washington on 14-16 January. Vallee's papers are now at Rice University's Woodson Research Center as MS 0672, and the finding aid lists a file titled "11. The Robertson Panel and the 'Pentacle Memorandum' — January 1953" in Series III. The collection is restricted: Series I and II open on 24 January 2028, Series III case files on 1 January 2031. The Department of Defense has never released the memorandum. Treat the document's existence as archivally attested and its full text as an open question, not a claim.

Special Report No. 14, dated 5 May 1955, is the payoff. Battelle's analysts sorted about 3,200 cases into knowns, unknowns and insufficient information, graded each on a four-point quality scale, and required unanimity among four analysts before a case could be called unknown — an unusually stringent test that biases toward suppressing the unknown count. About 22 percent came back unknown. The quality gradient ran the wrong way for the debunking thesis: roughly 35 percent of excellent-quality cases were unknowns versus about 18 percent of the poorest. Battelle's own summary nevertheless declared it "highly improbable" that any of the reports represented technological developments outside present-day knowledge. When the Air Force released the study in October 1955 under Secretary Donald Quarles, the public framing was that the report scientifically disproved flying saucers, with an unknown rate cited as 3 percent. The report itself was not distributed; the press release was. The cleanest surviving copy of the 312-page report sits in CIA's declassified holdings as CIA-RDP81R00560R000100060001-5 — which is itself worth noting, since the document is nominally an Air Force product.

What makes Battelle load-bearing for a recovery-and-exploitation thesis rather than merely for a history of statistical malpractice is what the institute became. Battelle's own site states it manages eight national laboratories for the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security under the government-owned, contractor-operated model, and partners in managing Canadian Nuclear Laboratories. It is the sole LLC member for Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Idaho National Laboratory (via Battelle Energy Alliance), the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center, and Savannah River National Laboratory; an LLC member of UT-Battelle for Oak Ridge; of Brookhaven Science Associates with Stony Brook; and of Triad National Security with the Texas A&M System and the University of California for Los Alamos, which Battelle describes as executing work for the Department of Energy, the Department of War and the Department of Homeland Security. Battelle's stated core competencies are advanced materials, biology and chemistry, and its national security portfolio includes an advanced functional materials line.

The analytic point is a continuity of institutional posture, not a proven chain of custody. The organization that in 1953 was negotiating with ATIC over what the CIA's scientists would be allowed to hear is the same organization that now holds the operating contracts for the laboratories where anomalous materials would plausibly be characterized. No public contract, appropriation line, or DD Form 254 has been produced connecting Battelle or any Battelle-operated laboratory to UAP materials exploitation. That absence is the research target, and Battelle's carve-out-eligible SAP work at those laboratories is exactly the space in which such an absence would be expected.
