Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, the Battelle statistical analysis, is dated 5 May 1955 and runs 312 pages; the cleanest publicly available copy is the version held in CIA's declassified document holdings under identifier CIA-RDP81R00560R000100060001-5.

Battelle's analysis classified about 22 percent of roughly 3,200 cases as "unknown," about 69 percent as known or identified, and about 9 percent as insufficient information; a case required unanimous agreement of all four analysts to be classified unknown.
The unknown rate rose with case quality: about 35 percent of excellent-quality cases were classified unknown versus about 18 percent of the poorest-quality cases.

The summary section of Battelle's final report declared it "highly improbable that any of the reports of unidentified aerial objects ... represent observations of technological developments outside the range of present-day knowledge," a conclusion at odds with the 240 charts, tables, graphs and maps in the body of the report.

When the Air Force made Special Report No. 14 public in October 1955 it claimed the report scientifically proved UFOs did not exist and stated an unknown rate of 3 percent rather than the roughly 22 percent the study actually produced.

Battelle's methodology included devising a standardized reporting form and coding about thirty characteristics per sighting for machine analysis — the first machine-assisted statistical treatment of the U.S. government's UFO corpus.

A file titled "11. The Robertson Panel and the 'Pentacle Memorandum' — January 1953" exists in Series III (Correspondence, Vallee group C, boxes 42-53) of the Jacques F. Vallee UFO and paranormal phenomena papers, MS 0672, Woodson Research Center, Rice University; the collection is donor-restricted, with Series I and II opening 24 January 2028 and Series III case files 1 January 2031.

Battelle manages or co-manages eight U.S. national laboratories for the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security — Brookhaven (Brookhaven Science Associates, with Stony Brook), Idaho (Battelle Energy Alliance, Battelle sole member), Los Alamos (Triad National Security, with Texas A&M System and University of California), the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center (Battelle National Biodefense Institute, sole member), the National Laboratory of the Rockies, Oak Ridge (UT-Battelle, with University of Tennessee), Pacific Northwest (managed by Battelle alone), and Savannah River (Battelle Savannah River Alliance, sole member) — and partners in managing Canadian Nuclear Laboratories.

Battelle states that Los Alamos National Laboratory "executes work for multiple government agencies including the U.S. Department of Energy, Department of War and Department of Homeland Security" spanning "nuclear security, intelligence, defense, emergency response, nonproliferation, counterterrorism, energy security, emerging threats and environmental management."

Battelle self-describes its core expertise as "advanced materials, biology and chemistry" and lists a National Security market comprising Advanced Functional Materials, CBRNE Defense, Cyber, and Emerging Threat Mitigation.

dossier.denialPosture: Battelle has issued no public statement about Project STORK, the Pentacle memorandum, or any materials-analysis role, and its corporate history pages do not mention the ATIC contract at all. The denial in this case is by omission: the institute's public account of its own past treats 1952-1955 as if the largest statistical study of UFO reports ever performed for the U.S. government was not its work.
connections: Edward J. Ruppelt, Chief of the ATIC Aerial Phenomena Branch, initiated the Battelle relationship in late December 1951 and briefed the Robertson Panel for roughly forty minutes on 14 January 1953.

J. Allen Hynek was the conduit: he described the STORK support to the CIA panel in 1953 as an associate member, and it was in his files that Vallee found the 9 January 1953 Battelle memorandum in 1967.
Howard C. Cross of Battelle is the reported author of the Pentacle memorandum; Miles Goll at Wright-Patterson AFB is the reported addressee.

Jacques Vallee — sole public custodian of the Pentacle text; his papers (Rice MS 0672) also contain field notes on cattle mutilations and on face-to-face meetings of NIDS and BAASS, linking the 1953 Battelle thread to the Bigelow thread in a single collection.
Robertson Panel — consumed Battelle's product; the panel's debunking recommendation and Battelle's public-facing statistics operate as a matched pair two years apart.
Air Technical Intelligence Center / Wright-Patterson AFB — the contracting activity; the same base the January 1985 USAF fact sheet uses to deny that extraterrestrial equipment was ever held there.

Los Alamos National Laboratory — Battelle is a Triad LLC member; the Durant Report separately records that the 1952 map of unexplained sightings showed clusters "in certain strategic areas such as Los Alamos" which the panel could not explain.
John B. Alexander ran non-lethal weapons work at Los Alamos before becoming a public face of Bigelow's NIDS, a personnel path from a Battelle-operated laboratory into private anomaly research.
Secretary of the Air Force Donald Quarles is the named signatory of the October 1955 public framing of Battelle's data.
openQuestions: The full text of the 9 January 1953 Battelle memorandum has never been released by DoD or Battelle; the only known copy sits in a Rice University collection restricted until 2031. What does the complete document say about what ATIC withheld from the CIA panel?
What was the contract number, contracting activity and dollar value of Project STORK, and how long did it run after Special Report No. 14 was delivered?
Battelle reportedly reacted with hostility when Hynek returned in 1967 to ask about the memorandum; no contemporaneous record of that exchange has surfaced.

Did Battelle perform materials characterization on any recovered debris, at Columbus or at any Battelle-operated national laboratory? No contract, appropriation line, DD Form 254 or facility clearance record establishing this has been produced.
Which Battelle-operated facilities hold SAP carve-out designations under 32 CFR 117.6, and does DCSA retain or lack industrial security cognizance over them?
Why does the cleanest surviving copy of an Air Force report reside in CIA's document holdings rather than in the Air Force's own accession to NARA?
Battelle's own corporate history omits the ATIC work entirely — was that omission a contract requirement, a classification consequence, or an editorial choice?

dossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, formally titled 'Analysis of Reports of Unidentified Aerial Objects,' dated 5 May 1955, is the largest statistical study of UFO reports the U.S. government has ever produced. The analysis was performed under contract by Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus, Ohio, under a project designation reported as Project STORK, using 3,201 cases with an information cut-off of the end of 1952. It was released publicly on October 25, 1955 through Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55.
dossier.whyImplicated: The gap between what the study found and what the government said it found is the cleanest documented instance of deliberate framing in the entire record, and it is verifiable from two documents that were published together. The press release and Secretary of the Air Force Donald Quarles's accompanying statement told the public that the unknowns amounted to three per cent, a figure drawn from 131 sightings in the first four months of 1955, not from the 3,201-case study sample the report actually analyzed. The report body shows unknowns running far higher, and highest precisely where witness reliability was rated Excellent. The release also declined to name Battelle, describing the analysis only as the work of a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio. The full 316-page report was then not distributed, on stated grounds of printing cost, until a private citizen reprinted it. Every element of a concealment operation is present and dated: a suppressed dataset, a substituted statistic, an unnamed contractor, and a restricted distribution.
dossier.narrative:
Start with what the report says about itself. Its own Summary states that the special study started in 1953, that to provide the study group with a complete set of files the information cut-off date was established as of the end of 1952, and that in these charts, 3201 cases have been used. It describes a three-part analytic method: a systematic attempt to find distinguishing characteristics in the data, a study of any trend or pattern, and an attempt to determine the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS represented observations of technological developments not known to this country. On the first of these it records a genuinely load-bearing finding: 'The first step in the analysis of the data revealed the existence of certain apparent similarities between cases of objects definitely identified and those not identified. Statistical methods of testing when applied indicated a low probability that these apparent similarities were significant.' Read plainly, Battelle tested whether the unknowns looked like the knowns and found that the resemblance did not hold up. That is the opposite of the conclusion the public was handed. The report then walks it back through re-evaluation, concluding that the probability the unknowns represented unknown technology was very small.

Now the release. Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55, dated October 25, 1955 and headlined 'AIR FORCE RELEASES STUDY ON UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL OBJECTS', opens with the flat assertion that no evidence of the existence of the popularly-termed flying saucers was found. It attributes the work to a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio, and never says the word Battelle. It then executes the substitution: since the instigation of the investigation more than seven years ago, methods and procedures have been so refined that of the 131 sightings reported during the first four months of 1955 only three per cent were listed as unknown. Secretary Quarles then attaches his name to that number: 'On the basis of this study we believe that no objects such as those popularly described as flying saucers have overflown the United States. I feel certain that even the unknown three per cent could have been explained as conventional phenomena or illusions if more complete observational data had been available.' The phrase on the basis of this study is doing enormous work. The study is the 3,201-case Battelle analysis. The three per cent is from a 131-case sample the study did not analyze, collected three years after the study's own cut-off date. The two are welded together in a single sentence and a Cabinet-level official signs it.

The attached Summary makes the substitution visible in its own numbers. For cases received before the end of 1952 it gives Unknown at 9 per cent; for the more recent tranche it gives Unknown at 3 per cent. Neither figure is the rate for the 3,201 cases whose charts and tables make up the report.

The body tells a different story, which is why the body was hard to get. Leon Davidson, a chemical engineer who had worked at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory and who reprinted the report photographically beginning in 1956, wrote in his publisher's analysis that the key to the answer is contained in Fig. 8 (orig. p. 24) and Tables A1, A2, and A3 (orig. pp. 107 and 108); that Fig. 8 shows Unknown sightings constitute 33.3 per cent of all the object sightings for which the reliability of the sighting is considered Excellent; and that Tables A1 through A3 agree, with the percentage of Unknown sightings not less than about 20 per cent even when sightings of lesser reliability are included. The distribution runs the wrong way for the official framing: the better the witness, the more likely the object stayed unidentified.

Distribution was the second layer of the concealment. Davidson reproduces a letter from Air Force Secretary Donald A. Quarles dated July 5, 1956 stating that it has been estimated that the cost of printing enough copies for distribution to the public through such outlets as libraries and academic institutions would be between $10 and $15 per copy. The 316-page full report was therefore never distributed. The non-availability became a matter of congressional record at the House Subcommittee on Government Information under Rep. John E. Moss on November 15, 1956. Davidson's privately financed edition, reproduced photographically page by page with the main text intact, is why the document exists in public hands at all.

One further anomaly sits in the photographic reproduction. Davidson points to original page 295, where the codes for Final Identification carry typewritten strikeovers: the category originally called Rockets and Missiles in the early analytic work was changed to read Insufficient Information, and the category originally called Electromagnetic Phenomenon was changed to read Unknown. If that reading of the page is correct, then the report's residual category was not an empty bin for the unexplained. It was a renamed bin for a hypothesis.

Battelle is the connective tissue. The same institute later formed UT-Battelle, the operator of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which per contemporary allegations received AARO's 2024 material analysis work. Battelle is also one of the entities Rep. Burlison named in his May 2026 MITRE interrogatories, alongside Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace. The organization that wrote the government's founding public statistical assessment of the phenomenon has never left the file.

l0.label: Project Blue Book

dossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book was the United States Air Force's public-facing unidentified flying object investigation, headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and running from March 1952 until Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans, Jr. announced its termination on 17 December 1969. It succeeded Projects SIGN and GRUDGE and logged 12,618 sightings, of which 701 were closed as "Unidentified." Its textual records were retired to the USAF Archives and subsequently to the National Archives, where they are open as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, publication T-1206, within Record Group 341.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Air Force's own termination paperwork states in plain language that Blue Book was not the channel through which serious UAP reporting flowed. The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender records that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system," and in the same paragraph that "there is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function." That is a signed admission of a two-channel architecture: a public channel with a press office and a phone number, and a separate operational reporting channel whose corpus has never been inventoried, indexed or transferred to any archive. The same document shows the Air Force weighing where to store the Blue Book files specifically to manage researcher access, with the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information agreeing to "rigidly limit the right of access" and to "screen researcher's notes." Blue Book therefore sits on this board twice: as the mechanism that absorbed and normalised public interest for seventeen years, and as a custody object whose public copy was deliberately shaped before release.
dossier.narrative:
Project Blue Book is the most examined document set in the history of the subject and the least useful, and both facts follow from the same cause: it was never the file where the answer would be.

The Air Force ran three named UFO efforts in sequence. Project SIGN began in 1948, Project GRUDGE followed in 1949, and Blue Book was stood up in March 1952 under Air Force Regulation 80-17, which required base commanders to provide a UFO investigative capability and Air Force Systems Command to continue the project. The Bolender document of 20 October 1969 describes the resulting establishment with some precision: "Project Blue Book has two officers, one NCO and one civilian assigned on a full-time basis," plus Dr. J. Allen Hynek as a scientific consultant until 1 July 1969. Four people, one part-time academic, and a stated mission to determine whether UFOs threatened national security and whether they exhibited advanced technology. For seventeen years this was the entire visible federal apparatus.

The Bolender document is the load-bearing artifact. It was written as the staff package recommending termination, was released to researcher Robert Todd in January 1979, and reads as an internal cost-benefit memorandum rather than a scientific finding. Paragraph 4 contains the sentence that reorganises everything around it: after noting that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs posed no direct physical threat, the document observes that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system," then states that national-security-relevant reports move under JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11 "and are not part of the Blue Book system." JANAP 146 is the joint communications instruction governing CIRVIS reporting of vital intelligence sightings; AFM 55-11 governs operational reporting. Neither corpus has ever been assembled, declassified or transferred as a body. Whatever came up those channels between 1952 and 1969 is not in T-1206 and never was.

The same document then explains, in operational terms, why Blue Book was kept alive after its own premise was disclaimed. Paragraph 8 recommends that if Blue Book is terminated the records "should be transferred to an appropriate archive and preserved for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts." The reason given for preservation is reputational management, stated openly. Paragraph 9 goes further. Because witnesses had been promised confidentiality, "access to these records and the publications must be carefully reviewed and controlled," and the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information judged that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because ready availability in Washington "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts." Air University agreed to take the files on three conditions: that SAFOI answer all queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained." The Air Force decided, in writing, where to put the archive on the basis of how hard it would be for the public to reach.

The public announcement two months later, Department of Defense release No. 1077-69 of 17 December 1969, carries none of that. It quotes Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," cites the Condon report and the National Academy of Sciences review, and closes with the three conclusions that have been repeated ever since: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, no "unidentified" case represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and no "unidentified" case indicated extraterrestrial vehicles. Read against Bolender, the first conclusion is a statement about a filing system rather than about the sky, because the reports that could affect national security were routed elsewhere by regulation.

Custody is the second reason Blue Book is on this map. The National Archives holds approximately 2 cubic feet of project and administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files arranged chronologically, and 3 cubic feet of records relating to the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, arranged by OSI district and overseas command. NARA states that the textual records are available "excluding names of people involved in the sightings." The public Blue Book is therefore a redacted copy of the Air Force's own Blue Book, and the confidentiality rationale from Bolender paragraph 9 is the reason. NARA also states flatly that it "has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico." The General Accounting Office found the same when it reviewed Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at Archives II during its 1994-95 Roswell audit: the analysis of sightings from 1946 to 1953 "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947." The single most famous American recovery event does not appear in the official American UFO file. That is either evidence the event did not happen or evidence the file was not where such events were recorded, and Bolender tells you which architecture the Air Force actually built.

What the record does not show is equally specific. The Bolender document carries sixteen attachments listed on a separate page. Several are known and were released separately; several have never surfaced. There is no public inventory of JANAP 146 CIRVIS traffic. There is no public accounting of the OSI material beyond the three cubic feet NARA holds. And the January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet that NARA reproduces contains the categorical sentence "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base" - a dated, attributable, institutional denial about a specific installation, which is exactly the kind of statement this board catalogues rather than weighs.

claims.text: The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender states that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system."
The same document states: "There is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function (Atch 8)."

The same document notes that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs were not a direct physical threat, and that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system" for a further sixteen years.
Paragraph 8 of the same document recommends that Blue Book records be transferred to an archive "for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts."

Paragraph 9 records Air University's conditions for accepting the records: that SAFOI answer all Blue Book queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained."

The same paragraph states SAFOI's view that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because Washington-area availability "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts."

Blue Book was staffed full-time by two officers, one NCO and one civilian, with Dr. J. Allen Hynek as scientific consultant until 1 July 1969; reporting procedures were defined in Air Force Regulation 80-17.

Department of Defense release No. 1077-69, 17 December 1969, announced termination, quoting Secretary Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," and stated that Blue Book records would be retired to the USAF Archives at Maxwell AFB with requests handled by SAFOI.

The National Archives states that Blue Book textual records are available for research "excluding names of people involved in the sightings," and comprise approximately 2 cubic feet of project/administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files and 3 cubic feet of AFOSI-related records, accessed via 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm (T-1206).
The National Archives states: "The National Archives has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico."
GAO reviewed Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at National Archives II and reported it "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947."

The January 1985 USAF fact sheet distributed by Wright-Patterson AFB, reproduced by the National Archives, records 12,618 sightings from 1947 to 1969 of which 701 remain "Unidentified," and states "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base."

The Bolender document carried sixteen attachments listed on a separate page; NICAP's published notes state that researcher Robert Todd spent years seeking their release and that several remain unidentified or unreleased.

dossier.denialPosture: The Air Force's position has been fixed since 17 December 1969 and restated verbatim for decades: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, none represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and none indicated extraterrestrial vehicles (DoD release No. 1077-69). The January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet adds the installation-specific denial that there are not now and never have been "any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base." Both are dated, attributable and institutional, and both are silent on the JANAP 146 and AFM 55-11 channel the Air Force's own termination paperwork describes.
openQuestions: No inventory, index or transfer of the JANAP 146 (CIRVIS) and AFM 55-11 UFO reporting corpus for 1952-1969 has ever been made public. Where does that traffic physically reside?

Several of the sixteen attachments to the 20 October 1969 Bolender staff package have never been released. What is in Atch 8, cited for the claim that Blue Book served no intelligence function, and Atch 10, cited for the JANAP 146 routing?
Does an unredacted Blue Book master copy containing witness names still exist in Air Force custody, and under what disposition authority?
The exact date, transfer authority and accession record for the movement of the files from Wright-Patterson to the USAF Archives at Maxwell and then to NARA is not stated on NARA's own page.
The text and successive amendments of AFR 200-2 (1953) and its provisions on public release of unidentified cases were not verified in primary form for this dossier and remain a research target.
Whether AFOSI retained a parallel UFO case series beyond the three cubic feet at NARA, and whether any of it was destroyed.

l0.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)

dossier.whatItIs: The Condon Committee was the University of Colorado UFO Project, funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research from 1966 to 1968 under physicist Edward U. Condon, which produced the report formally titled Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects. Its conclusions, released January 1969, were used by the Air Force as the basis for terminating Project Blue Book on 17 December 1969. It remains the most cited public document on the scientific status of the UFO question.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Condon Committee is the second and larger instance of the pattern the Robertson Panel established: a nominally independent scientific body whose framing was set before the work began and whose product retired the public investigative apparatus. Robert J. Low's memorandum of 9 August 1966, written to reassure University of Colorado administrators before the contract was signed, states the design explicitly: "The trick would be, I think, to describe the project so that, to the public, it would appear a totally objective study but, to the scientific community, would present the image of a group of non-believers trying their best to be objective but having an almost zero expectation of finding a saucer." The finished report contains an affirmative denial of concealment — "We have no evidence of secrecy concerning UFO reports" — offered by a committee that had simultaneously declined to independently evaluate the Air Force's national-security finding, writing "we felt that it was out of our province." A body that will not examine the defense question is not positioned to certify the absence of secrecy about it. The report also recommended against establishing any federal UFO agency, a recommendation that held for fifty-three years until AARO. Buried in Section IV, Chapter 2, the report's own Lakenheath-Bentwaters case assessment concludes "the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved appears to be fairly high."
dossier.narrative:
The chain of custody runs from the Air Force to itself. In March 1966 an ad hoc committee of the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board chaired by optical physicist Brian O'Brien recommended that the Blue Book program be strengthened, that contracts be negotiated with a few selected universities to provide scientific teams, and that one university or nonprofit coordinate. The Secretary of the Air Force referred the recommendations to the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, which combined recommendations A and C into a single contracting university with subcontracting authority and implemented recommendation B through Air Force Regulation 80-17, reprinted as Appendix B of the eventual report. Harvard, Berkeley, MIT and North Carolina declined. Hynek's Northwestern and McDonald's Arizona were rejected as too committed. Colorado accepted on 6 October 1966. The contract was publicly announced on 7 October 1966 and provided $313,000 for fifteen months, 1 November 1966 to 31 January 1968; total funding later rose above $500,000.

The contract terms are worth reading against what followed. The report states that "the contract provided that the planning, direction and conclusions of the Colorado project were to be conducted wholly independently of the Air Force," that the Air Force was ordered to furnish its records and base support, and that "we were assured that the federal government would withhold no information on the subject." Where sightings involved classified missile launches or classified radar systems, "this fact is merely stated as to do more would involve violation of security on these military subjects." The committee then reports that these reservations "have affected a negligible fraction of the total material." This is an assurance accepted on the word of the contracting party, by a project that had no independent means of verifying either the completeness of what it received or the existence of holdings outside Blue Book.

The Low memorandum predates the contract by two months. Written 9 August 1966 to two university administrators, it reassured them that the study "would be conducted almost entirely by non-believers who, though they couldn't possibly prove a negative result, could and probably would add an impressive body of thick evidence that there is no reality to the observations," before the sentence about the trick. James McDonald learned of it in July 1967 and located a copy in the project's own open files; NICAP severed ties on 30 April 1968; Donald Keyhoe circulated copies; John G. Fuller published "Flying Saucer Fiasco" in Look on 14 May 1968, describing the project as a "$500,000 trick." Condon fired David Saunders and Norman Levine for alleged incompetence; administrative assistant Mary Louise Armstrong resigned; Low resigned in May 1968. Representative J. Edward Roush asked the General Accounting Office to investigate; GAO declined. Condon resigned from the AAAS after Science published on the controversy without his input.

What the committee produced is not a single argument but a document whose front matter contradicts its interior. Condon's six-page Conclusions and Recommendations opens: "Our general conclusion is that nothing has come from the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge. Careful consideration of the record as it is available to us leads us to conclude that further extensive study of UFOs probably cannot be justified in the expectation that science will be advanced thereby." He recommended against a new federal agency, and on secrecy wrote: "It has been contended that the subject has been shrouded in official secrecy. We conclude otherwise. We have no evidence of secrecy concerning UFO reports. What has been miscalled secrecy has been no more than an intelligent policy of delay in releasing data so that the public does not become confused by premature publication of incomplete studies of reports."

Set that against the adjacent paragraphs. On the defense question Condon wrote: "We felt that it was out of our province to attempt an independent evaluation of this conclusion. We adopted the attitude that, without attempting to assume the defense responsibility which is that of the Air Force, if we came across any evidence whatever that seemed to us to indicate a defense hazard we would call it to the attention of the Air Force at once. We did not find any such evidence. We know of no reason to question the finding of the Air Force." The committee thus deferred to the Air Force on the national-security question and then, three paragraphs later, certified that no secrecy existed. Hynek's later count was that the committee had been unable to explain more than a quarter of the cases it examined. In Case 2 of Section IV, Chapter 2, on the 1956 Lakenheath-Bentwaters radar-visual event, the report states: "although conventional or natural explanations certainly cannot be ruled out, the probability of such seems low in this case and the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved appears to be fairly high."

The operational effect was immediate and durable. The Air Force had asked the National Academy of Sciences, before the report was finished, to independently assess its scope, methodology and findings; a panel chaired by Yale astronomer Gerald M. Clemence studied it for six weeks and endorsed it, concluding that "no high priority in UFO investigations is warranted by data of the past two decades." On 17 December 1969 the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project Blue Book, citing the Colorado report, the NAS review, past studies and Air Force experience. The Air Force fact sheet distributed from Wright-Patterson in January 1985 records the closing tally — 12,618 sightings reported 1947 to 1969, of which 701 remain "Unidentified" — and appends a categorical denial: "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base." That sentence, on a public affairs fact sheet from the base that housed ATIC and let the Battelle contract, is a dated, attributable claim about the specific installation most often named in recovery accounts. It is evidence about the denier.

The USAF fact sheet distributed by Wright-Patterson AFB Public Affairs in January 1985 states: "On December 17, 1969, the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project BLUE BOOK," that the decision rested on the University of Colorado report, the National Academy of Sciences review of it, past UFO studies and Air Force experience, and that of 12,618 sightings reported 1947-1969, 701 remain "Unidentified."
