l0.label: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)
l0.short: DoD Special Access Program Central Office

dossier.whatItIs: The DoD Special Access Program Central Office is the headquarters element that runs the Department of Defense's entire special access program enterprise. Its Director operates under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, reports directly to the Deputy Secretary, serves as Executive Secretary of the Special Access Program Oversight Committee and Senior Review Group and Chair of the SAP Senior Working Group, and holds delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information. It is also the Department's single point of contact for SAP matters with the Executive, Judicial and Legislative branches.
dossier.whyImplicated: If a legacy program exists inside the Department of Defense, DoD SAPCO is the office that knows where it sits in the architecture, who is read in, and what Congress has been told. Three provisions of the governing issuances make this office load-bearing rather than merely administrative. First, DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1.g bars any DoD contractor entity, employee, representative or consultant from providing SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the Director's approval — a regulatory chokepoint sitting directly across the path of every contractor whistleblower. Second, the Director accredits congressional SAP facilities and "maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress," which makes SAPCO both the conduit and the recordkeeper of its own conduct. Third, under DoDI 5205.11 the Director may approve the establishment and disestablishment of SAPs at tier 2 and below on his own authority with SSWG concurrence, meaning a single flag officer or SES can create and dissolve compartments. In March 2023 the then-Director, Major General David W. Abba, signed the memorandum that authorized AARO to receive sensitive U.S. Government information and effectively released NDA-bound personnel to speak to AARO — the single most consequential document in the government's handling of the whistleblower question, and it came from this office.
dossier.narrative:
DoD Directive 5205.07, "Special Access Program Policy," was reissued on 12 September 2024 over the signature of Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It cancels the July 1, 2010 version and, importantly, incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum of July 11, 2023, "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform." That reform memorandum was issued three days before the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act was unveiled and eight days before the Senate added it to the NDAA. The companion issuance, DoD Instruction 5205.11, was reissued the same day.

The Directive creates four governance bodies and one office. The SAP Oversight Committee is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and includes the four Under Secretaries who serve as SAP oversight authorities — Research and Engineering, Acquisition and Sustainment, Policy, and Intelligence and Security — plus the Comptroller, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the DoD General Counsel, the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation, the DoD Chief Information Officer, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the ASD for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, the Vice Chiefs of the Army and Air Force, the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps, and the Vice Chiefs of Naval and Space Operations. The Director of DoD SAPCO is its Executive Secretary. Below it sits the Senior Review Group, which the Directive pointedly says "has no designated individual as the Chair," and below that the SAP Senior Working Group, chaired by the Director of DoD SAPCO, whose voting members are the SAPCO directors of the four oversight-authority offices, the military departments, SOLIC, and the Joint Staff.

The Director's own portfolio in section 2.1 of the Directive is broader than the governance role. He is the "DoD-designated proponent" for SAP policy; the oversight authority for SAPs designated by the Deputy Secretary, "including those protecting capabilities and information shared with the DoD by foreign governments"; the cognizant authority for SAPs designated by the Deputy Secretary, for DoD components not supported by another SAPCO, for foreign-government-shared capabilities, and for "SAP studies, portfolios, and associated access management structures involving DoD SAPs"; and the DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with all three branches of government, "including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries." He is also Executive Secretary of the Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum of 21 November 2020. He publishes and maintains security classification guides for all DoD SAP umbrellas and is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for that purpose. He maintains the single authoritative repository of SAP personnel access and facility accreditation. He accredits congressional SAP facilities and maintains the records of what SAP information Congress received.

Paragraph 3.1.g of the Directive is the sentence to underline: "All personnel accessed to DoD SAPs will notify the Director, DoD SAPCO and OA SAPCO directors through their SAP CA SAPCO in a timely fashion when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff. No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval." A contractor employee who believes a program is being illegally concealed from Congress must, under this rule, ask the office that administers that program for permission to tell Congress about it.

DoDI 5205.11 supplies the operating mechanics. Only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary may alter the tier-1 architecture; the Director of DoD SAPCO may approve establishment and disestablishment of SAPs at tier 2 and below. New CPI enters through a "SAP project" assigned a number in the TR umbrella, and if a decision is not reached in 210 days it transfers automatically toward termination absent a waiver from the Secretary or Deputy Secretary. Access Approval Authority for non-waived SAPs may be delegated to component SAPCO staff; "AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee." DoD SAPCO coordinates on personnel access requests for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs — that is, the office decides which judges and which agencies get read in. The SAPOC's mandatory annual review must assess, among other things, "All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status."

The office intersects the UAP record at three documented points. In March 2023 Major General David W. Abba, then Director of DoD SAPCO, signed a memorandum — released to The Black Vault in FOIA case 24-F-0266 — stating that AARO was authorized to receive information relating to sensitive U.S. Government information and activities, the instrument on which AARO's repeated attempts to interview David Grusch rested. On 17 April 2024 Abba appeared alongside acting AARO director Tim Phillips in a classified UAP briefing to members of Congress. And in July 2024 former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick described briefing and testifying to members of Congress "with the SAPCO director and the CAPCO director from ODNI," saying that they had gone through everything and that none of the alleged hidden programs were what witnesses claimed.

That last item is the denial, and it is a good one to catalogue precisely because of who is standing next to whom. The office that administers waived SAPs, the office that controls contractor communication with Congress, and the office that keeps the records of what Congress was told, went to Congress to say there is nothing there.

claims.text: DoD Directive 5205.07, "Special Access Program Policy," effective September 12, 2024, was approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks; it reissues and cancels the July 1, 2010 directive and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum, "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform," July 11, 2023.

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 1.2.e provides that the Director, DoD SAPCO, "under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, will be a general officer, flag officer, or Senior Executive Service member or equivalent appointed to oversee day-to-day management of the SAP Enterprise. The Director, DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense."

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 2.1.b provides: "The Director, DoD SAPCO has jurisdiction over the protection of information contained within DoD SAPs and is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for purposes of issuing SAP security classification guides."

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 2.1.a(5) makes the Director the "DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch, including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries, unless otherwise specified by statute or regulation."

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 2.1.e requires the Director to accredit congressional SAP facilities and to "maintain records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress" — making the same office the conduit for, and the recordkeeper of, what Congress is told.

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1.g provides: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval."

The SAP Oversight Committee is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense with the Director, DoD SAPCO as Executive Secretary; its membership includes USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), USD(C)/CFO, USD(I&S), the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the DoD General Counsel, DCAPE, the DoD CIO, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, ASD(SO/LIC), and the service vice chiefs.

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 1.2.b provides that only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense may alter the tier-1 SAP architecture, while "The Director, DoD Special Access Program Central Office (SAPCO) may approve establishment and disestablishment of DoD SAPs at tiers 2 and below."
DoDI 5205.11 requires the SAPOC's annual review to assess "All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status."

DoDI 5205.11 provides that Access Approval Authority for non-waived SAPs may be delegated to component SAPCO staff, while "AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee," and that "DoD SAPCO will coordinate on PARs for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs."

DoDI 5205.11 assigns DoD SAPCO the duty to notify the congressional defense committees of changes to CPI protected by DoD SAPs, and the intelligence committees for intelligence or intelligence-related CPI, and to report proposed classification changes or declassifications with a description, the reasons, and notice of any planned public announcement.

DoDI 5205.11 states that Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency oversight for administration of the National Industrial Security Program "will be phased out in July 2029 in accordance with the carve-out provision of DoD Instruction (DoDI) 5220.31" — removing an independent industrial-security inspector from the SAP contractor base.

Major General David W. Abba, U.S. Air Force, served as Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office; a March 2023 memorandum signed by Abba stated that AARO was authorized to receive information relating to sensitive U.S. Government information and activities, and was released under FOIA case 24-F-0266. Abba also participated with then-acting AARO director Tim Phillips in a classified UAP briefing for members of Congress on April 17, 2024.

Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick stated in a July 17, 2024 interview that he had briefed and testified to members of Congress "with the SAPCO director and the CAPCO director from ODNI" and that all of the alleged hidden programs "have turned out to be other things that have nothing to do with extraterrestrial reverse engineering. And all of them have been reported to Congress."

dossier.denialPosture: DoD SAPCO does not speak publicly under its own name. Its position enters the record through others: the Abba memorandum authorizing AARO to receive sensitive information, and Kirkpatrick's account of the SAPCO director appearing alongside him before Congress to say that every alleged hidden program had been checked, was something else, and had already been reported.
connections: Administers the waived unacknowledged SAP mechanism created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e); controls congressional access under DoDI 5205.11 section 7.
Reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense — Kathleen H. Hicks signed the 2024 reissuance and chaired the SAPOC.
Maj. Gen. David W. Abba (Director) is the signatory of the March 2023 memorandum on which AARO's authority to interview cleared witnesses, including David Grusch, rested.
Paired in Kirkpatrick's account with ODNI's CAPCO (Controlled Access Program Coordination Office) as the two offices that jointly told Congress the alleged programs do not exist.
Absorbed the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum of July 11, 2023 on 'DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform' — issued three days before the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act was unveiled.
Also Executive Secretary of the Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee established by the November 21, 2020 Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum.
Directly targeted by FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687, which conditions funding for UAP activities 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' on disclosure to Congress.
openQuestions: Whether DoD SAPCO's records of 'DoD SAP information provided to Congress' have ever been examined by an independent body, and whether they would show what the eight recipients of any waived-SAP notification actually received.
The full text and classification markings of the March 2023 Abba memorandum, and whether it authorized disclosure to AARO of waived-SAP information or only of non-waived material.
Whether any request has been made under DoDD 5205.07 para 3.1.g by a contractor employee seeking approval to take SAP material to Congress, and how such requests are adjudicated and logged.
Who succeeded Abba as Director of DoD SAPCO and what that officer has told Congress about UAP.
What the July 11, 2023 SAP Enterprise Reform memorandum actually directed, given that it has now been cancelled and absorbed into DoDD 5205.07 without separate publication.
Which judicial personnel have been granted access to waived DoD SAPs, and in connection with which litigation.

l0.label: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
l0.short: Office of the Director of National Intelligence

dossier.whatItIs: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence is the coordinating headquarters of the US Intelligence Community, created by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 and headed by the Director of National Intelligence. Since 2021 it has been the statutory co-owner of the government's UAP reporting machinery: it published the June 2021 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' it is the office with which the Secretary of Defense must coordinate in establishing and running AARO, and it co-issues the annual consolidated UAP reports. Its Inspector General is also the channel through which UAP whistleblower complaints reach the congressional intelligence committees.
dossier.whyImplicated: ODNI sits on both sides of the ledger, and that is precisely what makes it useful. It is the office that publicly certified that most reported UAP 'probably do represent physical objects,' that eleven documented pilot near-misses exist, and — critically — that it could not confirm that any of the collected reports were attributable to classified US government or industry developmental programs. An intelligence headquarters that cannot deconflict a UAP dataset against its own black programs is either not being told, or is telling us it is not being told. At the same time, ODNI is the institutional counterparty for every DoD SAP that shares compartmented capabilities with the IC, and AARO is lodged inside the DoD office designated as ODNI's primary interface. Its Inspector General found David Grusch's complaint alleging concealed retrieval and reverse-engineering programs 'credible and urgent' and forwarded it to the DNI and both intelligence committees, after which nothing publicly followed. Even the FOIA-released version of its own 2021 assessment is redacted under (b)(1) and (b)(3), including the identity of the official it names as accountable.
dossier.narrative:
ODNI's formal entry into the UAP file came through an appropriations rider rather than through the intelligence community's own initiative. Senate Report 116-233, accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to submit an intelligence assessment of the threat posed by unidentified aerial phenomena and of the progress the Department of Defense Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force had made in understanding it. The resulting nine-page unclassified 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' dated 25 June 2021, is the single most-cited government document on the subject, and it repays close reading of the FOIA copy rather than the sanitised public one.

The drafting roster alone is analytically valuable. The report was 'drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and ODNI/National Intelligence Council.' That is a list of every organisation with an equity in the file as of 2021, and it is a map of where records exist.

The substantive findings are hedged but not empty. 'Most of the UAP reported probably do represent physical objects given that a majority of UAP registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation.' The UAPTF 'has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.' The dataset is limited primarily to US government reporting of incidents from November 2004 to March 2021. The report proposes five explanatory bins — airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or US industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other' — and then, on the third bin, delivers the sentence a program hypothesis must build on: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to classified USG aerospace programs or systems under development by commercial aerospace firms. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' On foreign adversaries: 'We currently lack data to determine any UAP are part of a foreign collection program or indicative of a major technological advancement by a potential adversary.' On collection: 'The UAPTF had no MASINT reporting on the events considered in this dataset' — which stands in direct tension with the later Immaculate Constellation allegation that a parent USAP holds high-quality IMINT and MASINT of UAP.

The redaction pattern is itself evidence. The FOIA version, approved for release on 24 March 2022 under case DF-2021-00275, still withholds material under (b)(1) — properly classified national defence information — and (b)(3), statutory exemption. The sentence identifying the accountable official reads, in the released copy, 'The UAPTF Director, is the official accountable for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP,' with the name removed. Passages describing unusual flight characteristics, GEOINT and SIGINT collection, and specific incidents are blank. The unclassified public product is therefore a curated fraction of what Congress received, and the delta is where the argument lives.

ODNI's second role is structural. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373 the Secretary of Defense must act 'in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence' in establishing AARO, and the reporting mechanism must be established 'in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence.' AARO is housed inside OUSD(I&S). And DoDD 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, designates USD(I&S) as the office that 'serves as the primary interface for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and members of the Intelligence Community (IC), including sharing with the DoD compartmented capabilities and information intended for inclusion and subsequent apportionment.' In other words, the same office that hosts the body Congress created to find unreported UAP programs is the office through which IC compartmented capabilities are moved into and out of DoD special access programs. Whether that is an oversight design flaw or the point is the question the board exists to press.

The third role is the whistleblower channel. In 2022, while at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, David Grusch filed a Presidential Policy Directive 19 urgent-concern complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General. Thomas Monheim, IC Inspector General from April 2020 to January 2025, found the complaint credible and urgent, and a summary went to the Director of National Intelligence and to the House and Senate intelligence committees. Grusch then testified publicly to House Oversight in July 2023. No ODNI product has since publicly addressed the substance of the referral.

Finally, ODNI has been the co-publisher of record for the successor reporting. The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, released 14 November 2024 the day after the House Oversight hearing, reported 757 UAP reports received, 485 of which occurred within the reporting period and 272 of which occurred in 2021-2022 but were reported late; 118 cases resolved to prosaic objects; 21 unresolved. That report is a DoD/AARO product carried on the ODNI website, and under this board's sourcing rules it is a primary record of what the government said, not of what is true.

What the record does not show is any ODNI statement about retrievals, materials, or reverse-engineering. There is no ODNI acknowledgement of a legacy program, and no public ODNI response to the Grusch referral.

claims.text: The 25 June 2021 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena' was produced by ODNI in response to a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, directing the DNI in consultation with the Secretary of Defense to assess the threat posed by UAP and the UAPTF's progress.

The assessment states it 'was drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and ODNI/National Intelligence Council.'

The assessment states: 'Most of the UAP reported probably do represent physical objects given that a majority of UAP registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation.'
The assessment states: 'The UAPTF has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.'

On the possibility that UAP are US black programs the assessment states: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to classified USG aerospace programs or systems under development by commercial aerospace firms. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.'
The assessment states: 'The UAPTF had no MASINT reporting on the events considered in this dataset.'

The assessment defines five explanatory categories into which resolved UAP incidents would fall: airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or U.S. industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other' bin.
The dataset described in the assessment 'is currently limited primarily to USG reporting of incidents occurring from November 2004 to March 2021.'

The FOIA-released version of the assessment, approved for release by ODNI on 24 March 2022 under case DF-2021-00275, withholds material under exemptions (b)(1) and (b)(3), including the name of the UAPTF Director identified in the text as 'the official accountable for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP,' redacted under (b)(3) and (b)(6).
The assessment notes 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems.'

DoD Directive 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, designates USD(I&S) as the office that 'serves as the primary interface for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and members of the Intelligence Community (IC), including sharing with the DoD compartmented capabilities and information intended for inclusion and subsequent apportionment' — the same office in which AARO is housed.

50 U.S.C. 3373 requires the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to establish the office known as the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, and requires the secure UAP reporting mechanism to be established in consultation with the DNI.

In 2022 Intelligence Community Inspector General Thomas Monheim found David Grusch's PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint credible and urgent, and a summary was transmitted to the Director of National Intelligence and to the House and Senate intelligence committees; Grusch subsequently testified publicly to House Oversight in July 2023.

Michael Shellenberger's November 2024 congressional testimony quotes DNI John Ratcliffe stating in 2021 that UAP demonstrated 'technologies that we don't have and, frankly, that we are not capable of defending against,' that analysts had 'high confidence' foreign adversaries were not behind the Tic Tac encounter, and that 'there are a lot more sightings than have been made public.'

The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, released 14 November 2024 and carried on the ODNI website, reports 757 UAP reports received, of which 485 occurred within the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were reported late; 118 cases were resolved to prosaic objects and 21 remain unexplained.

Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, require NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection consisting of 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence'; NARA established Record Group 615 for it, creating a statutory transfer obligation that reaches every IC element ODNI coordinates.

dossier.denialPosture: ODNI has never denied that a legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering program exists; it has denied confirmation. Its 2021 assessment states it was 'unable to confirm' that US classified aerospace programs accounted for any collected UAP report, and that it 'currently lacks data' to attribute UAP to a foreign collection program. The characteristic ODNI posture is epistemic hedging plus redaction, not categorical denial — which is a materially different artifact from the flat DoD denials on this board.
connections: ODNI to UAPTF to AARO: the same reporting lineage, with ODNI's National Intelligence Manager for Aviation as the drafting office in 2021 and AARO now lodged inside OUSD(I&S), ODNI's designated DoD interface under DoDD 5205.07.

The 2021 drafting roster names every agency with a UAP equity as of that date — DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, NCSC, NIC — and is therefore a target list for NARA Record Group 615 transfer compliance.
The redacted UAPTF Director's name under (b)(6) is a specific, resolvable identity gap; the same office is the accountability node the Senate report demanded be identified.

ICIG Thomas Monheim to DNI Avril Haines to the congressional intelligence committees is the documented Grusch referral path; the substance of what ODNI did with it is unaddressed in any public product.

The assessment's statement that the UAPTF had no MASINT reporting sits in direct conflict with the Immaculate Constellation allegation that a parent USAP holds high-quality IMINT and MASINT — either the UAPTF was walled off from that collection, or one of the two statements is false.

DNI John Ratcliffe's 2021 public statements are the most permissive on-record remarks by any DNI and are quoted into the congressional record by a November 2024 witness; DNI succession since (Haines, Gabbard, Clayton) is a change-of-posture axis worth tracking.
Michael Gold's testimony connects ODNI's collection problem to NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System and to CNES/GEIPAN as civil-side data sources the IC has not integrated.
openQuestions: Who is the UAPTF Director redacted under (b)(6) in the FOIA copy of the 2021 assessment?
What does the classified annex to the 2021 preliminary assessment contain, and who at ODNI has seen it?
What action, if any, did ODNI or the DNI take on the ICIG's credible-and-urgent referral of the Grusch complaint?
Has ODNI or any IC element transferred records to NARA Record Group 615, and what did they withhold?
Which ODNI element holds equity in any UAP-related compartmented capability shared with DoD SAPs through the USD(I&S) interface?
Why could the IC not deconflict its own UAP dataset against classified US aerospace programs — was the deconfliction attempted and refused, or never possible at the UAPTF's access level?

l0.label: National Reconnaissance Office

dossier.whatItIs: The National Reconnaissance Office is the joint Department of Defense / Intelligence Community agency that designs, builds, launches and operates United States reconnaissance satellites. Management arrangements creating it and the National Reconnaissance Program were signed on 6 September 1961 by Acting DCI General Charles P. Cabell and Deputy Secretary of Defense Roswell L. Gilpatric. Its very existence was classified for thirty-one years and was declassified only on 18 September 1992.
dossier.whyImplicated: The NRO is the existence proof for the central premise of this board: that the United States can operate a multi-billion-dollar technical enterprise for three decades with no public existence, no line item Congress could disaggregate, and no acknowledged budget. When it was finally pried open in August 1994 it emerged that the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence did not know the NRO had built a one-million-square-foot, $310 million headquarters in Chantilly, Virginia, because the money sat in the "base" portion of the budget rather than as a new initiative. By 1996 the agency was found to be sitting on billions of dollars in forward funding that had not been reported to CIA, the Pentagon, or Congress. It is also the agency that produced David Grusch, who served as the NRO's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force from 2019 to 2021 and whose subsequent complaint alleged a concealed multi-decade recovery and reverse-engineering effort. Finally, the NRO's own 1992 declassification memorandum is a template artifact of the concealment posture: it declassified the fact of the agency and then closed with a single sentence refusing everything else.
dossier.narrative:
Everything about the NRO is instructive for a board that asks not whether but how. Start with the birth certificate: not a statute, not a public charter, but management arrangements agreed on 6 September 1961 between the Acting Director of Central Intelligence and the Deputy Secretary of Defense, consolidating Air Force, CIA and Navy overhead reconnaissance programs into a single compartmented office. For thirty-one years the fact of the office was itself classified. It hired, contracted, launched, and spent, and the American public and most of the Congress did not know the name.

The 18 September 1992 declassification is worth reading closely because it is a study in minimum viable disclosure. Deputy Secretary of Defense Donald Atwood announced, in Memorandum for Correspondents No. 264-M, that there is an NRO, that it is an agency of the Department of Defense, that it is funded through the National Reconnaissance Program, that its mission is spaceborne and airborne collection, and that the Director reports directly to the Secretary of Defense while the Director of Central Intelligence sets collection priorities and jointly approves the budget. It named three officials — Faga, Hill, March — and gave a Pentagon mailing address and a phone number. Then it ended: "No other information relating to the National Reconnaissance Office was declassified." That is the entire architecture of managed disclosure in one sentence. Acknowledge the container; classify the contents.

The 1994 headquarters affair is the second lesson. On 8 August 1994 members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence held a press conference to disclose the existence of a secret $310 million headquarters complex under construction in Chantilly, Virginia, and to attack the intelligence community for not properly informing them of its size and cost. Two days later DCI James Woolsey produced a paper trail sufficient to argue there had been no deliberate concealment — but the paper trail was not the point. The point, as the Federation of American Scientists documented at the time, was that the project had been buried in the "base" part of the budget rather than broken out as a new initiative, and that base programs go essentially unscrutinized. The NRO's own headquarters project director, Roger Marsh, conceded in the agency's first open hearing: "We have been negligent, clearly negligent, for not showing the budget breakout for this project." Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan was blunter: "This is an agency which has lied to Congress before. Egregiously." Senator John Warner put the resource asymmetry on the record — the NRO had twenty-five people working budget matters; the Senate committee had one. The NRO's own share of the intelligence budget at the time was roughly $6.5 billion.

The third lesson is the money itself. Reporting in 1995 and 1996 established that the NRO had accumulated a very large pool of unspent forward funding — figures reported in the range of $1 billion to $1.7 billion initially, and ultimately around $3.8 billion — without informing CIA, the Pentagon or Congress. NRO Director Jeffrey K. Harris departed in February 1996. The relevance to a legacy recovery program is direct and mechanical: an agency inside the classified budget can accumulate carryover at a scale that would fund an entire concealed enterprise, and the discovery of that carryover required a scandal, not oversight.

The fourth lesson is personnel. David Grusch served as the NRO's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force from 2019 to 2021, and afterward as the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency's co-lead for UAP analysis and its task-force representative into July 2022. His allegations, published by Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal in The Debrief on 5 June 2023 and repeated under oath before the House Oversight Committee on 26 July 2023, did not originate with a UFO enthusiast off the street. They originated with the officer the NRO sent to the interagency table. Whatever one concludes about the substance, the provenance runs through this agency.

What the NRO has not done is speak to UAP at all. It has issued no denial, no confirmation, no historical review. It is not named in AARO's public historical reporting as a subject of interest. It has never been asked in open session what it holds. Under sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA the NRO is a "Government office" like any other and was obliged to review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by 20 October 2024; there is no public accounting of what it transmitted or withheld, and under section 1843 the postponement decision rests with its own original classification authority.

For an analyst, the NRO is best understood not as a suspect but as a calibration instrument. It tells you the maximum duration of full concealment achievable in the modern American system (thirty-one years), the mechanism (base-budget aggregation inside a compartmented program), the failure mode (a construction project too physically large to hide), the discovery mechanism (press and scandal rather than committee), and the recovery posture (declassify the container, refuse the contents). Any hypothesis about a legacy recovery program that requires less institutional capability than the NRO demonstrably possessed is, on the face of it, feasible.

claims.text: The Department of Defense announced the declassification of the existence of the National Reconnaissance Office on September 18, 1992, in Memorandum for Correspondents No. 264-M, attributed to Deputy Secretary of Defense Donald Atwood and made on the recommendation of the Director of Central Intelligence.
claims.source: https://irp.fas.org/nro/dod091802.html (DoD Memorandum for Correspondents No. 264-M, September 18, 1992)

claims.text: That 1992 memorandum ends with the sentence: "No other information relating to the National Reconnaissance Office was declassified."

The 1992 memorandum states the NRO is "organized as an agency of the Department of Defense and funded through a program known as the National Reconnaissance Program (NRP), which is the single, national program to meet U.S. Government intelligence needs through spaceborne and assigned airborne reconnaissance."

Per the same memorandum, the Director of the NRO reports directly to the Secretary of Defense; the DCI establishes collection priorities and requirements, jointly approves the NRP budget with the Secretary of Defense, and provides security policy guidance; and the Director executes NRO programs "through the Department of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency."
As of the 1992 declassification the Director of the NRO was Martin C. Faga, the Deputy Director was Jimmie D. Hill, and the Deputy Director for Military Support was Rear Admiral Daniel P. March, USN.

The management arrangements establishing the National Reconnaissance Program and the NRO were signed on 6 September 1961 by Acting Director of Central Intelligence General Charles P. Cabell and Deputy Secretary of Defense Roswell L. Gilpatric, consolidating CIA, Air Force and Navy overhead reconnaissance under a covert compartmented office.

On August 8, 1994, members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence publicly disclosed a previously secret $310 million, approximately one-million-square-foot NRO headquarters complex in Chantilly, Virginia, and criticized the intelligence community for failing to properly inform them of its size and cost; the committee subsequently held a hearing on the project.
claims.source: https://sgp.fas.org/bulletin/sec39.html (Secrecy & Government Bulletin No. 39, Aug-Sep 1994); see also S. Hrg. 103-997, "NRO Headquarters Project," Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, 103d Cong.

claims.text: NRO headquarters project director Roger Marsh testified in the agency's first open public hearing: "We have been negligent, clearly negligent, for not showing the budget breakout for this project."

Senator Daniel P. Moynihan said of the NRO during the 1994 headquarters controversy: "This is not the first time such a thing has happened, nor will it be, I fear, the last.... This is an agency which has lied to Congress before. Egregiously."

The headquarters project escaped congressional scrutiny because it was presented within the "base" portion of the classified budget rather than as a new initiative; Senator John Warner noted on August 10, 1994 that the NRO had 25 people working budget matters while the Senate intelligence committee had one staff person assigned to the task, and the NRO's share of the intelligence budget was then roughly $6.5 billion.
claims.source: https://sgp.fas.org/bulletin/sec39.html citing Cong. Rec., 8/10/94, p. S11142

claims.text: In the immediate aftermath the Senate passed an amendment requiring that any intelligence construction project costing $300 million or more be identified as a specific line item within the classified budget request.

Reporting in 1995-1996 established that the NRO had accumulated large unreported unspent balances — figures reported from $1 billion to $1.7 billion initially and around $3.8 billion in total forward funding — without informing CIA, the Pentagon or Congress; NRO Director Jeffrey K. Harris left the post in February 1996.

David Grusch served as the NRO's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force from 2019 to 2021, and from late 2021 to July 2022 as NGA's co-lead for UAP analysis and its task force representative, before going public on June 5, 2023.

As a "Government office" the NRO was subject to the FY2024 NDAA requirement that each agency review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by October 20, 2024; no public accounting exists of what the NRO transmitted or postponed.

dossier.denialPosture: The NRO has issued no public statement on UAP, no denial and no confirmation, and has never been examined on the subject in open session. Its institutional posture is the one modeled by its own 1992 declassification memorandum: acknowledge the container and refuse everything inside it.
connections: David Grusch was the NRO's representative to the UAP Task Force 2019-2021; his allegations of a concealed retrieval and reverse-engineering program originate from that detail.

Structurally joint with CIA: the DCI/DNI sets collection requirements and jointly approves the NRP budget, while the Director reports to the Secretary of Defense — a two-key arrangement that lets each principal point at the other.
The 1994 headquarters affair is the archetype for the FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687 problem: money hidden not by lying but by aggregation inside a base budget line.
Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (Moynihan, Warner, DeConcini, Kerrey, Wallop) as the oversight body that admitted it had not looked.
DCI James Woolsey and Deputy Secretary of Defense John Deutch as the officials who declassified the headquarters only under White House pressure, per FAS.
NRO is a covered 'Government office' under P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843 and therefore a custodian of record within the UAP Records Collection regime administered by NARA.
openQuestions: What, if anything, the NRO transmitted to the National Archives under sections 1841-1843, and how many of its records it postponed under section 1843.
Whether the NRO holds or has held any special access program with UAP equities, and whether any such program is waived under 10 U.S.C. 119(e).
What Grusch saw or was told in his capacity as NRO representative to the UAP Task Force, as distinct from what he was later told by others.
Whether the forward-funding practice uncovered in 1995-96 was unique to the NRO or characteristic of compartmented programs generally, and whether any comparable audit has been performed since.

The identity and disposition of NRO programs historically misidentified in the UAP record — AARO has asserted misattribution of classified U.S. programs generally but has not published an NRO-specific accounting.

l0.label: United States Department of Energy

dossier.whatItIs: The Department of Energy is the successor to the Atomic Energy Commission and the custodian of the United States nuclear weapons complex, including Los Alamos, Sandia, Lawrence Livermore and the Pantex assembly and disassembly plant, operated through the National Nuclear Security Administration. Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 it holds a government-wide classification authority, Restricted Data, that exists entirely outside the executive order classification system and is not subject to automatic declassification.
dossier.whyImplicated: DOE holds the one classification authority in the United States government that a legacy programme could hide behind indefinitely, because Restricted Data is created by statute rather than by executive order, applies government-wide, and never automatically declassifies. Its facilities are also the physical centre of gravity of the phenomenon's own documented history: the green fireball wave of 1948 to 1951 concentrated over Los Alamos and Sandia, Project GRUDGE recorded case clusters in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area and at Oak Ridge, and Congress now requires AARO to report annually on incidents at nuclear weapons production, transportation and storage facilities. In the most recent reporting year the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman sent AARO fifty incident reports, a 177.8 percent increase over the prior year, every one of which AARO records as not reported as UAP. A former DoD official named DOE under oath as one of the agencies with a role and no accountability. DOE has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
dossier.narrative:
The reason DOE belongs on a map of concealment has nothing to do with what anyone alleges and everything to do with statute. Restricted Data is defined by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and covers all data concerning the design, manufacture or utilisation of atomic weapons, the production of special nuclear material, and the use of special nuclear material in the production of energy. It is classified under the Act, not under an executive order. Everything else in the national security classification system flows from a presidential order, currently the 13526 lineage, and is therefore subject to automatic declassification at twenty-five years unless exempted. Restricted Data is not. It requires affirmative review before declassification, it cannot be declassified by an agency that did not originate it, and the authority is government-wide. DOE's implementing regulation is 10 CFR Part 1045, most recently overhauled by a final rule published in the Federal Register on 21 December 2018.

The practical consequence is that if a UAP incident occurred over a weapons production facility, a storage igloo, a transport convoy or a laboratory working on weapons physics, the record of it could be created as Restricted Data from the moment of its generation and would then be permanently outside the reach of the executive order declassification machinery that every UAP disclosure statute has assumed. The FY2024 NDAA's records collection provisions operate on federal records generally. They do not amend the Atomic Energy Act.

The history is dense. From late November 1948 through early 1951 a wave of green luminous objects was reported over New Mexico, concentrated near Los Alamos and Sandia and over other sensitive installations. On 16 February 1949 a conference at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory brought together laboratory director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller, Frederick Reines, representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the military, and Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico Institute of Meteoritics, who had personally observed the objects. LaPaz, after interviewing more than a hundred witnesses, advised the military and the AEC that the fireballs were most likely either unconventional defensive devices being tested by the United States or Soviet reconnaissance devices. The Air Force ran Project Twinkle from 1949 to 1951 to instrument the phenomenon, never fully implemented it, and concluded the objects were probably natural.

AARO's own Volume I preserves the pattern independently. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites. It records that AARO interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and elsewhere in connection with a narrative that UAP sightings near nuclear facilities resulted in malfunctioning missiles and a destroyed test reentry vehicle. It records that AARO continues to investigate these cases because of their potential impact on the readiness of the US nuclear programme. And it lists DOE among the agency archives AARO partnered with.

Congress has legislated the nuclear connection into permanent statutory reporting. Section 3373(k) of title 50 requires AARO's annual report to include the number and description of incidents of UAP associated with military nuclear assets, and separately the results of consultation with the Administrator for Nuclear Security regarding incidents at facilities or assets associated with the production, transportation or storage of nuclear weapons or their components, and with the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding nuclear power stations and fuel storage sites. That is a standing legal obligation on the nuclear weapons enterprise to account, annually, for anomalous objects over its facilities.

The FY2025 report is the most recent execution of it and the number is striking. AARO received fifty reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the NRC Chairman regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near US nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, a 177.8 percent increase over the eighteen reported the previous year. Forty-seven of the fifty occurred between 1700 and 0500 local. Five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours. AARO then adds the sentence that carries all the weight: none of these incidents were reported as UAP. The nuclear complex is reporting a rising volume of unexplained aerial activity over the most sensitive sites in the country and categorising all of it, in advance, as drones.

The 2015 Pantex incident is the clearest recent case. A Department of Energy report describes security personnel at the nuclear weapons assembly and disassembly plant near Amarillo observing a diamond-shaped object in September 2015, hovering and moving in a northerly trajectory at roughly ten to fifteen miles per hour, described by witnesses as around four feet tall and two feet wide at the base and thinner at the top, with conflicting colour descriptions. The object was tracked by ground radar and photographed from a nearby radar tower, and the imagery was analysed by DOE's Sandia National Laboratories. The report was released in more complete form during the 2026 executive-branch disclosure tranches after earlier heavily redacted releases.

Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, listed the Department of Energy among the White House, CIA, NASA and the Pentagon as agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading to unchecked power and corruption. As of the National Archives collection page's 22 May 2026 review, DOE had no transmittal listed in Record Group 615.

dossier.whatItIs: The Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI) is the Department of the Air Force's federal law enforcement and counterintelligence agency, established 1 August 1948 and operating as a Field Operating Agency under the Secretary of the Air Force Inspector General. Its first commander was Special Agent Joseph F. Carroll, a senior FBI official and assistant to Director J. Edgar Hoover, who in 1961 became the first Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency. AFOSI is currently chartered by Air Force Mission Directive 39, dated 12 February 2024.
dossier.whyImplicated: AFOSI sits on both sides of the concealment problem simultaneously, and its own charter says so. Under AFMD 39 paragraph 3.16 it "Executes independent special access program CI and LE investigations, operations, specialized investigative activities, compliance inspections, integrated technology protection, and program security responsibilities for all DAF special access programs, and non-DAF special access programs where the DAF has been assigned responsibility." That is the security envelope around Air Force black programs, held by one agency. Under paragraph 3.3 it is the Department's sole counterintelligence agency, and under 3.2 its investigations supersede any other Air Force entity's inquiry. Historically, AFOSI took over UFO investigation from Air Materiel Command shortly after its 1948 creation under the name Project Grudge, ran most of those investigations out of District 17 at Kirtland AFB in New Mexico - the district co-located with Sandia, Los Alamos and the Manzano weapons storage area - and in 1967 sent a piece of an alleged UFO to the FBI Crime Laboratory. And the single best-documented instance of a US counterintelligence element manufacturing UFO belief, the campaign run against Albuquerque physicist Paul Bennewitz in the late 1970s and 1980s, was run by an AFOSI special agent at Kirtland.
dossier.narrative:
Start with the charter, because it is unclassified and it is decisive. Air Force Mission Directive 39, signed 12 February 2024 by Lt. Gen. Stephen L. Davis as The Inspector General, states AFOSI's mission as identifying, exploiting, investigating, disrupting and neutralising criminal, terrorist and intelligence threats across all domains. Paragraph 3.3 designates AFOSI, by the Secretary of the Air Force, as the Department's counterintelligence component and its sole agency for counterintelligence investigations, collections, operations and analysis. Paragraph 3.2 gives it primary investigative authority over everything in its jurisdiction and provides that its investigations "will supersede any other DAF entity's investigation or inquiry." Paragraph 3.7 gives it counterintelligence responsibility for cleared contractor facilities under the National Industrial Security Program. Paragraph 3.8 gives it counterintelligence support to critical DoD research and development under DoDI-O 5240.24. Paragraph 3.16 gives it program security responsibility for all Department of the Air Force special access programs and for non-DAF SAPs where the DAF has been assigned responsibility, under AFPD 16-7 and AFI 16-701. And paragraph 2.2 requires the commander to notify the Secretary in writing of any instance in which a commander or any other Air Force official attempts to impede an investigation - an obligation that exists precisely because the situation arises.

Set that against the historical record published by AFOSI's own command historian, Dr. Deborah Kidwell, in August 2020. Her account states that at the inception of Project Sign, Air Force Materiel Command held responsibility for UFO reports, but that shortly after AFOSI's creation in 1948 it took over that responsibility under the name Project Grudge. Most investigations were run by District 17 at Kirtland AFB, New Mexico. The 1948 green fireball investigations drew in a University of New Mexico meteoriticist; District 17 briefed Sandia Base, Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, the University of California Geophysics Institute, the Atomic Energy Commission and the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project in early 1949. On the recommendation of an Air Force Scientific Advisory Board member in April 1949, District 17 established an observation post on the crest of the Sandia Mountains northeast of Albuquerque where agents manned spectrographic photo surveillance equipment twenty-four hours a day. The results were collected under OSI Letter Number 85: Unconventional Aircraft-Special Inquiry, classified file designation 24-185.

Two items in that same account matter disproportionately. First: "In 1967, agents briefed a scientific group on Neutron Activity analysis and sent a piece of an alleged UFO to the FBI Crime Laboratory. The lab concluded that while the item was unusual, there was no evidence that it belonged to an alien craft." This is an official, on-the-record acknowledgement of AFOSI custody and forensic routing of purported UAP material, and it is the same workflow that runs today through Oak Ridge. Second: AFOSI declassified its UFO investigative files in late 1975 and sent them to the National Archives, and Kidwell writes that "The National Archives has been unable to locate any documentation among the Blue Book records that discuss the incident in Roswell." The service whose district office covered New Mexico transferred its New Mexico UFO files to NARA and none of them mention Roswell - which sits alongside the GAO's separate finding that Roswell Army Air Field's outgoing messages for 1946-1949 were destroyed without recorded authority.

Then there is Kirtland in 1980. On 9 August 1980 security personnel at the Manzano Weapons Storage Area adjacent to Kirtland reported a bright light descending in a restricted area, and a report was filed with AFOSI at Kirtland. The investigating agent was Special Agent Richard C. Doty. In the same period Doty became the primary AFOSI contact for Paul Bennewitz, an Albuquerque physicist and businessman who had been filming and intercepting signals around Kirtland and Manzano. Rather than being turned away, Bennewitz was fed. Doty has since publicly acknowledged participating in counterintelligence disinformation directed at the UFO research community, and both Doty and documentary producer Linda Moulton Howe state they met at Kirtland AFB in April 1983. Bennewitz's mental deterioration is the documented outcome.

The reason this matters to a board about a legacy program is not that Doty's stories were true. It is that they were false, deliberately, and produced under colour of federal counterintelligence authority at the base where the Air Force's New Mexico UFO files, its nuclear weapons storage and its special access program security responsibilities all converged. Disinformation is expensive and is not deployed to protect nothing. AFOSI's own charter tells you what it protects at Kirtland: special access programs and nuclear surety. Whether the thing being screened was a conventional black program, a nuclear security vulnerability, or the retrieval architecture itself is exactly the question - and AFOSI is the agency whose files would settle it.

AFOSI remains inside the current reporting architecture. The May 2023 Joint Staff GENADMIN reproduced in AARO's FY2024 annual report directs Combatant Commands and Services to report all UAP incidents, incursions and engagements to Joint Operations Centers, Service Watch Centers, and respective counterintelligence elements within 96 hours. For the Department of the Air Force, per AFMD 39 paragraph 3.3, that counterintelligence element is AFOSI and only AFOSI.

l0.short: Congressional oversight of special access programs

dossier.whatItIs: The congressional oversight apparatus for the legacy program question spans four venues with mismatched authorities: the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (broad jurisdiction, no SAP access), the House and Senate Armed Services and Appropriations committees (SAP access, narrow appetite), the two intelligence committees (Controlled Access Program access), and the eight-member chairman-and-ranking-member channel through which waived Special Access Programs are reported under 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Since 2021 Congress has legislated repeatedly and specifically against concealment, and has been told, repeatedly and specifically, that there is nothing to conceal.
dossier.whyImplicated: Congress is not a bystander in this record; it is the party that wrote into permanent law the demand that the Executive account for 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.' That sentence exists in the United States Code because members with access to classified briefings concluded such programs might exist. Congress then legislated that AARO must enumerate every instance in which data was withheld from it on classification grounds, barred contractors from charging UAP-related independent research and development to overhead unless the material is furnished to Congress, and created a statutory UAP Records Collection at the National Archives. Each of those provisions is a countermeasure, and countermeasures are designed against something. What Congress has not obtained is compliance: the eminent-domain and Review Board provisions were stripped in conference, the annual SAP report requirement lapsed on 31 December 2021, and in September 2025 the chairwoman of the investigating task force told the public that DoD would not read her members in at all.
dossier.narrative:
Congressional oversight of the legacy program problem has a structural defect that no amount of legislative will has cured: the committees with the appetite lack the access, and the committees with the access lack the appetite.

The modern sequence begins on 26 July 2023, when the House Oversight Committee's National Security subcommittee convened 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency.' Former National Reconnaissance Office and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency officer David Grusch testified under oath alongside former Navy pilot Ryan Graves and retired Navy Commander David Fravor. Grusch alleged a decades-long crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering effort, recovery of non-human biologics, and misappropriation of funds to evade congressional oversight, and said the specifics required a classified setting. The hearing produced a printed transcript, a legislative wave, and no records.

The legislative wave crested in the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act. Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds had drafted the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, which passed the Senate with three teeth: a presidentially appointed nine-member Review Board, a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan, and federal eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private parties. Conference removed all three. What survived became sections 1841 through 1843 of Public Law 118-31, codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note: a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, populated by 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence,' housed by NARA in Record Group 615. The eminent domain provision — the only clause that would have compelled a private contractor to surrender physical material — was the one the private contractors did not have to face.

What survived elsewhere in the same law is less discussed and arguably sharper. Section 1687(b) of P.L. 118-31 provides that, consistent with DoDI 3204.01, 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses' on covered contracts 'unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Congress legislated, in the FY2024 NDAA, against a specific accounting mechanism by which a defense contractor could fund UAP work with taxpayer money routed through overhead and owe nobody an explanation. That provision is a fingerprint.

The permanent statute carries more. 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4) requires the AARO Director, every briefing period, to give the chairs and ranking members of the Armed Services and Intelligence committees 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.' Congress anticipated that its own office would be stonewalled by other parts of the Executive and built a tripwire. Section 3373(j) requires the Historical Record Report to reach back to 1 January 1945 and to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' together with 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information.' The Comptroller General was directed by section 6803 of P.L. 117-263 to audit that very report process with cleared GAO personnel and to brief Congress semiannually on it.

Congress kept legislating. Public Law 119-60, enacted 18 December 2025, amended 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) so that the data-sharing mandate binds every component of the Department of Defense, not merely elements of the intelligence community — an amendment that would be pointless unless DoD components had been withholding under the old text. The same act added subsection (l)(5), requiring briefings to include details of NORAD and USNORTHCOM intercepts of UAP, with the first post-enactment briefing to reach back to 1 January 2004. Section 1673(a) ordered the AARO Director to make, within 180 days, 'an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena.' Congress is now demanding an inventory of the classification instruments themselves.

Against all of this stands the access problem. On 11 February 2025 Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets under Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, authorized for six months under Committee Rules. On 9 September 2025 Luna told the public that DoD had informed her staff that only HASC and HAC-D members could be read into the relevant SAPs, and that any other Member required the approval of the chairman and ranking member of both. She added: 'Independent SAP oversight has presented a consistent problem for Congress as the program's budgets are classified.' That is the architecture of 10 U.S.C. 119 operating exactly as designed, against the committee investigating it.
