l0.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (Record Group 615)
l0.short: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection

dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection is a statutory records collection at the National Archives and Records Administration, created by sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act and codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note. NARA established it as Record Group 615. Every federal agency was required to review, identify and organise its UAP records for disclosure and transmission, and to transfer publicly releasable digital copies in advance of 30 September 2025.
dossier.whyImplicated: The collection is the concealment argument reduced to an inventory problem, and the inventory is nearly empty. Congress wrote a statutory definition that expressly reaches records concerning technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence, which is a legislature drafting for the existence of the thing rather than the possibility of it. It then stripped out the two provisions that would have given the statute teeth, the eminent domain power over privately held recovered material and the independent Review Board modelled on the JFK Act, leaving agencies to grade their own homework. What arrived is the measure of what compliance is worth: as of May 2026 the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations, and the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the Defense Intelligence Agency, NASA and the military departments are not among them. A parallel executive-branch release channel opened in 2026 that routes disclosures around the statutory collection entirely.
dossier.narrative:
The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, sponsored by Senators Schumer and Rounds, passed the Senate in July 2023 as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA. In its Senate form it would have created an independent Review Board with authority over agency withholding decisions, and it would have directed the federal government to exercise eminent domain over any recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private persons or entities. Neither survived conference. What was enacted in Public Law 118-31 on 22 December 2023 was the records collection framework alone.

What survived is still remarkable as legislative drafting. The statute directs NARA to build a collection consisting of copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence, or equivalent subjects by any other name, with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects. Congress wrote three categories into federal records law. Unidentified anomalous phenomena is the neutral one. Technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence are not neutral at all; they are the categories a legacy recovery programme would generate. The clause about equivalent subjects by any other name is anti-evasion drafting aimed at codeword renaming. The exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects is there to keep routine drone and balloon traffic out. Legislatures do not build statutory taxonomies for things they believe do not exist.

NARA implemented it. It established Record Group 615, issued guidance to agencies through memoranda AC 26.2024 and AC 04.2025, and set the mechanics: agencies identify all UAP records in any format, make digital copies, attach prescribed metadata, and transfer. NARA accepts only digital versions. Agencies were to complete identification and organisation by 20 October 2024 and to initiate transfer in advance of 30 September 2025. One provision deserves particular attention. Where a publicly releasable record includes redactions, the agency must simultaneously transfer redacted and unredacted copies to NARA. The National Archives therefore holds unredacted originals of redacted UAP records that it does not publish, which makes NARA itself a custody node with material it is sitting on.

The results are the story. As of the Record Group 615 page's stated review date of 22 May 2026, the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. That list is as notable for its absences as its contents. The Central Intelligence Agency, whose own historian documented decades of UFO cover story management, is absent. The Department of Energy, which holds the nuclear complex and the Restricted Data authority, is absent. The Defense Intelligence Agency, which AARO has confirmed holds the AAWSAP archive, is absent. NASA is absent. The Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force are absent, which means the services that ran Project SIGN, Project GRUDGE, Project Blue Book and Project Moon Dust have not appeared in the collection created to hold that history. AARO itself, whose Volume I lists partnering with the National Archives on locating UAP data as one of its four lines of effort, appears only through OSD.

The statutory architecture explains why. The Act imposes an obligation on agencies to identify their own records and to decide what is publicly releasable. There is no Review Board, no independent adjudicator of withholding, and no penalty for a null return. Independent tracking of the transfer deadline found that most agencies approached with records requests either produced nothing or did not respond at all. A statute that asks the holders of a secret to declare it, and provides no mechanism when they do not, produces exactly the collection that exists.

The 2026 development compounds rather than fixes this. A presidential directive in February 2026 launched a multiagency effort to identify, review, declassify and publicly release UAP records, with a centralised repository opened in May 2026 on the Department of War's own website and material issued in periodic tranches. The releases have included previously unseen material, including a Department of Energy report on a 2015 incident over the Pantex nuclear weapons plant. But the channel is executive, discretionary, and controlled by the departments whose compliance with the statutory channel was the problem. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation made the point directly in February 2026, noting that Congress had already passed laws establishing a public UAP records collection at the National Archives and that the existing statutory framework gave the administration a path it was not using, while warning that classification nuances could produce misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.

The collection is therefore best understood on this board as an instrument that works and a compliance record that does not. The statute is the strongest UAP disclosure law ever enacted and it names the categories precisely. Record Group 615 is real, it is growing, and NARA is holding unredacted copies the public cannot see. Seven agencies have delivered. The agencies at the centre of the argument have not.

claims.text: Sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, require NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and require each federal agency to review, identify and organise each UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission to the National Archives.

The statutory scope is 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).'
NARA established Record Group 615 as the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and will accept only digital copies of UAP records from agencies.

Agencies were required to identify and organise UAP records by 20 October 2024 and to initiate transfer of publicly releasable records in advance of 30 September 2025, with metadata prescribed by NARA guidance in memorandum AC 26.2024.

Where a publicly releasable record includes redactions, agencies must simultaneously transfer both redacted and unredacted copies to NARA, meaning the National Archives holds unredacted originals of redacted UAP records that it does not publish.

As of the Record Group 615 page's stated review date of 22 May 2026, the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the Defense Intelligence Agency, NASA and the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force do not appear among the organisations with transmittals listed in Record Group 615 as of 22 May 2026.

The eminent domain mandate over privately held recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence, and the independent Review Board, were contained in the Senate-passed UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 but were removed in conference and are not part of Public Law 118-31.
AARO lists 'Partner with the U.S. National Archives on locating UAP data, refining requests based on the discovery of new leads' as one of its four stated lines of effort for the historical review.
claims.source: AARO Historical Record Report Volume I, March 2024, Scope and Methodology; https://media.defense.gov/2024/Mar/08/2003409233/-1/-1/0/DOPSR-CLEARED-508-COMPLIANT-HRRV1-08-MAR-2024-FINAL.PDF

claims.text: NARA maintains a bulk catalog download facility for UAP records alongside the Record Group 615 series listings, allowing the collection's contents to be enumerated independently of NARA's own summaries.

In February 2026 a War Department official stated that AARO 'has made progress to make UAP information available and transfer those records to the National Archives in accordance with federal law,' while AARO's own historical and annual reports remained unpublished and overdue.

Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation, stated in February 2026 that 'Congress already has passed laws establishing a public UAP records collection at the National Archives' and that the existing statutory framework provided the administration a path it was not using, while warning that classification nuances risked misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.

A presidential directive issued in February 2026 established a multiagency UAP records release effort with a centralised repository on the Department of War website, releasing material in periodic tranches beginning May 2026, operating alongside and outside the statutory National Archives collection.
NARA's guidance to agencies on identifying, preparing and transferring UAP records is published as a records management guidance page and in agency memoranda AC 26.2024 and AC 04.2025.

dossier.denialPosture: NARA has made no substantive claim about the phenomenon and issues no denials; it is a records custodian executing a statute. Its published position is procedural, that it receives records from agencies on a rolling basis and will add to Record Group 615 as they are transferred. The absence of denial is itself significant: NARA has never stated that any agency has certified it holds no UAP records, and it publishes no compliance register.
openQuestions: NARA publishes no register of which agencies have certified compliance, which have made null returns, and which have not responded at all. Without it, the seven listed transmittals cannot be distinguished from a near total failure of compliance.
The statutory transfer deadline of 30 September 2025 has passed. No enforcement action, referral or public accounting of non-compliance has been identified.
NARA holds unredacted copies of redacted UAP records under the simultaneous transfer requirement. The volume of that unpublished holding is not disclosed anywhere.

Whether records classified as Restricted Data under the Atomic Energy Act are treated as within or outside the transfer obligation has never been addressed by NARA guidance, which matters directly for DOE and the nuclear weapons complex.

The relationship between the statutory Record Group 615 collection and the 2026 executive-branch release channel is undefined. It is not established whether material released through the executive channel is also being accessioned into RG 615, or whether it substitutes for it.
The Senate-passed Review Board and eminent domain provisions have not been reintroduced and enacted. Whether any subsequent NDAA restores them is a live tracking item.

l0.label: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)

dossier.whatItIs: A waived unacknowledged special access program is the most tightly held category in the Department of Defense classification system. Department of Defense training doctrine defines it in one sentence: 'Waived SAPs are unacknowledged SAPs for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting requirements under Section 119, Title 10 U.S. Code.' The waiver authority is 10 U.S.C. 119(e), under which the Secretary may withhold specified information from the statutory reports to Congress if he determines that including it would adversely affect national security, and must then provide the information and the justification for the waiver only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the mechanism. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering program exists and has been concealed from Congress, waived SAP status is the lawful instrument by which that concealment is accomplished, and no unlawful act is required to sustain it. The statute permits an entire program's existence, cost, milestones and technology to disappear from the reports Congress wrote to keep itself informed, on the unilateral written determination of a single official. The population read in on the legislative side collapses to eight members and, per DoD policy, their staff directors. Everyone else in Congress, including every member of both intelligence committees who is not chair or ranking, can hold a Top Secret clearance and still be told nothing exists. The system is designed to produce truthful denials from officials who genuinely do not know, which is the precise pathology alleged across every UAP whistleblower account since 2017.
dossier.narrative:
The architecture has four layers, and each one narrows the audience.

Layer one is the baseline reporting duty. 10 U.S.C. 119, added by Public Law 100-180 section 1132(a)(1) on December 4, 1987, required the Secretary of Defense to submit to the defense committees an annual report on special access programs by March 1 of each year, setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP, a brief description, its major milestones, its actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and its estimated total cost across the current year, the budget year and four succeeding years. Subsection (b) required a separate annual report by February 1 giving notice and justification for each new SAP designation, with the current total program cost estimate and an identification of existing programs or technologies similar in technology or mission to the one being hidden. Subsection (f), added by Public Law 101-510 section 1482(a)(2) in November 1990, added the hard gate: a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

Layer two is the waiver. Subsection (e)(1) provides that the Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security, with each waiver made on a case-by-case basis. Subsection (e)(2) then routes the withheld information and the justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists put the practical result plainly: waived SAPs are exempted by statute (10 USC 119e) from normal congressional notification requirements, and in such cases only eight senior members of the congressional defense committees may be advised of the program.

Layer three is DoD policy, which is more restrictive than the statute. Under the pre-2024 SAP policy framework, only the chair, the ranking minority member and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's oversight role, absent approval by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary. The currently effective directive, DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued September 12, 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, adds a provision that is the operational choke point for whistleblowers: no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval. The people most likely to hold the evidence are contractors, and the directive forbids them from handing it to Congress without permission from the office that runs the SAP system.

Layer four is the quiet erosion of the reporting baseline itself. The U.S. Code note under section 119 records that for termination, effective December 31, 2021, of the provisions in subsections (a) and (b) requiring submittal of an annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notification report, the two instruments the 1987 Congress built, were sunset by a general reporting-requirement cull. And the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 does not define waived SAP anywhere in its glossary. It defines SAP, SAP architecture, SAP umbrella, SAP compartment, SAP sub-compartment, Joint Force Integration SAP and Strategic Enabler SAP. The acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy that appears in DoD's own training material has been replaced in the public directive by a vocabulary that does not distinguish between programs Congress is told about and programs it is not. Whether that is reform or relabeling, the public governing document no longer names the category.

The rest of the directive maps the custody chain. All DoD SAPs are assigned to an oversight authority drawn from USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), USD(I&S) and the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. The Director of DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, holds delegated Top Secret original classification authority for all DoD SAP information, publishes and maintains the security classification guides for every SAP umbrella, accredits congressional SAP facilities, and maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is by exception and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. The senior governing body, the SAP Oversight Committee, is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. Approximately 75 to 80 per cent of all DoD SAPs are acquisition SAPs, which is the category that would cover a materials exploitation or reverse-engineering effort.

Congress has attacked the funding side rather than the classification side. FY2024 NDAA section 1687(b) makes independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material and information is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. That is an admission on the face of the statute that Congress believed UAP work was being charged to the taxpayer through contractor overhead and reported to no one. It is also a route around the waiver, because IR&D allowability is an accounting question, not a classification question.

claims.text: Department of Defense training doctrine defines the category: 'Under extremely limited circumstances, unacknowledged SAPs may also be waived. Waived SAPs are unacknowledged SAPs for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting requirements under Section 119, Title 10 U.S. Code. Waived SAPs have more restrictive reporting requirements and access controls.'
claims.source: Center for Development of Security Excellence (CDSE), Student Guide, Course SA001 'Special Access Program (SAP) Overview,' lesson 'SAP Lifecycle and Structure'; https://www.cdse.edu/Portals/124/Documents/student-guides/SA001-guide.pdf

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) requires that when the waiver authority is exercised, the withheld information and the justification for the waiver be provided 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Committee on Armed Services, the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate, and the same three bodies of the House of Representatives.

Waived SAPs 'are exempted by statute (10 USC 119e) from normal congressional notification requirements. In such cases, only eight senior members of the congressional defense committees may be advised of the program.'
claims.source: Steven Aftergood, 'Spotlight on DoD Special Access Programs,' Federation of American Scientists, February 7, 2013; https://fas.org/publication/dod_saps/

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(f) provides that a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified of the program and a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received; this subsection was added by Public Law 101-510, section 1482(a)(2), November 5, 1990.

Section 119 was enacted by Public Law 100-180, division A, title XI, section 1132(a)(1), December 4, 1987, 101 Stat. 1151, and the first report was required to set out SAP budget requests and appropriations for each of the five preceding fiscal years and to cover all then-existing special access programs.
claims.source: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim (source credit and 'Initial Reports on Special Access Programs' note)

claims.text: The annual reporting requirements in subsections (a) and (b) of 10 U.S.C. 119 were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328.

DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy,' effective September 12, 2024, was approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks; it reissues and cancels the July 1, 2010 directive and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum 'Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform,' July 11, 2023.

The September 12, 2024 DoDD 5205.07 glossary contains no definition of 'waived SAP', 'unacknowledged SAP' or 'acknowledged SAP'; it instead defines a new taxonomy of 'Joint Force Integration SAP' and 'Strategic Enabler SAP', the latter being a SAP protecting capabilities or information that 'warrant more limited and restrictive sharing than Joint Force Integration SAPs.'

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1.g states: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval', and requires all personnel accessed to DoD SAPs to notify the Director, DoD SAPCO when briefing or providing SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff.

The Director of the DoD SAP Central Office reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information, publishes and maintains security classification guides for all DoD SAP umbrellas, accredits congressional SAP facilities, and 'Maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress.'

Approximately 75 to 80 percent of all DoD SAPs are acquisition SAPs, established to protect sensitive research, development, testing and evaluation, modification and procurement activities; SAPs are referred to by both protection level and category, producing combinations such as 'unacknowledged waived operations and support SAPs'.

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue, because the Department has never publicly acknowledged any individual waived SAP; acknowledging one would defeat the category. What is on the record instead is a quieter act: the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoD Directive 5205.07 removed the acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy from the public policy document entirely, while DoD's own unclassified training material continues to teach it. The public governing directive no longer names the category by which programs are lawfully hidden from Congress.

l0.label: DoD Agency-Wide Financial Statement Audit (FY2018-present)

dossier.whatItIs: The Department of Defense's annual department-wide financial statement audit, first performed for fiscal year 2018 and repeated every year since, coordinated by the DoD Office of Inspector General across dozens of component audits. It has never produced a clean opinion. DoD is the only major federal agency that has never received an unmodified audit opinion on its financial statements, and its balance sheet is assembled through summary-level accounting adjustments, journal vouchers, that auditors have repeatedly found to be unsupported by documentation traceable to actual transactions.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the financial-concealment thread and it requires no exotic assumption. If a department cannot demonstrate where more than four trillion dollars in reported assets sits, cannot reconcile its subsidiary systems to its general ledger, and closes the gap each quarter with trillions of dollars in undocumented journal vouchers, then the accounting system itself functions as a laundering mechanism whether or not anyone designed it that way. Money moved into an unacknowledged program does not need a fake line item; it needs only to enter an environment where the difference between the books and reality is routinely papered over at a scale that dwarfs the transaction. The DoD Inspector General documented $6.5 trillion in unsupported year-end adjustments and $2.8 trillion in unsupported third-quarter adjustments to the Army General Fund in a single fiscal year against an Army budget of roughly $120 billion. GAO has found that identified material weaknesses directly affect over half of DoD's reported assets. The audit failure is therefore not merely a governance embarrassment; it is the enabling condition for any funding stream the board alleges. It also functions as an oversight artifact with a deadline: Congress has now set a statutory requirement for a clean opinion by 31 December 2028, which for the first time gives concealment a dated, enforceable test to fail.
dossier.narrative:
Start with the number that made the pattern famous. DoD Inspector General Report No. DODIG-2016-113, 'Army General Fund Adjustments Not Adequately Documented or Supported,' issued 26 July 2016, found that Army and Defense Finance and Accounting Service Indianapolis personnel did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third-quarter adjustments and $6.5 trillion in year-end adjustments made to Army General Fund data during the fiscal year 2015 financial statement compilation. The Army's entire enacted budget that year was on the order of $120 billion. The unsupported year-end adjustments were therefore roughly fifty-four times the money Congress actually authorized the Army to spend.

The mechanism deserves precision, because the scale invites dismissal. A journal voucher is a summary-level accounting entry made when balances between two systems will not reconcile. It is legitimate when it is documented and tied to identifiable transactions. It is what auditors call a plug when it is not. DoD's feeder systems for procurement, logistics, personnel and property were never built to talk to its accounting systems, so at each reporting cycle the difference is closed by hand. The Inspector General's finding was not that the Army stole $6.5 trillion. It was that the Army could not demonstrate what the adjustments represented. From an audit standpoint those are functionally identical: unsupported entries at that magnitude mean the books cannot be used to detect anything, including diversion.

This was not new in 2016. Reuters correspondent Scot J. Paltrow's 2013 investigative series 'Unaccountable: The High Cost of the Pentagon's Bad Bookkeeping,' culminating in a special report published 18 November 2013, documented that fabricating entries to force agreement was standard operating procedure at DFAS offices handling the Army, Navy, Air Force and other defense agencies, and cited a December 2011 Pentagon Inspector General report finding that a single DFAS office in Columbus, Ohio had made at least $1.59 trillion in errors, including $538 billion in plugs, in fiscal year 2009 Air Force financial reports.

The modern audit era begins with fiscal year 2018, the first full-scope department-wide audit. It has failed every year since. For fiscal year 2024, GAO reported that DoD received a disclaimer of opinion for the seventh consecutive year, meaning DoD could not provide auditors sufficient, appropriate evidence to support the information in its financial statements, owing to ineffective systems and processes. DoD reported over $4.1 trillion in assets on its balance sheet as of 30 September 2024. That balance sheet consolidated information from sixty-seven separate DoD components. Eleven components received clean opinions, contributing $1.8 trillion of reported assets, 42.8 percent, and $3.1 trillion of reported liabilities, 72.2 percent. But GAO added the detail that guts the headline: nearly all of the assets attributable to clean-opinion components related to the Military Retirement Fund, a pension trust, while nearly all assets attributable to disclaimer components related to the Army, Navy and Air Force. The parts of DoD that can be audited are the parts that do not buy anything.

The DoD Office of Inspector General identified twenty-eight department-wide material weaknesses for fiscal year 2024. GAO's own analysis found that several of those DoD-wide material weaknesses directly affected $2.1 trillion of DoD's reported assets, 50.3 percent, and $146.9 billion of reported liabilities, 3.4 percent, and cautioned that pervasive material weaknesses may affect all balance sheet data. Congressional Research Service analysis of the FY2024 results adds that entities receiving disclaimers accounted for 44 percent of DoD's total assets and at least 68 percent of its total budgetary resources, and that DoD extended the target date for correcting its department-wide financial management systems modernization material weakness from FY2028 to FY2031, a slippage past the statutory audit deadline itself.

That deadline is the newest and most useful fact for the board. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 requires DoD to receive an unmodified audit opinion by 31 December 2028; CRS identifies the provision as Section 1005. GAO states the requirement flatly in GAO-25-108052. The department has therefore been given a legal obligation to become legible on a specific date, while simultaneously moving its own systems-modernization fix three years past that date.

The fiscal year 2025 cycle continued the pattern. The DoD Office of Inspector General issued Report No. DODIG-2026-032, 'Independent Auditor's Reports on the DoD FY 2025 Financial Statements,' comprising three separate audit reports addressing the financial statements, internal control over financial reporting, and compliance with laws and regulations. DoD received a disclaimer of opinion for the eighth consecutive time, on reported assets of approximately $4.65 trillion and reported liabilities of approximately $4.73 trillion, with results released 18 December 2025. After the seventh failure, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform publicly sought GAO engagement on waste, fraud and abuse at DoD.

What this means for the legacy-program argument is narrow and strong. It does not prove that money was diverted. It proves that DoD's accounting environment cannot rule out diversion at any scale below the noise floor, and that the noise floor is measured in trillions. Every other funding hypothesis on the board, whether contractor-held Independent Research and Development recovery, unacknowledged Special Access Programs, waived SAPs briefed only to a handful of members, or overhead absorption on classified contracts, sits downstream of one structural fact: the Department of Defense's books do not close, have never closed, and the entries that make them appear to close are, by the Inspector General's own finding, undocumented. Set beside STAR GATE, which consumed roughly $20 million across two decades, the scale mismatch is the whole argument. A real, funded, denied program of that size would not register as a rounding error in a single quarterly journal voucher.

dossier.denialPosture: DoD does not deny the audit failures; it reframes them as a modernization timeline. The department's public posture is that disclaimers reflect systems and process immaturity rather than any inability to account for money, and that a clean opinion is achievable by the statutory 2028 deadline, while it simultaneously slipped its own financial-systems modernization remediation target from FY2028 to FY2031.
connections: Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) Indianapolis and DFAS Columbus are the named operational sites where unsupported adjustments are made; they are the specific offices any funding-trace inquiry has to reach.

The Army General Fund carries the documented $6.5 trillion unsupported year-end adjustment, and the Army is also the service that executed CRADA 19-15 with To The Stars Academy (ttsa-army-crada) - the same service is simultaneously the least auditable and a documented technology-transfer counterparty on anomalous material.
GAO Director Asif A. Khan, Financial Management and Assurance, is the named GAO contact on GAO-25-108052 and the obvious entry point for questions about which components are unauditable and why.

Section 1005 of the FY2024 NDAA and Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA are the two statutory levers Congress has actually pulled: one forces financial legibility by 2028, the other forced creation of AARO in 2022. They are the paired oversight instruments.

STAR GATE (stargate-program) cost roughly $20 million across two decades, an amount that would vanish entirely inside a single quarterly journal-voucher adjustment, illustrating the scale mismatch between a real black program and the audit noise floor.

The Military Retirement Fund is the anomaly worth exploiting analytically: it is the one enormous DoD balance that is auditable, establishing that auditability is achievable when an account has no operational spending attached.
Congressional Research Service product IF12627 is the standing annual summary of audit results and the cheapest way to track the disclaimer streak year over year.

l0.label: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
l0.short: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004

dossier.whatItIs: On 14 November 2004, during pre-deployment workups off southern California, the USS Princeton (CG-59) vectored two F/A-18F Super Hornets from VFA-41 aboard USS Nimitz (CVN-68) onto a radar contact. Four aircrew, including squadron commanding officer Cdr. David Fravor, visually observed a white, wingless, roughly forty-foot object above a patch of disturbed water. A later sortie captured the infrared video now known as FLIR1, which the Department of Defense formally released as an authentic unclassified Navy video on 27 April 2020.
dossier.whyImplicated: Nimitz is the modern case that cannot be argued away on witness quality, because the observation was multi-platform: an Aegis SPY-1 radar track held over weeks, four aircrew in two aircraft, and an ATFLIR recording. What happened to that data afterwards is the point. Fravor testified under oath in July 2023 that "the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken," and that no one from the government contacted him about it until Jay Stratton did so in 2009 on behalf of a Defense Department programme he had never heard of. Enlisted personnel from the Princeton and the Nimitz have separately said that unidentified individuals arrived by helicopter within a day and collected Aegis and aircraft data recordings; that account is testimonial and undocumented. Either way, the United States possessed the highest-quality sensor capture of an unexplained object in its history and produced no investigation, no incident report and no data package - until a compartmented programme quietly reached out five years later. That gap between the sensor and the file is the same architecture Bolender described in 1969.
dossier.narrative:
The Nimitz encounter is the case that made the modern era possible, and the reason it belongs on a map of the legacy programme is not the object. It is the handling.

Fravor's sworn statement to the House Oversight Committee, filed for the hearing of 26 July 2023, is the cleanest primary account and it is worth reading for the operational detail rather than the spectacle. He was commanding officer of Strike Fighter Squadron 41 attached to Carrier Air Wing Eleven, roughly two weeks into an at-sea period, briefed to lead a two-versus-two air combat training exercise controlled by Princeton. On launch, "we were told that training was going to be suspended for real world tasking." His flight was vectored west of the combat air patrol point. Critically, he records what the controller told him about the preceding fortnight: the Princeton "had been observing these objects on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks. They had been descending from above 80,000ft and coming rapidly down to 20,000ft would stay for hours and then go straight back up." This is not a single sighting. It is a two-week radar campaign by a cruiser's air defence system that generated no public record and no known written report.

At the merge the aircrew saw disturbed white water, then a small white object with its longitudinal axis pointed north-south, moving abruptly above it, with "no Rotors, No Rotor wash, or any visible flight control surfaces like wings." Fravor descended in a clockwise turn; the object shifted its axis to align with his aircraft and began a climbing turn in the same direction. At roughly half a mile it "rapidly accelerated and disappeared right in front of our aircraft," and the disturbed water was gone with it. The flight turned back toward the CAP point sixty miles east and the controller reported that the object had reappeared there on the Princeton's SPY-1 radar, having covered that distance in "less than a minute."

Back aboard Nimitz they mentioned it to the crew preparing to launch. That crew took the roughly ninety-second infrared video that would be released by the government in 2017. Fravor adds a detail about a second recording that has never surfaced: "What is not seen is the Radar tape that showed the jamming of the APG-73 radar in the aircraft." An electronic attack on a fighter's fire control radar off the coast of California is, by any ordinary standard, a reportable event.

And then, on his account, nothing. "What is shocking is that the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken, and after a couple of days, it turned into a great story to tell friends. Not until 2009 did Jay Stratton contact me to investigate what we observed. Unbeknownst to all of us, Jay was part of the ATIP . . . program led by Lue Elizondo out of the DOD." That single paragraph is the whole argument in miniature. The Navy's normal machinery - safety reporting, intelligence debrief, mishap investigation - did not engage. Five years later a compartmented Defense Department effort did, without announcing itself, and the resulting document circulated for years as what Fravor calls "the Unofficial Official Report." Fravor also notes that Lt. Cdr. Alex Dietrich, the other pilot in the flight, had been invited to the Pentagon multiple times to discuss the event and view other UAP videos while he had heard from no one at all - which means the government knew where the aircrew were and chose which of them to talk to.

Against that, there is a competing testimonial strand that must be tiered honestly. Petty Officer Gary Voorhis, aviation technician Patrick "PJ" Hughes and Senior Chief Kevin Day have described, in interviews and documentaries from roughly 2019 onward, unidentified individuals arriving by helicopter within about a day and taking Aegis data recordings, combat engagement centre recorders, optical drives holding radio communications and E-2 Hawkeye data bricks, with Voorhis instructed to erase even blank tapes. No document has ever been produced for this and no official Navy statement has addressed it. It is also not in tension with Fravor as often assumed: Fravor speaks for his aircrew and his squadron's tapes, the enlisted witnesses speak about the cruiser and the carrier's data systems. Both can be true. Neither is documented.

What is documented is the government's slow, deliberate concession of the artifact. On 27 April 2020 the Department of Defense issued a formal statement authorising release of three unclassified Navy videos, "one taken in November 2004 and the other two in January 2015, which have been circulating in the public domain after unauthorized releases in 2007 and 2017." It confirmed that "the U.S. Navy previously acknowledged that these videos circulating in the public domain were indeed Navy videos," stated that release "does not reveal any sensitive capabilities or systems, and does not impinge on any subsequent investigations of military air space incursions by unidentified aerial phenomena," and closed with the line that matters: "The aerial phenomena observed in the videos remain characterized as 'unidentified.'" Two things are conceded in that paragraph. The video is real, and there are subsequent investigations of airspace incursions by unidentified phenomena that a release could in principle impinge upon.

Fravor's closing testimony frames the oversight question the way this board frames it. He is explicit that the issue "is not about full public disclosure that could undermine national security" but about checks and balances, and he makes the structural point directly: "even Unacknowledged Waived programs have some level of oversight by the appropriate committee members in the House and Senate and this work that is said to be occurring from Whistleblower testimonies should not be exempt." That is a retired commander with a Top Gun background telling Congress, under oath, that he believes there is an activity operating outside the waived-programme oversight floor. Nimitz is on this map because it is the point where the sensor data, the missing file and the oversight gap all converge in one afternoon off San Diego.

claims.text: In sworn written testimony to the House Oversight Committee for the 26 July 2023 hearing, Cdr. David Fravor (USN, ret.) states that on launch his flight was told "that training was going to be suspended for real world tasking."

Fravor's statement records that the USS Princeton "had been observing these objects on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks. They had been descending from above 80,000ft and coming rapidly down to 20,000ft would stay for hours and then go straight back up."

Fravor describes an object with "no Rotors, No Rotor wash, or any visible flight control surfaces like wings" that aligned its longitudinal axis with his aircraft, then "rapidly accelerated and disappeared right in front of our aircraft" at approximately half a mile.
Fravor states the object reappeared on the Princeton's SPY-1 radar at the flight's CAP point roughly 60 miles east, having covered that distance "in a very short period of time (less than a minute)."
Fravor states that a second recording exists and has never been shown: "What is not seen is the Radar tape that showed the jamming of the APG-73 radar in the aircraft."

Fravor states: "What is shocking is that the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken, and after a couple of days, it turned into a great story to tell friends."

Fravor states that the first government approach came in 2009 from Jay Stratton, who "was part of the ATIP . . . program led by Lue Elizondo out of the DOD," and that the resulting document circulated as what he calls "the Unofficial Official Report."

Fravor states that Lt. Cdr. Alex Dietrich, the other pilot in the flight, "had been invited to the Pentagon multiple times to discuss the event and view other videos of UAPs" while he himself had not been contacted after 2009.

Fravor's closing testimony asserts an oversight gap: "even Unacknowledged Waived programs have some level of oversight by the appropriate committee members in the House and Senate and this work that is said to be occurring from Whistleblower testimonies should not be exempt."

The Department of Defense stated on 27 April 2020 that it authorised release of three unclassified Navy videos, one taken in November 2004, and that "the aerial phenomena observed in the videos remain characterized as 'unidentified.'"

The same DoD statement records that "the U.S. Navy previously acknowledged that these videos circulating in the public domain were indeed Navy videos," that they had circulated "after unauthorized releases in 2007 and 2017," and that the released files were posted to the Naval Air Systems Command FOIA reading room.

The same statement concedes the existence of an ongoing investigative effort, saying release "does not impinge on any subsequent investigations of military air space incursions by unidentified aerial phenomena."

Fravor testified under oath alongside Ryan Graves and David Grusch before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs on 26 July 2023 in the hearing "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency."
claims.source: House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, hearing transcript HHRG-118-GO06-Transcript-20230726, 26 July 2023, https://www.congress.gov/118/meeting/house/116282/documents/HHRG-118-GO06-Transcript-20230726.pdf

claims.text: Former crew members including Gary Voorhis, Patrick "PJ" Hughes and Kevin Day have stated in interviews since 2019 that unidentified individuals arrived by helicopter shortly after the encounter and collected Aegis data recordings, combat engagement centre recorders and E-2 aircraft data drives. No document supports this and no Navy statement addresses it; the compiled case file that reports these accounts states expressly that the point "remains anecdotal and is not confirmed by documentation."
The FLIR1 video was recorded on a later sortie the same day by a weapons systems officer, Lt. Cdr. Chad Underwood, using an ATFLIR pod; Underwood did not see the object visually.

dossier.denialPosture: There is effectively no denial to catalogue, and that is itself the finding. The Navy acknowledged the videos' authenticity in 2019 and the Department of Defense formally released them on 27 April 2020 while stating that the phenomena "remain characterized as 'unidentified.'" No component has denied the Princeton's Aegis tracks, denied the encounter, or produced a resolution. The only official position that has ever been asserted about Nimitz is that the imagery is real and the object is unexplained.
openQuestions: Do the USS Princeton's Aegis SPY-1 recordings and combat information centre logs for 10-16 November 2004 still exist, and under what disposition authority were they retained or destroyed?
Does the APG-73 radar tape Fravor describes, showing jamming of his aircraft's fire control radar, exist in any Navy holding?

Was any contemporaneous 2004 report of any kind generated - safety, intelligence, mishap or operational - and if not, under what authority was reporting waived for a two-week Aegis track and a fighter radar jamming event?
What is the provenance, classification history and custodian of the document Fravor calls the "Unofficial Official Report," prepared following Jay Stratton's 2009 contact?
Who directed the collection of data recordings from Princeton and Nimitz, if it occurred, and under what authority? No FOIA release has yet produced tasking, travel or custody documentation.
Why was Lt. Cdr. Dietrich brought to the Pentagon repeatedly while the flight lead was not contacted at all, and which office issued those invitations?

l0.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)

dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023 was submitted by Senator Charles Schumer on 13 July 2023 as Senate Amendment 797 to S. 2226, the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, and printed in full in the Congressional Record at pages S2953-S2959. It travelled into the Senate-engrossed NDAA as a freestanding division of fifteen sections. Its enforcement machinery - an independent nine-member Records Review Board, a federal exercise of eminent domain over privately held recovered materials, and a $20,000,000 authorisation - was removed before enactment, leaving only an archiving and postponement regime at sections 1841-1843 of Public Law 118-31.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only text ever adopted by a chamber of the United States Congress that legislates on the express premise that recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence exist and are held in part by private entities. Its definitions are not rhetorical: 'controlling authority' is defined to include any commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of such material, and 'legacy program' is defined to reach commercial, academic and private-sector reverse-engineering endeavours predating enactment. Six senators including the Majority Leader and the Vice Chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee put their names to a finding that records exist which have been shielded from mandatory declassification review by Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an over-broad reading of transclassified foreign nuclear information. The bill then directs the Federal Government to seize that material by eminent domain and hand it to a board explicitly barred from containing anyone who has ever worked on a legacy program. The provisions that would have moved custody, compelled testimony and paid for the effort are precisely the provisions that did not survive conference - which is the single most informative fact on this node.
dossier.narrative:
On 13 July 2023 the Senate Majority Leader rose and submitted an amendment to the defence bill. The Congressional Record entry is flat and procedural - 'SA 797. Mr. SCHUMER (for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich) submitted an amendment intended to be proposed by him to the bill S. 2226 ... which was ordered to lie on the table' - and what follows across seven pages of the Record is the most consequential UAP text in American law.

The structure is deliberately modelled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992: a records collection at the National Archives, a presumption of immediate disclosure, an independent review board with the power to override agency postponement, and a sunset. The differences are where the argument lives. The JFK Act dealt only with paper. This bill deals with objects.

The findings section states the premise. Congress finds that 'Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526 ... due in part to exemptions under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 ..., as well as an over-broad interpretation of "transclassified foreign nuclear information", which is also exempt from mandatory declassification, thereby preventing public disclosure under existing provisions of law.' That is a named legal mechanism of concealment, identified by the Senate, and it points at the Department of Energy and the Restricted Data regime rather than at the Department of Defense alone. The next finding says the Freedom of Information Act 'has proven inadequate.'

The definitions do the load-bearing work. 'Controlling authority' means 'any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.' A commercial company cannot be in physical possession of a thing that does not exist. 'Legacy program' is defined to include 'commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.' 'Non-human intelligence' means 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.'

The Review Board provisions establish 'as an independent agency a board to be known as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board"', appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, nine citizens, without regard to political affiliation. Board staff must be citizens 'of integrity and impartiality who ha[ve] had no previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence.' A statute does not write a conflict-of-interest bar against a category of person that Congress believes to be empty.

Then the section that made the bill unpassable. 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' Such material 'shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material.' The Board would then decide whether the material constitutes technologies of unknown origin 'beyond a reasonable doubt', whether it qualifies for postponement, and 'what changes, if any, to the current disposition of said material should the Federal Government make to facilitate full disclosure.' The Board would also 'have access to all testimony from unidentified anomalous phenomena witnesses, close observers and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers within the Federal Government's possession.'

The money section authorised $20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024 and, pending appropriation, permitted the President to use 'such sums as are available for discretionary use.'

What was enacted on 22 December 2023 in Public Law 118-31 is three sections - 1841, 1842 and 1843 - creating the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives, requiring agencies to review, identify, transmit and disclose UAP records, and setting out grounds for postponement. There is no Review Board. There is no eminent domain. There is no authorisation of appropriations. There is no witness-solicitation mandate. The surviving regime asks the original classification authorities that hold the records to identify their own records and to invoke their own postponement grounds, and gives no independent body the power to say no.

That is the argument. The Senate wrote a bill whose operative theory was that the material is held by controlling authorities including private companies, that those companies will not surrender it voluntarily, and that only compulsory acquisition plus an outside board with special access clearances could break the hold. Conference removed compulsion and removed the outside board. What remains is a filing cabinet with the same locks and the same keyholders.

claims.text: S.Amdt. 797 was submitted on 13 July 2023 by Sen. Schumer 'for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich' to S. 2226, and was ordered to lie on the table; the full text is printed at Congressional Record, Vol. 169, No. 120, pages S2953-S2959.

Congressional finding (a)(4): 'Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526 ... due in part to exemptions under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.), as well as an over-broad interpretation of "transclassified foreign nuclear information", which is also exempt from mandatory declassification, thereby preventing public disclosure under existing provisions of law.'

The definitions section defines 'controlling authority' as 'any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.'

'Legacy program' is defined to include 'commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.'

'Non-human intelligence' is defined as 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.'

The Review Board section states: '(a) ESTABLISHMENT.-There is established as an independent agency a board to be known as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board"' and '(1) IN GENERAL.-The President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall appoint, without regard to political affiliation, 9 citizens of the United States to serve as members of the Review Board.'

The Review Board staffing section requires that a person appointed to the staff 'shall be a citizen of integrity and impartiality who has had no previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence', and requires accelerated grant of 'all necessary special access program clearances'.

The eminent domain provision reads in full: '(a) EXERCISE OF EMINENT DOMAIN.-The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.'

The same section provides that '(b) AVAILABILITY TO REVIEW BOARD.-Any and all such material, should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material', and that the Board shall decide 'whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt'.

The Board was to 'have access to all testimony from unidentified anomalous phenomena witnesses, close observers and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers within the Federal Government's possession as of and after the date of the enactment of this Act'. The phrase 'legacy program personnel' is statutory text.

The authorisation section provides '$20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024' and adds that 'Until such time as funds are appropriated pursuant to subsection (a), the President may use such sums as are available for discretionary use to carry out this title.'

The National Archives states that it 'has established an "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection," per sections 1841-1843 of the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act (Public Law 118-31)', and that records received from federal agencies under that Act are accessioned into Record Group 615.

The disclosure machinery enacted in Public Law 118-31 consists only of the NARA records collection at sections 1841-1843; the Review Board, the eminent domain provision, the Review Board witness-access provision and the $20,000,000 authorisation have no enacted counterpart.

dossier.denialPosture: No executive branch office has ever publicly explained why the Review Board and eminent domain sections were removed in conference, and no conference report language identifying an objecting party has been made public. The Department of Defense has never responded on the record to the bill's finding that Atomic Energy Act exemptions and transclassified foreign nuclear information are being used to keep UAP records out of mandatory declassification review.
openQuestions: Which members or agencies asked for the Review Board and eminent domain sections to be struck in the FY2024 NDAA conference, and in what written form was the request made?
Did any executive branch agency submit a Statement of Administration Policy or legislative-referral objection to Division G, and is it retrievable?
Has any agency ever identified a specific record withheld under the 'transclassified foreign nuclear information' exemption that would otherwise be a UAP record?

The Senate text presupposes controlling authorities in physical possession; no controlling authority has ever been named in any public congressional document. Which entities did the drafters have in mind?

Section numbering differs between the Congressional Record print of SA 797 (SEC. __01 through __15) and the engrossed division; the engrossed section numbers used elsewhere on this board should be re-verified against BILLS-118s2226es directly.

The negative claim that no Review Board or eminent domain text survives in Public Law 118-31 was established here by comparison against NARA's description of the enacted sections rather than by a direct full-text search of the enrolled bill, which should be run to close the point.

l0.label: S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 (Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act amendment)

dossier.whatItIs: S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 was the Schumer-Rounds "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023," submitted in July 2023 and folded into the Senate-passed FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act on July 27, 2023 as Division G, sections 9001 through 9015. Modeled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992, it would have created a nine-member, Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena-adjacent powers, a government-wide records collection at the National Archives, a controlled disclosure process, and a mandate that the federal government exercise eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private parties.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only time the United States Senate has passed statutory text asserting, as a matter of legislative fact, that private entities may be holding recovered non-human technology and biological material and that the government should take it. The bill defines "legacy program," "non-human intelligence," "technologies of unknown origin" and "controlling authority" in statutory language, and its Review Board qualification clause bars anyone with "any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin" — a conflict-of-interest screen that presupposes the existence of the thing being screened against. Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, several of them sitting members of the Intelligence and Armed Services Committees, wrote that clause. The Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security then submitted a thirty-three page line-by-line rewrite to conferees in November 2023 stating that the Department "strongly urges consideration" of its revisions, and the Department's core objectives prevailed. The gap between what the Senate passed and what the President signed is the single cleanest measurement of institutional resistance available on this board.
dossier.narrative:
The UAP Disclosure Act was unveiled on 14 July 2023 with Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer as prime sponsor and Senator Mike Rounds as lead co-sponsor, with Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich joining. It was added to the FY2024 NDAA in an agreed bloc of amendments without floor debate or a separate vote, and the Senate passed the NDAA including it on 27 July 2023.

The findings section is short and remarkably direct. Congress would have declared that all federal records concerning UAP "should carry a presumption of immediate disclosure"; that "Legislation is necessary to create an enforceable, independent, and accountable process for the public disclosure of such records"; and that "Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526."

The definitions are where the bill does its most consequential work, because definitions survive in the mind even when the operative provisions die. "Legacy program" is defined as "all Federal, State, and local government, commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act." "Non-human intelligence" is "any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware." "Technologies of unknown origin" is a lawyer's inventory: "any materials or meta-materials, ejecta, crash debris, mechanisms, machinery, equipment, assemblies or sub-assemblies, engineering models or processes, damaged or intact aerospace vehicles, and damaged or intact ocean-surface and undersea craft associated with unidentified anomalous phenomena or incorporating science and technology that lacks prosaic attribution or known means of human manufacture." And "controlling authority" reaches "any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence." Whoever drafted that list was not speculating about the abstract; they were describing categories of custody.

The Review Board would have been nine citizens appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, nominated within ninety days after considering persons recommended by the four congressional leaders, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, the American Historical Association, and — a genuinely unusual inclusion in a statute — "the UAP Disclosure Foundation." Nominees had to include at least one current or former national security official, one current or former foreign service official, one scientist or engineer, one economist, one professional historian and one sociologist. They would have been "granted the necessary security clearances and accesses, including any and all relevant Presidential, departmental, and agency special access programs, in an accelerated manner." Confirmation ran through Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on compressed clocks: hearings within thirty days, committee vote within fourteen, floor vote within fourteen.

The eminent domain provision, section 9010(a), read: "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good." Subsection (b) required that any such material "should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination." Subsection (c) tasked the Board with deciding "whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt." Subsection (d) gave the Board access to all testimony from UAP witnesses, close observers, "and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers" in the government's possession, and subsection (e) directed it to solicit more, extending the whistleblower protections of section 1673(b) of the FY2023 NDAA, 50 U.S.C. 3373b(b).

Other operative provisions: government offices had 300 days to review, identify and organize their UAP records; the Board was to be treated as an agency of the United States for purposes of 18 U.S.C. 6001, the witness immunity statute; the Board would report to congressional leadership, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and House Oversight; and $20,000,000 was authorized for fiscal year 2024, with the President permitted to use available discretionary sums in the interim.

Then the Pentagon wrote back. In November 2023, during end-stage conference negotiations, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security transmitted to congressional negotiators a thirty-three page line-by-line rewrite of the Senate-passed text, presented as the Department's "informal views" but stating that the Department "strongly urges consideration" of the changes and that the position was arrived at "after conferring with NARA/ISOO." The document was first published by Douglas Dean Johnson in July 2024. Its treatment of section 9010 is the tell: OUSD(I&S) proposed replacing the mandatory "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over" with "It is the sense of Congress that the Federal Government should exercise eminent domain appropriately over" — while leaving the object of the sentence, "any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities," untouched. Asked why, former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick replied that "a compromise was proposed to allow for the exercising of eminent domain under AARO's authority to underscore that AARO could compel disclosure of anything, should anything exist. Since we know nothing exists, we didn't feel it made our job harder."

Kirkpatrick was blunter elsewhere. On 17 July 2024 he told interviewer Marik von Rennenkampff, "We convinced Congress last year not to go down that road." The Review Board, its staff, the eminent domain authority and the controlled disclosure process were all deleted in conference. Schumer, on the Senate floor on 13 December 2023, called it "really an outrage."

The bill's findings state that all federal UAP records "should carry a presumption of immediate disclosure"; that "Legislation is necessary to create an enforceable, independent, and accountable process for the public disclosure of such records"; and that "Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526."

The bill defines "controlling authority" to include "any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence."

The Review Board would have consisted of 9 U.S. citizens appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, without regard to political affiliation, nominated not later than 90 days after enactment, and all nominees "shall be granted the necessary security clearances and accesses, including any and all relevant Presidential, departmental, and agency special access programs, in an accelerated manner subject to the standard procedures for granting such clearances."

Review Board nominees "shall be impartial citizens, none of whom shall have had any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence."

Section __10(a) provided: "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good."

Section __10(c)(1) tasked the Review Board with deciding "whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt," and __10(d) gave the Board access to all testimony from UAP witnesses, close observers, "and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers" in the government's possession.

Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick said in a July 17, 2024 interview, regarding the 2023 UAPDA: "We convinced Congress last year not to go down that road," and by email on July 23, 2024 explained the retained eminent domain language: "a compromise was proposed to allow for the exercising of eminent domain under AARO's authority to underscore that AARO could compel disclosure of anything, should anything exist. Since we know nothing exists, we didn't feel it made our job harder."

dossier.denialPosture: The Department of Defense never denied the bill's premises in public. It filed a redline. The 'informal views' rewrite objected to structure, duplication with AARO's existing historical-report mandate, and burden on industry — Kirkpatrick's stated reasoning was that the Review Board would duplicate AARO and that 'we found no evidence of any of these allegations. None.' The Department nonetheless declined to strike the eminent domain object, which is the more interesting fact.
connections: Sponsors Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich — Rounds sits on both Senate Armed Services and Senate Intelligence; Rubio was SSCI vice chairman.
Modeled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992 and its Assassination Records Review Board.

OUSD(I&S) under Ronald Moultrie (who resigned effective February 29, 2024) was the office that transmitted the rewrite; AARO was administratively attached to OUSD(I&S) while its director reported to the Deputy Secretary of Defense on operational and security matters.
Sean Kirkpatrick, AARO director from mid-2022 to December 1, 2023, is the named actor claiming credit for defeating the bill.
The surviving remnant is P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843; the deleted provisions are catalogued in the Joint Explanatory Statement to H. Rept. 118-301 at page 1330.

The 'controlling authority' definition reaching commercial companies and academic institutions is the statutory hook that would have touched defense contractors directly — the point at which the bill stopped being about records and started being about property.

Refiled substantially intact as S.Amdt. 2610 to S. 4638 (FY2025 NDAA) on July 11, 2024, this time with Rounds as lead sponsor and Schumer as co-sponsor, printed at Cong. Rec. S4943-S4950; Gillibrand joined July 23 and Heinrich August 1, 2024.
openQuestions: Whether the text as filed in S.Amdt. 797 differs in any material respect from the text released by the Majority Leader's office in July 2023; congress.gov is the authoritative version and section numbering in the released draft is left blank.
Who drafted the definitions of 'legacy program,' 'controlling authority' and 'technologies of unknown origin,' and on what factual briefing those categories were built.
What 'the UAP Disclosure Foundation' is, why a private entity was written into a statutory nomination process, and who proposed it.

Which conferees specifically insisted on removing the Review Board and eminent domain provisions; Douglas Johnson attributes the outcome to a small group of senior Republican members but names none in the public record.
Whether the Senate ever received a classified justification from DoD for opposing the bill, distinct from the unclassified 'informal views' redline.
Whether NARA and ISOO, whom OUSD(I&S) said it consulted, supported the rewrite or merely commented on records-management feasibility.
