dossier.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, H.R. 2670, became Public Law 118-31 on December 22, 2023. It contains four UAP-related provisions: section 1687 (funding cutoff for unreported UAP special access programs), sections 1841-1843 (the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives), section 7341 (a reporting-channel adjustment) and section 7343 (the parallel Intelligence Authorization funding cutoff). It is what survived of the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act after House-Senate conference.
dossier.whyImplicated: The enacted law is simultaneously the strongest and the weakest document on this board. Strongest, because the Joint Explanatory Statement of the House-Senate conference committee states in the official legislative history that the section 1687 funding prohibition "could cover" activities including "Analyzing such craft, or pieces or components thereof," "Actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology or performance," propulsion "based on or derived from or inspired by inspection, analysis, or reverse engineering of recovered unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or materials," and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Conferees do not write six itemized categories of a thing that does not exist. Weakest, because everything with teeth was removed: the same JES records that "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process," and section 1843 hands the postponement decision back to "the original classification authority" — the same officials the Senate bill was designed to review. The difference between the Senate text and the enacted text is the measurable output of the concealment effort in a single legislative cycle.
dossier.narrative:
The FY2024 NDAA is a 973-page enrolled bill authorizing $886 billion. The Senate approved the conference version 87-13 on 13 December 2023, the House 310-118 the next day, and the President signed it on 22 December.

Section 1687, "Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs," is the money clause. Subsection (a): "None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024." Subsection (b) closes the contractor channel: citing DoD Instruction 3204.01, it provides that independent research and development funding relating to UAP "shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership." The missing preposition is in the enacted text. Subsection (c) defines the appropriate committees as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and congressional leadership as the four leaders.

That IR&D subsection is the sleeper. It is a legislative acknowledgment that UAP-related work might sit inside contractor overhead accounts rather than a government program element — funded by the government as an allowable indirect cost without ever appearing as a DoD program. Congress does not write a prohibition against a billing practice nobody uses.

The Joint Explanatory Statement explains what the conferees did to the Senate provision (formerly section 1646): they removed the direction to provide information to AARO, and summarized the prohibition. Then they wrote six numbered categories of activity the prohibition "could cover": recruiting, employing, equipping and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a mission of "capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft"; analyzing such craft or components "including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering of such craft or component technology"; protecting UAP activities and information "from disclosure or compromise"; actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating UAP technology or performance; development of propulsion technology or aerospace craft "based on or derived from or inspired by" reverse engineering of recovered UAP craft or materials; and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." That sixth category is a definition by exclusion of every propulsion method the conferees could not name.

Section 7343 does the same on the Intelligence Authorization side, substituting the DNI for the Secretary of Defense and adding the Appropriations Committees. Its IR&D subsection contains a dangling cross-reference — "contracts covered by such instruction," with no instruction identified anywhere in the section. The intelligence committee chairmen entered an Explanatory Statement in the Congressional Record on 14 December 2023 saying section 7343 was intended "to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist."

Sections 1841-1843 are the records regime. Section 1841 directs the Archivist, within 60 days of enactment, to commence establishing the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection," consisting of "record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)." Those three terms appear in enacted United States statute with no definitions attached, because the definitions lived in the Senate bill and were dropped. Congress legislated about non-human intelligence and then declined to say what it meant.

Section 1842 sets the mechanics. Each head of a government office had 300 days to review, identify and organize its UAP records; NARA fixed the operative date at 20 October 2024. No UAP record may be destroyed, altered or mutilated, and no record already publicly disclosed may be withheld, redacted, postponed or reclassified. Agencies must give precedence to records "that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence," to records under active FOIA litigation, and to records "with earliest provenance." Subsection (g)(2)(D) is the 25-year rule: each record must be disclosed in full not later than 25 years after creation unless the President certifies continued postponement is necessary because of "an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations" of "such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure."

Section 1843 is where the Senate's design was inverted. Postponement is decided not by an independent board but by "the original classification authority," on "clear and convincing evidence" of one of four enumerated harms.

The JES at page 1330 states the outcome without euphemism: "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process."

On 13 December 2023 Schumer told the Senate: "It is really an outrage that the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board... Now it means that declassification of UAP records will be largely up to the same entities that blocked and obfuscated their disclosure for decades." He added that multiple credible sources had notified them that UAP information was being withheld from Congress, "which, if true, is a violation of the laws requiring full notification to the legislative branch." Nine days later the President signed the bill and issued a signing statement listing section 1687 among provisions requiring submission of "highly sensitive classified information" to Congress.

claims.text: Section 1687(a) of P.L. 118-31 provides: "None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024."
claims.source: Pub. L. 118-31, sec. 1687(a) (Dec. 22, 2023), text at H. Rept. 118-301 pp. 489-490, https://douglasjohnson.ghost.io/content/files/2023/12/UAP-pages-only--final--from-NDAA--HR-2670--and-Joint-Explanatory-Statement-12-6-23.pdf

claims.text: Section 1687(b) provides that, consistent with DoD Instruction 3204.01 (August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2 dated July 9, 2020), "independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership."

Section 1687(c) defines "appropriate congressional committees" as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and "congressional leadership" as the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House.

The Joint Explanatory Statement to H. Rept. 118-301 records that the conferees amended the Senate provision (sec. 1646) to "Remove the direction to provide information to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office" before enactment.
claims.source: H. Rept. 118-301, Joint Explanatory Statement, pp. 1311-1312

claims.text: The Joint Explanatory Statement lists six categories the section 1687 prohibition "could cover," including "Recruiting, employing, training, equipping, and operations of, and providing security for, Government or contractor personnel with a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft"; "Analyzing such craft, or pieces or components thereof, including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering of such craft or component technology"; "Actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology or performance"; and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust."
claims.source: H. Rept. 118-301, Joint Explanatory Statement, pp. 1311-1312

claims.text: Section 1841(a)(1)(C) provides that the Collection "shall consist of record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)."

The enacted subtitle contains no definitions of "technologies of unknown origin," "non-human intelligence," "temporarily non-attributed objects," "record" or "Collection" — the definitions existed in sections 9001-9015 of the Senate amendment and were dropped in conference, leaving the terms undefined in United States statute.
claims.source: Pub. L. 118-31, subtitle C of title XVIII; H. Rept. 118-301 pp. 568-575 (no DEFINITIONS section appears in secs. 1841-1843)

claims.text: Section 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office to review, identify and organize each UAP record in its custody within 300 days of enactment; NARA implemented this as a deadline of October 20, 2024, and stated it would accept only digital versions.

Section 1842(g)(2)(D) requires each UAP record to be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation "unless the President certifies that (i) continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations; and (ii) the identifiable harm is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure."

Section 1843(a) vests the postponement determination in "the original classification authority" on a finding of "clear and convincing evidence" of one of four enumerated harms — restoring the decision to the classifying agency rather than the independent board the Senate had proposed; section 1843(b) permits Senior Agency Officials to withdraw records from the Collection determined to be both unrelated to UAP and properly classified on 60 days' advance notice to congressional leadership and the oversight committees, and section 1843(c) requires notice of any postponement within 15 days.

The Joint Explanatory Statement states: "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process."
claims.source: H. Rept. 118-301, Joint Explanatory Statement, p. 1330

claims.text: Section 7343 imposes a parallel funding cutoff on Intelligence Authorization funds, substituting the Director of National Intelligence for the Secretary of Defense and adding the Appropriations Committees to the notification list; its subsection (c) contains a dangling reference to "contracts covered by such instruction" with no instruction identified anywhere in that section.

The chairmen of the House and Senate intelligence committees entered an Explanatory Statement in the Congressional Record of December 14, 2023 stating that section 7343 "is also intended to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist."

In a colloquy with Senator Rounds on the Senate floor on December 13, 2023, Senator Schumer said: "It is really an outrage that the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board, which, by definition, needs bipartisan consent. Now it means that declassification of UAP records will be largely up to the same entities that blocked and obfuscated their disclosure for decades," and in the same colloquy: "We have also been notified by multiple credible sources that information on UAPs has also been withheld from Congress, which, if true, is a violation of the laws requiring full notification to the legislative branch, especially as it relates to the four congressional leaders, Defense Committees, and the Intelligence Committee."
claims.source: Cong. Rec., Dec. 13, 2023, pp. S5930-S5931; reproduced at https://douglasjohnson.ghost.io/uap-disclosure-act-pentagon-rewrite-nov-2023/

dossier.denialPosture: The Presidential signing statement of December 22, 2023 is the operative denial artifact: it identified section 1687 as one of several provisions compelling delivery of highly sensitive classified information to Congress and reserved to the Executive a construction of those provisions consistent with its own view of national security — a reservation aimed squarely at the one UAP provision with a funding sanction attached.
connections: P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843 are the surviving remnant of S.Amdt. 797, the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act; the deletions are itemized in the Joint Explanatory Statement at p. 1330.

Section 1687 aims directly at the waived and unacknowledged SAP mechanism of 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDI 5205.11 by conditioning appropriations on disclosure to the defense and intelligence committees and the four leaders.
Section 1687(b) and section 7343(c) target contractor independent research and development indirect expense under DoDI 3204.01 — the funding path that bypasses DoD program elements entirely.
The 300-day review obligation runs against every 'Government office,' expressly including the NRO, CIA, DOE and the military departments; NARA set the compliance date at October 20, 2024.

AARO is written into the statute at sec. 1842(c)(2)(E)-(F) and sec. 1842(c)(3) as a recipient of agency records, after conferees removed the Senate requirement that SAPs provide UAP material to AARO under sec. 1687.
Sean Kirkpatrick and OUSD(I&S) are the named actors whose November 2023 redline shaped the conference outcome.
Sec. 7341 shifted the annual UAP report obligation from the Secretary of Defense and the DNI to AARO and its director.
openQuestions: Whether any agency has ever certified compliance with section 1687, and whether any funds have been withheld or an activity terminated under it.

Which agencies transmitted records to the UAP Records Collection by the October 20, 2024 deadline, in what volume, and how many records were postponed under section 1843 and reported under the 15-day notice rule.
How many records have been withdrawn from the Collection under section 1843(b) by Senior Agency Officials, and on what basis.
Whether the President has ever made a section 1842(g)(2)(D) certification to continue postponing a UAP record beyond 25 years.

How agencies are interpreting the undefined statutory terms 'technologies of unknown origin,' 'non-human intelligence' and 'temporarily non-attributed objects' in their identification and review, and whether NARA issued any definitional guidance beyond the metadata template.

Whether any contractor has been denied recovery of independent research and development indirect costs under section 1687(b) or section 7343(c), which would be a Defense Contract Audit Agency and Defense Contract Management Agency record.
Who the 'multiple credible sources' were who told Schumer information had been withheld from Congress.

l0.label: FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 - secs. 1671-1673, NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefings and UAP classification-guide accounting

dossier.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, S. 2296 of the 119th Congress, signed into law on 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60. It carries three UAP-related provisions affecting AARO. It does not carry the UAP Disclosure Act, which was excluded for the third consecutive year.
dossier.whyImplicated: The FY2026 NDAA is the clearest available measurement of what Congress can and cannot pass on this subject. What survived is procedural: briefings, an inventory of classification guides, and reporting consolidation. What died — again — was every provision with teeth: records preservation, an independent Review Board, eminent domain over privately held recovered material, and mandatory declassification timelines. The pattern is now three cycles deep and consistent in kind: the disclosure architecture is introduced in the Senate with bipartisan leadership sponsorship, and it is removed in or around conference. One surviving provision is unusually revealing on its own terms — a directive that AARO account for the UAP-related security classification guides governing its own reports and investigations. A classification guide is a written instrument with an author, a date, and an original classification authority. Congress asking for an inventory of them is Congress conceding it does not know how many exist or who wrote them.
dossier.narrative:
S. 2296 passed the Senate on 10 October 2025 and became P.L. 119-60 on 18 December 2025. Three UAP provisions made the conferenced text, all of them modifications to the existing AARO framework rather than new authorities.

The first amends the AARO mandate to require the director to supply Congress with briefings and data on UAP intercepts conducted by U.S. Northern Command and the North American Aerospace Defense Command going back to 2004 — specifically the "number, location, and nature" of such intercepts, together with the procedures and protocols followed, "including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts." The 2004 start date is not arbitrary; it is the year of the USS Nimitz/USS Princeton encounters off southern California. That a statutory obligation was needed in 2025 to get NORTHCOM and NORAD intercept data in front of Congress establishes that, for twenty-one years, the commands responsible for defending North American airspace were not routinely providing it — not to Congress, not to AARO, and not to the scientific community. Christopher Mellon, the former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence who now chairs the Disclosure Foundation's board, has made precisely that point publicly: the United States operates some of the world's most advanced sensor systems, and what those systems capture about anomalous incursions has not been reaching oversight.

The second provision directs AARO to account for the UAP-related security classification guides that apply to information used in reports and investigations of the phenomena. This is the provision an analyst should mine. Security classification guides are the operative documents of concealment: they are what tells a program office which facts are classified at what level and for how long, and they are signed by an original classification authority. Disclosure Foundation officials, Mellon among them, have argued in public that DoD classification guides have been applied inconsistently with executive order standards and have been used to suppress material that was previously unclassified. An accounting of those guides would produce a list of instruments, custodians and dates. Whether AARO produces it, and whether the accounting is delivered classified, is the next measurable event.

The third provision consolidates duplicative reporting requirements and streamlines how federal agencies provide data and information to the Pentagon for AARO's investigations. Streamlining is double-edged: it reduces friction for AARO, and it reduces the number of separate documents Congress receives.

Against that, consider what was excluded. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) submitted the UAP Disclosure Act of 2025 as an amendment to the FY2026 NDAA in late August 2025. It would have prohibited the destruction or alteration of UAP records, created a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, established an independent UAP Records Review Board, and required public disclosure of UAP records within twenty-five years absent a presidential certification of a clear national security reason for delay. It failed in the House. On the Senate side the same architecture was offered as S.Amdt. 3111 to S. 2296. Neither survived. The UAP Disclosure Act has now been excluded from three consecutive defense authorization bills despite bipartisan Senate backing associated with Schumer, Rounds and Gillibrand, and Liberation Times has reported that sources attribute the FY2026 failure specifically to Senator Mitch McConnell.

The records-destruction prohibition is the provision whose repeated exclusion should be read hardest. It is cheap, non-controversial on its face, and imposes no disclosure burden — it merely freezes the evidentiary record in place. Its removal, three cycles running, from a bill that Congress has enacted for more than six decades without fail, is a fact about the removers. The precedent for why it matters is documentary and sixty years old: GAO found in 1995 that the administrative records and outgoing message traffic of Roswell Army Air Field for the relevant period were destroyed with no indication of by whom or under what authority (see gao-nsiad-95-187). A statutory bar on destruction is the one measure that would prevent the 1995 finding from recurring, and it is the measure that keeps not passing.

Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation — the rebranded UAP Disclosure Fund — characterized the three enacted provisions as "a meaningful, if incremental, step toward transparency and oversight," and noted that two of them mirror recommendations Mellon and his team had promoted for years. That is the accurate reading: the FY2026 NDAA moved the oversight perimeter a few feet and left the custody question untouched.

l0.label: House Oversight hearing, 26 July 2023 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'

dossier.whatItIs: A hearing of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability's Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, held 26 July 2023 at 10:06 a.m. in room 2154 of the Rayburn House Office Building, chaired by Rep. Glenn Grothman. The witnesses were Ryan Graves, David Grusch and retired Commander David Fravor. It was the first congressional hearing at which a former intelligence officer testified under oath that the United States operates a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme outside congressional oversight.
dossier.whyImplicated: This hearing converted the legacy programme allegation from journalism into sworn testimony before a committee of jurisdiction, and it did so with three specific mechanisms attached: how the programme is hidden (special access programs the witness was denied read-on to), how it is paid for (misappropriation of funds and self-funding), and who holds the material (contractors, described by the witness as 'the metal benders', who are under no requirement to report UAP). Fravor's written statement establishes that the most corroborated modern military encounter was never investigated and the tapes were never collected - an evidentiary vacuum that is itself the artefact. The hearing also demonstrated the ceiling on congressional capability: members were denied a SCIF, no contractor was called, no document production was compelled, and every substantive answer was deferred to a closed session that has never been publicly confirmed to have occurred on these terms. The committee's own wrap-up release then framed the day around pilot reporting and stigma, omitting the crash retrieval testimony entirely.
dossier.narrative:
The subcommittee met at 10:06 a.m. on 26 July 2023 in 2154 Rayburn. Present were Representatives Grothman, Gosar, Foxx, Sessions, Biggs, Mace, LaTurner, Armstrong, Perry, Garcia, Moskowitz and Frost; also present, waived on, were Luna, Burlison, Gaetz, Burchett, Comer, Ogles, Langworthy, Raskin and Ocasio-Cortez. The unusual size of the 'also present' list is the first fact about this hearing: members from outside the subcommittee, from both parties, came to sit in.

The second fact came in Burchett's opening. Members, he said, 'were even denied access to a classified briefing in a SCIF prior to this hearing due to the amount of hoops that we had to jump through to grant temporary clearance to witness Grusch, who has knowledge of classified information.' The committee therefore held a public hearing about compartmented programmes without the means to hear about compartmented programmes. Every subsequent deferral in the transcript traces back to that.

Grusch's written opening statement is the core document. He identifies himself as an intelligence officer of fourteen years, a USAF major, and from 2021 to 2023 a GS-15 at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, where he was his agency's co-lead for UAP and transmedium object analysis reporting to the UAP Task Force and then to AARO. He states that he became a whistleblower 'through a PPD-19 Urgent Concern filing with the Intelligence Community Inspector General (ICIG)'. He describes a specific tasking: 'In 2019, the UAPTF director tasked me to identify all Special Access Programs & Controlled Access Programs (SAPs/CAPs) we needed to satisfy our congressionally mandated mission.' And then the sentence the hearing is remembered for: 'I was informed, in the course of my official duties, of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program to which I was denied access to those additional read-on's.' His closing statement calls the programmes he reported the 'Non-Human Reverse Engineering Programs' and predicts their revelation would act as 'an ontological (earth-shattering) shock'.

Under questioning the mechanism claims sharpened. Asked by Rep. Moskowitz how such a programme gets funded, Grusch answered: 'I will give you generalities. I can get very specific in a closed session. But misappropriation of funds and self-fund.' Asked whether that meant money budgeted for one programme goes elsewhere, he said 'Yes. I have specific knowledge of that. Yes.' Asked by Rep. Ocasio-Cortez about interactions between defence contractors and UAP activities, he described 'the contractors, you know, or the metal benders, so to speak, the ones actually doing specific performance on government contracts.' Asked whether those contractors are required to report UAP sightings, he answered: 'In terms of the contractors? Not that I am aware of.' That single exchange is the cleanest statement on the record of the regulatory gap that would allow contractor custody to persist without disclosure.

On where and who, he refused in open session and said the information had gone elsewhere: 'I cannot discuss that publicly, but I did provide that information both to the intel committees and the Inspector General.' Asked by Burchett whether it could be given in a SCIF, he replied 'Sure, if you had the appropriate accesses.' Asked when the government first became aware, he said: 'I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's.' Asked by Rep. Burlison whether he had personally seen the craft or bodies, he distinguished carefully: on the craft, 'I have to be careful to describe what I have seen firsthand and not in this environment'; on bodies, 'That is something I have not witnessed myself.' The witness is testifying to what he was told and what he documented, not to personal observation, and the transcript is unambiguous that he drew that line himself.

Fravor's written statement supplies the other half. He commanded VFA-41 aboard USS Nimitz in November 2004 and describes the Princeton having tracked the objects on Aegis 'for the previous 2 weeks', descending from above 80,000 feet to 20,000 feet, staying for hours, and going 'straight back up'. His closing judgement is about oversight, not phenomenology: 'even Unacknowledged Waived programs have some level of oversight by the appropriate committee members in the House and Senate and this work that is said to be occurring from Whistleblower testimonies should not be exempt.' And the line that indicts the system: 'What is shocking is that the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken, and after a couple of days, it turned into a great story to tell friends.'

The official denial was read into the record by a member reciting AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick's prior testimony that there has been 'no credible evidence thus far of extraterrestrial activity' or of 'off-world technology brought to the attention of the office' - a formulation that is a statement about what reached one office, not about what exists.

What the hearing did not produce is as important as what it did. No contractor was called. No document was subpoenaed. The Committee's own wrap-up release, published the same day, lists its Key Takeaways as poor reporting processes and retaliation against pilots, and quotes Graves estimating that only 'somewhere near five percent' of pilot sightings are reported. Crash retrieval, non-human craft and contractor custody do not appear in the committee's summary of its own hearing.

No DoD or AARO witness appeared, and the Department made no on-the-record response to the funding-diversion or contractor-custody testimony.
openQuestions: Grusch stated he provided names, locations and documentation to the ICIG and the intelligence committees; none of that material has been published or acknowledged as received in any public committee document.
Whether the classified session Grusch repeatedly offered was ever held on the terms he described, and by which committee.
Which Special Access Programs Grusch identified in his 2019 UAPTF tasking, and whether that tasking product still exists as a retrievable document.

The publicly retrievable copies of the printed record (CHRG-118hhrg53022) and the committee transcript PDF both truncate before the closing rounds of questioning; a complete verified text of the final third of the hearing has not been obtained for this dossier.
No contractor named in open or closed session has been publicly identified, and no committee has issued a subpoena arising from this hearing.

l0.label: House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets hearing, 9 September 2025 - 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'
l0.short: House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets hearing, 9 September 2025

dossier.whatItIs: A hearing of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, held 9 September 2025 at 10:00 a.m. in HVC-210, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member, titled 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'. The witnesses were Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Senior Chief Petty Officer Alexandro C. Wiggins, George Knapp, Dylan Borland, and minority witness Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the hearing at which the enquiry stopped being about lights in the sky and became about programme architecture, contracts and custody. Knapp's written testimony placed on the congressional record a detailed account of AAWSAP/BAASS as a prime-contract intelligence programme - fifty cleared investigators, twenty-seven months, a 240,000-case data warehouse still reportedly in agency use, more than a hundred papers never released by DIA - and an account of a negotiated transfer of anomalous material from Lockheed Martin to a private contractor that was agreed and then not completed. Nuccetelli testified that documented, investigated UAP incursions over the National Missile Defense sites at Vandenberg produced records now held by AARO and the FBI, and that a witness was threatened into silence. Wiggins, an active-duty Navy Senior Chief, put multi-sensor Star SAFIRE EO/IR imagery of a transmedium object into the record with time, coordinates and platform. Taken together the hearing establishes that the material, the records and the contracts are locatable - and that the committee could name where they sit without being able to compel their production.
dossier.narrative:
The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets is a creature of the 119th Congress, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, and it exists because the 2023 and 2024 hearings demonstrated that a standing subcommittee without access to compartments could not move the file. The 9 September 2025 hearing was held in HVC-210, a House Visitor Center room, with five witnesses and written statements posted by the committee.

Jeffrey Nuccetelli, a former Air Force military police officer with sixteen years of active duty, testified to five UAP incidents at Vandenberg Air Force Base between 2003 and 2005 - the home, as his statement notes, of the National Missile Defense Project, during launches described by the National Reconnaissance Office as 'the most important in twenty-five years.' His formulation of the oversight failure is exact: 'Each incident was witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated, and reported up the chain of command. We sent information up, but no guidance came down.' The 14 October 2003 incursion - Boeing contractors reporting 'a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites' - is the incident Rep. Luna had raised at the 2023 hearing, and Nuccetelli states that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI.' That is a custody claim with two named holders. He also testified that after a later incident 'The witness was later threatened and told to kept quiet about the incident, discouraging further reports.'

Alexandro C. Wiggins, an active-duty Navy Senior Chief Petty Officer with roughly twenty-three years of service, gave the hearing its hardest sensor evidence. On 15 February 2023 at approximately 1915 PST, in the W-291 warning area off Southern California, aboard USS Jackson (LCS-6), a self-luminous Tic-Tac-shaped object was observed emerging from the ocean, joined three similar objects, and all four departed simultaneously with no sonic boom and no conventional propulsion signature. The event was recorded from the Combat Information Center on a Star SAFIRE multi-spectral EO/IR system with visible time and location stamps, the objects were held on radar, and reports were made to the Tactical Action Officer. His statement is careful about what the data does and does not show, and notes an approximate altitude reference of about 22,000 feet reflected in CIC operator conversation.

George Knapp's written testimony is the document that makes this hearing structurally important. He describes AAWSAP as conceived by DIA's Dr. James Lacatski and a colleague, funded through Senator Harry Reid and two other senior senators, and contracted to Robert Bigelow's BAASS, which 'managed to recruit and hire fifty full-time investigators for BAASS, most of them former military or law enforcement, and all of whom were able to qualify for top-secret security clearances.' In twenty-seven months the programme produced 'more than three dozen preliminary reports (DIRDs)' and 'compiled the largest known UFO database - or rather data warehouse - consisting of more than 240,000 case files obtained from multiple other collections, including files from other governments.' That warehouse 'was designed and overseen by Dr. Jacques Vallee and has reportedly been used by U.S. agencies up to the present date.' The programme also produced 'more than 100 highly detailed papers', of which 'None of these 100-plus reports have been released by DIA, though a few have been leaked.'

Knapp then puts two custody claims on the record. First, Lacatski's 2023 statement during Kona Blue discussions with a US senator and an undersecretary of the Department of Homeland Security that 'the U.S. is in possession of a craft of unknown origin and had successfully gained access to its interior', described as having 'a streamlined configuration suitable for aerodynamic flight but no intakes, exhaust, wings, or control surfaces.' Second, and more concrete: 'I have confirmed that Bigelow and a trusted colleague met with and negotiated with a senior executive at Lockheed and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that Lockheed was safeguarding at a facility in California. A source who was in the room for that discussion has confirmed this.' The material 'contained no unknown element, no unobtanium, but its composition suggested it had been crafted in a zero-gravity environment.' And then: 'The agreement was not completed.'

Knapp also notes, almost in passing, a fact that matters for how this file is now being worked: 'Mr. Grusch now works for Representative Burlison as an advisor on these matters.' The 2023 whistleblower is now congressional staff support on the same subject.

The Russian half of Knapp's testimony - Ministry of Defence documents from his 1993 and 1996 Moscow visits, Colonel Boris Sokolov's decade-long standing collection order 1978-1988, General Igor Maltsev's standing order to disengage, the October 1982 Ukraine missile base incident in which launch displays illuminated and could not be shut down - is presented as material already handed to AAWSAP and BAASS for analysis, with the resulting report 'included in one of those unreleased papers submitted to DIA and still bottled up there.'

The minority witness, Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight, was there for whistleblower protection rather than phenomena, which is the correct read of the hearing's title. The Task Force's theory is that the bottleneck is not evidence but the legal exposure of the people who hold it.

claims.text: The hearing 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection' was held on 9 September 2025 at 10:00 am in HVC-210 before the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets.

The witnesses of record were Jeffrey Nuccetelli (U.S. Air Force Veteran), Chief Alexandro Wiggins (UAP Witness), George Knapp (UAP Journalist), Dylan Borland (UAP Witness, U.S. Air Force Veteran) and, as minority witness, Joe Spielberger, Senior Policy Counsel, Project On Government Oversight.

Knapp's written testimony is addressed 'Good morning, Chairwoman Luna, Ranking Member Crockett, and Members of the Task Force', establishing Rep. Anna Paulina Luna as chair and Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member.

Nuccetelli testified to five UAP incidents at Vandenberg Air Force Base between 2003 and 2005, stating: 'Each incident was witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated, and reported up the chain of command. We sent information up, but no guidance came down.'

Nuccetelli testified that the 14 October 2003 incursion began 'when Boeing contractors reported a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites', and that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI.'
Nuccetelli testified that after a subsequent Vandenberg incident 'The witness was later threatened and told to kept quiet about the incident, discouraging further reports.'

Wiggins, an active-duty Navy Senior Chief Petty Officer (Operations Specialist) with approximately 23 years of service, testified to an event on 15 February 2023 at approximately 1915 PST in the W-291 warning area off Southern California aboard USS Jackson (LCS-6), involving a self-luminous Tic-Tac-shaped object emerging from the ocean, linking up with three similar objects, and departing simultaneously with no sonic boom or conventional propulsion signature.

Wiggins testified that the event was recorded inside the Combat Information Center on a Star SAFIRE multi-spectral EO/IR system, that 'The released, stabilized footage includes timestamps, lat/long, and platform readouts consistent with USS Jackson's location in W-291 at the time of the encounter', that the objects were held on radar, and that reports were made to the Tactical Action Officer.

Knapp testified that BAASS, the prime contractor for AAWSAP, 'managed to recruit and hire fifty full-time investigators for BAASS, most of them former military or law enforcement, and all of whom were able to qualify for top-secret security clearances.'

Knapp testified that in its 27-month existence AAWSAP/BAASS produced 'more than three dozen preliminary reports (DIRDs)' and a data warehouse of 'more than 240,000 case files', which 'was designed and overseen by Dr. Jacques Vallee and has reportedly been used by U.S. agencies up to the present date.'

Knapp testified that AAWSAP/BAASS 'also produced more than 100 highly detailed papers focusing on different issues and questions, including studies of the health effects on humans from encounters with UFO/UAP technology. None of these 100-plus reports have been released by DIA, though a few have been leaked.'

Knapp testified that during Kona Blue discussions with a US senator and an undersecretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Dr. James Lacatski revealed that 'the U.S. is in possession of a craft of unknown origin and had successfully gained access to its interior', with 'a streamlined configuration suitable for aerodynamic flight but no intakes, exhaust, wings, or control surfaces.'

Knapp testified: 'I have confirmed that Bigelow and a trusted colleague met with and negotiated with a senior executive at Lockheed and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that Lockheed was safeguarding at a facility in California. A source who was in the room for that discussion has confirmed this.' He added that the material's 'composition suggested it had been crafted in a zero-gravity environment' and that 'The agreement was not completed.'
Knapp stated on the record that 'Mr. Grusch now works for Representative Burlison as an advisor on these matters.'

dossier.denialPosture: No Department of Defense, AARO or DIA witness appeared and no departmental response to the hearing's custody claims - Air Force records held by AARO and the FBI, unreleased DIA papers, the Lockheed material negotiation - has been published. The Department's standing position, restated in AARO's annual reporting, remains that it has found no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial technology; it has not addressed the specific documentary and contractual allegations made under oath at this hearing.
openQuestions: Whether AARO and the FBI in fact hold the Vandenberg 2003 records Nuccetelli names, and whether either has been asked for them in writing by the Task Force.
The identity of the Lockheed Martin senior executive who negotiated the BAASS material transfer, the California facility involved, and why the agreement was not completed.
Whether the AAWSAP 240,000-case data warehouse designed by Jacques Vallee is still operational, in which agency's hands, and under what contract.
The disposition of the more than 100 unreleased AAWSAP/BAASS papers held by DIA, and whether any FOIA or committee request for them has been answered.
Whether the USS Jackson Star SAFIRE source video and radar tracks were ever transmitted to AARO, and whether the case was adjudicated.
Dylan Borland's testimony was not obtained for this dossier and his written statement has not been reviewed here.

dossier.whatItIs: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-81, enacted 27 December 2021 at 135 Stat. 2118, is the statute that created the office lineage running from the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force through the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and was rewritten wholesale a year later by section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 (Public Law 117-263), and amended again in 2023 and 2025.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only place in the United States Code where Congress wrote down, in operative statutory language, that programs concerning unidentified anomalous phenomena may have been 'protected by restricted access' and 'not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' and demanded an accounting of them going back to 1 January 1945. It is also the only statute that directs the Secretary of Defense to designate line organizations for 'the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models' relating to UAP, and to run a science plan whose stated purpose includes providing 'the foundation for potential future investments to replicate' anomalous performance characteristics. Congress did not merely authorize a reporting office; it authorized materials testing, medical study of exposed personnel, and replication research — the exact functional description of a reverse-engineering enterprise — and then required that any prior version of the same enterprise be disclosed. The statute's subsequent amendment history is a record of the Executive branch failing to comply.
dossier.narrative:
Section 1683 began as a modest reorganization and became, through two rewrites, the sharpest disclosure instrument in federal law. Read it as a chronology of what Congress learned.

The original enactment on 27 December 2021 stood up an office to absorb the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, in the wake of the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment. A year later, section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 amended the section generally — replacing it in full — and section 1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever the word appeared. That single-word substitution is not cosmetic. It extended the statute's reach from aircraft to transmedium objects and submerged objects, a definitional move that matters if what is at issue includes things recovered from water.

The rewritten statute names the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office and hardwires a dual chain of command. The Director is appointed by the Secretary of Defense in consultation with the DNI; the Deputy Director is appointed by the DNI in coordination with the Secretary. The Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence — and, separately, 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters.' That administrative reporting line runs to the same office that is a SAP Oversight Authority under DoDI 5205.11 and the DoD interface to the DNI's Controlled Access Program Central Office. The office chartered to find concealed compartments is administratively subordinate, in part, to the office that manages compartments.

Subsection (j) is the load-bearing clause. Within 540 days of 23 December 2022, the Director was to deliver to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership a written report on 'the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' drawn from intelligence community records, oral history interviews, open source analysis, interviews of current and former officials, and classified and unclassified national archives. It must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945. And it must include 'a compilation and itemization of the key historical record of the involvement of the intelligence community with unidentified anomalous phenomena, including — (I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.' Subsection (j)(2) obliges the Archivist of the United States to make classified NARA holdings available to the office for that purpose.

Subsections (e) and (g) are where the statute stops sounding like transparency legislation and starts sounding like a program charter. Under (e)(1), the Secretary of Defense in coordination with the DNI 'shall designate one or more line organizations that will be primarily responsible for scientific, technical, and operational analysis of data gathered by field investigations... including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.' Under (e)(2), both officials must issue directives ensuring those line organizations 'has authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.' Under (g), the science plan must account for performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation,' and 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.' Congress wrote replication into the law. Subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) then requires each annual report to include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

Definitions matter here too. Subsection (n)(6) defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense — pushing materials testing and medical studies out to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories, and therefore out to contractor-operated facilities. Subsection (n)(7) defines transmedium objects as those observed transitioning between space and atmosphere, or atmosphere and water.

The amendment history is the compliance record. In December 2023, P.L. 118-31 §7341 moved the annual report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly onto the AARO Director alone. In December 2025, P.L. 119-60 §1672(b) rewrote subsection (f)(1)(A) so the data-availability mandate binds 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' — the prior text covered only IC elements. Congress had to amend the statute to reach the Department of Defense's own components. Section 1671 added the NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept requirement with a 2004 lookback, and section 1673(a) demanded an accounting of the security classification guides themselves. Each amendment closes a door someone had walked through.

claims.text: Section 1683 was enacted as Pub. L. 117-81, div. A, title XVI, §1683, on 27 December 2021, at 135 Stat. 2118, and is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373.

Pub. L. 117-263 §6802(a) (23 December 2022) amended section 1683 generally, replacing its text, and §1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever appearing, extending the statute's definitional reach to transmedium and submerged objects.

The AARO Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, and reports 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters of the Office.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii) requires the historical record report to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.'

The same subsection requires itemization of 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

The historical record report must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945, and the Archivist of the United States must make available to AARO NARA holdings 'including classified information' as the Director considers necessary.

50 U.S.C. 3373(e)(1) directs the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, to designate one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(g) requires a science plan to account for characteristics 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.'
Each AARO annual report must include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

The statute defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense, pushing designated materials-testing and medical-study responsibility outward to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories.

Annual reports must name 'the line organizations that have been designated to perform the specific functions under subsections (d) and (e), and the specific functions for which each such line organization has been assigned primary responsibility.'
Subsection (m) required the Secretary of Defense to terminate the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force no later than the date the new office was established.

Public Law 119-60 §1672(b) (18 December 2025) rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to bind 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense'; the prior text reached only IC elements.

AARO published Volume I of its historical record report on 8 March 2024, asserting no verifiable evidence that any UAP sighting represented extraterrestrial activity and no verifiable evidence that the U.S. government or private industry has ever had access to extraterrestrial technology, and characterizing interviewees as having 'mistakenly associated' authentic classified programs with alien activity.
claims.source: AARO, 'Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), Volume I,' 8 March 2024 — https://media.defense.gov/2024/Mar/08/2003409233/-1/-1/0/DOPSR-2024-0263-AARO-HISTORICAL-RECORD-REPORT-VOLUME-1-2024.PDF

dossier.denialPosture: The statute contains no denial; the office it created does. AARO's Volume I historical record report (8 March 2024) states it found no verifiable evidence that the U.S. government or private industry has ever had access to extraterrestrial technology, and attributes whistleblower accounts to misidentification of authentic classified programs. That formulation concedes the existence of authentic classified programs proximate to the allegations while denying their nature, and it is the denial Chairwoman Luna attacked on the record on 9 September 2025.
connections: AARO and its first Director, Sean Kirkpatrick — the office created by this section; Kirkpatrick reported to the NASA UAP Independent Study Team's 31 May 2023 public meeting that AARO had collected more than 800 events.
Deputy Secretary of Defense and USD(I&S) — the reporting lines written into 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3), which run into the same offices that control the DoD SAP architecture under DoDI 5205.11.

NARA and the Archivist of the United States — obligated by subsection (j)(2) to open classified holdings to AARO; separately the statutory custodian of the UAP Records Collection created by the FY2024 NDAA.
NASA — named in subsection (c)(6) as a required coordination partner; NASA's own Independent Study Team reported in September 2023 with no access to the classified data this section covers.
GAO / Comptroller General — assigned by P.L. 117-263 §6803 to audit the historical record report process with cleared personnel.
David Grusch — his 2023 allegation of a program 'protected by restricted access' not reported to Congress tracks the exact statutory language of subsection (j)(1)(B)(ii)(I).

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories — Section II.4 demands identification of MITRE work performed for AARO, the UAP Task Force, AATIP and AAWSAP, connecting the statutory office lineage to contractor custody.
Pub. L. 118-31 §1687(b) — the companion prohibition on charging UAP-related IRAD to contract overhead without congressional disclosure.
openQuestions: Which line organizations were designated under subsections (d) and (e), and for which functions? The statute requires them to be named in annual reports; no unclassified naming has been published.
Was the science plan required by subsection (g) ever produced, and does it contain a replication program element as the statute contemplates?
Has any annual report actually addressed subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) — efforts 'to capture or exploit' discovered UAP — and what was said?
Did the Archivist open classified NARA holdings to AARO under subsection (j)(2), and what accession records document that transfer?
Why did Congress need to amend subsection (f)(1)(A) in December 2025 to reach DoD components — which components had withheld data under the prior text?

The original 27 December 2021 text of section 1683 differs materially from the 2022 rewrite; what provisions in the original were dropped, and at whose request? The Code preserves only a summary amendment note.
Has the AARO Director delivered the accounting of security classification guides required within 180 days of 18 December 2025, and does it list any guide covering recovered materials?

l0.label: IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102 — contractor turn-in of 'non-earth origin or exotic' UAP material

dossier.whatItIs: The contractor turn-in provision of the Fiscal Year 2024 Intelligence Authorization Act: a Gillibrand amendment adopted unanimously by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 14 June 2023, which required any person currently or formerly under federal contract holding government-derived UAP material to notify AARO within 60 days and, within 180 days, to hand over "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" for assessment, analysis and inspection. It carried a safe harbor, a sweeping funding ban on unreported UAP special access programs, and a Sense of Congress. It was numbered Sec. 1104 in S. 2103 as reported on 22 June 2023, renumbered as the bill moved, and was enacted in drastically narrowed form as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 on 22 December 2023.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the single most important statutory hook on the board because it is the only text Congress has ever voted out of committee that presumes, on its face, that private contractors are holding non-earth-origin material derived from federal programs and that treats getting it back as an administrative problem with a deadline. A safe harbor is not written for a hypothetical. Congress does not draft immunity from criminal and civil action "for receiving" material unless someone plausibly received it. The definition of covered activities is equally load-bearing: it contemplates government or contractor personnel with "a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft," and it defines the reverse-engineering perimeter as work on "any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Seventeen senators on the Intelligence Committee voted this text out. Then it was cut in conference.
dossier.narrative:
On 14 June 2023, nine days after The Debrief published David Grusch's allegations, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence adopted by voice vote a UAP amendment sponsored by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and cosponsored by Senators Mike Rounds (R-SD), John Cornyn (R-TX) and Marco Rubio (R-FL). The committee then approved the underlying Intelligence Authorization Act unanimously. The bill was filed and numbered on 22 June 2023 as S. 2103; the UAP text appeared as Section 1104, titled "Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena." Section 1102 of that same reported text was an unrelated provision on defense sensitive support; the board's identifier tracks a later renumbering as the IAA moved into the NDAA vehicle, and the substance — not the number — is what matters.

The operative mechanism had three parts.

First, a notification and turn-in mandate. The text reached "any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access." Such persons had 60 days from enactment to notify the AARO director, and 180 days to provide "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" in their possession and to make it available to the director for "assessment, analysis, and inspection." The AARO director then had 30 days to notify designated congressional committees and leaders of any notification, information or material received. That last clause is the accountability trigger: it would have created a dated congressional paper trail for each turn-in.

Second, a safe harbor: "No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving" the covered material or information, contingent on meeting the deadlines. Douglas Johnson, who first reported the text, read this as implying that a private entity holding non-human technology outside democratic oversight — and possibly profiting from it — would otherwise be in a legally tenuous position, and that the provision functioned as a time-limited amnesty to smooth an orderly return. Nothing in the provision created new criminal offenses, and nothing immunized threats, violence or perjury.

Third, a funding ban. No future federal funds, directly or indirectly, for any UAP-related special access program activity unless the program had been "formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified to the appropriate committees of Congress, congressional leadership, and the Director" of AARO. The designated recipients were the intelligence, armed services and appropriations committees of both chambers plus the Speaker, House minority leader, and Senate majority and minority leaders — 58 senators and 137 House members in total. The categories of covered activity were drafted in six expansive paragraphs and included recruiting, employing, training, equipping, operating and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a retrieval mission; managing and providing security for activities and information relating to UAP "from disclosure"; and reverse-engineering work reaching any aerospace craft using propulsion other than chemical propellants, solar power and electric ion thrust.

The Sense of Congress attached to the provision is the most candid language Congress has produced on the subject. It asserted that "due to the increasing potential for technology surprise from foreign adversaries and to ensure sufficient integration across the United States industrial base and avoid technology and security stovepipes... the Federal Government must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes." Read plainly: the government previously provided exotic technology antecedents to industry for R&D, secrecy has stovepiped that work, and the stovepiping is now a national security liability. Whether or not one accepts the premise, the drafters wrote it into a bill that a Senate committee approved unanimously.

The legislative arc from there is the concealment story in miniature. The Senate Armed Services Committee carried parallel but non-identical language at Section 1546 of S. 2226, without the safe harbor and without the Sense of Congress, and with the funding limitation confined to FY2024 DoD programs. On 20 July 2023 SSCI Chairman Mark Warner filed a revised version, SA 994, narrowing the IAA's funding limitation to FY2024 as well. The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence approved its own FY2024 IAA (H.R. 3932) on 13 July 2023 containing no UAP provisions at all, and the House Rules Committee blocked a floor vote on Rep. Mike Gallagher's parallel amendment to the House NDAA — reportedly because of objections from HPSCI leadership, whose chairman Michael Turner and ranking member Jim Himes had made dismissive public comments about secret alien technology on 6 June 2023. The Senate passed a combined NDAA-IAA on 27 July 2023. In conference, the turn-in mandate and safe harbor did not survive. What was enacted on 22 December 2023 as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 is a funding limitation only, conditioned on the Director of National Intelligence providing program details to the appropriate committees and leadership — which the Intelligence chairmen explained "provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area."

The deletion is the finding. A unanimous committee wrote a hand-back-the-material provision with an amnesty clause, and the amnesty and the hand-back both vanished behind closed doors.

claims.text: The UAP amendment was sponsored by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and cosponsored by Sens. Mike Rounds (R-SD), John Cornyn (R-TX) and Marco Rubio (R-FL); it was adopted by the 17-member Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on a voice vote on 14 June 2023, after which the full bill was approved unanimously.
claims.source: Douglas Dean Johnson, "Senate Intelligence bill gives holders of 'non-earth origin or exotic UAP material' six months to make it available to AARO," Mirador, 24 June 2023, https://douglasjohnson.ghost.io/senate-intelligence-bill-gives-holders-of-non-earth-origin-six-months/
