l0.label: 10 U.S.C. 119 — Special Access Programs: Congressional Oversight

dossier.whatItIs: 10 U.S.C. § 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight,' is the statute that governs how the Department of Defense must tell Congress about its special access programs. Enacted 4 December 1987 as section 1132(a)(1) of Public Law 100-180 and amended in 1990, 1996, 1999 and 2001, it requires an annual report on all SAPs, an annual report on each new SAP with justification, advance notice of classification changes, and — decisively — bars any SAP from being initiated until the defense committees have been notified and thirty days have elapsed. It also grants the Secretary of Defense a case-by-case waiver over the content of those reports.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the statute against which the concealment must be measured, and it is the statute a whistleblower report given to Congress in 2024 alleges is being deliberately circumvented. Subsection (f) is categorical: a special access program 'may not be initiated until' the defense committees are notified and thirty days pass. If a legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering effort exists as a DoD SAP and the defense committees were never notified, the illegality is not a matter of interpretation. Subsection (e) is the built-in escape hatch, letting the Secretary strip content from the reports on national-security grounds and narrow disclosure to eight members. And the reporting obligations in subsections (a) and (b) were terminated outright effective 31 December 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328 — the annual SAP report to Congress simply stopped, in the same window in which the UAP Task Force was being stood up and AARO was being legislated. Michael Shellenberger's sworn testimony that an alleged UAP USAP is White-House-controlled and DoD-executed 'to avoid compliance with Title 10' is a claim about this section specifically.
dossier.narrative:
Section 119 was Congress's answer to the black-budget expansion of the 1980s. Enacted in the FY1988 defense authorisation, it imposed a reporting discipline on a category of program that by design resists reporting. Read as a whole, the section is a fairly aggressive assertion of legislative prerogative, and its subsequent amendment history shows Congress tightening it further: in 1990 Congress added subsection (f), the thirty-day pre-initiation notification bar, effective 1 October 1991, and rewrote subsection (c) to require fourteen days' advance notice of classification changes rather than thirty days' notice after the fact.

The reporting architecture has four parts. Under subsection (a), by 1 March each year the Secretary of Defense must submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP in that budget, a brief description, a brief discussion of major milestones, the actual cost for every prior fiscal year of the program, and the estimated total cost plus estimates for the current year, the budget year, and each of the four succeeding years. Under subsection (b), by 1 February each year the Secretary must report every new SAP with notice of the designation, justification for it, the current estimate of total program cost, and — a provision with real analytic teeth — 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.' That clause exists to stop the Department from hiding duplicate or successor programs under new names. Under subsection (c), any planned classification change or public declassification announcement requires a report to the defense committees not less than fourteen days beforehand, unless exceptional circumstances make that impossible.

Subsection (e) is the pressure valve. The Secretary 'may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report' if inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' with the waiver made on a case-by-case basis. When a waiver is used, the withheld information and the justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — that is, to eight members across four committees, and to nobody else. This is the statutory basis of what practitioners call a waived SAP. The implementing directive confirms the practice: access to waived SAPs is limited to the chairs, ranking minority members and staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise.

Subsection (f) is the hardest edge in the statute and the one most relevant to this board: 'A special access program may not be initiated until— (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' There is no waiver of subsection (f) in subsection (e) — the waiver reaches only (a), (b) and (c). Congress can, in principle, be denied the content of a report about a SAP. It cannot lawfully be denied notice that a DoD SAP is being initiated.

Which makes the terminating note in the current code text the most consequential single fact in this dossier. Under the heading 'Termination of Reporting Requirements,' the statute records: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.' The annual comprehensive SAP report and the annual new-SAP report both lapsed at the end of 2021, under a sunset written into the FY2017 NDAA. The pre-initiation notification in (f) survives. The routine, systematic, year-over-year visibility does not. Any analyst working this board should note the coincidence of timing: the UAP Task Force was established in August 2020, the ODNI preliminary assessment landed in June 2021, AARO was legislated in December 2021 and stood up in 2022, and the statutory obligation to give Congress an annual accounting of every DoD special access program expired on 31 December 2021.

The implementing machinery underneath the statute is set out in DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It establishes the Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary, a Senior Review Group, a Senior Working Group, and the DoD Special Access Program Central Office whose Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary and is the 'DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch.' Two provisions in it bear directly on the concealment argument. First, establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is 'by exception' and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. Second, and more starkly: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' The contractor layer — precisely where a legacy program would sit — is prohibited by directive from talking to Congress about SAP material without permission from an office reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. And the same directive designates USD(I&S), the office housing AARO, as the primary interface with ODNI for sharing compartmented capabilities into and out of DoD SAPs.

Witnesses have made the statutory argument directly. Tim Gallaudet told House Oversight in November 2024 that 'even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight' and that 'any and all past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs and activities are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress by preventing it from exercising its legislative and oversight responsibilities.' Shellenberger's source described the alleged workaround with unusual precision: the White House directs the Secretary of Defense to run the program, so it is executed by DoD but controlled by the White House. 'But that's the loophole.' Whether such a structure escapes subsection (f) turns on whether it is a special access program 'of the Department of Defense' — a question no court and no committee has resolved on the public record.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) requires that 'not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs.'

10 U.S.C. 119(a)(2)(B) requires that for each special access program in the budget the report include a brief description, a brief discussion of major milestones, the actual cost for each prior fiscal year of the program, and the estimated total cost plus estimates for the current fiscal year, the budget year, and each of the four succeeding fiscal years.

10 U.S.C. 119(b) requires an annual report, not later than February 1, on each new special access program providing notice of the designation, justification for it, the current estimate of total program cost, and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.'

10 U.S.C. 119(c) requires the Secretary of Defense to report to the defense committees any planned change in the classification of a DoD special access program, or any planned declassification and public announcement, not less than 14 days beforehand, with a later-notice exception for 'exceptional circumstances' that must be explained in the report.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive any requirement under subsections (a), (b) or (c) that certain information be included in a report 'if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security,' with any such waiver made on a case-by-case basis.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) provides that when a waiver is exercised, the withheld information and the justification for the waiver go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — eight members in total.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) provides that 'a special access program may not be initiated until— (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' The waiver authority in subsection (e) does not extend to subsection (f).

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Committee on Armed Services, the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate, and the corresponding committees and Subcommittee on Defense of the House.

The section was added by Public Law 100-180, division A, title XI, section 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987, 101 Stat. 1151, and amended by Pub. L. 101-510 (1990), Pub. L. 104-106 (1996), Pub. L. 106-65 (1999) and Pub. L. 107-107 (2001).
Subsection (f), the 30-day pre-initiation notification bar, was added by Pub. L. 101-510, division A, title XIV, section 1482(a)(2), 5 November 1990, and took effect on 1 October 1991.

The statute carries a note headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' stating: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.' The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP report requirements therefore lapsed at the end of 2021.

DoD Directive 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, establishes the Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and provides that the Director, DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary and serves as the 'DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch, including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries.'

DoD Directive 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(g) provides that 'no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.'

DoD Directive 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(d) provides that 'establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments will be by exception' and that establishing SAPs to protect new and novel critical program information at any tier 'requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval.'

Michael Shellenberger testified on 13 November 2024 that a source told him an alleged UAP Unacknowledged Special Access Program 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code,' adding 'the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.'

Tim Gallaudet testified on 13 November 2024 that 'even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight, and all compartmented programs must be reported to the Senate Intelligence Committee,' and that any past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs 'are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress.'

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial attached to the statute itself. The relevant absence is that no DoD component has ever publicly identified a UAP-related special access program in any section 119 report, and the annual reporting obligations that would have carried such an identification lapsed on 31 December 2021. The Department's only categorical statement in this area is Sue Gough's denial that any SAP named IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION appears in its records.
connections: Section 119(f)'s unwaivable 30-day pre-initiation notice is the specific legal provision the alleged White-House-directed, DoD-executed USAP structure is said to be engineered around.
Section 119(e)'s eight-member disclosure floor is the statutory origin of the waived-SAP practice implemented through DoDD 5205.07, and is what Gallaudet means by 'Gang of Eight' reporting.

The 31 December 2021 termination of subsections (a) and (b) reporting, enacted by section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328 (FY2017 NDAA), coincides with the UAPTF-to-AARO transition and the enactment of 50 U.S.C. 3373 in December 2022.

DoDD 5205.07 places SAP governance under Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks as SAPOC chair and routes all congressional SAP contact through the DoD SAPCO Director, giving a single named office control over what Congress learns.

The contractor gag in DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(g) directly implicates the defence-contractor layer this board is mapping: contractors cannot lawfully brief Congress on SAP material without DoD SAPCO approval, which structurally converts contractor whistleblowing into a security violation.

USD(I&S) is both the ODNI/IC interface under DoDD 5205.07 and the parent organisation of AARO, meaning the office Congress created to find unreported UAP programs sits inside the office that brokers compartmented sharing between the IC and DoD SAPs.

Luis Elizondo's testimony that he 'managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council' describes the same White-House-to-DoD execution pattern the Immaculate Constellation source alleges, from the inside.
openQuestions: Has the section 119(e) waiver authority ever been exercised for a UAP-related program, and do the eight recipients' offices hold the resulting notifications?

Was the 31 December 2021 termination of the subsection (a) and (b) annual reports replaced by any successor reporting vehicle, or is there now no periodic comprehensive SAP accounting to Congress at all?

Is a program directed by the White House and executed by the Secretary of Defense a 'special access program of the Department of Defense' for purposes of subsection (f)? No court or committee has resolved this on the public record.
Who is the current Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office, and what records does that office hold of SAP material provided to Congress?

Does any section 119 report ever filed identify a program with a UAP, materials-exploitation or recovered-technology mission, and would the subsection (b)(2)(B) similar-technology identification requirement have forced such a disclosure?
How does section 119 interact with intelligence-community programs funded outside the DoD budget, where the reporting path runs to the intelligence committees rather than the defense committees?

l0.label: Waived Unacknowledged SAP (waived USAP) — the mechanism

dossier.whatItIs: The waived unacknowledged special access program is the most restrictive reporting category in the American national-security system. It is created when the Secretary of Defense, acting under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), waives the statutory requirement that specified information about a special access program appear in the reports to Congress, and instead provides that information and the justification for the waiver jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the four defense committees. That is eight members of Congress.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the mechanism that makes the board's premise legally possible without anyone committing a crime. A waived unacknowledged SAP is a program whose existence is affirmatively not acknowledged to anyone not cleared for it, whose contents are reported to eight members rather than four committees, whose professional staff are excluded by regulation, and whose contractor personnel are barred by DoD directive from taking material to any member of Congress without the approval of the DoD SAPCO director. Compounding this, the annual reporting requirements in 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) — the very reports the waiver operates on — terminated by operation of law on December 31, 2021 under section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, so the statutory baseline against which a waiver would be visible no longer runs. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort exists and has been kept from Congress, this is the container it fits in, and the container was designed and is administered lawfully.
dossier.narrative:
Read 10 U.S.C. 119 in order and the architecture assembles itself. Subsection (a) requires the Secretary of Defense to submit an annual report by March 1 on special access programs, including for each SAP a brief description, major milestones, actual cost by fiscal year, and estimated total and out-year costs. Subsection (b) requires a separate report by February 1 covering each new SAP — notice of the designation and the justification for it, plus the current total program cost estimate and, notably, "an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice." Subsection (c) requires 14 days' advance notice of any classification change or planned declassification. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. Subsection (g) defines "defense committees" as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees, and the defense appropriations subcommittees, of both chambers — four committees.

Then subsection (e) removes it. "The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis." And paragraph (2): if the Secretary exercises that authority, the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees." Four committees, two members each. Eight.

The Department's implementing regulations are more specific than the statute. DoD Instruction 5205.11, reissued 12 September 2024, states at paragraph 1.2.f: "The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight." That last sentence is the denial, and it is doing a great deal of work. The glossary of the same instruction defines a waived SAP as "A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs" — and an unacknowledged SAP as "A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information."

Section 7 of DoDI 5205.11 governs congressional access and is where the eight-member construct becomes operational. Paragraph 7.2.a(3): "Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense." Paragraph 7.2.a(2) closes a gap that would otherwise leak: when a member is granted access to a SAP umbrella, that access carries down to all compartments and sub-compartments "with the exception of waived sub-compartments." Paragraph 7.2.b confirms that committee members get access to all DoD SAPs in their jurisdiction "except for waived programs." Paragraph 7.2.c(1) allows one majority and one minority professional staff member per committee access only to non-waived SAPs. Paragraph 7.2.f: "The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs."

So the practical picture: a waived unacknowledged SAP is briefed to eight members plus staff directors and a security manager. Those members cannot discuss it with their own staff, cannot discuss it with colleagues, and cannot describe it publicly. The oversight that exists is the personal, unstaffed attention of eight busy legislators who cannot take notes out of the room.

Two further features deserve an analyst's attention. First, the sunset. The note to 10 U.S.C. 119 records that for termination, effective December 31, 2021, of the provisions in subsections (a) and (b) requiring submittal of an annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328. The reports the waiver was designed to redact stopped being statutorily required at the end of 2021. Whatever reporting occurs now occurs as a matter of practice, not obligation.

Second, the covert-action escape hatch. The Gang of Eight construct familiar from intelligence law lives at 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2): when the President determines it essential to limit access to a covert action finding, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking members of the intelligence committees plus the four congressional leaders. But 50 U.S.C. 3093(e) defines "covert action" as an activity to influence political, economic or military conditions abroad, and expressly excludes "traditional counterintelligence activities, traditional activities to improve or maintain the operational security of United States Government programs, or administrative activities," as well as "traditional diplomatic or military activities or routine support to such activities." A domestic recovery, custody and exploitation effort — material retrieval on U.S. soil, laboratory analysis, contractor engineering — is not an activity to influence conditions abroad. It is therefore not a covert action, it generates no Presidential finding, it triggers no reporting under 3093 at all, and the eight-member intelligence-committee mechanism never engages. The only mechanism that engages is 10 U.S.C. 119 — and 119(e) waives it.

That is the argument in its full form. Nothing in it requires anyone to have broken a law.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) provides: "The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis."

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) provides that when the waiver authority is exercised, the Secretary shall provide the withheld information and the justification for the waiver "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — and 119(g) defines the defense committees as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees plus the defense appropriations subcommittees of both chambers, i.e. four committees and eight members.

10 U.S.C. 119(b)(2)(B) requires each new-SAP report to include "an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice" — a comparative-technology disclosure that a 119(e) waiver can remove.
10 U.S.C. 119(f) prohibits initiating a special access program until the defense committees are notified and 30 days elapse after notification.

The annual reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) terminated effective December 31, 2021, pursuant to section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, as recorded in the Termination of Reporting Requirements note to section 119.

DoD Instruction 5205.11, September 12, 2024, paragraph 1.2.f states: "The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight."

DoDI 5205.11 defines a waived SAP as "A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

DoDI 5205.11 defines an unacknowledged SAP as "A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information."

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a(3) states: "Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense."

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a(2) provides that access to a SAP umbrella conveys access to all subordinate compartments and sub-compartments "with the exception of waived sub-compartments" — meaning a waived sub-compartment can sit inside a program a member has otherwise been read into.

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.c(1) limits committee professional staff access to non-waived SAPs only, and paragraph 7.2.f states flatly: "The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs."

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) is the statutory Gang of Eight provision: where the President determines it essential to limit access to a covert action finding, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate.

50 U.S.C. 3093(e) defines covert action as activity "to influence political, economic, or military conditions abroad" and expressly excludes "traditional counterintelligence activities, traditional activities to improve or maintain the operational security of United States Government programs, or administrative activities" and "traditional diplomatic or military activities or routine support to such activities" — so a domestic material recovery, custody and exploitation effort would generate no Presidential finding and no reporting obligation under section 3093 at all.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a limited-access statement of reasons is submitted, the President either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a renewed statement of reasons for continued limitation — a sunset discipline that has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

dossier.denialPosture: The Department's only public position on this mechanism is the single sentence in DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 1.2.f: "Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight." That assertion is true in the sense that eight members are notified and false in the sense that ordinary committee process, staff review, and institutional memory are excluded by regulation in the same document.
connections: DoD SAPCO administers waived SAPs, controls congressional access requests, and can delegate Access Approval Authority for waived SAPs to its Deputy Director.
The SAPOC, chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense, is required by DoDI 5205.11 to assess in its annual review 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.'

FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687 (P.L. 118-31) attacks this mechanism directly by cutting funds for UAP activities 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' unless details are given to the defense and intelligence committees and the four congressional leaders.

Senator Schumer's December 13, 2023 floor statement that information on UAP has been withheld from Congress 'especially as it relates to the four congressional leaders, Defense Committees, and the Intelligence Committee' is a direct reference to this reporting architecture.

David Grusch's allegation of programs concealed from congressional oversight is, in statutory terms, an allegation about either a waived SAP whose eight recipients were not told the truth, or an effort operating outside the SAP system entirely.
10 U.S.C. 119 was added by Pub. L. 100-180 sec. 1132(a)(1), December 4, 1987 — the SAP reporting regime postdates by decades any program alleged to have begun in the 1940s or 1950s.
openQuestions: How many waived DoD SAPs exist. The number has never been made public in any form, aggregate or otherwise.
Whether the Secretary of Defense has ever exercised 10 U.S.C. 119(e) with respect to a UAP-related program, and if so on what date and under which Secretary.

What replaced the 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) annual reports after their statutory termination on December 31, 2021, and whether any comprehensive SAP inventory is now provided to Congress as a matter of obligation rather than practice.
Whether a program predating the 1987 enactment of section 119 was ever brought into the SAP reporting system at all, or whether legacy arrangements were grandfathered.
How a program funded through contractor independent research and development indirect expense — rather than a DoD program element — would appear in any 10 U.S.C. 119 report, if at all.
Whether the eight recipients under 119(e)(2) are given the same material as the four committees would have received, or a summary.

l0.label: Wayne State University

dossier.whatItIs: Wayne State University is a public research university in midtown Detroit whose School of Medicine operates jointly with the Detroit Medical Center, a large urban academic hospital system. Inside that medical school sat a small, defense- and intelligence-facing neuroscience unit called the Emergent Technology Research Division, built around functional neuroimaging and cognitive-workload measurement. That division, not the university's public research portfolio, is the reason Wayne State appears on this board.
dossier.whyImplicated: Four of the thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents commissioned under the DIA's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications program are attributed on the government-derived DIRD list to two Wayne State men: Christopher C. "Kit" Green and Richard J. Genik II. Green is a career CIA analyst (1969-1985) who came to Wayne State as executive director for emergent technology research for the School of Medicine and Detroit Medical Center, and then as assistant dean; Genik directed the Emergent Technology Research Division that Green's role had seeded, and the two had already co-authored on "cognitive avionics" for spaceflight crews in 2005. Green's DIRD is the human-effects paper, the single AAWSAP deliverable about injured bodies rather than propulsion, and it states outright that clinical diagnosis of injured witnesses can be used to reverse-engineer the craft that hurt them. That makes a named academic medical centre in Detroit a node in the custody chain for injury data on people harmed by anomalous craft, and it makes the university's silence about that work the relevant fact. Wayne State has never issued any public acknowledgement of the DIA contract deliverables written by its faculty, and Green himself has since recast the entire enterprise as private consulting done outside any institutional review structure.
dossier.narrative:
The program reached into universities, and Wayne State is where it reached into a hospital.

The entry point is Christopher C. Green. His career is the point: senior division analyst and assistant national intelligence officer for science and technology at CIA from 1969 to 1985, then General Motors, then Wayne State. The National Research Council's own 2008 biography of him, published while he chaired a committee on military and intelligence methodology for emergent neurophysiological research, records that immediately prior to becoming assistant dean he was "executive director for emergent technology research for the SOM/DMC" and that he held clinical appointments in the Departments of Diagnostic Radiology and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurosciences of the School of Medicine and the Detroit Medical Center. Note what that means. A former CIA science-and-technology officer was running the emergent-technology research function of a large American medical school, with hospital-side appointments in the two departments that give access to brain imaging and to psychiatric case material.

By 2009 the unit had a name and a successor. Wayne State's own School of Medicine news office described Richard J. Genik II as "director of the Emergent Technology Research Division and assistant professor of the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurosciences," announcing that the U.S. Army had picked him as one of fifteen experts to direct two decades of Army neuroscience investment, and that he briefed the Pentagon, the Board of Army Science and Technology, the Army Research Lab and Training and Doctrine Command. The university publicised that. It has never publicised what came next.

What came next was AAWSAP. The DIRD list attributes to Genik three papers and to Green one. Genik's three are all verifiable in the released record: "Technological Approaches to Controlling External Devices in the Absence of Limb-Operated Interfaces" (DIA-08-1003-012, 23 March 2010), "Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft" (DIA-08-1101-001, 15 December 2010, ICOD 8 September 2010, issued in the "Defense Futures" series), and a quantum-computing paper dated 10 December 2010. Read together they are not miscellaneous: brain-machine control of external devices, cognitive ceilings on piloting multiple craft at once, and molecular computing. That is a specification sheet for operating something you do not fly with your hands.

Green's contribution is the one that matters most. "Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues," dated 11 March 2010 with an information cut-off of 1 December 2009, produced under the FY 2009 AAWSA program in the "Acquisition Threat Support" series, opens with three antenna engineers who suffered erythema, fever, hair loss, blood dyscrasia and, in one case, "signs of malignant transformations" after a near-field exposure centred at about 785 MHz. Its summary is the load-bearing sentence in the whole DIRD corpus: the paper "relates, summarizes, and analyzes evidence of unintended injury to human observers by anomalous advanced aerospace systems," and argues "that the subsequent work can inform (e.g., reverse engineer), through clinical diagnoses, certain physical characteristics of possible future advanced aerospace systems from unknown provenance." Later it states: "It is our contention that characteristics of the fields or mechanisms associated with close encounters with anomalous craft can even sometimes carefully be gleaned from archival records where effects on human physiology have been carefully reported." Its appendices draw on the Schuessler catalog of UFO-related human physiological effects and on Vallee's close-encounter typology. The internal references cite "Green C. 2009 & 1983 (Unpublished Personal Archives)" and "Green, CC 2001, 2009 Unpublished HIPPA files" — a defence intelligence reference document resting, in part, on one physician's private patient archive.

The custody problem is exactly there. The released PDFs redact every author name under FOIA exemption (b)(6); the attribution to Wayne State comes from the DIRD list, not from the documents. Green, interviewed in April 2022, said he was a consultant to AAWSAP facilitated by BAASS, that there were no control groups and no institutional review board because he was doing "case studies" and not research, that a client gave him a grant he would not name, and that DIA reviewers objected to his use of the word UFO and had him change the wording. So the human-effects paper commissioned by a defence intelligence agency was written by a Wayne State assistant dean, drew on patient material he holds personally, passed through no university IRB, and was scrubbed of the word that described what it was about. The institution's name is on the government's list; the institution's oversight machinery never touched the work; and the institution has said nothing since. That is not an accident of paperwork. It is how the program used a university: for the credential and the clinical access, not for the accountability.

Green's own posture is displacement rather than denial: he characterises the human-effects paper as private consulting and personal case studies conducted outside any university review structure, and declines to name the funder. The DIA's standing line that DIRDs are contractor-produced theoretical papers that do not represent agency positions performs the same function for the government side.

openQuestions: No evidence was found that Green ever held a named or endowed chair at Wayne State. The verifiable titles are assistant dean, adjunct/clinical professorial appointments in Diagnostic Radiology and Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurosciences, and earlier executive director for emergent technology research. Any claim of a 'chair' for anomalous-exposure research should be treated as unsupported until a Wayne State appointment letter or catalogue entry surfaces.

The exact start and end dates of Green's Wayne State appointments are not established in the sourced record; the 2008 NRC biography is the firm anchor, and his status in 2009-2010 when the DIRD was written is inferred rather than documented.

Whether any part of the AAWSAP work flowed through Wayne State accounts, contracts, facilities or the Emergent Technology Research Division's budget is unresolved. Green describes personal consulting; no subcontract, subaward or effort-reporting document has surfaced either way.

Whether Genik's three DIRDs were written under university affiliation or, like Green's, as private consulting is not established. He is attributed to Wayne State on the DIRD list, but no contract instrument has been located.

The document number on the human-effects DIRD is illegible in the released scan, so the paper is cited here by title and date only. The quantum-computing DIRD's number OCRs ambiguously and is likewise cited by date.
Whether Wayne State's institutional review board ever reviewed, or was ever asked to review, any of the clinical or imaging work Green describes conducting on 'experiencers' in later years.
The identity of 'Morris' in the DIRD's Appendix B 'Green/Morris' ICD-coding exercise, and whether that collaborator was a Wayne State colleague.
Whether the Emergent Technology Research Division still exists at Wayne State, when it was wound down or renamed, and where its records went.
Whether Wayne State has ever received a FOIA, records request or press inquiry about the DIA work, and what it said in response.

l0.label: Senado Federal do Brasil

dossier.whatItIs: The Senado Federal is the upper chamber of Brazil's National Congress. On 16 March 2022 it received Requerimento no 193, de 2022 (RQS 193/2022), tabled by Senator Eduardo Girao (PODEMOS/CE) with seven co-signatories, and approved it the same day; the resulting special plenary session was held on 24 June 2022. The requerimento's stated purpose was to hold a special session commemorating the 75th anniversary of World Ufology Day, and its justificacao entered into the Senate's permanent record a detailed account of Brazil's official UFO programmes and archive holdings.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Senate node is where the correction lives, and correcting it makes the comparison stronger rather than weaker. RQS 193/2022 is not a records-production instrument. Its ementa is a request for a commemorative special session under Article 199 of the Senate's internal rules, and its disposition reads 'Aprovada pelo Plenario' followed by 'SESSAO REALIZADA'. What it did instead is arguably more useful to this board: it wrote into the permanent legislative record of a G20 state, over eight senators' names, that the Aeronautica ran Operacao Prato and SIOANI, that FAB fighters chased 21 objects in 1986, that from 2007 the air force but not the army and not the navy transferred its files, and that the archive reference code BR DFANBSB ARX returns 758 documents. No US congressional instrument has ever put an equivalent set of specifics into the record as settled institutional history. The contrast is not that Brazil compelled disclosure through legislation. It is that Brazil did not have to, because the executive had already published, and the legislature's role was to hold a session about it in the plenary chamber with foreign witnesses at the rostrum.
dossier.narrative:
The premise that most needs correcting before this node is usable is the shape of the instrument. RQS 193/2022 is a requerimento, a procedural request, filed under Article 199 of the Regimento Interno do Senado Federal, asking for a special session at an appropriate date to commemorate 75 years of World Ufology Day. It carries the signatures of Eduardo Girao (PODEMOS/CE), Eliziane Gama (CIDADANIA/MA), Alessandro Vieira (CIDADANIA/SE), Izalci Lucas (PSDB/DF), Jorge Kajuru (PODEMOS/GO), Marcos do Val (PODEMOS/ES), Paulo Rocha (PT/PA) and Reguffe (PODEMOS/DF), which is a cross-party spread from left to right. It was read and approved on 16 March 2022, published in the Diario do Senado Federal no 32 of 17 March 2022 at pages 269 to 275 and page 62, the session was held on 24 June 2022 and published in DSF no 99 of 25 June 2022 at pages 7 to 67, and the matter was closed and sent to the archive coordination on 29 June 2022. It compelled nothing and produced no documents. Any claim on this board that the Senate passed an instrument seeking UAP records must be retired.

What survives, and what makes the node worth keeping, is the justificacao. Brazilian requerimentos carry a reasoning section that enters the permanent record with the instrument, and Girao's runs to several pages of institutional history. It states that Brazil was the first nation to officially admit that OVNIs exist and have extraterrestrial provenance, at a 1954 session at the Escola Superior de Guerra in Rio at which the then Aeronautica captain Joao Adil de Oliveira spoke to officers, civilians and press, and that France followed only in 1976. It states that since 1954 the Brazilian government has created several official UFO research programmes through the Aeronautica, naming Operacao Prato in 1977, SIOANI in 1969 at the IV Comando Aereo Regional in Sao Paulo, and the 1986 night in which 21 spherical objects, each given as 100 metres in diameter, were pursued for hours by Brazilian jet fighters. It states that the Aeronautica was always discreet about these facts but never denied them when asked. It states that from 2007 the Aeronautica, and expressly not the Exercito and not the Marinha, began sending its papers to the Arquivo Nacional, and that the total now exceeds 20,000 pages. It records that in August 2010 the then FAB commander determined by an instrument published in the Diario Oficial da Uniao that all OVNI cases across the force be concentrated at COMDABRA for onward transmission. It records the April 2013 meeting at the Ministry of Defence, convened at the invitation of then Foreign Minister Celso Amorim and held before the service commanders, at which researchers pressed for the Army and Navy files. And it gives the archive arithmetic directly: searching OVNI alone yields 137 registros, but the reference code BR DFANBSB ARX yields 758 documents, some of them more than 70 years old.

The justificacao also turns outward, and that is where the comparison it enables becomes explicit. It notes that at least 30 nations established research commissions, that the 2021 Pentagon UAP preliminary assessment examined 144 sighting cases of which only one was explained, and that on 15 March 2022 President Biden signed an omnibus funding bill including 782.5 billion dollars for defence with resources reserved for unexplained aerial phenomena research legislated within the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act. Brazil, in other words, put the American record into its own legislative record while noting that its own files were already open.

The session itself, on 24 June 2022, was held in the Senate plenary and is documented in the Senate's own file with individual presentation documents lodged for each invited speaker: Rony Vernet, Ademar Jose, Gary Heseltine, Geraldo Lemos Neto, Inajar Antonio Kurowski, Jackson Luiz Camargo, Robert Lambert Salas and Thiago Ticchetti. Agencia Senado's report of the session records Gevaerd calling the opening incomplete but fruitful, Robert Salas, a former US Air Force officer, describing unidentified objects disabling ten nuclear weapons at a launch facility he commanded, and the delivery to Girao at the close of a document the participants called the Carta de Brasilia, recommending creation of a permanent joint civil and military commission to enable organised research on the subject.

One error must be named and buried. A previous pass on this board asserted that Senator Girao brought the 1996 Varginha case to Capitol Hill in 2026. Nothing in the reporting located supports that. Girao's verified, documented action is RQS 193/2022 and the 24 June 2022 special session, and the board should carry that and nothing beyond it.

claims.text: Requerimento no 193, de 2022 (RQS 193/2022) was authored by Senador Eduardo Girao (PODEMOS/CE) with co-signatories Paulo Rocha (PT/PA), Izalci Lucas (PSDB/DF), Reguffe (PODEMOS/DF), Jorge Kajuru (PODEMOS/GO), Marcos do Val (PODEMOS/ES), Alessandro Vieira (CIDADANIA/SE) and Eliziane Gama (CIDADANIA/MA), and was presented and read on 16 March 2022.

The ementa of RQS 193/2022 is 'Sessao especial destinada a comemorar os 75 anos do Dia Mundial da Ufologia'. Its nature is recorded as 'Realizacao de sessao especial ou comemoracao no periodo do expediente'. It is a request for a commemorative plenary session under Article 199 of the Regimento Interno do Senado Federal, not an instrument compelling the production of records.

The requerimento was approved by the Plenary on 16 March 2022 and the special session was held on 24 June 2022; its tramitacao is closed, with the last recorded location the Coordenacao de Arquivo on 29 June 2022.

The instrument's official publications are: Diario do Senado Federal no 32 of 17 March 2022, pages 269 to 275 and page 62; and Diario do Senado Federal no 99 of 25 June 2022, pages 7 to 67 recording the special session.

claims.text: The justificacao of RQS 193/2022 names Operacao Prato (1977), the creation of SIOANI in 1969 at the IV Comando Aereo Regional in Sao Paulo, and the 1986 'Noite Oficial dos UFOs no Brasil' as official Brazilian government UFO research programmes run through the Aeronautica.

The justificacao states that a search of the Arquivo Nacional for the term OVNI alone returns 137 registros, while a search on the specific reference code BR DFANBSB ARX returns 758 documents, some over 70 years old.

The justificacao states that from 2007 the Aeronautica, but not the Exercito and not the Marinha, began sending its research papers to the Arquivo Nacional in Brasilia, totalling more than 20,000 pages of released files.

The justificacao records that in August 2010 the then commander of the FAB determined, by an instrument published in the Diario Oficial da Uniao, that all OVNI cases registered across the force's installations be concentrated at COMDABRA for transmission to the Arquivo Nacional.

The justificacao asserts that Brazil was the first nation to officially admit that OVNIs exist and are of extraterrestrial provenance, at a 1954 session at the Escola Superior de Guerra in Rio de Janeiro addressed by the then Aeronautica captain Joao Adil de Oliveira, with France following in 1976.
The justificacao states that the Aeronautica was always discreet about these matters but never denied them when questioned.

The justificacao cites the 2021 Pentagon UAP report as examining 144 sighting cases of which only one was explained, and cites the omnibus funding bill signed by President Biden on 15 March 2022 including 782.5 billion dollars for defence with resources reserved for UAP research legislated within the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act.

The Senate file for the matter lodges individual presentation documents dated 24 June 2022 for invited speakers Rony Vernet, Ademar Jose, Gary Heseltine, Geraldo Lemos Neto, Inajar Antonio Kurowski, Jackson Luiz Camargo, Robert Lambert Salas and Thiago Ticchetti.

At the 24 June 2022 session, former US Air Force officer Robert Salas told the Senate plenary that he had witnessed the presence of unidentified objects that deactivated ten nuclear weapons at a launch facility under his command.
claims.source: Agencia Senado, 'Em homenagem no Plenario, ufologos cobram liberacao de documentos sobre ovnis', 24 June 2022, https://www12.senado.leg.br/noticias/materias/2022/06/24/em-homenagem-no-plenario-ufologos-cobram-liberacao-de-documentos-sobre-ovnis

claims.text: At the close of the session the invited participants delivered to Senator Girao a document they called the Carta de Brasilia, recommending the creation of a permanent joint civil and military commission to enable organised research on the subject.

dossier.denialPosture: None on the part of the Senate. The chamber's posture is the inverse of denial: it approved a plenary session on the subject unanimously enough to be recorded simply as 'Aprovada pelo Plenario', gave the floor to foreign and domestic witnesses including a former US Air Force officer, and entered into its permanent Diario the specific archive reference code under which its own military's files can be retrieved.
connections: RQS 193/2022 documents the Forca Aerea Brasileira's programmes (fab), naming SIOANI, Operacao Prato (operacao-prato) and the 1986 night (ev-noite-ovnis-1986).
Cites the Arquivo Nacional's OVNI holdings (arquivo-nacional-ufo) by reference code BR DFANBSB ARX and by document count.

Its justificacao explicitly frames the Brazilian record against the US record, citing the 2021 Pentagon UAP preliminary assessment and FY2022 NDAA UAP funding, which places it directly alongside the nip node.
Robert Salas, a witness at the 24 June 2022 session, connects the Brazilian legislative record to the US nuclear-facility incident testimony stream.
A. J. Gevaerd, who interviewed Capitao Uyrange Hollanda in 1997, testified at the same session, linking the Operacao Prato node to the Senate node through a single individual.
The Carta de Brasilia's proposal of a permanent joint civil-military commission is the Brazilian counterpart to the US push for a UAP Records Review Board.
openQuestions: A previous research pass asserted that Senator Girao brought the 1996 Varginha case to Capitol Hill in 2026. No source located supports this. It should be treated as retracted unless a primary record is produced.

No Brazilian legislative instrument has been located that compels production of Army or Navy holdings, establishes a records review board, or creates the permanent joint commission proposed in the Carta de Brasilia.
The text of the Carta de Brasilia itself has not been retrieved; its content is known only through Agencia Senado's summary.
Whether any of the eight co-signatory senators pursued follow-on action after the session closed on 29 June 2022 is not established.

The full stenographic record of the 24 June 2022 session is published in DSF no 99, pages 7 to 67, but has not been read in this pass; individual statements beyond those summarised by Agencia Senado are unverified.

Several factual assertions inside the justificacao, notably the 100-metre diameter figure for the 1986 objects and the primacy claim for Brazil in 1954, are the author's assertions entered into the record, not independently verified findings.

l0.label: National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDS)

dossier.whatItIs: The National Institute for Discovery Science was a privately financed research organization based in Las Vegas, Nevada, formed by real-estate developer Robert Bigelow in October 1995 and disbanded in October 2004. It bought the 480-acre Sherman ranch in the Uinta Basin near Fort Duchesne, Utah — the property later known as Skinwalker Ranch — in 1996 and staffed it around the clock with scientists and a veterinarian. It was the direct organizational and personnel predecessor to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, the contractor that executed the Defense Intelligence Agency's AAWSAP contract from 2008.
dossier.whyImplicated: NIDS is the point at which anomaly research moved into private hands under conditions of contractual secrecy, and it is the documented bridge from that private effort into a DIA-funded government program. Within weeks of buying the ranch Bigelow had the previous owner, Terry Sherman, working for him under a nondisclosure agreement that Sherman told the Las Vegas Sun prevented him from discussing what happened on the property — a private-sector information control instrument doing exactly the work a security classification would do, without any of the accountability. NIDS drew its personnel directly from the national security research establishment: John B. Alexander, the former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratory, was the institute's public voice from its Las Vegas offices in 1996. And the continuity to government is not inferential: Rice University's published biography of Colm Kelleher states that he led the NIDS team on Skinwalker Ranch from 1996 to 2004 and that "in 2008, Kelleher became deputy administrator of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) where he led the day-to-day operations in executing the AAWSAP contract with Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)." NIDS is where the government's later program acquired its methodology, its site, its database concept and its senior staff.
dossier.narrative:
The sequence is tight and dated. In July 1996 the Sherman family broke years of silence and went public in the Deseret News and on national radio with accounts of strange lights, lights emerging from circular "doorways" that appeared in mid-air, three cows mutilated, several others vanished, unusual soil impressions and circles of flattened grass. Several weeks later Robert Bigelow met the Shermans and negotiated to buy the 480-acre ranch for about $200,000. By 23 October 1996, when the Las Vegas Sun published its account, Bigelow had erected an observation building, moved in a pair of scientists and a veterinarian, and had someone on the property twenty-four hours a day recording anything out of the ordinary. The Shermans relocated fifteen miles away. Terry Sherman stayed on as ranch caretaker, employed by Bigelow, and told the Sun he could no longer discuss the activity because of a nondisclosure agreement Bigelow had him sign. He also said he had been offered more money by a Colorado family and a local hunting club but did not want to put anyone at risk. His summary: "It's just been a bad deal all the way around. All that's really redeeming is that you have some knowledge that a lot of people don't have, for what it's worth."

The institutional framing was scientific and the operating posture was closed. Officially the research was conducted by the National Institute for Discovery Science, which Bigelow had formed the previous October. John B. Alexander — described in the same article as "former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratories in New Mexico" — spoke for the institute and articulated the public mission: "Our approach is to do good, high-quality research using a standard scientific approach and do what we can to get hard data. One of the missions of the institute is to make information widely available." He said results would be published in scientific journals and on the institute's web page. Bigelow declined to be interviewed. Alexander would not provide details of how or why the research was being conducted. Outside researchers, including Chris O'Brien, who had visited the ranch in July before Bigelow's involvement and called it "the most impressive case I've ever personally investigated," objected that "it should be public knowledge."

The cattle-mutilation program was built deliberately. Bigelow met Roosevelt, Utah veterinarian Dan Dennis on 15 October 1996 to ask for assistance performing necropsies on any animals whose deaths or mutilations might be tied to UFO or paranormal phenomena, and planned to write to area ranchers requesting notification of unusual animal deaths. From 1999 NIDS ran a public hotline; over five thousand reports arrived by phone and email, many later attributed to missile test launches and meteors. NIDS's stated research areas were cattle mutilation and black triangle reports. Colm Kelleher, deputy administrator, framed the scope: "We don't study aliens, we study anomalies. They're the same thing in a lot of people's minds, but not in our minds." NIDS disbanded in October 2004.

What matters for this board is what happened next. Kelleher went from NIDS to Prosetta in San Francisco from 2004 to 2008, where he was laboratory director executing Department of Defense contracts to discover drugs against Ebola virus and other viruses of interest to DoD — a four-year interval inside the DoD contracting system. Then, per Rice University's published biography, "in 2008, Kelleher became deputy administrator of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) where he led the day-to-day operations in executing the AAWSAP contract with Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)." Rice lists his affiliation on that page as "Program Manager, Advanced Aerospace System Weapons Application Program (AAWSAP) Contractor, Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)." From 2012 to 2020 he ran the Environmental Control and Life Support Systems department at Bigelow Aerospace, building life-support systems for expandable spacecraft. He co-authored Hunt for the Skinwalker (2005) with George Knapp and Skinwalkers at the Pentagon (2021) with James Lacatski and Knapp.

The archival record now treats NIDS and BAASS as a continuous object. The finding aid for the Jacques F. Vallee UFO and paranormal phenomena papers at Rice describes the collection as containing "field notes and press documents about related topics such as cattle mutilations, and face-to-face meetings of NIDS and BAASS, as well as various research proposals." Vallee — one of the reported NIDS science advisory board members — is thus the custodian of documentation on the meetings that connect the private institute to the DIA contractor, and that documentation sits in a collection restricted until 2028 and 2031.

The analytic significance of NIDS is not that it proved anything. None of the NIDS work was published in a peer-reviewed journal despite Alexander's 1996 commitment. The significance is structural. NIDS demonstrated that a private individual with sufficient capital could stand up an anomaly-research operation staffed by former national-laboratory and intelligence-community personnel, acquire physical custody of a site of interest, impose nondisclosure obligations on witnesses, collect data outside any government records system, and then — twelve years later — sell that same capability, that same site, that same database concept and that same staff back to the Defense Intelligence Agency under a contract. Whatever NIDS collected between 1996 and 2004 was never subject to FOIA, never subject to congressional oversight, and was never in a federal recordkeeping system. That is a concealment architecture built out of contract law rather than classification, and it is the model the AAWSAP era inherited.

claims.text: NIDS was formed by Robert Bigelow in October 1995; the Las Vegas Sun reported on 23 October 1996 that the ranch research was "being conducted by the National Institute for Discovery Science, which Bigelow formed last October."

Bigelow negotiated to buy the Shermans' 480-acre ranch for about $200,000 several weeks after the family went public in July 1996 with accounts of lights emerging from circular "doorways" appearing in mid-air, three mutilated cows, several missing cattle, unusual soil impressions and circles of flattened grass.

By October 1996 Bigelow had erected an observation building on the property, installed a pair of scientists and a veterinarian, and maintained someone on the property twenty-four hours a day recording anything out of the ordinary.
Terry Sherman, retained by Bigelow to maintain the ranch, told the Las Vegas Sun he could no longer discuss the activity because of a nondisclosure agreement Bigelow had him sign.

John B. Alexander, described as "former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratories in New Mexico," was among the scientists involved and spoke for NIDS from its Las Vegas offices, stating that "one of the missions of the institute is to make information widely available" and that results would be published in scientific journals and on the institute's web page.

Bigelow met Roosevelt, Utah veterinarian Dan Dennis on 15 October 1996 to request assistance performing necropsies on animals whose deaths or mutilations might be tied to UFO or paranormal phenomena, and planned to write area ranchers requesting notification of unusual animal deaths.

Bigelow declined to be interviewed and Alexander would not provide details of how or why the research was being conducted; outside researchers including Chris O'Brien, who had visited the ranch in July 1996, objected that the case "should be public knowledge."
NIDS operated from 1995 to 2004 and was disbanded in October 2004; its research areas were cattle mutilation and black triangle reports.
NIDS established a hotline in 1999 to receive reports of odd occurrences and received over 5,000 reports by phone and email; officials said many were explained as missile test launches and meteors.
Deputy Administrator Colm Kelleher characterized the institute's scope as: "We don't study aliens, we study anomalies. They're the same thing in a lot of people's minds, but not in our minds."

Rice University's published biography of Colm A. Kelleher states: "From 1996-2004, he led the National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDS) team on Skinwalker Ranch as well as multiple other NIDS projects."

The same Rice biography states: "In 2008, Kelleher became deputy administrator of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) where he led the day-to day operations in executing the AAWSAP contract with Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)," and lists his affiliation as "Program Manager, Advanced Aerospace System Weapons Application Program (AAWSAP) Contractor, Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)."

Between the NIDS and BAASS periods, from 2004 to 2008, Kelleher served as laboratory director at San Francisco biotechnology company Prosetta, leading teams executing Department of Defense contracts to discover drugs against Ebola virus and other viruses of interest to DoD.

The finding aid for the Jacques F. Vallee UFO and paranormal phenomena papers (MS 0672, Woodson Research Center, Rice University) states the collection contains "field notes and press documents about related topics such as cattle mutilations, and face-to-face meetings of NIDS and BAASS, as well as various research proposals"; the collection is restricted, with Series I and II opening 24 January 2028 and Series III case files 1 January 2031.

dossier.denialPosture: NIDS did not deny; it declined. Bigelow refused interviews, Alexander refused to explain how or why the research was being conducted, and the previous owner was placed under a nondisclosure agreement within weeks of the sale. Alexander's 1996 public commitment that results would appear in scientific journals was not fulfilled — no NIDS finding was published in a peer-reviewed journal in the institute's nine-year existence.
connections: Robert Bigelow — founder and sole financier; later founder of Bigelow Aerospace and Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, the AAWSAP prime contractor, and of the Bigelow Institute for Consciousness Studies.

Colm A. Kelleher — the load-bearing personnel link: NIDS Skinwalker team lead 1996-2004, DoD contract laboratory director 2004-2008, BAASS deputy administrator and AAWSAP day-to-day manager from 2008, Bigelow Aerospace ECLSS department head 2012-2020.
John B. Alexander — former director of non-lethal weapons testing at Los Alamos National Laboratory, a Battelle-co-managed facility, and the public voice of NIDS in 1996.

George Knapp — the KLAS-TV journalist whose 1996 reporting brought the ranch to Bigelow's attention; later co-author with Kelleher of Hunt for the Skinwalker (2005) and, with Kelleher and James Lacatski, Skinwalkers at the Pentagon (2021).
Jacques Vallee — reported NIDS advisory board member and the archival custodian of NIDS-BAASS meeting documentation now held at Rice under restriction.
James Lacatski — the DIA official associated with AAWSAP's creation and Kelleher's later co-author.
Defense Intelligence Agency — the government customer that in 2008 contracted with BAASS for AAWSAP, importing the NIDS methodology and staff into a federal program.
Terry and Gwen Sherman — the witnesses whose testimony was placed under a private nondisclosure agreement, and the Deseret News, the outlet that first published it in July 1996.

Los Alamos National Laboratory — Alexander's prior employer, operated by Triad National Security LLC of which Battelle is a member; the same installation the Robertson Panel identified in 1953 as an unexplained sighting cluster.

Christopher "Kit" Green, Hal Puthoff and John Schuessler are reported in secondary accounts to have served on the NIDS science advisory board alongside Vallee and Alexander; this roster is not established by any primary source located here.
openQuestions: The full NIDS science advisory board roster, its meeting minutes and its charter have never been published. Secondary accounts name Kit Green as chairman with Hal Puthoff, John B. Alexander, Jacques Vallee, John Schuessler, Edgar Mitchell and Harrison Schmitt among the participants; no primary document confirms this.
What became of the NIDS data holdings when the institute disbanded in October 2004? Were they transferred to Bigelow Aerospace, to BAASS in 2008, or destroyed?
The terms and scope of the Sherman nondisclosure agreement have never been disclosed. Is it still in force, and how many other witnesses signed comparable instruments?
Did any federal agency fund, task or receive NIDS product between 1995 and 2004, before the 2008 DIA contract?
NIDS ran a hotline receiving over 5,000 reports. Where is that report corpus now, and did any of it enter the AAWSAP database?
Alexander committed publicly in 1996 to journal publication. Was that commitment abandoned by choice, by the absence of results, or by an internal restriction?
Vallee's papers document face-to-face meetings between NIDS and BAASS. Who attended, when, and what was transferred? The files are restricted until 2028-2031.

The AAWSAP solicitation and contract numbers reported in secondary accounts (solicitation HHM402-08-R-0211; contract HHM402-08-C-0072, performance beginning 22 September 2008) have not been verified here against a primary contracting record.

l0.label: EarthTech International / Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin
l0.short: EarthTech International / Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin

dossier.whatItIs: EarthTech International, Inc. is a private research company in Austin, Texas, incorporated in 1991 as the corporate vehicle for the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin, which Harold E. Puthoff founded in 1985. Its declared research program covers spacetime and gravitation theory, the quantum vacuum and zero-point energy, modifications to standard electrodynamics, interstellar flight science, and SETI, framed as inputs to innovative space propulsion and energy generation. Puthoff is president, CEO and board chairman; Eric W. Davis is chief science officer.
dossier.whyImplicated: EarthTech is the intellectual clearinghouse where the legacy program's technical vocabulary was written down and then sold back to the government as reference literature. Under the Defense Intelligence Agency's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, EarthTech was subcontracted through Robert Bigelow's BAASS, and Puthoff and Davis commissioned the set of expert studies that DIA published as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on traversable wormholes, antigravity, metamaterials and invisibility cloaking. That output supplied the exact conceptual frame — non-chemical propulsion, spacetime metric engineering, exotic materials — that Congress later wrote into statute as the boundary of a covered reverse-engineering program. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I aims squarely at this network without naming it, attributing the reverse-engineering allegations to a group involved in UAP endeavors "since at least 2009" and tied to "a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE." AARO's own account therefore places these people at the center of both the DIA program and its DHS successor attempt, while insisting nothing was ever recovered.
dossier.narrative:
Harold E. Puthoff earned his PhD at Stanford in 1967 as a theoretical and experimental physicist working on lasers, and spent the 1970s running the SRI International parapsychology program with Russell Targ under intelligence-community sponsorship — the lineage that became Project STARGATE. In 1985 he founded the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin; in 1991 it was incorporated under EarthTech International, Inc. Both remain co-located in Austin. Eric W. Davis, whose declared specializations include breakthrough propulsion physics, beamed energy propulsion, directed energy weapons, general relativity, quantum field theory, quantum gravity and what he calls SETI-xenoarchaeology, is chief science officer of both entities.

The institutional significance is not the physics. It is that EarthTech occupied, for four decades, a specific structural position: a small, privately held, security-cleared research house with no shareholders to answer to, no publication obligations, and a standing relationship with the parts of the defense and intelligence enterprise that buy speculative propulsion analysis. That is precisely the shape of entity a legacy program would need — small enough to compartment, technical enough to be credible, private enough to sit outside the FOIA perimeter.

The documented engagement is AAWSAP. In 2008 the Defense Intelligence Agency awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, reported at up to $22 million over five years, to assess advanced aerospace threats. Puthoff served as the program's chief scientist on the BAASS side, and EarthTech was subcontracted to produce the written product. Puthoff and Davis commissioned a series of thirty-eight expert studies, which DIA then issued as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. The subjects released into the public record include traversable wormholes and negative energy, antigravity, metamaterials for aerospace applications, and invisibility cloaking. Whatever one makes of the science, the procurement fact is unambiguous: a U.S. intelligence agency paid, through a contractor and a subcontractor, for a reference library on how one would build and analyze a craft that violates the propulsion assumptions of every acquisition program in the department. Fifteen years later Congress drafted the covered-activity definition for UAP reverse-engineering as any aerospace craft using "propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust" — the DIRD library's subject matter, rendered as statutory text.

Davis is also the pivot of the two most consequential unofficial documents in the modern record. In October 2002 he met with retired Vice Admiral Thomas Ray Wilson, former director of DIA; the handwritten notes of that conversation, describing a special access program under contractor control that had denied access to a senior flag officer, surfaced publicly in 2019 as the Wilson-Davis memo. In July 2020 the New York Times reported that Davis, then a contractor for Aerospace Corporation, had briefed a Defense Department agency in October 2019 and Senate Armed Services Committee staff about retrievals from "off-world vehicles not made on this earth." Both items are contested; neither is invented. Both were produced by the chief science officer of EarthTech International.

The AARO response is where this entity becomes central rather than peripheral. Volume I never names EarthTech, Puthoff, Davis or Bigelow. It does not need to. It states that the modern reverse-engineering claims stem "largely" from "a consistent group of individuals who have been involved in various UAP-related endeavors since at least 2009," and that many of them were "involved in or supportive of a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE." The cancelled DIA program is AAWSAP. AARO's rebuttal is therefore built on the same population that AARO concedes staffed a real, funded DIA program and then attempted, unsuccessfully, to stand up a DHS prospective special access program to continue it. AARO also reports resolving a claimed anomalous material sample to magnesium "and bismuth with some other trace elements, such as lead" by materials characterization — the layered magnesium-bismuth specimen that has circulated through this network for decades and been analyzed by parties associated with it.

The network extends forward. Davis appears on the team roster of the Disclosure Foundation, the organization chaired by former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Christopher Mellon, whose published recommendations two of the three FY2026 NDAA UAP provisions mirror. So the same technical population that wrote the DIA reference library, that AARO identifies as the source of the circular reporting, and that pitched KONA BLUE to DHS, is also inside the advocacy apparatus that now shapes what Congress writes into the defense authorization act. That is not a contradiction. It is what a closed technical community looks like when the subject matter has no other constituency.

claims.text: The Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin was founded in 1985 by Harold E. Puthoff, PhD, and was later incorporated under EarthTech International, Inc., in 1991; both are based in Austin, Texas.

Harold E. Puthoff is president, CEO and chairman of the board of EarthTech International, Inc., and director of the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin; he received his PhD from Stanford University in 1967 as a theoretical and experimental physicist specializing in lasers.

Eric W. Davis, PhD, is chief science officer of EarthTech International, Inc. and the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin, with declared specializations including breakthrough propulsion physics for interstellar flight, beamed energy propulsion, directed energy weapons, quantum gravity theories and SETI-xenoarchaeology.

EarthTech's declared research interests include theories of spacetime, gravity and cosmology; studies of the quantum vacuum; modifications of standard theories of electrodynamics; interstellar flight science; and SETI, specifically as applied to developing innovative space propulsion and sources of energy.

EarthTech International was subcontracted by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies to produce the written product of the DIA's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program; Puthoff and his EarthTech colleague Eric W. Davis commissioned a series of 38 expert studies that DIA issued as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents.
claims.source: Vice, "Newly-Released Documents Shed Light on Government-Funded Research Into Worm Holes, Anti-Gravity and Invisibility Cloaks," https://www.vice.com/en/article/newly-released-documents-shed-light-on-government-funded-research-into-worm-holes-anti-gravity-and-invisibility-cloaks/

claims.text: The Defense Intelligence Reference Documents produced under AAWSAP include studies of traversable wormholes, antigravity, and invisibility cloaking.

AAWSAP was initiated in 2008 and awarded to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) under a contract reported at up to $22 million over five years, with the stated purpose of investigating potential aerospace threats including advanced technologies potentially linked to UAP observations.
claims.source: "Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)," WikiDisc, https://www.wikidisc.org/wiki/Advanced_Aerospace_Weapon_System_Applications_Program_(AAWSAP) ; see also Metabunk, "The Origins of AAWSAP," https://www.metabunk.org/threads/the-origins-of-aawsap.12484/

claims.text: Harold Puthoff served as chief scientist of the AAWSAP program on the BAASS side and oversaw its scientific studies.
