claims.text: Before founding the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin, Puthoff ran the SRI International remote-viewing research program with Russell Targ during the 1970s under U.S. intelligence-community sponsorship.

The New York Times reported that Eric W. Davis, then a contractor with Aerospace Corporation, briefed a Department of Defense agency in October 2019 and, separately, Senate Armed Services Committee staff, on retrievals from "off-world vehicles not made on this earth."

Unit Will Make Some Findings Public," The New York Times, 23 July 2020; discussion and document trail at Metabunk, https://www.metabunk.org/threads/debunked-pentagon-has-evidence-of-off-world-vehicles-not-made-on-this-earth.11334/

claims.text: AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I attributes modern reverse-engineering claims largely to "a consistent group of individuals who have been involved in various UAP-related endeavors since at least 2009," many of whom AARO says were "involved in or supportive of a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE" — a description that maps onto the AAWSAP/BAASS/EarthTech network without naming it.

claims.text: AARO reports resolving a claimed anomalous material sample to magnesium "and bismuth with some other trace elements, such as lead," on the basis of materials characterization.
claims.source: AARO Historical Record Report Volume 1 (2024), p. 9, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:AARO_Historical_Record_Report_Volume_1_2024.pdf/9

claims.text: Eric Davis is listed as a member of the team of the Disclosure Foundation, the advocacy organization chaired by former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Christopher Mellon.

claims.text: The FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act's proposed covered-activity definition for UAP reverse-engineering reached work on "any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust" — the subject matter of the AAWSAP reference library that EarthTech curated.
claims.source: Douglas Dean Johnson, Mirador, 24 June 2023, quoting S. 2103 Sec. 1104, https://douglasjohnson.ghost.io/senate-intelligence-bill-gives-holders-of-non-earth-origin-six-months/

dossier.denialPosture: EarthTech does not publish denials; it publishes physics. Its public posture is that of an ordinary small research institute working on quantum vacuum energy and advanced propulsion, with no reference on its own site to crash retrieval, custody of material, or the programs its principals are alleged to have served. That silence is itself a posture: the entity most persistently named in reverse-engineering allegations has never issued a dated, attributable statement addressing them, which leaves the government's characterizations — AARO's unnamed 'consistent group of individuals' — as the only on-the-record account.
connections: Robert Bigelow / Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) — prime contractor on the DIA AAWSAP award; EarthTech was the subcontractor producing the study product.
Defense Intelligence Agency — customer for AAWSAP and publisher of the 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents; the 'cancelled DIA program' in AARO's Volume I.
KONA BLUE / Department of Homeland Security — AARO's named prospective special access program, described as the failed attempt to reestablish the cancelled DIA program.
Vice Admiral Thomas Ray Wilson (USN, ret.), former DIA director — subject of Eric Davis's October 2002 meeting notes, the Wilson-Davis memo.
Christopher Mellon and the Disclosure Foundation — Davis is on the team roster; Mellon's recommendations are mirrored in FY2026 NDAA UAP provisions.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand's IAA amendment — the 'person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government' language is drafted to reach entities structurally identical to EarthTech.
AARO Historical Record Report Volume I — the official rebuttal aimed at this network, and the Volume II that would have carried the underlying interview record.
To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science — the 2017 vehicle where Puthoff, Luis Elizondo and Christopher Mellon overlapped publicly (relationship asserted in the popular record; see openQuestions).
openQuestions: The DIA contract number and full obligation history for AAWSAP, and the subcontract instrument and dollar value flowing from BAASS to EarthTech International.

dossier.whatItIs: The Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, the OSD principal staff element for defense intelligence, counterintelligence, and security policy, chartered by DoD Directive 5143.01 (24 October 2014, incorporating Change 2, 6 April 2020) under 10 U.S.C. 113 and 137 and Executive Orders 12333, 13470 and 13869. It owns DoD security policy, counterintelligence, and the department's interface with the DoD Special Access Program Central Office. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B)(i), the Director of AARO reports to the USD(I&S) on all administrative matters of the office.
dossier.whyImplicated: OUSD(I&S) is the office that produced the paper trail of the Elizondo counter-narrative, and that paper trail is the cleanest documentary evidence in the entire record of a deliberate, dated, signed effort by a defense component to control the public account of a UAP program. Its Director for Defense Intelligence, Garry Reid, wrote a memorandum for record in late December 2017 — within a week of the New York Times AATIP story — asserting that Luis Elizondo had 'aggrandized his role' and that to the best of Reid's knowledge Elizondo 'had no job responsibilities related to the AATIP,' while simultaneously initiating an AFOSI inquiry into Elizondo's handling of classified material. The Pentagon then sat on that determination for eighteen months before deploying it publicly through spokesman Christopher Sherwood in June 2019, and afterwards quietly amended the wording from 'no responsibilities' to 'no assigned responsibilities.' The same office holds administrative authority over AARO, the body Congress created to investigate the concealment, and it is the department's SAP security-policy owner. The entity that ran the counter-narrative also holds the keys to the compartments and supervises the investigators.
dossier.narrative:
OUSD(I&S) is where the security state's plumbing and its press strategy meet, and the December 2017 file shows both running at once.

The charter first. DoD Directive 5143.01, reissued 24 October 2014 and updated by Change 2 on 6 April 2020, sets the USD(I&S)'s responsibilities, functions, relationships and authorities pursuant to 10 U.S.C. 113 and 137, 50 U.S.C. 3001 et seq., Public Law 108-458, and Executive Orders 12333, 13470 and 13869. The 'and Security' in the title was added in 2019-2020 and is the whole point: this office does not merely produce intelligence, it writes the rules for who may know things. It coordinates with the Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office on SAP matters involving ODNI and the intelligence community, and it runs the department's counterintelligence, law enforcement and security enterprise. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B)(i), enacted by Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA, the Director of AARO 'shall report... to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters of the Office.' Operational and security matters go to the Deputy Secretary and the Principal Deputy DNI; administration — staffing, funding, personnel, facilities — goes to OUSD(I&S). Congress placed the investigative body's housekeeping under the office whose predecessor had spent five years managing the Elizondo problem.

Now the file. Records obtained by The Black Vault under FOIA establish the sequence.

3 October 2017: Elizondo submits a resignation letter, received by his direct supervisor John Garrity III. A second, differently worded resignation letter — the one public since 2018 — is later characterized in Reid's memo as having 'uncertain provenance' and as never delivered to the Secretary of Defense.

12 October 2017: Reid learns of the To The Stars Academy launch, at which Elizondo appears as Director of Global Security and Special Programs one week after leaving DoD and states that TTSA plans to provide 'never-before-released footage from real U.S. government systems.' Reid contacts the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. AFOSI finds no 'tangible indicators' of misconduct and declines to open a case.

7 December 2017: The New York Times contacts DoD about AATIP and Elizondo.

15 December 2017: The OUSD(I) Security Officer is notified that Elizondo may have 'misused government systems' and 'may intend to release [U.S. government] footage or information that he obtained during his employment with OUSD(I).'

16 December 2017: 'Glowing Auras and Black Money' publishes, carrying the FLIR1 and Gimbal videos captioned as released by AATIP and courtesy of the Department of Defense. The same two videos appear on TTSA's YouTube channel.

18 December 2017: OUSD(I) discovers a classified email Elizondo sent to a Navy civilian in August 2017 requesting assistance getting videos declassified, with the same videos attached.

21 December 2017: Reid meets AFOSI agents to initiate a formal inquiry into Elizondo's possible mishandling of classified materials. AFOSI concludes the investigation in April 2018. No charges are known to have followed.

23 December 2017: A copy of Reid's memorandum for record carries handwritten marginal notes and initials dated '12/23' believed to be those of Secretary of Defense James N. Mattis, including a question whether Elizondo's 'sudden departure' was a 'counter-intelligence alarm?'

The two propositions in that file cannot both be casually true. If Elizondo had no job responsibilities related to AATIP, the department's own security office had no reason to fear that he would release government footage 'obtained during his employment with OUSD(I),' and Reid had no reason to open a counterintelligence inquiry about material he possessed. The counter-narrative and the counterintelligence action are internally inconsistent, and both were produced by the same office in the same week.

The eighteen-month gap is the other artifact. The determination was reached in December 2017. It was not made public until June 2019, when spokesman Christopher Sherwood told The Intercept that Elizondo 'had no responsibilities with regard to the AATIP program while he worked in OUSDI... up until the time he resigned effective 10/4/2017.' That formulation was later revised to 'no assigned responsibilities' — a lawyer's edit, narrowing a claim about what a man did to a claim about what was written in his position description. Departments do not narrow their own denials unless the broader version is indefensible.

Reid himself was removed in April 2022, following a nearly two-year investigation by The Debrief; the stated cause was an inappropriate relationship and favoritism with a colleague, not the Elizondo matter, and sources described him as the person most directly responsible for preventing further UAP video releases and for retaliating against Elizondo. The office continued. Bradley Hansell was confirmed as USD(I&S) by the Senate 61-35 and took office 25 July 2025, succeeding acting Under Secretary Dustin Gard-Weiss.

For an analyst the significance is structural rather than personal. The record shows that when a UAP disclosure event occurred, the response was generated inside OUSD(I&S) by the Director for Defense Intelligence, coordinated with a service investigative agency, briefed to the Secretary of Defense within a week, and held in reserve for eighteen months before public deployment. That is not confusion. That is an information operation run through a security-policy office — and the same office now holds administrative authority over AARO and coordination authority over DoD SAPs.

dossier.whatItIs: Americans for Safe Aerospace (ASA) is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2023 by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18F pilot from strike fighter squadron VFA-11. It operates a confidential intake channel through which military and commercial aircrew report UAP encounters, and it functions as the principal non-governmental witness pipeline into Congress. Headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC, it describes itself as the world's largest UAP advocacy community and reported more than 30,000 members as of 2026, up from roughly 4,000 at its founding.
dossier.whyImplicated: ASA is the institution that solved the collection problem the government created. Because there is no protected, non-stigmatizing reporting route for commercial pilots, and because military witnesses face a confusing internal process, the observational data that would test the phenomenon has never been aggregated by the state. ASA aggregates it privately and then feeds it to Congress, which is why its founder's July 2023 testimony landed as the first public congressional hearing to take military pilot and whistleblower evidence. More importantly for a concealment map, ASA is where several people who were inside the classified system have landed: Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force; Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence; Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former head of NOAA and Oceanographer of the Navy; and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. That roster means ASA holds institutional memory of both the task force that collected the data and the committee staff that wrote the oversight statutes. It is a private organization staffed with the government's own former custodians.
dossier.narrative:
ASA's origin is a specific failure of the reporting system. Graves joined the Navy in 2009 and by 2014 was flying with VFA-11 near Virginia Beach when a radar upgrade began producing unknown tracks that were initially dismissed as software glitches and then corroborated on infrared, confirming their physical presence. The sightings became routine enough to appear in daily briefs. The pivotal event was in Warning Area W-72, an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach where all traffic enters through a single GPS point at a set altitude. As two jets crossed the threshold one hundred feet apart, one pilot saw a dark gray cube inside a clear sphere, motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. Both aircraft took evasive action and terminated the mission. The squadron filed a safety report. There was no official acknowledgement and no mechanism to report further sightings. Graves founded ASA to build the mechanism that did not exist.

The organization scaled faster than anyone planned. Its July 18, 2023 launch release for the UAP Witness Campaign stated that more than 30 commercial aircrew and military witnesses had already approached it and that ASA had more than 4,000 members. Eight days later, in written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, Graves reported nearly 5,000 members and more than 30 UAP witnesses being actively worked. By 2026 the public membership figure is over 30,000. The witness profile is itself a finding: the majority are commercial pilots at major airlines, often veterans with decades of experience, and their reports frequently open with an apology, in Graves's phrasing, 'I apologize, I realize this will sound crazy.' They describe objects at altitudes apparently above 40,000 feet, potentially in low earth orbit or in the grey zone below the Karman line, executing right-hand turns, retrograde orbits and j-hooks, with recurring clusters north of Hawaii and in the North Atlantic. They are adamant these are not Starlink flares.

ASA's process is deliberately witness-controlled. A pilot or veteran contacts the organization confidentially with an outline, ASA conducts an interview, brings in an advisor with relevant expertise for evaluation, and only then, and only with the witness's explicit permission, are next steps taken, which can include meetings with congressional staff and Members or with AARO. Most witnesses do not want to speak publicly and fear professional consequences; they want their account added to the data set. That design is a direct response to the retaliation problem that runs through the whole file.

The advisory bench is what makes ASA structurally significant rather than merely large. Its pilots include David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, the first former Navy pilots to meet with Congress about their UAP encounter, plus Michael Greene and Sam Fletcher. Its national security advisors are Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force, Christopher Mellon, Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff on the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is the committee that wrote the AARO statutes and whose chair and ranking member sit inside the eight-member waived-SAP notification group. Its policy advisors include Susan McCue, former chief of staff to Senator Harry Reid, and Bryan Bender, former defense editor at Politico, plus Mike Gold of the NASA UAP Independent Study Team and David Radzanowski, former CFO and Chief of Staff at NASA. Its science bench includes Avi Loeb of Harvard, Garry Nolan of Stanford, Robin Hanson of George Mason and Ravi Starzl of Carnegie Mellon.

The single most operationally important thing ASA has put on the congressional record came through Gallaudet. Graves testified that while serving as an Admiral with Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from the Operations Commander to all one- and two-star subordinates, titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue', attaching the GO FAST video and raising concerns about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach, with a note that the exercise might be shut down for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was removed from both of their systems, and despite routine in-person meetings with that group, no one ever discussed it again. Gallaudet's stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That is a flag officer, on the record through a congressional witness, describing the retroactive deletion of a safety-of-flight communication.

Graves also entered two hard data points into the House record: that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 there had been eleven near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment of June 25, 2021, and that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. He also flagged an unexplained reversal by AARO's director, who told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview shortly before the hearing that he had what he needed.

On policy, ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 in the 118th Congress, which would let civilian pilots report through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System with anti-retaliation protection and public release of all reports, a mechanism recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team. ASA's July 2023 release also documents the organization's read of the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023, sponsored by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, whose central mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena UAP witnesses and documents.

claims.text: Americans for Safe Aerospace is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy lieutenant and F/A-18 pilot, headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC 20006; Graves is Founder and Executive Director.

As of 2026 ASA publicly reports more than 30,000 members and describes itself as 'the world's largest UAP advocacy community dedicated to pilot support, aerospace safety, data-driven research, and analysis of UAP.'

In written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs on July 26, 2023, Graves stated ASA had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses who have approached us.'

Graves testified that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 that there were 11 near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment on UAP dated June 25, 2021.

Graves testified that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operation managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP.

ASA's national security advisory bench includes Jay Stratton (former Director, UAP Task Force), Christopher Mellon (former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence), Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet (former head of NOAA), and Kirk McConnell (former professional staff, Senate Armed Services Committee).

ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 (118th Congress), which would allow civilian pilots to report UAP through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System, provide protection against retaliation, and make all UAP reports publicly available; the mechanism was recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team.

ASA documented that the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 was proposed by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, and that its key mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to 'hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena [UAP] witnesses and documents' in connection with declassifying UAP documents for public distribution.

Its posture toward the government's own position is captured in Graves's testimony noting that AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview a week before the hearing that he had what he needed, a reversal Graves flagged on the record as unexplained.

l0.label: USS Theodore Roosevelt Encounters (2014-2015)

dossier.whatItIs: The sustained series of unidentified object encounters reported by U.S. Navy aircrews operating with Carrier Air Wing One and the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group off the U.S. East Coast from roughly the summer of 2014 through the Roosevelt's 2015 deployment work-ups. The episode produced the two ATFLIR infrared videos known publicly as GIMBAL and GOFAST, both of which the Navy has officially dated to 21 January 2015.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the case in which a U.S. Navy fighter squadron documented an unidentified object corridor over an active training range for months, and the institutional response was to erase the paperwork rather than identify the objects. Ryan Graves testified under oath that after a near-collision at the W-72 entry point his squadron submitted a safety report and there was "no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings." The stronger allegation, entered into the same congressional record, comes from Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet: a 2015 SIPRNET email from the Fleet Forces operations commander to all one- and two-star admirals, titled "Urgent safety of flight issue" and attaching the GO FAST video, was removed from his and his deputy's classified systems the next day and never discussed — which he attributes to a classified special access program. That is a documented instance of a compartmented program reaching into a flag officer's classified mail to delete a safety-of-flight warning. Meanwhile the Navy's own on-record position is that it "considers the phenomena contained/depicted in those 3 videos as unidentified" and will provide "no details on individual reports."
dossier.narrative:
In 2014, Lieutenant Ryan Graves was flying F/A-18F Super Hornets with Strike Fighter Squadron 11 out of the Virginia Beach area. Following an upgrade to the squadron's radar, aircrews began detecting unknown objects in their operating airspace. The tracks were initially dismissed as software glitches until they were corroborated with infrared sensors, at which point, in Graves's words, the sightings "became an open secret among our aircrew" and "were so frequent that they became part of daily briefs."

The pivotal incident occurred in Warning Area W-72, a block of restricted airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach through which all traffic enters at a single GPS point and set altitude. Graves testified: "Just at the moment the two jets crossed the threshold, one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere — motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. The jets, only 100 feet apart, were forced to take evasive action. They terminated the mission immediately and returned to base. Our squadron submitted a safety report, but there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings." His description of the objects' performance is specific and falsifiable: they "could accelerate at speeds up to Mach 1, hold their position against hurricane-force winds, and outlast our fighter jets, operating continuously throughout the day," with "no visible means of lift, control surfaces or propulsion."

The cover-up allegation is Gallaudet's, and Graves put it in the record. While serving as an admiral at Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from his boss, the Operations Commander, addressed to all one- and two-star admiral subordinates. The subject line was "Urgent safety of flight issue." Attached was the GO FAST video from a Navy F/A-18. The email asked whether anyone knew the objects' origin, expressed concern about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach — the same airspace as Graves's encounters — and raised the possibility of shutting down the exercise for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was gone from both their systems. Despite routine in-person meetings of that same group, no one ever discussed it. Gallaudet presumes it was removed in connection with a classified special access program, and has stated publicly that after seeing the report he did not believe the objects represented any known human technology.

The Navy's public position is a study in minimal concession. In September 2019, Joseph Gradisher, official spokesperson for the Deputy Chief of Naval Operations for Information Warfare, told The Black Vault that the Navy's official identifiers for the videos do not match the TTSA names FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast — the Navy identifies them by the dates of the observations — and then supplied the dates: "[The] dates are 14 November 2004 for 'FLIR1' and 21 January 2015 for both 'Gimbal' and 'GoFast.'" That single sentence established for the first time that GIMBAL and GOFAST were recorded on the same day and may be two aspects of a single event. Gradisher went on: "The Navy has not publicly released characterizations or descriptions, nor released any hypothesis or conclusions, in regard to the objects contained in the referenced videos," while conceding that "The Navy considers the phenomena contained/depicted in those 3 videos as unidentified." Asked for the location, the answer was: "We will not be providing any details on individual reports." The Navy also confirmed the footage had never been cleared for public release when To The Stars Academy published it in December 2017 and March 2018.

Geography can be reconstructed anyway. Filmmaker Dave Beaty worked the deck logs of USS Normandy, the cruiser escorting the Roosevelt, and placed her on 21 January 2015 slightly more than 100 miles east, roughly equidistant between Jacksonville and Savannah — the JAX operating area. A cruiser stays with the carrier during operations, so the deck log fixes the approximate position of the encounter that the Navy declined to disclose.

What happened afterward is the concealment argument's second half. Graves testified that "all UAP videos since 2021 are classified Secret or above, which prevents the American people and even some Members of Congress from seeing UAP videos like the full GIMBAL video recorded by my squadron." The 2021 UAP Task Force preliminary assessment reported eleven near misses with UAP; Graves said he understood the number had grown. In April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia had experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. Graves founded Americans for Safe Aerospace, which by July 2023 had nearly 5,000 members and was working with more than 30 UAP witnesses, most of whom refuse to speak publicly for fear of professional consequences; he also chairs the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics' UAP Integration and Outreach Committee with roughly 80 volunteer PhDs and aerospace engineers. In his testimony he noted that among the accounts reaching ASA, "in several, sensor data was escalated for analysis and there were profound irregularities in how the data was handled" — the same signature as the deleted email, reported independently by other witnesses.

The loop closes in June 2026. Gallaudet — the flag officer whose deleted email is the strongest public evidence that a special access program suppressed a UAP safety warning about this exact airspace — was named to the government's new UAP Science Advisory Council, seated for oceanography, and restricted to unclassified data.

l0.label: Langley AFB Drone Incursions (December 2023)

dossier.whatItIs: A sustained wave of unidentified aerial incursions over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Hampton, Virginia, beginning the evening of 6 December 2023 and running for roughly seventeen nights into late December. The objects overflew the home of the 1st Fighter Wing and the headquarters of Air Combat Command, the East Coast's principal F-22 Raptor base and a linchpin of the NORAD air-defense mission for Washington, D.C. Neither the Air Force, NORTHCOM, the FBI, nor the Pentagon's UAP office has ever publicly identified what the objects were, who operated them, or where they launched from.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the cleanest modern test case of the board's central proposition: that the United States government maintains a category of aerial object it will not name, and that its institutional response to encountering one is to reach for a label rather than an answer. For seventeen consecutive nights, objects that a four-star general watched from a rooftop transited restricted airspace over the most defended fighter base on the Atlantic seaboard, and the response was to move the F-22s, call in a NASA high-altitude imaging aircraft, hold two weeks of interagency meetings, and then say nothing for three months until a trade publication forced the acknowledgment. The objects were classified as 'uncrewed aerial systems' without a single one being downed, captured, tracked to a launch point, or attributed to any operator, and the Pentagon's own anomaly office told a reporter in May 2024 that it had never received a report on the incident at all. The government therefore produced, in the same event, a defense failure it could not explain and a taxonomy it could not justify: a 'drone' with no drone attached to it. Langley is the node where the concealment apparatus and the air-defense apparatus become visibly the same apparatus, because the thing that stopped the inquiry was not an absence of sensors but an official noun.
dossier.narrative:
The incursions began after dark on 6 December 2023. A Langley Air Force Base spokesperson, responding to The War Zone three months later, confirmed the outline in language that has never been amended: the installation 'first observed UAS activities the evening of December 6' and 'experienced multiple incursions throughout the month of December,' with the number of objects fluctuating and their size and configuration varying. The same statement declined to discuss impacts to operations or force protection measures, and noted only that the FAA had been made aware.

What that statement omitted was the scale of the response. Flight-tracking hobbyists watching Newport News in mid-December saw F-16s flying what looked like combat air patrols with tanker support around 12 December. The following week, one of NASA's three WB-57F high-altitude research jets, civil registration N927NA, flew circular orbits with Langley at their center. NASA's own public airborne-science calendar listed N927NA as tasked with 'Imagery Support' on 18 and 19 December 2023. Asked about it, NASA's Langley Research Center said the aircraft had been on the East Coast to image the SpaceX CRS-29 capsule's return and that 'while in the area, the aircraft provided additional imaging support in Virginia.' A NORAD/NORTHCOM spokesperson told The War Zone in December that NORTHCOM 'has been coordinating with [the] FBI' and referred further questions to the Bureau. The FBI declined to comment then and declined again in March 2024.

The senior officer on the ground was Gen. Mark Kelly, then commander of Air Combat Command, headquartered at Langley. He went to the roof of a squadron building for an unobstructed view. His account, given to 60 Minutes in March 2025, is the most detailed first-person military description on the record: 'The reports were coming in 20-to-30 sightings, same time every evening, 30-to-45 minutes after sunset.' The objects varied in size, altitude, and speed. 'The smallest, you know you're talking about a commercial-size quadcopter. And then the largest ones are probably size what I would call a bass boat or a small car.' The Wall Street Journal, reporting in October 2024, had one object at roughly twenty feet long, moving at more than 100 miles an hour at 3,000 to 4,000 feet, with others following one by one and sounding at distance like a parade of lawn mowers.

Gen. Glen VanHerck was the NORAD and NORTHCOM commander at the time. He provided fighters, AWACS, and helicopters to try to characterize the objects, and could not. NORAD's radars, built to see high-altitude bombers and missiles, could not see things a person could see with the naked eye. Asked by CBS whether he could rule out hobbyists, VanHerck said no: 'It would be my assessment they weren't hobbyists because of the magnitude of the events, the sizes of some of the drones, and the duration.' He added the sentence the board treats as load-bearing: 'It certainly could have a foreign nexus, a threat nexus.' A senior official in the Biden White House told 60 Minutes, anonymously, that it was likely the work of hobbyists. Both statements describe the same seventeen nights. Only one of them is attributable.

The first public official acknowledgment came on 14 March 2024, when VanHerck's successor, Gen. Gregory Guillot, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that counter-UAS had dominated his first month in command, that he 'wasn't prepared for the number of incursions,' and that he had 'gone into the events at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, and I'm using that as the centerpiece of my 90-day assessment.' The War Zone published its investigation the next day. Everything the public knows about Langley therefore entered the record either through a reporter's persistence or through a general's aside at a budget hearing, never through an announcement.

The subsequent posture is instructive. In October 2024 Guillot told reporters at Peterson Space Force Base that 'the only thing I can tell you about the Langley drones is roughly the number and roughly the altitude,' that he did not know whether they had been tracked to a recovery point or launched from a vessel offshore, and that he knew of no 'organized or unorganized foreign nexus.' That same month, Langley's 633rd Contracting Squadron posted a sources-sought notice for counter-drone netting to be draped over up to 42 open-ended aircraft sunshades: a base that could not identify what flew over it buying nets to catch it. In February 2025 Guillot told the SASC there had been 350 drone detections at 100 different military installations in 2024, and that only about half of U.S. installations even qualify as 'covered installations' with authority to act under 10 U.S.C. 130i.

Then came New Jersey. Beginning November 2024, thousands of sightings across the Northeast produced a joint DHS/FBI/FAA/DoD statement on 16 December 2024 asserting that the agencies had 'not identified anything anomalous.' The statement is the concealment posture in its purest form: an assurance issued about a phenomenon the same document concedes generated more than 5,000 tips and roughly 100 open leads. Langley is what that assurance is built on top of, and Langley was never solved.

VanHerck, retired and unconstrained, closed the loop in August 2026 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium. 'There were no surprises, at least for myself and the team at NORAD/NORTHCOM and others,' he said of learning about the incursions. He had told Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin on 16 December 2021, two years to the week before Langley, that he lacked the domain awareness to do his mission, and that 'we're not set up to fight in and from our own land.' Installation commanders, he said, 'really felt a lack of trust' about whether they would be covered if they shot at something. The record therefore shows an air-defense system that knew it was blind, wrote it down, briefed it upward, and then watched seventeen nights of objects it could not name pass over its own F-22s.

dossier.denialPosture: The government's Langley posture is not denial of the event but denial of its significance, executed through a taxonomy: the objects were declared 'uncrewed aerial systems' without a single one being recovered, downed, tracked, or attributed, which converts an unexplained penetration of restricted airspace into a routine force-protection problem. That posture has four dated, attributable artifacts - the Air Force's 'none of the incursions appeared to exhibit hostile intent' (March 2024), Gen. Guillot's 'I do not know of any organized or unorganized foreign nexus' (October 2024), an unnamed Biden White House official's characterization to 60 Minutes of the affair as likely hobbyists, and the 16 December 2024 four-agency joint statement's 'we have not identified anything anomalous.' It is contradicted on the record by VanHerck, who commanded the response and who says magnitude, size, and duration rule hobbyists out. AARO's May 2024 statement that it had 'not yet received a report or any information on this incident' is the strangest artifact of the set: the office chartered to resolve unidentified objects was, by its own account, never told about the largest unresolved domestic airspace event in decades.
connections: Gen. Glen VanHerck - NORAD/NORTHCOM commander during the incursions; ordered the F-22 shootdown of the Chinese surveillance balloon ten months earlier; the only four-star to publicly reject the hobbyist explanation; his 16 December 2021 warning to SecDef Lloyd Austin about lack of domain awareness predates Langley by two years and establishes documented foreknowledge of the vulnerability.

Gen. Gregory Guillot - VanHerck's successor from February 2024; made the first public acknowledgment before the Senate Armed Services Committee on 14 March 2024 and made Langley the centerpiece of his 90-day assessment; directed in November 2024 to serve as DoD's synchronizer, integrator and coordinator of counter-small-UAS activity within the continental United States and Alaska; the official through whom nearly all subsequent government characterization of Langley flows.

Gen. Mark Kelly - commander of Air Combat Command, headquartered at Langley; the senior military eyewitness and the source for the WSJ's physical description. Distinct from Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), SASC and Intelligence Committee member, who separately told reporter Matt Laslo that some base incursions are 'very likely to be foreign nationals that are doing surveillance with low-cost systems that are somewhat expendable.'

AARO (All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office) - reported to have joined two weeks of interagency meetings on Langley, yet told Liberation Times in May 2024 it had received no report; Guillot separately said in October 2024 that he 'coordinates frequently' with AARO. Connects Langley to the board's AARO node and to the pattern of service-level withholding from AARO also alleged of the Navy.

FBI - held jurisdiction outside the base perimeter, received witness video from civilian eyewitness Jonathan Butner, and has declined comment on the investigation since December 2023; the agency in whose files the primary evidentiary record most plausibly sits.

FAA - notified of the incursions; later a signatory to the December 2024 joint statement; the agency whose airspace authority creates the jurisdictional seam VanHerck describes as ending 'at the fence line.'

NASA - the WB-57F N927NA orbits over Langley on 18-19 December 2023 place a civilian science agency's high-altitude imaging asset inside a military anomaly response, with NASA's public explanation (SpaceX CRS-29 support, plus 'additional imaging support in Virginia') covering the tasking.

Chinese surveillance balloon (February 2023) - shot down by an F-22 flown from Langley; the immediately preceding demonstration that NORAD's radar clutter gates were misconfigured for non-traditional aerial objects, and the precedent Guillot cites for 'lessons learned.'

New Jersey / Picatinny Arsenal drone wave (November 2024 onward) - the mass-sighting event that forced the four-agency joint statement and generated the congressional pressure Langley alone had not; the Army confirmed 11 drone sightings over Picatinny Arsenal beginning in November 2024.

Prior and parallel incursion nodes - Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station (2019), the Colorado plains ICBM-field drone reports (winter 2019-2020), the USS Paul Hamilton and other warships off Southern California (2019), Air Force Plant 42 in Palmdale (2024), the Energy Department's Nevada National Security Site nuclear-weapons experiment facility (October 2023), Wright-Patterson AFB, Guam's THAAD battery, and the RAF Lakenheath/Mildenhall/Feltwell cluster in the UK (November 2024).

10 U.S.C. 130i and the 'covered installation' regime - the statutory bottleneck that made non-engagement lawful; Sens. Tom Cotton and Kirsten Gillibrand pushed expansion legislation, and the later Safer Skies Act extended limited mitigation authority to DHS, DOJ, and certain state, local and tribal agencies.

Sen. Roger Wicker - SASC chairman; the ranking legislator to state on camera that the incursions have a military intelligence dimension and that the executive branch remains mystified despite top-level classified briefings.

House Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs (Chairman William Timmons, Ranking Member Suhas Subramanyam) - the 29 April 2025 'Securing the Skies' hearing, the closest thing to a dedicated congressional examination of the base-incursion pattern.

Fengyun Shi prosecution - the only criminal case to emerge from Hampton Roads airspace in that window, involving a separate January 2024 flight over Newport News Shipbuilding; frequently conflated with the December incursions in secondary coverage and useful chiefly as a control case demonstrating what identification, attribution and prosecution look like when they actually occur.

Joint Base Langley-Eustis ISR units - the 363rd and 480th Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Wings are based at JBLE, meaning the incursions occurred over an installation hosting national-level ISR analytic capability.
Falcon Peak (2024, 2025) - the NORTHCOM-led counter-small-UAS demonstration series at Fort Carson, Colorado, created as a direct downstream product of the Langley assessment.

Ross Coulthart and Liberation Times - the disclosure-side journalists who pressed the eyewitness account and the AARO non-receipt statement into the record; Coulthart has publicly flagged the classification problem, noting that if no craft were ever recovered, the word 'drones' is doing unearned work.
openQuestions: No launch or recovery point was ever identified. Guillot stated in October 2024 that he did not know whether the objects were tracked to a recovery point or whether they could have been launched from a vessel offshore, leaving the maritime-launch hypothesis neither confirmed nor excluded.

On what basis were the objects classified as 'uncrewed aerial systems'? None was downed, captured, or attributed. The Air Force has never disclosed the identification methodology, and the 'UAS' label is the single act that removed the event from the anomaly-resolution track.

Why does AARO say it received no report when other reporting places AARO personnel in two weeks of interagency meetings on the incident? Either the office was excluded from a case squarely within its charter, or its public statement is incomplete. Both readings are consequential.

What did the NASA WB-57F N927NA record on 18-19 December 2023? No imagery, sensor tasking order, or product from those flights has been released, and NASA's public explanation attributes the deployment to a spacecraft-reentry imaging mission.

The FBI investigative file remains unreleased and the Bureau has declined comment continuously since December 2023. It is not publicly known whether the investigation was closed, and if so on what finding.

What did Langley's own counter-UAS equipment register? Security Forces are equipped with handheld Dronebuster-type detection and jamming devices, yet seventeen nights of activity produced no publicly acknowledged operator geolocation or radio-frequency signature.
Whether Gen. Guillot's 90-day NORAD/NORTHCOM assessment, of which Langley was the stated centerpiece, contains a Langley-specific annex, and whether any portion of it is releasable.

Civilian eyewitness Jonathan Butner described orb-shaped objects and a separate low-flying saucer-form object, and provided his video to the FBI. Whether any government entity analyzed that footage and what it concluded is unestablished; his morphological description and the official 'UAS' classification have never been reconciled.
Which specific F-22 airframes were relocated, to which base, and under whose order. The relocation is confirmed by 60 Minutes and VanHerck but no unit-level movement record has surfaced.

Whether the October 2023 drone overflights of the Energy Department's Nevada National Security Site, reported by the Wall Street Journal two months before Langley, are operationally connected to the Virginia events or merely contemporaneous.

Whether any classified session of the Senate or House Armed Services Committees produced a finding on Langley attribution, and whether such a finding, if it exists, differs from the public 'no known foreign nexus' posture Wicker's 'still mystified' remark implicitly denies.

Whether the F-16 combat air patrols observed over southeastern Virginia around 12 December 2023 were flown in direct response to the incursions, and whether any airborne sensor track of the objects exists from those sorties or from the AWACS and helicopter assets VanHerck says he provided.

l0.label: NASA UAP Independent Study Team

dossier.whatItIs: The NASA Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Independent Study Team was a 16-member external panel convened by NASA in 2022 under the Earth Science Advisory Committee, chaired by astrophysicist David Spergel of the Simons Foundation, with Dr. Daniel Evans of NASA Headquarters as Designated Federal Official. It held a single public meeting on 31 May 2023 and delivered its final report on 14 September 2023. On the same day NASA created a Director of UAP Research position and initially declined to name the appointee.
dossier.whyImplicated: The panel is a study in the shape of a hole. It was chartered to advise NASA on UAP using only unclassified civilian, commercial and open-source data, and it says so plainly — which means the one body assembled to bring scientific rigor to the question was structurally barred from the classified holdings where the question actually lives. Its report says the quiet part in print: military and intelligence sensor data are classified 'often because of what the imagery could reveal about U.S. technical capabilities to our adversaries, and not because of what is actually in the images,' and that these classified observations 'enhance the sense of mystery and conspiracy surrounding UAP, and they present an obstacle to scientific inquiry.' That is a federally chartered panel, in an official NASA publication, stating that classification is generating the appearance of concealment. Three of its sixteen members came from commercial remote-sensing, space-hardware and private-equity defense firms — Maxar, Redwire and AE Industrial Partners — and two from the FAA, making the panel a map of who holds the civilian sensor data that would matter. And the harassment record around the panel and the withheld name of NASA's UAP research director are themselves artifacts: the cost of association was high enough that the agency initially treated the identity of a civil servant as a security matter.
dossier.narrative:
NASA's Independent Study Team was born of a specific institutional bet: that the agency with the most public trust and the least security baggage could drag UAP into normal science. The bet was placed by Administrator Bill Nelson and executed by the Science Mission Directorate under Nicola Fox, following her predecessor Thomas Zurbuchen, with the activity graciously hosted, in the report's own words, by NASA's Earth Science Division under the Earth Science Advisory Committee. That administrative placement is worth pausing on: a panel about unidentified objects in the airspace was parked in the division that studies the planet's surface and atmosphere. It kept the activity out of astrophysics and out of anything that would have implied a search for technology.

The roster reads as a deliberate coalition of civilian instrumentation. Chair David Spergel of the Simons Foundation. Anamaria Berea of George Mason, Federica Bianco of Delaware, Paula Bontempi of Rhode Island, Jennifer Buss of the Potomac Institute for Policy Studies, science journalist Nadia Drake, David Grinspoon of the Planetary Science Institute, retired astronaut Captain Scott Kelly, Matt Mountain of AURA, Joshua Semeter of Boston University, and Shelley Wright of UC San Diego. Then the operators: Warren Randolph and Karlin Toner from the Federal Aviation Administration, Walter Scott from Maxar Technologies, Mike Gold from Redwire Space, and Reggie Brothers from AE Industrial Partners. Two FAA officials, one commercial satellite imaging executive, one space infrastructure executive, and one defense-focused private equity operator who had previously been Under Secretary for Science and Technology at DHS. If the panel's recommendations pointed anywhere, they pointed at data these institutions own.

And they did. The report recommends NASA leverage its Earth-observing assets to probe local environmental conditions associated with UAP detected by other means, and 'explore enhancing collaborations with the U.S. commercial remote-sensing industry, which offer powerful constellations of high-resolution Earth-observing satellites.' It recommends multispectral and hyperspectral acquisition, AI and machine learning applied to anomaly detection, a crowdsourcing system built on open-source smartphone apps, and better leveraging of the Aviation Safety Reporting System, which NASA operates for the FAA, as 'a critical database for the whole-of-government effort.' Every one of those recommendations routes future UAP data through civilian and commercial channels rather than military ones. Read charitably, that is a strategy for building an evidentiary base outside the classification perimeter. Read uncharitably, it is a strategy for building an evidentiary base that will never intersect the classification perimeter.

The panel's own frustration surfaces in the passage that matters most. Discussing why existing observations cannot resolve UAP, the report states: 'In addition, much of the data collected by military sensors or intelligence satellites are classified—often because of what the imagery could reveal about U.S. technical capabilities to our adversaries, and not because of what is actually in the images. While essential for security, these classified observations enhance the sense of mystery and conspiracy surrounding UAP, and they present an obstacle to scientific inquiry.' A federal advisory panel wrote, in a public report, that the government's classification practice is manufacturing the appearance of a cover-up and blocking the science that would dispel it. That sentence is a finding about the concealment architecture, delivered by scientists who could not see inside it.

On the evidence question the report is careful and narrow: 'To date, in the peer-reviewed scientific literature, there is no conclusive evidence suggesting an extraterrestrial origin for UAP.' The qualifier is doing work — peer-reviewed literature is precisely the corpus from which classified holdings are absent. The panel also recorded that then-AARO Director Sean Kirkpatrick reported at its 31 May 2023 public meeting that AARO had collected more than 800 reported events, against 263 reports filed in the 17 years before March 2021.

The cost of participation is documented in the report itself: team members received hate mail from colleagues, were ridiculed and criticized on social media, and had firsthand knowledge of colleagues warned away from technosignature research on the grounds that it could damage scientific credibility and promotion prospects. On 14 September 2023 NASA announced the creation of a Director of UAP Research and Administrator Nelson said the identity would be withheld to prevent harassment. NASA reversed within hours and named Mark McInerney, a former NASA liaison to the Department of Defense on UAP matters. The reversal is instructive twice over: it shows the agency's first instinct was concealment framed as protection, and it shows how quickly that instinct collapsed under press pressure — which is not how the Department of Defense's instances of the same instinct have behaved.

The statutory tie is direct. 50 U.S.C. 3373(c)(6) requires AARO to coordinate with NASA, among other agencies. Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories demand identification of all UAP-related work MITRE performed for or with NASA. NASA sits inside the legal architecture of the program question while its own expert panel sat outside the data.

l0.short: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

dossier.whatItIs: The U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is the House's principal investigative committee, chaired in the 118th and 119th Congresses by Rep. James Comer. Since 2023 it has been the primary congressional venue for sworn public testimony about a concealed UAP retrieval and reverse-engineering program, holding hearings in July 2023, November 2024 and September 2025, and continuing a documentary investigation into AARO through the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna.
dossier.whyImplicated: Oversight is the institution against which the concealment is measured. The claim on this board is not merely that a program exists but that it has been withheld from Congress; the only way to test that is to watch what happens when a committee with subpoena power asks. The pattern across three hearings and multiple document requests is consistent: witnesses testify under penalty of perjury to firsthand or near-firsthand knowledge, the executive branch responds through public affairs rather than document production, and the committee escalates to written demands. In April 2026 Chairwoman Luna wrote to the Secretary of War stating that 'The Task Force has found responses from AARO, when questioned about UAP sightings and provided data, less than adequate' — a sitting subcommittee chair putting on the record that the executive's designated UAP office is not answering. That is an oversight failure documented by the overseer, which is the most probative kind of evidence available for a concealment argument.
dossier.narrative:
Three hearings define the record.

On 26 July 2023 the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, chaired by Rep. Glenn Grothman, held 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency' in 2154 Rayburn. The witnesses were Ryan Graves, Executive Director of Americans for Safe Aerospace; Commander David Fravor, former commanding officer of the Black Aces squadron; and David Grusch, former National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAP Task Force. Grusch testified under oath that in the course of his official duties he was informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program to which he was denied access, that he had interviewed dozens of witnesses over several years, and that recoveries included non-human biologics, repeatedly stating he could provide specifics in a secure setting. Fravor described the November 2004 Nimitz encounter. Graves testified on reporting stigma and aviation safety. It was the first time a sworn witness told a House committee, on camera, that the United States operates a concealed retrieval program.

On 13 November 2024 the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation and the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs held a joint hearing, 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth.' Witnesses were Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, USN (Ret.), CEO of Ocean STL Consulting; Luis Elizondo; Michael Gold, former NASA Associate Administrator for Space Policy and Partnerships and member of the NASA UAP Independent Study Team; and Michael Shellenberger, founder of Public. Shellenberger testified to the existence of a claimed program he identified as 'Immaculate Constellation,' described as collecting UAP imagery and sensor data from military personnel and sequestering it from the rest of the government. The full transcript was published as HHRG-118-GO12-Transcript-20241113 and the hearing was printed as CHRG-118hhrg57440. The composition of the witness panel is itself notable: a retired flag officer, a former NASA associate administrator, a former DoD official, and a journalist, three of whom held senior federal positions.

On 9 September 2025 the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, held 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection' in HVC-210. Witnesses were Jeffrey Nuccetelli (USAF veteran), Chief Alexandro Wiggins, George Knapp, and Dylan Borland (USAF veteran). Luna's announcement stated the hearing would 'analyze the work and effectiveness of DoD's congressionally mandated All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)' and that whistleblowers 'should be able to' provide information on spending, classification and declassification 'without retribution.'

The institutional vehicle matters. The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets was created in early 2025 under the Oversight Committee, with a portfolio spanning the JFK, RFK and MLK assassinations, COVID origins, 9/11, the Epstein files, and UAP and unidentified submerged objects. Members include Reps. Lauren Boebert, Nancy Mace, Jasmine Crockett and Raja Krishnamoorthi. Placing UAP inside a declassification task force rather than a national security subcommittee is a deliberate reframing: it treats the subject as a records-access problem rather than a threat-assessment problem, which is the correct frame if the hypothesis is concealment.

The investigation did not end with the hearing. A committee press release dated 1 April 2026 announces a letter from Luna to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth requesting specific UAP video files, quoting her: 'On September 9, 2025, the Task Force held a hearing focused on UAP concerns. Whistleblowers informed the Task Force that AARO possesses additional video records of potential UAP sightings.' The release states this is 'part of the Committee's larger investigation into the work and effectiveness of the Department of War's congressionally mandated AARO,' and quotes Luna concluding that AARO's responses have been 'less than adequate' and that 'The presence of UAPs in and around the sensitive airspaces of U.S. military installations poses a threat to the security of the armed forces and their readiness.'

Who matters by name: James Comer (full committee chair), Anna Paulina Luna (task force chair and the most persistent driver), Tim Burchett (co-founder of the UAP caucus and a principal mover of the 2023 hearing), Glenn Grothman (2023 subcommittee chair), Nancy Mace, Eric Burlison, Jared Moskowitz and Robert Garcia on the minority and bipartisan side. What the record shows is a committee that has taken sworn testimony, published transcripts, created a dedicated task force, and escalated to written demands on the Secretary of War. What the record does not show is a single document production from the executive branch responsive to the central claim.

dossier.denialPosture: The Committee is the recipient of denials rather than the issuer. Its own published position, stated by Chairwoman Luna in April 2026, is that AARO's responses to its questions have been 'less than adequate' and that the lack of disclosure 'regarding the very real threat posed by UAPs in and around U.S. restricted airspace is concerning.'
connections: Anna Paulina Luna chairs the task force and is the direct correspondent with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth; her letters are the current front line of the documentary fight.

Tim Burchett and Anna Paulina Luna were the members most responsible for securing witnesses; Glenn Grothman chaired the first hearing; Nancy Mace chaired the Cybersecurity/IT subcommittee side of the November 2024 joint hearing.
David Grusch's path runs NRO to UAP Task Force to NGA to ICIG to this committee, making Oversight the terminus of the whistleblower channel.
Luis Elizondo testified here in November 2024, connecting the AATIP naming dispute directly to a congressional record under oath.
Michael Shellenberger's 'Immaculate Constellation' testimony introduces a claimed program name into the congressional record that no executive branch document has yet addressed.
AARO is the committee's principal adversary-in-fact: the office whose effectiveness the task force is investigating and whose video holdings it is demanding.
George Knapp, a witness in September 2025, is also the journalist who first reported the AATIP-Bigelow story in Nevada, tying the 2025 hearing back to the 2008 procurement.
The FY2024 NDAA UAP Records Collection at NARA and the stripped Schumer-Rounds eminent domain and review board provisions define the statutory terrain the committee is operating on.
openQuestions: Has the Committee ever issued a subpoena, as opposed to a request letter, for UAP records? No published subpoena has surfaced.
Grusch told the Committee he could provide specifics in a SCIF. Did a classified follow-on session occur, and is there a record of it?

Did the Committee ever obtain the classified annex to the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment?
Why has the Senate Armed Services and Intelligence side never held a comparable open hearing, and does that split reflect a jurisdictional bargain?

l0.label: Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets
l0.short: Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets

dossier.whatItIs: The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets is a panel of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, established by Chairman James Comer on 11 February 2025 and chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL), authorized for six months under Committee Rules. Its announced portfolio spans the Kennedy, Robert Kennedy and King assassination records, UAP and USO, the Epstein files, COVID-19 origins and the 9/11 files. It has become the principal congressional venue for the legacy program question since 2025.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the first congressional body to run at the concealment architecture rather than at the phenomenon. Its members subpoena-adjacent letters go to contractors and federally funded research and development centers rather than to the Pentagon press office, on the theory that the records are in private hands under federal sponsorship. Its chairwoman has stated on the record that the Department of Defense refused to read her members into the relevant special access programs, naming HASC and HAC-D as the only committees with access — which converts a suspicion about compartmentation into a documented, dated institutional fact. Its member Eric Burlison has converted that finding into legislative interrogatories to MIT Lincoln Laboratory and The MITRE Corporation demanding enumeration of SAPs, ACCMs, cover programs, hidden funding and instructions to avoid certain vocabulary. And its chairwoman has used her opening statement to attack the credibility of the former AARO director by name, making the government's own denial instrument a subject of the investigation.
dossier.narrative:
The Task Force exists because a different theory of the problem won an internal argument. For four years the congressional approach to UAP was to demand better reports from the Executive branch. The Task Force's approach is to demand records from whoever physically holds them, and to treat classification as a claim to be adjudicated rather than an answer to be accepted.

It was created on 11 February 2025 when Chairman James Comer announced the panel and named Rep. Anna Paulina Luna to lead it, following President Trump's 23 January 2025 executive order on declassification of records concerning the assassinations of President Kennedy, Senator Robert Kennedy and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Comer framed it in institution-repair language: 'This secrecy has sowed distrust in our institutions.' Luna's own statement laid out a portfolio nobody expected a single panel to carry: 'We will also investigate UAPs/USOs, the Epstein client list, COVID-19 origins, and the 9/11 files.' The Task Force was authorized for six months pursuant to Committee Rules, and Comer and Luna transmitted eleven letters the same day. Its first hearing addressed the JFK files; Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) was initially the ranking member, and by the September 2025 UAP hearing Luna was yielding to Ranking Member Crockett.

The 9 September 2025 hearing, 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection,' is the panel's substantive turn. Four witnesses testified: Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp, and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland. Luna's opening statement is the single most useful congressional document on the access problem. She described following a lead from active-duty Air Force pilot whistleblowers alleging a cover-up of UAP activity at Eglin Air Force Base, pursued with former Rep. Matt Gaetz and Rep. Tim Burchett. She said pilots decline to come forward out of fear for their flight status and careers. And then she stated the mechanism: 'In preparation for previous UAP hearings, the Committee repeatedly asked DoD to allow Members to view videos and files relating to UAP incidents. Unfortunately, DoD notified Committee staff that due to the Department's special access program (SAP) rules, only members of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) and the Defense Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee (HAC-D) were allowed to be "read in" on such programs. For a non-committee Member to be allowed to view these documents and videos, individual Members must be approved by the Chairman and Ranking Member of both HASC and HAC-D.' She added that 'Independent SAP oversight has presented a consistent problem for Congress as the program's budgets are classified.'

That is 10 U.S.C. 119 operating as designed, quoted from the receiving end by a committee chairwoman. It also identifies precisely four people — the chairs and ranking members of HASC and HAC-D — as the gatekeepers for any Oversight Committee member seeking access.

Luna also went after AARO directly, calling former director Sean Kirkpatrick 'a documented liar' and questioning 'what his purpose at AARO really was if it was not to follow up on investigations and disclose his findings to Members of Congress.' She entered into the record former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Chris Mellon's characterization of an AARO report as 'the most error-ridden and unsatisfactory government report I can recall reading during or after decades of government service,' noting Mellon's claims that it was the first AARO report submitted to Congress without the DNI's sign-off, that it omitted agencies with known UAP investigations, and that it omitted any discussion of efforts to hide information — including at U.S. Customs and Border Protection. A congressional task force treating the government's own investigative office as a suspect witness is a meaningful shift in posture.

The Task Force's method matured into contractor-directed process in 2026. On 7 May 2026 Burlison wrote to MIT Lincoln Laboratory about a reel-to-reel recording catalogued as 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52' from the Beacon Hill Study, labeled 'flying saucer talk,' with Edward J. Ruppelt as briefer. On 22 May 2026 he transmitted ten pages of legislative interrogatories to MITRE, copied to Luna, Comer, and Information Security Oversight Office Director Michael D. Thomas. Both letters run on the same statutory theory: sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, create a UAP Records Collection at NARA in Record Group 615 that encompasses government-funded records, and contractor custody does not defeat it. Burlison's framing in the accompanying release is the Task Force's thesis in one sentence: FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records.'

The backdrop by 2026 is a Trump administration declassification push. Following a 19 February 2026 Trump directive, the Department of War began publishing declassified UAP files in May 2026 under the banner PURSUE — Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters — at war.gov/ufo. Burlison's press release places his MITRE inquiry explicitly inside that effort, testing whether agencies, contractors, FFRDCs and laboratories are actually complying.

l0.label: Congressional UAP Caucus

dossier.whatItIs: A bipartisan House caucus launched by Rep. Tim Burchett (TN-02) in August 2023 and co-chaired with Rep. Jared Moskowitz (FL-23). Its founding cohort — the six members who signed its first act, a letter to the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community — were Burchett, Moskowitz, Anna Paulina Luna (FL-13), Nancy Mace (SC-01), Eric Burlison (MO-07) and Andy Ogles (TN-05).
dossier.whyImplicated: The caucus is the only organised bloc in Congress whose founding premise is that UAP crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programs exist and have been concealed from the committees of jurisdiction. Its very first act, less than a month after David Grusch's July 2023 testimony, was to demand from the IC Inspector General the names of the people and the identities of the facilities involved in those programs. Its members subsequently drove the FY2024 NDAA's UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, the House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, the September 2025 whistleblower hearing, and the UAP Disclosure Act amendment adopted into the House FY2027 NDAA on 22 July 2026 with its eminent domain provision intact — a provision that would order the government to seize recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private entities. In August 2026 the relationship inverted: the executive branch authorised Burlison's House office to publish ODNI memo ES 2026-00818, making the oversight bloc the administration's distribution channel for its own IC directive.
dossier.narrative:
On 26 July 2023 the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs held the first public UAP hearing to take testimony from military pilots and whistleblowers. David Grusch, a former intelligence officer, testified that he could not provide specific details regarding UAP crash retrieval or reverse engineering programs because those details are classified, but that he had provided them to the Office of the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community. Twenty-seven days later, on 22 August 2023, Tim Burchett announced that he had launched the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Caucus and had led five colleagues in a letter to IC IG Thomas A. Monheim asking for follow-up on Grusch's testimony — specifically, in the caucus's own words, "information from the Intelligence Community Inspector General regarding which people and facilities are involved with UAP crash retrieval programs and reverse engineering programs."

That question has never been publicly answered. The caucus's subsequent trajectory is best read as successive attempts to answer it by other means.

The statutory route came first. The FY2022 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-81, § 1683, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373) created AARO. The FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-263, § 1673, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373b) required a secure channel for authorised disclosure of UAP information relating to any government or contractor activity, notwithstanding NDAs, EO 13526, the Atomic Energy Act and Section 798 of the Espionage Act, and prohibited retaliation by agencies and by contractors, subcontractors, grantees and subgrantees. The FY2024 NDAA (Pub. L. 118-31, § 1841) then created the UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, defining covered records as any "Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence." That statutory phrase — "technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence" — is now U.S. public law, drafted by a Congress that would not have needed the category if nothing occupied it.

The FY2024 NDAA also contained the sharpest instrument the caucus era produced and the one that quietly died: sections 1687 and 7343 prohibited the use of FY2024 funds for any UAP-related secret program until the Secretary of Defense or the Director of National Intelligence fully disclosed the relevant details to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership. Those funding limitations were not renewed in subsequent enactments. Whoever allowed that lapse removed the only appropriations-side leverage Congress had ever applied to the question.

The Senate route was the UAP Disclosure Act, which passed the Senate in 2023 as Division G of S. 2226 by unanimous-consent incorporation of Amendment No. 935 and would have created an independent review board empowered to advise the President on declassification and release of UAP records. Its most aggressive clause orders the government to "exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good." It was stripped in conference. On 22 July 2026 the House adopted its own version — including the eminent domain provision — as an amendment to the FY2027 NDAA, recorded as Amendment No. 315 at H.R. Rep. 119-755, pages 419-442. The named sponsors are Burlison of Missouri, Crane of Arizona, Carson of Indiana, Luna of Florida, Moskowitz of Florida and Begich of Alaska: three of the six are caucus founders, and Crane, Carson and Begich extend the coalition. The House bloc carried into law-adjacent text the provision the Senate had been unable to protect.

The hearing route continued through the 119th Congress. Luna chairs the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, which held a hearing on 9 September 2025 titled "Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection," taking testimony from Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland. That task force also runs the JFK files declassification work — the same members, the same theory of the case, applied to two record sets.

The most revealing development is procedural rather than legislative. On 21 July 2026 Burlison publicly invited anyone covered by President Trump's UAP NDA directive to contact his office for help navigating the process — a member of Congress standing up an informal whistleblower intake because the official one did not yet exist. Eleven days later, ODNI signed memorandum ES 2026-00818. On 1 August 2026 Burlison released it, noting that "the administration authorized Congressman Burlison's office to publicly distribute the memorandum." A national-level Intelligence Community directive to the Director of the CIA and the heads of every IC element reached the public through the website of a backbench House member from southwest Missouri who had spent three years accusing that same community of concealment. Whether that is co-option or capitulation is the open question; either way it is the clearest measure of the caucus's leverage in 2026. It is also worth noting what the memo Burlison distributed does not give him: it forecloses disclosure to Congress outside AARO, meaning the caucus published an instrument that routes around itself.

One cataloguing caution for downstream analysis: the domain uapcaucus.com belongs to a private advocacy organisation, not to the congressional caucus, and the House caucus has never published an official membership roster.

dossier.denialPosture: The caucus issues no denials; it exists to contest them. Its own weak point is documented rather than asserted: it has never published an answer from the IC Inspector General to its founding question about the people and facilities involved in crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programs, and the FY2024 funding prohibition on undisclosed UAP programs — the only appropriations lever ever applied — was allowed to lapse without public explanation.
