l0.label: Immaculate Constellation 12-page report entered into the Congressional Record
l0.short: Immaculate Constellation 12-page report entered into the Congressional Record

dossier.whatItIs: A twelve-page document that Michael Shellenberger delivered to Congress on the morning of 13 November 2024 and that Rep. Nancy Mace moved into the Congressional Record from the dais during the House Oversight Committee hearing 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth'. Its first section describes an unacknowledged special access program named Immaculate Constellation; its second section concerns United States Government imagery intelligence. It is listed in the hearing's Index of Documents as 'Report, Pentagon, "Immaculate Constellation"; submitted by Rep. Mace.'
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only artefact in the entire public record that purports to be an internal description of a UAP parent compartment, and a chairwoman of a House committee put it into the Congressional Record while the Department of Defense was on record saying it has no record of the programme it names. The document is therefore a test case for the whole disclosure machinery: a congressional committee can receive, distribute to every member on the dais, and formally enter a document about an unacknowledged SAP, and nothing follows. No agency was compelled to search for it, no author was subpoenaed, no classification review was triggered, and no executive branch office has addressed its contents. It is the disclosure mechanism working exactly as designed and producing exactly nothing.
dossier.narrative:
The document arrived on the morning of the hearing. Rep. Mace flagged it in her opening remarks before the witnesses were sworn: 'there is a document that will be entered into the congressional record today. Mr. Tim Burchett from Tennessee has this document, and we just distributed it to every Member up here on the dais, this document. But this is going to be the original document from the Pentagon about Immaculate Constellation that Michael Shellenberger delivered to Congress today.' She then characterised it: '12 pages about this unacknowledged special access program that your government says does not exist.'

Later in the hearing, after the last of the opening statements, she performed the formal act: 'Committee staff asked me to go ahead, and I will do it, to enter into the Congressional Record this 12-page document that Michael Shellenberger brought today that describes the Immaculate Constellation government program. So, we will do that now. Every Member up here has a copy of it.' She then described its structure on the record: 'The first section talks about the unacknowledged special access program called Immaculate Constellation, and the second section about USG imagery intelligence.' She added the FISA warning she had just received from Rep. Luna, and closed with 'But, without objection, entered into the record.'

The printed hearing record's Index of Documents lists it as 'Report, Pentagon, "Immaculate Constellation"; submitted by Rep. Mace', alongside a Mellon hearing letter submitted by Mace, documents related to UAPs submitted by Burchett, and Questions for the Record to Elizondo, Gallaudet, Shellenberger and Gold submitted by Burlison. The record states that 'The documents listed above are available at: docs.house.gov.'

The contents, as read into the record by Shellenberger in his oral statement and set out at greater length in his written testimony, are consistent between the two. The report describes a parent USAP consolidating UAP observations from tasked and untasked collection platforms; a holdings profile of high-quality IMINT and MASINT from low Earth orbit, the upper atmosphere, aviation altitudes and maritime environments; a shape taxonomy of spheres and orbs, discs and saucers, ovals and tic-tacs, triangles, boomerang and arrowhead forms and irregular or organic shapes; and seven categories of evidence. The written testimony says the report 'describes in detail various UAP sightings collected by technical assets and US military personnel', and that the underlying material sits in defence HUMINT databases 'accessible to the Intelligence Community'.

Two incident descriptions are quoted directly from the report in the written testimony. The F-22 encounter: 'The F-22 broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs', with one object holding station off the cockpit through multiple evasive manoeuvres before the aircraft 'was forced out of the mission area under the escort of the UAP formation.' And the carrier deck event, in which a small orange-red sphere descended from high altitude to within 100-200 yards directly above the flight deck of a CVN.

The evidentiary character of the document is worth stating plainly, because the argument does not need it inflated. It is an anonymous report, delivered by a journalist, whose author Shellenberger says he knows and will not name. Under questioning from Rep. Higgins he confirmed 'I do' when asked whether he knew the author, and when pressed on the author's sources referred back to the report itself. He offered one internal check: that when he compared its cases against publicly known cases he 'did not find it based on existing cases; it was new cases for me', which he presented as an argument against circular reporting. That is a weak check, and he said so in effect by presenting it as the only one he could make.

What gives the document its standing is not its provenance but its position. It sits in the Congressional Record. It was distributed to every member on the dais of a House committee. It names a compartment. And the executive branch response to it, before and since, has been a single sentence from a public affairs office - Sue Gough's statement that 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION"' - which addresses records holdings and not existence, and which was itself printed in the witness's own testimony rather than issued in response to the congressional entry.

Since 13 November 2024 the document has been followed by nothing. No agency has confirmed conducting a search. No committee has published a referral. No classification authority has asserted that the document is classified, which would be the ordinary response to an authentic Pentagon report on an unacknowledged SAP appearing in a public hearing room; nor has any authority asserted that it is a forgery, which would be the ordinary response to a fabrication. That double silence is the most interesting fact about the artefact. The disclosure machinery accepted the document and then had nowhere to put it, because the mechanism Congress built in 2023 - a records collection administered by the agencies that hold the records - has no procedure for a document that arrives from outside the agencies and describes a compartment the agencies say they cannot find.

Mr. Tim Burchett from Tennessee has this document, and we just distributed it to every Member up here on the dais ... this is going to be the original document from the Pentagon about Immaculate Constellation that Michael Shellenberger delivered to Congress today.'
Rep. Mace described the document as '12 pages about this unacknowledged special access program that your government says does not exist.'

l0.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
l0.short: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026

dossier.whatItIs: A ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests dated 22 May 2026, sent by Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO-07) to Dr. Mark Peters, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Christopher Land, Senior Vice President and General Counsel, of The MITRE Corporation at 7525 Colshire Drive, McLean, Virginia. Copied to Task Force Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna, Oversight Chairman James Comer, and Michael D. Thomas, Director of the Information Security Oversight Office at NARA. The enclosure runs eleven numbered sections and more than forty specific requests, with a relevant time period beginning 1 January 1930.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the first congressional instrument that treats a federally funded research and development center as a potential custodian of the legacy program's paper. It does not ask MITRE whether UAP are real. It asks MITRE which Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, Managed-Need-To-Know codewords, DOE Restricted Data compartments and SIGMA categories it participated in touching UAP subject matter, and for each one, 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks for any classification guide, nondisclosure agreement or sponsor communication that instructed MITRE personnel to avoid the words UAP, UFO, USO, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, technology of unknown origin or non-human intelligence in their records. It asks for funding routed through 'a cover program' whose 'public description differed materially from the responsive work performed,' and for funding MITRE understood to be 'hidden from, not briefed to, or not readily visible to ordinary sponsor budget channels.' And it names twelve companies by name. The letter is a map of the concealment hypothesis rendered as a document request.
dossier.narrative:
Burlison's MITRE package is the moment the congressional inquiry stopped asking the Pentagon and started asking the people who hold the Pentagon's files.

The premise is stated in the cover letter's second paragraph. MITRE operates multiple FFRDCs, and 'By design, FFRDCs often receive special access to government facilities, data, sponsor requirements, and sensitive technical information that ordinary private contractors may not receive. This special public-trust role makes records stewardship, sponsor accountability, and congressional visibility especially important.' The statutory hook is sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA and NARA's Record Group 615: if government-funded UAP records sit in a contractor's archive, the statute reaches them, and MITRE's status as a nonprofit operator does not create a safe harbor. DefenseScoop reported that FFRDCs are largely shielded from public disclosure by FOIA exemptions, and that some officials have warned this lets them hold government information the public has a right to see.

The scope is deliberately enormous. 'Unless otherwise specified, the relevant time period is January 1, 1930, to the present.' MITRE was incorporated in 1958; the 1930 start date is a trap for inherited archives, telling MITRE that if it contends the request is overbroad for a legacy period it must 'identify the earliest date for which MITRE can search reliably, the reason older records cannot be searched, and the custodian or sponsor most likely to hold the older records.' The definition of 'UAP-related' extends to any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving' UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, 'or equivalent terms.' Euphemism is named as a category of evidence.

The deadlines are tight and sequenced. Within five business days, designate a vice-president-level officer to coordinate. Within ten business days, issue and confirm a written preservation hold covering 'restricted systems, air-gapped environments, classified repositories, personal workspaces used for official business, archived systems, email, collaboration platforms, backup media, contractor/subcontractor systems, and offsite storage.' Within fourteen days, contact the office to coordinate a classified briefing for Task Force Members and cleared Committee staff at 'the appropriate TS/SCI/SAP level.' Within thirty days, written answers plus a records-location index naming repositories, custodians, contract vehicles, sponsors, classification authorities and record schedules. Within forty-five days, production of all unclassified responsive records in native electronic format with complete metadata, plus a segregated classified annex and a privilege and classification log. The letter warns that 'False statements, concealment, alteration, destruction, or obstruction in connection with this inquiry may implicate federal law, including but not limited to 18 U.S.C. §§ 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519, and 2071.'

The eleven enclosure sections read as a taxonomy of how a program stays hidden. Section I demands an accounting of records destroyed, degaussed, sanitized, reclassified, moved to a restricted system or 'placed under sponsor control,' with the authority and the responsible personnel named. Section II demands identification of every contract, IDIQ, GWAC, BPA, OTA and CRADA under which MITRE touched UAP information, and every individual involved with 'their specific functions and duties' — and names AARO, the UAP Task Force, AATIP, AAWSAP, DIA, CIA, NSA, NRO, NGA, ONI, NRL, DARPA, IARPA and DOE laboratories, 'or any successor, predecessor, cover, compartment, or renamed activity.' Section II.6 asks whether MITRE 'provided cover' for another entity's UAP work.

Section III is the compartmentation audit already described. Section IV asks what MITRE has and has not sent to NARA under the UAP Records Collection. Section V asks for sensor work across radar, optical, infrared, acoustic and undersea domains, expressly including 'SOSUS/IUSS-related' systems and 'unidentified submerged objects.' Section VI asks about recovered anomalous materials, isotope ratios, chain of custody, metamaterials, propulsion and 'cognitive interface systems' — and, in VI.4, about 'biological material, biological samples, human physiological effects, medical monitoring, occupational exposure, anomalous injury, cognitive or neurological effects, or environmental hazards associated with UAP-related materials, objects, fields, occupants, or events,' with the careful caveat that the request 'seeks records and safety documentation only and does not presume the validity of any particular biological claim.' The word 'occupants' is doing a great deal of work in a congressional document.

Section VII asks for SCIFs, SAPFs, vaults and 'material-containment work.' Section VIII asks for internal disclosures, retaliation, and nondisclosure instruments 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations' that restricted personnel from reporting to Congress, IGs, AARO, NARA or law enforcement. Section IX names Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace or its successors. Section X goes at the money. Section XI demands a certified response signed by a responsible MITRE officer and counsel.

MITRE's answer, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was custodial rather than responsive: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That is a statement that anything found goes back to the sponsor, not to Congress. A member of Burlison's staff told DefenseScoop the letter was informed by 'advice from many whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations, and those working at FFRDCs.'

The MITRE package was not the first shot. On 7 May 2026 Burlison had written to MIT Lincoln Laboratory Director Melissa G. Choi and counsel David A. Suski about a single object: a reel-to-reel recording catalogued as 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52' from the Beacon Hill Study, labeled 'flying saucer talk,' with Edward J. Ruppelt — then head of Project Blue Book — listed as the briefer. That letter demanded the laboratory determine whether the recording is extant, preserve it, digitize it to preservation grade, and transmit it with metadata to NARA for Record Group 615. It also instructed the laboratory to coordinate with the cognizant sponsor, the original classification authority, ISOO and the Public Interest Declassification Board if an active Security Classification Guide still applies to a 1952 tape.

l0.label: Senate Armed Services Committee

dossier.whatItIs: The Committee on Armed Services of the United States Senate, one of the four congressional defense committees named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g), and therefore one of the bodies whose chairman and ranking minority member sit inside the eight-member group that may be advised of a waived special access program. SASC is also the drafting venue for the annual National Defense Authorization Act provisions that created the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, defined unidentified anomalous phenomena in statute, and progressively tightened the reporting obligations attached to them.
dossier.whyImplicated: SASC occupies the structural pinch point: it is simultaneously the committee that is supposed to receive notification of the most closely held programs and the committee that keeps writing new statutes because it apparently is not receiving it. The language it has enacted is an admission. 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) requires AARO's historical record report to itemize any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress, and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about UAP. Congress does not write that sentence about a subject on which it believes it has been told the truth. Subsection (l)(4) goes further, requiring the AARO Director to hand the SASC and SSCI chair and ranking member an enumeration of every instance in which UAP data was withheld from AARO because of classification restrictions or for any other reason, which is a statutory acknowledgment that data is being withheld from the office created to collect it. And in December 2025 Congress had to amend the statute again to extend the immediate data-availability requirement beyond intelligence community elements to Department of Defense components, meaning that for three years the mandate did not reach the department that owns the special access program system.
dossier.narrative:
Follow the statutory ratchet, because it is a record of what did not work.

In December 2021, section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, 135 Stat. 2118, created the office structure and authorities to address what were then called unidentified aerial phenomena. Twelve months later, in December 2022, Public Law 117-263 rewrote the section twice over: section 1673(c) of the NDAA substituted anomalous for aerial throughout and added congressional leadership to the notification list, while section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act amended the section generally, standing up the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office proper. The Senate-side drive came from SASC members, principally Senator Kirsten Gillibrand working with Senator Marco Rubio.

What the rewritten section actually demands is the interesting part. AARO's duties include developing procedures to synchronize and standardize the collection, reporting and analysis of UAP incidents, including adverse physiological effects, across the entire Department of Defense and intelligence community. The Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence must jointly designate an official responsible for ensuring the expertise, authorities, accesses, data, systems, platforms and capabilities exist for rapid response to and support for field investigations, and must designate one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of data, including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models. Congress wrote materials testing and medical studies into the statute. It also required that each designated line organization have authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the federal government with appropriate security clearances, and it listed the Department of Energy among the elements that may detail personnel to be physically located at the office.

The historical record report in subsection (j) is the closest thing to a congressional charge sheet in U.S. law. It requires a written report to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership covering the period beginning January 1, 1945, compiling the key historical record of intelligence community involvement with UAP, and specifically itemizing three things: any restricted-access program or activity not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track UAP; and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect information, classified or unclassified. The Archivist of the United States is directed to make NARA holdings, including classified holdings, available to AARO for that purpose. Congress then attached an auditor: section 6803 of Public Law 117-263 required the Comptroller General to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the historical record report process, to conduct work on site as appropriate, and to brief the intelligence committees, the defense committees and congressional leadership semiannually on AARO's progress and its compliance with legislative requirements. That requirement was extended by Public Law 118-159 section 6802 in December 2024.

The FY2024 NDAA added the money lever. Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 made independent research and development funding relating to UAP unallowable as an indirect expense on contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. This is the appropriations-side answer to the classification-side problem, and its existence implies a belief that contractors were recovering UAP-related costs through overhead.

The FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60, enacted December 18, 2025, shows what still was not working. Section 1671 added a new subsection (l)(5) requiring every semiannual briefing to include details on any UAP intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or United States Northern Command, including the number, location and nature of the intercepts and a description of the procedures and protocols followed, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts, and requiring the AARO Director to inform Congress of any failure by NORAD or NORTHCOM to provide timely information. Section 1671(b) reached backward, requiring the first briefing after enactment to cover intercepts not previously reported going back to January 1, 2004. Section 1673(a) gave the AARO Director 180 days to produce an accounting of the security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, with discretionary authority to issue a consolidated security classification matrix. Section 1672(b) rewrote the data-availability clause so that the immediate-production requirement now binds each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with UAP data, where the prior text bound only intelligence community elements.

That last amendment is the single most damning line in the sequence. From December 2022 to December 2025, the statutory command to hand UAP data over immediately did not reach Department of Defense components as such. The department that operates the special access program system, that houses DoD SAPCO, and that owns the classification guides sat outside the mandate for three years, and it took an act of Congress in December 2025 to close it.

What SASC has not delivered is the enforcement architecture. The UAP Disclosure Act, offered by Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds as an NDAA amendment and modeled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act, would have created a nine-member presidentially appointed civilian Review Board with subpoena power and would have asserted federal eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private entities. The Review Board and the eminent domain provision were stripped in conference in FY2024, and the Act was excluded again from the FY2026 NDAA. What survived was a records collection with no independent adjudicator. The one provision that would have reached into contractor custody, eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin, is the one that has never made it into law.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1) names the Committee on Armed Services of the Senate as one of the 'defense committees' entitled to special access program notification, making its chairman and ranking minority member two of the eight members who may be advised of a waived SAP under section 119(e)(2).

The statutory basis for AARO originates in section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, division A, title XVI, December 27, 2021, 135 Stat. 2118, and was amended generally by Public Law 117-263 section 1673(c) and Intelligence Authorization Act section 6802(a) on December 23, 2022.

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(I) requires AARO's historical record report to include 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(III) requires the report to include 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4) requires the AARO Director to provide to the chair and ranking member of the Senate and House Armed Services Committees and the congressional intelligence committees 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.'

Section 1672(b) of the FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 (December 18, 2025, 139 Stat. 1202), amended 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to require that 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' with UAP data make it immediately available to AARO; the prior text bound only intelligence community elements.

Section 1671(a) of Public Law 119-60 added 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(5), requiring each semiannual briefing to detail any UAP intercepts conducted by NORAD or U.S. Northern Command, including 'the number, location, and nature of such intercepts' and 'a description of the procedures and protocols followed during the intercepts, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts', and requiring notice to Congress of any failure by NORAD or NORTHCOM to provide timely information.
Section 1671(b) of Public Law 119-60 requires the first post-enactment briefing to include previously unreported NORAD and NORTHCOM UAP intercepts occurring from January 1, 2004 onward.

Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60 requires the AARO Director, within 180 days of December 18, 2025, to make an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix for UAP-related programs.

50 U.S.C. 3373(e) requires designation of one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of UAP data 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models', and requires that each such organization have authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the federal government with appropriate security clearances.

50 U.S.C. 3373(i) lists the Department of Energy among the elements that may provide detailees to be physically located at AARO, alongside CIA, DIA, NSA, NGA, the service intelligence elements and DHS.

Section 6803 of Public Law 117-263 required the Comptroller General to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the AARO historical record report process, including on-site work, and to brief the intelligence committees, defense committees and congressional leadership semiannually on AARO's progress and compliance with legislative requirements; the requirement was extended by Public Law 118-159 section 6802 (December 23, 2024).

Section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA, Public Law 118-31 (137 Stat. 621), bars UAP-related independent research and development funding from being allowable as an indirect expense on contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, HPSCI, SSCI and the four congressional leaders.

The UAP Disclosure Act, offered by Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA and modeled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act, would have created a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths and subpoena witnesses and documents, and would have asserted eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private entities; the Review Board and eminent domain provisions were stripped in conference and the Act was again excluded from the FY2026 NDAA.

dossier.denialPosture: SASC issues no denials of its own; it is the body to which denials are owed. The relevant posture is the executive branch's, restated through 2026, that government officials have not uncovered evidence verifying any UAP case involving extraterrestrial activity or technology. That position is worth dating against the committee's own enacted text, which since December 2022 has required a formal itemization of restricted-access programs never reported to Congress and of efforts to hide or provide incorrect information about UAP.

l0.label: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc. (later To The Stars Inc.)
l0.short: To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science Inc.

dossier.whatItIs: To The Stars Academy of Arts and Science Inc. was a Delaware public benefit corporation incorporated in 2017 and registered with the SEC under Commission File Number 024-10728, CIK 1710274, EIN 82-0601064. Its directors were Tom DeLonge, former CIA Directorate of Operations officer Jim Semivan, and physicist Harold Puthoff; Lockheed Skunk Works veteran Steve Justice and former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo were listed as significant employees. It raised money through a Regulation A offering, hosted the first officially released US military UAP videos, and signed a research agreement with the US Army before winding down its aerospace work and reverting to entertainment as To The Stars Inc.
dossier.whyImplicated: TTSA matters to this map not as a research institution but as a legal vehicle. For roughly three years it was the corporate person through which men carrying intelligence, special-access and black-aerospace careers could act in public, hold material, sign agreements with the government, and speak to Congress and the press without a government employer's prepublication apparatus sitting on top of every sentence. Its SEC filings are the single richest primary record on this board of who those people were, what clearances and career histories they carried, and what the venture was actually organised to do. In October 2019 it converted that standing into a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering 'material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage' - a government laboratory relationship with a private company that held claimed anomalous material. AARO's own history records the same personnel network attempting to reconstitute the AAWSAP effort inside the Department of Homeland Security as the prospective special access programme KONA BLUE.
dossier.narrative:
To The Stars Academy is the most thoroughly documented entity on this board, for a reason that has nothing to do with UAP: it sold securities. A company that offers stock under Regulation A must file with the SEC, and the filings are public, dated, signed and auditable. The FY2017 Form 1-K is therefore the closest thing this subject has to a sworn organisational chart.

What it shows is a very small company with a very unusual staff. Officers and directors were Tom DeLonge as president and interim chief executive; Jim Semivan as vice president of operations and director; and Harold E. Puthoff as vice president of science and technology and director. The filing states that Semivan 'retired from the Central Intelligence Agency's Directorate of Operations after 25 years working as an operations officer both overseas and domestically,' that he 'was a member of the CIA's Senior Intelligence Service,' and that he 'currently holds Top Secret Clearances.' It states that Puthoff is president and chief executive of EarthTech International and director of the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin. Two significant employees are listed: Steve Justice, Director of Advanced Programs and Technology, part-time at twenty hours a week, whose industry background the filing ties to the Lockheed organisation 'known as the "Skunk Works"'; and Luis Elizondo, Chief of Security and Special Programs, full-time, described as a career intelligence officer. As of 31 December 2017 the company had eleven employees.

The financial picture in the same filing is stark. Revenues for 2017 were $1,376,215 against cost of revenues of $750,932, producing gross profit of $625,283 - essentially a merchandise and music business. The net loss for 2017 was $30,665,436, against $422,670 the prior year, almost entirely non-cash stock compensation. Gravity Holdings LLC, whose sole member is the DeLonge Family Trust, held 60,000,000 Class A shares, 85.7 per cent of the class. This was not a research budget. It was a capital structure wrapped around a founder and a small group of named individuals.

What the company did with that structure is the part that belongs on this map. It became, as the filing puts it, 'the very first company to obtain official U.S. Government footage of unidentified aerial phenomena ("UAP") that had gone through the declassification process and been approved for public release,' publishing the footage through its online Community of Interest. The videos that entered the mainstream through the New York Times in December 2017 - the material now known as FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast - reached the public through a private securities issuer, not through a Pentagon press release. That routing is itself a finding. A declassification review was completed and the product was handed to a company in which a serving-until-recently Pentagon official was chief of security and special programs.

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command 'to advance TTSA's materiel and technology innovations in order to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles.' The announcement described the technology set as leveraging 'developments in material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage,' and set out the exchange: 'TTSA will share its discoveries with Ground Vehicle System Center (GVSC) and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection (GVSP) and the U.S. Army shall provide laboratories, expertise, support, and resources to help characterize the technologies and its applications.' Dr Joseph Cannon of US Army Futures Command called the partnership 'an exciting, non-traditional source for novel materials and transformational technologies.' Steve Justice, by then TTSA's chief operating officer and aerospace division director, said the agreement brought 'additional, critically important expertise that is necessary to advance the state-of-the-art in both our near and long-term technology areas of study.'

Read against the rest of this board, the CRADA is the important document. A private company holding material it described as anomalous obtained access to Army laboratories to characterise it, under an instrument that is not a procurement contract and does not require the government to pay. A CRADA moves capability and data across the government-private boundary in both directions with far less contractual and oversight furniture than a prime contract, and it does so without a competitive solicitation. Whether or not anything anomalous was ever in those laboratories, the mechanism is precisely the kind of low-visibility government-private research channel this board is built to map.

The network did not begin with TTSA and did not end with it. AARO's Historical Record Report records that after AAWSAP was terminated, 'its supporters unsuccessfully attempted to convince DHS to support a new version of this effort dubbed KONA BLUE,' which AARO characterises as 'a UAP-related Prospective Special Access Program (PSAP) called KONA BLUE that was proposed to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and supported by individuals who believed the USG was hiding off-world technology,' and which 'was never approved by DHS.' The same people, in sequence: a DIA contract, a proposed DHS special access programme, a Delaware public benefit corporation, a congressional hearing.

Elizondo, Christopher Mellon and Justice departed in December 2020, the aerospace and materials work wound down, and the entity renamed itself To The Stars Inc. and returned to entertainment. What it leaves behind is a documentary trail that is unusually hard to argue with, because it was filed under penalty of securities law: names, ages, clearances, prior employers, share counts, losses, and an executed agreement with a US Army laboratory command.

AARO reports that it acquired a sample from an alleged crashed off-world spacecraft 'from a private UAP investigating organization and the U.S. Army' and concluded it is 'a manufactured, terrestrial alloy' primarily composed of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with trace elements including lead.

The executed text of the TTSA-CCDC CRADA, its period of performance, its data-rights provisions, and any chain-of-custody documentation for material delivered to Army laboratories have not been publicly released.

dossier.denialPosture: TTSA has not been the subject of an official denial addressed to it by name. The nearest thing in the record is AARO's 2024 finding that a sample it acquired 'from a private UAP investigating organization and the U.S. Army' is a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with no exceptional qualities, and its characterisation of KONA BLUE - proposed by the same personnel network - as a prospective special access programme that DHS never approved and whose supporters 'never provided empirical evidence to support their claims.'
openQuestions: The full executed CRADA between TTSA and the Army Combat Capabilities Development Command has not been released; its statement of work, data rights, term and any material transfer provisions are unknown.

Whether the sample AARO says it obtained 'from a private UAP investigating organization and the U.S. Army' is the same material that moved under the TTSA CRADA is not established by any document reviewed here.

The route by which the FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast videos passed prepublication review and reached a private securities issuer rather than a government release channel is not documented in the public record.
What happened to TTSA's materials holdings when the aerospace and science divisions wound down in 2020-2022, and who holds them now.

Whether any TTSA principal was under a live nondisclosure or special-access indoctrination instrument at the time of the company's public statements, and whether DoD SAPCO approval under DoDD 5205.07 Section 3.1.g was sought or given for any briefing to Congress.

l0.label: New York Times, 'Glowing Auras and Black Money: The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program'
l0.short: New York Times, 'Glowing Auras and Black Money

dossier.whatItIs: 'Glowing Auras and "Black Money": The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program,' a New York Times article published 16 December 2017 by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal and Leslie Kean. It revealed the existence of the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, its $22 million funding, its origin at the request of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, and its management by Luis Elizondo from the fifth floor of the Pentagon's C Ring. It was accompanied by the release of US Navy FLIR gun-camera footage.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the date on which the concealment failed in public, and the article says so in its own lede: $22 million inside a $600 billion budget 'was almost impossible to find. Which was how the Pentagon wanted it.' The piece establishes three facts the program argument rests on: that the Defense Department had never before acknowledged the program's existence, that DoD said it shut down in 2012, and that the program's own backers said it did not — that officials continued to investigate episodes for five more years while carrying out other duties. That is a documented, contemporaneous dispute about whether a UAP program continued to run after the government said it had stopped. Every subsequent institutional response — the UAP Task Force, the 2021 ODNI assessment, AARO, the 2023 and 2024 hearings, the NARA records collection — is downstream of this article, and a whistleblower report given to Congress in 2024 alleges that a new Unacknowledged Special Access Program was created in 2017 in direct response to it.
dossier.narrative:
The article is short on speculation and long on institutional fact, which is why it has held up. Its reporting basis is stated in the second paragraph: the program was documented 'according to Defense Department officials, interviews with program participants and records obtained by The New York Times.' Three sourcing streams, one of them documentary. Those records have never been published in full, and their contents remain one of the most valuable unexploited leads on the board.

The factual core is compact. The Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program was funded at $22 million within Defense Department budgets of roughly $600 billion a year. It was run by Luis Elizondo, a military intelligence official, from the fifth floor of the Pentagon's C Ring. The Defense Department had never previously acknowledged that it existed. DoD said it shut the program down in 2012. And — the sentence that does the most work — 'its backers say that, while the Pentagon ended funding for the effort at that time, the program remains in existence. For the past five years, they say, officials with the program have continued to investigate episodes brought to them by service members, while also carrying out their other Defense Department duties.'

That construction is the whole concealment argument in miniature. A program is funded through a line item that is hard to find. Its existence is not acknowledged. When it becomes inconvenient, funding is ended and the government says the program is over. The work continues anyway, distributed across officials' other duties, which is exactly the arrangement that makes a program invisible to the reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. 119 — there is no new SAP to notify, no budget line to report, and no milestone schedule to submit. Whether that is what happened is not proven by the article. What the article proves is that people with direct knowledge asserted it on the record in December 2017, and that DoD's contrary position was already a matter of dispute at the moment of first disclosure.

The money trail the article opened has been independently corroborated by the government's own subsequent releases. Steven Aftergood, writing for the Federation of American Scientists in January 2019 on the occasion of DIA's FOIA release of the 38 funded research titles, described the same program in the same terms: 'From 2007 to 2012, the DIA spent $22 million on the activity, formally known as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program. It was apparently initiated at the behest of then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, with most of the funding directed to a Nevada constituent of his' — and cited this article by name. The Debrief's 2021 investigation into BAASS likewise anchors its $22 million figure to this piece. So the article's central financial claim has been ratified by a FOIA release, by an arms-control watchdog, and by a subsequent investigative outlet using different documents.

The article's second, less-discussed effect was on the evidentiary record itself. It carried Navy infrared gun-camera footage into mainstream circulation, which the Navy later confirmed as authentic imagery of unidentified aerial phenomena. That transformed the subject from a testimony problem into a sensor-data problem, and it is the reason later official documents — including the 2021 ODNI assessment's observation that a majority of UAP 'registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation' — are framed in terms of instrumentation rather than eyewitnesses.

The third effect is the one that matters most for this board, and it is alleged rather than established. In written testimony to House Oversight on 13 November 2024, Michael Shellenberger reported that a whistleblower's report provided to congressional committees alleges that DoD created an Unacknowledged Special Access Program called IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION in 2017, after this article was published, to serve as a 'central or parent USAP' consolidating UAP observations and enforcing internal information security by detecting, quarantining and transferring collection incidents before they circulate within the Military Intelligence Enterprise. If true, this article did not merely expose a program — it caused a new and better-hidden one. DoD spokesperson Sue Gough has denied that any SAP by that name exists in its records.

There are also unresolved discrepancies that a careful analyst should hold onto. The article and FAS both date the program 2007-2012 and call it AATIP; the DIA contracting record dates the BAASS contract to 2008 and calls the effort AAWSAP; Shellenberger's testimony dates AAWSAP 2009-2017 with reports ending in 2010 and the program running through 2012. The government has never issued a clean, consistent account of the relationship between AATIP and AAWSAP, and that inconsistency is not incidental — it is the kind of ambiguity that survives only when nobody is compelled to resolve it.

What the article does not do: it does not allege retrievals, materials, or reverse-engineering. It does not name a contractor in its lede. Its claims about the program's survival past 2012 are attributed to unnamed backers, and its documentary basis has never been made public.

claims.text: 'Glowing Auras and "Black Money": The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program' was published by The New York Times on 16 December 2017 and written by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal and Leslie Kean.

The article opens: 'In the $600 billion annual Defense Department budgets, the $22 million spent on the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program was almost impossible to find. Which was how the Pentagon wanted it.'
The article states the program 'was run by a military intelligence official, Luis Elizondo, on the fifth floor of the Pentagon's C Ring, deep within the building's maze.'

The article states: 'The Defense Department has never before acknowledged the existence of the program, which it says it shut down in 2012. But its backers say that, while the Pentagon ended funding for the effort at that time, the program remains in existence.'

The article states: 'For the past five years, they say, officials with the program have continued to investigate episodes brought to them by service members, while also carrying out their other Defense Department duties.'

The article's stated evidentiary basis is 'Defense Department officials, interviews with program participants and records obtained by The New York Times'; those records have never been published in full.

The Federation of American Scientists, writing in January 2019 on the DIA's FOIA release of 38 funded research titles, corroborated that 'from 2007 to 2012, the DIA spent $22 million on the activity, formally known as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program' and that it was 'apparently initiated at the behest of then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, with most of the funding directed to a Nevada constituent of his,' citing this article by name.
The Debrief's January 2021 investigation into BAASS anchors the $22 million DIA-to-Bigelow figure directly to this New York Times article.

Michael Shellenberger testified to House Oversight on 13 November 2024 that a whistleblower alleges DoD created the Unacknowledged Special Access Program IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION in 2017 'after the New York Times published an article describing an informal Pentagon UAP program called Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, or AATIP.'
DoD spokesperson Sue Gough responded to the Immaculate Constellation reporting with: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION."'
Co-author Leslie Kean maintains a dated record of the article's publication on her own website under 16 December 2017.

Shellenberger's testimony sets out a Pentagon program timeline in which AAWSAP ran 2009-2017 with reports ending in 2010 but running through 2012 'according to the DOD,' the UAP Task Force ran 2020-2022, and AARO began in 2022 by order of Congress — a chronology that conflicts with the 2007-2012 AATIP dating in the NYT article and in the FAS account.

Luis Elizondo, the official the article identified as running the program, testified to Congress on 13 November 2024 that in his last position he 'managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council' and that 'the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies.'

Michael Gold testified in November 2024 that Lt. Commander Alex Dietrich's USS Nimitz encounter might have been 'lost to history' but for AAWSAP, tying the program the article exposed to the 2004 Nimitz case whose video the article helped make public.

dossier.denialPosture: The article itself records the Defense Department's position that the program was shut down in 2012, and simultaneously records that program backers say it continued — making the denial and its contradiction contemporaneous and jointly attributable. DoD's later flat denial of IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION, the program allegedly created in response to this article, is the second denial in the same chain.
connections: Luis Elizondo is the named program manager here and a sworn witness before House Oversight seven years later; the article is his standing credential.
Harry Reid appears as the program's political originator, connecting the article to the DIA solicitation, to BAASS, and to Nevada contracting.
The 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents released by DIA under FOIA in January 2019 are the article's documentary aftershock, and FAS explicitly links the two.
The article is the alleged causal trigger for IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION in 2017 per the whistleblower report entered into the record at the 13 November 2024 hearing.
It is the origin point for the sensor-data framing later adopted by ODNI's 2021 assessment, which describes UAP registering across radar, infrared, electro-optical and weapon seekers.
Co-author Leslie Kean later co-reported the David Grusch allegations, making her a through-line from 2017 disclosure to 2023 whistleblower testimony.

The unpublished 'records obtained by The New York Times' are a discrete, identifiable body of documents that no FOIA has surfaced and that would now fall within the scope of the NARA UAP Records Collection if they originated as government records.
openQuestions: What were the 'records obtained by The New York Times,' who provided them, and do copies exist in government custody subject to the NARA Record Group 615 transfer obligation?
Who were the 'backers' who said the program continued after 2012, and in what capacity did they continue investigating episodes?

Are AATIP and AAWSAP the same program, sequential programs, or a program and a successor portfolio? The NYT, FAS, DIA contracting records and Shellenberger's testimony give three incompatible date ranges.

l0.label: The MITRE Corporation

dossier.whatItIs: The MITRE Corporation is a private not-for-profit spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1958 that operates exclusively as a manager of federally funded research and development centers. It runs six FFRDCs on behalf of the Department of Defense, the Federal Aviation Administration, Treasury and the IRS, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Health and Human Services, and NIST. It is headquartered in McLean, Virginia, and also provides the administrative home for JASON, the government's standing outside scientific advisory panel.
dossier.whyImplicated: MITRE is on this map because of the legal mechanism it embodies, not because a witness has named it as a custodian of material. An FFRDC is granted, by regulation, access to government and contractor data 'beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship' - including sensitive and proprietary data, installations, equipment and real property - and its sponsoring agreement gives the sponsor's Executive Agent approval authority over the classification, publication and distribution of its output. That combination produces a private organisation holding federal program records under a disclosure obligation that runs to a sponsoring agency rather than to Congress or to the public, and whose corporate files are not agency records for FOIA purposes. The DHS sponsoring agreement goes further: MITRE's own staff sign non-disclosure agreements that expressly preserve the right to report substantial violations of law to Congress, but subcontractors and consultants are required to sign the same NDA with that whistleblower carve-back removed. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison put this exact structure in writing, telling MITRE that FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records' and demanding a search back to 1 January 1930.
dossier.narrative:
MITRE occupies a category that exists nowhere else in the federal enterprise. It manufactures nothing, competes for nothing, and sells nothing. It exists to hold institutional memory and technical judgement on behalf of government sponsors, and the Federal Acquisition Regulation builds that role out of a single privilege: an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.' That sentence, FAR 35.017(a)(2), is the load-bearing beam of this dossier. Everything a prime contractor knows about its own black programmes, and everything the government knows about the prime, can lawfully sit inside the FFRDC that sits between them.

MITRE currently operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for DoD; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and the IRS, co-sponsored by Veterans Affairs, the Social Security Administration and Commerce; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC for NIST. Its own fact sheet notes there are only forty-two FFRDCs in total and that operating six of them is 'a high honor.' The relevant point for this board is not prestige but coverage: one nonprofit sits inside the defence establishment, the intelligence-adjacent national security enterprise, and the civil aviation regulator that owns the primary radar picture of American airspace.

The governing document that shows how this works in practice is the FY2009 sponsoring agreement between DHS and MITRE for HS SEDI, signed by MITRE's president and by the Acting Under Secretary for Science and Technology on 13 March 2009. It is worth reading as a specification for exactly the kind of custody problem this board is mapping. Section 3 states that SEDI's work 'will often require privileged access to information, including sensitive Government information and industry proprietary data not normally available to non-Government organizations.' Section 5(h) obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data.' Section 6(c)(9) records the routine practice: 'Ordinarily, sponsors release classified, privileged, no-contractor, and other sensitive material directly to SEDI.' Section 5(a) states plainly that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects.'

Then the agreement closes the loop on disclosure. Section 6(b)(9) gives the DHS Executive Agent authority to review and approve 'the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications.' Section 9(g) defines 'Privileged Information' so broadly that it captures every deliverable, note, lab record, test result and analysis MITRE produces for the sponsor, and forbids disclosure except as required by law or 'as expressly authorized in writing by the DHS Executive Agent.' Section 9(g)(2) then carves back the whistleblower statutes, stating that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.' That is the protective clause. And Section 5(j)(iv) requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2).' The people at the outer edge of the work - the ones brought in for specialised expertise MITRE does not hold in-house - are contractually bound by the secrecy terms without the clause that preserves their right to tell Congress.

This is the structural argument, and on 22 May 2026 a member of Congress made it out loud. Rep. Eric Burlison, of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, sent a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE's president Mark Peters and its general counsel Christopher Land. The relevant time period is 'January 1, 1930, to the present.' The definitions section reaches every MITRE-operated FFRDC, every subcontractor, and any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, or equivalent terms.'

The interrogatories are targeted at exactly the mechanism described above. Section III demands identification of every Special Access Program, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword and DOE SIGMA category MITRE participated in or supported in connection with UAP records, and asks whether each 'was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks MITRE to identify any classification guide, NDA, access roster or sponsor communication that instructed personnel to avoid using the terms UAP, UFO, crash retrieval or reverse engineering in records. Section VIII asks for every NDA or indoctrination instrument 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress.' Section IX asks MITRE to identify any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems or Bigelow Aerospace. Section X asks whether responsive funding was routed through a cover programme 'whose public description differed materially from the responsive work performed.' The letter warns that concealment or destruction may implicate 18 U.S.C. sections 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519 and 2071.

MITRE's reply, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was a single sentence from a spokesperson: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That answer is not evasive so much as accurate. It restates the architecture the letter was written to expose. An FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor. Congress asks MITRE; MITRE asks the sponsor; the sponsor is the same authority that classified the work. What the record does not contain, as of this writing, is the certification of search methodology, the records-location index, the preservation hold, or any production - all of which the letter demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks.

claims.text: Federal Acquisition Regulation 35.017(a)(2) states that an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.'

MITRE operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center (DoD), the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development (FAA), the Center for Enterprise Modernization (Treasury/IRS, co-sponsored by VA, SSA and Commerce), the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute (DHS), the Health FFRDC (HHS), and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC (NIST).

The DHS-MITRE sponsoring agreement for HS SEDI obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data ... including that which is not normally available to non-government organizations' (Section 5(h)).

Under Section 6(b)(9) of the same agreement, the DHS Executive Agent 'Reviews and approves the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications' - meaning the sponsoring agency, not MITRE, controls whether MITRE's work product can be released.

Section 5(j)(iv) of the same agreement requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) secrecy terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2)' - the clause that preserves the right to make disclosures to Congress essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.

Section 9(g)(2) of the same agreement states that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law' - a protection extended to MITRE's own personnel but expressly withheld from its subcontractors and consultants.

Section 5(a) of the same agreement states that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects and shall strictly comply with the provisions of the National Industrial Security Program ... as set forth in DOD Directive 5220.22-M as amended.'

On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison transmitted a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE president Mark Peters and general counsel Christopher Land, setting the relevant search period as 'January 1, 1930, to the present.'

The Burlison interrogatories demand that MITRE identify all Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, Managed-Need-To-Know codewords and DOE SIGMA categories it participated in or supported in connection with UAP-related records, and state for each 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify any nondisclosure agreement, indoctrination record or sponsor communication 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress, Inspectors General, AARO, NARA, federal law enforcement, or appropriate cleared oversight officials.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify 'any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems, Bigelow Aerospace or its successors/affiliates.'

Burlison's accompanying statement of 26 May 2026 says FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records - especially records Congress has directed to be identified, preserved, reviewed, and transferred for public release.'

MITRE's public response, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets'; a member of Burlison's staff told the same outlet that the letter was informed by 'advice from many whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations, and those working at FFRDCs.'

MITRE's certification of search methodology, records-location index, preservation hold and production of unclassified responsive records - all demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks from 22 May 2026 - have not been placed on the public record.

dossier.denialPosture: MITRE has not denied holding UAP-related records. Its only public statement on the Burlison inquiry, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was that it was reviewing its archives and that 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' No certification, denial of possession, or records-location index has been made public.
openQuestions: Did MITRE issue the preservation hold demanded within ten business days, and if so, which systems, archives and air-gapped environments does it cover?

Whether the subcontractor/consultant NDA construction found in the DHS HS SEDI sponsoring agreement - Section 9(g) secrecy terms without the Section 9(g)(2) congressional-disclosure carve-back - also appears in the sponsoring agreements for MITRE's DoD, FAA, Treasury, HHS and NIST FFRDCs, which are not public in comparable form.
Which federal sponsor would have to authorise release of any responsive MITRE record, and whether any sponsor has been asked.

Whether MITRE's National Security Engineering Center or its work for the FAA ever handled UAP sensor, radar or anomaly-detection data, which Section V of the interrogatories asks about directly and which has not been answered publicly.
MITRE's role in administering JASON, and whether JASON was ever tasked on UAP or anomalous materials questions, is not addressed anywhere in the public record reviewed here.

l0.label: RAND Corporation

dossier.whatItIs: The RAND Corporation is a nonprofit research institution created by the U.S. Army Air Forces in 1946 as Project RAND, operating under contract to the Douglas Aircraft Company, and spun out as an independent California nonprofit in 1948 with initial capital from the Ford Foundation. It operates federally funded research and development centers for the Department of Defense, including Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute and the Army Research Division, and has published on unidentified aerial phenomena in both 1968 and 2023.
dossier.whyImplicated: RAND is the original defense-contractor-adjacent think tank, born inside an airframe manufacturer and chartered to think about things the Air Force could not think about in uniform. It sat at the center of the 1946-1968 window in which any recovery and exploitation effort would have needed exactly RAND's product: threat framing, capability assessment, and analytic cover. Its 1968 internal draft "UFOs: What To Do?" states flatly that the phenomenon is "unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms" — a judgment produced inside the Air Force's own analytic arm during the same period the Condon Committee was preparing to declare the subject scientifically barren. RAND stamped that document for internal use only and reportedly refused to acknowledge its existence for thirty-two years. Fifty-five years later, RAND published an OSD-sponsored study whose central finding is that public UAP reports cluster around military operations areas — analytically useful, and also the most institutionally comfortable finding available, since it relocates the phenomenon inside U.S. military activity without ever addressing recovery or custody.
dossier.narrative:
Project RAND was created in 1946 under contract between the Army Air Forces and the Douglas Aircraft Company, expressly to retain the civilian scientific talent that had won the war. Its first assignment, delivered on a three-week deadline, was the design of a world-circling spaceship; the resulting "Preliminary Design of an Experimental World-Circling Spaceship" was released in May 1946. The organization incorporated as a California nonprofit on 14 May 1948, and on 1 November 1948 the Project RAND contract was formally transferred from Douglas Aircraft to the RAND Corporation, with the Ford Foundation supplying the initial capital for the spin-off.

That founding sequence is the point. RAND was a defense contractor's internal analysis shop that became a national institution by changing its corporate wrapper without changing its customer. The July 1947 Roswell events fall squarely inside the Douglas-contract period; the FBI teletype GAO later recovered records that the recovered disc and balloon were "being sent to Wright Field... for examination" — Wright Field being Air Materiel Command, the same enterprise for which Project RAND was doing its earliest work on exotic aerospace concepts. GAO in 1995 could find no Air Materiel Command records from 1947-1950 mentioning the crash or any examination of debris.

RAND's documented engagement with the phenomenon comes in two widely separated bursts.

The first is DRU-1571, "UFOs: What To Do?", by George Kocher, 1968, forty-three pages. RAND's own abstract for the document is unusually direct: "Since World War II, however, there seems to have been a drastic increase in the number of sightings. We have enough data — both visual and photographic — on some of these sightings to know that the phenomenon is unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms." Kocher examines UFO brightness, size and maneuvers, discusses the frequency and location of sightings, and closes by proposing standardized reporting so that times and locations of appearances may be anticipated and objective data obtained. He recommended going beyond a national collection to worldwide data with intensive investigation of the most interesting reports. The document is dated 27 November 1968 and was stamped for RAND use only, with instructions not to quote or cite externally; researchers report that RAND did not acknowledge the paper's existence and authenticity until 2000. RAND now files it in a series it describes as unrestricted drafts that "were not usually formally edited or peer reviewed" — a retrospective classification that softens a document written by its own staff during the exact months the Air Force was preparing to shut down Project Blue Book on the strength of the Condon report.

The timing is the finding. In late 1968 the Air Force's analytic contractor produced an internal paper saying the phenomenon was real, extraordinary and inexplicable, and recommending a global standardized collection architecture. In January 1969 the Condon report was released and Blue Book was terminated. The Kocher draft was suppressed for a generation.

The second burst is 2023. RAND published "Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America," report number RR-A2475-1, by Marek N. Posard, Ashley Gromis and Mary Lee. The research was sponsored by the Office of the Secretary of Defense and conducted within the Acquisition and Technology Policy Program of the RAND National Security Research Division. The authors analyzed 101,151 public UAP reports across 12,783 U.S. Census Bureau locations. The headline result is that reports cluster near Military Operations Areas — designated blocks of airspace for military training and maneuvering, not necessarily near airbases. RAND completed the report in May 2023, sent it to the Department of Defense for review, and published it on 25 July 2023 — the day before the House Oversight Committee's UAP hearing at which David Grusch testified.

For an analyst, the 2023 study is a two-edged artifact. Its finding is genuinely useful: whatever is being reported, it is being reported disproportionately where the military flies. That is consistent with misidentification of military activity, and it is equally consistent with the phenomenon exhibiting interest in military activity — the correlation does not discriminate. What the study does not do, and was not scoped to do, is ask a single question about recovery, custody, materials, or program structure. An OSD-sponsored study, reviewed by the Department before release, published the day before the most consequential UAP hearing in fifty years, framing the entire subject as a geography-of-misidentification problem, is exactly the deliverable a concealment posture would commission. That does not make the analysis wrong. It makes the timing and the scoping evidence about the sponsor.

RAND's structural position remains what it was in 1946: an FFRDC operator with continuous classified access across Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute and the Army Research Division, publishing an unclassified fraction of its output and disclaiming that its publications "do not necessarily reflect the opinions of its research clients and sponsors." Between 1968 and 2023 the public record shows nothing. Fifty-five years of an FFRDC's silence on a subject its own analyst called unambiguously extraordinary is itself a data point.
