Sol states that the council 'reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board, an interagency body coordinating across military, law enforcement, and intelligence community agencies' and that 'All data shared with the council will be unclassified.'

Sol characterises the appointments as 'a fulfillment of its founding mission,' adding that 'Sol can now share its insight to the highest levels of government deliberation about disclosure, amplifying our impact.'

The Sol Foundation solicits membership and donations on its own site but names no donors, foundations or corporate supporters anywhere in its published material.

openQuestions: Who funds the Sol Foundation. No donor, foundation or corporate supporter is named in any published Sol material, and there is no public filing reviewed here that discloses its revenue sources.

The foundation's own founding date is inconsistent across its publications (2022 in some material, 'established in 2023' in the June 2026 council announcement); the incorporation record has not been checked.
Whether any Sol principal or adviser holds or has held a security clearance or special-access indoctrination that would constrain what they can say about the concealment thesis they publish on.
Whether the McConnell whistleblower restitution fund proposal has been introduced in any legislative vehicle, and by whom.

What relationship, if any, exists between Sol and the government bodies its people now advise beyond the individual appointments - whether any contract, agreement, data-sharing arrangement or funding flows between the foundation and ODNI, AARO or the FBI.

l0.label: Lockheed Martin Corporation

dossier.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Corporation is the largest single recipient of United States defense contract obligations, formed by the 1995 merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta. It operates cleared facilities accredited for Special Access Program work and runs the Advanced Development Programs organisation, the Skunk Works, which has built the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 among other classified aircraft. It is the only corporation named on the record, by a sworn witness in a congressional hearing, as a holder of recovered non-terrestrial material.
dossier.whyImplicated: Lockheed Martin sits at the intersection of the two conditions this board treats as necessary for a legacy programme to survive without congressional visibility: a company with the industrial capacity to store and work on recovered material, and a legal regime that can lift normal industrial security oversight off it. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of National Industrial Security Program oversight for DoD special access programs whenever the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves a carve-out provision. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee or consultant may provide SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. Two sworn witnesses - George Knapp in September 2025 and Luis Elizondo in November 2024 - have testified to a specific, dated, blocked transaction in which material collected in the 1950s and held at a California facility was to move from a corporation to Bigelow's BAASS, and did not. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of that sworn testimony.
dossier.narrative:
The Lockheed Martin allegation is unusual on this board because it is the one that has been made under oath, in a hearing room, with a company name attached. On 9 September 2025, before the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, George Knapp told the committee: 'It has been widely reported and suspected that Lockheed Martin is one of the contractors - the defense contractors, that has held this stuff, stored it away in secrecy, and tried to figure out how it works.' He then went further and put his own reporting on the record: 'I have confirmed on the record that Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.' Later in the same hearing Rep. Tim Burchett asked which corporations hold the material. Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.' He added a line that is, for the purposes of this map, more revealing than the accusation itself: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Ten months earlier, on 13 November 2024, Luis Elizondo had testified to the same transaction from inside the government side of it. Asked by Rep. Burlison whether the government or defence contractors possess technology, Elizondo said one reason his predecessor programme AAWSAP was trying to collect material of unknown origin was that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material ... that was collected in the 1950s. Unfortunately, that did not actually occur.' Burlison then put the Christopher Sharp reporting to him directly - a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace, and a CIA block - and Elizondo answered: 'What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.' He described the missing instrument: 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

The official record does not name the company, but it does record the allegation. AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, logs an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.' A separate entry logs a claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly intact, under a CIA partnership that ended in 1989. AARO says it found no empirical evidence for either. AARO's denial is procedurally notable in its own right: 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, on what date, and describes no verification step beyond the meeting itself. Under this board's sourcing rule, that is an artefact of a statement, not evidence of the fact asserted.

What makes the allegation structurally survivable rather than merely unproven is the regulatory architecture around a company like Lockheed Martin. Industrial security oversight of cleared contractors is normally exercised by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency under the National Industrial Security Program. But 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.' A carve-out programme is therefore a cleared contractor facility from which the government's own standing industrial security inspector has been formally removed by name, at the direction of the second-ranking official in the Department.

The congressional side is narrowed by the same directive. DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' That is a standing prior-restraint on contractor-to-Congress disclosure inside the SAP world, in an unclassified, publicly posted directive. The statutory reporting channel is narrower still: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content of any SAP report to the defence committees on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - eight people, not four committees.

So the record on Lockheed Martin has an unusual shape. Two witnesses under oath, one of them a former Pentagon official, describing the same blocked transfer with the same missing Secretary of the Air Force memorandum. An official report that catalogues the allegation, does not name the company, and reports an unverified denial from unnamed executives. A statutory and regulatory framework that would make exactly this kind of holding invisible to the ordinary inspection and reporting machinery. And, on the other side of the ledger, no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no inventory, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record statement from Lockheed Martin responding to sworn testimony that named it.

That material was not made here.'

Elizondo testified at the same hearing that 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07' - the legal mechanism by which a cleared contractor facility can be removed from the government's standing industrial security inspection regime.

claims.text: DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy,' effective 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g that 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive the inclusion of specified information in required SAP reports on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information and the waiver justification go only 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, records an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.'

The same AARO report records a separate interviewee claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from different crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly 'intact,' and that the CIA had a partnership with the company that ended in 1989.

AARO's stated basis for rejecting the corporate custody allegation is that 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology' - without naming the executives, the companies, the dates, or any verification step beyond the meeting.

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE list Lockheed Martin first among the entities whose UAP-related work MITRE must identify, placing the company's name in a formal congressional production request rather than only in testimony.

No contract, facility designation, transfer or shipping document, inventory record, subpoena, inspection report, or on-the-record corporate response from Lockheed Martin to the sworn testimony naming it has been placed in the public record.

dossier.denialPosture: Lockheed Martin has issued no public, on-the-record rebuttal of the sworn testimony of September 2025 naming it. The only denial in the documentary record is AARO's summary statement in its 2024 Historical Record Report that unnamed 'executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees' met the Director of AARO and denied ever having recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered extraterrestrial technology.

The identity of the 'facility in California' described in Knapp's sworn testimony, and whether it is a company-owned site or leased space on a government-owned installation.
Whether the Secretary of the Air Force memorandum Elizondo described as necessary and never issued exists in draft, and in whose files.
Whether Lockheed Martin executives were among those AARO says met its Director, and on what date - AARO names neither the companies nor the individuals.

l0.label: EG&G (Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier)

dossier.whatItIs: EG&G — Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier — was founded in 1947 by three MIT-connected figures whose wartime work instrumented and photographed nuclear detonations, and became the Atomic Energy Commission's principal test-instrumentation contractor at the Nevada Test Site. Its Las Vegas-based Special Projects division provided engineering, technical, radar and logistical support to classified programs at the Air Force operating location near Groom Lake and operated the unmarked passenger airline known as Janet from a dedicated terminal at McCarran International Airport. The name and the contracts have since passed through the Carlyle Group, URS Corporation, AECOM and Amentum.
dossier.whyImplicated: EG&G is the connective tissue of the American black-site system: the same firm that instrumented nuclear tests ran the workforce airlift, the technical support and the site services that make an unacknowledged installation function. Its employees are the population at the center of the only litigation that has ever forced a court to decide what legal protection a denied facility enjoys. When Groom Lake workers sued in August 1994 alleging illegal open-air burning of hazardous waste, the Secretary of the Air Force filed a formal military and state secrets privilege claim covering categories that expressly included "security sensitive environmental data"; the President signed an annual RCRA exemption for "the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada"; and the Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that seemingly innocuous information forming part of a classified mosaic may be withheld and that a court cannot order the government to disentangle it. That sequence — contractor workforce, denied facility, state secrets, presidential exemption, dismissal — is the complete legal template a legacy program would require, and it is fully documented in the Federal Register and the Federal Reporter.
dossier.narrative:
Harold "Doc" Edgerton, Kenneth Germeshausen and Herbert Grier came out of MIT and out of the Manhattan Project's photographic and timing instrumentation work, and in 1947 incorporated the company that carried their initials. EG&G's core business for decades was the measurement of nuclear detonations for the Atomic Energy Commission — high-speed photography, timing and firing, diagnostics — making it one of very few private firms holding continuous clearances into the most sensitive American technical programs. From that base it grew into site services, security support, range operations and personnel logistics across the Nevada complex.

The most visible artifact is the airline. EG&G Special Projects operated the passenger service, universally known by its Janet callsigns, that moves the workforce from Las Vegas to the Air Force operating location at Groom Lake and to the Tonopah Test Range. A Nevada Department of Transportation diagram for McCarran dated May 1999 labels the building on the west side of the field the "EG&G Airlift Terminal." Reporting places the first Las Vegas-to-Groom flights in 1972 with a Douglas DC-6, and current operations at roughly twenty round trips per weekday carrying one to one and a half thousand workers on unmarked aircraft. This is what a routinized, industrial-scale commute to an unacknowledged facility looks like, and it has looked like that for over fifty years.

The legal history is the part that matters most for this board. In August 1994, Professor Jonathan Turley of the National Law Center at George Washington University filed two suits based on field research by the Project on Government Oversight: Frost v. Perry against the Secretary of Defense and Kasza v. Browner against the EPA Administrator, both in the District of Nevada, both under the citizen-suit provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Helen Frost was the widow of a former worker at the site; Walter Kasza was another. Six plaintiffs were permitted to proceed under pseudonyms because, in the district court's finding, "there is a substantial danger here that the Plaintiffs will be subject to retaliation by the government or possible physical attack and harassment from third parties in Nevada."

The government's response was not to deny the allegations. Once discovery began, the Air Force refused to furnish almost all requested information on privilege grounds, and Secretary of the Air Force Sheila Widnall invoked a formal claim of military and state secrets privilege over categories of national security information associated with the operating location near Groom Lake, "specifically including '[s]ecurity sensitive environmental data.'" The claim was supported by an unclassified declaration and a classified declaration reviewed in camera, and the court also reviewed in camera a classified declaration by Air Force Vice Chief of Staff General Thomas S. Moorman, Jr. The district court found the privilege properly invoked and held that it covered the requested information "even though her need for discovery was compelling." The Air Force then moved for summary judgment on the ground that the privilege barred any evidence tending to confirm or disprove that hazardous waste had ever been generated, stored or disposed of at the location — an essential element of every claim. Summary judgment was granted.

On the EPA side, the district court held that RCRA itself contains no exception for disclosure of classified information, but that the President may exempt a federal facility under 42 U.S.C. 6961(a), and gave the Administrator time to obtain one. On 29 September 1995 the President issued Presidential Determination No. 95-45, published at 60 Federal Register 52823, which reads in operative part: "I find that it is in the paramount interest of the United States to exempt the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada (the subject of litigation in Kasza v. Browner (D. Nev. CV-S-94-795-PMP) and Frost v. Perry (D. Nev. CV-S-94-714-PMP)) from any applicable requirement for the disclosure to unauthorized persons of classified information concerning that operating location." It exempted the location from "any Federal, State, interstate or local provision respecting control and abatement of solid waste or hazardous waste disposal that would require the disclosure of classified information concerning that operating location to any unauthorized person," and stated: "This exemption shall be effective for the full one-year statutory period." One year. It must be renewed, and it has been.

The Ninth Circuit decided the consolidated appeals on 8 January 1998. Kasza v. Browner, 133 F.3d 1159, cert. denied, 525 U.S. 967 (1998). The panel held that the state secrets privilege is absolute; that "if seemingly innocuous information is part of a classified mosaic, the state secrets privilege may be invoked to bar its disclosure and the court cannot order the government to disentangle this information from other classified information"; and that RCRA section 6001 does not preempt the privilege — "we discern no Congressional intent to replace the government's evidentiary privilege to withhold sensitive information in litigation by providing an exemption from RCRA's regulation of hazardous waste." The Supreme Court declined review.

What that sequence establishes is not that anything exotic was buried in the Groom Lake trenches. It establishes that a contractor-operated installation the government declines to name can be placed outside an ordinary environmental statute by a one-page presidential memorandum; that a cabinet secretary's declaration can foreclose discovery of the physical facts; that federal courts will accept a mosaic theory under which even innocuous data is protected; and that the workers who get sick have no remedy. Every element a concealed recovery and exploitation effort would need to survive litigation was demonstrated in public between 1994 and 1998.

The corporate lineage matters for tracking who holds the contracts today. EG&G's technical services business was acquired in August 1999 by a Carlyle Group entity and operated as EG&G Technical Services; URS Corporation acquired it in August 2002; URS was absorbed by AECOM in 2014; and the Janet operation is reported to have passed with AECOM's federal business to Amentum. The initials survive on the fuselages of nothing, but the function has never been interrupted.

Nev. Accordingly, we hold that RCRA § 6001 does not preempt the state secrets privilege."

dossier.denialPosture: Neither EG&G nor its successors has ever publicly described the Groom Lake work. The government's posture in the Frost and Kasza litigation was not denial but non-cognizability: it did not deny that hazardous waste had been burned, it asserted that the existence or non-existence of such information is a state secret. Presidential Determination 95-45 preserves that posture explicitly, stating that nothing in it is intended to "imply that in the absence of such a Presidential exemption, the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) or any other provision of law permits or requires disclosure of classified information to unauthorized persons."

The Carlyle Group, URS Corporation, AECOM and Amentum — the ownership chain that now holds the successor contracts, all publicly traded or private-equity entities with no separate public accounting for the classified Nevada work.

Kasza v. Browner is one of the most cited modern state secrets precedents and appears in Department of Justice briefing in later privilege cases, making the Groom Lake litigation the doctrinal ancestor of subsequent dismissals.

l0.label: Nolan, Vallee, Jiang & Lemke (2022), Progress in Aerospace Sciences 128:100788
l0.short: Nolan, Vallee, Jiang & Lemke (2022), Progress in Aerospace Sciences 128:100788

dossier.whatItIs: A peer-reviewed review article, "Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics," by Garry P. Nolan, Jacques F. Vallee, Sizun Jiang and Larry G. Lemke, published in Elsevier's Progress in Aerospace Sciences, Volume 128, January 2022, article 100788 (online 9 December 2021), DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2021.100788. Its first half reviews mass-spectrometry and imaging methods for characterizing unknown solids; its second half applies them to a preserved sample, designated CB_JV-1, from the 17 December 1977 molten-metal fall at Council Bluffs, Iowa. It is the first materials-analysis paper on a UAP-associated sample to appear in a mainstream aerospace journal.
dossier.whyImplicated: This paper is the methodological hinge of the entire material-evidence question. It puts on the record, in a journal that describes itself as invitation-only and that is read by the aerospace engineering community, a replicable protocol for exactly the task a legacy exploitation program would have been performing in secret for decades: determining whether a recovered solid was manufactured, by whom, and by what process. Its lead author, Garry Nolan, is a Stanford professor of pathology whose analytical lab work brought him into contact with the contractor-adjacent UAP community; its second author, Jacques Vallee, holds the sample catalogue that has been the reference set for physical-trace UFO cases since the 1960s. The paper cites, on page 3, one of the Defense Intelligence Reference Documents produced under the DIA-funded Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP) - Maxim Tsoi's "Metallic Spintronics" (2010) - which drags a government UAP-program artifact into the open Elsevier literature and into a citation graph that can be followed. Finally, the paper's actual result is the inconvenient one: isotope ratios consistent with terrestrial norms, but an inhomogeneity pattern the authors say would not be expected to form naturally and that they cannot source to any identified industrial process. That is the shape of an evidentiary problem, not a claim of proof - which is what makes it usable.
dossier.narrative:
The Council Bluffs event is one of the very few physical-trace cases in the UFO record with a same-night, multi-agency chain of custody. At approximately 1945 CST on 17 December 1977, two residents of Council Bluffs, Iowa, watched a red luminous mass descend near the northern city limits. When they reached the site they found ground covered by molten metal glowing red-orange and igniting grass. Police and fire personnel were on scene within roughly fifteen minutes and all of them saw the mass, which they estimated at 35 to 55 pounds. Investigators at the time ruled out re-entering space debris, falling aircraft material, a meteorite (there was no crater), and a hoax. Two of the eleven witnesses described a round object hovering in the sky edged with red blinking lights. Vallee took possession of a fragment. Forty-four years later Nolan's Stanford laboratory - which had developed Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging (MIBI), a mass-spectrometric imaging technique built for tissue but capable of resolving a much broader isotope range than the 1978-era instruments - ran it again.

The result was not what either camp wanted. The paper reports that all isotopic ratios were similar between the samples and did not show statistically significant deviations from expected terrestrial normal, with one exception involving 57Fe for which the authors themselves offer a conventional explanation. In other words: the sample is made of Earth atoms. What the paper does not do is stop there. The elemental map shows local homogeneity inside individual measured grains but pronounced inhomogeneity across subsamples, which the authors read as incomplete mixing - the fingerprint of a process, not a natural formation. Their published summary of the Council Bluffs material is that it shows no evidence of having been engineered or designed, would not be expected to form naturally, and has unusual inhomogeneity. The origin, handling history and delivery mechanism remain unidentified.

The hostile reading of the paper is worth cataloguing because it is specific and it is on the record. The most detailed public critique, a long-form analysis at Metabunk, argues that the four most abundant elements identified in the paper's Figure 9 - aluminium, silicon, iron and magnesium - are the 3rd, 2nd, 4th and 7th most abundant elements in Earth's crust and are all consistent with a thermite or improvised-thermite reaction; that the MIBI-SIMS configuration used cannot detect oxygen, which would be the discriminating element for a redox reaction; that two of five subsamples returned compromised ion counts; that the paper's citation of Southall and Oberly's 1979 paper on airborne superconducting generators does not support the liquid-metal and novel-propulsion inferences drawn from it; and that roughly 350 words are reused near-verbatim from Vallee's own 1998 paper "Physical Analyses in Ten Cases of Unexplained Aerial Objects with Material Samples" without being marked as reused. None of these critiques have produced a retraction, and none of them contradict the isotopic finding. They are, for an analyst, a checklist of what a replication attempt has to close out.

The reason this paper matters to a board about a concealed program is structural rather than evidentiary. Every version of the legacy-program hypothesis reduces, eventually, to a claim about custody of physical material. Every official denial reduces to a claim about the absence of such material. Both claims are testable by exactly the instruments described here, and only by them. The Nolan-Vallee paper is therefore the open-literature specification of the test that the government has consistently declined to submit its holdings to - and, notably, the government has since begun performing a shadow version of the same test on its own terms. AARO's FY2024 annual report to Congress states plainly that Oak Ridge National Laboratory "provided analysis for a material claimed to be from a UAP" and that AARO S&T, in coordination with ORNL, wrote and posted a materials-analysis report on its website, with supplemental data promised. That is the same workflow, run inside the fence, with the sample provenance and the raw data controlled by the party with the strongest institutional interest in the answer.

The analyst-facing question the paper leaves open is not whether CB_JV-1 is alien. The authors expressly refuse that framing, writing that the objective is to provide data in an open-source manner so that others might replicate the analytic approaches or derive a testable hypothesis for how such materials are deposited. The question is who else has run this protocol, on what, and where those results went. Nolan has stated publicly that he has analysed other samples; the paper itself notes further analyses in progress. The gap between the published Council Bluffs work and whatever else has passed through that instrument is one of the more tractable research targets on this board.

claims.text: The paper is Nolan, G.P., Vallee, J.F., Jiang, S., Lemke, L.G., "Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics," Progress in Aerospace Sciences, Vol. 128, January 2022, article 100788; made available online 9 December 2021.
Progress in Aerospace Sciences is an Elsevier review journal that describes itself as an invitation-only international review journal, which means the paper was solicited rather than submitted cold.

The paper's case study is the Council Bluffs, Iowa event of 17 December 1977 at approximately 1945 CST, in which a red luminous mass fell near the northern city limits and police and fire personnel arriving within about 15 minutes observed molten metal estimated at 35-55 pounds; investigators ruled out re-entering space debris, aircraft material, a meteorite and a hoax.

The paper reports that "All isotopic ratios were similar between the samples and did not show any statistically significant deviations from expected terrestrial normal except for 57Fe," and offers a conventional explanation for the 57Fe deviation.

The analysed fragment is designated CB_JV-1 and was supplied by Vallee from his own retained portion of the 1977 material; the analysis used Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry and Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging (MIBI), an instrument capable of a broader isotope range than the 1977-78 analyses.

The paper's published conclusion on the material is that "The materials from Council Bluff show no evidence suggesting it was been engineered or designed. The material would not be expected to form naturally, and has been shown does have unusual inhomogeneity." (quoted with the paper's own grammatical errors).

The paper states its purpose as open-source replication: "The objective is to provide data in an open-source manner so that others might replicate the analytic approaches or divine a testable hypothesis of why and how such materials are deposited or left behind."
On page 3 the paper cites a Defense Intelligence Reference Document produced under the DIA-funded AAWSAP program, specifically Maxim Tsoi's "Metallic Spintronics" (2010).

The four most abundant elements identified in the paper's Figure 9 (page 15) are aluminium, silicon, iron and magnesium; the MIBI-SIMS configuration used could not detect oxygen because of its low mass.
Subsamples 2 and 4 of five were excluded from the paper's Figure 8A because of low ion counts, which the authors attributed to possible oxidation.

Approximately 350 words of the 2022 paper are reproduced near-verbatim from Vallee's 1998 paper "Physical Analyses in Ten Cases of Unexplained Aerial Objects with Material Samples" without being identified as reused text, including an unattributed quotation from a source identified only as "J. Roser" that in the 1998 paper referred to a different specimen (from Bogota).

The paper's citation of Southall, H.L. and Oberly, C.E., "System Considerations for Airborne, High-power Superconducting Generators" (1979), is contested on the grounds that the cited paper concerns engine-driven superconducting generators for aircraft and contains no reference to liquid-metal technology or novel airborne platforms.

The US Government has run a parallel, non-public version of the same workflow: AARO's FY2024 report to Congress states that Oak Ridge National Laboratory "provided analysis for a material claimed to be from a UAP" and that AARO S&T, in coordination with ORNL, wrote a materials-analysis report and posted it on AARO's website, with supplemental data to follow.
The authors state in the paper that they are conducting analyses on other pieces of unusual material beyond CB_JV-1, none of which had been published as of the 2022 article.

dossier.denialPosture: The paper issues no denial and makes no claim of non-terrestrial origin; it explicitly refuses that framing and reports terrestrial isotope ratios. Its posture is one of deliberate under-claiming, which the authors themselves anticipate will feel "incomplete or insufficient" to readers on both sides.
connections: Garry P. Nolan (Stanford School of Medicine, Baxter Laboratory) is the analytical bridge between academic mass spectrometry and the private/contractor UAP materials network; his co-authorship with Vallee links the modern instrumentation to the 1960s-1990s physical-trace sample catalogue

Jacques F. Vallee held custody of the Council Bluffs fragment from 1977 to the 2021 analysis; his 1998 paper 'Physical Analyses in Ten Cases of Unexplained Aerial Objects with Material Samples' is the source text partially reused in the 2022 paper
Larry G. Lemke is a former NASA Ames Research Center engineer, which places a NASA-affiliated author on the paper
Sizun Jiang was a member of the Nolan lab and provides the MIBI instrumentation lineage

The paper cites an AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Document ('Metallic Spintronics', Maxim Tsoi, 2010), connecting it directly to the DIA-funded AAWSAP/AATIP program lineage and to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies
Oak Ridge National Laboratory now performs the government-side equivalent analysis for AARO, per the FY2024 annual report - the same protocol run inside classification
Frank Laukien, co-founder of the Galileo Project, is chairman and CEO of Bruker Corp., a manufacturer of exactly the mass-spectrometry and imaging instrumentation class reviewed in this paper
openQuestions: The chain of custody for CB_JV-1 between the 1977 recovery by Council Bluffs police/fire and Vallee's retained fragment is not documented in the public record
The identity and institutional affiliation of 'J. Roser', quoted in both the 1998 and 2022 papers without citation, is unresolved
What other samples the Nolan laboratory has run using this protocol, at whose request, and where those results went
Whether the AARO/ORNL materials analysis used comparable isotopic methods, and whether its raw data has been released as promised
Whether the thermite hypothesis raised in the Metabunk critique has ever been tested experimentally against the CB_JV-1 elemental profile

l0.label: The Galileo Project

dossier.whatItIs: The Galileo Project for the Systematic Scientific Search for Evidence of Extraterrestrial Technological Artifacts is a Harvard-hosted, cross-institutional research programme launched in July 2021 and co-founded by Avi Loeb, the Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science at Harvard, and Frank Laukien, chairman, president and CEO of the scientific instrument manufacturer Bruker Corporation. It operates three branches: the study of interstellar objects near Earth, the search for unidentified aerial phenomena using multimodal ground-based observatories, and the study of interstellar meteors. It is funded entirely by private donation.
dossier.whyImplicated: Galileo is the control experiment for this entire board. Every version of the legacy-program hypothesis and every official denial of it reduce to claims about physical evidence held under classification. The only structural way to break that is an independent, uncleared, publishing instrument capable of producing calibrated data on the same phenomena - data that is not subject to prepublication classification review because it was never collected on government money or on government sensors. Galileo is the first serious institutional attempt to build one, and its funding structure is the mechanism: $1.755 million raised in the first two weeks from named private donors, which means its outputs go to arXiv rather than to a DOPSR queue. Its director also co-authored a March 2023 draft paper with Sean Kirkpatrick, the sitting Director of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office - the only documented instance of a joint technical product between the Pentagon's UAP office and an independent academic programme. And its IM1 interstellar meteor work is the most instructive public failure mode on the board: a physical-recovery campaign that produced material, published it, and could not establish a chain from the material to the event, generating a citation war that maps precisely onto the epistemics of the whole subject.
dossier.narrative:
Loeb's framing paper, "Overview of the Galileo Project," was posted to arXiv on 2 August 2022 as arXiv:2209.02479 and published in a special issue of the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation in 2023. Its abstract describes the project as "the first systematic scientific research program in search for potential astro-archaeological artifacts or remnants of extraterrestrial technological civilizations (ETCs) or potentially active equipment near Earth," and characterises the approach as taking a path not taken and conceivably picking low-hanging fruit. That is a statement about method, and the method is the point: Galileo's premise is that the subject has been starved of instrumented, calibrated, continuous data, not of anecdotes.

The UAP branch built to that premise. Wesley Watters and colleagues published "The Scientific Investigation of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Using Multimodal Ground-Based Observatories" in the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation, volume 12, article 2340006 (2023), laying out the sensor architecture: synchronised optical, infrared, radio, magnetometric and acoustic channels producing a continuous census of everything above an observation site, so that anomaly is defined by exclusion from a measured baseline rather than by the surprise of an observer. The first instrument came online at Harvard. Commissioning results for the all-sky infrared camera array were posted as arXiv:2411.07956, and a system architecture paper followed as arXiv:2506.00125. Loeb has publicly discussed commissioning data covering roughly half a million objects. No Galileo detection has been shown to be non-human technology, and the project has not claimed otherwise.

The interstellar meteor branch is where the project collided with the discipline. CNEOS 2014-01-08, designated IM1, is a bolide detected over the western Pacific whose inferred velocity implied a hyperbolic, interstellar trajectory. In summer 2023 Galileo mounted an ocean expedition off Papua New Guinea, dragging a magnetic sled across a roughly ten-kilometre region around the fireball localisation across twenty-six runs and recovering approximately 700 sub-millimetre spherules. Loeb and colleagues reported that a subset had a distinctive composition rich in beryllium, lanthanum and uranium - the 'BeLaU' type - which they argued was inconsistent with solar-system materials. The chemical classification work was eventually published in Chemical Geology (2024), with the preprint at arXiv:2401.09882.

The response was immediate and formal, and it is worth cataloguing precisely because it is the model of how a materials claim gets adjudicated in the open. Steve Desch and Alan Jackson published a direct critique, arXiv:2311.07699, arguing among other things that the spherules plot on or extremely near a terrestrial fractionation line and that a body entering at the assumed IM1 velocity would have been essentially vaporised, so that recovered iron spherules cannot be attributed to that event. A separate paper, arXiv:2403.05161, proposed the BeLaU signature as microtektites of terrestrial laterites. Most damaging to the localisation, Fernando and colleagues published "Seismic and acoustic signals from the 2014 'interstellar meteor'" in Geophysical Journal International, volume 238, issue 2 (2024), concluding that the seismic signal used to pin the impact site changed direction over time in a way that matched a road running past the seismometer - a truck, not a bolide. Galileo replied with "Peak-Brightness Localization of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Fireball," arXiv:2403.07696, arguing that the search region was set by the NASA/JPL CNEOS localisation box - 11.112 km on a side, centred at 1.3 degrees south, 147.6 degrees east - and not by the seismic data at all.

Whichever way that dispute resolves, its structure is the finding. A privately funded team recovered candidate material, published composition data, and could not establish provenance linking material to event; independent groups published falsifying analyses within months; the original team responded in the same channel. This is exactly the adjudication process that has never been available for any material alleged to be in government custody, and the contrast is the argument. The Nolan-Vallee 2022 paper faces the same problem from the other direction - a sample with a documented same-night recovery but a forty-four-year custody gap.

The most direct institutional connection on the board is the Loeb-Kirkpatrick paper. Dated 7 March 2023 and titled "Physical Constraints on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena," it derives physical constraints on interpretations of highly manoeuvrable UAP from standard physics and known forms of matter and radiation, and it is co-authored by the serving Director of AARO. The draft circulated publicly, drew criticism from multiple directions, and was never formally issued as an AARO product. It nonetheless establishes that the Pentagon's UAP office and Galileo were in direct technical collaboration during Kirkpatrick's tenure, which bears on how one reads AARO's later categorical statements and on what data, if any, moved in either direction.

For an analyst, Galileo's value is threefold. It produces a public, timestamped, instrumented baseline that any future disclosure has to be consistent with. Its funding graph - Eugene Jhong, Vinny Jain, Teddy Jones, Eric Keto, the Laukien Science Foundation, Joerg Laukien, William A. Linton, Adnan Sen, the Brinson Foundation - identifies the private capital willing to underwrite the question outside the appropriations system. And through Laukien and Bruker it sits one step from the mass-spectrometry instrument industry whose products define what any materials claim, government or otherwise, can actually be tested with.

claims.text: Loeb, A. (on behalf of the Galileo Project, Harvard University), "Overview of the Galileo Project," arXiv:2209.02479, submitted 2 August 2022, published in Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation (Special Issue), 2023, describes the project as "the first systematic scientific research program in search for potential astro-archaeological artifacts or remnants of extraterrestrial technological civilizations (ETCs) or potentially active equipment near Earth."
The Galileo Project was launched in July 2021, co-founded by Avi Loeb of Harvard and Frank Laukien, chairman, president and CEO of Bruker Corporation.

The project received donations totalling $1.755 million in its first two weeks; named donors include Eugene Jhong, Vinny Jain, Teddy Jones, Eric Keto, the Laukien Science Foundation, Joerg Laukien, William A. Linton, Adnan Sen and The Brinson Foundation. It receives no government funding.
The project operates three branches: the study of interstellar objects near Earth, the search for UAP using multimodal ground-based observatories, and the study of interstellar meteors.

Watters, W. et al., "The Scientific Investigation of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Using Multimodal Ground-Based Observatories," Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation 12, 2340006 (2023), sets out the observatory sensor architecture combining optical, infrared, radio, magnetic and acoustic channels.
Commissioning results for the Galileo Project's all-sky infrared camera array were published as "Commissioning An All-Sky Infrared Camera Array for Detection Of Airborne Objects," arXiv:2411.07956.
The observatory system design was published as "Galileo Project Observatory Class System Architecture," arXiv:2506.00125.

In 2023 the Galileo Project conducted an ocean expedition near Papua New Guinea targeting the site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) bolide, recovering approximately 700 sub-millimetre spherules across 26 magnetic-sled runs criss-crossing a roughly 10-kilometre region around the fireball location.

Loeb and colleagues reported a subset of the recovered spherules with a distinctive beryllium-, lanthanum- and uranium-rich ('BeLaU') composition claimed to be of extrasolar origin; the chemical classification work was published as "Chemical classification of spherules recovered from the Pacific Ocean site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) bolide," Chemical Geology (2024), preprint arXiv:2401.09882.

Steve Desch and Alan Jackson published a formal critique, arXiv:2311.07699, "Critique of arXiv submission 2308.15623, 'Discovery of Spherules of Likely Extrasolar Composition in the Pacific Ocean Site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Bolide', by A. Loeb et al.", arguing the spherules plot on or near a terrestrial fractionation line and that a body at the assumed IM1 velocity could not have survived entry in the recovered form.
A competing terrestrial explanation for the BeLaU signature was published as "Be,La,U-rich spherules as microtektites of terrestrial laterites: What goes up must come down," arXiv:2403.05161.

Fernando et al., "Seismic and acoustic signals from the 2014 'interstellar meteor'," Geophysical Journal International 238(2):1027 (2024), concluded that the seismic signal used to localise the IM1 impact site changed direction over time in a way matching a road running past the seismometer, i.e. a truck rather than a bolide.

The Galileo Project responded with "Peak-Brightness Localization of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Fireball," arXiv:2403.07696, arguing the search region was set by the NASA/JPL CNEOS localisation box measuring 11.112 km on a side centred at 1.3 degrees south, 147.6 degrees east, and not by the seismic data.

Avi Loeb and Sean Kirkpatrick, then serving Director of the Department of Defense All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, co-authored a draft paper dated 7 March 2023 titled "Physical Constraints on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena," deriving constraints on interpretations of highly manoeuvrable UAP from standard physics and known forms of matter and radiation.

dossier.denialPosture: Galileo issues no denials; it is the party against which official denial is directed. Its own posture is one of null results honestly reported - no Galileo observation has been shown to be non-human technology, and the project has repeatedly declined to assert probabilities. That posture is itself evidentially useful, because it establishes that the project's later claims, if any, would not be the product of a group predisposed to affirm.
connections: Avi Loeb (Harvard, Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science) and Frank Laukien (Bruker Corporation) are the co-founders; Bruker manufactures the mass-spectrometry and imaging instrument class that the Nolan-Vallee 2022 protocol depends on

Sean Kirkpatrick, first Director of AARO, co-authored the March 2023 'Physical Constraints on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena' draft with Loeb - the only documented joint technical product between the Pentagon UAP office and an independent academic programme
Wesley Watters (Wellesley College) leads the observatory instrumentation work; Richard Cloete holds the Laukien-'Oumuamua Postdoctoral Fellowship
Steve Desch and Alan Jackson (Arizona State University) and Benjamin Fernando are the principal published critics of the IM1 spherule and localisation work
NASA/JPL's CNEOS database is the source of the IM1 detection and of the localisation box that defined the search region

The private funding graph - Eugene Jhong, Vinny Jain, Teddy Jones, Eric Keto, Laukien Science Foundation, Joerg Laukien, William A. Linton, Adnan Sen, The Brinson Foundation - identifies capital willing to fund the question outside the appropriations system, and is a distinct network from the Bigelow/AAWSAP funding lineage
Galileo's arXiv-first publishing model is the structural inverse of AARO's DOPSR-cleared reporting, and the two produce non-overlapping evidence classes on the same phenomena
The IM1 material-provenance failure is the direct methodological analogue of the Council Bluffs custody gap in the Nolan-Vallee paper
openQuestions: Whether Galileo observatory data has ever been requested by, shared with, or offered to AARO under 50 U.S.C. 3373, and whether any such exchange is documented
What became of the Loeb-Kirkpatrick draft paper - whether it was ever submitted, reviewed, or suppressed, and whether AARO reviewed it as an official product
Whether the BeLaU spherules can be independently re-analysed by a laboratory with no stake in the outcome, and whether sample material has been distributed
Whether any Galileo observatory site has been sited near locations with historical UAP incident density, and how site selection was made
Whether the project has retained legal or classification advice regarding what would happen to its data if a detection were judged to implicate a classified US programme
The extent of overlap between Galileo's donor network and the private funders of other UAP research vehicles

l0.label: University at Albany (SUNY), Department of Physics
l0.short: University at Albany (SUNY), Department of Physics

dossier.whatItIs: The University at Albany (SUNY), a public research university at 1400 Washington Avenue, Albany, New York, and specifically its Department of Physics. The department houses an established dark matter group working on the LZ (LUX-ZEPLIN) experiment and the Snowball Chamber, and it is the institutional home of Professor Kevin H. Knuth, Associate Professor Matthew Szydagis and Associate Professor Cecilia Levy. As of November 2025 it also hosts UAlbany Project X (UAPx), an endowed academic collaboration devoted solely to the scientific study of unidentified anomalous phenomena.
dossier.whyImplicated: The standard defence of the concealment is that no serious scientist will touch the subject, therefore the absence of scientific data proves there is nothing there. UAlbany is the counter-example, and it is institutional rather than biographical: Matthew Szydagis's official departmental faculty page lists his research interests as "Experimental astroparticle physics, in particular direct detection of dark matter WIMPs ... and general detector development for rare event searches, neutron activation, and Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" - a state university publishing UAP as a declared faculty research interest on a .edu page alongside dark matter. In June 2025 the department placed two peer-reviewed UAP papers in Progress in Aerospace Sciences, one of them a 34-author historical review led by Knuth. In November 2025 the university accepted a named endowment gift specifically to fund UAP research in perpetuity and announced the launch of UAlbany Project X. And in the same announcement Knuth confirmed that physicist Eric W. Davis had joined the physics department as visiting adjunct faculty - placing one of the most heavily implicated figures in the legacy-program record inside a public university physics department, on the record, in a university press release.
dossier.narrative:
The University at Albany physics department is a small, instrument-heavy group whose day job is looking for signals that are rare, faint and easy to confuse with noise. That is exactly the skill set the UAP problem has always lacked. Cecilia Levy and Matthew Szydagis both work on LZ, the multi-tonne xenon time-projection chamber operating a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota; Szydagis wrote NEST, the Noble Element Simulation Technique package the wider noble-liquid detector community depends on. Levy's second research line is the Snowball Chamber, a supercooled-water low-mass dark matter technology unique to the UAlbany group. Kevin Knuth came from a different direction: a PhD in physics from Minnesota, brain-imaging work at the Nathan Kline Institute and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, then four years as a GS-14 Research Scientist in the Intelligent Systems Division at NASA Ames Research Center from 2001 to 2005, designing inference algorithms for astrophysical data. He joined UAlbany as an Assistant Professor in 2005, was promoted to Associate in 2009 and to full Professor in 2023, and has been Editor-in-Chief of the MDPI journal Entropy since 2012.

Knuth's route into the phenomenon ran through the numbers. His 2019 paper with SCU collaborators, "Estimating Flight Characteristics of Anomalous Unidentified Aerial Vehicles", published in Entropy, worked out minimum speeds and accelerations for several documented cases including the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter off southern California. The Nimitz case is what drove the fieldwork: in July 2021 Knuth, Szydagis and Levy joined the non-profit UAPx for a week-long expedition to the Catalina Channel - the same water where the Nimitz strike group's aircrew recorded the Tic Tac - deploying visible-light and infrared cameras, Cosmic Watch scintillation-based radiation detectors, and National Weather Service Doppler radar data.

What came out of that expedition is the part that matters institutionally. It was not a conference talk or a preprint that died on arXiv. It was two papers in a June 2025 special edition of Progress in Aerospace Sciences, an Elsevier review journal with no prior history of publishing on this subject. Szydagis was lead author of "Initial results from the first field expedition of UAPx to study unidentified anomalous phenomena" (DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2025.101099), with Knuth, Benjamin Kugielsky and Levy. The paper reports approximately one hour of triggered visible and night-vision video, over 600 hours of untriggered far-infrared video, and 55 hours of background radiation measurement. The team plausibly explained all but one candidate anomaly: a dark spot in the visible/near-IR camera captured at roughly 4am Pacific on Friday 16 July 2021, possibly coincident with ionizing radiation, which has resisted prosaic explanation. Szydagis built a new analysis tool for the work, the Custom Target Analysis Protocol (C-TAP), applying pixel-by-pixel frame-differencing with AI assistance and human verification - the same logic used to separate a dark-matter recoil from detector noise.

The companion paper, "The new science of Unidentified Aerospace-Undersea Phenomena (UAP)" (DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2025.101097), had Knuth as lead author and, per the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies, thirty-four authors in total. It reviews roughly twenty historical government studies from 1933 to the present across Scandinavia, wartime Europe, the US, Canada, France, Russia and China, plus private studies in France, the UK and the US, and current instrumented research programmes in Ireland, Germany, Norway, Sweden and the US. Its stated purpose is to demonstrate that UAP "can be, and have been, scientifically investigated" and to dispel the misconception that this is an American phenomenon. Project Condign sits inside that review as one of the government studies catalogued - the two nodes on this board touch directly through that paper.

On 27 June 2025 SCU announced that Knuth had received its inaugural Distinguished Scholar Award, presented at SCU's Sixth Annual Conference at the Von Braun Center in Huntsville, Alabama, on 6-8 June 2025. The distinction worth preserving is that Knuth is an award recipient and paper author, not an SCU officer: the SCU release identifies Rich Hoffman as the Executive Board member who presented the award and describes Knuth only as a University at Albany professor and former NASA research scientist. Knuth does hold a science-and-technology role at UAPx, but that is a separate organisation.

The institutional consolidation came on 5 November 2025. UAlbany announced an endowment gift from Albany businessman Tony Gorman, formerly a principal owner of the Gorman Group highway construction and materials firm, who had seen a local news segment about the physicists' work. Knuth told The Debrief the gift funds the team for five years and "sets up an endowment that funds us in perpetuity." The gift launched UAlbany Project X, which absorbs the mission of the non-profit UAPx co-founded by Navy veterans Kevin Day and Gary Voorhis - both connected to the 2004 Nimitz encounter. The university's own release positions the group alongside academic UAP efforts in Sweden, Germany and at Harvard. Planned instrumentation includes diffraction gratings for spectroscopy, magnetic and electric field sensors, and portable multi-camera sky-monitoring arrays - categories Knuth notes are "often omitted from study".

Buried in Knuth's quote in that release is the sentence that puts UAlbany on this board rather than merely in a science-news roundup: "the physics department's UAP research base grows, with the recent addition of physicist Dr. Eric W. Davis as visiting adjunct faculty. Dr. Davis has cooperated with recent congressional UAP hearings." Davis is a central figure in the legacy-program record. A public university has just given him a faculty affiliation, and said so in its own press release.

What makes the node durable is that the team is deflationary about its own data: Szydagis's public line is that "we did not find evidence indicating that UAP have anything to do with non-human intelligence." That is what instrumented science looks like, and it is the thing the concealment has always been able to point to as absent. It is no longer absent. It is endowed, it is on a .edu faculty page, and it now has Eric Davis in the building.

claims.text: The field expedition took place in July 2021 over the Catalina Channel, the same water as the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter. The arXiv version places it at "Avalon, California, located on Catalina Island, and nearby"; the UAlbany press releases describe it as a field expedition "in Laguna Beach, California"; Szydagis has called it "the Catalina-Laguna mission".

Szydagis developed a new analysis tool for the expedition data, the Custom Target Analysis Protocol (C-TAP), combining artificial intelligence with human verification for pixel-by-pixel frame-differencing analysis of infrared imagery, explicitly modelled on dark-matter search methodology; the study also made the first use of public National Weather Service Doppler radar data to corroborate observations from other instruments.

Knuth received the inaugural SCU Distinguished Scholar Award, presented at SCU's Sixth Annual Conference held 6-8 June 2025 at the Von Braun Center in Huntsville, Alabama. The SCU release identifies Rich Hoffman as the Executive Board member who presented the award and describes Knuth solely as a UAlbany professor and former NASA research scientist; it attributes no SCU board seat or officer post to him.

On 5 November 2025 UAlbany announced an endowment gift from businessman Tony Gorman, formerly a principal owner of the Gorman Group, funding UAP research in perpetuity and launching UAlbany Project X (UAPx), which continues the mission of the non-profit UAPx co-founded by Navy veterans Kevin Day and Gary Voorhis. Knuth stated the gift funds the team for five years plus an endowment "that funds us in perpetuity."

In the same 5 November 2025 release, Knuth stated: "the physics department's UAP research base grows, with the recent addition of physicist Dr. Eric W. Davis as visiting adjunct faculty. Dr. Davis has cooperated with recent congressional UAP hearings." Szydagis separately confirmed that Davis works with the team on a volunteer basis as an adjunct researcher in an advisory position.

Knuth's 2019 paper "Estimating Flight Characteristics of Anomalous Unidentified Aerial Vehicles", published in Entropy (DOI 10.3390/e21100939), estimated minimum speeds and accelerations for documented UAP cases including the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter, and is archived in UAlbany's institutional repository.

dossier.denialPosture: None from the institution. UAlbany publicises the work through its own news centre and advancement office, with its vice president for university advancement describing the university as "one of the few universities worldwide leading academic research into UAPs". The team itself is scrupulously deflationary about its own results: Szydagis states "we did not find evidence indicating that UAP have anything to do with non-human intelligence", and the group explained away all but one candidate anomaly from the 2021 expedition. That restraint is what makes the node useful rather than what undercuts it.
connections: Eric W. Davis - visiting adjunct faculty in the UAlbany Department of Physics as of November 2025, per the university's own release; a primary node elsewhere on this board for the legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering record and for congressional engagement.

Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies (SCU) - collaborator on Knuth's 2019 Entropy paper, awarding body for his 2025 inaugural Distinguished Scholar Award, and source of a substantial bloc of co-authors on the 2025 Progress in Aerospace Sciences review.

UAPx (the non-profit), co-founded by Navy veterans Kevin Day and Gary Voorhis - both connected to the 2004 Nimitz encounter; the non-profit's mission was absorbed into UAlbany Project X in November 2025.
The 2004 USS Nimitz / Tic Tac encounter - the case anchoring Knuth's 2019 flight-characteristics paper and the geographic choice of the Catalina Channel for the 2021 expedition.
Project Condign (doc-condign-vol3) - one of roughly twenty historical government studies catalogued in Knuth et al. 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2025.101097.

Progress in Aerospace Sciences (Elsevier) - the June 2025 special edition also carried a study by Luc Dini, Geoffrey Mestchersky and Jacques Vallee estimating energy values for a historic UAP incident, placing Vallee in the same issue as the UAlbany group.
LZ (LUX-ZEPLIN) at the Sanford Underground Research Facility and the NEST simulation package - the rare-event-search infrastructure and methodology transferred into the UAP work.
Tony Gorman and the Gorman Group - private donor who endowed the programme, the funding mechanism that made a permanent university UAP research line possible without federal money.
Caroline Cory / OMnium Media and the 2022 documentary "A Tear in the Sky" - private funder of the original 2021 fieldwork.
Comparable academic efforts named by UAlbany itself: programmes in Sweden and Germany and the Galileo Project at Harvard.
AARO (All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office) - the federal counterpart effort against which the UAlbany programme is repeatedly contrasted in coverage.
openQuestions: What is the dollar value of the Gorman endowment? Neither the university release nor The Debrief states a figure.

What are the terms of Eric W. Davis's visiting adjunct appointment - duration, whether compensated, whether it carries any research-supervision or data-access role? The Debrief reports it is unpaid and advisory; the university release does not specify.

The one unresolved 2021 anomaly - a dark spot with possible coincident ionizing radiation at roughly 4am on 16 July 2021 - has not been explained or independently reanalysed by anyone outside the team.

Szydagis's departmental faculty page lists UAP as a research interest; whether UAP or UAlbany Project X appears as a formal departmental research area or registered centre on the department's research overview or the university's institutes/centres/labs listing was not checked in this pass.
Whether any of the UAP work has drawn federal or DoD funding, or whether it remains entirely privately endowed, is not established by the public record.

Author-count discrepancy: SCU states the 2025 review "brings together thirty-four authors" while the UAlbany release says Knuth's article was "co-written by Szydagis and more than 30 other researchers". The exact byline count has not been confirmed against the published Elsevier version.

Whether UAlbany Project X will publish raw data and instrument logs, or only analysed results, is unstated - the single most important question for whether this node becomes independently checkable science.
Knuth's role at the non-profit UAPx has been described in third-party sources as Vice President of Science & Technology; this was not confirmed against a UAlbany or UAPx primary source in this pass.

l0.label: Arquivo Nacional (Brazil) - UFO/UAP collection

dossier.whatItIs: The Fundo Objeto Voador Nao Identificado (OVNI), reference code BR DFANBSB ARX, is a discrete archival collection held by Brazil's Arquivo Nacional, the national archives, and produced by the Comando da Aeronautica. It contains reports, occurrence questionnaires, correspondence, photographs, drawings, video, audio and press clippings concerning objects observed in Brazilian skies. It is open to the public and searchable online through SIAN, the Arquivo Nacional's information system.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the physical answer to the question the US disclosure fight keeps asking in the abstract: what does it actually look like when a state moves its military UAP holdings into civilian custody and publishes them. It looks like a reference code, a finding aid, a login page and a holding count. The archive is the endpoint of the pipeline the FAB built through Portaria 551/GC3, and its existence dismantles the premise that this material is intrinsically unreleasable, because a NATO-adjacent air force with a real air defence mission released it and continues to accession into it annually. It is also honest about its own limits, and the board should be too: the collection covers one service, the Aeronautica, and not the Army or the Navy, and its holding count is reported differently by the archive and by the Senate. Those limits do not weaken the comparison. They sharpen it, because even a partial, imperfect, single-service release is more than the United States has produced in seventy-nine years.
dossier.narrative:
Brazil's national archive holds the world's most accessible body of military records on unidentified aerial objects, and it holds them under an ordinary archival reference code with an ordinary finding aid, which is precisely what makes it remarkable. The Arquivo Nacional describes the collection plainly on its own website: the Fundo Objeto Voador Nao Identificado, BR DFANBSB ARX, produced by the Comando da Aeronautica do Brasil and held in the archive's custody, composed of 743 registros comprising reports, occurrence questionnaires, correspondence, photographs, drawings, videos, audio and clippings from newspapers and magazines about objects seen in Brazilian skies over the years. The earliest occurrence in the fund dates from 1952 and, per the archive's own description, the most recent from 2016. Access runs through SIAN, the Sistema de Informacoes do Arquivo Nacional, and a curated image set is published on the archive's Pinterest account, which is not a detail one expects from a body of military intelligence records.

The holding count is contested and the board should present both figures rather than pick one. The Arquivo Nacional says 743 registros. The Brazilian Senate's own record, in the justification to RQS 193/2022, says that searching the term OVNI alone returns 137 records but that entering the specific reference code BR DFANBSB ARX returns 758 documents. These are almost certainly counting different things, registros as archival units versus digitised items as retrieved by a code search, and the gap may also reflect accruals between the two dates. Neither figure is wrong and neither is authoritative for the other's purpose. Both are cited here. Layered on top, the ufologist A. J. Gevaerd told the Senate plenary in June 2022 that the Brazilian government and the Aeronautica had released more than 20,000 pages, which is a page count rather than an item count and is not in conflict with either.

The collection's provenance runs through the FAB's documentation and archival machinery rather than through litigation or leak. From 2007 the Aeronautica began sending its papers to the archive. In April 2009 CENDOC forwarded the first Operacao Prato material. In August 2010 Portaria no 551/GC3 formalised the flow, making the archive the default destination for reports received through the aerospace operations command. The consequence is that the fund is not a historical dump frozen at a cut-off date but a live series. In August 2026 Brazilian media reporting off documents released through the archive identified at least eighteen unidentified-object cases reported in Brazil during 2025 by pilots, controllers and other aviation personnel, with five clustered at Londrina in Parana and four in Ceara, including a LATAM captain's report near Guarulhos on 1 September 2025 and a Londrina tower controller's 23 November 2025 report of a white, round object that appeared and disappeared on the traffic display. A citizen can read the form.

The archive is not an advocate, and its framing is worth cataloguing precisely because it is not. Its public page carries an explicit caveat that OVNI does not necessarily mean flying saucers or extraterrestrials, and that the term designates any flying object whose origin was not immediately identified, which may include satellites, drones, balloons or natural phenomena. On this board that sentence is an artefact rather than a rebuttal: it is the institutional hedge a records body attaches when it publishes material a defence ministry produced, and its presence tells you the archive expected the material to be read as more than administrative residue. The important thing is that the hedge is attached to published records rather than used as a reason not to publish.

The boundary of the collection is the sharpest single fact in this dossier. The Senate record states without qualification that from 2007 it was the Aeronautica, and not the Exercito and not the Marinha, that sent its papers. Brazilian researchers went to the Ministry of Defence in April 2013, at the invitation of then Foreign Minister Celso Amorim and before the service commanders, specifically to press for the Army and Navy holdings. Those holdings have not been released. So the Fundo OVNI is a one-service archive, which means Brazil's disclosure is real but partial, and means the comparison with the United States should be drawn carefully: Brazil is not a state that opened everything, it is a state where one armed service unilaterally chose publication as its default and the other two did not. That variance is the most useful thing about it, because it isolates the decision. The material did not force the outcome. The institution chose it. And in the United States, no service has chosen it, at any point, in any decade, for any category of this material.

dossier.denialPosture: The archive itself does not deny; it disclaims. Its public description states that OVNI does not necessarily mean flying saucers or extraterrestrials and that the label covers satellites, drones, balloons and natural phenomena. That is a records body inoculating itself against the reading its own holdings invite, and it is catalogued here as an institutional hedge attached to published material rather than as a reason for withholding it.
connections: Custodian of the records produced by the Forca Aerea Brasileira (fab) through CENDOC and COMDABRA/COMAE under Portaria 551/GC3.

Subordinate to the Ministerio da Justica e Seguranca Publica, which places custody of the records outside the defence establishment.
The structural counterpart the United States lacks: there is no NARA record group equivalent for a live, annually accruing US military UAP reporting series.
openQuestions: The 743 versus 758 discrepancy has not been reconciled. The two figures come from different bodies, are counting differently (archival registros versus documents returned by a reference-code search), and are separated in time. The Arquivo Nacional gives 2016 as the fund's most recent occurrence while the FAB states transfers run through 2025 and 2025 reports are demonstrably being released. Whether the archive page is simply out of date, or whether post-2016 accruals sit under a separate series, is unresolved.
