Whether any material was withheld, redacted or reclassified during the transfers from CENDOC and GSI is not addressed in any located source.
Whether the fund contains any material relating to physical residue, recovered objects or materials analysis has not been established from the finding aid.

l0.label: Operação Prato (Operation Saucer)

dossier.whatItIs: Operacao Prato, literally Operation Plate and usually rendered Operation Saucer, was a field operation mounted by the Forca Aerea Brasileira in the state of Para in 1977 and 1978, centred on Colares and neighbouring riverine communities on the Atlantic coast of the Amazon delta. It was commanded by Capitao Uyrange Bolivar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima, who named it, and ran under I COMAR with involvement from the Servico Nacional de Informacoes. Its stated object was to investigate a wave of reports of luminous objects that residents said projected beams of light at them, a phenomenon locals called the chupa-chupa.
dossier.whyImplicated: Operacao Prato is the specific thing the United States has never produced: a military UAP field operation with a name, a commanding officer identified by rank and full name, a defined area of operations, dated phases, a case count, a written final report, and a paper trail that a member of the public can now request from a civilian archive. The US analogue would be if Project Blue Book had deployed officers into a county for two months with cameras, and the resulting negatives, logs and the captain's signed report were downloadable from NARA. Everything about the operation that would in the American context be cited as a reason for permanent classification, that it was run under a military dictatorship, that it involved a domestic intelligence service, that it concerned civilians who claimed physical injury, and that it produced imagery, turned out not to prevent release. That is the contrast. The concealment argument in the US rests on the proposition that this class of record cannot be released; Brazil released this class of record, and the state did not fall.
dossier.narrative:
In the second half of 1977 the coastal and riverine municipalities of Para began generating a volume of reports that local authorities could not absorb. Residents described luminous objects hovering over houses at night and directing narrow beams of light at people, and a hospital in Colares filled with patients presenting with burns, puncture-like marks and profound weakness. The mayor of Colares appealed for help. What the Brazilian state did next is what puts this node on the board: it sent the air force.

Operacao Prato was organised out of I COMAR, the First Regional Air Command in Belem, and placed under Capitao Uyrange Hollanda. It ran in phases across the last months of 1977 and into 1978, with a team on the ground carrying cameras and observation logs, and it operated in coordination with the Servico Nacional de Informacoes, the dictatorship's civilian intelligence service. Case counts in the surviving documentation are substantial. Material now in the Arquivo Nacional includes a compilation described as Registros de Observacoes de OVNI, drawn up from data gathered by I COMAR on the recommendation of the Minister of Aeronautics, forwarding 130 OVNI records catalogued between 2 September 1977 and 28 November 1978. Alongside the paper there are photographs and drawings, and elsewhere in the same fund the archive holds audio recordings of exchanges between pilots and control tower operators.

The written product of the operation was a report signed by Hollanda that recorded no evidence of extraterrestrials. That report is the operation's official position and, on the board's own method, it is the document that must be handled as an artefact rather than as an answer. It is dated, it is signed, it is attributable, and it was produced by an officer inside a chain of command under a military government. Twenty years later Hollanda repudiated it. In August 1997, at Cabo Frio in Rio de Janeiro state, he gave a long interview to the researchers A. J. Gevaerd and Marco Petit for Revista UFO in which he described what he said the team had actually encountered in the field, including close-quarters encounters, and described unexplained phenomena in his own home afterwards. On 2 October 1997 he was found dead in his apartment at Cabo Frio. The coroner recorded death by asphyxiation due to hanging and the death was ruled suicide.

The temptation with a witness who recants a signed military report and dies weeks later is obvious, and the record does not support taking it. Gevaerd, who had spent the hours of the interview with him and who has every professional incentive to say otherwise, has stated flatly that no one 'suicided' him for talking, that Hollanda acted for his own reasons, and that Hollanda had disclosed a previous attempt on his own life, a fall from the fourth floor of a building. The honest formulation is that the board has a commanding officer who signed a negative report, publicly contradicted it two decades later, and died by his own hand within weeks, and that the person best placed to allege foul play declines to. That is a knot, not a proof, and it belongs in the open questions.

The archival afterlife is where the contrast with the US becomes concrete. In April 2009 the Air Force's documentation centre, CENDOC, sent the first tranche of Operacao Prato material to the Arquivo Nacional. Later in 2009 the Gabinete de Seguranca Institucional of the Presidency released dozens of pages of former SNI documents on the same operation. The two streams converged into the collection coded BR DFANBSB ARX, the Fundo OVNI, where they sit digitised and searchable through SIAN, the Arquivo Nacional's online information system. The mechanism that made this routine was administrative rather than political: Portaria no 551/GC3 of August 2010 established that the Aeronautica registers and forwards, and the archive publishes.

What Operacao Prato does not do is establish recovery or reverse-engineering. There is no crash, no hardware, no custody chain in the released material. Its evidentiary function on this board is different and arguably stronger: it is a fully documented instance of a state deciding that objects it could not identify were interfering with its citizens, tasking a named officer to go and look, and then, three decades on, handing the whole file to the reading public. Every element of that sequence has a missing US counterpart, and the absence of the counterpart is the finding.

dossier.denialPosture: The operation's own final report, signed by its commanding officer, is a negative finding: no signs of extraterrestrials at Colares. That report is the denial, and it is exactly the kind of denial this board catalogues rather than accepts, because it is dated, signed and attributable, and because the signatory publicly repudiated it twenty years later before dying by suicide within weeks. The FAB has never withdrawn or reaffirmed the report; it has simply released the file.
connections: Run by the Forca Aerea Brasileira (fab) through I COMAR, with participation by the Servico Nacional de Informacoes.

openQuestions: The precise phase dates of the operation vary by source. One commonly cited framing gives two phases, 20 October to 11 November 1977 and 25 November to 5 December 1977, while other accounts extend the operation into 1978 and the archive compilation covers 2 September 1977 to 28 November 1978. No primary FAB order fixing the phases has been retrieved.
The identity and archival citation of Hollanda's signed final report inside BR DFANBSB ARX have not been pinned to a specific SIAN item number in this pass.
The attribution of the ARX 184 compilation to a report signed by Brigadeiro Jose Pessoa Cavalcanti de Albuquerque rests on a secondary blog account and has not been verified against the archive item.
Whether the Colares hospital admissions were medically documented in the military file, and whether those medical records were transferred with the rest, is unresolved.

The circumstances of Hollanda's death are recorded as suicide and the principal interviewer rejects foul play. The board should not treat the sequence of recantation followed by death as evidentiary without a document that has not been produced.
No released Operacao Prato material speaks to recovery of material, custody of hardware, or reverse-engineering.

l0.label: Noite Oficial dos OVNIs - the Brazilian 'Night of the UFOs', 19 May 1986

dossier.whatItIs: The 'Noite Oficial dos OVNIs', the Official Night of the UFOs, is the night of 19 May 1986, when Brazilian civil and military radar tracked multiple unidentified returns across several states in the country's south-east and centre-west and the Forca Aerea Brasileira launched interceptors against them. Five fighters, a mix of F-5E and Mirage aircraft, were scrambled from Santa Cruz air base in Sao Paulo state and Anapolis air base in Goias. Four days later the Minister of Aeronautics, Brigadeiro Octavio Julio Moreira Lima, held a press conference at the ministry in Brasilia, presented controllers and pilots involved, and said the air force had no technical explanation.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the single most important comparison point on the board, because it is the event the United States has never had and, on the concealment thesis, cannot have. A cabinet-rank defence official stood at a podium four days after a multi-aircraft intercept mission against radar-confirmed unidentified objects, named the mission, produced the aircrew and the controllers, and stated on the record that the state could not explain what it had chased. Nothing about Brazil's position in 1986 made this cheap: the country was two years out of military rule, the air force ministry was a serving-officer institution, and the radar and intercept performance data at issue were exactly the sort of material the US cites as the reason such events cannot be discussed. The 1986 night therefore converts the US argument from a claim about the sensitivity of the phenomenon into a claim about the sensitivity of the institution. It also carries its own lag, which is the honest half of the story: the minister promised a written document within thirty days and the report did not reach the public until September 2009, twenty-three years later.
dossier.narrative:
The evening of 19 May 1986 produced a cascade rather than a single sighting. Radar returns began appearing on civil scopes serving Sao Paulo airports and on the military picture held by CINDACTA, the Integrated Air Defence and Air Traffic Control Centre, and the objects were also acquired visually from the air. Among the airborne witnesses was Ozires Silva, at the time president of Petrobras and one of the most consequential figures in Brazilian aviation as the founder of Embraer, who was flying in an executive Xingu and who, with his pilot, pursued lights for roughly twenty-five minutes. The reported speeds spanned a wide band, from a few hundred kilometres per hour to well over a thousand, which is itself a characteristic of the case: the objects were not behaving like a single misidentified class of target.

The air force treated it as an air defence problem. Five interceptors went up, two F-5E from Santa Cruz in Sao Paulo state and three Mirage from Anapolis in Goias. Pilots reported acquisitions and losses, and the objects did not resolve into anything the crews could identify. In the Brazilian Senate's own later account of the night, twenty-one objects were involved and were pursued for hours.

What makes the date load-bearing is 23 May, not 19 May. The scale of the press coverage forced a response, and the response was a press conference at the Ministry of Aeronautics in Brasilia at which Moreira Lima appeared with air traffic controllers and air force pilots from the mission. He confirmed that five FAB fighters had pursued unidentified objects over Brazilian territory and, asked to account for them, said that technically he would tell them there was no explanation. Contemporary and retrospective Brazilian reporting has treated the phrase as the moment the state conceded, in public, at ministerial level, that its air defence system had engaged something it could not name. Documents later associated with the case describe the objects as solid bodies displaying intelligent behaviour, including formation flight and the ability to track aircraft.

The US comparison is not close. The nearest American analogue in kind, the Washington DC overflights of July 1952, produced a press conference that went the opposite way: the Air Force convened the largest such briefing since the Second World War in order to deliver an explanation, temperature inversion, and to close the matter. In 1986 Brasilia did not reach for an explanation because it did not have one, and said so. Nothing in the subsequent four decades suggests the admission harmed Brazilian air defence, deterrence, or public order. That absence of consequence is the evidence.

The concealment element sits in the timeline afterwards. The minister undertook to produce a written document on the incident and to release it within thirty days. That did not happen. The report became public only in September 2009, which places it inside the same window as the FAB's initial transfers to the Arquivo Nacional and just ahead of Portaria 551/GC3 in August 2010. So the correct reading of the 1986 night is two-part. The verbal disclosure was immediate, unqualified and at cabinet level. The documentary disclosure took twenty-three years and arrived only once the Aeronautica had built an archival pipeline that made release the default. A board tracking concealment should treat that gap as the ordinary metabolism of a defence bureaucracy, and should note that even a system with a twenty-three year documentary lag still ended in publication, which the US system has not.

Today the material sits in the Arquivo Nacional's Fundo OVNI. The archive itself flags 1986 as one of the best known cases in the collection, with around twenty-one unidentified objects detected on 19 May, and the fund includes audio recordings of exchanges between pilots and control tower operators alongside the written reports. In May and June 2026 the fortieth anniversary drew substantial Brazilian press coverage, including detailed reconstructions in the military press, which is a measure of how thoroughly the event has become part of the country's public record rather than its classified one. The comparison the board is built to make is therefore not rhetorical. It is a specific, dated, documented sequence in one country against a specific, dated, documented absence in another.

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue for 19 May 1986, and that absence is the point of the node. The Minister of Aeronautics affirmed the intercept mission at a press conference four days later and stated that the air force had no technical explanation, which is the opposite of the American pattern of supplying an explanation in order to close a case. The only concealment behaviour attaching to this event is procedural delay: a written report promised within thirty days that did not become public until September 2009.
connections: Executed by the Forca Aerea Brasileira (fab); the intercepts ran through CINDACTA and the air defence structure that later became COMDABRA/COMAE.
Its file is held in the Arquivo Nacional's Fundo OVNI (arquivo-nacional-ufo), BR DFANBSB ARX, alongside audio of pilot and tower exchanges.
Named in Senado Federal RQS 193/2022 (senado-brasil) as an official FAB engagement with 21 objects.
Ozires Silva, founder of Embraer and then president of Petrobras, is an airborne civilian witness of unusual institutional standing.
Direct comparison node to the July 1952 Washington DC overflights, where the US Air Force convened a press conference in order to supply an explanation rather than concede its absence.
The 2009 release of the 1986 report is contemporaneous with the CENDOC transfers of Operacao Prato material and precedes Portaria 551/GC3 of August 2010.
openQuestions: No verbatim transcript of the 23 May 1986 press conference has been located in a primary Brazilian government source in this pass; the minister's most quoted sentence rests on Brazilian press reporting.

The object count varies. The Arquivo Nacional and the Senate record both use 21; some English-language accounts say 'as many as twenty'. The underlying FAB tally has not been checked against the archive item.
The specific SIAN item number for the September 2009 report on the 1986 events has not been identified.
The names of the intercept pilots and the tail numbers of the five aircraft have not been confirmed against a primary FAB source.
Whether any radar tape, gun-camera film or onboard sensor data from the intercepts was retained, and whether it was included in the transfer to the Arquivo Nacional, is unresolved.

l0.label: Força Aérea Brasileira / Ministério da Aeronáutica
l0.short: Força Aérea Brasileira / Ministério da Aeronáutica

dossier.whatItIs: The Forca Aerea Brasileira (FAB), the air arm of the Comando da Aeronautica, formerly the Ministerio da Aeronautica, which existed as a cabinet ministry from 1941 until the Ministry of Defence absorbed it in 1999. It is the Brazilian state organ that holds the air-defence radar picture, controls civil and military air traffic through CINDACTA and COMDABRA/COMAE, and receives pilot and controller reports of unidentified aerial objects. Since 2010 it has operated under a published administrative rule requiring it to register those reports and forward them to a civilian national archive.
dossier.whyImplicated: The FAB is the board's control case. It is a mid-sized air force inside a country that spent 1964 to 1985 under a military dictatorship, which means it had every institutional reason to behave like the US Air Force did after 1947, and for a period it did: SIOANI in 1969, Operacao Prato in 1977 under a named captain, and an air-defence scramble in 1986 that it initially treated as a security event. What it then did is what makes it load-bearing. It did not build a permanent denial apparatus around the subject; it built a filing pipeline out of it. Portaria do Comando da Aeronautica no 551/GC3 of 9 August 2010 does not classify unidentified aerial phenomena reports, it routes them to the Arquivo Nacional for public consultation, and the FAB says on the record that everything it holds from 1952 to 2025 has gone there. Every structural argument the US posture rests on (national security, sources and methods, the danger of public panic, the need to protect radar performance data) was equally available to a Cold War military government in Brasilia, and Brasilia declined to use it.
dossier.narrative:
The Brazilian Air Force arrives on this board not as a suspected participant in a legacy recovery programme but as the measuring stick against which the US posture is read. Its value is that it controls for almost every variable the US concealment argument depends on. Brazil had an air force with a genuine air-defence mission, a real radar network, supersonic interceptors, a military intelligence service (the SNI), and, for twenty-one years, a military government answerable to nobody. If the argument for permanent secrecy about anomalous aerial objects were driven by the intrinsic sensitivity of the subject, the FAB should look like the most closed institution on the map. Instead it is the most open, and the openness is administrative rather than rhetorical, which is what makes it hard to dismiss.

The institutional history runs in three phases. The first is investigative. In 1969 the FAB stood up the Sistema de Investigacao de Objetos Aereos Nao Identificados, SIOANI, inside the 4a Zona Aerea in Sao Paulo, the command later renamed IV COMAR. SIOANI ran for roughly three years before ceasing operations quietly in 1972, and left behind a documentary residue that is now in the Arquivo Nacional. The second and best known phase is Operacao Prato, the field operation the FAB mounted in Para in 1977 and 1978 under Capitao Uyrange Hollanda, which put uniformed personnel into riverine villages with cameras and orders to observe. The third is the 19 May 1986 night, when CINDACTA and civil radar produced returns the FAB could not reconcile, five fighters were launched, and the Minister of Aeronautics stood in front of the press four days later and said the Air Force had no technical explanation.

What happened after 1986 is the part that matters most for comparison. The FAB did not sustain a public debunking programme. It did not issue a terminal report closing the file the way Project Blue Book was closed in 1969 with the Condon Committee as its warrant. Its posture, as characterised in the Brazilian Senate's own record, was discretion without denial: reticent when unasked, non-denying when asked. Then, in stages between 2007 and 2010, it converted the material into an archival stream. From 2007 the Aeronautica began sending its ufological papers to the Arquivo Nacional in Brasilia. In April 2009 CENDOC, the Air Force's documentation and history centre, sent across the first tranche relating to the Para operation. In August 2010 the Comando da Aeronautica published Portaria no 551/GC3 in the Diario Oficial da Uniao, formalising the pipeline: reports of aerial phenomena received by the aerospace operations command are received, registered, catalogued and forwarded to the Arquivo Nacional, where they are made available for consultation.

That rule is the single most consequential artefact in this dossier, because it inverts the default. Under 551/GC3 the resting state of a Brazilian military UAP report is public. There is no analytic gate, no adjudication of credibility before release, no requirement that the object be resolved before the paperwork moves. A LATAM captain reporting lights over Guarulhos in September 2025 and a Londrina tower controller reporting an intermittent radar-and-visual target in November 2025 both end up as scanned forms a citizen can pull down. In August 2026 the FAB restated the position in a written note to CNN Brasil: all documents, videos, photographs and reports available within the Comando da Aeronautica concerning unidentified aerial phenomena for the period 1952 to 2025 have already been transferred to the Arquivo Nacional, where they are in the public domain.

The limits are real and should be stated. The transfer was one service only. The Senate record is explicit that from 2007 it was the Aeronautica, and not the Army and not the Navy, that sent its papers to the Arquivo Nacional, and a 2013 approach to the Ministry of Defence by Brazilian researchers was aimed specifically at prying loose the Army and Navy holdings. So Brazil is not a case of total disclosure. It is a case of one service unilaterally choosing custody-with-publication while its sister services did not, which is itself an argument that the choice was institutional rather than physically compelled by the nature of the material. Nothing in the FAB record establishes retrieval of a craft or reverse-engineering activity, and nothing here should be read as claiming otherwise. What it establishes is narrower and sharper: a military that scrambled interceptors against unresolved radar contacts, said so at a podium, and then put the file in a civilian archive did not find that any of those three acts destabilised the state. The US argument that it cannot do the first two, let alone the third, is therefore not a claim about the subject matter. It is a claim about the US institution.

dossier.denialPosture: The FAB does not deny; it defers to the archive. Its standing public answer, restated in a written note in August 2026, is that everything it holds from 1952 to 2025 is already in the Arquivo Nacional and in the public domain, which converts every substantive question into a records query rather than a security refusal. That posture is itself the artefact: an air force that treats the subject as a filing matter has decided the subject is not a secret.
connections: Ran Operacao Prato (operacao-prato) in Para in 1977-78 under Capitao Uyrange Hollanda, and ran SIOANI at IV COMAR from 1969 to 1972.
Scrambled the interceptors in the 19 May 1986 event (ev-noite-ovnis-1986); its minister, Brigadeiro Octavio Julio Moreira Lima, gave the 23 May 1986 press conference.
Is the producing body of the Arquivo Nacional's Fundo OVNI (arquivo-nacional-ufo), reference BR DFANBSB ARX, via CENDOC and COMDABRA/COMAE.
Named repeatedly in Senado Federal RQS 193/2022 (senado-brasil) as the state organ that opened the files while the Army and Navy did not.
Structural counterpart to the US Air Force's Project Sign / Grudge / Blue Book lineage and to AARO: same problem, opposite disposal.
Worked alongside the Servico Nacional de Informacoes (SNI) on the Para operation; SNI holdings on the case were later released by the Gabinete de Seguranca Institucional.
openQuestions: The full text of Portaria no 551/GC3 of 9 August 2010 as published in the Diario Oficial da Uniao has not been retrieved directly; the date and content are attested by the FAB's own note and by the Senate record, not yet by the DOU page itself.

The Senate record spells the 2010 FAB commander as 'Junichi Saito'; the commander of the Aeronautica in that period is conventionally rendered Juniti Saito. The discrepancy has not been resolved against a primary FAB or DOU source.

The FAB says it has transferred everything through 2025, but the Arquivo Nacional's own description of the fund gives the most recent occurrence as 2016. Whether this reflects a lag in accessioning, a separate accrual series, or a genuine gap is unresolved.
No document has been located establishing why the Aeronautica transferred and the Exercito and Marinha did not, or what the Army and Navy holdings contain.

Nothing in the FAB record located here speaks to material recovery, custody of hardware, or reverse-engineering. Absence of such records in an otherwise open service is itself a datum but is not evidence either way.

l0.label: UAP Science Advisory Council

dossier.whatItIs: An external scientific advisory body stood up in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, ODNI, the FBI and the wider Intelligence Community, chaired by Harvard astrophysicist Abraham (Avi) Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board co-established by ODNI, the FBI and the Department of War, which held its first meeting on 16 June 2026. Every dataset the council is given is unclassified by design.
dossier.whyImplicated: The council is the scientific-legitimacy layer bolted onto the 2026 disclosure architecture, and its terms of reference are the tell. It exists to advise on the coordinated declassification of UAP information under Executive Order 13526, yet its own members are restricted to unclassified data — a body chartered to resolve the mystery is structurally barred from the evidence that would resolve it. Its membership includes Rear Admiral (ret.) Tim Gallaudet, whose account of a 2015 SIPRNET email titled "Urgent safety of flight issue" being deleted overnight from a flag officer's classified system is one of the most concrete public allegations of a special access program reaching into fleet communications; and Prof. Garry Nolan, whose laboratory work on claimed anomalous materials is the closest civilian science has come to the custody question. The council therefore places people with direct knowledge of concealment inside the advisory apparatus while denying them access to the compartments. Loeb's own public framing — that the "down-to-Earth interpretation" is adversary technology and compromised espionage defence — supplies the administration with an alarm-raising narrative that never touches the legacy retrieval question.
dossier.narrative:
On 16 June 2026, Avi Loeb published a Medium post announcing that he had been "tasked by the White House, the Pentagon's All Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and the Intelligence Community, to assemble a 'UAP Science Advisory Council'." The following day DefenseScoop's Brandi Vincent confirmed the arrangement with an ODNI official, who described the parent UAP Governance Board as an interagency body created "to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies," and confirmed that it had met for the first time the previous day. The ODNI official declined to identify the board's original participants — the body that will control declassification sequencing is itself anonymous.

The council's composition is the most analytically useful fact about it, and the two authoritative lists do not match. Loeb's own 16 June account names fifteen members: Prof. Liberty Vittert Capito (data analysis and statistics), Prof. Carol Cleland (anomaly identification), Dr. Richard Cloete (data analysis and AI tools), Dr. Omer Eldadi (data management, AI, human psychology), Dr. Tim Gallaudet (oceanography), Prof. Robin Hanson (statistics and economics), Ross Howard (communication), Dr. Kevin Knuth (physics and instrumentation), Ben Lamm (oceanography and biology), Dr. Devesh Nandal (numerical analysis and astrophysics), Prof. Garry Nolan (molecular biology and materials science), Dr. Michael Shermer (the study of anomalies), Dr. Peter Skafish (anthropology), Prof. Matthew Szydagis (instrumentation and data collection), and Dr. Jennice Vilhauer (quantitative psychology). The list Loeb supplied to DefenseScoop one day later drops Vittert Capito, Hanson and Knuth — three of the four quantitative-methods seats — and is otherwise identical. Whether that is editorial compression or a roster in flux within twenty-four hours is unresolved, but it is a documented discrepancy between two dated statements by the same source.

Loeb is explicit about the design intent behind Shermer's inclusion: "Including at least one member with a skeptical perspective (or a designated 'devil's advocate') in every committee is highly important. The skeptic prevents blind spots, reduces cognitive biases, and actively protects groups from disastrous decision-making as a result of groupthink." Read against the stance of this board, a council that pre-installs its own debunker and pre-commits to unclassified-only inputs has been engineered for a specific class of output: methodological recommendations, sensor procurement advice, and the repeated observation that better data is needed. It cannot produce a finding about custody, because it will never see a custody record.

The council's first substantive engagement with government product illustrates the boundary. Loeb pointed to an AARO report dated 5 June 2026, signed by AARO Director Dr. Jon Kosloski and posted in the third PURSUE tranche as DOW-UAP-D077, "Unresolved Case Analysis Update — Western United States Event." Loeb's summary: during two days in October 2023, law enforcement officials observed anomalous phenomena including an orange "mother" orb launching smaller red orbs, and about 40 percent of the reported phenomena lack a reasonable explanation and remain unresolved. That is the council's raw material — a published, unresolved case file, offered to outside scientists after AARO has already declined to resolve it.

The personnel overlaps are where the network becomes legible. Gallaudet is the former Oceanographer of the Navy, former commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, and former Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere. He is also an advisor to Ryan Graves's Americans for Safe Aerospace, and it was through Graves's sworn July 2023 testimony that his account of the deleted Fleet Forces Command email entered the congressional record. The man whose story is the strongest public evidence that a special access program suppressed a safety-of-flight warning about the very encounters that produced the GO FAST video now sits on the government's own science council — advising on declassification, with unclassified data only.

Loeb's institutional history matters too. He served on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) in 2019-2020, chaired Harvard's Astronomy department 2011-2020, chaired the National Academies' Board on Physics and Astronomy 2018-2021, and has run the Galileo Project since roughly 2021, which now operates three observatories scanning for objects outside the performance envelope of human technology. He is, in short, exactly the kind of credentialed outsider whose participation converts a political disclosure exercise into something that reads as science — and whose access constraints guarantee it will remain an exercise. The sequencing underlines the point: three PURSUE tranches had already gone public before the council was constituted, so the scientific advisory body was assembled after the declassification pipeline was already running.

l0.label: National Archives Record Group 615 - UAP Records Collection

dossier.whatItIs: Record Group 615, the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the U.S. National Archives, created by Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act (Public Law 118-31, div. A, title XVIII, subtitle C, December 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 699). It is the statutory destination for record copies of all Government, Government-provided or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.
dossier.whyImplicated: RG 615 is the first time Congress has created a records collection whose statutory scope explicitly includes 'technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.' A legislature does not write a records-collection statute around a category it believes to be empty; the statutory text is itself a congressional finding that such records are believed to exist and to be held by federal agencies. But the enforcement architecture was hollowed. The Senate-origin design contemplated an independent review board to push postponed records toward disclosure; the enacted subtitle contains none. Postponement is decided by 'the original classification authority' -- the agency holding the record -- and postponed records physically remain with the originating body until NARA stands up a security programme. So the collection that was supposed to break the compartment is, for the withheld portion, still inside the compartment. What has actually arrived at RG 615 by 2026 is the readily releasable material from FAA, NRC, ODNI, OSD, NSA, State and FBI.
dossier.narrative:
Read the statute rather than the coverage.

Section 1841(a)(1)(A) required the Archivist to commence establishing the collection within 60 days of enactment. Section 1841(a)(1)(C) defines its contents with unusual reach: 'record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).' Three features of that sentence are load-bearing. First, 'Government-funded' reaches contractor holdings. Second, 'or equivalent subjects by any other name' is an anti-euphemism clause -- a direct legislative anticipation that the material will be filed under cover terminology. Third, the sole carve-out is for temporarily non-attributed objects, i.e. drones and balloons, which is Congress saying the collection is not about the prosaic.

Section 1841(a)(1)(D) requires the Archivist to 'prepare and publish a subject guidebook and index to the Collection.' Section 1841(b) requires that transmitted records be available for inspection and copying at the National Archives within 30 days of transmission and digitally within not more than 180 days thereafter. Section 1841(e) assigns continuing oversight jurisdiction to Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services and Intelligence, and to House Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services and Intelligence.

Section 1842 governs the agencies. Subsection (c)(1) gave each head of a Government office 300 days from December 22, 2023 to review, identify and organise every UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission. Subsection (a)(2)(A) is absolute: 'No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way.' Subsection (a)(2)(B) forbids withholding, redacting, postponing or reclassifying any UAP record already made available or disclosed to the public before enactment -- a retroactive lock on the existing public record, including documents like the Halt memo. Subsection (a)(2)(C) extends the same protection to records created by persons or entities outside the federal government.

Subsection (c)(2)(G) sets priorities, and the priority order is revealing. Agencies must give precedence first to records not already public; second to 'all records that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence'; third to records already in FOIA litigation; fourth to earliest-provenance records. Congress wrote a triage rule that puts the most explicitly non-human material at the front of the queue.

Then the gate. Section 1843(a) permits postponement 'if the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' that the threat to military defence, intelligence operations or foreign relations 'is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure' and that disclosure would reveal a currently protected agent, a currently used source or method, or 'any other matter currently relating to the military defense, intelligence operations, or conduct of foreign relations of the United States, the disclosure of which would demonstrably and substantially impair the national security.' Additional grounds cover the Privacy Act, unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, and confidentiality understandings with cooperating individuals.

'Clear and convincing evidence' is a demanding standard on paper. The problem is who applies it. The original classification authority is an official of the agency that owns the record and, on the allegations at issue, may be the same institutional actor accused of the concealment. There is no independent adjudicator in the enacted text. This is the JFK Records Act model with the Assassination Records Review Board removed.

Section 1842(g) supplies the only ongoing pressure. Postponed records must be reviewed periodically by the originating agency and the Archivist. Every continued postponement 'shall require an unclassified written description of the reason for such continued postponement relevant to these specific records,' provided to the Archivist and published in the Federal Register. And section 1842(g)(2)(D) sets the backstop: each record must be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation, unless the President personally certifies that continued postponement is necessitated by an identifiable harm of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest. On a 25-year rule, anything created before 2001 is already past due absent a presidential certification.

Section 1841(d)(2) and section 1842(f) together create the physical bottleneck. NARA's National Security Program Office, with the Information Security Oversight Office, must establish a programme to secure the postponed and classified portion of the collection -- and until that programme exists, postponed records are 'held for reasons of security and preservation by the originating body.' The withheld material does not move.

What has actually landed is documented on NARA's RG 615 page, last reviewed May 22, 2026: series from the Federal Aviation Administration (National Archives Identifier 493468575), the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (488808322), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (493468579), the Office of the Secretary of Defense (493468580), the National Security Agency (580103959), the Department of State (608806625), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (580705010). NARA issued AC Memo 04.2025 to agencies on the transfer of publicly releasable UAP records, and describes transfers as arriving on a rolling basis.

By 2026 a parallel executive channel has opened alongside the statutory one. Following a presidential order to disclose collected UAP records, the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters -- the PURSUE Task Force -- released a fourth tranche of records on July 10, 2026, published at war.gov/ufo, and ODNI issued memorandum ES 2026-00818 on July 31, 2026 waiving nondisclosure agreements for anyone speaking to PURSUE or AARO. The analytically important question is whether PURSUE releases are being routed into RG 615 as section 1842(e) requires, or are accumulating in a separate executive-branch publication stream outside the Archivist's custody and outside the Federal Register accountability of section 1842(g)(2)(B).

claims.text: Record Group 615, the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection, was created by Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, div. A, title XVIII, subtitle C, December 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 699.
claims.source: Pub. L. 118-31, secs. 1841-1843, reproduced as a note to 44 U.S.C. ch. 21 at https://www.archives.gov/about/laws/nara.html#uaps; collection page at https://www.archives.gov/research/topics/uaps/rg-615

claims.text: Section 1841(a)(1)(C) provides that the Collection 'shall consist of record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).'

Section 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office to review, identify and organise every UAP record in its custody for public disclosure and transmission to the Archivist not later than 300 days after December 22, 2023.
Section 1842(a)(2)(A) provides that 'No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way.'
Section 1842(a)(2)(B) bars any UAP record made available or disclosed to the public before December 22, 2023 from being withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified.

Section 1842(c)(2)(G)(ii) directs agencies to give precedence to 'the identification, review, and transmission of all records that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.'

Section 1843(a) permits postponement of disclosure only where 'the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of enumerated harms; the enacted subtitle establishes no independent review board to adjudicate those determinations.

Section 1842(g)(2)(B) requires that every continued postponement carry 'an unclassified written description of the reason for such continued postponement relevant to these specific records,' provided to the Archivist and published in the Federal Register.

Section 1842(g)(2)(D) requires each UAP record to be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation unless the President certifies that continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm whose gravity outweighs the public interest in disclosure.

Section 1841(d)(2) requires NARA's National Security Program Office, with the Information Security Oversight Office, to establish a security programme for postponed records, and section 1842(f) provides that postponed records are held by the originating body until that programme exists -- so withheld records physically remain with the agency that withheld them.

As of the page's May 22, 2026 review date, RG 615 contains series transferred from the Federal Aviation Administration (NAID 493468575), the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (488808322), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (493468579), the Office of the Secretary of Defense (493468580), the National Security Agency (580103959), the Department of State (608806625), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (580705010).
claims.source: National Archives, "Record Group 615: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection," https://www.archives.gov/research/topics/uaps/rg-615

claims.text: Section 1841(e) assigns continuing legislative oversight of the Collection to the Senate Committees on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services and Intelligence, and to the House Committees on Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services and Intelligence.

NARA issued AC Memo 04.2025, 'Transfer of Publicly Releasable Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) Records,' to federal agencies governing identification, preparation and transfer of records into Record Group 615.

In 2026 a parallel executive disclosure channel is operating: the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) Task Force released a fourth tranche of records on July 10, 2026, published at war.gov/ufo, following a presidential order to disclose collected UAP records.
claims.source: Douglas Messier, "Guidance Published for UAP Disclosure," August 2, 2026, https://douglasmmessier.substack.com/p/guidance-published-for-uap-disclosure; releases at https://www.war.gov/ufo/

dossier.denialPosture: No agency has publicly asserted that it holds no UAP records; the posture is instead procedural. Agencies transfer 'publicly releasable' material under AC Memo 04.2025 while postponement determinations remain with each originating agency's own original classification authority under section 1843(a), and postponed records stay physically in agency custody under section 1842(f) pending a NARA security programme. The result is that the withholding is never articulated as a denial -- it is expressed as a classification determination made by the withholder.
connections: RG 615 is the disclosure end-state of the same statutory sequence that begins with 50 U.S.C. 3373b (FY2023 NDAA sec. 1673), which Grusch helped draft.
Section 1843's 'original classification authority' gate imports the self-adjudication principle described in classified-annex.
Records like the Halt memo and the DEFE 24 files bearing on rendlesham-1980 fall under section 1842(a)(2)(B)'s bar on re-withholding already-public UAP records.

AARO is named in sections 1842(c)(2)(E), (F) and (3) as an office that other agencies must make records available to -- giving the office accused of being non-neutral a statutory role in the records pipeline.
The KONA BLUE and AAWSAP/AATIP documents released by DoD and DHS in partnership are precisely the class of record section 1842 was written to capture.
The 2026 PURSUE Task Force and ODNI memorandum ES 2026-00818 (Aaron Lukas, July 31, 2026) run alongside RG 615 and raise the question of dual custody.
Presidential libraries and archival depositories under 44 U.S.C. 2112 are given expedited-review priority by section 1842(c)(3), reaching back into the 1944-1970 period this board covers.
openQuestions: Whether the subject guidebook and index required by section 1841(a)(1)(D) has been prepared or published.

How many records have been postponed under section 1843, by which agencies, and whether any unclassified written descriptions of continued postponement have been published in the Federal Register as section 1842(g)(2)(B) requires.
Whether NARA's National Security Program Office has stood up the security programme required by section 1841(d)(2) -- until it does, no postponed record can leave agency custody.
Whether any President has issued a certification under section 1842(g)(2)(D) to continue postponing records older than 25 years, and how many records are past that deadline without one.

Whether any agency has certified completion of the section 1842(c)(1) 300-day review, and whether the Department of Energy, CIA, DIA, NRO, NGA and the military departments have transferred anything into RG 615.
Whether contractor-held records are being captured under the 'Government-funded' clause of section 1841(a)(1)(C), and whether any contractor has been served a records demand.
Whether PURSUE tranche releases at war.gov are also being transmitted to the Archivist for inclusion in RG 615, or are a parallel channel outside the statutory accountability structure.

l0.label: ODNI Memorandum ES 2026-00818 - Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver

dossier.whatItIs: An Office of the Director of National Intelligence memorandum titled "Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver," bearing control number ES 2026-00818, dated 31 July 2026, from the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence to the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency and other IC element heads. It directs the Department of War and the Intelligence Community to build a process by which current and former employees and contractors may disclose UAP information to AARO or to designated representatives of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) Task Force notwithstanding existing non-disclosure agreements, agreements, oaths or commitments.
dossier.whyImplicated: The memo is an admission written in the form of a remedy. No government waives non-disclosure obligations for a subject about which nothing is being withheld. Its most consequential sentence is the one instructing the IC to make its workforce aware that any NDA prohibiting disclosure to the President, the PURSUE Task Force or other designees is no longer in force — an instruction that only makes sense if such instruments exist, and DLA Piper's government contracts practice notes that an NDA barring disclosure to the President "would be unusual if not unlawful" because the President is the ultimate classification authority. It was not published by ODNI. The administration authorised the House office of Rep. Eric Burlison, a founding member of the Congressional UAP Caucus, to distribute it — routing an IC-wide directive through the oversight bloc rather than dni.gov. And it is materially narrower than the statute it purports to implement: 50 U.S.C. § 3373b already authorises disclosure to AARO notwithstanding Executive Order 13526, the Atomic Energy Act, and Section 798 of the Espionage Act, while the memo reaches only contractual and oath-based restrictions.
dossier.narrative:
On 31 July 2026 the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence signed a memorandum, numbered ES 2026-00818, addressed to the Director of the CIA and the heads of the other Intelligence Community elements. Two days later Rep. Eric Burlison (MO-07) posted it on his House website, noting that "the administration authorized Congressman Burlison's office to publicly distribute the memorandum." That single procedural fact deserves more attention than the memo's contents. The executive branch chose, as the public release channel for a national-level intelligence directive, the congressional office of a member who had spent three years accusing the executive branch of hiding UAP records — and who ten days earlier, on 21 July 2026, had publicly invited anyone who believed the President's directive applied to them to contact his office for help navigating the process. Burlison's office was, in effect, standing up a parallel intake channel for whistleblowers while the official one was still being written.

What the memo does: it directs the Department of War and the IC to implement a process ensuring that current and former governmental employees and contractors holding alleged UAP information may disclose it to designated government representatives in AARO or the PURSUE Task Force notwithstanding contravening NDAs, agreements, oaths or commitments. It instructs every IC element, within thirty days of receipt, to coordinate with ODNI to establish a PURSUE designee and to "inform their workforce of the President's order." It states that NDAs prohibiting disclosure to the President, to PURSUE or to other designees are no longer in force. And it flags two further tranches of guidance to come — implementing guidance for the preliminary guidance itself, and a separate ODNI/DoW package for the broader PURSUE transparency project.

What the memo does not do is the more informative half. It does not authorise public disclosure of classified information. It does not authorise disclosure to Congress other than through AARO or existing channels — a striking limitation given that the standard ODNI classified information nondisclosure agreement, Standard Form 312, already contemplates disclosure to Congress in some form. It does not tell government contractors, as distinct from IC employees, how to make an authorised disclosure at all, even though the FY2023 NDAA's anti-retaliation protection expressly extends to any "contractor, subcontractor, grantee, subgrantee, or personal services contractor" of a covered department or agency. For an entity board built on the premise that the retrieval and reverse-engineering work sits inside cleared private industry, that omission is the operative fact: the memo waives the secrecy instruments of the government workforce while leaving the contractor workforce — the population most likely to hold the material — without a documented route.

The memo is also narrower than the law. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. No. 117-263, 136 Stat. 2959-62, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373b(b)(1)) authorises disclosure to AARO notwithstanding not merely NDAs but any regulation or order issued under Executive Order 13526, anything under the Atomic Energy Act, Section 798 of the Espionage Act, and any other "provision of law relating to the disclosure of information." ES 2026-00818 speaks only to "[NDAs], agreements, oaths, or commitments." As agency guidance it is not binding law, and DLA Piper's alert notes that it "does not, by itself, confer legal rights with respect to making authorized disclosures beyond those established by statute." A person weighing whether to come forward is therefore being handed a document that sounds like permission and is legally less protective than the statute already on the books — and told that the real guidance is still being drafted. That is a structure that produces delay.

The scale problem is visible in AARO's own reporting. Its Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report states that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, seven individuals contacted AARO with UAP-related claims that AARO judged warranted a request for a follow-on interview. Seven. The same report asserts that AARO is legally authorised to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs. Those two statements coexisting is the concealment argument in miniature: an office with unlimited statutory reach and a single-digit annual intake.

Context matters for dating. The PURSUE Task Force was launched by the Department of War on 1 May 2026 following President Trump's 19 February 2026 Truth Social directive; the first tranche of records went public on 8 May 2026, with further tranches on 22 May, 12 June, 10 July and 7 August 2026. ES 2026-00818 arrives at the end of that sequence, nearly three months into a rolling public release — the NDA waiver follows the file dumps rather than preceding them, which means the population best able to contextualise those files was still under contractual gag while the files were being published.

One further structural note. AARO sits inside the Department of War but reports to ODNI on operational and security matters under 50 U.S.C. § 3373(b)(3)(B)(ii). ES 2026-00818 was issued by ODNI, while the FY2023 NDAA assigns the establishment of the secure disclosure mechanism to the Secretary of War acting through the head of AARO in consultation with the DNI. The guidance therefore comes from the consulted party rather than the responsible one — a jurisdictional wrinkle that any contractor's counsel will find, and that gives every recipient a colourable argument that the instrument binding them has not yet been properly issued.

dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act as adopted by the U.S. House of Representatives on 22 July 2026 as an amendment to the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (H.R. 8800, 119th Congress). It would create a permanent UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, stand up an independent Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority, and extend disclosure obligations to covered government contractors. It is the first time the full JFK-Act-style disclosure architecture has cleared a chamber of Congress since the original Schumer-Rounds text was gutted in conference in December 2023.
dossier.whyImplicated: The amendment is written on the assumption that UAP records exist outside the reach of ordinary congressional oversight, in agency holdings and in contractor holdings, and that the agencies holding them will not surrender them voluntarily. Three design choices give that away: the records collection is compulsory and on a statutory timeline rather than voluntary; the review board is given subpoena power rather than a request authority; and disclosure obligations are extended to 'covered government contractors,' which is meaningless unless Congress believes private firms hold federal UAP records. Burlison's own framing, that records have 'remained scattered across agencies and outside meaningful oversight,' is a sitting member of Congress stating on the record that the existing oversight architecture does not reach the material. The amendment also explicitly positions itself as statutory backstop to a presidential declassification effort (PURSUE), which is an admission that executive-branch goodwill is not considered durable. Every one of those features is a legislative inference about the concealment structure, drawn by people with access to classified briefings.
dossier.narrative:
The Burlison amendment is the third act of a five-year legislative arc, and the arc itself is the evidence.

Act one was July 2023, when Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds introduced the UAP Disclosure Act as Senate Amendment 797 to S.2226, the FY2024 NDAA, explicitly modeled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992. That text carried a presumption of immediate disclosure, an independent review board, presidential authority to overturn board determinations, a hard 25-year outer deadline, and — the provision that made the defense industry move — federal eminent domain over 'recovered technologies of unknown origin' and biological evidence held by private persons. The Senate adopted it 84 to 0. An eminent domain clause is not written into a defense bill as an abstraction. It is written because the drafters believe there is specific property, in specific private hands, that the government cannot presently compel.

Act two was December 2023. In conference with the House, the review board, the eminent domain provision and the presidential certification mechanism were stripped. What survived became Sections 1841 through 1843 of Public Law 118-31, which directed the Archivist to establish a UAP Records Collection at NARA and required agencies to identify, organize and begin transmitting UAP records. The surviving language was the filing cabinet without the locksmith: a collection with no independent body empowered to second-guess an agency's decision to withhold, and no reach into contractor vaults. Agencies were left as the sole judges of what constituted a covered record.

Act three is 2025-2026. Burlison, a Missouri Republican on the House Oversight Committee, reintroduced the disclosure act as an NDAA amendment during FY2026 consideration; it did not reach a floor vote. He came back for FY2027. On 22 July 2026 the House adopted his amendment to H.R. 8800, and later that day passed the underlying bill 216 to 212 on Roll Call 278. The press release from his office is precise about what the amendment restores: 'a permanent UAP Records Collection at the National Archives,' 'an independent, Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority to review records, hear testimony, and determine whether information should remain protected under standards established by law,' and extension of disclosure requirements 'to covered government contractors.' The review board is back. The contractor reach is back. Eminent domain is not mentioned.

The contractor clause is the load-bearing provision for anyone mapping the legacy program. Under the existing FY2024 architecture, a record physically held by a prime or a subcontractor under an IRAD-funded or SAP-funded effort is not obviously a 'federal record' subject to transmission. The FY2023 statutory scheme had already tried to grip this problem from a different angle: 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(1)(B) protects authorized disclosure of any activity 'by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency' relating to UAP including 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering,' and 3373b(b)(3)(A) ordered federal agencies and their contractors to conduct comprehensive searches of records relating to UAP nondisclosure orders and hand copies to AARO. A subpoena-armed review board with contractor jurisdiction is the enforcement mechanism those provisions never had.

The PURSUE relationship is the other tell. The press release says the amendment would 'support President Trump's Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE)' by 'bolstering in law authorities for carrying out disclosure.' PURSUE is a Department of War declassification and release effort standing at war.gov/ufo, running on rolling tranches. A legislator who trusted an executive declassification program to be complete and permanent would not spend a year of floor strategy building a Senate-confirmed board with subpoena power to sit alongside it. The amendment is insurance against the possibility that PURSUE releases what the executive branch chooses to release and stops there.

What happens next is a conference fight. The FY2027 NDAA moved to the Senate; the House-passed disclosure architecture will meet whatever the Senate produces, and the 2023 precedent is that the strongest provisions die quietly in conference without a recorded vote. Conference is where the concealment structure has historically been most effective, because it is the one stage of the legislative process with no roll call, no floor debate and no public amendment text.

dossier.whatItIs: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the U.S. civil space agency. Since 2022 it has been a formal participant in the government's UAP effort through a commissioned Independent Study Team, whose final report it published on 14 September 2023 alongside the appointment of a Director of UAP Research. Since 2026 it has been a contributing agency to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, supplying Apollo- and Gemini-era imagery and astronaut accounts.
dossier.whyImplicated: NASA's role in the concealment architecture is not custody; it is certification. It is the civilian, scientifically credentialed institution that repeatedly states there is no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while holding, by its own design choices, no access to the compartmented material where the question would actually be settled — its Independent Study Team used unclassified data only, and its charter expressly excluded review of past incidents. The sharper fact is a custody claim. In 2025 NASA's Office of Communications told a records researcher that it has no UAP records qualifying for transfer to the National Archives under the FY2024 NDAA because "any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That single sentence removes NASA's UAP holdings from the statutory records regime by attributing ownership to the department least likely to release them. Ten months later NASA's own Administrator publicly identified NASA-provided Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 lunar-surface imagery as "some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure." Both statements cannot sit comfortably together: an agency with nothing to transfer, holding the most interesting data.
dossier.narrative:
NASA entered the modern UAP file formally in 2022, when it commissioned an outside Independent Study Team to advise on how the agency might contribute. The team's final report was published on 14 September 2023 under NASA release 23-106, chaired by David Spergel, president of the Simons Foundation, with sixteen members. Its overall recommendation was that NASA play a prominent role in the whole-of-government effort by using its open-source resources, technological expertise, data analysis techniques, federal and commercial partnerships, and Earth-observing assets to curate a better dataset for understanding future UAP. The report explicitly is not a review or assessment of previous UAP incidents. That boundary is the point: NASA's charter for the study excluded the historical record, which is where the legacy program question lives.

Spergel described the methodological constraint as a virtue: "Using unclassified data was essential for our team's fact-finding, open-communication collaboration, and for upholding scientific rigor to produce this report for NASA." The team reported that there are currently a limited number of high-quality observations of UAP, which make it impossible to draw firm scientific conclusions about their nature. The same architecture reappears three years later in the UAP Science Advisory Council chaired by Avi Loeb — unclassified data only, chartered to recommend how to get better data, structurally incapable of reaching a custody finding. NASA built the template.

With the report NASA named Mark McInerney its Director of UAP Research. McInerney had previously served as NASA's liaison to the Department of Defense "covering limited UAP activities for the agency" — meaning the agency's UAP function had already existed as a DoD liaison billet before it was given a public title. Administrator Bill Nelson framed the role in terms of instrumentation and analytics: the director would apply "artificial intelligence and machine learning to search the skies for anomalies," and "NASA will do this work transparently for the benefit of humanity." McInerney's career runs through NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, NOAA and the National Hurricane Center since 1996 — a NOAA lineage he shares with Tim Gallaudet, the retired admiral now on the 2026 UAP Science Advisory Council.

Then came the records question, and with it the most consequential NASA statement in the public record. The FY2024 NDAA, sections 1841-1842, required federal agencies to identify and transfer UAP records to a new collection at the National Archives, with digital transfers due by 30 September 2025. Record Group 615 was created to hold them. Over the course of 2025 the FAA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the National Security Agency, ODNI and the Office of the Secretary of Defense transferred records into the online catalog. NASA did not. Asked why, NASA's Office of Communications replied: "Per the requirements in Section 1841-1842 of the Fiscal Year 2024 National Defense Authorization Act for handling records related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), NASA does not have any records that meet the requirements to submit records to the National Archives. Any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That is not a denial of possession. It is an assertion of foreign ownership over material NASA holds — a jurisdictional argument that keeps agency UAP records outside a statutory public-release regime by routing their custody back into the Department of War.

The 2026 disclosure wave then produced the contradiction. On 27 May 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that the newly declassified files show "real unexplained phenomena" but no recovered craft: "What's being surfaced isn't crashed ships or alien bodies, but real unexplained phenomena," and "There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships." Note the construction — personal awareness, from a political appointee without read-in to the compartments where such material would be held. In the same interview Isaacman said agencies "really didn't take this quite as seriously in the past until President Trump put out the tweet, basically giving an order to government agencies and going out and saying, look, this time you better go through the files, you better start searching your databases and bring things up" — a sitting NASA Administrator stating that federal agencies did not conduct records searches for UAP material until a presidential post compelled them.

And on NASA's own contribution: "I would say that some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure was taken on the surface of the moon from Apollo 12 and 17. You can't be a moon landing denier and also believe that those photos captured unexplained phenomenon." Fox News reported that the PURSUE material includes astronaut and NASA-related accounts from the Apollo and Gemini eras describing strange lights and unidentified objects observed in space, alongside 2023 infrared footage of an F-16 engaging a diamond-shaped object over Lake Huron and reports from military operations in Iran, Syria, Iraq and Greece. Set against the 2025 Office of Communications statement — NASA has no qualifying records because DoD owns them — the position is that NASA's most interesting UAP data was released through the Department of War's website rather than deposited in the National Archives collection Congress created for exactly that purpose. One route is statutory, permanent and indexed; the other is a rolling, discretionary web publication controlled by the Secretary of War. NASA's material went down the second.

A loose thread worth pulling: on the war.gov PURSUE page, the Release 05 slideshow of 7 August 2026 carries an image described as "A photograph of an unidentified object in low-Earth orbit, taken from Space Shuttle Columbia in 1996," while the underlying file is named DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953.jpg. A 1996 Columbia photograph filed under a 1953 film analysis is either a metadata error or an indexing artifact, and either way it is a checkable discrepancy in the government's own release. The Columbia 1996 imagery in question is almost certainly from STS-75, the tethered satellite mission whose downlink footage has been argued over for thirty years — meaning the 2026 disclosure has quietly placed a long-contested NASA video into an official unresolved-case release.

dossier.whatItIs: The Central Intelligence Agency is the United States civilian foreign intelligence service. Its documented involvement with the UFO question runs from the Office of Scientific Intelligence study group of 1952 through its convening of the Robertson Panel in January 1953 to its management of the U-2 and OXCART cover stories through the 1950s and 1960s. Its own in-house historian published a detailed account of that record in Studies in Intelligence in 1997.
dossier.whyImplicated: The CIA is the only agency in this dossier set that has published, in its own classified-origin journal, a first-person institutional admission that it directed the government to debunk UFO reports, concealed its sponsorship of the panel that recommended doing so, and knowingly allowed the Air Force to issue misleading and deceptive statements about more than half of all UFO reports for over a decade. That is not an allegation; it is the CIA's own historian describing the machinery of a UFO cover story and calling it by name. Once an agency has demonstrably run one UFO cover story for a real classified programme, the argument that it would not run a second for a different one loses its force. The Agency also sits at the point in the concealment argument where a recovery capability would have to live if the operations occurred on foreign soil, and it has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
dossier.narrative:
The primary document here is Gerald K. Haines, CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90, published in Studies in Intelligence in 1997 and posted on the Agency's own website. Haines was a government historian with access to Agency files. What he wrote is more damaging to the Agency's credibility on this subject than anything a critic has written.

The Robertson Panel convened in January 1953 at CIA's instigation, following a recommendation from the Intelligence Advisory Committee to enlist selected scientists to review and appraise the available evidence in light of pertinent scientific theories. The panellists had expertise in nuclear physics, high-energy physics, radar, electronics and geophysics. Their formal conclusion was that there was no evidence of a direct threat to national security and no evidence of extraterrestrial visitation. Their operational recommendation was something else entirely. Haines writes that to meet these problems, the panel recommended that the National Security Council debunk UFO reports and institute a policy of public education to reassure the public of the lack of evidence behind UFOs. It suggested using the mass media, advertising, business clubs, schools, and even the Disney corporation to get the message across. In the same breath, reporting at the height of McCarthyism, it recommended that private UFO groups including the Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators in Los Angeles and the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization be monitored for subversive activities.

That is a US intelligence agency recommending, at national security council level, a domestic public-opinion management campaign on a scientific subject and the surveillance of American civil society organisations that took an interest in it. The Agency then concealed its own role. When public pressure built for release of the panel report in 1956, Philip Strong, Deputy Assistant Director of the Office of Scientific Intelligence, refused to declassify it and declined to disclose CIA sponsorship of the panel. Haines records that the Agency instead prepared a sanitized version which deleted any reference to CIA and avoided mention of any psychological warfare potential in the UFO controversy. When Donald Keyhoe told Mike Wallace on CBS in March 1958 that the CIA was deeply involved and had sponsored the panel, the Agency held firm to its policy of not revealing its role in UFO investigations and refused to declassify the full report.

The U-2 passage is the strongest single piece of documentary evidence anywhere in the official record that the United States Government has deliberately generated false explanations for aerial phenomena and sustained them for years. Haines writes that Air Force BLUE BOOK investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights tried to explain away such sightings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and temperature inversions, that by checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in Washington they were able to attribute many UFO sightings to U-2 flights, and that they were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public. He then reports that according to later estimates from CIA officials who worked on the U-2 and OXCART projects, over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s were accounted for by manned reconnaissance flights, namely the U-2, over the United States, and that this led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily sensitive national security project. Haines adds that while perhaps justified, this deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup controversy of the 1970s.

The Agency also drafted, and then abandoned, a National Security Council Intelligence Directive on UFOs following the Robertson Panel findings. A directive of that class would have assigned standing intelligence community responsibility for the subject. That it was drafted at all establishes that the Agency treated UFOs as a candidate for permanent national intelligence tasking in 1953.

The modern allegations against the Agency are thinner and must be marked as such. Journalist Ross Coulthart has reported, on the basis of David Grusch and other sources, that an office within CIA has coordinated crash retrievals on foreign soil for many years. No document supporting that has been released, no named official has confirmed it on the record, and this board carries it at Tier 3 as a research direction rather than a finding. AARO's Volume I addresses a related allegation and reports that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which is an on-the-record denial obtained by an interested party rather than a document from the period.

What can be said cleanly is this. AARO states it partnered with CIA archives for the historical review, so the Agency's UAP holdings were at least nominally opened to the office writing the government's history. Yet as of 22 May 2026 the CIA does not appear among the seven organisations with a transmittal in the National Archives UAP Records Collection. Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, named the CIA first among the agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading in his words to unchecked power and corruption. An agency with a published institutional history of running UFO cover stories, no statutory records transmittal, and a named place in sworn whistleblower testimony belongs on this map.
