dossier.denialPosture: CIA's public position at termination was that remote viewing had never produced data used to guide an intelligence operation and that the program was scientifically unsupported, a verdict delivered through a contracted outside evaluator rather than in CIA's own voice. The 1995 internal memorandum shows that position was arrived at before the evaluation was contracted, and that the declassification package was scoped in parallel by CIA and DIA to exclude 'the most sensitive aspects of the program.'
connections: Harold Puthoff and Russell Targ ran the SRI research leg under CIA and later DIA sponsorship; Puthoff is a recurring node in the modern UAP-contracting record (NIDS, AAWSAP-era work, To The Stars Academy). His exact TTSA officer title and dates should be confirmed against SEC filings for CIK 0001710274.

SAIC as STAR GATE prime contractor from 1991 to 1995 places the program inside the same cleared-contractor ecosystem as later phenomenon-adjacent work; SAIC's successor entities are standing nodes for the funding thread.

DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate (DT-S) hosted the program from 1985 to 1991; DIA is the same agency that later hosted AAWSAP, making DIA the most persistent institutional host across both threads.
Richard D'Amato, Senate Appropriations Committee staff, is the named congressional staff recipient of the 27 March 1995 CIA briefing, a specific and findable oversight contact point.
Army INSCOM at Fort Meade is the operational home; INSCOM connects to the Army-side custody question raised by the TTSA-Army CRADA (ttsa-army-crada) four decades later.

The pattern of serial renaming and inter-agency transfer is the template the board applies to the alleged legacy recovery program; STAR GATE is the control case where the template is documented rather than inferred.

American Institutes for Research and its president David Goslin are the named third-party validators used to close the program, the same 'independent review' device later used with the NASA 2023 UAP study panel and AARO's Historical Record Report.
openQuestions: What material was withheld under the 1995 decision to declassify 'all but the most sensitive aspects of the program,' and under whose signature was the withholding line drawn?
Which DIA support contractor performed the 1995 document identification and declassification sorting alongside CIA?

l0.label: UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports I-VII (Stringfield, 1978-1994)

dossier.whatItIs: The Status Reports are a series of seven self-published monographs by Cincinnati ufologist Leonard H. Stringfield (1920-1994), issued between 1978 and 1994, compiling anonymized first- and second-hand accounts of alleged U.S. military recoveries of crashed craft and occupant bodies. The first, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody,' was presented at the Ninth Annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio in July 1978. The series is the foundational corpus of the modern crash-retrieval literature.
dossier.whyImplicated: Every modern claim about a legacy retrieval program is downstream of a source pool that Stringfield assembled first. His method — solicit military and medical personnel, strip identities, publish coded case abstracts — created a body of testimony in the late 1970s and 1980s whose content is structurally identical to what witnesses told the House Oversight Committee in 2023 and 2024: recovery of intact and damaged craft, transport to secure facilities, autopsy of non-human remains, compartmented handling outside normal channels. If those 2023 claims are a modern fabrication, the fabrication is forty-five years old and was published in monograph form by a MUFON public relations director with a documented Air Defense Command reporting relationship. If they are not, Stringfield's files are the earliest systematic index of the program's personnel. Either way, the corpus is a testable object: the sources are anonymous, but the cases carry dates, units and installations, and the underlying files exist as a physical archive. The honest tier here is low on the substance and high on the provenance.
dossier.narrative:
Stringfield's standing rests on a career that predates the crash-retrieval work by two decades. In 1954 he founded Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects (CRIFO) in Cincinnati and published the newsletter ORBIT. He wrote 'Inside Saucer Post...3-0 Blue: CRIFO Views the Status Quo' in 1957, the same year he became public relations adviser to Donald Keyhoe's National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena. From 1967 to 1969 he served as an 'Early Warning Coordinator' for the Condon Committee at the University of Colorado, screening incoming reports for possible scientific study. He was later Director of Public Relations for the Mutual UFO Network. His day job, throughout, was Director of Public Relations and Marketing Services for DuBois Chemicals, a division of Chemed Corporation. He died of lung cancer on 18 December 1994.

The relevant biographical detail for a concealment analysis is the reporting arrangement. NICAP's own biography states that Stringfield worked in cooperation with the U.S. Air Force from 1953 to 1957 investigating and reporting UFO activity, having been assigned a special code number for reporting to the Air Defense Command in Columbus, Ohio. A civilian researcher holding an assigned reporting code to ADC is an unusual artifact and it explains why military personnel later approached him rather than a journalist.

The Status Report series, with titles and dates as published: Status Report I, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A case study of alleged UFOs and occupants in military custody' (1978, from the Ninth Annual MUFON Symposium, Dayton, Ohio, July 1978); Status Report II, 'The UFO Crash/Retrieval Syndrome: New Sources, New Data' (1980); Status Report III, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Amassing the Evidence' (1982); Status Report IV, 'The fatal encounter at Ft. Dix-McGuire: A case study' (1985); Status Report V, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Is the coverup lid lifting?' (1989); Status Report VI, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: The Inner Sanctum' (1991); Status Report VII, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Search for Proof in a Hall of Mirrors' (1994). All were self-published. A 2019 compilation reissued all seven in one volume.

The method is the weakness and also the reason the corpus is worth auditing. Stringfield presented cases as numbered abstracts summarizing accounts from unnamed informants, most described as military or medical personnel. Some abstracts are explicitly composites; the widely cited 'Abstract XXII: Biological data relating to retrieved alien bodies' is described as a composite assembled from anonymous medical and military sources. No abstract in the published series can be independently verified from the text alone, because the text withholds the identifying information that would permit verification. That is a disqualifying defect for any individual claim and simultaneously the exact behavior one would expect from a researcher protecting serving personnel.

Status Report IV is the outlier and the best single entry point for an analyst. It abandons the abstract format for a single named case study, the alleged January 1978 incident at Fort Dix and McGuire Air Force Base in New Jersey, with a specific installation, a specific date window, and identifiable military police and security police units. That case is checkable against Army and Air Force records in a way the composite abstracts are not.

The physical archive survives. MUFON's Project Aquarius Library lists the Stringfield Files as a private collection. The underlying correspondence, informant notes and case files in that collection are the actual evidentiary object; the published monographs are only the redacted output. Whether the collection contains unredacted informant identities is the single most consequential unanswered question about this entity.

What the record shows: a well-documented researcher with an unusual official reporting relationship who, over sixteen years, published seven monographs compiling anonymous military testimony about recoveries and autopsies, and who left an archive. What the record does not show: any named source, any document, any physical item, or any independent corroboration of a single abstract. Tiered honestly, the existence, authorship, dating and archival survival of the Status Reports are Tier 1 or 2; every substantive claim inside them is Tier 3 pending identification of sources.

l0.label: The Roswell Report: Case Closed (1997)

dossier.whatItIs: The Roswell Report: Case Closed is a 231-page official United States Air Force publication authored by Capt. James McAndrew of the Secretary of the Air Force Declassification and Review Team at the Pentagon, printed by the U.S. Government Printing Office and released on 24 June 1997. It is the follow-on to the 1994-95 Air Force report The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert by Col. Richard L. Weaver and then-1st Lt. James McAndrew. Its purpose is to account for the reports of 'alien bodies' that the 1995 report had left unaddressed.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is a denial artifact, and it is catalogued here as evidence about the denier rather than about Roswell. It is dated, signed, congressionally provoked, and printed at government expense, which makes it the most attributable statement the Air Force has ever made on the subject - and its internal logic reveals precisely which claims the Air Force judged it could not leave standing. Its core mechanism is temporal: it asserts that Air Force activities spread across many years have been consolidated by witnesses into two or three days in July 1947, and that UFO proponents mis-dated the 'alien' observations "in some instances by more than a decade." It was released on the 50th anniversary of the Kenneth Arnold sighting, a date choice that is itself a communications decision. And it is the direct product of a General Accounting Office audit initiated at the request of a sitting member of Congress, which means the Air Force wrote it under external compulsion rather than voluntarily - the only such instance in the pre-2017 record. The GAO audit that produced it also established, on the record, that Roswell Army Air Field's administrative records for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing messages for October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, with no indication of by whom or under what authority.
dossier.narrative:
The sequence matters more than the content. In 1993 Rep. Steven H. Schiff (R-New Mexico) began asking the Department of Defense about Roswell and, dissatisfied, referred the matter to the General Accounting Office. The GAO tasking forced the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force into an exhaustive records search that concluded in July 1994 and produced roughly 1,000 pages of material, published in 1995 as The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert. Secretary of the Air Force Sheila E. Widnall released interviewees from any security obligations that might have restricted their statements. The 1995 report's answer was Project Mogul: a then-classified balloon-borne acoustic sensor program whose train components, it said, accounted for the debris. Notably, the Mogul records that carried the explanatory weight had never been classified at all; other Mogul records had been declassified en masse under Executive Order 11652, signed by President Nixon on 6 March 1972.

Mogul explained debris. It did not explain bodies. Case Closed exists to close that gap, and its four stated conclusions are worth reading as a list of the specific narrative threads the Air Force needed cut. First, that Air Force activities occurring over a period of many years "have been consolidated and are now represented to have occurred in two or three days in July 1947." Second, that "'Aliens' observed in the New Mexico desert were probably anthropomorphic test dummies that were carried aloft by U.S. Air Force high altitude balloons for scientific research." Third, that the reports of military units arriving shortly after a crash to retrieve a saucer and its crew "were actually accurate descriptions of Air Force personnel engaged in anthropomorphic dummy recovery operations." Fourth, that claims of bodies at the Roswell Army Air Field hospital were most likely a conflation of a 1956 KC-97 accident in which eleven airmen were killed and a 1959 manned balloon mishap in which two pilots were injured.

Read as an intelligence product, this is a substitution table. Each item on the left is a witness-reported element of a retrieval operation - non-human bodies, a cordon, a convoy, a hospital, injured or dead personnel - and each item on the right is a real, documented, unclassified Air Force activity that produces the same observable. The Air Force is not arguing that nothing happened. It is arguing that everything happened, repeatedly, over fifteen years, and that the witnesses stacked it. The named substitutes are Projects High Dive and Excelsior, the Holloman-based dummy-drop and high-altitude-bailout programs; the dummies are identified in the report's own figures as Alderson Laboratories and 'Sierra Sam' type anthropomorphic dummies. Appendix B is a set of signed sworn statements from in-person interviews, including Col. Charles A. Coltman Jr. (USAF Medical Corps, retired), Col. Dan D. Fulgham (retired) - the pilot injured in the 1959 balloon mishap - and Bernard D. Gildenberg, the Holloman balloon engineer.

The report's own framing gives away its function. It states that its findings run "Contrary to allegations that the Air Force has engaged in a cover-up and possesses dark secrets involving the Roswell claims." That sentence is not a finding; it is a rebuttal, and it identifies the audience. The title itself - Case Closed - is a declaration of jurisdiction over when an inquiry ends, which is the specific authority a service branch does not actually have with respect to Congress.

What the report does not address is the record-destruction finding that emerged from the same GAO audit. GAO/NSIAD-95-187, released 28 July 1995, reported that RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, and that the document disposition form did not indicate what organization or person destroyed them, when, or under what authority. The GAO also found that Army Air Force regulations in 1947 required air accident reports to be maintained permanently, that four such accidents were reported in New Mexico in July 1947 - all after 8 July, the date the RAAF public information office announced recovery of a flying disc - and that USAF officials told GAO there was no requirement to report the crash of a balloon.

Case Closed has since been absorbed into the current official narrative without qualification. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume 1, published 8 March 2024, cites it approvingly, restating the dummy explanation and the 1956/1959 hospital conflation verbatim as established results. That continuity is the point: the 1997 denial is not a historical curiosity, it is a live load-bearing element of the 2024 denial.

l0.label: Aztec, New Mexico claim, March 1948

dossier.whatItIs: A retrieval story with no retrieval behind it: the documented history is a Denver oil-fraud scheme
dossier.whyImplicated: Aztec is on this board for one reason, and it is not that a saucer came down in Hart Canyon. It is the earliest fully traceable example of a crash-retrieval narrative whose entire provenance can be reconstructed end to end - source, motive, transmission, monetisation, exposure, conviction, and revival - and that makes it the control case against which every other retrieval claim on this board has to be measured. Everything the story needed to survive it had: named military witnesses, a specific canyon, a specific craft diameter, a specific body count, a bestselling book, a metal sample, and a federal-sounding cover-up. What it did not have was a crash.
dossier.narrative:
Aztec is on this board for one reason, and it is not that a saucer came down in Hart Canyon. It is the earliest fully traceable example of a crash-retrieval narrative whose entire provenance can be reconstructed end to end - source, motive, transmission, monetisation, exposure, conviction, and revival - and that makes it the control case against which every other retrieval claim on this board has to be measured. Everything the story needed to survive it had: named military witnesses, a specific canyon, a specific craft diameter, a specific body count, a bestselling book, a metal sample, and a federal-sounding cover-up. What it did not have was a crash.

The chain begins with Silas Mason Newton, a Denver oil promoter whose name first reached the FBI on 24 September 1938 on a suspected wire-fraud referral, and Leo (Leonard) A. GeBauer, a Phoenix electronics merchant who appears in the literature under the pseudonym 'Dr. Gee', the 'magnetologist'. On 8 March 1950 Newton, billed only as 'Mr. X' or 'Scientist X', lectured a room of science students at the University of Denver. He told them he had seen two recovered flying saucers held in a secret government facility; one had come down near Aztec, New Mexico, brought down by a 'magnetic fault line', the other near Durango, Colorado. The occupants of the first had been burned dark brown when a porthole blew out; the crew of the second had suffocated from a change in atmosphere. He described the beings as between 38 and 42 inches tall, dressed in cloth that could not be torn, probably from Venus, flying on magnetic propulsion at twice the speed of light.

Frank Scully, a Variety columnist, had already begun retailing the story in his 1949 columns. In 1950 Henry Holt published 'Behind the Flying Saucers', which turned Newton's lecture into a bestseller and into the template. Scully's version put the event in March 1948, a 99-foot craft - the largest UFO reported to that date - containing sixteen humanoid bodies, recovered by the military after a controlled landing in Hart Canyon roughly twelve miles northeast of Aztec, and hauled away for secret research. Scully added that the craft ran on 'magnetic principles', that the crew carried concentrated food wafers and heavy water, and that every dimension of the vehicle was divisible by nine. Martin Gardner, in 'Fads and Fallacies in the Name of Science', took the book apart as 'wild imaginings' and 'scientific howlers'.

The monetisation is the part that matters. Through the late 1940s and early 1950s Newton and GeBauer were travelling the Four Corners selling 'doodlebugs' - devices that in the oil business claim to locate deposits by remote sensing - and their sales pitch was that the doodlebug was built from, or reverse-engineered out of, the alien technology recovered at Aztec. Herman A. Flader, a Denver industrialist, put in $50,000 for a partnership in GeBauer's Colorado Geophysics & Development company, on the represented understanding that each unit cost around $800,000 to build. Dr. Alfred D. Kleyhauer, a Denver optometrist, lost $15,000. When investigators opened the devices they found surplus military radio parts; the estimated build cost was about $3.50 each. When J. P. Cahn of the San Francisco Chronicle demanded a sample of the miracle metal, the sample tested as ordinary aluminium. Cahn published the exposure in True magazine in September 1952 and returned in August 1956 with a second piece cataloguing further victims. Flader pressed charges. Newton and GeBauer were convicted of fraud in 1953 and also faced federal charges for moving the proceeds across state lines. Neither did jail time; the Denver Public Library's account records Newton still on probation and in violation of its terms by June 1955, and on 30 April 1969 he pleaded guilty again, this time to salting the Buckhorn Mine at Silver City, New Mexico. He died in 1972, probably still on probation.

The story should have died in 1956 and did, for about fifteen years - through the mid-1950s to the early 1970s most ufologists treated it as radioactive. It came back because the surrounding mythology gave it somewhere to live. In 1974 Robert Spencer Carr publicly claimed alien bodies recovered near Aztec were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, drawing official Air Force denials. Leonard Stringfield in the late 1970s went further, arguing the craft was one of many the US military had captured and stored. From there the Aztec details - the small burned bodies, the intact hull, the fast military sanitisation of the site - migrated wholesale into later allegedly first-hand accounts of Roswell, which is the single most important structural fact in this dossier: a documented hoax became a donor of detail to the case that the modern disclosure argument rests on.

It also acquired a paper artefact that will not go away. On 22 March 1950, two weeks after Newton's Denver lecture, Guy Hottel, special agent in charge of the FBI's Washington Field Office, filed a one-page memo relaying a third-party account of three recovered circular craft in New Mexico, 'approximately 50 feet in diameter', each holding three bodies 'only three feet tall' in 'metallic cloth', allegedly downed by high-powered radar. The memo ends 'No further evaluation was attempted'. When the FBI launched The Vault in April 2011 the Hottel memo became its most-viewed document, and in March 2013 the Bureau published a statement that it 'does not prove the existence of UFOs; it is simply a second- or third-hand claim that we never investigated', adding that some believe it simply repeats a hoax then in circulation.

Revisionism continues. Aztec's public library ran an annual UFO Symposium as a library fundraiser from 1997 to 2011. Scott and Suzanne Ramsey, with journalism professor Frank Thayer, spent three decades on the case and published 'The Aztec Incident: Recovery at Hart Canyon' (2012) and 'The Aztec UFO Incident' (2016), arguing the crash was real and independently witnessed; Ramsey placed a commemorative plaque at the canyon site in 2007. Nothing in that body of work has displaced the trial record. Tier it accordingly: the fraud is documented, the retrieval is not.

dossier.narrative: The group that receives notification of a WAIVED Department of Defense special access program is not the Gang of Eight, and conflating the two is the single most common error in public argument about how a legacy programme could be hidden. The waived-SAP channel is created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Subsection (e)(1) provides: 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Subsection (e)(2) then specifies where the withheld material goes instead: 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' The term 'defense committees' is defined not by the general Title 10 definition but by section 119's own subsection (g): 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate' and 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six bodies, each contributing a chairman and a ranking minority member: twelve members of Congress. This is deliberately narrower than a full committee and deliberately wider than eight. Note that 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines a different, similar-sounding term, 'congressional defense committees,' as only the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of the two chambers - four bodies, eight chairs and rankings. Section 119 does not use that definition; it uses its own, which adds the two Defense Appropriations Subcommittees. A board that cites 101(a)(16) for the waived-SAP group would be naming the wrong set. The Gang of Eight is a separate creature governing covert action, not DoD SAPs. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2), where the President determines that it is essential to limit access to a covert action finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, 'the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Different committees (intelligence, not armed services or appropriations), different people (the four party leaders sit in the Gang of Eight and are absent from the 119(e) group; the appropriators sit in the 119(e) group and are absent from the Gang of Eight), and different subject matter. The structural comparison is where the argument actually lives, and it cuts against the covert-action statute being the tighter one. Title 50 contains two escape valves that Title 10 does not. First, 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) imposes a 180-day clock: within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limiting access, the President must either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a fresh statement of reasons for continuing to withhold. Section 119(e) contains no sunset, no periodic re-justification, and no mechanism that ever widens the circle. A waiver, once made, is permanent as to that report. Second, 50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires the President to tell all members of the intelligence committee that a limited notification occurred and to give them a general description of it. Section 119 has no analogue: the members of the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees who are not chair or ranking are never told that a waiver happened at all. They cannot ask about what they do not know exists. That asymmetry - no sunset, no notice of bypass - is the load-bearing limit on congressional oversight of a waived programme, and it is a limit written into the statute rather than an abuse of it. What the twelve can see is also bounded. They receive the withheld report content and the Secretary's justification. They do not thereby acquire subpoena power over the programme, staff who can read the material, or any statutory right to share it with colleagues. What they cannot see is anything the Department declines to characterise as a DoD special access program at all - the recurring allegation in the UAP context being that recovery and reverse-engineering activity was moved into contractor-held or non-DoD structures where section 119 does not reach. Finally, the mechanism's present scope is narrower than it was. Pub. L. 114-328 section 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among the reporting requirements it terminates, and section 1061(b)(1) provides that each such report still required as of December 31, 2021 'shall no longer be required to be submitted to Congress after that date.' The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries this as a Termination of Reporting Requirements note under section 119. The annual SAP budget report and the annual new-SAP designation-and-justification report are therefore gone. Because 119(e)(1) can only waive a requirement 'under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' the waiver authority now has live operation only as to subsection (c), the report on a planned change in classification or a planned declassification and public announcement. Subsections (d), (f) and (g) survive and are not waivable at all - notably 119(f), which bars initiating any SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) directs waived-SAP information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve members, given the six bodies listed in 119(g).

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' for this section as the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senate Appropriations Committee, Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, House Armed Services Committee, House Appropriations Committee, and House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee.

10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines the different term 'congressional defense committees' as only '(A) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate; and (B) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the House of Representatives' - four bodies, not the six used by section 119.

The Gang of Eight under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) consists of 'the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' It governs covert action findings, not DoD special access programs.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) forces re-justification or widened access within 180 days of a limited covert-action notification. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) contains no sunset and no re-justification requirement, so a SAP reporting waiver is permanent as to that report.

50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires that all members of the intelligence committee be told a limited notification occurred and be given a general description of it. Section 119 imposes no equivalent duty, so non-leadership members of the defense committees are never informed that a waiver has been exercised.

Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among terminated reporting requirements, and sec. 1061(b)(1) ends them after 31 December 2021. The OLRC note under section 119 records the termination as effective 31 December 2021.

Because 119(e)(1) reaches only 'a requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' and (a) and (b) terminated on 31 December 2021, the waiver authority retains live operation only as to subsection (c) - reports of a planned classification change or declassification. This is an inference from the statutory text, not a statement carried in the statute itself.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) bars initiating a special access program until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. Subsection (f) is outside the reach of the 119(e)(1) waiver, which by its terms covers only subsections (a), (b) and (c).

DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, sets DoD special access program policy and its glossary defines SAP, SAP umbrella, SAP compartment, Joint Force Integration SAP and Strategic Enabler SAP. It does not define or use the terms 'acknowledged', 'unacknowledged' or 'waived' SAP, which appeared in the superseded July 2010 version.

DoDD 5205.07 para. 3.1.g requires all personnel accessed to DoD SAPs to notify the Director, DoD SAPCO through their cognizant authority SAPCO when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff, and bars any DoD contractor entity, employee, representative or consultant from providing SAP material to members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.
DoDD 5205.07 para. 2.1.e assigns the Director, DoD SAPCO responsibility to accredit congressional SAP facilities and to maintain records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress.

openQuestions: Whether the Department of Defense continues in practice to provide SAP budget and new-programme information to the defense committees after the 31 December 2021 termination of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) - for example under classified annex direction in annual authorisation or appropriations acts, or voluntarily - and whether the 119(e)(2) chair-and-ranking channel is still used for that material. This could not be established from statutory text and would require the classified annex language or committee report language to resolve.

Whether any waiver under 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) has ever been exercised in connection with UAP-related activity. No public record establishes this either way, and the statute creates no public reporting of the fact that a waiver occurred.

The precise date on which Howard P. 'Buck' McKeon replaced John M. McHugh as the senior Republican on the House Armed Services Committee in 2009. The December 2009 Congressional Directory shows McKeon in the seat and army.mil records McHugh taking office as Secretary of the Army in 2009, but the exact date of the House Armed Services succession was not confirmed from a primary source. For any claim tied to a specific 2009 date, verify which of the two held the ranking seat on that date.

The name of the 2009 Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee ranking minority member is taken from the first-listed Republican in the 111th Congress committee assignment publication rather than from an explicit 'ranking member' designation. The publication marks chairmen explicitly but identifies minority seniority only by list order. The reading is that Thad Cochran held it, consistent with his position as the full committee's senior Republican, but the publication does not label it.

Whether the September 2024 reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 formally retired the acknowledged / unacknowledged / waived taxonomy or merely omitted it from the directive while retaining it in the subordinate instruction DoDI 5205.11, which was reissued the same day and was not retrieved. This matters for how the board should label the waived-usap node.
